title: China shares follow Asian bourses lower as oil rally fizzles
text:
SHANGHAI (Reuters) - China's fragile stock markets ended sharply lower on Thursday as oil prices failed to sustain a bounce from 13-year lows and other Asian markets went into reverse.

With tumbling oil prices indicative of slowing global growth, in which China plays a central part, the benchmark Shanghai Composite Index ended down 3.2 percent.

That followed a morning of up and down trade as the market lived up to its reputation for volatility, with moves amplified by low volumes.

The index has slumped more than 18 percent in 2016 as China's currency has come under pressure and economic indicators have confirmed its declining growth, putting the world's second-largest economy at the foreground of global investors' concerns.

At this level, investors who bought back into the market at the lowest point after regulators arrested a 40 percent crash last summer are back to square one.

The CSI300 index of the largest listed companies in Shanghai and Shenzhen shed 2.9 percent, taking its losses for the year to more than 17 percent.

Lu Jie, head of China research at Robeco Asia Investment Center, said there was a vicious cycle in the markets.

"China falls trigger declines in overseas markets, which in turn fuel further slides in China markets. Panic has been amplified," he said.

However, he said the market could stabilize around March, when Chinese leaders are expected to unveil policies to support the economy at the National People's Congress, and believed that 2,800 points could be the SSEC's floor for this year.

Shi Wei, who manages roughly 4 billion yuan ($608 million) at Shanghai-based hedge fund Broad Capital, said ample liquidity would prevent an extended bear market, but a poor economy means there's not much room to go up either.

"The investment strategy this year is to be brave enough to buy during slumps and quick to take profit during rebounds," he said.

China has come in for criticism that it has left markets confused about its policies, and occasionally its stated intentions such as keeping its currency stable have not always matched its actions.

At the World Economic Forum in Davos, International Monetary Fund director Christine Lagarde said China needed to communicate better with financial markets.

"There is a communication issue, which markets do not like," she said.

Fang Xinghai, vice chairman of the securities regulator, also at Davos, said China was learning to "communicate seamlessly" with the markets, which he said ought to do more to support the economy.

YUAN STEADY

The yuan has had a volatile start to 2016, after depreciating about 5 percent since August.

After jolting global markets by allowing the currency to slide sharply early in January, the People's Bank of China (PBOC) has kept a steady course for the yuan's daily midpoint fix in the last two weeks.

Thursday's fix was barely changed at 6.5585 per dollar.

"The yuan is under depreciation pressure, but China has the ability to control its pace, and indeed the yuan has already stabilized," said David Dai, Shanghai-based investor director at Nanhai Fund Management Co.

A Reuters poll showed that bearish positions on the currency have eased a little in the last two weeks, deterred by the central bank's determined intervention.

In the spot market, the yuan was at 6.5788, just a few pips softer than Wednesday's close, while offshore it was nearly 0.5 percent weaker at 6.6084.

The central bank was also generous with liquidity ahead of the Lunar New Year holiday by injecting a net 315 billion yuan ($48 billion) into the banking system for the week to avoid a cash crunch during the long holiday.

It was the biggest weekly injection since January 2014, and came on top of other recent PBOC moves to avert any undue strains in coming weeks.

HONG KONG SPILLOVER

The PBOC has acted aggressively to deter speculators from shorting the yuan, also known as the renminbi (RMB), but the yuan's bumpy fall in the past six months, heavy capital outflows and a cooling economy have reinforced market expectations that something will have to give.

Speculators have taken to using the yuan's cheaper offshore forwards market to wager China will finally devalue the currency around March or April.

China's foreign exchange regulator said on Thursday that net capital outflows had eased in the fourth quarter last year, and risks were under control.

Hao Hong, Managing Director at Research BOCOM International, said the consequences of China's attempts to manage its currency and support its stocks were spilling over into Hong Kong.

"Interventions in mainland assets such as the RMB and A-shares have prevented market prices from adjusting toward China’s deteriorating fundamentals, and forced volatility to manifest in Hong Kong assets," he said.

The Hong Kong dollar fell to its lowest in more than eight years on Wednesday as the market tested the city's long-standing peg to the U.S. dollar, though the currency was steady on Thursday.

Hong Kong's Hang Seng share index, however, dropped another 1.5 percent to plumb lows not seen since August 2012.

title: Should We Worry About The Hong Kong Dollar? -- Barron's Blog
text:
Winter is coming to Hong Kong. The Hong Kong dollar breached its 2007 low today, down to as low as 7.8226, just haircuts away from the 7.85 level that would prompt the Hong Kong Monetary Authority to intervene.

After China decoupled its loosely pegged yuan from the dollar last August, we Hong Kong residents are understandably worried Hong Kong may de-peg its currency as well.

But really, rather than the Hong Kong dollar, we should worry about the Hong Kong economy instead.

First of all, it is highly unlikely Hong Kong would want to rock the boat even though Hong Kong's economy is more closely tied to China (and so should its monetary policy be). After all, this is the government that lets its citizens kidnapped across the border without consequences.

Second, HKMA has enough gun power to defend its currency when it comes to it. Hong Kong's foreign reserve is currently at $359 billion, which covers 1.75 times its monetary base. See my last week's blog for Credit Suisse's commentary on the possibility of Hong Kong de-pegging.

But what this means is that Hong Kong has to raise its interest rates to compensate for the Hong Kong dollar outflow, estimated to be around 300 billion Hong Kong dollars, or $38 billion. This certainly is not good news for the Hong Kong economy, especially when it is already in the downturn. In 2015, Hong Kong retail sales, a growth engine in recent years, is expected to slump over 5%, even worse than the SARs epidemic in 2003.

Hong Kong investors are catching up to reality today, sending the Hang Seng Index down 3.1% a new 40-month low. No surprise, Hong Kong property developers tumbled today. Cheung Kong Property ( 1113.Hong Kong) fell 5.6%, Wheelock ( 20.Hong Kong) dropped 4.8%, Wharf Holding ( 4.Hong Kong) was down 3.7%.

Year-to-date, the iShares China Large-Cap ETF (FXI) fell 13.5%, the iShares MSCI China ETF (MCHI) fell 13.4%, the iShares MSCI Hong Kong ETF (EWH) was down 10%.

title: CNH TRACKER-Dim sum bond sale commissions shrink, volume halves in 2015
text:
HONG KONG, Jan 14 (Reuters) - Yuan bond sale underwriting fees in the offshore market shrank last year as Chinese issuers found cheaper funding on the mainland while foreign buyers stayed away due to yuan weakness and volatility.

The offshore debt market saw its first annual primary issuance decline since it kicked off nearly a decade ago, with issuance more than halving in 2015 from the previous year.

Banks received an estimated $51.2 million from underwriting dim sum bonds last year, down 62 percent from $136 million recorded a year earlier, according to Thomson Reuters/Freeman Consulting.

The average commission per deal also fell to $0.13 million last year from $0.22 million, the statistics showed.

"Underwriting fees this year can be even lower than last year as the dim sum bond supply is expected to fall further and commission rates also have room to be squeezed," said a debt capital market banker at a Chinese bank in Hong Kong.

"We will not recommend the dim sum bond market to our clients who plan to raise funds unless they want to, but switch our focus to the dollar bond market," the banker said.

Dim sum bond issuance fell to 163 billion yuan ($24.8 billion) in 2015, less than half of that sold a year earlier, Thomson Reuters data shows. The slide was heaviest in the second half of the year as China markets crashed and Beijing unexpectedly devalued the yuan in early August.

The debt market is still facing strong headwinds this year given demand will continue to be curbed as foreign investors sell off yuan assets amid weak economic fundamentals in China and on expectations the yuan is set to weaken further.

Chinese issuers that used to be key players in the market mostly disappeared last year after funding costs on the mainland fell much lower than in Hong Kong, especially for high-yield issuers such as property firms.

A 10-year Chinese government dim sum bond fetched a yield of 3.7 percent on Thursday, compared with 2.8 percent for its counterpart onshore.

The trend appears set to continue this year with the People's Bank of China (PBOC) expected to maintain a loose monetary policy to shore up the sluggish economy, while yuan liquidity remains tight in Hong Kong.

Implied overnight interest rates for China's yuan hit a record high of 94 percent in Hong Kong on Tuesday, as suspected intervention from the PBOC drained liquidity in the offshore market.

"Despite the weak sentiment in the dim sum bond market, it may see some technical support this year as there will not be much supply," said a fixed income fund manager in Hong Kong.

The total return of dim sum bonds in U.S. dollar terms slid to -3.2 percent in 2015, the worst level since the market came into being, Standard Chartered said.

WEEK IN REVIEW:

* China has allowed a second batch of foreign institutions to enter China's interbank foreign exchange market, including Reserve Bank of India, Monetary Authority of Singapore and Bank of International Settlements.

title: Bets Against Yuan Face Rocky Road
text:
HONG KONG--In mid-November at the Grand Hyatt hotel in midtown Manhattan, prominent hedge-fund investor David Tepper told an audience gathered to hear money-making ideas that "the problem with China right now is they have a very overvalued currency."

The Chinese currency's gyrations so far this year have in part borne out forecasts made by the likes of Mr. Tepper, whose Appaloosa Management LP is one of Wall Street's most successful firms. They have also underscored one big risk faced by those betting against the yuan--the chance the People's Bank of China could intervene at any time to stem the currency's fall.

Now, following the PBOC's successful fight back against what it has called "speculators" driving down the yuan's value, the question is whether the markets will continue to test the central bank's resolve.

Investors from New York to Hong Kong stepped up bets against the yuan late last year in the so-called offshore market for the currency, convinced it was set for another fall against the dollar following the International Monetary Fund's decision on Nov. 30 to add the yuan to its elite basket of reserve currencies.

The offshore yuan slid as much as 2.7% in the first four trading days of the year, a major move by currency market standards. But from Friday onwards, heavy yuan buying by Chinese state-owned banks--prompted by the PBOC--saw the currency bounce back as much as 2.9% from its weakest level last week.

"It's a risky trade," said Allen Sing, a portfolio manager at SAIL Advisors Ltd. in Hong Kong, which invests in hedge funds. "It's a bet against policy intervention, which doesn't make sense in this environment."

After 2016's rocky start, investors and traders say they now expect a period of calm and are reluctant to place new bets just yet. Sentiment toward the yuan, though, remains fragile.

Many said they expect the yuan to gradually weaken as the PBOC grapples with giving market forces a bigger role to allow the yuan to decline against the U.S. dollar, with its familiar urge to maintain a tight grip on its currency and fight speculators.

"Certainly the PBOC has discovered a new way of managing the currency, which is through liquidity," said one hedge-fund manager that has been betting against the yuan. "The difficult part is what's next. I think we stay in a pretty stable zone."

Investors bearish on the Chinese currency last year expected the IMF's decision would encourage Beijing to show its currency regime had become more liberal, reducing the risk of any sudden government intervention if, as they expected, the yuan headed downwards.

"There was a sentiment that 'OK, we can take our chances now,'" said SAIL Advisors' Mr. Sing. "There was a sense of extreme bearishness, especially the further away you got from Asia."

Yet traders say anxiety was still running high that Beijing would eventually step in. Some investors darted in and out of the trade, putting on bearish positions for just hours at a time, according to traders. One hedge-fund manager betting against the yuan said he cut a two-week old position by about 75% over the past week, satisfied with the profit he had made.

The warning sign for many was the increased divergence between the yuan's value in offshore markets, where it was falling fast, and its price in the less open domestic Chinese market, where it was dropping less quickly. Traders sensed the PBOC wouldn't allow the gap to widen too far for fear it would only encourage offshore investors to increase their negative bets.

That hunch proved correct as Chinese banks started buying up the yuan in Hong Kong late last week, a sign the central bank was intervening, traders say. Their buying pushed the cost of borrowing yuan up sharply, making it more expensive to carry out trades betting against the currency.

Some nimble investors have been rewarded. Carl Huttenlocher, who runs the $4 billion Hong Kong hedge fund Myriad Asset Management, scored on bearish bets against the yuan, according to people familiar with the matter.

One of Asia's best-known traders, Mr. Huttenlocher had been building the position over the past year, one of the people said.

Mr. Huttenlocher and other investors used bearish currency-options and forwards to build up positions that the yuan would weaken, according to people familiar with the matter.

A spokesman for Mr. Tepper declined to comment on his bets against the yuan.

Many, like Adam Levinson, a former star trader at Fortress Investment Group LLC executive who runs Singapore-based hedge fund Graticule Asset Management Asia, expect further declines for the yuan.

In a letter to investors dated Jan. 12, Mr. Levinson said his fund had made money betting on a weaker yuan with profitable options trades as recently as last month.

"We maintain our view that the yuan will continue to depreciate over the medium-term," Mr. Levinson wrote in the letter, referring to the currency traded onshore. He didn't respond to requests for comment.

title: Beijing Flexes Muscle to Put Yuan in Line
text:
HONG KONG--Beijing escalated the battle for control of its currency, effectively shutting down the offshore market where traders had been betting on a decline in the yuan.

Traders said a surge of yuan buying by state-owned banks on Friday and Monday in Hong Kong sent the cost of borrowing yuan overnight soaring past 66% by Tuesday, making it prohibitively expensive for investors to finance bets against the currency, known as a short sale. The move has boosted the currency's value by as much as 1.8% since Friday against the U.S. dollar.

Beijing typically enlists state-owned financial firms to do its bidding and has intervened in the offshore market in the past.

The show of force followed strong warnings from Chinese officials and the central bank in recent days that the country wouldn't let currency depreciation spiral out of control.

The government hopes to gradually weaken the yuan to help stimulate the country's slowing growth, according to interviews with Chinese officials and advisers to the central bank. But it is a perilous effort that risks being overrun by traders trying to get ahead of the depreciation.

China is sensitive about signals being sent by the $230 billion-a-day offshore yuan market in Hong Kong, the main center for free trade in the currency. The gap between the value of the yuan in Hong Kong and in mainland China widened to a record last week, as offshore traders bet the country would need to further weaken the currency after a pair of jarring depreciations.

The People's Bank of China sets the yuan's rate against the dollar in the onshore, or domestic, market, and the currency is allowed to trade 2% above or below that level. In the offshore market, principally Hong Kong, its value floats freely.

The currency fell as much as 2.7% last week in Hong Kong, much deeper than the 1.1% decline the People's Bank of China had guided in the onshore market, leading to speculation that the central bank was losing its touch. Inside China, consumers rushed to banks to buy dollars and sell yuan, also known as the renminbi.

Now, China's central bank is trying to reassert who is boss. In recent days, its officials have dialed up their attacks on the people they blame for the yuan's earlier decline, branding them "speculators."

On Monday, Han Jun , deputy director of the office of the Central Leading Group on Financial and Economic Affairs, said market bets that the yuan could slump by 10% or more against the dollar were "ridiculous and impossible." He confirmed the central bank had intervened in the offshore market on Friday and Monday.

"Attempts to sell short the renminbi will not succeed," Mr. Han, a senior aide in President Xi Jinping 's economic advisory group, told an audience in New York. "The expectations of markets can be changed."

Last week, the central bank had pointed to "speculative forces" that were driving its currency down, saying the fall had "nothing to do with [China's] real economy."

Officials at the central bank have consistently defended the way they are managing the yuan, saying it has remained largely stable against a basket of currencies, even when it fell against the dollar.

Priorities for the currency have shifted for Beijing. Last year, its main effort was to cast the yuan as a stable, global currency. When the International Monetary Fund added the yuan to its basket of global reserve currencies in November--part of Beijing's efforts to expand its use world-wide--officials shifted their goals to using the yuan to stimulate the economy, according to Chinese officials and advisers to the central bank. A weaker currency can help an economy by boosting inflation and exports.

The central bank appears to have overshot in that effort and is now resorting to intervention to regain control.

It was the central bank's own actions that triggered a selloff in the offshore yuan market in the first trading days of 2016.

From Monday to Thursday last week, the central bank set the onshore rate significantly weaker against the dollar, sparking fears it was more worried about the health of the Chinese economy than it had previously let on.

Traders said the central bank shifted tack and began propping up the swiftly declining yuan beginning Friday, when they saw large state-owned Chinese banks step in to sell greenbacks and buy the yuan in overseas markets. The offshore yuan strengthened as much as 1.5% late Monday against the dollar and continued to advance Tuesday.

Chinese banks' buying spree, seen as a sign of central-bank intervention, effectively shut down the yuan market in Hong Kong on Tuesday, as supply of the currency all but disappeared. The benchmark rate at which banks borrow yuan from each other surged to an unprecedented 66.8%, up from what had been a record level of 13.4% on Monday. The benchmark is based on rates contributed by 18 domestic banks each morning. Traders said the actual yuan borrowing rate reached as high as 110% during the day.

"There's no cash in the market," said a senior trader at a bank in Hong Kong, referring to the yuan's availability.

The rise in borrowing costs has made it much more expensive for investors to pursue trading strategies that bet against the yuan, said Khoon Goh, foreign-exchange strategist at Australia & New Zealand Banking Group Ltd . in Singapore.

As the cost of funding for such bets rose Tuesday, investors tried to close remaining trades, fearing deeper losses later if they didn't act soon.

The retreat allowed the central bank to achieve its aim of bringing its value inside and outside China back in line, a shift that restricts traders from profiting from the differences between the yuan's offshore and onshore value in the future. As the currency strengthened in offshore markets Tuesday, at one point it traded at a premium to its onshore counterpart.

Late Tuesday, the yuan traded onshore closed at 6.5695 against the U.S. dollar, and the offshore yuan was at 6.5746.

"It's so far the biggest signal from the [central bank]," a Hong Kong-based senior trader at a Wall Street bank said of the intervention.

Still, the central bank's efforts, while effective for now, could come at both a short- and long-term cost.

The central bank's actions raise concerns over Beijing policy makers' pledges to give markets a bigger say over the yuan. Investors in Hong Kong said the central bank's willingness to intervene heavily in the offshore market could hinder the yuan's development as a widely traded global currency.

"This has had a quite a dramatic impact on the market," said Alexandra Edstein, a portfolio manager at hedge fund the Cambridge Strategy. "Whether it lasts is the question."

Meanwhile, the rise in interbank borrowing costs in Hong Kong, engineered to support the yuan, could crimp new lending by banks that don't have enough yuan deposits and need to borrow, said Michael Wu, senior equity analyst at Morningstar Investment Management Asia. Hong Kong banks already have been paring back their yuan lending businesses as China's growth slowed, he said.

Also, the recent turbulence in yuan markets could keep the trading and issuance of offshore yuan-denominated bonds, dubbed dim-sum bonds, subdued, analysts said.

Julie Steinberg and Lingling Wei contributed to this article.

title: China Tumble Leads Asian Markets Lower
text:
China shares plunged Monday, approaching their low reached during the summer crash, as regulators appeared to refrain from propping up the market.

The Shanghai Composite Index fell 5.3% to 3016.70, the lowest finish for the benchmark in more than three months. It has shed 15% so far this year. Another 3% drop, or 89 points, would put the benchmark below its close of 2927.29 reached on Aug. 26. At that point, Shanghai had lost more than 40% from its June peak.

The smaller Shenzhen Composite Index fell 6.6% to 1848.10.

Shares in Hong Kong sank to their lowest in roughly 2½ years. The Hang Seng Index was off 2.8% at 19888.50, closing below 20000 for the first time since June 2013. A gauge of Chinese firms listed in the city fell 3.9%.

Australia's benchmark S&P/ASX 200 lost 1.2% and South Korea's Kospi fell 1.2%. Japan's market was closed for a national holiday.

Traders said state-owned funds were notably absent from the market Monday. Buying by China's so called "National Team" had helped stabilize the market last summer and, at times, late last year.

The central bank's lack of aggressive easing measures over the weekend to boost the economy also disappointed investors. While some say they still expect officials to take action, including further cuts to interest rates and the amount of reserves banks are required to hold, a lack of clear communication from authorities is worrying.

"[All] this may have conveyed a sense of sanguinity from regulators and the government regarding recent market volatility," said Bill Bowler, equities sales trader at Hong Kong-based research and brokerage firm Forsyth Barr Asia Ltd.

Poorly telegraphed moves last week exacerbated volatility in China and triggered selling that spread to the rest of the region, the U.S. and Europe

Meanwhile, worries about weakness in the Chinese yuan and how authorities convey their market expectations continue to unnerve investors, though the currency stabilized in the past two days.

The yuan's weakening by 1.5% against the U.S. dollar last week sparked selling in commodities and currencies of China's trading partners and sent investors to assets perceived as safe.

Earlier Monday, China's central bank fixed the yuan at 6.5626 against the dollar, guiding the currency stronger from its 6.5636 fixing on Friday. It was the second day the bank guided the yuan stronger, after eight sessions of weaker guidance. The onshore yuan can trade up or down 2% from the fix.

The onshore yuan was last at 6.5833 against the U.S. dollar, compared with 6.5938 late Friday. It reached a five-year low of 6.5956 last Thursday.

The offshore yuan, which trades freely, was last at 6.6727 to the U.S. dollar, compared with 6.6820 late Friday. It reached a five-year low of 6.7511 on Thursday.

China's central bank appears to have spent huge amounts of dollars to support the yuan amid decelerating economic growth and the onset of higher U.S. interest rates.

The country's foreign-exchange regulator said over the weekend that its reserves are "relatively sufficient." Reserves dropped by $107.9 billion in December, the biggest monthly drop ever.

In Hong Kong, the short-term rate Hong Kong banks charge each other to borrow Chinese yuan jumped to a record 13.4% from 4% on Friday, an indication that China's currency turmoil is spreading to Hong Kong. The increase comes as traders said large Chinese banks intervened offshore to buy yuan last week, effectively tightening liquidity.

Worries about slackening demand in China, one of the world's biggest consumers of commodities from oil to copper, trammeled prices early Monday. Copper fell to a six-and-a-half year low of $4,416 a ton before recovering to $4,485.

title: UPDATE: Chinese companies are betting on further yuan weakness
text:
By Craig Stephen, MarketWatch

Record-breaking purchases in Hong Kong make sense if they are hedges against a falling currency

HONG KONG (MarketWatch) -- In recent weeks it has appeared the worst is over for the yuan, which has been under pressure since its surprise August devaluation.

October data showed China had reversed (http://www.wsj.com/articles/chinas- foreign-exchange-reserves-rise-11-39-billion-in-october-1446870527?alg=y)five months of currency outflows, while there was also better news on China's hopes for the yuan's inclusion by the IMF as one its special drawing right reserve currencies, helping it on its way to being a reserve currency. This looks increasingly likely after positive comments (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/imfs-lagarde-and-staff-support-adding-chinas- currency-to-sdr-basket-2015-11-13) by IMF Managing Director Christine Lagarde.

Yet there remain various question marks over whether the yuan has really turned a corner after its summer wobbles. There is scant evidence the economy has, and much more of concerted intervention by the People's Bank of China to support the currency, including in offshore markets.

Another way to gauge the market's view on the yuan is to ignore the government and watch what China's corporations are doing with their money. Increasingly it seems they are going long overseas assets, while loading up on yuan debt at home -- a trade that would be advantageous if there were further currency weakness.

As China's de facto offshore financial center, Hong Kong needs to be watched.

Its commercial property market has witnessed a remarkable influx of buying by mainland Chinese corporates. Last week there was a record-breaking purchase (http://www.mingtiandi.com/real-estate/outbound-investment/evergrande-buys-hk-office-tower-from-chinese-estates-for-1-61b/)by("http://www.mingtiandi.com/real-estate/outbound-investment/evergrande-buys-hk-office-tower-from-chinese-estates-for-1-61b/)by") Guangzhou-based property giant China Evergrande when it paid HK$12.5 billion for an office tower in Wanchai district.

Despite not being in prime Central, this set a new mark for the highest price paid per square foot in Hong Kong at HK$36,232. Earlier this year, Hopewell Holdings secured $35,000 for sale of a floor in 9 Queen's Road.

On the same day, China Life announced it had purchased an en bloc office tower with a two-story retail block for HK$5.85 billion from local conglomerate Wheelock.

Analysts have questioned the steep price of the Evergrande purchase in particular. Yet these investments would look different if there were an expectation of yuan depreciation. Due to the Hong Kong dollar's peg to the greenback , such assets offer a natural hedge.

If you rewind all the way to 1994 when China last had a significant yuan depreciation, there was an influx of money from over the border seeking similar protection.

Meanwhile, another sign that Chinese corporations are positioning for currency realignment is in the growth in onshore debt raising at the same time wider foreign acquisitions are skyrocketing.

According to Dealogic, year to date China's onshore corporate debt capital market volume has reached 312.8 billion yuan ($50.2 billion), almost four times levels from a year earlier. The financing is also cheaper than overseas. Earlier this year, Evergrande raised 40 billion yuan in the domestic bond market, at less than half the cost it paid for an offshore issuance of US$1 billion in February.

This comes at the same time Chinese corporations are also ramping up acquisitions of overseas companies. So far this year Chinese acquirers have announced a total of $486.1 billion in mergers and acquisitions, up more than 50% on the same period last year, according to Dealogic. This has been given a push by authorities, who in May relaxed rules so that any Chinese firms looking to invest less than US$1billion in overseas firms no longer needed to seek government approval.

Other signs of ongoing currency pressure can be seen in Hong Kong, the main offshore yuan hub.

Since the initial yuan devaluation there has been a waning appetite for yuan, which fell some 84 billion ($13 billion) in September from August to 895 billion yuan, according to Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) data. Meanwhile the HKMA had to intervene several times last month to stop the local currency rising, buying more than $10 billion, the highest monthly intervention since 2009. At the same time this pushed the Hong Kong interbank offered rate (HIBOR) down to record low levels.

Meanwhile analysts remain cautious about the prospects for the yuan, despite the likely positive news on SDR inclusion. Societe General writes in a new report that, although there is likely to be modest short-term positive reaction, inclusion by itself is unlikely to drive the trend.

They estimate we may see capital flows relating to SDR allocation of just $30 billion and $40 billion depending on the weights. Furthermore, this inclusion does not mean that reserve managers will have to mechanically buy more Chinese assets now or in the future.

UBS is similarly sanguine on IMF endorsement providing much of a boost to the yuan as reserve currency. They write in a new report that more needs to be done by Chinese authorities to open up China's capital accounts and convince global reserve managers to invest meaningfully in Chinese reserve-related assets.

For now when it comes to having a view on the yuan, it looks best to follow what Chinese corporations are doing, rather than what their government is saying.

-Craig Stephen; 415-439-6400; AskNewswires@dowjones.com

title: China Must Speed Up Financial Reform, Says PBOC Official
text:
BEIJING—China must intensify its efforts to open up its financial system to the outside world despite the country's recent market volatility, a senior Chinese central-bank official warned, in an apparent effort to shore up support for reforming China's vast but creaky financial plumbing.

Sheng Songcheng, head of the survey and statistics department at the People's Bank of China, said at a forum in Shanghai on Friday that there is "no direct connection" between volatility in China's financial markets and China's recent effort to give foreign investors greater access. Foreign ownership accounts for only 2.5% of Chinese stocks, Mr. Sheng said, according to a copy of his remarks reviewed by The Wall Street Journal.

On the other hand, slowing down the pace of freeing cross-border money flows would only "prolong the uncertainty" over China's commitment to reforms, he said. Mr. Sheng said stalled reform would encourage differences in interest rates and exchange rates between China and other countries, encouraging speculators.

"Reform should be sped up," Mr. Sheng added.

The comments come as China's central bank is fighting to stick with a year-end timetable it set for greater openness in the country's markets. Following a stock-market meltdown in the summer and recent currency fluctuations, some officials within the Chinese bureaucracy are raising concerns over continued opening at a time of persistent economic weakness and growing worries about financial instability.

Earlier this year, PBOC Gov. Zhou Xiaochuan pledged greater openness for the financial system of the world's No. 2 economy by the end of 2015. Yi Gang, a deputy PBOC governor responsible for day-to-day oversight of China's financial flows, said in late August that China would move forward with opening its markets up to foreign investors according to its timetable.

Mr. Sheng reiterated that sentiment on Friday, saying reform "shouldn't be put off because of market volatility." Rather, freer movements of money across China's borders could help smooth out the fluctuations, he said.

For instance, Mr. Sheng said, the Chinese yuan currently trades at different values inside and outside the country. That creates problems for regulators, as some investors seek to profit from the difference and as the central bank tries to forge a unified exchange rate in its bid to get the International Monetary Fund to declare the yuan an official reserve currency.

The yuan trades both in the domestic market and in what is known as the offshore market in Hong Kong, a Chinese city which operates under its own laws. In mainland China, authorities strictly limit the way the yuan trades. In Hong Kong, it can be bought and sold freely. Since Aug. 11, when China surprised the world by devaluing its currency, investors in Hong Kong have been pounding the yuan weaker in expectation of more devaluation to come. The offshore yuan has traded at a discount of 1% or more to its mainland cousin at times since then, while the two were largely in line before the devaluation.

That widened spread is complicating China's ambitions to raise the yuan's global profile. Beijing is trying to persuade the IMF to include the yuan in its elite basket of reserve currencies, giving it the same status as the U.S. dollar, the euro, the British pound and the Japanese yen. But people familiar with the IMF's thinking say it is unlikely to deem a currency with two exchange rates "freely usable," as the organization requires.

To narrow the gap, the PBOC in recent weeks has intervened in both the mainland and the Hong Kong markets to bring the onshore and offshore yuan more in line with each other.

If China sufficiently opens the capital account and gives foreign investors easier access to the mainland market, Mr. Sheng said, the division between the offshore and onshore yuan would be reduced significantly.

He added that China remains attractive to long-term foreign capital, adding that foreign direct investment in China increased $1.51 billion year-over-year to $8.71 billion in August.

Grace Zhu.

title: Hong Kong Stocks Still Cheap Despite Cash Inflows Into City
text:
The Hong Kong stock market was dragged down by China over the summer, and even a massive flow of cash into the city hasn't been enough to bring it back from its lowest valuation in years.

Normally, the combination of low valuation and money inflows signals a good buying opportunity, said Chris Wood, a strategist at Asian brokerage firm CLSA. While the Hang Seng Index has risen 6% in the last two weeks, it is still at its cheapest level since the financial crisis.

Much of the inflows are driven by people converting their Chinese yuan into Hong Kong dollars after the Chinese currency's devaluation in August. Many expect the yuan, known officially as the renminbi, to weaken further next year, and Hong Kong is usually the first stop when mainland Chinese start moving money abroad.

"For mainland investors looking to diversify away from home-country renminbi assets, Hong Kong just happens to be the easiest outward step," said Michael Kurtz, chief Asia strategist at Nomura.

The Hong Kong dollar is pegged to the U.S. dollar, so it has risen along with the greenback in recent months. The Chinese currency had been strengthening on the same path until Beijing devalued it by 2% in August.

The money flowing out of China has forced the Hong Kong Monetary Authority to intervene in the market at least seven times since Sept. 1, spending HK$47 billion ($6.1 billion) by selling local currency and buying dollars to keep the Hong Kong dollar from rising too far. The last time the HKMA intervened by selling Hong Kong dollars was in April, when the Hong Kong stock market rallied to its highest level since 2007.

"Lots of money has come to Hong Kong recently," said Alan Yandong Wang, investment director at Hong Kong-based investment firm Value Partners, which manages $10 billion in Hong Kong, China and Taiwan. "But instead of going into investments, it seems so far they have only parked here."

Despite the strong inflows into the city, money has been flowing out of Hong Kong equities because of a lack of confidence from global investors. The market has experienced 13 consecutive weeks of fund outflows, the longest period since 2010 when the data became available, according to EPFR Global, which tracks such flows. A total of $1 billion has flowed out of Hong Kong markets in the last three months.

After a 15% fall since April, the Hang Seng Index now trades at 8.4 times its trailing earnings, just above the low of 7.69 reached during the global financial crisis in 2008, according to Wind, a data provider that tracks Chinese markets. Currently, Hong Kong's price-to-book ratio is just 1.03, even lower than the 1.25 hit in October 2008.

Cash moving into Hong Kong also typically flows into real estate. But the residential market has been weak with shrinking volumes as buyers expect the retail downturn and higher interest rates to squeeze the local economy and property demand.

Two things are keeping investors away from Hong Kong markets--the prospect of higher U.S. interest rates and the large number of Chinese companies listed in Hong Kong. Because of the currency peg, the increase in U.S. rates expected by the end of the year will drive up Hong Kong rates. For Chinese companies, the slowdown in growth at home could hurt profits.

"Any rally in Hong Kong can be short-lived," said Alan Xi Wang, portfolio manager and head of Greater China equity at Principal Global Investors, an asset management firm that oversees more than $300 billion globally. Mr. Wang said he has limited his Hong Kong market exposure to defensive stocks.

Value Partners is also taking a cautious approach to Hong Kong. At the end of August, its funds were mostly 90% to 95% invested, slightly lower than its normal ratio of 95% to 100%.

As global investors flee emerging markets, one group of investors is turning more positive about Hong Kong. Chinese investors are moving cash into Hong Kong via Shanghai through the link between stock exchanges. Those flows have totaled $2.4 billion over nine consecutive weeks of inflows, according to Nomura Securities. This has helped narrow the price premium of dual-listed companies' China shares versus their Hong Kong shares to 31% from 41% two months ago.

"After all, Hong Kong stocks have deeper value than mainland stocks and the Hong Kong dollar is an alternative to renminbi downside risks," added Mr. Kurtz.

The Shanghai Composite, despite having fallen 39% from its June peak, still trades at 13.3 times of trailing earnings and 1.6 times its book value. Francis Cheung, head of China and Hong Kong Strategy at brokerage firm CLSA, expects Shanghai stocks to fall another 15% from current levels.

title: China  central bank  seen ready to  intervene  again if offshore pushes yuan too far
text:
HONG KONG (Reuters) - A spike higher in the offshore yuan following suspected rare intervention by Chinese state banks is expected to be short-lived, especially with a looming U.S. interest rate rise likely to add to the attraction of owning dollars.

But those betting on a further depreciation in the yuan are likely to have only limited room to push the offshore rate down relative to the onshore rate without drawing the ire of the Chinese central bank and the risk of further state intervention, market sources said.

"The central bank will not stand aside if depreciation expectation is formed again and more intervention may happen," said a Hong Kong-based currency trader, who declined to be identified.

The offshore yuan <CNH=D3> shot up by more than 1 percent on Thursday on suspected intervention that was seen by traders as a gesture by authorities to shake out speculators betting against the yuan.

Authorities have spent the country's foreign exchange reserves heavily to hold the yuan steady onshore since a surprise devaluation in August prompted fears the Chinese economy was in worse shape than previously thought and that the yuan therefore could fall further.

Thursday's spike narrowed the offshore yuan's discount against the onshore rate to 0.38 percent from 1.56 percent on Wednesday and forced traders with short positions to cover. Traders suspect the sudden move was prompted by buying by state banks at the behest of the central bank.

"The Chinese central bank's purpose was to narrow the gap between the offshore and onshore rates, but I don't see any fundamental that supports yuan appreciation against the dollar going forward," said Penny Chen, a fixed-income fund manager at Manulife Asset Management in Taiwan.

Since the Aug 11 devaluation, several investment banks, including Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley and UBS, have revised down their forecasts for the yuan's performance this year.

The Chinese currency will remain under pressure as long as U.S. interest rates are set to rise, analysts said. U.S. market rates have already risen in anticipation the Federal Reserve will raise its policy rate by the end of this year for the first time since 2006.

In contrast, the Chinese central bank has cut lending rates five times since last November and analysts expect further easing of monetary policy to support China's economy.

The interest rate differential will be reflected more in the offshore market, where China's central bank has less influence, analysts said. The offshore yuan was quoted at 6.4150 per dollar late on Friday in Asia, compared with an onshore rate of 6.3740 - a gap of 410 pips. It was 200 pips earlier in the day, but traders said the gap widened after London offshore markets kicked into action.

Some traders believe the central bank will not allow the gap to widen to 500 pips for fear that would strengthen expectations of further yuan depreciation.

Still, the central bank has less influence in the offshore market, which is more driven by market forces, and so leaves more room for the yuan to fall, said Liao Qun, China chief economist at Citic Bank International in Hong Kong. "The gap between CNH (offshore) and CNY (onshore) will be widened to 500-600 pips again in the coming months," Liao said.

Liao expected the onshore and offshore rates to fall to 6.45 and to more than 6.5 per dollar, respectively, by the end of the year if the Fed increases its benchmark rates.

title: Asian Trader: Hong Kong Real Estate At Risk -- Barron's
text:
(FROM BARRON'S 9/7/15) 
   By Shuli Ren 

For years, Hong Kong made money by selling goods to China's wide-eyed middle class and arranging financing for Beijing's projects. But as China devalues the yuan, and the Federal Reserve looks to raise rates, the island city is in a bind. One result could be that residential property prices fall sharply over the next year.

Since China devalued the yuan three weeks ago, there has been speculation that Hong Kong will abandon its dollar peg. Last week, for the first time since April, the Hong Kong Monetary Authorityintervened in the currency markets, buying more than US$3.5 billion in two days, as its own currency, the Hong Kong dollar, hit the 7.75 upper band of the peg. Investors rushed to sell yuan and move into the more stable Hong Kong dollar.

However, a stronger HK dollar deters mainland shoppers, the island's big growth engine. From 2009 through 2013, Hong Kong's retail sales rose at a brisk 11.3% per annum, far outpacing its overall 2.8% economic gain. But starting a year ago, many Chinese opted for shopping destinations such as Korea and Japan, where the yuan went further. In July -- even before the yuan was devalued -- retail sales fell 2.8%. The number of Chinesevisitors to Hong Kong has slumped 10% from the total a year ago. Last week, U.S. handbag brand Coach (ticker: COH) closed the store that had been its Hong Kong flagship.

De-pegging might help retailers, but it wouldn't be a wise thing to do. Trade, of everything from raw materials to consumer electronics, is still the largest piece of the pie, accounting for 19% of the goods and services that Hong Kong generates, versus retail's 4.5%. A simple peg trims traders' exchange-rate risk -- "a considerable advantage" for a small, open economy, says Capital Economics' Chang Liu. Financial services generate 15% of total value-add, and this sector benefits from a firm Hong Kong dollar in a volatile time.

Global trade is barely expanding, while Hong Kong's financial center is alarmingly quiet after China's stock market rout. The benchmark MSCI China index, which tracks Hong Kong-listed mainland stocks, fetches just eight times earnings, 30% below its historical average. And average daily turnover on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange fell from HK$164 billion (US$21 billion) in the second quarter to under HK$100 billion in August.

Over the past six years, hot money and low interest rates have pushed property prices 75% above the previous peak, hit in 1997. A 540-square-foot apartment now is quoted at $780,000. That makes analysts worry that residential property prices are vulnerable, particularly because debt is so high. Private nonfinancial sector debt now exceeds 180% of the city's gross domestic product, about 60 percentage points above 1997's level.

A UBS analysis finds Hong Kong's property sector responds more to the city's economic growth than to mortgage rates. If GDP contracts 2% next year, UBS estimates, residential property prices could fall 16%. Economists polled by Bloomberg expect Hong Kong to grow by 3% next year, in line with 2014's 2.5%, but that might be too bullish. The poll also showed that the consensus forecast is for China's economy to expand by 6.9% this year and 6.7% in 2016. However, Citigroup's top economist, Willem Buiter, thinks the real growth rate is "something closer to 4.5% or less." And of all Asian economies, Hong Kong is the most exposed to China's slowdown.

title: UPDATE How Much Did China Spend Defending The Yuan? -- Barron's Blog
text:
After moving to a more market-oriented currency regime on August 11, the People's Bank of China let the yuan go for only three days and has been trying to prop up the yuan by intervening in the currency market, selling its dollar reserves.

$150 billion, estimates Societe Generale, is the amount China spent in August. For comparison purposes, China's foreign exchange reserves fell $50 billion in July, itself a monthly record.

To be sure, China has a deep pocket. It held $3.65 trillion foreign exchange reserves as of the end of July.

Societe Generale's Wei Yao and Jason Daw admitted their estimate was very rough. The actual amount can be anywhere between $100 and $200 billion.

If the actual amount turned out to be $100 billion, then the PBoC may be asking its state-owned commercial banks to do the dirty work:

If the PBoC's figure surprises on the upside (ie. less decline than expected), one possible reason could be that state banks, policy banks or SOE's bought RMB at the behest of the PBoC and kept the risk on their balance sheet. Capital controls may have also tightened for corporates and households.

Nice. Is this partly why China's banks are now even cheaper than before? See also my Septemtber 2 blog " Value Trap: China Banks Report The Worst Earnings In A Decade".

Well, consider the Hong Kong Monetary Authority a beneficiary. The PBoC guided its yuan fix rate higher earlier this week - to make China look strong and steady ahead of the big military parade yesterday, many commentators said. Households and businesses took advantage of this window and rushed out of their yuan accounts to buy Hong Kong dollars. As a result, the HKMA had to intervene twice, buying over $3.5 billion U.S. dollars in two days with mint money to keep the Hong Kong dollar within the strong end of the 7.75 peg range. See also my blog yesterday " Will Hong Kong Keep The Dollar Peg?".

The offshore yuan was trading at 6.4481 recently. Societe Generale re-iterated its year-end forecast of 6.80. Overnight, the Powershares DB US Dollar Index Bullish Fund ( UUP) rose 0.5%.

UPDATE: Every Wall Street bank is coming up with some estimates today. Societe Generale's estimate is on the high end. Deutsche Bank's Zhiwei Zhang for instance thinks China spent $90 billion defending the yuan:

We estimate that the PBoC may have intervened heavily on 3 days since the RMB depreciation on August 11, with average daily intervention at some US$16bn. On other days the average daily intervention may be in the range of US$4bn to US$8bn, and it seems to have declined substantially in recent trading days. We believe the most intensive episode of intervention may have passed. Monthly intervention in the next few months will probably not exceed US$90bn.

Chill, people! The PBoC will announce the official number next Monday. We will find out then!

title: Will Hong Kong Keep The Dollar Peg? -- Barron's Blog
text:
The Hong Kong Monetary Authorityintervened again on Wednesday to hold onto its currency peg.

The central bank injected 12.5 billion Hong Kong dollars, after buying HK$15.5 billion worth of U.S. dollars on Tuesday, the first time since April.

Under the current system, the Hong Kong dollar is pegged at 7.8 per U.S. dollar but can trade between 7.75 and 7.85. HKMA is obliged to intervene when the Hong Kong dollar hit 7.75 or 7.85. The Hong Kong dollar was hitting the strong end of 7.75 this week as businesses and households move out of their yuan deposits and into Hong Kong dollar accounts, expecting the yuan to depreciate further.

Since the People's Bank of China devalued the yuan three weeks ago, markets have been speculating that Hong Kong will abandon the dollar peg. An expensive currency is hurting the island's retail sales. In July - even before the yuan devaluation - retail sales fell 2.8% from a year ago, sharpening from June's 0.4% decline. In addition, since the Hong Kong dollar is pegged, its monetary policy follows the US as well. As the Federal Reserve Bank is on track to raise interest rates, cost of capital in Hong Kong will spike up too, exerting pressure on the local economy.

But economists think that Hong Kong's central bank won't give up the dollar peg easily.

First, global trade growth is already anemic. The dollar peg reduces exporters' exchange rate risk. "In a small, highly trade-dependent economy, with exports the equivalent of over 200% of GDP, this represents a considerable advantage," wrote Capital Economics' Chang Liu.

Second, HKMA firmly believes changing the peg would hurt investor confidence, which could trigger catastrophic capital outflow, according to UBS strategist Teck Leng Tan. After all, what's the alternative?

Third, how expensive is the Hong Kong dollar really? Looking back the history, the Hong Kong dollar now is not that expensive compared to 1998, and the HKMA adamantly defended its currency then, argued UBS:

While the HKD real effective exchange rate (REER) has indeed risen to levels seen in 2009, the economic growth and inflation situation now is quite different. Also, the current level of HKD REER is still almost 40% below that seen during the 1998 Asian Financial Crisis, when HK economy was in a much more dire situation.

HKMA certainly has the means to keep the dollar peg for a while. The currency board system means that changes in Hong Kong's monetary base are exactly matched by changes in the HKMA's US dollar holdings. Currently, HKMA has $340 billion foreign exchange reserve, almost twice Hong Kong's entire monetary base of $183 billion. The central bank can keep on buying dollars for quite a while.

title: Lower Yuan Keeps Hong Kong Money-Changers Busy
text:
China's devaluation of its currency, its slowing economy and tanking stock market are weighing on Hong Kong's key industries--retailing and real estate.

But fears that things will worsen in China is a boon for the money-changers, bankers and wealth managers who are getting flooded with business from nervous Chinese eager to get their cash overseas.

Hong Kong has long been the financial entry point for foreigners into China and the first place mainland Chinese visited and parked their cash. Now fears that the yuan will fall further is making the former U.K. colony, where the currency is pegged to the U.S. dollar, a haven.

"The devaluation of the [yuan] and the volatility of the domestic market are forming a perfect storm," said Kenny Lam, group president of Noah Holdings, a Chinese wealth management firm. Mr. Lam said the company's 80-strong Hong Kong office, set up three years ago, is scrambling to meet "tremendous increase in demand" for its foreign-currency denominated products from investors who see the yuan continuing to fall.

"Hong Kong is our clients' first stop abroad," said Mr. Lam, who worked at McKinsey & Co. before joining New York-listed and Shanghai-based Noah in March.

Noah's revenues rose 500% in the quarter ended June over the same period last year, the company disclosed in its recent earnings report.

The flood of cash into Hong Kong has gotten so strong the city's de facto central bank was forced to act on Tuesday. In its first intervention since April, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority sold 15.5 billion Hong Kong dollars, or $2 billion, to the market in an effort to push down the currency, which was pushing at the high end of the narrow band in which it is allowed to trade against the U.S. dollar.

The pressure on the Hong Kong dollar has been building since China devalued the yuan on Aug. 11, allowing the currency to fall 2.6% in a week. Investors had expected China to keep its currency steady, and the switch sent investors fleeing the yuan.

An officer at a Chinese bank in Hong Kong said the number of people who are transferring $50,000 worth of foreign currency--the maximum annual limit allowed a Chinese resident--from China into Hong Kong has increased several-fold in recent weeks since Beijing's devaluation of the yuan.

"Generally, money moving into a city benefits a local economy because it provides more liquidity, which can fuel more investing," said Ken Peng, Asia investment strategist at Citi Private Bank in Hong Kong, adding that the bank has seen a pickup in inquiries from clients seeking to move more of their holdings into U.S. or Hong Kong dollars in recent weeks.

But Mr. Peng said benefits for the Hong Kong economy "remain to be seen" because the impact of China's slowing economy and market selloff may make investors more reluctant to make risky investments.

Already, interest rate cuts in China and a depreciating yuan have damped a lucrative line of business for the city's bank lending into China. Chinese companies have been big borrowers from Hong Kong in recent years, taking advantage of the city's lower interest rates and a rising yuan to borrow money they then deposited in higher-earning accounts back home.

Such cross-border lending "probably was a key driver for demand the last few years" in Hong Kong for trade finance, said Jim Antos, a banking analyst at Mizuho Securities Asia Ltd.--and the recent devaluation of the yuan will depress demand further still.

Banks in Hong Kong reported a 5.2% drop in loans to finance trade in July from June, the latest data from the HKMA show.

The search for havens is also keeping Hong Kong's ultra-high-end real estate homes in heavy demand, with luxury retail rents up 13% in July, over the year, according to property consultancy Colliers. A large part of that has been driven by mainland Chinese buying.

But outside high-end real estate, the outlooks for property prices and retail look grimmer. Taken together, the two sectors account for just over 10% of Hong Kong's gross domestic product.

Falling numbers of Chinese tourists, and China's anticorruption crackdown, are hurting spending in the city. The number of visitors to Hong Kong fell 8.4% in July, from a growth of 11.2% a year earlier, according to data from the Hong Kong Tourism Board released Monday. Most of that was from an almost 10% drop in mainland Chinese tourists that month. Even before the yuan's devaluation, spending by Chinese tourists in Hong Kong had been falling, with retail sales down for its fifth straight month by 2.8% in July.

On Tuesday, New York-based handbag maker Coach shut its flagship store on Queen's Road Central, a road in the heart of Hong Kong's business district and home to some of the world's highest rents. Coach is backing out of a lease set to expire in 2017, according to retail leasing brokers. Coach declined to comment on its lease.

"The retail network is saturated for many brands in Hong Kong," said Karim Azar, general manager of retail leasing at International Financial Center, a luxury shopping mall.

Real estate sales volumes fell 30% in Hong Kong in July over the previous year, according to the Land Registry, showing that the weakening Hong Kong economy, which is increasingly linked to the economic well-being of China, is hurting confidence and sentiment.

For now, however, analysts say the biggest risk to Hong Kong lies in higher U.S. interest rates, which the city would have to mirror because of the peg.

"The real risk for the [Hong Kong] economy comes from [Hong Kong] interest rates rising alongside U.S. interest rates at a time when [Hong Kong] faces a peaking credit cycle and property market, reduced China tourist spending, weakening exports and a China economic slowdown," UBS Group AG said in a note Tuesday.

title: Investors Bet That  Currency  Pegs Will Come Under Strain
text:
With global markets thrown into a twist, some investors are betting that long-standing currency pegs might come under strain.

Traders and investors said a buildup in bets against currency pegs in Hong Kong and Saudi Arabia accelerated after China's central bank devalued its currency this month. The wagers picked up further after Kazakhstan and Vietnam moved to free their exchange rates, too.

"[Investors] are looking at who's next," said Cynthia Wong, head of Société Générale SA's emerging-market Asia fixed-income and currency trading in Hong Kong and Singapore.

Policy makers in places including Saudi Arabia and Hong Kong intervene in the market to keep their currencies in narrow trading bands. Wild swings in the currency market can make that task more difficult.

Hong Kong's 32-year-old peg to the U.S. dollar, backed by its de facto central bank's currency board, has weathered bouts of volatility. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority closely monitors the peg against the U.S. dollar and intervenes if the currency tests the limits of HK$7.75 or HK$7.85 ($1 or $1.01) against the dollar.

The Saudi central bank has effectively fixed the riyal's exchange rate with the U.S. dollar since 1986. Some analysts said the peg could be vulnerable due to the rapid fall in the price of oil.

"Saudi is a big oil exporter, and oil-exporting currencies have been hit hard this year," said Chris Turner, a currency strategist at ING in London.

A senior central-bank official responded to the speculation on Tuesday, telling Saudi Arabia's Al Arabiya news channel that the kingdom is committed to pegging the riyal to the dollar.

The Saudi and Hong Kong central banks wouldn't lightly abandon the pegs, which provide a degree of stability to their economies, most analysts said. Still, there are signs that some traders believe the pegs could be strained in the current market turmoil, which has led to erratic moves in some currencies.

There has been a surge in bets in the options markets that the Hong Kong dollar and Saudi Arabian riyal could see increased volatility over the next few months. Futures markets indicate that investors expect both currencies to weaken despite their pegs over the next 12 months.

In the Hong Kong dollar options market, in which investors can make bets to protect against a change in Hong Kong's peg against the U.S. dollar over the next month, the cost of such positions has surged to its highest level in more than a decade.

"When everyone is talking about pegs, the Hong Kong dollar will come into consideration," said Société Générale's Ms. Wong.

A representative from the Hong Kong Monetary Authority said "the exchange rate and interest rates have remained steady" and "there is no sign of significant net inflows or net outflows of funds." The representative said the Hong Kong government "is fully committed" to maintaining its peg.

Recent concerns about China's economy have put the Hong Kong dollar under the spotlight, said Ian Gunner, a fund manager at Altana Wealth in London.

"The people making the markets feel there is an increased risk" of the peg breaking, he said. "If you want to bet on the peg being removed, it is going to cost you a lot more than before."

Still, Mr. Gunner noted that Hong Kong is "wedded to the idea of exchange-rate stability" and said the payoff for betting against the peg is less favorable than it was a few weeks ago.

BNP Paribas SA economist Mole Hau said the rise in bets on increased swings in Hong Kong's currency comes as investors and companies convert funds from Chinese yuan into Hong Kong dollars. "Safe-haven demand for the Hong Kong dollar has been rising," he said.

Strains in global markets have forced central banks in several countries to abandon long-held currency policies. Late last year, Russia's central bank said that it would let the ruble float freely as the country's economy came under stress. Switzerland's central bank abandoned a cap on the value of the franc earlier this year, sending the currency soaring against the euro.

"The market appears to have turned more nervous about regime shifts for other currency pegs," based on moves in the foreign-exchange forwards and options markets, strategists from Barclays PLC wrote in a note Tuesday.

Last week, Kazakhstan's government decided to remove the dollar peg for its currency, the tenge, as prices for copper and oil fell. The decision led to a depreciation of the currency of more than 20% in a few minutes.

Some investors said Kazakhstan's move, which followed soon after the Chinese currency devaluation, helped prompt traders to look for other pegs that could break.

"Following Kazakhstan's abandonment of its peg to the dollar, we have seen increased trading activity on our option desk with hedge funds speculating in devaluations in Saudi Arabia and Hong Kong," said Per Hammarlund, economist at Swedish bank SEB.

Laurence Fletcher and Carolyn Cui contributed to this article.

title: China Woes Drive Hong Kong, Taiwan to Bear Market
text:
Stocks in Hong Kong and Taiwan fell into bear-market territory Thursday, as the effects of China's volatility spills across its borders.

Both Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index and Taiwan's Taiex fell 20% from their peaks in April earlier Thursday before retracing losses. The Hang Seng Index closed down 1.8% and Taiwan's Taiex, which was down as much as 0.9%, rebounded to end 0.1% higher.

The accessibility of Hong Kong's market's to foreigners--in contrast to China's markets--make it a proxy for investing in China. That easier access makes Hong Kong vulnerable to losses amid mounting worries about the health of China's markets and economy. About half of shares listed on the Hang Seng are so-called H-shares, which represent Chinese companies listed in the city.

For example, when mainland stocks were suspended from trading in the throes of China's stock turmoil--with as few as 3% of stocks available for trading at one point--some investors who wanted to pull money from the Chinese market had to sell their stocks in Hong Kong instead, said Binay Chandgothia, a portfolio manager at Principal Global Investors.

Meanwhile, the streak of volatility continues to rattle investors in China's markets, with heavy selling in the last 15 minutes of trading Thursday.

The Shanghai Composite Index ended down 3.4% at 3664.29 and the smaller Shenzhen Composite fell 3% to 2155.49.

Global investors withdrew 1.34 billion yuan ($209.45 million) from Shanghai via a trading link with Hong Kong.

Uncertainty about the pace of government intervention in Shanghai and Shenzhen has spurred much of this week's rocky trading, as the funds tasked with supporting the market don't disclose details of what and when they are buying. Earlier this week, some listed firms announced government-held stakes, which lifted shares, though performance across the market has been uneven.

Those that disclosed Wednesday after market hours that the state fund Central Huijin Investment has increased its stake, for example, contained their losses Thursday: Agricultural Bank of China Ltd. fell 0.3%, Bank of China Ltd. slipped 0.5% and Industrial and Commercial Bank of China Ltd. declined 0.4%. Losses in other big state-owned companies were steeper. For example, PetroChina Co. sank 4.4%, while China Citic Bank Corp. shed 4.2%.

Elsewhere, worries about the timing of a rise in U.S. interest rates, which could crimp growth and profits, drove losses, with Australia's S&PASX 200 down 1.7%, Nikkei's Stock Average down 0.9% and South Korea's Kospi down 1.3%.

On Wednesday, minutes from the Federal Reserve's policy meeting provided no clear sign the central bank would raise rates as soon as September.

"Investors are in a state of heightened nervousness so comments about global uncertainty get latched on to," including the Fed's minutes, said Shane Oliver, an investment strategist at AMP Capital.

A rush to safer assets drove gold prices to a near five week-high in Asia trade. Spot gold rose to an intraday high of $1,141.80 before cooling to $1,137.90.

The Chinese yuan weakened in the morning, after the International Monetary Fund confirmed an earlier proposal to a delay in the five-year reshuffling of the basket, which currently doesn't include the yuan. Late Wednesday, the IMF's executive board approved an extension of the current basket of reserve currencies included in its special drawing rights to Sept. 30, 2016.

AMP's Mr. Oliver said that the IMF decision added to jitters among Asian investors even though a selloff in the region was already under way after China devalued its currency last week.

The yuan recovered to finish roughly flat onshore. Offshore, it was last 0.2% stronger at 6.4451 against the U.S. dollar.

Brent crude oil was down 1.4% at $46.51 a barrel in Asia trade, amid worries about future demand from China.

Biman Mukherji contributed to this article.

title: HKMA sells HK$14.88 bln to keep Hong Kong dollar in trading band

HONG KONG, April 27 (Reuters) - The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) intervened in the currency market again late on Friday, selling a total HK$14.88 billion ($1.92 billion) in Hong Kong dollars as the local currency hit the strong end of its trading range.

The city's de-facto central bank, which has intervened multiple times in the market in the past fortnight, had sold HK$13.18 billion ($1.70 billion) earlier that day.

The Hong Kong dollar is pegged at 7.8 to the U.S. dollar, but can trade between 7.75 and 7.85. Under the currency peg, the HKMA is obliged to intervene to keep the currency within its band.

title: China stocks hit 7-yr high despite weak factory activity; Hong Kong also up

* CSI300 +0.2 pct; SSEC: 0.2 pct; HSI: 0.6 pct               

* China April flash HSBC PMI contracts to one-year low               

* Net flow into China's stock market totalled 781.4 billion yuan last week               

By Samuel Shen and Pete Sweeney               

SHANGHAI, April 23 (Reuters) - China stocks advanced to fresh seven-year highs on Thursday as weaker-than-expected factory activity data reinforced expectations that Beijing will roll out more stimulus measures and keep the financial system flush with cash.               

The flash HSBC/Markit Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI) showed that China's factory activity in April contracted at its fastest pace in a year, suggesting that economic conditions are still deteriorating.               

Investors also shrugged off the prospects of weaker company earnings. A Reuters survey showed that earnings growth at China-listed companies is likely to be the slowest in three years in 2015.               

"No one cares about price/earnings ratios, or price/book ratios now. Investors only care about the attitude of the government, which has so far appeared tolerant (of the rise)," said Du Changchun, analyst at Northeast Securities in Shanghai.               

"Upward momentum is still very strong, as money keeps flooding in. I don't dare to forecast the market's peak."               

The CSI300 index rose 0.2 percent to 4,751.24 points by midday, while the Shanghai Composite Index  gained 0.2 percent to 4,407.72 points.               

The Hang Seng index added 0.6 percent to 28,091.63 points, while the Hong Kong China Enterprises Index  gained 0.4 percent to 14,722.25.               

Despite the market's 80 percent surge since last November, new investors keep piling in. Last week alone, there was a net flow of 781.4 billion yuan ($126.08 billion) into the stock market, marking the fourth consecutive week of net inflows.               

And new stock trading accounts hit a record 3.3 million last week, almost doubling from the previous week, although that also  reflected a rule change that let investors open multiple share accounts.               

In the words of UBS' Asian strategists, the action seen in Chinese stocks is what happens "when 'Animal Spirits' meet liquidity."               

Earlier this week, The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA), intervened in the currency market again, selling Hong Kong dollars to keep the local currency within the trading band against the U.S. dollar, reflecting strong money inflows.               

Chinese steelmakers rose sharply as investors' interest shifts to some relatively cheaper cyclical stocks. Internet-related stocks were also strong.

title: CORRECTED-China charge into HK stocks both boon and bane
text:
(Corrects figure in second paragraph to 68 billion yuan, not $68 billion)

* Mainland inflows through stock connect programme flood HK

* Push Hang Seng index to 7-year high

* Mainland retail investors seen more volatile

* Complicates management of liquidity, dollar peg

By Pete Sweeney and Michelle Chen

SHANGHAI/HONG KONG, April 16 (Reuters) - Surging investment from mainland China has jolted Hong Kong's stock market from the doldrums, but the volatility of such flows, driven by an unfamiliar breed of investor, presents new risks to the stability of the city's economy and currency.

A Reuters analysis shows that Chinese investors have moved a net 68 billion yuan ($10.97 billion) into Hong Kong-listed stocks via the Shanghai-Hong Kong stock connect programme since its launch in November, the vast bulk of it during just a few days in April.

That new money, plus tens of billions of dollars from a separate channel for Chinese institutional investors and untold flows from Chinese-controlled offshore funds, has helped push the market's capitalisation to HK$28.6 trillion ($3.7 trillion) in April from HK$25.5 trillion in November.

That is driving profits in Hong Kong's financial industry, presenting opportunities for companies to raise capital and perhaps boosting consumer confidence.

But this tide of cash can flow out as quickly as it flowed in, especially if investors conclude the rally has run too far ahead of the slowing economies on both sides of the border.

"With the help of China's opening up, Hong Kong's status as a global financial centre has been enhanced. However, its economy is also entering into a bubble cycle, and it's just the beginning," said Raymond Yeung, analyst at ANZ in Hong Kong.

The Shanghai Composite Index has gained over 70 percent since late November when the central bank made a surprise cut to interest rates, and the rally began overflowing into Hong Kong stocks in April, pushing the Hang Seng index up more than 11 percent so far this month to a seven-year high.

"(Inflows) will add pressure to the already high property prices and cause inflation," said Yeung. "It will also bring more risks when sudden capital outflows happen."

According to exchange data, 62 percent of mainland Chinese investors in Hong Kong in 2014 were ordinary retail investors, who tend to behave very differently to the institutional fund managers Hong Kong is accustomed to.

On average, domestic Chinese investors hold a stock for as little as 24 days, compared with 260 days in Hong Kong, UBS analyst Lu Wenjie said in a research note.

"These two groups of investors are totally different, and there will be certain chemical reactions as they meet," wrote Charles Li, CEO of the Hong Kong exchange (HKEx), on his blog.

CURRENCY PEG

HKEx data for 2014 shows mainland investors made up only 5.1 percent of its total cash market trading by value, lagging institutional funds from the UK and United States, which together accounted for over 20 percent.

But that equation is changing rapidly.

The stock connect scheme means Chinese investors can invest up to 250 billion yuan ($40.3 billion) in Hong Kong markets, and that quota is expected to be widened this year. And the Chinese flows are amplified by foreign money riding on its coat tails.

All of which has pushed volatility in the Hong Kong and Shanghai bourses to record highs, producing wide price swings.

The potential for vast and sudden moves of liquidity in and out of the Hong Kong dollar will also complicate monetary policy.

Hong Kong operates one of the world's last remaining currency pegs to the U.S. dollar, which means it must buy or sell dollars when the currency looks set to exceed its daily trading band.

In recent days, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) was forced to intervene multiple times as demand for Hong Kong dollars spiked.

"Invariably the investment opportunity at any one time will be on one side or the other, and this is likely to create sudden inflows and outflows that will put pressure on the Hong Kong dollar peg," said Francois Perrin, head of Greater China Equities for BNP Investment Partners.

Two individuals familiar with the exchange's thinking said Hong Kong, not Beijing, had originally requested the imposition of quotas for the programme for fear an exodus of capital into China could put pressure on the exchange's trading system and the dollar peg.

HKEx said the quotas "were mutually agreed between the regulators and the exchanges as a means of managing risk in the initial stages".

HKMA declined to directly answer questions related to the impact these flows might have on monetary strategy, but reiterated its policy to "monitor the market developments closely and maintain the stability of the Hong Kong dollar". ($1 = 7.7504 Hong Kong dollars) ($1 = 6.2037 Chinese yuan renminbi) ($1 = 6.1977 Chinese yuan renminbi) (Additional reporting by Samuel Shen in SHANGHAI, Michelle Price and Saikat Chatterjee in HONG KONG; Editing by Will Waterman)
