US STOCKS 

Stocks kicked off November with their biggest single-day rally in weeks, in a day packed with economic data that raised investors' spirits ahead of Friday's key jobs report.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 136.16 points, or 1%, to 13232.62, on its second trading day after megastorm Sandy forced two days of market closures. The average marked its biggest one-day advance in both points and percentage terms since Sept. 13.

The Standard & Poor's 500-stock index rose 15.43 points, or 1.1%, to 1427.59, also posting its biggest gain since Sept. 13. The Nasdaq Composite gained 42.83 points, or 1.4%, to 3020.06.

Materials, technology and industrials shares were the top performers. The climb in the industrials sector was led by Masco, a provider of building supplies, which was one of the top gainers in the index. Masco has risen 10% since Sandy hit the East Coast.

Tech giants Intel and Microsoft propped up the Dow's gains, posting some of the largest increases in the average.

"Tech has been getting clobbered. So as people come back from being out of the office, tech is the place they are looking for deals," said Uri Landesman, president of New York hedge fund Platinum Partners, which oversees $1.1 billion in assets.

The rally was sparked by a line-up of economic reports, mostly positive, that pushed blue chips to a triple-digit increase in morning trade. A pair of labor-market reports boosted optimism ahead of Friday's employment data.

"These numbers give us the sense that it's going to be okay," said J.J. Kinahan, chief derivatives strategist at TD Ameritrade. "The economy is taking body punch after body punch, but it still seems pretty strong."

The Institute of Supply Management's reading on the manufacturing sector indicated that it expanded in October, and came in slightly higher than economists expected. The Conference Board reported that consumer confidence rose to its highest level since early 2008. Spending on construction projects rose in September as home building jumped, the Commerce Department reported.

Automatic Data Processing reported 158,000 new private-sector jobs were created in October. The report didn't have a consensus expectation, since ADP switched to a new methodology. The report is seen as a preview to the closely watched government employment report due Friday.

"This certainly isn't enough to bring unemployment down, so it's discouraging in that sense. But it is encouraging that the job growth we're getting is broad-based across most parts of the economy," said Mark Zandi, chief economist for Moody's Analytics, which helped develop the report's new methodology.

In earnings news, Pfizer fell 1.3% after the pharmaceutical giant's third-quarter earnings and revenue came in well below analyst expectations.

Exxon Mobil was 0.5% higher after its third-quarter earnings and revenue exceeded analyst expectations.


 
 
ASIAN STOCKS 

Asian markets were higher on Friday, as positive U.S. economic data released Thursday contributed to growing optimism over the global economy, pushing Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index to its highest level since August 2011.

Regional stocks took their cue from Wall Street, where markets started November on an upbeat note following positive economic data. At the forefront was the Institute of Supply Management's reading on manufacturing, which showed a slightly better-than-expected expansion in October.

The U.S. factory numbers followed Chinese manufacturing data, released early Thursday, which was taken as a sign that Asia's largest economy is recovering from its recent slowdown.

The next dose of economic data from the U.S. will be the government's employment report due later Friday. After that, the world's two largest economies will decide on their new leaders, with the U.S. Presidential election and the start of China's party congress both taking place next week.

The strong economic data helped the Hang Seng Index climb above the 20,000 mark for the first time in fifteen months. The index was up over 1%, benefiting from increased confidence in the Chinese economy as well as liquidity inflows into the city, as evidenced by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority's recent interventions to defend the local currency's peg to the U.S. dollar.

"There are four stages in a stock market cycle, including hope, optimism, worry and disappointment. The Hong Kong market is in the hope stage," said Edward Huang, strategist at Haitong International in Hong Kong.

Big movers in Hong Kong included Sands China, which was up 4.8%; retailer Esprit Holdings, which gained 3.2%; and Bank of East Asia, which advanced 2.5%.

In mainland China, the Shanghai Composite was 0.1% higher, moderating after jumping 1.7% on Thursday following the most recent Chinese manufacturing data.

Sharp fell 4.1% after posting a loss for the latest quarter and predicting a second straight year of record deficits; while Sony added 3.3% after announcing that its net loss in the second quarter narrowed from a year earlier.

Panasonic, which plummeted 19.5% on Thursday after releasing disappointing earnings, continued to fall, albeit at a slower pace - down 0.2%.

Australia's S&P/ASX 200 was just 0.2% higher, paring early gains as caution set in ahead of next week's risk events. Risk-aversion has characterized trading in Australia for much of the week, with local stocks underperforming regional peers - down less than 0.1% week-to-date.

However, Wall Street's overnight gains bolstered Australian resource companies: BHP Billiton was 1.7% higher, Rio Tinto added 2.0%, and Fortescue Metals Group rose 1.5%.

FOREX

The increase in risk appetite was also evident in the movement in the yen, which weakened against the U.S. dollar. The U.S. dollar was at Y80.28 Friday, extending its 0.4% overnight rise against the yen.


METALS 

Comex gold futures settled lower, giving up earlier gains as the dollar strengthened against the euro and brighter economic data damped investor appetite for the haven asset.

Base metals on the London Metal Exchange closed higher after positive economic data sparked a buoyant session and dollar weakness in the London session helped to underpin gains.

Nymex oil futures advanced Thursday after the U.S. government said oil stockpiles unexpectedly fell last week, while analysts warned tighter fuel supplies could be on the way in the wake of Hurricane Sandy.

title: WORLD  FOREX : Dollar Firms Ahead Of Payrolls; Greece Concerns Build
text:
--Dollar firmer ahead of US payrolls data

--Concerns over Greece build, weighing on sentiment to the euro

--Hong Kong Monetary Authorityintervenes again


 
   By Clare Connaghan 
 

The dollar was firmer across the board ahead of a U.S. employment update Friday, rising to a three-week high against the euro, as new worries about Greece and weak data from the 17-country euro region dampened sentiment towards currencies perceived as risky.

The euro hit $1.2865 against the dollar in European trading hours after data showed manufacturing activity shrank for the 15th straight month in October. That indicates the overall euro-zone economy deteriorated at the start of the fourth quarter.

European stock markets also fell, while yields were steady on bonds issued by fiscally-stressed European governments like Italy and Spain.

"The euro weakness against the dollar appears driven by positioning and squaring up ahead of payrolls, though market participants are now paying more attention to the risks surrounding the Greek parliamentary vote next week," said Elsa Lignos, a senior currency strategist at RBC Capital Markets.

Greek lawmakers are expected to vote next week on a 13.5 billion euro ($17.5 billion) austerity package that international creditors have demanded in exchange for aid. A vote on the government's 2013 spending plan is likely to follow a few days later. Analysts expect the votes to be close.

Aside from Greece, Spain also continues to worry the market with data showing Spanish manufacturing activity declined faster in October and Spanish car registrations fell 21.7% on the year in October.

"Everyone in the market keeps pushing back expectations for when Spain will ask (for financial assistance), until they are tested....there is no real political impetus for them to do so," said Adam Myers, senior currency strategist at Credit Agricole in London.

Investors are generally less optimistic about European situation right now, said Mr. Myers, and that is weighing on the euro and helping the dollar in European trading. The greenback is also stronger against the yen and commodity-linked currencies of Canada, New Zealand and Australia.

Looking ahead, attention is immediately focused on U.S. non-farm payrolls for October to be released at 1230 GMT. Economists surveyed by Dow Jones Newswires expect an increase of 125,000 jobs, compared with 114,000 in September.

Elsewhere, the pound bounced off session lows against the dollar and rose to a one-month high against the euro after data showed the U.K.'s construction sector returned to muted growth in October. Data provider Markit and the Chartered Institute of Purchasing and Supply said the purchasing managers index for the construction sector in October was 50.9, up from 49.5 in September. By 1147 GMT, the pound was trading at $1.6090 against the dollar, compared with $1.6129 late Thursday in New York.

In other news, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority sold another 5.038 billion Hong Kong dollars (US$650 million) during European trade Friday to defend the Hong Kong dollar's peg to the U.S. dollar, according to market data. The HKMA's latest move was triggered by the U.S. dollar hitting HK$7.7500, the strong side of the Hong Kong dollar's trading band, as a flood of capital inflows amid global central banks' stimulus measures continued to strengthen Asian currencies, including the Hong Kong dollar.

title: Asian Shares Up, Hong Kong Hits 15-Month High
text:
-- Asian markets rise on positive U.S. economic data

-- Hang Seng Index hits 15-month high above 22,000

-- Investors await near-term events including U.S. jobs data and the U.S. Presidential election

Asian markets were higher on Friday, as positive U.S. economic data released Thursday contributed to growing optimism over the global economy, pushing Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index to its highest level since August 2011.

Regional stocks took their cue from Wall Street, where markets started November on an upbeat note following positive economic data. At the forefront was the Institute of Supply Management's reading on manufacturing, which showed a slightly better-than-expected expansion in October.

The U.S. factory numbers followed Chinese manufacturing data, released early Thursday, which was taken as a sign that Asia's largest economy is recovering from its recent slowdown.

The next dose of economic data from the U.S. will be the government's employment report due later Friday. After that, the world's two largest economies will decide on their new leaders, with the U.S. Presidential election and the start of China's party congress both taking place next week.

The strong economic data helped the Hang Seng Index climb above the 20,000 mark for the first time in fifteen months. The index was up 1.3% at 22,099.82, benefiting from increased confidence in the Chinese economy as well as liquidity inflows into the city, as evidenced by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority's recent interventions to defend the local currency's peg to the U.S. dollar.

"There are four stages in a stock market cycle, including hope, optimism, worry and disappointment. The Hong Kong market is in the hope stage," said Edward Huang, strategist at Haitong International in Hong Kong.

Big movers in Hong Kong included Sands China, which was up 4.8%; food company Want Want China Holdings, which was 4.7% higher; and retailer Esprit Holdings, which gained 3%.

In mainland China, the Shanghai Composite was down 0.3%, moderating after jumping 1.7% on Thursday following the most recent Chinese manufacturing data.

The increase in risk appetite was also evident in the movement in the yen, which weakened against the U.S. dollar. The U.S. dollar was at Y80.24 Friday, extending its 0.4% overnight rise against the yen.

The weaker yen was a boon for Japanese stocks, with the Nikkei up 1.1%, while major electronics companies responded to earnings reports.

Sharp fell 4.1% after posting a loss for the latest quarter and predicting a second straight year of record deficits; while Sony added 2.6% after announcing that its net loss in the second quarter narrowed from a year earlier.

Panasonic, which plummeted 19.5% on Thursday after releasing disappointing earnings, continued to fall, albeit at a slower pace -- down 0.7%.

South Korea's Kospi was 1.0% higher.

Australia's S&P/ASX 200 was just 0.1% higher, paring early gains as caution set in ahead of next week's risk events. Risk-aversion has characterized trading in Australia for much of the week, with local stocks underperforming regional peers -- down 0.2% week-to-date.

However, Wall Street's overnight gains bolstered Australian resource companies: BHP Billiton was 1.8% higher, Rio Tinto added 2.0%, and Fortescue Metals Group rose 1.3%.

title: HK Shares End Higher; Continued Fund Inflows, China PMI Boost Interest
text:
HONG KONG--Robust manufacturing data out of China and continued fund inflows into Hong Kong helped boost the city's benchmark index Thursday, even as overnight declines on Wall Street and weakness in other Asian stock markets capped gains.

The blue-chip Hang Seng Index rose 180.05 points, or 0.8%, to 21,821.87, its highest close since Aug. 4, 2011, when the index ended at 21,884. The index recovered from a low of 21,506.05 early in the session after the release of China's official gauge of manufacturing activity for October indicated an expansion after two months of contraction.

Market volumes for the session totaled 58.70 billion Hong Kong dollars (US$7.6 billion), up from HK$47.94 billion Wednesday.

Gains on Thursday added to the 1.0% rise the previous day, as the Hong Kong Monetary Authorityintervened in the foreign exchange market for the second straight day to cap gains in the local currency against the U.S. dollar, signalling continued fund inflows.

If the last period of major liquidity inflows was any measure, there remains significantly more room for more hot money to flow into Hong Kong, said Francis Lun, managing director at brokerage Lyncean Holdings. For many months between 2008 and 2009, the HKMA intervened aggressively to defend the local dollar's peg to the greenback as liquidity poured into Hong Kong following the first round of U.S. quantitative easing.

Now, "there's also a lot of speculative inflows betting on further gains in the Chinese yuan," said Mr. Lun, as the Hong Kong currency has for years been seen as a proxy for the yuan's movements, which isn't freely convertible. The Chinese currency has in recent weeks been rising against the U.S. dollar amid further signs of a steady recovery in the domestic economy.

The broker said the continued inflows will help further lift the city's benchmark index, forecasting the next resistance level at around 23,000 points.

Australia's benchmark S&P/ASX 200 closed down 1.3% at a four-week low, while South Korea's Kospi dropped 0.7% to 1,898.44. Overnight, the Dow Jones Industrial Average slipped 10.75 points, or 0.08% from Friday's close, to 13096.46, after two days of closures due to superstorm Sandy.

Blue-chip property stocks in Hong Kong rose further as they recovered more from Monday's declines, after the government slapped a tax on foreign residential property buyers.

"The rebound in the stocks show that investors aren't too worried about property prices coming down sharply from the measures, even if transaction volumes may fall," said Conita Hung, a director at Delta Asia Financial.

Among the real estate firms, New World Holdings ended up 0.8% at HK$12.08, Wharf Holdings rose 0.6% to HK$53.35, and Cheung Kong added 0.4% to HK$115.0.

Chinese shippers also outperformed the broad market, led by China Shipping Container Lines after brokerage Daiwa upgraded the stock to Buy from Hold. Daiwa revised its 2012 earnings forecast for China Shipping to a CNY41 million net profit, versus an earlier forecast of a CNY371 million loss. The house also raised its target price to HK$2.74 from HK$2.70. The stock jumped 8.2% Thursday to HK$2.24.

title: WSJ Has Hong Kong popped its bubble?
text:
If this is a fair characterization of Hong Kong property, it is the drivers of investment demand that matter most. Have the fundamentals really changed?

Investors will likely be reconsidering political risk and the potential for further government intervention. Financial Secretary John Tsang said on Friday the government was ready to introduce further measures, which would likely include further taxes.

But for mainland Chinese investors, there are an assortment of reasons supporting property investment in Hong Kong from offshoring money to a more attractive tax regime.

The other gorilla in the room is the currency play. The peg of the Hong Kong dollar to the U.S. dollar has been an important dynamic in mainland Chinese investing.

For one, it means Hong Kong property has appeared less expensive after the yuan has gained over 30% against the dollar in recent years.

And keeping some money or assets in Hong Kong also gives all investors an option on a potential currency appreciation.

A longstanding belief is the Hong Kong currency should eventually be pegged to the yuan or a basket of currencies. The timing, however, is not expected before China is ready to make the yuan fully convertible. But this may not be just up to Beijing.

Another risk with the latest move is that it again flags to international investors the stresses facing the 29-year-old currency peg as its strains under "hot money" flows. Arguably, it is at the root of local asset inflation by forcing the importation of low interest rates and a weak currency value from the U.S.

Over the past 10 days, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority has repeatedly had to intervene to stop the currency from strengthening by selling Hong Kong dollars.

Some investors will interpret the new tax as sign such pressures are escalating.

There have already been questions about how effective the tax will be in curbing wider capital flows. Some property experts predict the tax will simply divert investment into commercial and industrial property. There have already been some signs of this, as investors try to skirt stamp-duty resale restrictions in the residential market.

Higher prices here will also be a problem. It would mean increased costs for businesses at a time when exports, retail sales and stock-market turnover have all been declining.

All said, Hong Kong will struggle to find a painless way out of its asset bubble.

title: WSJA(10/26) Once Staid, Yuan Starts To Swing -3-
text:
(From THE WALL STREET JOURNAL ASIA)

By Lingling Wei

BEIJING -- The once-predictable Chinese yuan has become increasingly volatile, a development that signals a stronger role for markets in the currency's moves but poses greater foreign-exchange risks for businesses and investors alike.

China still keeps a tight grip on the yuan, also known as the renminbi, by limiting its trading within a range. In terms of volatility, the currency still pales in comparison to more freely traded counterparts.

But since late September, as China's economy started to show signs of stabilizing from a slowdown earlier in the year, traders betting on the yuan's rise have pushed the currency to the upper limit of the Beijing-imposed trading range more frequently than in the past, according to an analysis by The Wall Street Journal. The intraday moves have been much bigger than suggested by changes in the daily rate set by China's central bank. Traders say they are increasingly taking advantage of an April move by the People's Bank of China to expand the yuan's trading territory.

On Thursday, the yuan again hit the upper limit of its daily trading band, finishing at the day's high of 6.2417 to the dollar. The level is the highest since the launch of modern foreign-exchange trading in China in 1994.

China's lighter hand on the currency is one reason why the yuan has experienced a rare bumpy ride this year. The yuan is now up 0.8% against the U.S. dollar for the year, after falling as much as 1.6% in July. Back then, as investors worried over China's economic slowdown, traders sold the yuan, aiding Beijing's effort to make it weaker against the dollar.

In effect, the new volatility underscores the increasing willingness of Beijing to allow market forces to play a bigger role in setting the yuan's value, though the PBOC still guides the currency's longer-term moves. The volatility shows that "the PBOC is not intervening much these days, and the market is taking full advantage of the widened trading band," said analyst WoonKhien Chia at Royal Bank of Scotland.

PBOC officials didn't respond to requests for comment.

The yuan's recent rise comes as China prepares for a once-a-decade leadership change set to begin next month. Some market analysts expect the transition to pave the way for more monetary-easing measures aimed at keeping China's economy humming. Stimulus measures would typically put downward pressure on a currency, but any increase in optimism over the economy could help strengthen the yuan.

The Chinese currency also has been buffeted by the same forces hitting other Asian markets. Money has poured into Asian assets as investors seek higher returns in response to declines in interest rates that have resulted from Western central banks' efforts to aid growth.

The Hong Kong Monetary Authority has intervened several times in the past week to weaken the Hong Kong dollar after it hit the top of its trading band against the U.S. dollar. Shares in Hong Kong hit a 14-month high Thursday.

Chinese stocks have risen recently as well after a dismal year, in part because of the inflow of new cash. Net flows of cash into Hong Kong and mainland China equity mutual funds have totaled $1.3 billion over the past four weeks, the most for any part of Asia excluding Japan, according to research by Deutsche Bank.

Chinese officials have said the country will push ahead with establishing a market-based exchange-rate system, whereby the yuan would move up and down like any other major currency. The change is part of China's broader plan to overhaul its creaky financial sector, elevate the country's status in the international monetary system and someday challenge the U.S. dollar as the de facto global currency.

Russian Prime Minister Vladimir Putin said Thursday that Russia and China should move toward settling trade in their own currencies and that full convertibility for the yuan is "a matter of time."

China's growing flexibility also could help deflect criticism by the U.S., where the yuan's value has become an issue in the current election campaign. Some U.S. businesses and lawmakers say China undervalues the yuan to make its exports more attractive abroad. Republican contender Mitt Romney has pledged that if he is elected, he will label China a currency manipulator on his first day in office.

The increased swings are causing problems for exporters like Du Hanbing, who runs a business in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen that makes embossing machines and sells them in the U.S. and Canada. Mr. Du said he usually would adjust prices based on how the yuan is trading.

"If the yuan depreciates, I would bump up the dollar prices for our products, and vice versa," he said. "But nowadays, the yuan seems to be switching courses faster than we could adjust our prices."

Mr. Du said the company hasn't tried to hedge against the yuan's swings because that could be expensive for a small business like his.

The volatility has increased the yuan's appeal for financial investors like hedge funds that profit from swings either way. Andy Seaman, a portfolio manager at hedge-fund firm Stratton Street Capital, said he has been increasing his exposure to renminbi all year.

Mr. Seaman manages a yuan-bond fund with about $180 million in assets under management. But the London-based fund doesn't hold any yuan bonds due to what he views as a lack of liquidity in Hong Kong's yuan-bond market. Rather, it buys Asian dollar-denominated bonds and enters into forward contracts that allow the fund to get renminbi by selling dollars.

The fund is up 2.8% this month and nearly 23% this year, he said. It has benefited from both yuan appreciation and rising yields on the underlying bonds.

Mr. Seaman said the fund has also benefited from the yuan's increased volatility. Prices on the yuan-linked forward contracts he buys are lower than they otherwise would be, reflecting the uncertain outlook, leaving his fund with bigger gains if the yuan continues to appreciate.

"Money is flowing from the debtor nations to the creditor nations, such as China, building up the pressure on Asian currencies, such as renminbi, to appreciate," he said.

The new volatility doesn't preclude Beijing from taking a stronger hand. A year ago, the PBOC pushed the yuan to strengthen against the dollar even as investors tested its trading band by pushing the currency the other way.

The PBOC keeps a leash on the yuan's trading in mainland China by setting a daily rate for it, known as the parity rate. In April, it widened the range in which the yuan is allowed to rise and fall daily to 1% above or below the parity rate from 0.5% previously. The move reflected China's belief that the currency is fairly valued and ready to take a more prominent role globally.

"The wider band was seen as a step for the spot rate to be more flexible, allowing greater volatility," said Paul Mackel, head of Asian currency research at HSBC.

title: ICBC-HKMA continues to curb HK dollar
text:
Release date - 25102012

The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) said Wednesday it will continue to intervene in the market to keep Hong Kong dollar from exceeding the top end of the trading band with the U.S. dollar as strong demand is driving up the value of the currency.

In its latest intervention, the HKMA injected over 3 billion HK dollars (about 408 million U.S. dollars) into the market this morning, bringing the total amount to over 14 billion HK dollars since Saturday.

The move came as the local currency hit 7.75 HK dollars to one U.S. dollar, the stronger end of the trading band under the Currency Board Mechanism. The buying of U.S. dollars is triggered automatically when the exchange rate hits the upper limit.

Deputy Chief Executive of the HKMA Eddie Yue said there are various reasons in the recent spike in demand for the Hong Kong dollar, for instance, the latest round of monetary easing in the United States may increase demand for Asian currencies, equities and bonds. Other investors who had previously held U.S. dollar assets may also switch back to the local currency.

Yue said he expects the high demand to persist, and the authority is obliged to sell the local currency to keep its value from the peg range. He said the currency still remains stable against the U.S. dollar.

Once the transaction is settled on Wednesday, the total balances on clearing accounts maintained by banks with the HKMA will reach 163 billion HK dollars. The HKMA said the increase is unlikely to affect the close-to-zero interbank rates in the short term.

The authority said it will closely monitor market developments and ensure the stability of the Hong Kong dollar.

The last time Hong Kong’s currency reached a similar level was back in 2009, when the HKMA sold over 2 billion HK dollars on the market.

title: Hong Kong Keeps Up Heat on  Currency
text:
Hong Kong's banking system is awash in cash, pushing lending rates down and threatening to push up property prices, as the de facto central bank continues to intervene in the currency market.

The Hong Kong Monetary Authority has sold a combined 14.36 billion Hong Kong dollars (US$1.85 billion) in four interventions since Friday as it seeks to keep the currency from strengthening out of its trading band against the U.S. dollar. The HKMA said Wednesday it expects funds will continue to flow into the Hong Kong dollar on a net basis "for some time" and pledged to maintain the currency's stability.

Cash has surged into the banking system from the intervention, and as overseas fund managers, more willing to take on risk as a result of global stimulus measures, snap up the city's stocks. As a result, Hong Kong's benchmark three-month interbank lending rate has fallen to 0.25%, from 0.35% before the first intervention, and 0.5% two weeks ago. When that rate falls, it brings down benchmark borrowing rates for companies and mortgage rates for individuals.

Barclays said that if interest rates remain low, there will likely be more lending, which would support the property market. The city's housing prices have already risen 16% from the start of the year through to August. When borrowing rates fell even more dramatically, from 4% to below 1% in 2009, home prices jumped 29%.

Still, "the rates drop hasn't been drastic, and its impact on the financial market wouldn't be as substantial as it was during 2008-2009," said Tommy Ong, head of wealth-management solutions at DBS Group Holdings Ltd.'s Hong Kong unit.

A measure of liquidity among banks in Hong Kong, the so-called aggregate balance, has climbed to HK$163 billion, from around HK$149 billion before the first injection Friday in New York trade. The last time the HKMA intervened was during 2008 and 2009, when the Hong Kong dollar was seen as a haven during global market turmoil. At the time, the currency was also boosted by the Federal Reserve's first round of quantitative easing.

Eddie Yue, deputy chief executive of the HKMA, said Wednesday that the U.S. stimulus measures announced in September may trigger demand for Asian currencies, equities and bonds. Some investors who have held U.S. dollars are switching back to the local unit as investors world-wide become more willing to take on risk, he added.

This time, the HKMA has been mostly stepping in during the U.S. day, when trading volume is less, making it easier for speculators to move the market if they wish to test the top end of the band. The Hong Kong dollar is allowed to trade between HK$7.7500 and HK$7.8500 per U.S. dollar. Late Wednesday, the rate was HK$7.7505.

One-year forward contracts for Hong Kong dollars were priced at HK$7.7440 per dollar late Wednesday, a level beyond the strong end of the trading band. Still, few are predicting any quick change to the peg, which was created in 1983 as confidence in the former British colony wavered ahead of its handover to China in 1997.

"The cost of change is substantial, while the benefits are highly uncertain," said Robert Minikin, senior foreign-exchange strategist at Standard Chartered PLC's Hong Kong unit. "Any change to the peg will be long-delayed until the yuan becomes fully convertible."

The Chinese yuan is seen as a possible hook for the Hong Kong dollar, as the city's economy is increasingly integrated to the mainland.

"But [yuan's full convertibility] will unlikely happen in the next decade," said Mr. Minikin.

title: HK Shares End at Fresh 14-Month High; 10-Day Winning Streak

By Clement Tan

HONG KONG, Oct 24 (Reuters) - Hong Kong shares rose to their highest level for the year on Wednesday, buoyed by expectations of further capital inflows into the city said to be mainly due to a third round of quantitative easing by the United States Federal Reserve.

The Hang Seng Index ended up 0.3 percent at 21,763.8, its ninth-straight daily gain helping the benchmark to its highest 2012 close after hitting its highest intra-day level this year at 21,802.5 in late afternoon trade.

Wednesday's gains were the benchmark's ninth in a row, equalling a winning streak recorded in June 2010. It last rose 10 sessions in a row in June 2006. The Hang Seng Index is now up 18.1 percent this year after slumping 20 percent in 2011.

In the mainland, the CSI300 Index of the top Shanghai and Shenzhen listings slipped 0.2 percent, while the Shanghai Composite Index edged up 0.1 percent.

"Incoming fund flows are sure to further buoy Hong Kong markets further, with local developers and Chinese construction-related plays likely to see further short-term buying interest," Edward Huang, equity strategist with Haitong International Securities said.

The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) intervened in the currency market for the fourth time since Oct. 19 on Wednesday, selling a total HK$14.4 billion ($1.85 billion) of Hong Kong dollars to weaken the territory's currency and protect its 29-year-old peg to the U.S. dollar.

On Monday, shares of bourse operator Hong Kong Exchange (HKEx) jumped 2.9 percent to its highest close since late April. After lagging the broader market for most of the year, it is now up more than 10 percent this month after surging 13.8 percent in September.

The Hong Kong property sector was also among the outperformers. Cheung Kong Holdings jumped 4.4 percent, extending its 2012 gains to nearly 30 percent. Sun Hung Kai Properties rose 3.6 percent.

With valuations of some Chinese growth-sensitive names near historic lows, market watchers expect further gains leading into China's 18th Party Congress meeting starting on Nov. 8.

A rise in the HSBC Flash Manufacturing Purchasing Managers Index for China to a three-month high of 49.1 in October with gains in new orders and output provided further signs that the slowdown in the world's second-largest economy could be stabilizing.

"Talking to my clients, it seems their pessimism on China is ebbing after recent data," said Huang.

IN FOCUS: EARNINGS OF CHINA CYCLICAL SECTORS

Third-quarter corporate earnings remained a focus. Investors rewarded in-line results, particularly for battered growth-sensitive sectors, partly on expectations that a stabilizing Chinese economy could help improve profitability.

China Coal Energy Co Ltd rose 2.1 percent in Hong Kong after posting a 22 percent decline in third-quarter net profit late on Tuesday that were largely in line with expectations.

After lagging the broader Hong Kong market for much of this year, shares of China's second-largest coal producer are now up almost 11 percent in October after jumping 10 percent in September.

It is still down 6.2 percent for the year, compared to the Hang Seng Index's 18.1 percent gain and the China Enterprises Index's 7.1 percent rise. China Coal currently trades at a 47 percent discount to its historic median 12-month forward price-to-book value, according to Thomson Reuters StarMine.

Anhui Conch Cement slipped 3.9 percent in Hong Kong, trimming its 2012 gains to 12.1 percent ahead of its third-quarter earnings expected later on Wednesday.

Currently trading at 8 percent discount to its historical 12-month forward earnings median, eight out of 28 analysts have upped their full year earnings-per-share estimates for Anhui Conch Cement by an average of 0.4 percent in the last 30 days, according to StarMine.

Esprit Holdings plunged 9.5 percent after it announced plans to raise $677 million to fund a restructuring of its key businesses.

Losses on Wednesday brought Esprit's share price to its lowest since early August, paring gains after the company appointed an executive from larger rival Inditex as its new CEO.

title: FX  GLOBAL CALL: Our Take on the Day's Big  FX  News
text:
The FX Global Call covers the main talking points from a news meeting involving DJ FX Trader editors in New York, London and Singapore, as well as other FX hot spots when warranted.


 
    By Michael Casey

1. Japanese authorities are finally getting their way. Dollar/yen got above Y80 for the first time in three-and-a-half months during Tokyo trading as speculation continued to mount over the prospect of action to weaken the Japanese currency to combat a softening economy. Yet one factor in that gain was a somewhat flimsy report in a Japanese newspaper, which claimed that the Bank of Japan was planning on increasing its asset purchases by a whopping Y20 trillion at its next meeting. The report was later widely denied by Japanese officials and the dollar later dipped below Y80 again. But given their persistent efforts to talk down the yen, there must be some relief inside the Ministry of Finance that dollar has at least briefly been quoted with an 80 handle again.

2. The People's Bank of China again injected funds into the money market in what has been its chosen method of adding monetary stimulus for some weeks. But analysts are expecting the market to show a net drain on liquidity by the end of the week as banks' prior borrowings from the PBOC will mature. With QE3 having sent foreign inflows back into the region and some indicators suggesting that China's slowdown may have bottomed, there mightn't be much more stimulus coming from the central bank. Some hopeful souls are still betting that it will cut banks' reserve requirement ratios, but there could be too much flux in the political process right now for that to happen, with the leadership transition still uncompleted.

3. In a mark of how QE3 is having this effect on the region, the Hong Kong Monetary Authorityintervened for the second time in recent days to defend the Hong Kong dollar's peg to the dollar. The inflows have pushed the local currency to the top end of its trading band, which compels the HKMA to step in. Under the currency board arrangement, these interventions amount to naked injections of local currency liquidity into the local banking system and have the effect of ensuring that local interest rates stay very close to zero. In recent years that has spurred periods of intense property price appreciation as well as consumer inflation and so has occasionally stirred debate over the prospect of Hong Kong abandoning the peg. But that would do such profound damage to Hong Kong's peg-dependent financial system that very few people foresee this coming anytime soon. In the meantime, expect routine HKMA interventions.

4. This time it was Reserve Bank of Australia board member Heather Ridout's turn to warn that the Australian economy is slowing and that the Australian dollar must fall. Coming on the back of comments to us Monday from her colleague Jillian Broadbent, Ms. Ridout's comments have reinforced the view that the RBA is gearing up for another rate cut.

5. Moody's downgraded the debt of five Spanish regions, which put the euro under a modicum of pressure. But with Prime Minister Mariano Rajoy widely expected to ask for an EU bailout, which would trigger bond-buying by the ECB, currency markets are mostly stuck in a holding pattern.

6. It's also quiet in the Americas today. The Bank of Canada will start and finish its policy meeting Tuesday and is not expected to make any change to its 1% benchmark rate. The Fed starts the first of a two-day meeting in which most economists similarly do not expect it to do anything [largely because it only just recently embarked on its game-shifting third round of quantitative easing.] The Treasury sells $35 billion in two-year notes and the Richmond Fed releases its manufacturing survey results.

title: Asian Shares Mostly Lower; Utility Plays Struggle In Tokyo
text:
Asia stocks traded in a downbeat fashion Tuesday as dividend worries weighed on Japanese utility firms while concerns over lackluster third-quarter earnings dragged on shares in Shanghai.

Japan's Nikkei put in a flat performance, while the Shanghai Composite Index lost 0.9% and South Korea's Kospi declined 0.8%.

Australia's S&P/ASX 200 index managed to gain 0.1%, and Singapore's Straits Times Index was up 0.2%. Markets were closed for a holiday in Hong Kong, which made new headlines on the foreign-exchange front.

The Hong Kong Monetary Authorityintervened in the currency markets for a second time in less than a week on Tuesday, stepping in to sell the Hong Kong dollar in an attempt to halt appreciation of the currency after it traded near the lower channel of its trading band against the U.S. dollar

The authority sold $3.914 billion Hong Kong dollars ($505 million), on the heels of having sold last Friday HK$4.67 billion during New York trading, its first intervention since 2009.

Most Asian markets have gained so far this month, gains that have been made against emerging Asian economies that "are not really booming but [are] still quite robust," said Lucinda Chan. division director at Macquarie Private Wealth.

In addition, U.S. earnings results out in recent days "have been quite reasonable," she said, while the U.S. economy has shown some signs of improvement.

The third and final debate between President Barack Obama and Republican challenger Mitt Romney took place during Asian morning trade. U.S. stock futures edged lower after the debate wrapped up, then deepened further.

Both contenders commented on China, with Obama saying he will insist that Beijing play by the same rules as everyone else. Romney echoed those comments and reiterated his pledge to immediately label China a currency manipulator should he be elected.

"Coming into tonight's debate, President Obama retained a small structural advantage, and I suspect that he will retain that advantage after this debate," said Nomura economist Lewis Alexander in a note.

Dividend concerns weighed on the Japanese utility sector, as Kansai Electric Power Co. fell 13% after a Nikkei report that the electricity supplier won't pay a dividend at the end of the fiscal year. This would be its first dividend omission in 61 years. Kansai Electric's rivals also traded weak, with shares of Chubu Electric Power Co. shedding 9.9% and Tokyo Electric Power Co. falling 1.5%.

Energy-sector firms likewise declined in Tokyo, with JX Holdings Inc. down 1.6% and Japan Petroleum Exploration Co. down 1%. The pullback came after a 1.5% drop for crude-oil futures in New York on Monday.

In the currency market, the U.S. dollar briefly traded over 80 Japanese yen for the first time since early July, up from Y79.91 on Monday, before falling back to Y79.77 as immediate central bank-easing hopes faded.

The euro reached its highest point against the yen since May but then also retreated. Despite the yen's rebound, the dollar was still at relatively elevated levels against the Japanese currency, and some exporters held their gains in Tokyo on Tuesday, with Casio Computer Co. trading up 2.8%, Nikon Corp. adding 1.6% and Panasonic Corp. nudging ahead by 0.6%.

Meanwhile, shares of Fuji Heavy Industries, maker of Subaru brand vehicles, gained 3.8% after raising its net profit view to Y40 billion from a prior estimate of Y23 billion.

In South Korea, steel makers were adding pressure to the market, with Posco, the world's fourth-largest producer, trading 2.1% lower ahead of its earnings report due late Tuesday.

Standard & Poor's downgraded its long-term-debt rating on Posco to BBB+ from A- late Monday, saying that the firm will struggle to secure financing and that its operational performance will likely be weaker than previously expected. Among its rivals, Hyundai Steel Co. declined 1.7% while Dongbu Steel Ltd. eased 0.1%.

Mainland-listed Chinese commodity firms were weak, with Aluminum Corp. of China trading down 1% in Shanghai. Mainland steel makers were also lower amid expected sluggish earnings and what's believed to be government plans for a forced consolidation of the sector. Shares of Angang Steel Co. fell 1.4% as Baoshan Iron & Steel retreated 0.2%.

Air China Ltd. dropped 1% after abandoning a plan to raise funds in a private placement with China National Aviation Holding Co., its state-owned parent. Tuesday's session marked the first for the Beijing-based carrier since its shares were suspended earlier in October.

In Australia, commodity extractors underpinned gains for Sydney stocks, with Oz Minerals Ltd. up 1.9% after saying that it's on track to meet its fiscal-year production targets for copper and gold. Also in the sector, Fortescue Metals Group Ltd. advanced 1.7% while Rio Tinto Ltd. rose 0.1%.

title: HEARD ON THE STREET: Hong Kong's Not off the Peg
text:
Hong Kong's U.S. dollar peg is under threat again. It will surely withstand the challenge for a long while yet.

The peg, in place since 1983, was pushed to its limit last week. Friday, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, the de facto central bank, intervened to keep the currency from rising above its permitted band, the first such action in nearly three years.

The problem is that loose monetary policies around the world, as well as improving market sentiment toward China, have sent capital flowing into Hong Kong.

By tying its currency to the U.S. dollar, Hong Kong gives up the ability to conduct its own monetary policy. The peg means Hong Kong mirrors the ultra-low interest rates of the U.S. and risks high inflation and asset bubbles, particularly in the volatile property market. Earlier this year, no less an authority than Joseph Yam, the former manager of the HKMA, said that Hong Kong should consider alternatives such as Singapore's system of setting the exchange rate against a basket of currencies.

But any change to the peg risks substantial disruption, especially at a time when global markets are still uncertain. The peg underpins the entire Hong Kong financial system. The case for a switch would have to be overwhelming--and it is not. Comparing inflation rates in Hong Kong and Singapore, the evidence for one currency system over the other is not clear-cut. For instance, over the past 15 years, Hong Kong's inflation rate has been more volatile than Singapore's but it has also been much lower too, on average. The property markets in Singapore and Hong Kong are prone to big fluctuations, and authorities in both cities are fretting over soaring prices.

The peg must surely go eventually. Linking Hong Kong's currency to the yuan is a real possibility--though only once the Chinese unit becomes a fully viable international currency, and that could be some way off. For now, there is too much downside for the monetary authorities to give the go-ahead to such a major change. Hong Kong's dollar peg is under pressure. But it is not likely to buckle in the foreseeable future.

title: WSJ BLOG/Korea Real Time: South Korea: On  FX , We're Not Hong Kong
text:
(This story has been posted on The Wall Street Journal Online's Korea Real Time Report blog at http://blogs.wsj.com/korearealtime .)

By Kwanwoo Jun

South Korea is shrugging off speculation that it might intervene to slow recent gains in the won after Hong Kong's central bank stepped in to damp its currency's rise.

The won has risen more than 4% against the U.S. dollar this year, hitting a 13-month high last Friday after seven straight days of gains.

The concern for Seoul is that the strong won is a weight on local exporters. Most Korean newspapers last week quoted traders and analysts who said they were closely watching whether authorities would step into the market as the exchange rate approached the psychologically important level of 1,100 won per dollar. Some speculated the government might move to tighten existing curbs on capital flows.

Recent stimulus measures by the U.S. Federal Reserve Board and the European Central Bank have led money managers to pump more liquidity into emerging markets, including South Korea and Hong Kong in Asia.

In response, some central banks in the region have sought to stop their currencies from strengthening further, to help keep their exports competitively priced.

The Hong Kong Monetary Authority on Saturday said it had bought US$603 million to prevent the Hong Kong dollar from rising too much. The Bank of Japan has recently threatened to slow the yen's appreciation.

So far South Korean authorities have not acted visibly to curb the won's rally, but some traders suspect they've intervened stealthily through their agent banks or by mobilizing state-linked corporations to invest in money markets.

After hitting a high of 1,103.30 on Friday, the dollar traded in a band of 1,103-1,106 on Monday.

Asked Friday if he was concerned about the won's recent rise, Finance Minister Bahk Jae-wan gave an oblique response.

"I'm not supposed to comment on the pace of the won's rise," Mr. Bahk told reporters on the sidelines of a conference.

But he added: "You may want to look at the average base exchange rate, on which the budget was drawn up a year ago."

Ministry officials later confirmed the budgeted rate for 2012 was 1,070 won per dollar -- still above the current level. It may be a leap to assume that 's a level Seoul wants to defend, but it's clear Mr. Bahk keeps it in mind.

For next year's budget, the Finance Ministry has set the average base exchange rate at 1,130. Ministry officials cautioned that rate is relevant for dollar-based buying of military equipment or crude oil, for example, but doesn't necessarily bind monetary-policy makers.

"If the won keeps rising next year, it would be a big concern for Korean exporters, but not for us because we could pay less in U.S. dollars" for government purchases overseas, said one Finance Ministry official responsible for budget policy, who asked not to be named.

It added that the HKMA intervening "may foretell a rally of other asset classes, similar to the situation after the global financial crisis stabilized."

Base metals on the London Metal Exchange closed lower amid quiet trading conditions and a gloomy start to the week for investor risk sentiment.

FOREX: 

The dollar jumped Monday to its highest level against the yen in over three months, after weak Japanese trade data raised expectations for further Bank of Japan easing.

The dollar traded up to Y79.97, its strongest level against the yen since July 12. It ended the day at Y79.95, up from Y79.32 late Friday.

Japan posted a wider-than-expected $7.2 billion deficit in September, its third consecutive trade deficit. Japan's territorial dispute with China over islands in the East China Sea took its toll on the domestic economy as exports to China dropped 14.1% in September from a year earlier.

The Bank of Japan also downgraded its economic outlook for eight of Japan's nine regions in October, noting in its quarterly report that the economic recovery has "paused or moderated" in these regions.

"With the situation getting worse and worse in Japan and the BoJ already reducing forecasts, it'd be surprising for the BoJ not to ease," said Brian Kim, currency strategist at RBS in Stamford, Conn. "People are expecting some form of easing, but the question is how much."

The dollar has already appreciated 2.6% against the yen this month on expectations the BoJ will ramp up the size of its asset-purchase program, which was increased by Y10 trillion at the bank's last meeting in September.

The euro also rose to a 5 1/2-month high against the yen of Y104.46, before ending the session at Y104.40 from Y103.26.

Meanwhile, the euro edged higher against the dollar after German Prime Minister Angela Merkel told the Wall Street Journal that Germany is likely to support extending the deadline for Greece to meet its fiscal austerity targets. Greece remains locked in negotiations with international creditors over whether it should receive the next tranche of its bailout loan.

The euro last traded at $1.3061, up from $1.3023 late Friday.

The Australian dollar dipped against the greenback to $1.0322 from $1.0332.

On Tuesday, the Federal Reserve begins its scheduled two-day policy meeting, its first since announcing a new round of quantitative easing in September. While Fed statements are generally market-moving events, "this week's meeting should be less dramatic and less of an issue for markets since most of the fireworks from the Fed came last month," said Robert Lynch, head of G10 foreign-exchange strategy at HSBC in New York.

Without fresh economic data to guide trading, Treasury investors focused on preparing for the upcoming auctions, which kick off with a $35 billion two-year notes sale Tuesday. That is followed by a $35 billion five-year offering Wednesday and $29 billion seven-year sale Thursday.

Bond analysts broadly expect these auctions to be greeted with decent interest given the Federal Reserve's efforts to keep borrowing rates suppressed in its bid to stimulate the economy. That ultra-accommodative policy should keep Treasurys in constant demand, even amid recent signs that the U.S. economy is improving and as tensions surrounding Europe's debt crisis abate, marking an easing of two factors that have fueled relentless appetite for safe-haven Treasurys over the past year. title: WSJ(10/22) Hong Kong Takes Action To Weaken Its Dollar
text:
(From THE WALL STREET JOURNAL) 
   By Fiona Law 

HONG KONG -- After weeks of capital inflows from abroad that have pushed up the value of the Hong Kong dollar to the top of its trading band, the city's de facto central bank intervened on Friday to weaken the local currency for the first time in nearly three years.

The U.S. Federal Reserve's latest round of stimulus measures and the European Central Bank's recent pledge to buy sovereign bonds has restored global investor confidence and led money managers to buy a wide range of assets around the world, including in Hong Kong.

The influx of money has pushed up the Hang Seng Index -- the benchmark of local shares that is closely tied to the fortunes of China -- to a six-month high, making it one of Asia's best performers in 2012.

The Hong Kong Monetary Authority sold 4.67 billion Hong Kong dollars (US$602.6 million) in the foreign-exchange market on Friday during New York trading as the U.S. dollar hit HK$7.7500, the upper limit of where the Hong Kong dollar is allowed to trade against the greenback.

The move on Friday was small and not surprising to traders, given that the currency has been trading around HK$7.76 for weeks. The HKMA undertakes to buy or sell the local unit whenever it touches either side of the band that ranges from HK$7.75 to HK$7.85.

Still, the reason for this intervention -- improved global risk appetite -- was different from the last time Hong Kong stepped into the foreign-exchange market, during the height of the financial crisis. From October 2008 to December 2009, the HKMA repeatedly intervened to tame the Hong Kong dollar, as the dollar-pegged local currency was seen as a haven asset amid global market turmoil.

title: WSJ UPDATE: HKMA Moves to Weaken  Currency  for First Time in Three Years
text:
HONG KONG--After weeks of capital inflows from abroad that have pushed up the value of the Hong Kong dollar to the top of its trading band, the city's de facto central bank was forced to intervene Friday and weaken the local currency for the first time in nearly three years.

The Federal Reserve's latest round of stimulus measures and the European Central Bank's recent pledge to buy sovereign bonds has restored global investor confidence and led money managers to buy a wide range of assets around the world.

The influx of money has also pushed up the Hang Seng Index--the benchmark of local shares that's closely tied to the fortunes of China--to a six-month high, making it one of Asia's best performers in 2012.

The Hong Kong Monetary Authority sold 4.67 billion Hong Kong dollars (US$603 million) in the foreign-exchange market on Friday during New York trading as the U.S. dollar hit HK$7.7500, the upper limit of where the Hong Kong dollar is allowed to trade against the greenback.

The move on Friday was small and well expected by traders given the currency has been trading around HK$7.76 for weeks. The HKMA undertakes to buy or sell the local unit whenever it touches either side of the band that ranges from HK$7.75 to HK$7.85.

Still, this intervention was different from the last time Hong Kong stepped into the foreign-exchange market during the height of the financial crisis. From October 2008 to December 2009, the HKMA repeatedly intervened to tame the Hong Kong dollar, as the tightly controlled dollar-pegged local currency was seen as a safe-haven asset amid global market turmoil.

An HKMA spokeswoman, who declined to be named, said Saturday there had been robust demand for the local currency recently, driven by a stabilized European market and a weak greenback.

Hong Kong's intervention this time around also comes as other central banks in region also seek to stop their currencies from strengthening further to help keep their exports competitively priced. The Bank of Japan recently threatened to intervene in the currency markets to slow the yen's appreciation while the Bank of Korea is suspected of curbing the won's rally.

The Hong Kong dollar is also partly seen as a proxy for China's yuan, also called the renminbi, which is trading near a 19-year high against the U.S. dollar, but isn't fully convertible so difficult for foreign investors to buy.

"Capital inflow to Asian currencies could continue, at least, through the end of this year, should the greenback remain weak ahead of the U.S. presidential election in November. The Hong Kong dollar will be one of the currencies to remain bolstered, as it's more liquid, and the renminbi is strengthening," said Woody Chan, treasurer of Citic Bank Corp.'s Hong Kong unit. "Further invention from the HKMA could be seen in the near future."

Hong Kong's linked exchange-rate regime was established in 1983, partly to defend the currency from panic selling amid escalating concerns on the former British colony's future, ahead of its handover to China in 1997.

The peg bolts Hong Kong's monetary policy to that of the U.S., meaning the city has had ultralow interest rates recently, spurring rising property prices because money is cheap to borrow for real estate purchases.

That's led to calls for a review of the system, including from the former head of the HKMA, Joseph Yam, who said in a research paper earlier this year that it was time for the government to look at options including a switch to pegging to a basket of currencies or a complete float.

"The re-appreciation in the renminbi has given the Hong Kong dollar a further boost and led to some speculation on the dollar peg regime," said Credit Agricole senior strategist Frances Cheung.

The HKMA says it has no intention to change the linked exchange rate system, citing it as an anchor of Hong Kong's financial and economic stability.

title: India  Central Bank  Deputy Gov: May  Intervene  More In  Currency  Markets If See 'Strong One Way Risk' For Rupee
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--India's central bank may intervene further in the currency markets if it sees a "strong one way risk" for the Indian rupee, Deputy Gov. Subir Gokarn said Friday.

"We see the return of some instability in the currency," Gokarn told Dow Jones Newswires in an interview on the sidelines of the Credit Suisse Asian Investor Conference.

"We don't target a range (for the rupee), but when there's a risk of moving strongly one way, that's something we want to avoid," he said.

Gokarn's comments come as the rupee is trading at an over two-month low to the dollar. The rupee slipped to a record low against the dollar last year following mounting global uncertainty and slowing growth in Asia's third-largest economy, which has been impacted by an extended period of inflation.

The senior Reserve Bank of India official said the nation's currency was relatively stable between January and February. In the last few days, however, he said there has been some instability in the rupee.

On Thursday, RBI Adviser Ashima Goyal said the central bank should continue to intervene in the market to ensure that the rupee doesn't weaken significantly beyond its fair value of INR50 to the dollar.

Currency fluctuations affect software companies to a large extent as they book most of their revenue in dollars, but settle the majority of their costs in rupees.

On the inflation front, Gokarn said he has seen some moderation in inflation, while domestic demand remains strong. However, he warned that the recent sharp rise in oil prices will pose new risks to price pressures.

Earlier Friday, Gokarn said the central bank is moving toward looser monetary policy, though the timing for easing will depend on the state of the economy.

At its rate-setting meeting on March 15, the central bank left its key lending rate unchanged, saying risks to inflation have increased due to a recent spurt in crude oil prices, a wide fiscal deficit and a weakening rupee.

-By Chester Yung, Dow Jones Newswires; 852-2832 2331; chester.yung@dowjones.com [ 03-23-12 0309ET ]

title: Paul Tudor Jones: US Can  Intervene  In HKD To Encourage Yuan Rise
text:
Renowned hedge fund manager Paul Tudor Jones said an "easy policy tool" for the U.S. to push for a correction in the undervalued Chinese currency would be to intervene in the Hong Kong dollar.

The heart of Jones's argument, made in a Feb. 14 research paper sent by the founder of Tudor Investment Corp. to investors, is that the Hong Kong dollar and the Chinese currency, the renminbi, are now closely intertwined. Pushing up the value of the Hong Kong dollar would put pressure on Chinese authorities to increase the value of the renminbi, also known as the yuan. By intervening in the Hong Kong dollar, the U.S. could "make a statement that would be highly symbolic if only slightly impactful."

Jones didn't address the political consequences that might result from such a dramatic policy.

Jones said it would be fairly inexpensive to push up the value of the Hong Kong dollar. "Countervailing intervention in the Hong Kong dollar may not require a 10% premium to spot" exchange rate, he said. "Inevitably, the Hong Kong dollar is going to have to adjust to an appreciating renminbi and intervening in this market is tantamount to intervening in the RMB itself."

Unlike other currencies, Hong Kong dollars trade in a narrow band around the rate of HK$7.8 to one U.S. dollar. If the exchange rate steers towards either end of the trading range, the city's de facto central bank, backed by its U.S. dollar reserves, steps in to intervene.

Jones said there is a sizeable pool of yuan in the city of Hong Kong. Citing a recent estimate by the head of the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, he said there is approximately $50 billion in yuan circulating in Hong Kong and the number is growing by $10 billion per month.

Jones, a heavyweight fund manager and one of the most respected macro traders, added that the U.S. could also launch targeted intervention in other non-Japanese Asian currencies to help reduce the U.S.'s growing trade imbalances.

In the paper, he argued the Chinese currency was highly undervalued. On a productivity-adjusted purchasing power parity basis, he said the renminbi was between 35% and 72% cheaper against the U.S. dollar in 2010 than in 1993.

As an alternate to the intervention, Jones said the U.S. could state its desire for the Chinese currency to appreciate at least 10% a year in nominal terms for the next three years. The U.S. could during that time profit from investing in renminbi.

"It would be a good investment and could continue until RMB was at an appropriate level," he said.

Calling China's monetary policy one that is "drawn from textbooks that are centuries old," Jones said it is in China's and Asian nations' interest to let their currencies rise.

"The recent popular uprisings in countries across North Africa are instructive because they are partly triggered by food price inflation," he wrote. "This may mark a turning point in how Asia views the continued merits of currency suppression."

Hedge funds have a complex history in the region, dating back to the Asian financial crisis of the late 1990s. At the time, many politicians blamed hedge funds for making speculative trades on the rise and fall of the region's currencies and contributing to their collapse.

Then-Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad singled out billionaire investor George Soros in particular and famously called him a "moron."

-By Amy Or, Dow Jones Newswires; 212 416 3142; amy.or@dowjones.com [ 02-25-11 1726ET ]

title: FX  ASIA: HK IPO Fever Boosts Local Rates, HK Dollar
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Hong Kong dollar is poised to rise in coming weeks toward the top end of its parity band against the U.S. dollar, driven by the latest rally in stocks and a jump in local rates on the territory's recent IPO fever.

That means the Hong Kong Monetary Authority may soon be forced to join Japan and other Asian countries in their efforts to control surging currencies.

A continued slide in U.S. rates is the main reason for Hong Kong dollar strength. As the U.S. Federal Reserve hints that it will keep ultra-low rates in place until 2011 or even longer, interbank dollar rates used by commercial banks, or Libor, have tumbled to five-month lows.

That diminishes the appeal of carry trades where investors borrow in Hong Kong dollars -- normally at cheaper rates due to the territory's status as a banking hub -- and then buy U.S. dollars, capturing the spread between the two. A narrowing spread between local and Libor means such trades, traditionally a key source of greenback demand in the territory, are unlikely to be attractive anytime soon.

The spread rose to 0.3 percentage points in late May but after narrowing for weeks it turned negative Monday as the benchmark 3-month Hibor rate for Hong Kong banks rose to 0.32%, while the equivalent 3-month Libor rate dropped to 0.29%.

Hong Kong traders say a flurry of initial public offerings expected in the territory in the next three weeks is behind the uptick in Hibor, which some expect may reach 0.4%. Meanwhile, Libor may fall further if the U.S. Fed expands its quantitative-easing policy as some expect.

Traders say Hibor rates should drop back below Libor once demand for Hong Kong dollars flags, as happened after an earlier IPO-driven Hibor spike in late June-early July. But Fed policies weighing on Libor rates mean spreads are likely to remain minuscule, discouraging carry trades in the US dollar and keeping the Hong Kong unit strongly supported.

"We are seeing central banks in the developed world flooding markets with liquidity, including the Fed," said Erik Lueth, a Hong Kong-based economist with Royal Bank of Scotland. "All that liquidity has to go somewhere, and it's going to Asia, places like Hong Kong."

RBS is forecasting that the U.S. dollar may fall to $7.7500 by the end of this month and stay there through year-end, from $7.7630 last. That means the Hong Kong Monetary Authority would likely intervene in forex markets by selling additional Hong Kong dollars, Lueth added, something it hasn't done since December 2009.

The HKMA, which keeps the U.S. dollar pegged between HK$7.7500-HK$7.8500, flooded the market with Hong Kong dollars in 2008 and 2009 as the local currency stayed near the low end of the parity band. That ended up feeding a property bubble in the territory -- and could well do so again.

title: =DJ UPDATE: China, Singapore Sign CNY150B  Currency  Swap Agreement
text:
(Adds details, background on currency swap; other moves to encourage wider use of the yuan) 


 
   By Aaron Back and David Roman 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

BEIJING (Dow Jones)--The People's Bank of China Friday signed a currency swap agreement with the Monetary Authority of Singapore worth CNY150 billion, or S$30 billion, the latest in a series of moves by China to promote wider global use of its currency.

The agreement, which was signed in Beijing, is effective for three years, during which both central banks will be able to exchange their currency from that of their counterpart.

The deal can also be extended beyond that period with the consent of both, the PBOC said in a statement.

Over the last two years, China has signed a series of similar deals with countries including Indonesia, Malaysia, South Korea, Brazil, Belarus and Argentina.

Analysts say these have little effective value beyond the symbolic, as the yuan is not freely traded in financial markets and isn't widely used in business with China. But, they note the removal of some restrictions in recent months and efforts to boost yuan transactions in Hong Kong show Beijing is looking to raise the yuan's global profile, even as it keeps tight controls on the currency.

Earlier this week, China signed a deal that allows more yuan-denominated investment products to be offered in Hong Kong, including insurance policies and wealth-management plans, and lifts restrictions on some account transfers and the opening of accounts for corporate clients.

The deal also keeps other restrictions in place, including a CNY20,000 ($2,950) cap on daily yuan purchases for individuals, and rules that allow mainland regulators to intervene in yuan transactions conducted in Hong Kong.

Analysts say the removal of these and other constraints, such as controls on cross-border flows, could add to already excessive liquidity and market bubbles in China, a key headache for Beijing policymakers.

-By Aaron Back and David Roman, Dow Jones Newswires; (8610) 8400-7701; aaron.back@dowjones.com

title: UPDATE:  FX  ASIA: Wider Use Of Yuan A Long-Term Prospect
text:
(Adds details on China-Singapore deal announced Friday.)

By David Roman

A Dow Jones Newswires Column

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Recent moves by China to encourage wider use of its currency overseas are unlikely to produce significant results for years due to major constraints on the use of the yuan, which remains hard to obtain outside the mainland.

This week, China signed an agreement with Singapore that allows the two countries' central banks to swap yuan for Singapore dollars, and another with Hong Kong removing some restrictions on yuan usage and circulation in Hong Kong. They're the latest moves in Beijing's campaign to boost use of the yuan as it seeks a more prominent international profile.

But those deals also showed that Chinese authorities are taking only baby steps for now and remain far from committed to the sort of radical changes needed to turn the yuan into a rival to the dollar. Such changes, such as allowing more freedom in cross-border flows and yuan usage for non-trade purposes, could add to already excessive liquidity and market bubbles in China, a key headache for Beijing policymakers, analysts say.

The Hong Kong agreement, the most wide-ranging, allows more yuan-denominated investment products to be offered in Hong Kong, including insurance policies and wealth-management plans, and lifts restrictions on some account transfers and the opening of accounts for corporate clients. But many restrictions remain in place despite lobbying from Hong Kong's financial industry.

Among these, there's a CNY20,000 (US$2,950) cap on daily yuan purchases for individuals, and rules that allow mainland regulators to intervene in yuan transactions conducted in Hong Kong.

In addition, China is still dragging its feet on other key issues like allowing cross-border yuan transactions for financial investments, and the development of a market for yuan forwards that would make it easier to hedge deals in yuan.

These pending reforms may be hard to implement, said Kelvin Lau, a Hong Kong-based economist with Standard Chartered, one of several banks that plan to offer structured investment products in Hong Kong paying interest in yuan.

"China doesn't allow yuan to be channeled onshore. It needs to create more channels, but they're concerned about the effect of inflows," Lau said. "We do expect future liberalization steps to be taken on a quarterly, semiannual or yearly basis... one step at a time."

China's cautious pace in pushing the yuan, even in Hong Kong, has meant that measures taken until now have had little impact. Six years after the territory's residents were allowed to start keeping yuan deposits they remain a footnote for the island's economy, accounting for just over 1% of total deposits, roughly unchanged from a year ago. The U.S. dollar accounts for close to 30% of deposits.

That doesn't bode well for similar efforts outside of China. Previous "internationalization" efforts opened up trade invoicing in yuan to exporters and importers in 20 mainland provinces and around the world, but the impact has been muted due to strict controls on yuan convertibility that analysts blame on Beijing's concerns about hot-money inflows.

These controls limit the usefulness of the swap announced Friday with Singapore, which comes after China's central bank signed similar deals with countries ranging from Brazil to Belarus. But these have had mostly symbolic value so far as the yuan is not freely traded in financial markets.

In addition, companies that want to conduct trade with China in yuan must operate through just a handful of authorized banks, all based in mainland China, except for the Bank of China (Hong Kong).

title: HK Exchange Fund may see loss on market volatility-HKMA

HONG KONG, July 22 (Reuters) - The Hong Kong Monetary Authority's Exchange Fund may suffer some paper losses because of volatility in certain asset classes, the HKMA said on Thursday, amid a weak performance by the territory's stock market.

Europe's moves to implement fiscal austerity measures should also address investor concerns about the long-term financial health of European nations, HKMA Deputy Chief Executive Eddie Yue said in a statement.

"Surely we hope that investor sentiment could improve and the investment environment could become more accommodating in the second half of the year," Yue said. "But current uncertainties in the market are such that it is hard to take this optimistic view."

title: UPDATE: HKMA: Yuan Flexibility Doesn't Affect HK Dollar/US Dollar Peg
text:
(Adds trader, strategist's comments on outlook for the HK dollar, former HKMA chief's comment on yuan.)

By Chester Yung

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--The Chinese central bank's announcement over the weekend that it will increase the flexibility of its exchange-rate regime hasn't affected the Hong Kong dollar's peg to the U.S. dollar, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority said Monday, adding a stronger yuan will have a "modest" impact on the city's inflation.

Analysts said the move by the People's Bank of China will place pressure on the U.S. dollar/Hong Kong dollar pair this week but Hong Kong's de facto central bank isn't likely to intervene to cap the Hong Kong dollar's rise.

The Hong Kong dollar was up sharply against the U.S. dollar Monday morning after the PBOC said over the weekend it would increase the flexibility of its exchange-rate regime, implying it would allow the yuan to resume its gradual rise against the U.S. dollar. The freely convertible Hong Kong currency is often traded as proxy for the yuan.

At 0820 GMT, the U.S. dollar was at HK$7.721, down from HK$7.7856 late Friday.

However, a HKMA spokesman said: "We have no plan to alter the USD/HKD peg as the currency regime has been effective."

Under Hong Kong's currency board system, the Hong Kong dollar is allowed to trade between HK$7.75 and HK$7.85 to the U.S. dollar.

"I don't expect the U.S. dollar to fall back to the lower limit of the trading band in the near term as some market players are eager to buy back the U.S. dollar for bargain-hunting near the HK$7.76 level. There is no need for the HKMA to step in (to buy back the U.S. dollar) now," said a senior trader at a U.K. bank.

Patrick Bennett, chief strategist at Standard Bank, said: "The move in the U.S. dollar/Hong Kong dollar pair reflects the general move in U.S. dollar/Asia currencies, of course led by the PBOC announcement."

He said as long as the U.S. dollar continues to weaken against other Asian currencies and investors are in risk-seeking mode, the U.S. dollar will remain under modest pressure against the Hong Kong dollar.

Both the Singapore dollar and South Korean won rose sharply against the U.S. dollar Monday due to expectations that the yuan will appreciate.

Former HKMA head Joseph Yam said: "The Renminbi (yuan) exchange rate against a basket of currencies will resume a long-term appreciation trend."

But Yam said he expects short-term volatility in the yuan's exchange rate against the U.S. dollar due to the uncertainty in the global foreign exchange and financial markets.

-By Chester Yung, Dow Jones Newswires; 852-2832 2331; chester.yung@dowjones.com [ 21-06-10 0840GMT ]
