title: WSJA(2/23) Hong Kong Property Market Reheats
text:
WSJA(2/23) Hong Kong Property Market Reheats

(From THE WALL STREET JOURNAL ASIA)

HONG KONG -- Strong results in a Hong Kong government land auction are the latest sign that the city's real-estate market is surging after a brief lull, as government officials here and elsewhere in the region grapple with how to cool off overheating property prices.

On Monday, blue-chip developer Sun Hung Kai Properties Ltd. agreed to pay 3.37 billion Hong Kong dollars (US$434 million) for a 130,000-square-foot site in the suburbs of Hong Kong. That price, reached after an intense bidding session, was above the average US$362 million forecast of six surveyors and analysts polled earlier by Dow Jones Newswires, and was 69% above the reserve price of US$258 million.

The big purchase came just after Sun Hung Kai, Hong Kong's biggest developer with a market capitalization of about US$34 billion, sold 900 apartment units in a major new residential complex over the weekend for a total of US$541 million. The units, ranging from about 400 to 1,400 square feet, sold for about US$700 per square foot, a steep premium to other apartments in the area. That indicates the mass-residential market could be vulnerable to the speculation that led to a jump of about 50% in Hong Kong's luxury-apartment prices last year.

Around the region, easy credit and ample liquidity is fueling fears that real-estate prices may be rising to irrational levels.

In China, where by some official measures home prices have risen as much as 25% in the past year and land values have doubled, officials are keen to tamp down the market. Beginning Thursday, the People's Bank of China will require banks to hold more cash in a bid to clamp down on excessive lending.

Last week, Singapore's government made an attempt to 'temper sentiments and pre-empt a property bubble' by imposing a tax on those who flip properties within a year of purchasing them while capping residential mortgages to 80% of a home's value, from 90%.

In spite of cooling measures instituted last autumn, Singapore's government said 'there are recent signs that [the property market] is starting to heat up again,' noting that the number of primary-home sales in the city-state last month was triple that of the month before, accompanied with a sharp price increase that outpaced previous rebounds.

'There is a risk that the market could overheat in the next few months, fueled by low global interest rates and positive sentiments associated with the economic recovery,' the government said, pledging to take further action if required later. Singapore also said it would boost housing supply.

Unlike China and Singapore, however, Hong Kong has little control over interest rates because its currency board system, which pegs the local currency to the U.S. dollar, forces it to import U.S. monetary policy.

Instead, Nicole Wong, a property analyst with CLSA Asia-Pacific Markets, says there is little Hong Kong's government can do about what she describes as a full-blown housing bubble in the city's mass-residential markets.

'Hong Kong property buyers have been in a prolonged low-interest-rate environment, and now they're behaving like drunken drivers on the road -- they don't think about consequences,' Ms. Wong says, estimating that prices have increased 5% this year. While speculative activity has been subdued, she argues the public is 'overstretching' itself, convinced that 'prices will go up forever.'

The Hong Kong government has tried its best to tamp down overexuberance in recent months. Chief Executive Donald Tsang has said the government would monitor property prices and fine-tune its land-sales policies if necessary. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority also told banks late last year to raise the standard down-payment ratio on luxury properties to 40% from 30%.

Keith Yeung, a property analyst at Mirae Asset Research, expects Hong Kong's financial secretary to announce a policy response Wednesday, when he delivers Hong Kong's annual budget. 'The government is now under tremendous pressure to intervene in the Hong Kong residential market,' Mr. Yeung says.

Not everyone is worried about home prices. Kelvin Lau, a Hong Kong-based economist with Standard Chartered Bank, says he doesn't see a bubble, pointing to low levels of speculation and an official mortgage-debt-servicing ratio of 36.4% as of last autumn, lower than Hong Kong's 20-year average of 52.6%.

Alva To, head of consultancy for brokers DTZ in Hong Kong, says the participation of a broad range of developers in Monday's auction, and the 'very expensive' auction sale price, were signs that prices could continue to spiral upward. Mr. To isn't worried yet, however: 'The public can still afford this, because interest rates have been as low as 0.7%.'

-By Jonathan Cheng and Aries Poon

But the Hong Kong dollar is likely to gain less than most other Asian currencies in the near term because of Hong Kong's passive foreign-exchange intervention policy and strong local corporate demand for the U.S. dollar at the beginning of a year, traders said.

In late Asian trade, the U.S. dollar was at HK$7.7549, down from HK$7.7552 late Monday. The U.S. unit was fixed at HK$7.7547 earlier Tuesday.

"The Hong Kong dollar will likely be less volatile relative to other Asian currencies, such as the Singapore and Taiwan dollar, because the latest inflows to Asia seem to be drawn to markets where central banks actively intervene," a senior trader at a local bank said.

Under Hong Kong's currency board system, the Hong Kong dollar is allowed to trade between HK$7.75 and HK$7.85 to the U.S. dollar. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority intervenes only when the U.S. dollar trades outside the range.

The U.S. dollar will likely find strong support at HK$7.7530 this week, the trader said.

title: FX  ASIA: Asian Reserves Down In Dec, Hit By Stronger Dollar
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Asia's foreign exchange reserves fell for the first time in 10 months, hit by a strong rise in the U.S. dollar that lowered the value of non-greenback holdings, but may resume their climb in coming months.

According to calculations by Dow Jones Newswires, reserves held by 11 key Asian central banks, excluding China's, stood at US$2.753 trillion at the end of December, down from US$2.783 trillion at the end of November, a fall of 1.1% on the month.

The dollar rallied in December against the main alternative reserve currencies, which together account for around 30% of central bank reserves. The dollar rose 7.6% against the Japanese yen, 4.8% against the euro and 1.8% against the British pound in December.

But the dollar was flat or lower for the month against key Asian currencies, a trend that analysts expect to continue this year, given strong economic growth and foreign inflows anticipated across East and South Asia. Many Asian currencies remain shy of the highs they hit against the dollar just before the financial crisis exploded in mid-2008, which should keep reserves across the region on the upswing in the next few months.

China, which releases its data on a quarterly basis, is expected to provide a reserves update later this week. Last week, state-run Shanghai Securities News said reserves at the end of 2009 may have exceeded US$2.4 trillion, citing an unnamed source at a state-run big bank. That compares with US$2.273 at the end of September.

Analysts say the expected continuation of strong inflows to Asia will be the main reason for increases in Asian reserves this year.

Sebastian Barbe, a foreign exchange strategist with Calyon, noted the inflows are a consequence of the region's persistent current account surpluses, which will continue to exert appreciation pressure on currencies. To respond to this, most Asian central banks - wary of how strong currencies affect local exporters - will keep a policy of intervening to buy dollars, Barbe added.

Even in December, as the dollar rose against the likes of the euro and yen, several Asian central banks, including in South Korea and Taiwan, were suspected of buying dollars in forex markets to slow the rise of their own currencies.

"The intervention story is part of the balance-of-payments story," Barbe said.

Still, any increase in reserves in 2010 is likely to be slower than last year's frantic pace. Excluding China, reserves were 14% higher in December from the year earlier, with whopping increases of 40% seen in Hong Kong, 33% in South Korea and 28% in Indonesia.

In some cases, a stronger dollar and weaker valuation of other currencies in central bank reserves should slow reserve accumulation considerably. That's especially the case in Hong Kong, where forex intervention accounted for most of the reserve increase last year but is expected to fall dramatically as the local dollar, which is pegged to the greenback, weakens on expectations of coming U.S. interest rate hikes.

title: MONEY TALKS: Hibor-Libor Spread To Make Life Easier For HKMA
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Hong Kong dollar's drop from very strong levels against the U.S. dollar reduces the pressure on the territory's long-standing currency peg and should make life easier for the Hong Kong Monetary Authority.

The slump in the Hong Kong currency to nine-month lows this week is very much a U.S. dollar story, and probably marks the end of a year of Hong Kong dollar strength. Supported by a growing view the Federal Reserve may start raising interest rates around midyear, the greenback could rise in coming months toward HK$7.8000, the midpoint of the HKMA's band for the currency pair, from HK$7.7566 now.

Higher policy rates in the U.S. imply an increase in interbank rates, used by commercial banks. This would encourage investors to borrow Hong Kong dollars and buy U.S. dollars, to capture the widening spread between Hong Kong's Hibor rates and U.S. dollar Libor rates.

The HKMA keeps the local currency pegged in its policy band against the U.S. dollar and moves in lockstep with the Fed on policy rates, but the Hibor-Libor spread fluctuates, widening when rates generally are rising because Hong Kong interbank rates rarely rise as fast as Libor. The benchmark three-month Hibor is usually 10 to 100 basis points below Libor, reflecting the low interbank risk in wealthy, bank-friendly Hong Kong.

The spread has been a fairly reliable indicator of Hong Kong dollar performance in recent years: the currency has at times been weak despite rallies in Hong Kong stocks and gained even as stocks fell back.

The spread narrowed to almost zero this year and stayed at 5 to 10 basis points most of the second half as the Fed vowed to keep rates extremely low for quite some time. The U.S. currency remained stuck at the bottom of the HKMA's band, with the de facto central bank selling over HK$640 billion to defend the peg since October last year.

The Fed Wednesday kept its key rate target at zero to 0.25% and repeated this will stay low for "an extended period," but was more upbeat about the economy, prompting speculation it's preparing the way for rate hikes. The Hibor-Libor spread has inched up to 14 basis points and looks set to widen further, boosting the greenback against the Hong Kong dollar.

Federal-fund futures now price a 36% chance of a Fed hike to 0.5% by June--twice the probability implied just two weeks ago. This shift should boost the three-month Hibor from its recent record low of 0.25%, and the pace of the rise is likely to dictate the greenback's rally against the Hong Kong dollar.

Libor rates are bottoming just as Hibors are falling on a large increase in Hong Kong dollar liquidity from the HKMA's massive interventions in recent months. Monetary base stands at HK$312.4 billion, 30 times higher than 18 months ago.

The Hibor-Libor spread will keep widening as long as this excess liquidity remains in the system. There's no incentive for Hong Kong banks to push interbank rates higher until the HKMA begins to mop up the extra cash.

title: UPDATE 2-HK "very concerned" about asset bubble risk
text:
* Hong Kong govt says no property bubble apparent yet

* No suggestion of further measures to control prices

* Echoes concerns of other emerging markets

* Industry executives see little threat of bubble so far (Adds details, industry quotes)

By Susan Fenton

HONG KONG, Dec 7 (Reuters) - Hong Kong's government is "very concerned" about the risk of an asset bubble developing although one is not apparent yet, Financial Secretary John Tsang said on Monday.

Tsang did not point to any potential measures to combat the city's main concern which is property prices, but his remarks reflect worries in many emerging markets over a flood of cash flowing into their economies seeking higher returns.

Both Brazil and Taiwan have imposed capital controls to try to limit the inflows and policymakers elsewhere are talking about potential measures they could take. [ID:nLJ437424]

"We are very concerned about the risk of an asset bubble," Tsang told legislators. "The risk is there but it is not very apparent."

In Hong Kong, residential property prices have jumped 30 percent this year and the luxury sector is up more than 40 percent after the city drew a record $73 billion in capital inflows between October 2008 and Nov. 13, 2009.

Tsang said the financial system was sound and the city could cope with capital inflows and outflows, but he echoed similar concerns voiced by Hong Kong Chief Executive Donald Tsang and central bank chief Norman Chan.

Hong Kong, like other economies in Asia, is watching warily for the formation of asset bubbles to avoid compromising nascent economic recovery.

The Hong Kong Monetary Authority, the central bank, recently reduced the maximum mortgage for luxury properties to 60 percent from 70 percent of the price in an effort to cool the market, and mortgage demand has eased from a few months ago.

But the HKMA is more tied than many central banks because the Hong Kong dollar's currency peg to the U.S. dollar means it has to adopt Federal Reserve monetary policy. U.S. rates have been held between zero and 0.25 percent since December.

The inflow of capital is putting the Hong Kong dollar under pressure and prompting the HKMA to intervene in markets to keep the currency within its tight trade band.

Some industry executives in Hong Kong said there was little threat of prices bubbles in the property sector because surges had been limited to certain sectors and particular regions.

"We cannot completely rule out that relatively severe bubbles are forming in some parts of Asia-Pacific," Leung Chun-ying, Asia-Pacific chairman of property agency DTZ, told a news conference.

"But in general, I think the Asia property market, including Hong Kong, doesn't have any problems of bubbles forming for now," he said.

A government economist told legislators that speculation in the property market was not too heated and that demand was mainly user-oriented, with 90 percent of transactions for mass-market property. Housing affordability meanwhile was above a 20-year average. (Additional reporting by Lee Chyen Yee; Editing by Chris Lewis and Neil Fullick)

HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--The Hong Kong dollar was steady near the upper limit of its trading band against the U.S. dollar Thursday, as further intervention in the market by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority continued to be offset by fund inflows.

Traders said the Hong Kong dollar is likely to hover around the current level for the rest of the year as inflows persist. They said they expect the U.S. dollar to stay in a tight range between HK$7.7500 and HK$7.7503 Friday.

In late Asian trade, the U.S. dollar was at HK$7.7501, steady from late Wednesday. The U.S. unit was fixed at HK$7.7501 earlier Thursday.

"Although we may be seeing some investor fatigue, as inflows have slowed a bit recently and the stock market rose less aggressively today, the flows are still considered strong and will probably keep the Hong Kong dollar strong," said a trader at a local bank.

The inflows prompted the city's de-facto central bank to sell HK$3.88 billion Thursday to defend the Hong Kong dollar's peg to the U.S. dollar. The intervention was triggered by the U.S. dollar hitting HK$7.7500, the strong side of the Hong Kong dollar's trading band.

Under Hong Kong's currency board system, the Hong Kong dollar is allowed to trade between HK$7.75 and HK$7.85 to the U.S. dollar.

Traders said Hong Kong's positive economic outlook will likely lure more funds to the city.

The International Monetary Fund said in a report Thursday that it expects Hong Kong's economy to continue to grow steadily, though the recovery remains fragile.

Goldman Sachs on Thursday raised its 2010 forecast for Hong Kong's gross domestic product growth to 5.8% from 5.0%.

The one-year U.S. dollar/Hong Kong dollar forward contract was quoted at a discount of 245 points to the spot rate, compared with a 247-point discount late Wednesday.

title: GLOBAL YIELD:Hong Kong Snaps Up Treasurys To Defend Dollar Peg
text:
NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--Hong Kong, the world's seventh-largest holder of foreign reserves, has become one of the biggest buyers of Treasury securities outside the U.S. this year as local officials stepped up efforts to defend the 26-year-old currency peg.

The interventions by Hong Kong, which is part of China but administered separately, reflects the challenge facing policy makers in many Asian economies: managing the influx of investments, fueled by cheap U.S. dollars, while at the same time preventing their local currencies from appreciating sharply and hurting their export industries, for many of these countries the key driver of growth.

Hong Kong's close links with China make it particularly attractive to foreign investors, but other export-driven Asian economies--from Indonesia to Thailand--have intervened to keep their domestic currencies from appreciating sharply.

The U.S. dollar's weakness has forced the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, or HKMA, to intervene since March, selling the Hong Kong dollar and buying the U.S. currency sometimes several times a day to maintain the peg at a rate of HK$7.8 to the U.S. dollar. The local dollar is allowed to trade between HK$7.75 and HK$7.85 to the U.S. dollar. The interventions have been aggressive: the HKMA sold HK$9.68 billion in the foreign exchange market Tuesday to defend the currency peg, after selling HK$2.33 billion Monday.

As a result, foreign currency reserves of Hong Kong have risen to $240.1 billion at the end of October from $182.5 billion at the end of last year, mostly held in U.S. dollars.

"All central banks will buy U.S. assets when they intervene," said Steven Major, global head of fixed-income research at HSBC Holdings Plc in London. That's to prevent the additional liquidity from exacerbating already rising asset prices.

The HKMA, Hong Kong's de facto central bank, bought $55 billion in U.S. Treasurys this year through the end of September, accounting for about 13.7% of net purchases by foreign investors and 23.8% of net buying by foreign central banks, according to data compiled by Dow Jones Newswires based on records from the Treasury Department.

In the same period, China, the largest foreign holder of U.S. Treasurys, purchased $71.5 billion in Treasurys and Japan, the second-largest holder, bought $125.5 billion.

More than 90% of Hong Kong's purchases this year was in Treasury bills, whose maturities are one year or less.

Parking cash in the most liquid part of the Treasury market gives the Hong Kong authorities more flexibility should capital suddenly flow out of the territory if sentiment on global economic growth turns sour, said Rachel Ziemba, an analyst in New York at Roubini Global Economics who closely monitors foreign central bank activities in the Treasurys market.

Along with demand from hedge funds, banks and mutual funds to improve their balance sheets ahead of the year end, buying by foreign central banks has helped keep Treasury yields at relatively low levels. That's kept funding costs down at a time when the U.S. government recently reported a budget deficit around $1.4 trillion in the fiscal year 2009 that ended in September.

Wednesday, as the U.S. dollar fell sharply amid expectations that U.S. interest rates will remain low even as the global economic recovery gathers pace, the Hong Kong dollar was trading around HK$7.7501 against its U.S. counterpart.

HKMA Chief Executive Norman Chan last week reiterated that the government has no plans to alter the Hong Kong dollar peg to the U.S. dollar, saying that it has helped to maintain currency stability.

(Min Zeng, a reporter on the Treasury desk, writes about global government bond markets for Dow Jones Newswires. He can be reached at 212-416-2229 or via email at: min.zeng@dowjones.com.)

 This followed a total HK$16.663 billion intervention by the HKMA during Hong Kong trading hours on Friday as the Hong Kong dollar repeatedly hit the top of its trading band at 7.7500 as funds continued to flow into the territory for initial public offerings in the stock market and amid some speculation that China could soon resume appreciation of its yuan <CNY=CFXS> currency.

 The Hong Kong dollar is pegged at 7.80 to the U.S. dollar but can trade between 7.75 and 7.85.

 Under the linked exchange rate mechanism, the HKMA is usually obliged to intervene in the market to keep the trading band intact if the currency hits 7.75 or 7.85.

title: MONEY MARKETS-Aussie swaps up as rate expectations build
text:
* Greater chance seen for more Australia rate increases

 * Hong Kong aggregate balance at record high

 * Dollar borrowing cost at new trough

 HONG KONG, Nov 13 (Reuters) - Australian swaps rose on Friday as investors grew increasing certain the central bank will raise interest rates at its Dec. 1 policy meeting after positive employment data supported the case for monetary tightening.

 The Reserve Bank of Australia is seen raising interest rates by 25 basis points to 3.75 percent as part of a policy tightening campaign expected to run through 2010. A Reuters poll showed 15 out of 18 respondents expect such a move. [ID:nSYD33220]

 On Thursday, data showed Australian employment rose 24,500 in October, a second month of surprisingly strong growth.

 One-year swap rates <AUDQM3AB1Y=> rose 3 basis points (bps) to 4.74 percent while the one-month overnight indexed swaps <AUD1MOIS=> rose 2 bps to 3.5825 percent.

 But the rates market has still not fully priced in a rate increase, preferring to wait for Tuesday's release of the central bank's minutes.

 It is still seeing only an 84 percent chance the central bank will tighten by 25 basis points <CSRBA=CSAU> next month, but that is higher than 68 percent at the start of the week.

 "The market is underpriced for a December tightening," said Annette Beacher, senior Strategist at TD Securities.

 "Tuesday's the last chance for the RBA to communicate they didn't mean to suggest a pause. We are saying yes for another 25 bps increase in rates," Beacher said.

 The central bank has already raised rates by 25 basis points in both October and November, becoming the first in the G20 to tighten since the global credit crisis blew up. If the RBA hikes rates in December, it would be the first time it would have tightened three months in a row.

 In Hong Kong, interbank rates continued to decline as repeated central bank intervention in the foreign exchange market injected increased liquidity in the domestic banking system.

 One-year Hibor <HIHKD1YD=> was fixed at 0.63929 percent, down from Thursday's 0.64929 percent. It has fallen 9 basis points this week. Short-dated interbank rates continue to hover around zero.

 Money is flowing into Hong Kong ahead of big upcoming IPOs in the territory, including a jumbo $4 billion offering by China's seventh-biggest bank China Minsheng Banking Corp .

 Since October, the HKMA has injected more than HK$140 billion in the territory's banking system to defend the currency peg, including Friday's intervention.

 As a result, the aggregate balance -- the sum of balances on clearing accounts maintained by banks with the HKMA -- will increase to a record HK$294.368 billion by Nov. 17 when the latest intervention is settled.

 The borrowing cost of dollars continued to fall in Asia after the European Central Bank Governing Council Member Michael Bonello told Reuters on Thursday the bank would ensure pulling back its liquidity lifeline did not disrupt markets. [ID:nLAG005916]

 In Singapore, 3-month dollars <SIUSDD=ABSG> are quoted at an average 0.27607 percent, a fresh low.    (Reporting by Umesh Desai; Editing by Kim Coghill)

HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--The latest intervention by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority temporarily curbed the Hong Kong dollar's strength, leading the unit slightly lower against the U.S. dollar late Friday.

But the HKMA said inflows to Hong Kong will continue in the near term, keeping the local unit near the strong end of its trading band against the U.S. dollar.

The HKMA sold HK$4.65 billion in the foreign-exchange market earlier Friday when the U.S. dollar hit HK$7.7500. In late Asian trade, the U.S. dollar was at HK$7.7502, compared with HK$7.7501 late Thursday. The U.S. unit was fixed at HK$7.7501 earlier Friday.

Inflows to Hong Kong have been strong since the second quarter, mainly because of the economic recovery in Hong Kong and China, the HKMA said in a document presented to the Legislative Council on Friday.

"With upbeat economic growth in China and renewed appreciation pressure on renminbi (the Chinese yuan), investment demand for Hong Kong dollar (denominated) assets is likely to remain strong," the HKMA said.

Hong Kong's de facto central bank said strong inflows "may (also) give rise to inflation in asset prices and consumer prices, which could pose threats to macroeconomic stability."

A trader at a Chinese bank said: "Capital inflows (to Hong Kong) are being boosted by renewed expectation of a stronger yuan."

Those expectations came after the People's Bank of China said in its quarterly monetary policy report issued this week that it will take into account "changes in international capital flows and the trends of major currencies" in exchange-rate policy, a phrase it hadn't used previously.

The one-year U.S. dollar/Hong Kong dollar forward contract was quoted at a discount of 243 points to the spot rate, compared with a 248-point discount late Thursday.

The HKMA said in the document a discount of around 200 points "suggests little speculation on the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate." It didn't elaborate.

A strategist at a U.K. bank said: "Market talk of Hong Kong dollar peg changes are hyperbole and highly unlikely."

Under Hong Kong's currency board system, the Hong Kong dollar is allowed to trade between HK$7.75 and HK$7.85 to the U.S. dollar.

title: 2nd UPDATE: HKMA October  Interventions  Hit Peak For Year
text:
(Adds value of HKMA interventions in October hit monthly peak for this year.)

By Chester Yung and Aries Poon

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--The value of the Hong Kong Monetary Authority's interventions in the foreign-exchange market in October has hit a peak for the year, as the de facto central bank defends the Hong Kong dollar's peg to the U.S. currency in the face of a continued influx of foreign funds into Asia.

The HKMA has sold about HK$74 billion to defend the Hong Kong dollar's peg to the U.S. currency so far this month. The total surpassed May's figure, when the HKMA sold HK$73.78 billion in the foreign-exchange market.

Bolstered by the strong start to the third-quarter earnings season, foreign investors have poured funds into Asia on expectations of increased U.S. and European demand for commodity and other exports from emerging markets, analysts said.

Traders said there is no indication the Hong Kong dollar will weaken before the end of the year and they expect more interventions by the HKMA. At 1002 GMT, the U.S. dollar was trading at HK$7.7502.

"The local property and stock markets are still holding firm. There is no incentive to push investors out of Hong Kong," said a trader with a U.K. bank.

The HKMA has injected HK$27.13 billion in the foreign-exchange market so far this week. The HKMA interventions were triggered by the U.S. dollar hitting HK$7.7500, the strong side of the Hong Kong dollar's trading band. Under Hong Kong's currency board system, the Hong Kong dollar is pegged at HK$7.80 to the U.S. dollar but is allowed to trade between HK$7.75 and HK$7.85.

The interventions this year have pushed the aggregate balance, a measure of commercial banks' clearing and reserve account holdings with the central bank, to HK$235.60 billion.

According to fund tracker EPFR Global, the amount of funds dedicated to emerging-market stocks totaled US$4.03 billion in the week ended Oct. 14, its highest level this year. The region's bond markets also absorbed US$967 million worth of new funds over that week. Separate data on inflows into Hong Kong were not available.

Hong Kong is one of the preferred destinations for funds in the region, traders and fund managers said, adding demand for shares of locally listed Chinese heavyweights such as Industrial & Commercial Bank of China and PetroChina is strong among foreign investors.

The benchmark Hang Seng Index has been hovering above the psychological 20,000 level since Sept. 3, and hit a 14-month intraday high of 22,620.01 Friday afternoon.

Traders said investors' expectations the Chinese yuan will appreciate on the back of a strong domestic economy have also lured funds to Hong Kong.

Law Ka-Chung, the chief economist at Bank of Communications, warned of a possible correction in the local stock market by end of the year, which could trigger capital outflows, pulling the Hong Kong dollar back from the high end of its trading band.

title: EM ASIA  FX -Yuan NDFs scale back appreciation, HK dlr fwds wider
text:
* Yuan NDFs off lows, but price in 3.5 percent gains in year

 * Hong Kong dollar forwards move on risk of revaluation

 By Vidya Ranganathan

 SINGAPORE, Oct 21 (Reuters) - Chinese yuan non-deliverable forwards rose on Wednesday, showing a slight scaling back of market expectations for appreciation of the yuan, while Hong Kong dollar forwards moved to price in the risk of a revaluation of that currency.

 Other Asian currencies fell, with the Korean won the worst hit, as the dollar <.DXY> rallied against commodity and high-yielding currencies and after Brazil's decision to impose a tax on foreign investment led to some nervousness among emerging market investors.

 CHINESE YUAN

 Chinese yuan NDFs were off Tuesday's lows, at which level they had priced in more than 4.5 percent of appreciation within 12 months -- a bullishness last seen in August 2008.

 Yet, they still priced in 3.5 percent of appreciation in the currency within the next 12 months from the spot rate of 6.827. Much of that has been spurred by foreign capital inflows into Chinese assets and punts on an economy that is recovering rapidly from the crisis, albeit aided by government stimulus.

 Traders said some investors might be getting carried away with speculating on yuan gains, given it has been tightly held for months and has not appreciated at all so far this year.

 "For you to be short NDFs, the negative carry is insane. So it only means they are expecting something out of the ordinary, like a revaluation of something," said one NDF trader in Singapore.

 Onshore yuan forwards <CNYXFWD=CFXS> have fallen to 6.7 in the one-year tenor over the past week from 6.75 per dollar, as hedge funds and traders locked in the arbitrage between NDF and onshore. The onshore one-year yuan is still way cheaper than NDF, where it is quoted at 6.6 per dollar. Traders said that had limited the drop in NDFs.

 "I suspect CNY will be at least 4 percent stronger a year from now but I doubt too many of the yuan buyers in NDFs are buy-and-hold types, in which case they're probably premature," said Sean Callow, a strategist at Westpac Bank.

 "I wouldn't be chasing it myself since I get the impression that the ultimate decision makers in China are still inclined to go full throttle on fiscal, monetary and FX policy i.e loose fiscal, no rate hikes, falling yuan NEER," Callow said.

 HONG KONG FORWARDS

 Hong Kong dollar forwards in the nine months to one-year tenors moved in step with recent movements in yuan NDFs, pricing the local currency at a higher premium to the U.S. dollar and thereby implying a risk to the peg.

 The currency has been hugging the top of its 7.75-7.85 per U.S. dollar band since June, while the Hong Kong Monetary Authority has been intervening heavily to defend the band.

 The growing speculation of yuan appreciation appeared to have further boosted expectations either of the Hong Kong dollar being pegged at a stronger level or being pegged to the yuan.

 "The rise in yuan appreciation expectation also appears to be spilling into market interests on a Hong Kong dollar move, as option-related interests on downside U.S. dollar/Hong Kong dollar emerge," analysts at JPMorgan said in a note.

 "However, we retain the expectation for the peg to remain in place."

 Hong Kong dollar 9-month forwards show the U.S. dollar at a 165 pips discount, compared with 125 pips a week ago. The options market showed options to be long the Hong Kong dollar <HKDVOL=GFI> were at a premium to those being long U.S. dollars.

title: =DJ CHINA VIEW: Dollar Weakness Sends Ripples Across Asia
text:
The fall in the U.S. dollar to 14-month lows is generating increased media coverage in recent days and ratcheting up political tensions.

U.S. policy on the dollar is a particularly sensitive topic in Asia, as where the dollar goes, so too does the yuan and the Hong Kong dollar. This makes finding ways to preserve capital in a time of currency weakness a priority.

This currency relationship between the U.S. and China has long been a source of periodic tensions. We are used to hearing the Chinese complaining about the declining dollar eroding its mountain of greenback reserves, while at the same time the gripe of the U.S. is that the yuan is undervalued. Now, the decline in the dollar is only dragging the yuan lower with it.

After allowing the yuan to appreciate by roughly 20% against the dollar from mid-2005, Beijing put the brakes on that movement when export growth contracted.

At least the silver lining for China of this new bout of dollar weakness is that its exports will get a much-needed boost, particularly in Europe and Japan, where "Made in China" products are now looking that much cheaper.

At a time when everyone would like to hold their currencies low to support flagging exports, it hasn't gone unnoticed that the Chinese manufacturing giant has seen a competitive devaluation.

Last week it was reported that central banks around Asia, including Thailand, Malaysia, Taiwan and Singapore, were intervening to buy dollars. These countries will be wary of letting their currency appreciate against the U.S. dollar (and hence, the yuan) and making their exports less competitive.

Hong Kong also is acutely sensitive to the movements in the dollar, thanks to its 26-year-old currency peg.

Last week, Hong Kong's new monetary chief Norman Chan did not quite get a baptism of fire, but was given warning his tenure at the helm of the Hong Kong Monetary Authority will not be all calm. After marking his first day in office the previous week with a reiteration of his support for the dollar peg, he was then forced to follow words with action. HKMA needed to intervene twice Thursday to keep the Hong Kong dollar within its trading band, injecting HK$8.525 billion into the money market in total.

Typically the weak U.S. dollar makes Hong Kong assets attractive, and funds pour into the territory.

As the financial system gets swamped by fund flows, money market rates have been driven to the floor. This is all good for owners of property or equities, who tend to gain from asset inflation, although worries exist that these conditions are setting up a new bubble.

For many, however, the downside is the dwindling purchasing power of their hard-earned Hong Kong dollars, amid the nearing of 0% interest rates on deposit.

What's hard to swallow is that the puny state of the Hong Kong dollar is not down to the government here running a gargantuan deficit or a blown-out financial system, but just to the peg. This comes at a time when regional neighbors in Asia, and even those across the border in mainland China, are seeing their purchasing power increase.

The only thing left to do is position for capital preservation. Gold and the Aussie and New Zealand dollars are all becoming favored plays, once again. And the Hong Kong dollar is becoming the new carry trade, due to the plentiful and cheap financing, while the dollar peg makes it a one-way bet.

This is all good as long as the HKMA keeps its promise of not changing the rules of the game and announcing a wider peg or new dollar valuation. The consensus is that there will be no change until China makes its capital account fully convertible, which should be years away.

But China might have to act faster in the event we do get a full-blown dollar crisis leading to much higher interest rates in the U.S. Then there would be little advantage of being attached to the greenback.

Another dynamic we are beginning to see involves countries benefiting from strong inflows of funds needing to raise rates to curb growth. Last week for instance, Australia raised interest rates. This could accelerate current currency moves, as investors go after the yield advantage. We have seen this cycle before, and for now it looks as if it will repeat.

The best advice is to watch announcements on currency policy carefully. And that's not just the U.S. policy on the dollar, but any hint from mainland Chinese officials of what they plan for the yuan and the Hong Kong dollar.

(Craig Stephen is a freelancer for MarketWatch. He can be reached at 415-439-6400 or via email at AskNewswires@dowjones.com.)

title: GLOBAL MARKETS-Asia shares hit 14-mth peak, dollar slumps
text:
* Asia shares hit 14-mth highs after strong U.S. retail sales

* Rising risk appetite sends U.S. dollar to 14-month low

* Oil rises to one-year high near $76

* Aussie, NZ currencies jump as rate rise speculation grows

* Korea, Taiwan intervene to curb appreciating currencies

By Susan Fenton

HONG KONG, Oct 15 (Reuters) - Asian shares rose to 14-month highs on Thursday as upbeat retail sales and surprisingly bullish earnings reports in the United States buoyed risk appetite, pushing the U.S. dollar to a 14-month low.

Shares in Japan jumped more than 2 percent as investors bought exporters who might benefit from rising U.S. demand and stocks in the rest of Asia firmed to their highest levels since last August.

Positive sales and earnings data from the United States -- including from Intel Corp and JP Morgan Chase & Co -- pushed the Dow Jones up 1.5 percent on Wednesday and above 10,000 points for the first time in a year.

U.S. government data showed that retail sales, excluding autos, rose for a second straight month in September.

Growing confidence that the United States can fuel a global economic recovery encouraged investors to buy riskier assets, such as higher-yielding currencies, including the Australian and New Zealand dollars, which were additionally boosted by rising expectations for interest rate hikes.

Authorities in Taiwan, Korea and the Philippines were spotted buying U.S. dollars to curb strength in their currencies. Several Asia countries have intervened in recent weeks to cap their currencies and keep them competitive in export markets.

The Aussie dollar hit a 14-month high at $0.9183 to the U.S. dollar after the Reserve Bank of Australia pointed to more rate rises. Last week, it became the first central bank in the Group of 20 to tighten policy as the global financial crisis eases.

"We have said that, over time, interest rates will need to be adjusted towards a more normal setting as the economy recovers," Governor Glenn Stevens said in a speech. "A step in that direction was taken last week."

In New Zealand, data showing stronger-than-expected inflation raised the likelihood of a rise in interest rates in coming months and sent the Kiwi to a 15-month high of $0.7485.

The flow of cash into riskier assets has knocked the U.S. dollar, a trend that pushed the currency to a 14-month low of 75.284 against a basket of currencies and against the euro at $1.4958.

Expectations of healthy global growth prodded NYMEX crude futures to a one-year high near $76 a barrel after U.S. industry data showed a surprise drop in inventories.

Gold gold held above $1,060 an ounce, just below Wednesday's record high above $1,070.

JAPAN EXPORTERS GAIN

Tokyo's Nikkei average rose 2.1 percent to 10,272.62, helped by auto maker Honda Motor Co, which gained 2.5 percent.

The MSCI index of Asia Pacific stocks traded outside Japan rose 1.4 percent to 414.96, its highest level since August last year. The Thomson Reuters index of regional shares was up 0.8 percent.

Shares in Hong Kong rose 1.6 percent and those in Shanghai increased 0.8 percent.

Bullish U.S. earnings reports boosted technology shares in Taiwan, lifting Taiwan's benchmark stock index by nearly 1 percent.

Shares in Acer Inc, which surpassed Dell Inc in the third quarter to become the world's No. 2 PC maker behind Hewlett-Packard, rose 1 percent. (Additional reporting by Gyles Beckford in WELLINGTON and Anirban Nag in SYDNEY; Editing by Neil Fullick)

title: MARKET SIGNALS-Asia and implications of an ugly dollar
text:
HONG KONG, Sept 14 (Reuters) - The dollar's slide in the past week has prompted the usual chorus of reasons used to explain every such decline: the inflationary impact of the Federal Reserve's quantitative easing, which has been belatedly tagged to a rise in gold, and central bank reserves diversification.

Then there's the persistent equity rally and money still chasing risk. Funds leaving safe-haven money markets -- and thus dollar deposits -- have swelled to $285 billion so far this year. That's well over half the money committed to money market funds last year.

But what stands out is how steady the dollar drop has been. It slid broadly to a one-year low last week but there were no remarkable milestones in terms of the dollar's percentage drop against major currencies.

It's hard to see a case for G7 intervention unless it turns more volatile. That said, Asia may soon face questions about how aggressively to intervene. South Korea is in the spotlight.

GOLD GAINS ACROSS BOARD

For a chart on gold's rise in terms of the pound and Swiss franc, click on: http://r.reuters.com/sat46d

This is not strictly a dollar story, so it's hard to hit the dollar alone with the inflation/quantitative easing stick.

The precious metal's latest push above $1,000 <XAU=> has unleashed a wave of commentary pinning big-picture reasons to the move. Beyond the technical nature of the move -- the break of a sideways triangle pattern in place for months -- other major currencies have fallen in tandem versus bullion.

So there is a shift towards gold generally (Asian central banks are rumoured to be behind the move, as always), which has coincidentally happened at a time when the dollar is vulnerable.

DOGGED BY DIVERSIFICATION

For a chart on the Hong Kong dollar's smaller dips during each Hang Seng pull-back: http://r.reuters.com/ner46d

Diversification: It's always happening, but for some reason reserve diversification only makes the headlines when the dollar is falling.

If trade surpluses are starting to rise in Asia and hot money is coming in, then that would mean more reserves in need of rebalancing.

Looking at Hong Kong's Hang Seng <.HSI> and the HK dollar <HKD=D4> as a proxy of how inflows/outflows are unfolding, it does seem that any drop in stocks is seen as an opportunity to shovel some hot money back into the Hang Seng and Hong Kong dollar, with each bout of outflows weakening the Hong Kong dollar less.

And some of that money is probably spilling over into the Chinese yuan <CNY=CFXS> from the Hong Kong dollar.

INTERVENTION AND JAPAN

For a graphic on the yen's trade-weighted rise and daily historical volatility: http://r.reuters.com/tyq46d

The dollar's weakness has also raised the question of intervention, with a fair bit of focus on Japan after the change of guard in government. Will the Democratic Party of Japan (DPJ) live up to its stated intentions to have a hands-off currency policy even as the yen reaches a seven-month high?

Japan's economy is very weak and very dependent on trade at this point because any capital spending recovery is going to take time.

Yet Japan has many other considerations. A desire to have the yen play an even greater role in Asian trade is creeping up the agenda just as China promotes the yuan. The yen has always suffered because Japan never really pushed the yen as an international currency and long intervened to weaken it.

But since 2004, Japan has gone quiet -- even during last year's record yearly surge, market volatility and a green light from the G7 to intervene. Yen volatility is now falling even as the currency strengthens, making it hard to build a case for intervention to fight volatility.

So given recent history, Japan may keep surprising on this front by staying out of the market. In the past few years, there was even debate within Japan on how it could reduce its reserves stockpile.

INTERVENTION AND KOREA

For a graphic on how the South Korean won's advance has stalled: http://r.reuters.com/ter46d("http://r.reuters.com/ter46d")

But what of the rest of Asia? There has clearly been intervention to stem currency strength, not a surprise as authorities rebuild reserves depleted last year to fight against the capital outflows. The big question is how aggressive they will get.

On that front, South Korea bears watching. The Bank of Korea signalled last week it is poised to raise interest rates in coming months, a move that would certainly lure more foreign funds.

Yet the won <KRW=> has had a tough time breaking beyond 1,220 to the dollar. A senior FX trader in Hong Kong described the Bank of Korea's efforts to stem the won's rise as, so far, "passive".

But local traders have not spotted intervention. Will they get more aggressive? Keep an eye out. It could set the tone for how other countries approach intervention.

title: ASIA LOCAL BONDS-Malaysian, Thai curves flatten on rate views
text:
HONG KONG, Sept 2 (Reuters) - The Malaysian yield curve extended a two-week flattening trend on Wednesday, with strong demand for new benchmark five-year debt helping sustain a decline in longer-end yields.

Thailand's bond yield curve also saw spreads tightening on views the central bank would keep its rate unchanged until early next year to spur the domestic economy.

For intraday updates, click on [ASIA-EMRG-FIXI]

VIEWS AND FLOWS

Malaysia's yield curve has flattened over the past two weeks, with the spread between the three-year and five-year bonds falling to 85.8 basis points (bps) on Wednesday from 98.7 on Aug 14. The flattening has been led by a drop in 5-year debt yields.

"Economic recovery is not yet very certain in Malaysia, so demand for government bonds continues. We have seen strong interest on the new five-year benchmark. Being a new issue, it is very liquid," a Kuala Lumpur-based trader said.

Even before the government sold the the 5-year debt on Aug. 26, investors had been buying the bond in a forward market, traders said.

At the same time, investors had been avoiding the short end of the curve, leading to the flattening.

The risk of a sell-off in three-year debt on views the central bank's easing cycle has ended, and supply concerns at the 10-year tenor were also driving investors toward the five-year security, said Suresh Kumar Ramanathan, rates and currency strategist at CIMB Investment Bank.

Malaysia's central bank kept its rate on hold for a fourth straight meeting on Aug. 25, after cutting it by a total of 150 bps between November and April.

Traders expect the flattening trend to be sustained, on expectations the five-year yield would extend its fall.

THAI YIELD CURVE FLAT

The Thai yield curve has bear-flattened since last week, led by a rise in short-end yields as the market priced in steady policy rates until the first half of 2010 from a central bank that has already paused policy for a while.

The spread between one-year and five-year bond yields fell to 148.5 bps on Wednesday from 182 on Aug. 24. The flattening was led by a rise in the one-year yield.

"The short-end of the curve, particularly the one-year, is being sold off because of expectations that monetary policy will remain unchanged for the rest of the year and maybe until early next year," a trader from Bangkok said.

"So there is no incentive to hold on to the one-year sector because of the limited upside."

At its last meeting on Aug. 26, the Bank of Thailand kept its rates unchanged at 1.25 percent for the third meeting in a row, after aggressive cuts from December to April totalling 250 bps.

Elsewhere, Philippine five-year bonds <PH5YT=RR> extended a steep fall to take their yield up 7 bps to 6.38 percent. Traders said investors were selling the maturity in anticipation of a new retail Treasury bond.

The government is in advanced talks with banks to manage the retail issue and is considering maturities of 3, 5, and 7 years. [ID:nMNB002456]

A two-year bond sale in Hong Kong was hugely oversubscribed, reflecting high liquidity in the banking system following central bank intervention to stabilise the pegged Hong Kong dollar.

The government sold HK$3.5 billion of the debt, with total tenders at HK$22.584 billion.

title: HK's Yam does not see  currency  speculation, asset bubble
text:
(Adds quotes, details)

HONG KONG, Aug 6 (Reuters) - Hong Kong's central bank chief Joseph Yam said on Thursday that strong fund flows into Hong Kong assets in recent months, which have pushed the Hong Kong dollar <HKD=> to the top of its trading band, are not related to currency speculation.

Funds have poured into Hong Kong assets -- pushing stock prices up 84 percent since a global equity rebound began on March 9, while property prices are up about 20 percent this year -- but Yam said he did not see any signs yet of excessive credit creation that could lead to an asset price bubble.

"Judging by information from our market contacts, these inflows were largely 'real money' -- that is, not related to any speculative activity in the currency -- from investors attracted by the opportunities here and looking to position themselves to benefit from the strong outlook for the mainland (China) and Hong Kong economies," Yam wrote in a weekly column on the bank's website www.info.gov.hk/hkma/eng/viewpt/index.htm("http://www.info.gov.hk/hkma/eng/viewpt/index.htm").

In addition, a narrowing of the differential between U.S. and Hong Kong interest rates had discouraged selling Hong Kong dollars for U.S. dollars and put further upward pressure on the local currency, Yam said.

"While we do not see any signs yet of excessive credit creation, which might fuel speculation in asset markets, we are mindful of the potential negative impact that asset-price bubbles, if they were to occur, could have on financial stability and especially the stability of the banking system," he said.

Hong Kong has no control over monetary policy because its currency is pegged to the U.S. dollar, forcing it to track U.S. monetary policy. However, Yam said the city could introduce supervisory measures to ensure that banks did not expand their lending to asset markets imprudently.

"This would help restrain credit expansion arising from strong capital inflows, and banks' credit-risk exposure, which might increase sharply if an asset-price bubble were to burst," he said.

Yam also warned that capital flows could reverse if economic conditions or corporate earnings disappoint, if U.S. interest rates rise -- Hong Kong rates would follow suit -- or, more positively, if investment opportunities overseas improved.

The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) has had to intervene repeatedly since March, selling Hong Kong for U.S. dollars, to keep the Hong Kong dollar within its fixed trading band with the U.S. dollar.

Many analysts say the territory's asset markets are at risk of forming a bubble -- excessive price appreciation that will result in a sharp correction -- over the next year.

Hong Kong is seen as attractive because its currency is reasonably stable thanks to its peg to the U.S. dollar and because it gives exposure to China, one of few major economies that is likely to see significant growth this year. (Reporting by Susan Fenton, Editing by Chris Lewis)

title: CORRECT: HK Shares End At Another 10-Month High
text:
("HK Shares End At Another 10-Mo High Led By China Mobile,Cnooc," published at 0944 GMT, misstated Sichuan Expressway's gain on its trading debut in the 10th paragraph. The correct version follows:)

HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--Gains in heavyweight China Mobile and oil giant Cnooc on hopes they will list on the mainland soon led Hong Kong shares to another 10-month closing high Tuesday.

The blue-chip Hang Seng Index rose 372.92 points, or 1.84%, to 20,624.54, its highest closing level since Sept. 8. The index traded between 20,664.48 and 20,109.55 during the session.

Turnover totaled HK$84.84 billion, up from HK$80.90 billion Monday.

Analysts said they expect a pullback in the market after July futures expire Thursday, with strong support at 19,000 because of abundant liquidity in the territory.

The HSI has risen for nine sessions out of the past 11 for total gains of 19.54%.

"A bubble appears to be forming in the Hong Kong stock market, with too much cash chasing a limited supply of stocks," said Francis Lun, general manager at Fulbright Securities.

Continued capital inflows prompted the Hong Kong Monetary Authority to intervene in the currency market again Tuesday, injecting HK$3.1 billion to maintain the local currency's peg to the U.S. dollar.

"Bullish sentiment continues to grow while valuations have gone well ahead of the expected improvements in economic activity and corporate earnings," Tai Fook Securities said.

Lun said Hong Kong shares will likely track any consolidation in Shanghai after the mainland's benchmark index has repeatedly hit 13-month highs. The benchmark Shanghai Composite Index ended up 0.1% Tuesday at 3438.37, its highest close since June 2, 2008.

Analysts said Sichuan Expressway's 203% rise on its trading debut in Shanghai on Monday reflects the level of demand for new listings in China and bodes well for large Hong Kong-listed companies that hope to list on the mainland, including China Mobile and Cnooc.

China Mobile rose 4.0% to HK$83.60 and Cnooc was up 2.84% at HK$10.86.

Chinese steel makers were among the biggest gainers after Goldman Sachs upgraded the sector on stronger demand related to infrastructure spending and property investments in China, resulting in the country becoming a net importer of steel products from a net exporter.

Goldman Sachs raised Angang Steel to buy from neutral and raised its target price to HK$20.00 from HK$12.90. Angang jumped 8.6% to a 13-month high of HK$16.96, and Maanshan Iron & Steel surged 7.9% to HK$5.84, the highest level since June 2, 2008.

Property developers were mostly higher on expectations abundant liquidity will continue to drive asset prices and support the local property market.

New World Development rose 4.4% to a 13-month high of HK$18.16. Wharf jumped 5.2% to HK$36.60, and Cheung Kong was up 1.4% at HK$102.80, its highest level since June last year.

Hang Seng Bank rose 4.5% to HK$122.10 after Morgan Stanley raised the lender's price target to HK$135 from HK$105 on an improved 2009 earning outlook.

title: CORRECT: HK Shares End At 10-Mo High Led By China Mobile

HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--Friday's gains on Wall Street and continued liquidity inflows led Hong Kong's benchmark index to close above 20,000 points Monday at a 10-month high, while heavyweight China Mobile caught up with the broader market's recent gains.

The blue-chip Hang Seng Index rose 268.83 points, or 1.35%, to 20,251.62, its highest closing level since 20,491 on Sept. 9. It traded between 20,096.17 and 20,385.69 during the session.

Turnover totaled HK$80.90 billion, down from HK$83.64 billion Friday.

Traders said they expect the ample liquidity in the territory to continue to lend near-term support to the blue-chip index, which could test 20,500 this week.

"The momentum is still strong, fueled by strong liquidity inflows," said Peter Lai, a director at DBS Vickers Securities. "But I expect the Hang Seng Index to see more profit-taking pressure with the index facing strong resistance at 20,800-21,000."

The continued fund inflows prompted the Hong Kong Monetary Authority to sell a total HK$33.73 billion in the foreign-exchange market since July 17 to maintain the Hong Kong dollar's peg to the U.S. dollar.

Local shares rose after a 0.26% gain in the Dow Jones Industrial Average on Friday. For the week, the DJIA was up 3.99%.

China Mobile led the blue-chip rally, rising 4.2% to HK$80.35 and contributing 76.06 points to the index's rise.

"China Mobile is lagging the recent market rally, and its valuation is becoming more attractive," said Eugene Law, research director at Celestial Securities.

Law said China Mobile is trading at a forward price/earnings ratio of about 12, while the average forward P/E of companies in the Hang Seng Index is 16-17.

"The stock is also trading at an unjustified discount versus peers China Unicom and China Telecom," said Law, who set a price target of HK$92.00 for the stock.

Aluminum Corp. of China, or Chalco, rose 4.5% to HK$9.22 though the company said it expects to swing to a net loss in the first half. Investors shrugged off the warning due to strengthening metals prices and bought the stock amid hopes of a turnaround in profitability in the second half, analysts said

On January 4, 2022, the CAC, in conjunction with 12 other government departments, issued the New Measures for Cybersecurity Review (the "New Measures") on January 4, 2022. The New Measures amends the Draft Measures released on July 10, 2021 and became effective on February 15, 2022.

● Loan receivables, net

Loans receivables are carried at unpaid principal balances, less the allowance for loan losses and charge-offs. The loans receivables portfolio consists of real estate mortgage loans, commercial and personal loans.

Loans are placed on nonaccrual status when they are past due 180 days or more as to contractual obligations or when other circumstances indicate that collection is not probable. When a loan is placed on nonaccrual status, any interest accrued but not received is reversed against interest income. Payments received on a nonaccrual loan are either applied to protective advances, the outstanding principal balance or recorded as interest income, depending on an assessment of the ability to collect the loan. A nonaccrual loan may be restored to accrual status when principal and interest payments have been brought current and the loan has performed in accordance with its contractual terms for a reasonable period (generally six months).

If the Company determines that a loan is impaired, the Company next determines the amount of the impairment. The amount of impairment on collateral dependent loans is charged off within the given fiscal quarter. Generally, the amount of the loan and negative escrow in excess of the appraised value less estimated selling costs, for the fair value of collateral valuation method, is charged off. For all other loans, impairment is measured as described below in Allowance for Loan Losses.

● Allowance for loan losses ("ALL")

The adequacy of the Company's ALL is determined, in accordance with ASC Topic 450-20 Loss Contingencies includes management's review of the Company's loan portfolio, including the identification and review of individual problem situations that may affect a borrower's ability to repay. In addition, management reviews the overall portfolio quality through an analysis of delinquency and non-performing loan data, estimates of the value of underlying collateral, current charge-offs and other factors that may affect the portfolio, including a review of regulatory examinations, an assessment of current and expected economic conditions and changes in the size and composition of the loan portfolio.

The ALL reflects management's evaluation of the loans presenting identified loss potential, as well as the risk inherent in various components of the portfolio. There is significant judgment applied in estimating the ALL. These assumptions and estimates are susceptible to significant changes based on the current environment. Further, any change in the size of the loan portfolio or any of its components could necessitate an increase in the ALL even though there may not be a decline in credit quality or an increase in potential problem loans.

Leases with a term greater than one year are recognized on the balance sheet as right-of-use assets, lease liabilities and long-term lease liabilities. The Company has elected not to recognize on the balance sheet leases with terms of one year or less. Operating lease liabilities and their corresponding right-of-use assets are recorded based on the present value of lease payments over the expected remaining lease term. However, certain adjustments to the right-of-use assets may be required for items such as prepaid or accrued lease payments. The interest rate implicit in lease contracts is typically not readily determinable. As a result, the Company utilizes its incremental borrowing rates, which are the rates incurred to borrow on a collateralized basis over a similar term an amount equal to the lease payments in a similar economic environment.

In accordance with the guidance in ASC Topic 842, components of a lease should be split into three categories: lease components (e.g. land, building, etc.), non-lease components (e.g. common area maintenance, consumables, etc.), and non-components (e.g. property taxes, insurance, etc.). Subsequently, the fixed and in-substance fixed contract consideration (including any related to non-components) must be allocated based on the respective relative fair values to the lease components and non-lease components.

The Company made the policy election to not separate lease and non-lease components. Each lease component and the related non-lease components are accounted for together as a single component.

● Income taxes

The Company adopted the ASC Topic 740 Income tax provisions of paragraph 740-10-25-13, which addresses the determination of whether tax benefits claimed or expected to be claimed on a tax return should be recorded in the consolidated financial statements. Under paragraph 740-10-25-13, the Company may recognize the tax benefit from an uncertain tax position only if it is more likely than not that the tax position will be sustained on examination by the taxing authorities, based on the technical merits of the position. The tax benefits recognized in the consolidated financial statements from such a position should be measured based on the largest benefit that has a greater than fifty percent (50%) likelihood of being realized upon ultimate settlement. Paragraph 740-10-25-13 also provides guidance on de-recognition, classification, interest and penalties on income taxes, accounting in interim periods and requires increased disclosures. The Company had no material adjustments to its liabilities for unrecognized income tax benefits according to the provisions of paragraph 740-10-25-13.

The estimated future tax effects of temporary differences between the tax basis of assets and liabilities are reported in the accompanying balance sheets, as well as tax credit carry-backs and carry-forwards. The Company periodically reviews the recoverability of deferred tax assets recorded on its balance sheets and provides valuation allowances as management deems necessary.

Overview

We are a Nevada holding company with operations conducted through our subsidiaries based in Singapore and Hong Kong. The Company, through its subsidiaries, is engaged in two business segments: (i) the physical arts and collectibles business, and (ii) the financing/money lending business.

Through our physical arts and collectibles business, we provide authentication, valuation and certification ("AVC") service, sale and purchase, hire purchase, financing, custody, security and exhibition ("CSE") services to art and collectibles buyers through traditional methods as well as through leveraging blockchain technology through the creation of Digital Ownership Tokens ("DOTs").

DOT is an integrated, best in class, smart contract for art and collectible pieces. We use blockchain technology to help resolve the issues of provenance, authenticity and ownership in the arts and collectibles market. For each art or collectible piece, we create an individual DOT that includes an independent appraisal, a 3D rendering of the piece, high-definition photo of the piece, AI recognition file of the piece and a set of legal documents to provide proof of ownership and provenance of the piece to the blockchain. Our DOTs are intended to provide assurance on the authenticity of art or collectible pieces as well as act as a record of ownership transfers using blockchain technology to establish provenance of the piece. As the owner of a DOT, the buyer will be able to take the necessary legal action against those who breach the digital ownership rights. We initially intend to focus on customers located in Hong Kong and expand throughout Asia and the rest of the world.

We conduct our DOT operations from Singapore. In Singapore, cryptocurrencies and the custodianship of such cryptocurrencies are not specifically regulated. Cryptocurrency exchanges and trading of cryptocurrencies are legal, but not considered legal tender. To the extent that cryptocurrencies or tokens are considered "capital market products" such as securities, spot foreign exchange contracts, derivatives and the like, they will be subject to the jurisdiction of the Monetary Authority of Singapore ("MAS"), Securities and Futures Act, anti-money laundering and combating the financing of terrorism laws and requirements. To the extent that tokens are deemed "digital payment tokens," they will be subject to the Payment Services Act of 2019 which, among other things, require compliance with anti-money laundering and combating the financing of terrorism laws and requirements. According to the Payment Services Act of 2019, "digital payment token" means any digital representation of value (other than an excluded digital representation of value) that (a) is expressed as a unit; (b) is not denominated in any currency, and is not pegged by its issuer to any currency; (c) is, or is intended to be, a medium of exchange accepted by the public, or a section of the public, as payment for goods or services or for the discharge of a debt; (d) can be transferred, stored or traded electronically; and (e) satisfies such other characteristics as the Authority may prescribe. Our DOTs, therefore, are not securities or digital payment tokens subject to these acts.

We receive fiat and cryptocurrency from the sale of art and collectibles and collection of transaction fees derived from the secondary and subsequent sales of the collectibles. In order to minimize the risk of price fluctuation in cryptocurrency, after we receive the cryptocurrencies, we will recognize the value by immediately exchange them into US dollar or stable currencies that are pegged with US dollar.

We conduct our financing/money lending business through our Hong Kong subsidiaries which are licensed under Hong Kong's Money Lenders Ordinance. We primarily provide unsecured personal loan financings to private individuals. We also have a small portfolio of mortgage loans. Revenue is generated from interest received from the provision of loans to private individual customers.

There may be prominent risks associated with our operations being in Hong Kong. We may be subject to the risks of uncertainty of any future actions of the PRC government including the risk that the PRC government could disallow our holding company structure, which may result in a material change in our operations, including our ability to continue our existing holding company structure, carry on our current business, accept foreign investments, and offer or continue to offer securities to our investors. These adverse actions could change the value of our common stock to significantly decline or become worthless. We may also be subject to penalties and sanctions imposed by the PRC regulatory agencies, including the Chinese Securities Regulatory Commission, if we fail to comply with such rules and regulations, which could adversely affect the ability of the Company's securities to continue to trade on the Over-the-Counter Bulletin Board, which may cause the value of our securities to significantly decline or become worthless.

As a U.S.-listed company with operations in Hong Kong, we may face heightened scrutiny, criticism and negative publicity, which could result in a material change in our operations and the value of our common stock. It could also significantly limit or completely hinder our ability to offer or continue to offer securities to investors and cause the value of such securities to significantly decline or be worthless. Commentary on our Revenue - an overview

In this quarter, we have seen strong and continued revenue growth. The total revenue for 2022 Q2 was approximately US$4.7 million consisting of approximately $3.05 million from the DOT business segment and $1.65 million from the lending segment. Our DOT revenue are primarily attributable to: (i) our MetaMall/Resale transactions of approximately US$3.04 million; (ii) primary DOT sales (revenue from sales of new collectible DOTs) of approximately US$198,000; and (iii) Coinllectibles Sports of approximately US$35,000.

Commentary on DOT Revenue - our key growth driver

As a whole, the 2022 Q2 revenue growth is in line with Management's expectations. Our business model focuses on the rights of ownership through a digital ownership token attached to physical art or some other collectible with real world tangible value. The business is fundamentally different from the model NFT marketplaces like OpenSea or Rarible that list third party NFTs for sale. Given the business model targets the physical art and collectibles market, the relative growth in the overall art markets sales at major auction houses and art fairs, we were less affected by the recent negative sentiment in the crypto and NFT markets.

We currently generate revenue from primary sales, or sales of new collectibles DOTs and resale transaction fees between 8% and 10% each time the DOT is sold in the secondary market. Because each collectible has the potential of generating revenue beyond the initial sale, we intend to focus on bringing quality primary sales DOT for long term ownership as well as resale potential to market. A key focus of the company is to work with appropriate partners to mint and sell DOTs attached to high quality collectibles in an increasing range of art such as photographs and sculptures and a range of other market segments including sports. We feel that DOTs are an attractive way for artists, galleries, auction houses to engage with existing and new buyer bases in addition to their current sales strategies. We see further opportunity to engage with partners to support strategies using applications of DOTs such as in the luxury goods segment.

The sports collectibles market is another area of potential application for DOTs. According to Market Decipher, the market value of sports collectibles - which is currently at US$26.1billion, is expected to reach US$227 billion by 2032. Sports related NFTs, with a current estimated market value of US$1.4 billion, is also expected to reach an estimated market value of US$92 billion by 2032.

Commentary on finance revenue - providing stability to the business

The lending segment is providing a stable revenue to the Group, and we generated approximately US$1.65 million and US$1.65 million for the six months ended June 30, 2023 and 2022, respectively. Our finance companies are licensed to originate personal loans, company loans and mortgage loans in Hong Kong, and generate interest income from these loans. In contrast to the significant growth in DOT revenue, our finance companies have long been established in Hong Kong and thus, the growth of the business is relatively steady. Despite the global economic situation and consequences caused by the pandemic, we believe that there is always a need for borrowing, and anticipate our lending segment to continue to provide stable revenue in the near future.

The COVID-19 pandemic has significantly impacted health and economic conditions throughout Asian region. National, regional and local governments took a variety of actions to contain the spread of COVID-19, including office and store closures, quarantining suspected COVID-19 patients, and capacity limitations. These developments have significantly impacted the results of operations, financial condition and cash flows of the Company included in this reporting. The impact included the difficulties of working remotely from home including slow Internet connection, the inability of our accounting and financial officers to collaborate as effectively as they would otherwise have in an office environment and issues arising from mandatory state quarantines.

While it is not possible at this time to estimate with sufficient certainty the impact that COVID-19 could have on the Company's business, the continued spread of COVID-19 and the measures taken by federal, state, local and foreign governments could disrupt the operation of the Company's business. The COVID-19 outbreak and mitigation measures have also had and may continue to have an adverse impact on global and domestic economic conditions, which could have an adverse effect on the Company's business and financial condition, including on its potential to conduct financings on terms acceptable to the Company, if at all. In addition, the Company has taken temporary precautionary measures intended to help minimize the risk of the virus to its employees, including temporarily requiring employees to work remotely, and discouraging employee attendance at in-person work-related meetings, which could negatively affect the Company's business. These measures are continuing. The extent to which the COVID-19 outbreak impacts the Company's results will depend on future developments that are highly uncertain and cannot be predicted, including new information that may emerge concerning the severity of the virus and the actions to contain its impact.

title: Hong Kong banks' usage of HKMA discount window hits 3-year high in July
text:
HONG KONG, Aug 3 (Reuters) - Hong Kong banks borrowed a record amount from the central bank in July as demand from companies paying seasonal dividends and intervention by the monetary authorities in currency markets drove cash levels down.

The scramble for cash lifted interbank rates to a two decade-high and saw banks borrowing HK$8.2 billion ($1.05 billion) from the Hong Kong Monetary Authority's discount facility - the highest monthly amount in over three years.

The discount window is an overnight liquidity facility available to banks at the city's base rate, which is 5.75%, and currently higher than inter-bank rates.

Analysts said banks were forced to tap the discount window more than usual in July as listed corporates needed more Hong Kong dollars to pay dividends, even as the HKMA's intervention to defend its currency peg drove down the aggregate banking system balance.

The overnight Hong Kong Interbank Offered rate (HIHKDOND=) rose as far as 5.6%, a 17-year high in July, as cash conditions tightened.

"Banks normally wouldn’t tap the discount window if the funding demand can be met in the interbank market," said Sam Wong, an analyst at Jefferies.

Hong Kong’s main policy rate, the base rate, is tethered to rates in the United States by the currency peg that moves in a tight range of 7.75-7.85 per U.S. dollar.

As the U.S. Federal Reserve raised interest rates in one of the fastest tightening cycles since the 1980s, Hong Kong's base rate has outpaced the rise in interbank rates, the latter more influenced by domestic demand and supply, analysts said.

But banks are also beginning to feel the pinch from a thinning aggregate balance, or interbank cash balance, which since May has stayed below HK$45 billion at the lowest levels since 2008.

The HKMA does not disclose information about which banks have used the facilities, but banks with a higher ratio of liquid assets appear not to have needed to borrow from the monetary authority.

"With our liquidity coverage ratio at over 230% and above the regulatory requirement, we are able to plan our liquidity need for the second half, said Saw Say Pin, Hang Seng Bank's chief financial officer. "...we have not tapped the discount window".

The July spurt in use of the discount window may be a one-off, as the seasonal dividend pressures will fade after August and interbank rates would then likely ease, said Kiyong Seong, lead Asia macro strategist at Societe Generale. title: Hong Kong dollar interbank rates could meet or overshoot U.S. rates, says HKMA
text:
HONG KONG, June 14 (Reuters) - Hong Kong dollar interbank rates could catch up with, or even overshoot their U.S. dollar counterparts as companies' demand for the local currency for dividend payments peaks in the three months to August, the head of the city's central bank said.

This is a seasonal factor unique to Hong Kong that affects the city's interbank rates, as listed companies need to stock up on Hong Kong dollars to pay dividends, said Hong Kong Monetary Authority's Chief Executive Eddie Yue in an "Insight" article published on its website on Wednesday.

The peak season for dividend payments is usually in June to August. Such funding demand sends the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate higher, he said.

Such seasonal factors will continue to influence interbank rates in the coming weeks or months, Yue said.

"The possibility that HKD interbank rates will catch up with, or even overshoot, their USD counterparts on certain days cannot be ruled out," said Yue.

The Hong Kong dollar was up 30 pips on Wednesday, at 7.8308 per dollar and the highest in two weeks.

The Hong Kong overnight interbank offered rate reversed two straight days of decline and rose to 3.88%, the highest since May 30, after having peaked at nearly 5% on May 19 at a nearly 16-year high.

Seasonal factors aside, Hong Kong's interbank rate is affected by the U.S. interest rate trend due to the Hong Kong dollar's peg to the greenback. The Hong Kong dollar is pegged within a band of 7.75 to 7.85 versus the U.S. dollar.

A widening of the interest rate gap between the Hong Kong dollar and U.S. dollar had incentivized carry trades and weakened the Hong Kong dollar, thereby leading to over 40 rounds of intervention by the HKMA since the U.S. Federal Reserve began hiking rates in March 2022 up to May.

(Reporting by Georgina Lee; Editing by Kim Coghill)
