title: HKMA  intervenes  to support HK dollar, buys HK$390 mln.
text:
HONG KONG, March 29 (Reuters) - The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA), the territory's de facto central bank, said on Tuesday that it bought HK$390 million from banks in exchange for U.S. dollars to support the local currency.   

Under Hong Kong's currency board system, the HKMA is committed to defending the pegged rate of HK$7.8 by buying Hong Kong dollars in exchange for U.S. dollars.   

A Reuters page showed the transaction occurred at 0820 GMT.   

At 0824 GMT, the Hong Kong dollar was trading at 7.7999/7.80 per U.S. dollar.   

The latest move by the HKMA will reduce the aggregate balance - the sum of balances on clearing accounts maintained by banks with the HKMA - to HK$3.85 billion after settlement on Thursday.

title: HKMA continues buying HK dollars in offshore market.
text:
HONG KONG, March 17 (Reuters) - The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA), the territory's de facto central bank, reported it bought HK$390 million from banks in exchange for U.S. dollars in offshore trade overnight to support the local currency.   

The intervention followed the purchase of HK$148 million during Hong Kong trading hours late on Wednesday. On Tuesday, it had bought HK$780 million in London trade.   

Under Hong Kong's currency board system, the HKMA is committed to defending the pegged rate of HK$7.8 by buying Hong Kong dollars in exchange for U.S. dollars.   

Real time information available on Reuters page showed the transaction.   

At 0136 GMT, the Hong Kong dollar was trading at 7.7996/97 per U.S. dollar versus 7.7998/99 in late Asian trade on Wednesday.   

The latest move by the HKMA will reduce the aggregate balance - the sum of balances on clearing accounts maintained by banks with the HKMA - to HK$4.358 billion after settlement on Friday, its lowest level in five months, from HK$15.789 billion at the beginning of the year.   

A recent decline in the aggregate balance in the banking system and rising interbank rates have increased pressure on local banks to raise interest rates.

title: HK dollar remains weak despite  interventions .
text:
HONG KONG, March 16 (Reuters) - The Hong Kong dollar remained
weak against the greenback on Wednesday as investors continued to
draw funds from the territory in search of higher yields
elsewhere, prompting the Hong Kong's de facto central bank to
intervene to support the local currency.
    The Hong Kong Monetary Authority stepped in twice within 24
hours to support the Hong Kong dollar. It bought HK$148 million
in exchange for U.S. dollars from banks late on Wednesday,
following the purchase of HK$780 million in London trade on
Tuesday.
    Under the currency board system, the HKMA is committed to
defending the pegged rate of HK$7.80 by buying Hong Kong dollars
in exchange for U.S. dollars.
    "The outflows were mainly due to interest rate differentials
and a further decline in the aggregate balance, reflecting an
imminent interest rate hike in Hong Kong," one dealer at a local
bank said.
 
    Some dealers also said such speculative trades would push
banks to raise rates.
   


    Hong Kong interest rates usually move in tandem with U.S.
   

rates due to the local currency's peg to the U.S. dollar, but   

banks here have ignored recent U.S. rate increases because the   

local banking system was awash with cash.    


 
    However, excessive liquidity in the banking system has shrunk
in recent months.
    The latest move by the HKMA will reduce the aggregate balance
   

- the sum of balances on clearing accounts maintained by banks   

with the HKMA - to HK$4.748 billion after settlement on Friday,   

its lowest level in five months, from HK$15.789 billion at the   

beginning of the year.

title: UPDATE 1-HKMA  intervenes  to support HK dollar.
text:
HONG KONG, March 9 (Reuters) - The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) stepped in four times on Wednesday afternoon to support the Hong Kong dollar amid accelerating arbitrage trade on speculation that interest rates will rise soon.   

"People are seeing that low interest rates in Hong Kong are in danger of disappearing and they want to take advantage of them while they can," said Tim Condon, chief economist at ING Financial Markets. "That's the arbitrage trade."   

Under Hong Kong's currency board system, the HKMA is committed to defending the pegged rate of HK$7.8 by buying Hong Kong dollars in exchange for U.S. dollars at that level.   

On Wednesday afternoon the dollar hit 7.8 several times and the HKMA intervened four times within half an hour, soaking up HK$2.148 billion in exchange for U.S. dollars.   

By 1041 GMT, the Hong Kong dollar was trading at 7.998/99 per U.S. dollar.   

Speculation that Hong Kong banks might raise rates ahead of a possible U.S. rate rise when the Federal Reserve meets on March 22 heightened on Wednesday.   

Raymond Or, general manager of HSBC, the territory's biggest bank, indicated that rates could go up soon if the overnight interest rate remained at current levels. However, HSBC Chairman David Eldon said pressure for an early rate hike was not significant.   

Ample liquidity in the Hong Kong banking system has enabled Hong Kong to ignore a recent upturn in U.S. rates, giving investors the opportunity to earn an interest rate pick up they sell Hong Kong dollars for U.S. dollars.   

However, fund flows to the territory have been easing in recent months, on expectations that interest rates will have to follow U.S. rate moves sooner or later and on declining demand for the Hong Kong dollar as a proxy to a revaluation of China's yuan currency.   

Though liquidity is still ample, the aggregate balance has fallen to around HK$8 billion from more than HK$15 billion in late January, raising the prospect that banks will have to raise rates.   

"I think banks may raise interest rates this week as the aggregate balance has been reduced quite a lot in recent months," a dealer at a European bank said.   

Once Wednesday's outflows are settled on Friday, the aggregate balance will fall to HK$5.541 billion. However, that is still well above the normal average of between HK$500 million-HK$1 billion.   

Speculation that China would soon allow its currency to appreciate slightly - which triggered heavy investment in Hong Kong-listed Chinese companies last year - has eased as recent comments by Chinese officials suggested an imminent revaluation of the yuan was unlikely.   

China's Finance Minister Jin Renqing told a news conference on Wednesday that the yuan's exchange rate was appropriate.   

"The renminbi (yuan) exchange rate conforms with China's economic development and our foreign trade situation and should be kept basically stable," Jin said.

title: HK dlr eases as U.S. dlr bolstered by ECB comments.
text:
HONG KONG, Nov 9 (Reuters) - The Hong Kong dollar edged lower
on Tuesday as the greenback regained some lost ground after
supportive comments from European central bank officials.
    The local currency        fell to a session low of 7.7783 per
U.S. dollar before trading back to 7.7763/65 at 0905 GMT, weaker
than 7.7736/37 in late Asian trade on Monday.
    "The dollar traded to 105.70 yen, and remarks from European
Central Bank officials helped the U.S. dollar," said a dealer
from a Japanese bank.
    The pause in the dollar's downtrend came after European
   

Central Bank President Jean-Claude Trichet warned against the   

euro's rapid rise on Monday. ECB Governing Council member Guy   

Quaden followed Trichet's comments, telling a Belgian newspaper   

that further appreciation of the euro would be undesirable.   

However, some dealers said the dollar's downtrend was not yet   

over and it would remain under pressure by concerns about the   

U.S. budget and current account deficits.   

Another trader from a local bank said the fall in the local   

currency was due to some players covering short dollar positions   

after the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) intervened on   

Monday to stem the local currency's rise against the greenback.   

The discount on one-year forwards was quoted at   

1,365/1,350 pips by late afternoon, narrower than Monday's close   

of 1,410/1,380 pips.   

The U.S. Federal Reserve is holding its policy-setting   

meeting on Wednesday. Dealers said the market has already priced   

in a 25 basis points rise in rates but they are are anxious to   

see the accompanying statement, which could hint at the future   

pace of monetary tightening.   

"People previously thought the Fed would pause in raising   

rates in December ... but the strong U.S. employment data for   

October has raised the prospects of another rate increase next   

month," one trader said.   

Hong Kong tends to track U.S. rate moves because of the   

territory's currency peg to the U.S. dollar. But Hong Kong banks   

are unlikely to follow the Fed's lead this time due to a banking   

system awash with funds.   

The aggregate balance, the sum of balances on clearing   

accounts maintained by banks with the HKMA, will rise to   

HK$14.118 billion on Wednesday.

title: =DJ Hong Kong Dollar Rises To 31-Wk High On China Yuan Talk
text:
NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--The Hong Kong dollar surged versus its U.S. counterpart Friday, buoyed by renewed speculation that China is nearing a plan to revalue its currency as it faces more pressure from the Bush Administration.  

The speculation about China's currency policy re-emerged following reports that President George W. Bush had discussed the issue, amongst others, via telephone Thursday with Chinese President Hu Jintao. In recent months Chinese officials have reiterated their long-standing intention to loosen their tightly-controlled currency policy - which acts as a defacto peg versus the dollar - at some point, but have given no specific details and no timeline for such a move.  

The yuan's exchange rate is almost entirely government-controlled and gyrates in a narrow band with a central point of around 8.28 yuan against the dollar. The Hong-Kong dollar is also pegged to the U.S. dollar under a currency board system in which the entire monetary base is backed with U.S. dollars, but the currency can occasionally deviate from that value.  

In late New York trading, the U.S. dollar was fetching HK$7.7815, compared to HK$7.7962 when trading opened. It was the lowest level for the dollar versus the Hong Kong currency since late February.  

During London trade, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority intervened in the currency markets to resist upward pressure on the Hong Kong dollar. The HKMA sold a total of HK$1.557 billion, buying around US$199.9 million.  

Ali Rada, of Radaforex, an independent interdealer broker in New York, said the Hong Kong dollar's surge could also be linked to the pending initial public offering of China Power International Development Ltd. (2380.HK), which is expected to make a strong debut on the Hong Kong stock exchange next week.  

Any revaluation of the yuan is widely seen as a positive for the region's currencies, including Hong Kong's dollar. Under that theory, other Asian governments would be more prone to allow their own currencies to appreciate if the yuan was also appreciating against the dollar.  

Though the Chinese government has given no specific plans for any revaluation, markets have recently taken rumors seriously as rhetoric from the Bush Administration has heated up ahead of the U.S. presidential election.  

Market watchers said that while speculators are placing bets based on the rumors, most analysts are dismissing the possibility of a near-term revaluation.  

'This is a very political issue, and it's being taken seriously,' said Tetsu Hisa Hayashi, Foreign Exchange Manager at Bank of Tokyo Mitsubishi in New York. 'But I have to say it is not so realistic. We think China would have given some information after last week's (Group of Seven) meeting if they did have near-term plans.'  

For the first time, China was a guest at the meeting of finance ministers from Group of Seven leading industrialzed nations last week in Washington.  

The rise in the Hong Kong dollar follows some similar action in related markets. China's yuan rose Friday in the offshore forwards market on the same news of Bush's conversation with Hu Jintao.  

In the Asian session, in the freely traded market for nondeliverable forwards, the dollar's one-year discount widened to 2475/2375, according to a late afternoon quote from Prebon Yamane, from 2150/2080 on Thursday.  

-Steven Vames; Dow Jones Newswires; 201-938-5063; steven.vames@dowjones.com  

(Jeff Meyer in Shanghai contributed to this report)

title: Dollar off vs Asia on persistent China speculation.
text:
NEW YORK, Oct 8 (Reuters) - The dollar tumbled across the board following a below-consensus U.S. jobs report on Friday, but the heaviest selling was against Asian currencies, amid mounting speculation that China could soon relax its currency controls.  

The dollar posted its biggest one-day loss in over a year against the yen; and despite intervention from the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, the Hong Kong dollar surged to its highest level since the end of February.  

"The euro is not the focus: it's Asia," said a senior trader at a large U.S. bank in New York.  

The dollar hit multi-month lows against several rivals on Friday - and in the case of the Canadian dollar, a new 11-year low - after the Labor Department said 96,000 new jobs were created last month. Economists had expected 148,000 new jobs.  

But the gains in most major currencies are being eclipsed by the sharp upticks in Asian currencies, particularly the yen.  

Around 1:00 p.m. EDT (1700 GMT) in New York, the dollar was trading around three-week lows of 109.39 yen , marking the biggest single-day drop since Sept. 22 last year, according to Reuters data.  

And the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA), the territory's central bank, intervened, selling HK$1.557 billion for U.S. dollars on Friday to maintain the Hong Kong currency's peg to the greenback.  

But "it doesn't seem to have done much good," the senior trader said, noting that the Hong Kong dollar was trading at HK$7.7819 per dollar. The currency is pegged at around HK$7.80 per dollar. Forward contracts also showed increased bets on some sort of upward revaluation.  

A major factor at play here is China and the mounting speculation that Beijing may soon loosen the peg keeping the yuan around 8.28 per dollar. Analysts generally expect any moves along these lines would strengthen the yuan and lead to Asian currency appreciation across the board.  

Chinese officials told the Group of Seven finance ministers and central bankers meeting in Washington last weekend that they remain on a path toward adopting a more flexible currency regime. But they also repeated they will proceed at their own pace and gave no timetable.  

Speculation, however, shows no sign of dissipating. A Korean newspaper reported China could revalue the yuan as soon as next week. And the White House confirmed on Thursday that forex was raised in President George W. Bush's telephone conversation with Chinese President Hu Jintao that day.  

"Speculation is building of a China revaluation," said a dealer at a Japanese bank in New York. This and the payrolls data were the two "triggers" that shot down the dollar on Friday, he added.

    Under Hong Kong's currency board system, the HKMA is
committed to defending the pegged rate of HK$7.80 by buying Hong

    Dealers said there was some profit taking on the U.S. dollar
in the wake of the HKMA intervention. But they expected the Hong
Kong dollar's bounce to be short-lived as investors would
continue to take advantage of comparatively higher U.S. interest
rates.
   


    "As long as Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates remain
below U.S. dollar rates, this provides an arbitrage trading
opportunity," one trader said.

amid heavy fund outflows triggered by arbitrage plays as Hong
Kong lags behind the United States in hiking interest rates.

because the banking system is awash with funds and on concerns
that higher rates could hobble weak loan growth in the city.
    Strong capital inflows to Hong Kong late last year boosted
bank liquidity. But the aggregate balance -- the sum of balances
on clearing accounts maintained by banks with the HKMA -- has
been declining in recent months, from a peak of HK$54.665 billion

told reporters on Thursday.

title: HK shares end slightly lower but retailers rise.
text:
HONG KONG, July 26 (Reuters) - Hong Kong's leading share index dropped a slight 0.27 percent on Monday, but retailers rose on hopes that they will win back some pricing power soon as the territory's six-year deflationary spiral comes to an end.  

China plays such as cement maker Anhui Conch fell on fears that corporate earnings would be hurt by measures to rein in the country's booming economy.  

The Hang Seng Index , which groups 33 blue-chip stocks, ended down 33.16 points at 12,319.83. Investor confidence was hurt after the U.S. benchmark Dow Jones industrial average fell below the key 10,000-point level.  

Turnover was HK$7.9 billion, making it this year's lightest day of trade, according to Reuters data.  

Intervention by Hong Kong's central bank to support the local currency on Friday also weighed on sentiment, indicating that more funds are leaving Hong Kong's equity market.  

Retailers such as Bossini International Ltd (0592.HK) jumped after the government said after the market close on Friday that Hong Kong prices were little changed in June from the previous month against a year earlier.  

"People think deflation is coming to an end," said Kenny Tang, associate director at Tung Tai Securities.  

Basic clothing retailer Bossini jumped 11.46 percent to HK$2.675, while women's clothing chain Moiselle International Ltd. (0130.HK) jumped 18.94 percent to HK$1.57 and Veeko International (1171.HK) climbed 13.82 percent to HK$0.28.  

But some brokers cautioned that trade on these second liners was speculative.  

Deflation robs companies of the ability to raise prices.  

Blue-chips were mixed. Bank of East Asia Ltd. (0023.HK) was up 0.88 percent at HK$22.85. It is forecast to report robust results on Friday, kicking off what is expected to be a strong first-half earnings season for Hong Kong companies.  

Cathay Pacific Airways Ltd (0293.HK) slipped 1.42 percent to HK$13.90 as investors speculated that a new air services agreement between China and the United States, signed over the weekend, could hurt Hong Kong-based airlines.  

The deal, which allows U.S. carriers greater access to Chinese cities, could result in less traffic being funnelled through Hong Kong, analysts said.  

CHINA PLAYS  

The Hang Seng China Enterprise Index , which groups Chinese firms listed here, dropped 1.09 percent to 4,301.64.  

China's largest cement maker Anhui Conch Cement Co. Ltd. (0914.HK) fell 2.44 percent to HK$8 after a Hong Kong newspaper quoted a company executive as saying its cement prices had declined by 20 percent in May and June against the first quarter this year.  

The executive attributed the decline to China's economic cooling measures.  

"They'll show excellent earnings growth for this half but it's concerns over future earnings that's affecting sentiment," said Alex Tang, research director at Core Pacific-Yamaichi International.  

Jiangxi Copper (0358.HK) fell 3.92 percent to HK$3.675, while Angang New Steel Co. Ltd. (0347.HK) shed 4.07 percent to HK$2.95.  

The China Securities Journal said on Monday the country's consumer inflation was likely to exceed five percent in the year through July. Central bank officials said earlier this year that China may need to raise interest rates if inflation hits five percent.  

Beijing Capital Land Ltd. (2868.HK) rose 3.76 percent to HK$1.93 after its proposed China domestic share issue was rejected by Chinese regulators. The news removed fears of a share dilution.  

However, some traders said overall sentiment remained optimistic with the Hang Seng ending off session lows.  

"There's strong support at the 12,000-to 12,200-points level, so I am quite confident," said Peter Lai, sales director at DBS Vickers Securities.

title: WEEK AHEAD-HK stocks seen up on high earnings expectation.
text:
HONG KONG, July 25 (Reuters) - Hong Kong stocks are seen rising this week, boosted by high expectations for earnings from Bank of East Asia, which kicks off the latest reporting season.  

But weak U.S. markets, hurt by disappointing earnings and high oil prices, may limit gains as investors eye further volatility on Wall Street.  

Bank of East Asia Ltd. (0023.HK), Hong Kong's fifth-largest lender, is expected to post strong interim earnings on Friday due to low provision charges.  

The results will also give a taste of earnings ahead from global bank and Hang Seng heavyweight HSBC Holdings Plc. (0005.HK), and its local unit Hang Seng Bank Ltd. (0011.HK).  

"Investors are expected to position themselves on hopes that blue chips will post upbeat earnings," said Linus Yip, strategist at First Shanghai Securities Ltd.  

A slew of smaller firms will also provide an early peek into the health of regional earnings including operators of the Peninsula hotel chain Hongkong and Shanghai Hotels Ltd (0045.HK), TV maker Skyworth Digital Holdings Ltd (0751.HK) and chip designer Solomon Systech (International) Ltd along with Internet firm TOM Online Inc. .  

Traders see the benchmark Hang Seng Index , which is heavily weighted toward banks and property, trading as high as 12,600.  

The Hang Seng gained 2.44 percent last week, closing at 12,352.09 on Friday.  

Property shares, such as Sun Hung Kai Properties (0016.HK) and property-heavy conglomerate Wharf Holdings (0004.HK) may gain further ground.  

"Property has recorded strong home sales over the past few weeks," said Lionel Kwok, chief investment officer at BOCI-Prudential Asset Management  

Investment bank J.P. Morgan expects office rents in prime business districts to rise by up to 40 percent this year due to strong demand and limited supply.  

Investors are also watching property companies that rent heavily sought after retail space such as Causeway Bay landlord Hysan Development Co. Ltd. (0014.HK).  

The firm's shares have more than doubled in the past year, but analysts are tempted by Hysan's modern shopping malls amid a retail boom spawned by a flood of mainland Chinese tourists.  

WALL STREET WEIGHS  

But an earnings-related rally is likely to be weighed down early in the week by a tumbled on Wall Street on Friday after disappointing earnings reports.  

More U.S. companies are set to report in the coming week. Investors are also nervously eyeing security concerns during the U.S. Democratic convention in Boston along with persistently high world oil prices which still hover above US$40 a barrel.  

The blue-chip Dow Jones industrial average fell for the fifth week in a row last week and closed below the key 10,000 level for the first time in two months.  

The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index notched a fresh low for the year on Friday, falling 2.12 percent to 1,849.28.  

Renewed signs that international investors are moving funds out of Hong Kong could also limit upside for Hong Kong shares.  

The territory's de facto central bank last week was seen intervening in the currency market to prop up the Hong Kong dollar, which is pegged to the U.S. unit.  

International fund flows are viewed as a key indicator for the Hong Kong market. A flood of money entered the territory late last year thanks to a weak U.S. dollar and high profile China IPO's, but traders said funds had been moving out of the territory in recent weeks due to lacklustre local stocks and arbitrage trades on higher U.S. interest rates.

title: HK stocks end 0.60 pct lower, China plays sag.
text:
HONG KONG, July 22 (Reuters) - Hong Kong stocks fell 0.60 percent on Thursday but still managed to hold above the key 12,300 points level after worries over slowing corporate earnings growth dragged Wall Street lower.  

The benchmark Hang Seng Index ended down 74.90 points at 12,320.21 after racking up gains of 270 points on Wednesday. Turnover was light at HK$9.6 billion (US$1.23 billion) - down from HK$14.5 billion on Wednesday.  

China plays suffered heavier losses than the broader market. The H-share index of Hong Kong-listed Chinese-registered firms fell 1.28 percent to 4,379.10, after running into stubborn resistance at the 4,400 level in the previous session.  

UBS said that a soft landing for China's economy would be insufficient to spur the sector further. It said a slowdown would not be enough to stem overinvestment and overcapacity, which have already spawned a poor industrial structure in the country.  

"The sector came under heavy selling pressure because news that the country may engineer a soft landing had overpowered China plays way too much in the past few sessions," said Alex Wong, a research director at Rexcapital Asset Management.  

Most blue chips ended in negative territory, led by tech plays after the U.S. tech board tumbled more than two percent.  

Ports-to-telecom conglomerate Hutchison Whampoa Ltd. (0013.HK), an index heavyweight, dipped 0.93 percent to HK$53.50. Local newspapers said Japanese electronics giant NEC Corp. is interested in buying stakes in the planned listing of Hutchison's emerging markets telecoms business.  

Other index majors also weighed on the market. China Mobile (Hong Kong) Ltd. (0941.HK) slipped 0.65 percent to HK$23.10 while HSBC Holdings Plc. (0005.HK) (HSBA.L) lost 0.43 percent to HK$116.  

China plays sagged, led by power firms on fears that high coal prices would hit their margins. Datang International Power Generation (0991.HK) lost 3.01 percent to HK$6.45 while Huadian Power (1071.HK) fell 2.375 percent to HK$2.375.  

FUND OUTFLOW FEARS  

Worries that more funds may leave Hong Kong also curbed investor sentiment.  

The local currency has been pressured in recent weeks after the U.S. raised interest rates at the end of June. Hong Kong banks left their rates unchanged, making U.S. dollar denominated investments more attractive.  

Market players have speculated funds may leave Hong Kong given the interest rate differential and the prospect that the spread may widen if the U.S. lifts rates further in August.  

But dealers dismissed worries of another meltdown reminiscent of the 1997 Asian financial crisis. They said there were no signs of unusually large short stock positions and that the outflow of funds from Hong Kong was merely arbitrage trade.  

During the Asian financial crisis, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority intervened heavily in the stock and currency markets to foil speculators who had simultaneously attacked the Hong Kong dollar and taken short positions in stocks and futures to benefit from falling stock prices.  

"Unlike 1998 when financial markets were rattled by a weak Hong Kong currency and property market, our economy is now riding on healthy retail, tourism and real estate sectors. Interest rates are also low," said Francis Kwok, director at Peace Town Securities Ltd.  

Meanwhile, shares in Hong Kong property developer Far East Consortium International Ltd. (0035.HK) bucked the market downtrend, jumping 10.67 percent to HK$1.66 after the firm said it planned to sell a property in the heart of Kowloon for HK$468.8 million.  

Shares of ship chartering and00Jewellery chain operator Hang Fung Gold Technology Ltd. (0870.HK) tumbled 11.33 percent to HK$1.33 after the firm posted a 26 percent drop in full year earnings during the midday break.

title: REPEAT/ CENTRAL BANK  WATCH:HKMA Rule Deters Rate Arbitrage
text:
By Raymond Tsoi 
 
   A Dow Jones Newswires Column 
   

HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--For months, Hong Kong banks have left their huge hoard of excess funds idle, rather than parking the money in U.S. dollars and earning 1%.  

Even the prospect of the Federal Reserve raising its federal funds target rate from the 46-year low of 1% as soon as the end of this month isn't enticing bankers who say they worry more about foreign exchange risks - a threat that has at its roots, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority's own policies.  

"Banks need to balance interest rate concerns and foreign exchange risk," said Dai Daohua, economist of Bank of China (Hong Kong), pointing out the latter now appears to be the bigger risk.  

A money trader with a local bank added "the higher U.S. dollar interest rate is inadequate to cover foreign exchange risk if the Hong Kong dollar surges again."  

"It takes one full year to earn that extra one percent, but that profit can be wiped out in a day if the exchange rate moves sharply against you," the trader said, referring to the rollover of short term funds for a full year to earn the 1%.  

The Hong Kong dollar is pegged at HK$7.80 to the U.S. dollar, but in reality, trades in a very narrow, accepted range around it. Under its currency board system, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority is obliged to buy the local unit at that rate. This essentially puts a floor to the Hong Kong dollar, but theoretically not a ceiling as there is no provision to cap the local unit at a specific level when it strengthens - what is known locally as "strong side undertaking."  


 
   Proxy For China Yuan 
   

During the 1997-1998 regional crisis, falling Asian currencies exerted strong pressure on the Hong Kong dollar to do likewise, but the latter stayed supported by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, the territory's de facto central bank. More recently, however, the local currency faces a different threat as foreign exchange participants use it as a proxy to the China yuan, buying it up whenever speculation mounts the Chinese authorities are ready for an appreciation of the yuan.  

This was what happened last September when the international pressure gathered after the Group of Seven industrialized nations called for more flexible exchange rates - interpreted as an euphemism for a stronger Chinese yuan, and hence, the Hong Kong dollar. At the same time, the territory faced a deluge of funds anticipating a recovery in Hong Kong's stock and property markets.  

The Hong Kong dollar suddenly strengthened well beyond its usual narrow range around the HK$7.80 peg rate.  

The Hong Kong Monetary Authority subsequently injected over HK$50 billion into the market to ease the upward pressure on the local unit. Today, much of that money remains in the territory's banking system. The aggregate balance, a measure of interbank liquidity, stood at over HK$35 billion Tuesday, compared with its usual historical level of about HK$1 billion. That large amount of idle funds in the interbank market has kept short-term interest rates near zero percent.  

The Hong Kong Monetary Authority has tried - unsuccessfully - to cajole banks to deposit the local dollars in U.S. dollars, with the authority's Chief Executive Joseph Yam pointing out that the one full percentage point interest rate earned on overnight funds was no small opportunity cost for large sums - which are what the banks are holding.  

But banks remain wary, arguing that the risks stack up against them as long the Hong Kong Monetary Authority is vague about its currency policy regarding the upside limit of the Hong Kong dollar.  

The rush of funds into Hong Kong last year caught most currency players by surprise. The Hong Kong dollar strengthened to around HK$7.70 to the U.S. dollar within days, forcing many scrambling to cover their short positions with deep losses.  


 
   Wary Of Sharp Rise In HK Dollar 
   

"Such unpleasant memory kept players highly wary of the possibility the Hong Kong dollar can rise sharply on big fund inflows," the trader said, adding that "the flow of funds is highly unpredictable."  

The Hong Kong Monetary Authority did later intervene to stabilize the market, and it has said it will act as needed to prevent volatility on the strong side of the peg.  

But it has stayed ambiguous over what it considers an excessively strong level for the currency.  

Hong Kong Monetary Authority's Yam, for instance, has repeatedly said he sees no need to create a strong side undertaking. He argues that kind of commitment would be undesirable because it would encourage speculators to short the Hong Kong dollar if the outlook on the city's economy suddenly turns bearish.  

"To fix a level to sell the Hong Kong dollar will enable speculators to calculate their costs and risks (precisely)," Yam told legislators recently.  

For banks, that will be enough for them to shy away from the idea of converting their excess interbank funds into U.S. dollars, and short term rates will continue to hover near zero.  

For now, the low rates have given Hong Kong's recovering economy an extra kick, helping to encourage domestic consumption and investment.  

The city posted a 6.8% year-on-year expansion in gross domestic product in the first quarter of 2004, as domestic consumption picked up, adding to growth in exports and tourism. The worst seems to be over for weak domestic appetite, with the composite consumer price index bottoming in the third quarter of last year. The territory still faces declining prices although the falls are moderating. April CPI registered a 1.5% fall from the year before.  

Economists warn though that the abnormally low rate environment, if it is allowed to continue for a lengthy period, could lead to problems. Asset bubbles may result from excessive speculation.  


   -By Raymond Tsoi, Dow Jones Newswires; 852-2802-7002; raymond.tsoi@dowjones.com 
   (Raymond Tsoi is a reporter at Dow Jones Newswires' Hong Kong bureau. He has reported on money market for the last two years.)

The Hong Kong Monetary Authority has tried - unsuccessfully - to cajole banks to deposit the local dollars in U.S. dollars, with the authority's Chief Executive Joseph Yam pointing out that the one full percentage point interest rate earned on overnight funds was no small opportunity cost for large sums - which are what the banks are holding.  

But banks remain wary, arguing that the risks stack up against them as long the Hong Kong Monetary Authority is vague about its currency policy regarding the upside limit of the Hong Kong dollar.  

The rush of funds into Hong Kong last year caught most currency players by surprise. The Hong Kong dollar strengthened to around HK$7.70 to the U.S. dollar within days, forcing many scrambling to cover their short positions with deep losses.  


 
   Wary Of Sharp Rise In HK Dollar 
   

"Such unpleasant memory kept players highly wary of the possibility the Hong Kong dollar can rise sharply on big fund inflows," the trader said, adding that "the flow of funds is highly unpredictable."  

The Hong Kong Monetary Authority did later intervene to stabilize the market, and it has said it will act as needed to prevent volatility on the strong side of the peg.  

But it has stayed ambiguous over what it considers an excessively strong level for the currency.  

Hong Kong Monetary Authority's Yam, for instance, has repeatedly said he sees no need to create a strong side undertaking. He argues that kind of commitment would be undesirable because it would encourage speculators to short the Hong Kong dollar if the outlook on the city's economy suddenly turns bearish.  

"To fix a level to sell the Hong Kong dollar will enable speculators to calculate their costs and risks (precisely)," Yam told legislators recently.  

For banks, that will be enough for them to shy away from the idea of converting their excess interbank funds into U.S. dollars, and short term rates will continue to hover near zero.  

For now, the low rates have given Hong Kong's recovering economy an extra kick, helping to encourage domestic consumption and investment.  

The city posted a 6.8% year-on-year expansion in gross domestic product in the first quarter of 2004, as domestic consumption picked up, adding to growth in exports and tourism. The worst seems to be over for weak domestic appetite, with the composite consumer price index bottoming in the third quarter of last year. The territory still faces declining prices although the falls are moderating. April CPI registered a 1.5% fall from the year before.  

Economists warn though that the abnormally low rate environment, if it is allowed to continue for a lengthy period, could lead to problems. Asset bubbles may result from excessive speculation.

title: HK stocks seen pressured by weak global markets.
text:
HONG KONG, May 18 (Reuters) - Hong Kong stocks are expected to face further selling pressure on Tuesday, although a technical rebound after recent sharp declines may lift the benchmark index initially.   

The blue-chip Hang Seng Index fell 2.74 percent on Monday to 10,967.65.   

Traders said the index had support at 10,800 although getting back above the 11,000 level would prove difficult given weak global market conditions.   

A list of factors have hurt global stock market sentiment including global security fears, high oil prices, anticipation of a U.S. interest rate hike and an overheating Chinese economy.   

"All these factors will continue to dominate in the short term," said Ben Kwong, associate director at KGI Asia Ltd.   

U.S. stocks stumbled on Monday after the killing of a key figure in Iraq's new government heightened investor worries about global security and helped send oil prices to fresh record highs.   

The blue-chip Dow Jones industrial average fell 1.06 percent to 9,907, while the tech heavy Nasdaq Composite Index lost 1.45 percent to 1,877.   

Asian markets showed signs of a slight rebound early on Tuesday after a sharp regional sell off on Monday.   

Japan's benchmark Nikkei average opened firmer on after the country's first quarter growth figures came in stronger than expected.   

Taiwan shares also opened slightly firmer on Tuesday after a sharp drop on Monday.   

Investors will be on the look out for further signs that funds are moving out of the Asia region.   

Hong Kong's de facto central bank intervened in the market late on Monday afternoon in order to maintain the Hong Kong dollar peg to the U.S. currency. Traders say funds are moving money back into U.S. dollar-denominated money market funds in anticipation of a U.S. rate rise as early as next month with funds squaring positions in Hong Kong blue chips and China plays after solid gains.   

Investors will also watching for further macroeconomic measures to cool China's surging economy.   

China will continue to control bank loans and money supply, and actively studying means, such as interest rate hikes, to rein its economic growth, central bank monetary policy committee member Li Yang said on Monday.   

Li said if consumer prices moved above five percent the government may raise interest rates, though under current conditions he believed China would not raise rates in the next six months.   

China shares traded in New York were hammered overnight.   

Asia's largest oil refiner Sinopec Corp (0386.HK) (SNP.N) fell 8.19 percent to US$32.08, while China's largest oil producer PetroChina Co Ltd (0857.HK) (PTR.N) lost 5.71 percent to US$41.63.   

China Eastern Airlines Ltd (CEA.N) (0670.HK) fell 5.14 percent to US$16.79.

title: HK stocks knocked by China overheating, high oil prices.
text:
HONG KONG, May 17 (Reuters) - Leading Hong Kong shares ended sharply lower on Monday, tapping fresh year lows as investors worried that China's economy may be overheating and global oil prices hit new record highs.   

Hong Kong shadowed other regional stocks markets which were all bruised by a rising U.S. dollar and a highly anticipated interest rate hike in the U.S. next month, encouraging funds flows out of Asia in favour of dollar-denominated assets.   

"These factors are all negative for the region and unfortunately they are all happening at the same time," said Aaron Pong, investment director at Standard Life Investments.   

The benchmark Hang Seng Index ended down 2.74 percent, or 309.21 points, at 10,967.65.   

Volume was above recent averages with HK$16.13 billion (US$2.06 billion) changing hands.   

Shares in China registered companies listed in Hong Kong were particularly hard hit with commodity stocks such as Yanzhou Coal (1171.HK), Asia oil refining giant Sinopec Corp (0386.HK) (SNP.N) and top Chinese oil producer PetroChina (0857.HK) (PTR.N) all falling by more than five percent.   

Hong Kong blue-chip property and interest-rate sensitive financial stocks such as Sun Hung Kai Properties (0016.HK) and the Bank of China's Hong Kong arm, BOC Hong Kong (Holdings) Ltd (2388.HK), also tumbled. Sun Hung Kai fell 5.3 percent and BOCHK dropped nearly seven percent.   

FUNDS LEAVING ASIA   

Crude oil hit a new all-time high of US$41.64 a barrel in electronic trade on Monday, fuelling fresh inflation fears and sending stocks lower across Asia.   

Traders also cited fresh evidence of international funds selling Asia stocks in favour of U.S. money market assets.   

Hong Kong's de facto central bank intervened in the market late on Monday afternoon in order to maintain the Hong Kong dollar peg to the U.S. currency.   

"Right now a lot of regional funds are trying to clean up their portfolio. They are aggressively removing second-tier stocks," said Herbert Lau, research director of Celestial Asia Securities.   

Investors also cited frustration with the lack of direction on China's plans to cool its economy.   

Chinese Vice Finance Minister Li Yong on Monday warned against applying the brakes too strongly on his country's racing economy.   

Li, who oversees financial reform, repeated the government's target for seven percent growth this year, but did not say how the country would get there.   

"Authorities continue to focus on administrative policy and I think this gives investors the feeling that the policy plan is still being adjusted on a day-to-day basis," Pong said.   

Chinese authorities have restricted lending to some industries and told local officials to forego new development zones for manufacturing.   

But some investors believe Beijing will eventually move to raise lending rates in China for the first time in nine years.   

The H-share index of China registered companies listed in Hong Kong fell 5.36 percent to 3,546.25.   

PROPERTY SUFFERS   

Hong Kong property stocks took a further battering on signs that activity in the city's property sector is cooling after at least six months of strong buying activity.   

The Hang Seng properties sub index fell 4.76 percent to 12,809.35.   

Shares in global bank global bank HSBC Holdings (0005.HK) fell 0.9 percent to HK$109.50 after three small bombs exploded outside branches of HSBC branches in Turkey on Sunday ahead of a visit by British Prime Minister Tony Blair. HSBC makes up one-third of the weighting of the benchmark Hang Seng Index.   

Free to air broadcaster Television Broadcasts Ltd (TVB) (0511.HK) was the biggest blue chip loser of the day, sliding nearly 12 percent following media reports over the weekend that the firm was suffering further delays in its bid to secure broadcasting rights in mainland China.   

Traders said market was looking oversold with the 10,800 level expected to provide some support for the Hang Seng on Tuesday.

title: HK stocks seen range trading, fund flow worries persist.
text:
HONG KONG, May 13 (Reuters) - Hong Kong stocks are expected to track sideways on Thursday with investors sharing global concerns over high oil prices and escalating Middle East violence while eyeing fund flows out of the territory.   

But badly bruised China plays may get a boost from the latest measures announced to tame China's sizzling economy, after the central bank said late on Wednesday that it will expand open-market operations from once to twice-weekly.   

Investors are on alert for a raft of possible measures China may implement to cool economic growth of 9.7 percent.   

Speaking in Dublin on Wednesday, Chinese Premier Wen Jiabao expressed concern about the pace of investment growth in some sectors of the economy as well as the over-expansion in money supply.   

The blue chip Hang Seng Index gained a slim 0.17 percent on Wednesday, closing at 11,528.18.   

Investors will also be on watch for further signs that funds are leaving Hong Kong after the city's de facto central bank intervened repeatedly on Wednesday to maintain the Hong Kong dollar peg to the U.S. currency.   

"That will continue to make investors a little worried. We need some positive news." said Ben Kwong, associate director at KGI Asia Ltd.   

Wall Street was mixed with bargain hunting setting in despite persistent worries about skyrocketing oil prices, rising interest rates and violence in Iraq. The blue-chip Dow Jones industrial average ended up 0.26 percent at 10,045.16, after tumbling by nearly 1.5 percent by midday. The tech heavy Nasdaq Composite Index fell 0.30 percent to 1,925.59.   

Oil prices settled in New York at their highest level ever at US$40.77 a barrel due to worries over escalating violence in the Middle East and a worries about inventory levels of gasoline heading into the summer driving season.   

China oil stocks traded in New York, however, put in a mixed performance.   

China's largest oil producer PetroChina Co Ltd (0857.HK) (PTR.N) fell 0.84 percent to US$44.67.   

Asia's largest oil refiner Sinopec Corp (SNP.N) (0386.HK) rose 1.01 percent to US$34.90.   

Hong Kong's Cathay Pacific Airways Ltd (0293.HK), the world's third largest airline by market value, said on Wednesday it was considering a fuel surcharge on ticket prices because of surging oil prices.   

"I'd say strong oil prices are here for the balance of the year," Cathay Chairman James Hughes-Hallett told reporters after the airline's annual general meeting.   

"It (a fuel surcharge) is under active review at the moment," he added.   

Hughes-Hallett said that should jet fuel prices remain high it would affect the airline in an "unfavourable way", adding that fuel accounts for 20 percent of operating costs.

title: Asian Stocks End Mixed; Techs, Car Makers Sink Tokyo
text:
A Wall Street Journal Online News Roundup   

Shares across the Asian-Pacific region closed mixed Monday. Concerns over the weakness of the dollar hurt tech stocks and car makers in Tokyo. Hong Kong and China markets rose on expectations of good earnings reports.  

Tokyo's benchmark stock index sank to a six-week low, as the dollar's slide against the yen and the approaching March 31 fiscal-year end prompted investors to sell technology and exporter blue chips.  

The Nikkei Stock Average of 225 issues closed down 58.31 points, or 0.6%, at 10402.61, after having risen more than 100 points earlier.  

The dollar was trading at 105.55 yen in Tokyo late Monday, down 49 yen from late Friday in Tokyo and also below the 105.91 yen it bought in New York later that day.  

Stocks were initially buoyed by signs that Tokyo had won concessions from G-7 nations at their weekend meeting to halt the yen's surge.  

Technology blue chips NTT DoCoMo and Fujitsu, auto makers Toyota Motor and Honda Motor. Major banks were mostly lower. UFJ Holdings slipped 0.2% and Mizuho Financial lost 1.7%.  

Sony added 1.2% and Canon edged up 0.4%.  

In a joint statement at the end of a two-day meeting in Boca Raton, Florida, G-7 finance officials said they support "more flexibility" in currency markets, but also noted concerns about "excess volatility and disorderly movements in exchange rates." The statement appeared to both endorse U.S. dollar's recent dive against major currencies while warning that Japan and European countries might intervene to hold the dollar steady.  

Hong Kong shares advanced Monday as hopes of upbeat earnings news from blue chips drove the key index sharply higher for the second consecutive session.  

The blue-chip Hang Seng Index ended up 267.08 points, or 2%, at 13576.68. The broader S&P/HKEx LargeCap finished ahead 313.29 points at 14945.28.  

"Investors are expecting good news from blue chips. Improved earnings can also help to lower the price-to-earnings ratio of Hong Kong shares," said Mark Wan, head of research at Tanrich Financial Group.  

Analysts are expecting much-improved earnings for Hong Kong companies on a recovering domestic economy. Blue chips Bank of East Asia and Esprit Holdings will kick off the reporting season this week. Bank of East Asia climbed 1.8%. Most of its banking peers also gained. HSBC Holdings rose 1.6%, Hang Seng Bank rose 1.4%, and BOC Hong Kong finished 2.8% higher. Fashion retail Esprit Holdings rose 3.6%, lifted by expectation a strong euro will continue to help its Europe-based operations.  

All but one of the 33 blue chips rose, with laggards producing the strongest gains. CITIC Pacific jumped 6%, while fixed-line telecom operator PCCW rose 4.1%.  

China's shares ended higher, with the benchmark Shanghai Composite Index closing above 1700 for the first time in eighteen months on hopes more foreign money could flow into the stock market.  

The Shanghai Securities News reported Monday that so-called qualified foreign institutional investors were looking to increase their investments in the stock market, and that UBS may ask for its investment quota in China to be raised. UBS declined to comment.  

The benchmark Shanghai Composite Index, which tracks both A and B shares, rose 1.5% to close at 1703.53. It was the highest level for the index since July 19, 2002. The Shenzhen Composite Index gained 2.1% to end at 435.75.  

Retail stocks led the gainers after Nanjing Xinjiekou Department Store said a company called Huamei became its second largest shareholder by buying shares in the secondary market. Analysts said Huamei, also based in Nanjing, could help restructure Xinjiekou, giving investors hope other retailers could be restructured in the future.  

Shanghai No.1 Department Store rose by the 10% daily limit, Shanghai Hualian also rose 10%, and Nanjing Xinjiekou Department Store rose 2.3%.  

The Australian share market closed 0.5% higher, supported by gains on Wall Street and a quarterly statement from the Reserve Bank of Australia. The star performers were market heavyweight News Corp. and resource and banking stocks.  

The benchmark S&P/ASX 200 closed 14.9 points higher at 3287.1.  

The Australian central bank's quarterly statement on monetary policy Monday painted a positive picture of domestic and global growth. News Corp., which generates 77% of its revenue in the U.S., rose 1.2% although volume was light ahead of the media group's second quarter and first half results due Thursday.

title: HKMA's Yam says no limit on HK dlr  intervention .
text:
HONG KONG, Jan 19 (Reuters) - The Hong Kong Monetary Authority, which has repeatedly sold local dollars in the recent months to stabilise the currency, said on Monday there was no limit on the amount of intervention if needed.    

 "There are, of course, large numbers (of interventions) but there is no limit as to how large they can become," HKMA Chief Executive Joseph Yam told a luncheon.    

 The Hong Kong dollar is pegged to the U.S. dollar at HK$7.80 per dollar.    

 But the HKMA has had to intervene regularly since late September to keep it close to that level, buying U.S. dollars and selling local dollars.    

 The Hong Kong dollar has strengthened amid strong demand from overseas investors as the local stock market rallies and the territory's economic recovery accelerates.    

 Some dealers said the local currency was likely to remain strong in anticipation of more 'hot money' flowing into the territory, given that a number of Chinese firms are planning initial public offerings on the Hong Kong bourse this year.    

 The local unit  eased to 7.7660/61 at 0350 GMT on Monday morning, compared with 7.7632/33 on Friday in Asian trade.    

 Yam said the HKMA's interventions have totalled US$6.7 billion.    

 "There is no limit to the amount of domestic money that can be created if the demand is there," he said.    

 The HKMA could issue more exchange fund paper to mop up a large pool of Hong Kong dollars in the aggregate balance.    

 "(We have) an open mind on this possibility," Yam said.    

 He also said currency stability is essential to the proper function of the economy and monetary policy.    

 Speculation that China will widen its currency band has also prompted some players to take positios on the Hong Kong dollar.    

 But Yam said he did not see the need for an appreciation of China's yuan exchange rate.    

 China is running a current account surplus, which is less than one percent of gross domestic product, and is shrinking under the influence of the World Trade Organisation, indicating that there is nothing fundamentally wrong with the level of its exchange rate, he said.    

 "There is no need to mess around with the exchange rate," he added.

title: INTERVIEW-HK dlr peg architect defends it, sees no change.
text:
SINGAPORE, Jan 16 (Reuters) - John Greenwood, the economist credited with designing the Hong Kong dollar peg, on Friday rejected criticism that the currency had caused the city's economic troubles and said he saw no need to change the system.    

 "Fundamentally, there is no need for the HK dollar peg to be revalued or devalued," said Greenwood, the chief economist of London-based INVESCO Asset Management Ltd and a member of the Hong Kong Monetary Authority's currency board.    

 "The desire to repeg represents a misunderstanding of the way in which the mechanism is designed to operate," he told Reuters.    

 In 1983 the Hong Kong Monetary Authority adopted Greenwood's suggestion that the Hong Kong dollar's  value be fixed against the U.S. dollar.    

 The Hong Kong dollar rate was steady near 7.75 until 1999, and then near 7.8 per U.S. dollar until September 2003, when speculation on a revaluation pushed the currency above 7.7 per dollar.    

 Prices for the Hong Kong dollar in the forward market  imply further appreciation.    

 Greenwood dismissed the idea that the currency needed a lower peg or to trade freely, either to resolve economic problems or to mimick any revaluation of the Chinese yuan .    

 Also, undesirable political interference tended to come with the different types of managed exchange rate bands that other Asian economies had adopted, he said.    

 "The Singapore way has been supported in the past by some degree of controls either on balance sheets or directing of savings or restrictions on certain types of capital and derivative transactions," Greenwood said.    

 "Hong Kong has never had those sort of controls and Hong Kong does not want to go down that route. The background is different and the objective is to keep markets very open and very liquid."    

 THE ECONOMY SWAYS    

 Hong Kong's economy and prices had in the past made the adjustments needed to keep the peg steady, he said.    

 "The mechanism is very strong. There is no reason why the Hong Kong dollar should move if the renminbi is changed."    

 The peg has been regarded as the pillar of the Hong Kong economy, the world's 27th largest in 2002 if counted separately from China's, and as a necessity for its open, service-based structure. But critics blame the peg for the territory's five years of deflation and high joblessness.    

 Greenwood defends his brainchild fiercely. Circumstances have been extraordinarily harsh, he says.    

 "The system wasn't really designed to take into account 40 to 50 percent devaluations of its neighbours," he said, referring to Asia's financial crisis in 1997/98.    

 "And the dramatic opening of China would have required very significant (economic) adjustments in any case. The fact that those two things came together has intensified the difficulty of the past five-six years."    

 LONG LIFE    

 Still, Greenwood said, the Hong Kong peg had been a success until the crisis and there was no reason it could not salvage that reputation.    

 Besides, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority was pumping cash into the economy by intervening in the foreign exchange market, buying US$7 billion in the past four months to push Hong Kong dollar back down towards 7.8 per dollar.    

 This would drive interest rates lower, encourage borrowing and stimulate greater activity, he said.    

 Greeenwood said the Hong Kong dollar need not always be anchored to the U.S. dollar and that the yuan might make a good choice when it became convertible.    

 But the peg would stay.    

 "I was criticised initially for saying this system will be around for many decades," Greenwood said.    

 "It has lasted for two decades. As long as the economy is flexible and can adjust to the exchange rate, it doesn't really matter whether the economy is in the era of sailing ships, battle ships or space ships."

text:
HONG KONG, Jan 13 (Reuters) - The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA), the territory's central bank, sold HK$737 million and bought U.S. dollars on Tuesday afternoon in its latest move to try and weaken the local currency.   

Real time information available on Reuters page showed the transaction at 0730 GMT.   

The Hong Kong dollar was trading at 7.7631 per U.S. dollar soon after the intervention versus 7.7630/31 earlier in the day.   

The Hong Kong dollar is pegged to the U.S. dollar at HK$7.80 per dollar. However, the HKMA has had to intervene regularly in recent months to keep it close to that level and offset strong demand for Hong Kong dollars by investors amid growing signs of economic recovery in the territory.

title: HKMA Sells HK$737 Mln Tuesday In Latest  Intervention
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--The Hong Kong Monetary Authority sold HK$737 million Tuesday, buying about US$95 million, as it continued its regular market activities to stabilize the Hong Kong dollar's exchange rate.  

After the sale, the U.S. dollar was quoted at HK$7.7628, unchanged from its level earlier in the day. The discount on Hong Kong dollar forwards was also largely unmoved, with the one-year contract quoted at 775 to 755 below the spot rate.  

The HKMA also sold HK$4.17 billion in similar interventions Monday. Including Tuesday's sale, it has sold nearly HK$47 billion into the market since late September, when the Hong Kong dollar's strength first prompted the moves.  

Traders said the recent HKMA sales are merely offsetting massive, ongoing capital inflows seeking to profit from the city's share rally and recovering property prices.  

Despite the HKMA's efforts, a return by the local currency to its peg rate of HK$7.80 to the U.S. dollar is unlikely until those strong fund inflows into Hong Kong reverse, traders said.  

One main consequence of the fund inflows has been a surge in interbank liquidity, pushing local interest rates to historical low levels near zero.  

-By Andrew Batson, Dow Jones Newswires; 852-2802-7002; andrew.batson@dowjones.com  

-Edited by John Viljoen

title: WRAP: HKMA Sells HK$1.59 Bln In Tuesday  Interventions
text:

Since the Hong Kong dollar first strengthened beyond its peg rate of HK$7.80 to the U.S. dollar in late September, the HKMA has sold more than HK$50 billion in the markets, including Tuesday's transactions, to stem the local unit's rise. The sales are now happening nearly every day: the HKMA sold HK$4.17 billion Monday in similar transactions.  

After the last of Tuesday's sales, the U.S. dollar was quoted around HK$7.7630, still within its recent tight range. Traders said the HKMA appears to be selling Hong Kong dollars to prevent the currency from moving any higher than that level.  

But since the HKMA's sales are just offsetting large purchases of the currency by investors interested in the rising local stock and property markets, they are mainly preventing swings in the exchange rate rather than pushing it back toward the peg.  

A return to the peg rate is unlikely until the strong fund inflows to Hong Kong reverse, traders say. And with investor interest still strong, that isn't expected to happen any time soon.  

Though its currency is pegged to the U.S. dollar, Hong Kong's system doesn't prevent the local unit from strengthening if, as at present, there are large and continuing flows of funds into Hong Kong dollar assets.  

The main consequence of the HKMA's sales to ease the currency's strength has been a surge in interbank liquidity, which is pushing down local interest rates to historical lows near zero.

title: Bank of China HK cuts savings rate in liquid market.
text:
HONG KONG, Jan 12 (Reuters) - Bank of China (Hong Kong) Ltd (2388.HK) said on Monday it would cut its local currency savings deposit rate to 0.001 percent from 0.01 percent, the latest such move amid a flood of liquidity in the city's banking system.   

The rate reduction on Hong Kong dollar accounts is effective Tuesday and would apply only to savings accounts with daily balances of HK$10,000 (US$1,282) or above. Accounts with lower balances would earn no interest, the bank said in a statement.   

Accounts with daily balances of HK$200,000 or above will enjoy a bonus rate of 0.005 percent per annum.   

The bank's shares fell 1.34 percent to end at HK$14.70 in Hong Kong on Monday.   

The interest rate reduction followed similar cuts made on Monday by HSBC Holdings Plc's (0005.HK) (HSBA.L) Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corp Ltd, Hang Seng Bank Ltd (0011.HK) and Bank of East Asia Ltd (0023.HK).   

Hong Kong's banking system is awash with liquidity as foreign investors pile into the city's stock market and park cash there for investments in booming mainland China.   

The territory's central bank has repeatedly intervened in money markets in recent months, selling Hong Kong dollars in a bid to curb growing spot market strength in the local currency, which is pegged to the U.S. dollar.

title: WRAP: HKMA Sells HK$1.64 Bln Monday In  Interventions
text:

title: HKMA Sells Another HK$854 Mln In Day's 2nd  Intervention
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--The Hong Kong Monetary Authority sold another HK$854 million, buying about US$110 million, in its second intervention Monday to stabilize the local currency.  

The latest sale brings the day's total to HK$1.24 billion, which would buy about US$160 million. But the additional injection of funds didn't have any immediate effect on the currency in the spot and forward markets.  

After the sale, the U.S. dollar was quoted at HK$7.7628, still within its recent tight range around HK$7.7630. Currency traders expect the HKMA to continue to sell Hong Kong dollars as needed to prevent the local unit from strengthening beyond that level.  

Since the Hong Kong dollar first strengthened beyond its peg rate of HK$7.80 to the U.S. dollar in late September, the HKMA has sold HK$46 billion in the markets, including Monday's transactions, to ease the local unit's rise.  

Traders said the HKMA's sales of Hong Kong dollars are primarily offsetting large purchases of the currency by investors seeking to profit from the recent strong performance of local stocks and rising Hong Kong property prices. Some buyers of Hong Kong dollars are also speculating on the possible appreciation of the Chinese yuan.  

Though the currency is pegged to the U.S. dollar, the system doesn't prevent the local unit from strengthening if, as at present, there are large and continuing flows of funds into Hong Kong dollar assets.  

While the HKMA's sales can help prevent dramatic swings in the exchange rate in this situation, a return to the peg rate is unlikely until the strong fund inflows reverse, traders said.  

-By Andrew Batson, Dow Jones Newswires; 852-2802-7002; andrew.batson@dowjones.com

title: UPDATE 1-Bank of East Asia, Hang Seng cut HK savings rates.
text:
HONG KONG, Jan 10 (Reuters) - Hong Kong's Bank of East Asia Ltd (0023.HK) and Hang Seng Bank Ltd (0011.HK) announced on Saturday lower local currency deposit rates amid a flood of liquidity in the city's banking system.   

The banks said separately they would cut their savings rates for Hong Kong dollar deposits to 0.001 percent from 0.01 percent, with effect from Monday.   

Their moves tracked that of HSBC Holdings Plc (0005.HK) (HSBA.L) announced on Friday, and may be followed by other Hong Kong lenders.   

Bank of East Asia, the territory's fifth-largest lender, said in a statement the new rate would apply to accounts with balances of HK$5,000 (US$641) or more, while accounts with less than that amount will get no interest, as before.   

Hang Seng Bank, the local unit of HSBC, said the new rate would apply to deposits of HK$10,000 or more, while those below that amount will receive no interest.   

Shares in Bank of East Asia closed at HK$24.70 on Friday, having gained about 14 percent in the past three months. Hang Seng shares ended at HK$102.50, and had added more than six percent during the same period.   

Hong Kong's banking system is awash with liquidity as foreign investors pile into the city's stock market and park cash there for investments in booming mainland China.   

The territory's central bank has repeatedly intervened in money markets in recent months, selling Hong Kong dollars in a bid to curb growing spot market strength in the local currency, which is pegged to the U.S. dollar.   

The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) has sold HK$11.45 billion this week alone, bringing the aggregate balance - a key measure of interbank liquidity - to nearly HK$44 billion. (US$1=HK$7.8).

title: UPDATE 3-HSBC cuts HK savings rate amid liquidity flood.
text:
HONG KONG, Jan 9 (Reuters) - HSBC Holdings Plc (0005.HK) (HSBA.L) on Friday announced a steep cut in Hong Kong dollar deposits rates amid a flood of liquidity, a move that may spark similar cuts by other banks and stoked fears of negative rates.  

HSBC's local arm, the Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corp Ltd (Hongkong Bank), said in a statement it would cut its savings rate in Hong Kong for local dollar deposits to 0.001 percent from 0.01 percent, effective on Monday.  

It did not rule out negative interest rates for local currency deposits in the future.  

The new rate will apply to accounts with balances of HK$10,000 (US$1,282) or more. Depositors with less than that will get nothing, as before.  

However, Hongkong Bank said it would not change its best lending rate, currently 5.0 percent.  

HSBC shares added 0.8 percent to end at HK$126.50 in Hong Kong on Friday.  

No official at the bank was immediately available for comment but analysts said the savings rate cut was prompted by the ample liquidity in the banking system.  

"I think it (the unexpected HSBC cut) mainly reflects high liquidity," said Tony Liu, an analyst at DBS Securities.  

"The HIBOR rate has been very weak in the past quarter," he said, referring to the Hong Kong interbank offered rate.  

Hong Kong's banking system is awash with money as foreign investors pile into its surging stock market and park cash for investments in booming mainland China.  

The territory's central bank has also repeatedly intervened in money markets in recent months, selling Hong Kong dollars in a bid to curb growing spot market strength in the local currency, which is pegged to the U.S. dollar.  

The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) has so far sold HK$11.45 billion this week alone, bringing the aggregate balance - a key measure of interbank liquidity - to nearly HK$44 billion.  

"When a bank cuts its interest rates, other banks may follow suit," Peter Wong, chairman of the Hong Kong Association of Banks, told reporters.  

However, Liu said other banks may not wish to follow suit to keep customers. He noted HSBC traditionally had the lowest savings rates of Hong Kong banks given its dominant market position.  

In view of the large balances held in banks' clearing accounts with the HKMA, the central bank has warned that it might impose a charge on large balances "in extreme or exceptional circumstances".  

"If the HKMA imposes a punitive charge, we will consider passing it onto customers," Raymond Or, general manager of Hongkong Bank, told reporters. Transferring that charge to customers could lead to negative savings rates.  

However, the HKMA said later on Friday it had no current plan to impose such charges on banks.  

"The HKMA currently does not envisage the need to introduce such deposit charges," an HKMA spokesman told Reuters.

title: UPDATE 1-HSBC cuts HK savings rate amid liquidity flood.
text:
HONG KONG, Jan 9 (Reuters) - HSBC Holdings Plc (0005.HK) (HSBA.L) said on Friday it would cut its savings rate in Hong Kong for local dollar deposits to 0.001 percent from 0.01 percent, a move analysts say is prompted by a flood of liquidity.   

The bank said the rate applies to accounts with balances of HK$10,000 (US$1,282) or more, effective on Monday. Depositors with less than that will get nothing.   

HSBC's Hong Kong unit said in a statement that it would not change its best lending rate, currently 5.0 percent. Bank spokespeople were not immediately available for comment.   

"I think it (the unexpected HSBC cut) mainly reflects high liquidity," said Tony Liu, an analyst at DBS Securities.   

"The HIBOR rate has been very weak in the past quarter," he said, referring to the Hong Kong interbank offered rate.   

Hong Kong's banking system is awash in money as foreign investors pile into its surging stock market and park cash here for investments in booming mainland China.   

The territory's central bank has also repeatedly intervened in money markets in recent months, selling Hong Kong dollars in a bid to curb growing spot market strength in the local currency, which is pegged to the U.S. dollar.   

The Hong Kong Monetary Authority sold HK$11.45 billion so far this week alone, bringing the aggregate balance - a key measure of interbank liquidity - to nearly HK$44 billion.   

Liu said that HSBC traditionally had the lowest savings rates of Hong Kong banks given its dominant market position. Other banks may not wish to follow suit to keep customers, he added. (US$=HK$7.8)

text:

Christmas shopping and a steady stream of tourists from mainland
China but markets are unlikely to react to the lagging indicator.

Hong Kong's central bank did little to budge the local dollar
from its recent range on Wednesday morning as foreign investors
continued to pour money into the surging stock market.

bank.

around the current levels, because the stock market is still

HK$28.5 billion for the day.

has been under upward pressure since September on speculation   

about a revaluation of the Chinese yuan, brighter domestic   

economic prospects and capital inflows.   

"I think there are some forces speculating about further   

strengthening in Asian currencies amid the weakness in the U.S.   

dollar," said a dealer from a European bank.   

The Hong Kong Monetary Authority is obligated to defend the   

HKD from weakening below its HK$7.80 peg with the U.S. dollar but   

has no mandate to stop it from strengthening above that level.   

"As the HKMA interventions are transparent, people are   

testing the upper limit of the HK dollar. As the HKMA had   

intervened at about 7.7630, people now think that it will   

invariably be buying U.S. dollars around that level," the dealer

balance - a key measure of interbank liquidity - to a new high   

of HK$41.251 billion on Friday.

further and the interbank interest rates softened on rising   

interbank liquidity.

as a number of Chinese firms will seek listings in Hong Kong that

title: HK Dlr Mkts Late: Hibors Fall On Increased Liquidity
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--Hong Kong interbank offered rates eased Wednesday after fresh Hong Kong dollar sales by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority boosted interbank liquidity.  

The quasi-central bank sold HK$4.27 billion Wednesday in its latest effort to weaken the local unit.  

The newest injections from the HKMA will likely boost the interbank surplus to more than HK$41 billion Friday when the transactions are settled. These large amounts of excess funds kept Hibors under downward pressure.  

The one-month Hibor was quoted at 0.03%, compared with 0.04% Tuesday. The 12-month Hibor was quoted at 0.50%, down from 0.62% previously.  

"It looks like this large amount of excess funds will stay in the market for quite sometime," one trader said.  

With excess liquidity possibly lasting months, banks are more willing to lend money for longer periods - six months and beyond.  

"There is almost no return anyway if banks lend for shorter maturity," the trader added.  

The discount on Hong Kong dollar forwards widened further, following the decline in Hibors.  

The one-year contract was quoted at 730-710 below the spot rate, compared with 685-675 Tuesday. It traded as low as 760 during the day.  

Despite another day of aggressive intervention by the HKMA, the Hong Kong dollar hardly budged.  

The U.S. dollar was quoted at HK$7.7631, compared with HK$7.7628 Tuesday.  

"If there are ongoing equity-driven inflows leading to solid demand for the Hong Kong dollar, further HKMA moves will still have little impact in weakening the currency," the trader said.  

Hong Kong Exchange Fund note yields fell in tandem with U.S. Treasury yields.  

The 10-year EF note was quoted at 4.27%, compared with 4.37% Tuesday.  

Chief Executive Tung Chee-hwa's policy address Wednesday was generally ignored by market participants as his speech offered few policy initiatives on the economic front. Tung said the government would maintain its objectives of keeping business costs low and deepening ties with mainland China.

title: HKMA Sells Another HK$1.01 Bln In Latest  Intervention
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--The Hong Kong Monetary Authority again sold Hong Kong dollars in the currency market Tuesday, in its latest effort to prevent the local unit from strengthening.  

The sale of HK$1.01 billion in the afternoon, after a sale of HK$776 million in the morning, brought the day's total sales to HK$1.79 billion, buying about US$230 million.  

Traders said the HKMA's sales were intended to offset the impact on the exchange rate from inflows of money into Hong Kong, as investors look to invest in the local stock market or speculate on a possible appreciation in the Chinese yuan.  

The spot exchange rate of the local currency was unmoved following the latest intervention. The U.S. dollar was quoted at HK$7.7628. However, the discount on Hong Kong dollar forwards deepened, to 700 to 680 below the spot rate, from 685 to 675 earlier.  

Hong Kong's currency board system automatically prevents the local unit from weakening away from the peg rate of HK$7.80 to the U.S. dollar, but there is no such provision in the system to prevent it from strengthening - only the HKMA's discretion to sell the currency in individual transactions.  

Since late September, the Hong Kong dollar has been trading at a rate stronger than its official peg, an unusual situation driven by heavy flows of foreign investment into Hong Kong assets.  

During that time, the HKMA has sold more than HK$32 billion in its interventions.  

Its efforts have, however, managed only to cap the rise of the local unit at a level of around HK$7.76. With continued inflows of funds into Hong Kong, the sales haven't been enough to push it back to its usual narrow range around the peg rate.  

-By Andrew Batson, Dow Jones Newswires; 852-2802-7002; andrew.batson@dowjones.com

Since late September, the Hong Kong dollar has been trading at a rate stronger than its official peg to the U.S. dollar at HK$7.80, an unusual situation driven by a combination of flows of foreign investment into Hong Kong assets, and speculation on the possible appreciation of the yuan, using the Hong Kong dollar as a proxy.

title: MONEY MARKETS-Dollar funding rate falls further in Asia
text:
* Dollar 3-month lending rate slides to another low

* LIBOR seen nearing bottom, pace of decline likely to slow

* New Zealand IRS down after soft producer price data

By Umesh Desai

HONG KONG, May 18 (Reuters) - The cost of dollar funding in Asia slipped further on Monday extending its near 2 week falling streak while New Zealand swaps dipped on data that supported the central bank's pledge to keep interest rates low.

In Hong Kong, interbank rates remained soft as the banking system was flush from the recent intervention in the currency market.

In Singapore, interest rates on 3-month dollars fell to yet another record low of 0.81333 percent from Friday's 0.84714 percent, as global money market benchmarks tumbled.

Three-month dollar Libor slipped to 0.82563 percent on Friday, another record low, from 0.85438 percent on Thursday, and in the interest rate swaps market, the cost to exchange two-year fixed-rate dollars for floating-rate ones fell to their lowest since May 2007.

But some analysts say rates appear to be nearing bottom and a significant decline from these levels would need major pronouncements from policy makers.

"The LIBOR coming down is enticing people to return to markets but I don't see it (LIBOR) going down a lot more from these levels," said Suresh Ramanathan, a strategist with CIMB Bank.

Stock markets have rallied with the improvement in risk appetite as investors bet the global economy freefall has bottomed out. The MSCI index covering Asia ex-Japan has surged 53 percent from its 2009 low on March 4 to its yearly high on May 11.

"We need to see more really dovish comments from the central banks for LIBOR to come down a lot more and I don't see that happening," he said referring to Friday's comments from ECB President Jean-Claude Trichet.

Late on Friday, Trichet said the measures taken by the European Central Bank to stimulate the ailing euro-zone economy can be removed quickly when the economy improves.

In New Zealand, data showed producer prices fell the quickest pace on record in the first quarter, lending support to expectations the central bank will keep rates low.

The New Zealand economy has been in recession since the beginning of 2008, the worst in more than 30 years, and forecasters expect the weakness to continue for much of 2009 because of the weak global outlook.

Swap rates were softer along the curve, with two year swaps at 3.36 percent and five-year swaps at 4.66 percent.

Swap rates have slowly eased back towards levels in late April when the central bank pledged to keep rates low until late next year. They spiked in March and early April as investors priced in an end to the central bank's easing cycle.

"So the inflationary burst we got from commodity prices is unwinding which is helpful, it allows the Reserve Bank to ease with less concern," said Robin Clements, senior economist with UBS.

In Hong Kong, the three-month Hibor was fixed at 0.52143 percent -- its lowest level since early January 2005 and down 2 basis points from Friday.

Liquidity has remained flush in the local interbank market on frequent intervention by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) in the currency market to curb the strength of the Hong Kong dollar and keep it within its trading band against the U.S. dollar.

The intervention lifted the aggregate balance -- the sum of balances on clearing accounts maintained by banks with the HKMA -- to a record HK$256.97 billion on Monday.

The Hong Kong currency is pegged at 7.80 to the U.S. dollar but can trade between 7.75 and 7.85. Under the currency peg, the HKMA is usually obliged to intervene when the Hong Kong dollar hits 7.75 or 7.85 to keep the band intact.
