title: Q+A-Why is the Hong Kong dollar so strong?
text:
HONG KONG, May 8 (Reuters) - Hong Kong's central bank has been injecting massive amounts of funds into the money market to stem an appreciating Hong Kong dollar <HKD=> and keep the currency within its fixed trading band with the U.S. dollar.

 Under Hong Kong's currency peg system, the Hong KongMonetary Authority (HKMA) is obliged to intervene if the local dollar hits the upper or lower limit of its trading band between 7.7500 and 7.8500 to the U.S. dollar.

 By Friday the HKMA had sold HK$58.760 billion ($7.6 billion) for U.S. dollars since April 21. That brought the aggregate balance -- the sum of the balances of banks' clearing accounts with the HKMA -- to a record high HK$211.033 billion <HKMAOOC>.

 That is a five-fold increase in the past six months and four times bigger than a 2004 peak when the peg came under speculative pressure. For a graphic see:

http://graphics.thomsonreuters.com/059/HK_DLR0509.jpg("http://graphics.thomsonreuters.com/059/HK_DLR0509.jpg")

 Following are some questions and answers about the HKMA's interventions:

 WHY IS THE HONG KONG DOLLAR SO STRONG?

 The currency has been trading at or close to the top of its band since last October as risk-averse investors saw it as a safe place to park funds amid the global financial crisis. The currency is pegged to the U.S. dollar and the HKMA last October guaranteed customer deposits at Hong Kong banks for two years.

 As risk aversion receded, the Hong Kong dollar has again hit the top of its band as funds flow back into the territory, both into surging Hong Kong shares and as a place to park money before allocating it to other Asian markets.

 Average turnover on the Hong Kong stock exchange has risen 60 percent in the past two months as the benchmark Hang Seng Index <.HSI> has rallied 51 percent to a seven-month high.

 An upturn in China's yuan <CNY=CFXS> currency to a seven-month high this week has also helped the Hong Kong dollar.

 WHAT ARE THE IMPLICATIONS FOR HONG KONG'S CURRENCY PEG?

 The currency peg is not under pressure. There is no sign that speculators are buying the Hong Kong dollar to bet that the currency will be de-pegged or its trading band widened.

 Hong Kong government officials and the HKMA have repeatedly stressed the currency peg underpins financial stability, and market players appear to accept there will be no change.

 WHAT ARE THE RISKS OF SUCH A JUMP IN THE AGGREGATE BALANCE?

 Massive fund injections by the HKMA into the money market are similar to quantitative easing and are boosting market liquidity and pushing down Hong Kong interbank rates <HIBOR=R>.

 Extra liquidity raises the risk of inflation, though analysts say inflationary pressure is low because Hong Kong's economy is still suffering from the hits to trade and the financial sector.

 But liquidity does risk an asset price bubble by fuelling gains in equity and property prices. HKMA Chief Executive Joseph Yam said on Friday that heavy fund inflows into Hong Kong could inflate asset prices. [ID:nHKG346756]

 HKMA intervention to curb the Hong Kong dollar's strength poses little risk to Hong Kong's financial stability because the HKMA increases foreign exchange reserves by selling Hong Kong dollars and buying U.S. dollars.

 CAN THE HKMA KEEP INTERVENING INDEFINITELY?

 In theory the HKMA has unlimited room to keep intervening. It has also been issuing Exchange Fund notes, which mop up excess liquidity in the market and reduce the aggregate balance, and is considering selling more bills, a move analysts say is aimed at sterilizing the proceeds of HKMA intervention in the market.

 The HKMA said demand for Exchange Fund bills by banks was strong for liquidity management. Despite their low yields, banks prefer to hold the paper than maintain non-interest bearing balances in their clearing accounts, the HKMA said.

 IS THE HK DOLLAR LIKELY TO REMAIN AT THE TOP OF ITS BAND?

 Yes in the short term, as the territory is likely to keep attracting funds intended for the stock market and initial public offerings, with several new listings in the pipeline.

 However, financial markets are riding on growing optimism that the worst is over for the global economy. If that view were to reverse, Hong Kong could quickly see an outflow of funds and downward pressure on its currency.

 Later in the year, analysts see the Hong Kong dollar falling back toward 7.80 to the U.S. dollar, arguing that carry trades -- where investors sell Hong Kong dollars for U.S. dollars to make a profit on the interest-rate differentials -- could resume. title: MONEY MARKETS- Hong Kong  interbank rates fall after  intervention
text:
* HIBOR edges lower on liquidity injection

 * U.S. dollar funding costs remain below 1 percent

 By Umesh Desai

 HONG KONG, May 8 (Reuters) - Hong Kong interbank rates slumped again on Friday as authorities injected liquidity to keep the currency within its trading band while the cost of borrowing dollars in Asia remained below 1 percent as credit markets heal.

 Funds are streaming into Hong Kong's financial markets on growing signs China will lead the territory out of the economic downturn and this has pushed the pegged Hong Kong dollar to the top of its trading band.

 Under Hong Kong's currency peg, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) is obliged to intervene if the Hong Kong dollar, which can trade between 7.7500 and 7.8500 to the U.S. dollar, hits the upper or lower limit of its trading band.

 On Thursday, the HKMA confirmed it injected HK$4.263 billion (US$550 million) into the money market lifting the aggregate balance -- sum of balances on clearing accounts maintained by banks with the HKMA -- to a record HK$211.033 billion by May 11.

 The liquidity injection in the local market sent the interbank rates lower.

 The three-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR) was fixed lower at 0.69321 percent from the previous 0.70500 percent.

 "They are happy with it (the Hong Kong dollar) testing 7.75 and with injecting liquidity especially at a time when there are deflationary forces," said Craig Chan, analyst with Nomura Securities in Singapore.

 HKMA chief Joseph Yam warned on Thursday hefty fund inflows could inflate asset prices in the territory, while local economic conditions remained difficult. He said the HKMA had issued extra exchange fund bills to absorb some of the funds, otherwise the aggregate balance would have been about HK$300 billion.

 Asian dollar funding costs remained below 1 percent as dollar London interbank offered rates remained low, indicating banks' increased willingness to lend amid easing credit strains.

 The 3-month dollar London interbank offered rate (Libor) was fixed at a record low of 0.95625 percent on Thursday.

 In Asia, three-month dollar funding rates in Singapore fell to 0.95333 percent, down from 0.96857 percent.

 Australian overnight index swaps showed steady to slightly lower rates for a year ahead, as the central bank on Friday slashed its forecasts for economic growth.

 The Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) sees a sharp contraction this year, but expects record-low interest rates and fiscal stimulus to generate a gradual recovery through 2010.

 "The RBA sounds like it's comfortably on hold now and perhaps believes it may be done cutting this cycle," said Rob Henderson, head of market economics at National Australia Bank.

 "But its outlook for inflation also suggests that rates may stay low for longer, with no hike until 2011 even," he added.

 The RBA skipped a chance to ease at its monthly meeting on Tuesday, after its slashed its cash rate by 425 basis points since September last year to a record low of 3.0 percent.  (Editing by Neil Fullick)

title: UPDATE: HK Exchange Fund Has Record HK$81.0B Net Invest Loss
text:
(Adds comments from Yam on outlook for financial markets, and comments from analysts on fund's asset allocation; breakdown of exchange fund performance.)

By Chester Yung

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--Sliding stock markets pushed Hong Kong's Exchange Fund to a record net investment loss of HK$81.0 billion (US$10.4 billion) in 2008, and Hong Kong Monetary Authority Chief Executive Joseph Yam said it is difficult to predict when a turnaround can start.

A loss had been widely expected in the Exchange Fund, which has a target allocation of 77% bonds and 23% local and foreign stocks, and analysts said the loss announced Tuesday was manageable although it could make a case for the HKMA to show more flexibility in the Exchange Fund's asset allocations.

The Exchange Fund's assets totaled HK$1.558 trillion on Dec. 31, up from HK$1.414 trillion a year earlier. The increase came about as the Hong Kong Monetary Authority carried out repeated interventions in the currency market in the last four months of 2008, adding to its aggregate balance.

Yam told a news conference the Exchange Fund faces more difficult times in 2009, with a rebound tough to call.

"The global financial system remains unsettled," Yam said.

"Whether monetary easing and large fiscal stimulus packages in major economies will be effective in restoring investor confidence remain to be seen," Yam said. "Financial markets are under immense stress and we expect volatile conditions to continue for some time."

The Exchange Fund's net investment loss, its first since 2001, compared with a net gain of HK$132.2 billion in 2007. The Exchange Fund had a negative investment return last year for the first time, of 5.6%. In 2007, its return on investment was 11.8%.

The Exchange Fund lost HK$77.9 billion on Hong Kong stocks last year, when the benchmark Hang Seng Index slid 48%, and HK$73.2 billion on foreign stocks. It had a foreign exchange loss of HK$12.4 billion, mainly due to the depreciation of the U.S. dollar against other currencies. The Hong Kong dollar is pegged to the U.S. dollar.

A gain of HK$88.6 billion from bonds offset some of the losses.

Analysts said that while the loss was widely expected, the Exchange Fund might do better with more flexibility in its asset allocation so it could respond better to market conditions.

"For example, the HKMA could allocate more assets from overseas stocks to bonds when bonds are rising and review the allocation frequently," said Frances Cheung, fixed income strategist of Standard Chartered Bank.

DBS senior investment strategist Daniel Chan also said it would be good to review the asset allocations, but he said the loss was not alarming.

"With over HK$1.5 trillion of fund total assets, we are still able to afford the temporary losses," Chan said.

-By Chester Yung, Dow Jones Newswires; 852-2802-7002; chester.yung@dowjones.com [ 21-01-09 1209GMT ]

title: UPDATE 1-Yam says inflow of funds to HK dollar welcome
text:
(Adds quote, details)

HONG KONG, Jan 15 (Reuters) - Recent fund flows into the Hong Kong dollar, which have pushed the currency to the top of its trading band, are causing a quantitative easing of monetary conditions, Hong Kong's chief central banker said on Thursday.

"The inflow of funds to the Hong Kong dollar that we have been seeing is a welcome development," Joseph Yam, Chief Executive of the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, said in a weekly column on the HKMA's Website www.info.gov.hk/hkma("http://www.info.gov.hk/hkma").

"Although we do not practise discretionary monetary management, quantitative easing is made possible by the substantial inflow of money that we have been seeing since the global financial crisis turned sharply worse with the collapse of Lehman Brothers," he said.

Hong Kong does not have control over monetary policy because its currency peg with the U.S. dollar forces it to track U.S. monetary policy.

Yam said monetary easing was appropriate given that Hong Kong is in recession and inflation is easing. Short-term interbank rates have fallen to near zero as a result of the HKMA injecting massive funds into the market to stem appreciation of the Hong Kong dollar and keep it within its pegged trading band with the U.S. dollar, he said.

Yam reiterated a warning earlier this month that fund flows could reverse but said that should be an orderly process. The HKMA has U.S. dollars it can sell back into the market and make a profit, unlike authorities elsewhere that have increased liquidity by buying up domestic financial assets, he said.

"Our position contrasts favourably with that of jurisdictions that have injected money into the banking system through buying domestic financial assets," Yam said. "Domestic circumstances may not be conducive to selling these assets back to the market when it becomes necessary to exit from quantitative easing."

The Hong Kong dollar <HKD=> has been trading at or close to the top of its fixed trading band with the U.S. dollar since the Lehman Brothers collapse in mid-September as risk-averse investors have unwound carry trades and as some have seen Hong Kong, with its currency link to the U.S. dollar, as a safe haven to park funds.

Heavy fund inflows have forced the HKMA to intervene in the market and sell massive amounts of Hong Kong dollars for U.S. dollars to keep Hong Kong's currency within its trading band. (Reporting by Susan Fenton; Editing by Nick Macfie)

HONG KONG, Jan 1 (Reuters) - The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) confirmed on Thursday it had sold HK$1.94 billion ($250 million) for U.S. dollars late on Wednesday in New York trading to curb the strength of the Hong Kong dollar.

According to data on Reuters page <HKMAOOC>, the latest intervention will lift the aggregate balance -- the sum of balances on clearing accounts maintained by banks with the HKMA -- to a record HK$175.48 billion by Jan. 5.

Hong Kong's currency has been boosted by the liquidation of carry trades, repatriation of capital and inflow of funds into the territory in recent months, dealers said.

title: MONEY TALKS: Stocks May Not Keep Propping Hong Kong Dollar
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Hong Kong dollar has been an outperformer amid the regional currency sell-off in recent months, but its reliance on inflows to the stock market may yet leave it vulnerable.

The flow of money in and out of Hong Kong is a large driver of the domestic currency, within the peg arrangement against the U.S. dollar, of course.

In recent weeks, the Hong Kong dollar has pushed a fair few times against the upper bound of its peg range, forcing intervention from the Hong Kong Monetary Authority.

Part of that has been due to a rise in domestic interbank rates and the unwinding of carry trades into the U.S. dollar, and part of it has been due to resilience in the Hong Kong stock market.

Indeed, the Hang Seng Index has risen 8.3% so far in December, gaining three of the past four trading days, though it remains down 45.9% year-to-date.

But Monday's action suggests the gains may prove vulnerable.

The HSI surged 8.7% on Monday in heavy volume to its highest close in almost two months, over the key 15,000 level, led by gains in China-based companies.

Part of that was due to hopes for further efforts by Beijing to support the mainland economy (and thus Hong Kong by association, given the dual listing of many companies and the reliance of some Hong Kong companies on income from Chinese operations).

This week brings the annual Central Economic Work Conference in China, too, a key summit of leaders which some think could yield fresh measures to stimulate the economy - or at least flesh out the details of the fiscal plans already announced.

Another key driver of Monday's rally was hopes the long-delayed program aimed at allowing mainland Chinese residents to directly invest in Hong Kong's stock market, known as the "through train," would finally get the go-ahead; Hong Kong Financial Secretary John Tsang said the program at least hadn't been scrapped.

That prompted a flurry of money into the Hong Kong stock market on hopes among investors generally that mainland Chinese would soon be pumping shedloads of cash in.

But we've seen previous episodes where hopes have been raised for its start, only for them to later be dashed and for cash to move back out of Hong Kong.

The latest anticipation is likely to prove inflated.

Tsang himself noted the ongoing difficulties in getting the program up and running, none the least on the logistical side.

And with the large interest rate cuts, liquidity operations and fiscal stimulus measures underway in China, the central government is not about to torpedo the Shanghai stock market by allowing Chinese to exit en masse and invest in Hong Kong.

JPMorgan's Managing Director for China equities, Jing Ulrich, believes officials will turn their focus in the new year to supporting stocks and encouraging property purchases; "with the economy expected to further weaken in the near-term, the risk of rising unemployment and income insecurity could create stumbling blocks for a sustained recovery," she says.

Her counterpart at JPMorgan, economist Frank Gong, has also warned of the risk of social unrest after the Chinese new year period, especially if many migrant workers fail to find jobs in February.

That's hardly a time to be letting money leave in large scale from the stock market, which has risen 10.6% over the past four trading days but remains 60% lower year-to-date and tends to be volatile..

As well, the expectations surrounding the Central Economic Work Conference may be overblown; we could see a steady drip-feed of commentary from key officials talking about the need to support the economy, but little in the way of fresh specifics.

That could dent sentiment on the China-linked plays listed in Hong Kong.

And that in turn could put a lid on the Hong Kong dollar in the near term.

title: ANALYSIS-Safety rather than speculation in HK dollar strength
text:
HONG KONG, Nov 25 (Reuters) - A rush of cash into safe-haven markets has flooded Hong Kong's banks with funds and forced the Hong Kong dollar to the top of its trading band, belying market expectations for the currency to eventually weaken.

Demand for Hong Kong dollars has surged as volatile credit markets have prompted a heavy unwinding of carry trades while Hong Kong's robust banking system and the currency's peg to the U.S. dollar have made the territory a safer place to park funds.

The currency has repeatedly hit the top of its pegged trading band with the U.S. dollar at 7.75 <HKD=>, and the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) has injected $7.1 billion into the market in the past month to keep the currency within its band.

Most currency analysts and economists see little danger to the Hong Kong dollar peg. There is also little fundamental support for the currency from an economy in recession.

"When the liquidity squeeze normalises, market trades will go back to fundamentals," said Emmanuel Ng, a strategist at OCBC Bank in Singapore. "Demand for Hong Kong dollars will ease and the currency will head back to the centre of its trading band."

As of now, even the forward markets contradict that outlook. As investors and banks use swaps to pile into Hong Kong, the forward market <HKDF=> <0#HKDF=> is pricing the currency at around 7.73 to the U.S. dollar within 12 months.

Such is the nature of Hong Kong's Currency Board that the HKMA has to keep intervening, selling Hong Kong dollars and mopping up the foreign currency to preserve the peg. The surplus cash in the banking system is around HK$84 billion, a record level compared with levels of just HK$5 billion in August.

Defending the peg has become a challenge for the HKMA, not to mention the inflationary pressures that could ensue.

Yet, the Hong Kong authorities are in the enviable position of fighting an appreciating currency and influx of cash, at a time when most central banks are trying to staunch capital flight.

Bank-to-bank lending rates <HIBOR=R> are at 5-month lows, and even below U.S. dollar rates.

"They have a problem which a lot of countries would love to have at the moment -- the rich man's dilemma," said an analyst in Singapore, who declined to be named.

YUAN PLAY

Unlike in 2007, when speculators pushed the Hong Kong currency to the top of its trading limit, this time the currency seems to be driven purely by a flight to safety. Nor is it considered undervalued for it to become a speculative bet.

Rather, real demand for the currency during a market panic -- heightened by banks' requirement for extra liquidity amid tight credit -- masks a shift in longer-term sentiment.

"The market no longer expects the Hong Kong dollar to appreciate (long term). It expects it to depreciate. That's a structural change," said Joe Lo, senior economist at Citigroup.

The Hong Kong dollar is often seen as a proxy for the Chinese yuan, which is not fully convertible, and the shift in sentiment coincides with a reversal in expectations for yuan appreciation.

A rising yuan had been viewed as a one-way bet since the yuan was revalued in July 2005 but is now seen to be putting too much pressure on exporters struggling with weakening global demand.

Still, in the short term, the Hong Kong dollar is likely to remain strong as investors continue to seek safe havens.

"Against the current backdrop, investors are asking, not "Where can I make money?" but "Where can I avoid losing too much money?" said Sebastien Barbe, senior economist at Calyon in Hong Kong.

HKMA Chief Executive Joseph Yam said last week the central bank had not seen any anomalies in the market and was ready to continue injecting liquidity to keep the currency in its band.

"The (recent) strong demand for Hong Kong dollars was probably due to repatriation of funds and unwinding of interest carry trades as global financial jitters led market participants to deleverage and reduce their exposure to risk," Yam said.

Hong Kong's decision last month to guarantee all customer bank deposits in the territory, and its peg to the U.S. dollar while other Asian currencies remain volatile, have reinforced Hong Kong's attraction as a safe haven.

As the collapse of U.S. investment bank Lehman Brothers in mid-September sparked panic in global financial markets, Hong Kong's banking system drew net inflows of HK$90 billion that month -- the largest amount in 11 months, according to Citigroup.

Hong Kong banks have had limited exposure to U.S. subprime risk and their aggregate classified-loan ratio is at less than 1 percent, down from more than 10 percent after the Asian financial crisis a decade ago, according to the HKMA.

Analysts expect global investors to remain risk averse for now but say confidence could improve in a few months.

If credit markets stabilise, carry trades could resume, pushing the currency to the weak side of its trading band between 7.80 and 7.85 where it was entrenched before Lehman's collapse.

The Hong Kong dollar is pegged at 7.8 to the U.S. dollar but can trade between 7.75 and 7.85.

And if the yuan keeps slowing meanwhile, the Hong Kong dollar could head to the bottom of its band at 7.85, analysts say.

That would be the time to worry about the peg. (US$=HK$7.8) (Editing by Vidya Ranganathan and Kazunori Takada)

title: UPDATE: HKMA Exchange Fund Jan-Sep Invest Losses HK$83.3B
text:

HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--The Hong Kong Exchange Fund's investment losses more than doubled in the third quarter to HK$48.3 billion when compared with the previous quarter as global stock markets fell, Hong Kong Monetary Authority Chief Executive Joseph Yam said Friday.

The latest loss compared with a HK$20.4 billion loss in the second quarter and brought the Exchange Fund's losses for the nine months ended Sept. 30 to HK$83.3 billion, Yam told lawmakers.

Yam told lawmakers the fund will incur losses in the fourth quarter due to a "very bad" investment environment in October and November. He said the full-year loss will exceed HK$83.3 billion, but didn't provide a specific estimate.

The investment losses this year come after the Exchange Fund posted record earnings of HK$142.2 billion in 2007, up from HK$103.8 billion in 2006.

The Exchange Fund's loss on its Hong Kong stock investments during January-September totaled HK$56.9 billion, as the benchmark Hang Seng Index fell 35% during the period.

It had a loss of HK$43.2 billion on overseas stock investments and a loss of HK$13.8 billion on foreign exchange during the nine-month period, but a HK$30.6 billion gain from bonds over the same period pared some losses.

The Exchange Fund, made up of a variety of assets, including stocks and bonds, amounted to HK$1.426 trillion as of Sept. 30 and is used by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority to maintain the Hong Kong dollar's peg to the U.S. dollar and ensure financial stability in the territory.

Yam attributed the recent strengthening of the Hong Kong dollar to the unwinding of long U.S. dollar positions due to growing risk aversion among market participants and possible repatriation of funds by domestic corporations.

Strong demand for the Hong Kong dollar in recent weeks prompted the HKMA to intervene in the foreign exchange market more than a dozen times this week to maintain its currency peg to the U.S. dollar. Hong Kong's de facto central bank sold a record HK$18.2 billion Thursday over seven interventions, pushing Hong Kong's aggregate balance to HK$84.27 billion.

title: HKMA Yam: Remain Fully Committed To US Dollar Peg
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--Hong Kong monetary chief Joseph Yam reaffirmed his commitment to the territory's currency peg, and said Thursday recent intense intervention in the foreign exchange market should bring down borrowing costs.

The Hong Kong Monetary Authority intervened seven times during the Asian trading day Thursday, selling a total of HK$18.21 billion to meet demand for the local currency that has surged to the upper limit of its trading band versus the U.S. dollar.

Yam said the strong demand was caused by investors deleveraging long U.S. dollar positions and corporations repatriating funds.

"We do not notice any market anomalies at the moment," he said.

Recent interventions have pushed Hong Kong's aggregate balance to HK$84.27 billion and Yam said there was no upper limit to the balance.

He said the large aggregate balance would provide ample liquidity to the banking system and help keep interbank interest rates soft.

"This may help translate into lower commercial rates and ease the cost of borrowing," Yam said.

In the face of an economic slowdown, the low interest rates are unlikely to fuel excessive credit creation and inflationary concerns, he said.

title: WSJA: Asian Shares Drop,  Currencies  Sharply Lower
text:
OF THE WALL STREET JOURNAL ASIA 
 

HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--Asian stocks were sold off heavily Thursday, knocking many of the region's currencies sharply lower and prompting governments to intervene.

Markets in Tokyo, Hong Kong and South Korea fell in response to a broad selloff overnight in the U.S. Tokyo's benchmark index fell 6.9%, while Hong Kong and Seoul were down 4% and 6.7% respectively. Australia's major benchmark dropped 4.2% and Shanghai fell 1.7%. Mumbai and Singapore were down 4.1% and 2.8% late Thursday. Jakarta was down 2.8% late.

The selling continued in Europe, where the DJ Stoxx 600 index was 3% lower. U.S. stock futures were down 1% to 1.5% in screen trade.

The stock hits reflect fears of deflation in the U.S., a major market for Asia-made goods, and the impact of a slowdown on commodity-rich nations like Australia and Indonesia.

That has led to a flight to safer investments typically denominated in U.S. dollars and the Japanese yen, taking money out of Asian markets and contributing to a drop in local currencies.

"It's part of the wholesale destruction of wealth across the planet," said Patrick Bennett, a strategist with Societe Generale in Hong Kong. "With asset and equity prices tumbling, investors are being encouraged to cut exposure completely."

Weaker currencies can boost big exporting nations because it makes their goods cheaper to sell in other markets. But declining currencies also hit countries with extensive foreign borrowing needs, can drive up inflation by making imports more expensive and can scare off foreign investment.

Among the hardest hit, Indonesia's rupiah and South Korea's won fell to their lowest level against the U.S. dollar since the Asian financial crisis a decade ago.

Thailand's baht fell to its weakest level since March 2007, while Taiwan's dollar hit a three-week low and the New Zealand and Australian dollars also weakened further.

The central banks of South Korea, Malaysia, the Philippines, Indonesia, Singapore and India intervened to defend their currencies, local traders said. Australia's central bank issued data that showed it plowed A$3.15 billion into currency markets last month to defend the Australian dollar against a sharp decline.

Japan and Hong Kong have defied the trend, the former because its currency is seen as a safe haven and the latter because it is pegged to the value of the appreciating U.S. dollar. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority, the city's de facto central bank, put roughly HK$15 billion into the market Thursday to bring the currency's value within its trading band with the U.S. dollar.

Economists cautioned that the current environment hasn't reached the point of the Asian currency crisis, when domestic funds followed foreign investors as they ran for the exits. Most governments have moved to back bank deposits to reassure consumers. Regional financial institutions have cleaner balance sheets than a decade ago, and bad loans have so far had only a minor effect on regional banks.

Still, continuing hits to currencies continue could erode consumer confidence, leading locals to consider moving their money elsewhere. "The impact on confidence could become a much bigger problem," said Sim Moh Siong, an economist at Citigroup in Singapore. "If this goes beyond how much money foreigners remove from Asia, the situation could broaden out."

In Tokyo, the Nikkei Stock Average of 225 companies ended down 6.9% at 7703.04. Shares of major banks and brokerages were hammered, with Sumitomo Mitsui Financial Group tumbling 10% to Y281,500 and Nomura Holdings ending down 11% at Y666.

Shares of nonlife insurers dropped after sector companies reported dismal fiscal first half results Wednesday and sharply reduced their earnings forecasts for the full fiscal year ending March.

Although most of the bad news had already been factored in by investors, forecast revisions confirmed the grim outlook. Tokio Marine Holdings went limit-down at Y2,220, and Mitsui Sumitomo Insurance Group Holdings also went limit-down at Y2,035.

Real estate stocks also sank, dogged by credit concerns, with Mitsui Fudosan skidding 14% to Y1,070, and Mitsubishi Estate falling 13% to Y1,077.

In Seoul, the Korea Composite Stock Price Index, or Kospi, finished down 68.13 points, or 6.7%, at 948.69, based on skepticism over conditions in the U.S., particularly among financials.

Shinhan Financial Group declined 9.7% to KRW26,400, and KB Financial Group plunged by the daily limit of 15% to KRW24,550. Among builders, Hyundai Engineering & Construction and GS Engineering & Construction both dropped by the daily 15% limit to KRW42,100 and KRW45,200, respectively.

In Shanghai, the benchmark Shanghai Composite Index, which tracks both A and B shares, ended down 1.7%, or 33.71 points, at 1983.76. Railway companies and insurance companies fell on profit-taking.

China Railway Group Ltd. dropped 4.1% to CNY5.82 after gaining 4.7% Wednesday, while China Life Insurance Co. fell 4.0% to CNY20.24 after rising 6.1% in the previous session.

-By Carlos Tejada, The Wall Street Journal; carlos. tejada@wsj.com

title: 2nd UPDATE: Asian Shares Mixed; Japan Falls But HK Up
text:
(Adds information, quotes, updates and adds market levels)

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Asian share markets were mixed Wednesday in low trading volume despite a rise in U.S. stocks, with tech stocks pressured by worries about the outlook for consumer spending around the globe.

Japan's Nikkei 225 ended with a 0.7% decline 2.5% after falling 2.3% Tuesday, with Korea's Kospi Composite finishing down 1.9% after a 3.9% drop Tuesday; Australia's S&P/ASX 200 slipped 0.7%, following a 3.6% fall Tuesday, with the lifting of a ban there on short-selling of most non-financial stocks. But there was some bounceback in Chinese stocks with Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index adding 1.6% after a 4.5% drop Tuesday, taking its lead from the Shanghai Composite Index, which had jumped 5.6% in a late-day rise.

Even so, sentiment on the Chinese economy remained wobbly at best, despite the recent news of a large-sized fiscal stimulus package.

The market mood generally was cautious in Asia, and trade was volatile.

"Investor confidence has been decimated and all of us are looking for a catalyst, but it continues to be a struggle for many companies worldwide," said Barry Lindsay, director of research at First NZ Capital.

"People have got it into their heads that the downturn is going to be deep, protracted and ugly really. They have got no confidence about earnings and can't seem to price shares."

U.S. stock futures were down 0.5% to 1% in screen trade, with European spreadbetting firms calling stocks there to open slightly lower; overnight, the Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 1.8% in a late-day rally, but the Nasdaq Composite only managed to end 0.1% higher.

"Overall, concerns over the extent of the global economic slowdown continue to weigh across the board for stocks - something that will be played out with falling commodity prices and continued pressure on banks," said CMC Markets dealer Matt Buckland.

Tech stocks failed to get much help from Hewlett-Packard's 14% rise in the U.S. after the computer maker forecast fiscal 2009 profit ahead of the average Wall Street estimate, showing that its diversified business model would help it avoid the most painful effects of a slowdown in computer sales.

H-P's approach seemed company-specific, analysts said; also, the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 2% Tuesday amid broad concerns about the demand outlook in the U.S.

Markets were awaiting the release later Wednesday of U.S. CPI data and the latest Federal Open Market Committee meeting minutes.

They were also watching for news on the U.S. auto sector with the Senate potentially gearing up to vote on a rescue package for the industry, amid warnings from several large carmakers that they might run out of cash; some lawmakers were critical of the idea of bailing out auto firms.

"The troubled U.S. automotive industry poses a large economic and potentially systemic risk, so a lack of a rescue plan is bad news for risky assets in the near term," said analysts at Barclays Capital.

Lower trading volume was exacerbating volatility; "on the plus side, selling seems to be drying up, but it's just not clear where the positive catalysts are going to come from for a sustainable rally," said a trader a local brokerage in Singapore.

In Japan, financial shares tumbled on Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group's poor results for the six months ended September; Mitsubishi sank 6.4% while Mizuho Financial Group fell 7.5%.

Exporter stocks were hurt by a rising yen with Tokyo Electron down 5.5% and TDK off 2.8%.

In Australia, the main index briefly hit its lowest level since May 2004; "share prices would indicate there's some shorting out there," said Patrick Crabb, senior sales trader at Goldman Sachs JBWere in Melbourne, with falls in large-cap stocks like BHP, Woolworths, Woodside and Brambles, though some banking shares were higher.

title: UPDATE 1-HKMA  intervenes  three times to curb HK dollar
text:
(Adds details, background)

HONG KONG, Nov 11 (Reuters) -TheHong Kong Monetary Authority was forced to intervene three times in less than an hour on Tuesday afternoon to curb a strong Hong Kong dollar <HKD=>, injecting HK$5.8 billion (US$750 million) to keep the currency within its pegged trading band.

Hong Kong's currency is pegged at 7.8 to the U.S. dollar, but it can trade between 7.75 and 7.85 and hit its upper limit at 7.7500 repeatedly on Tuesday.

Traders attributed the currency's strength to continued unwinding of carry trades, which have become less attractive as interbank rates have been volatile since the global financial crisis deepened two months ago.

Previously, investors were selling Hong Kong dollars for U.S. dollars to earn a profit on the interest rate differential between Hong Kong and U.S. dollars. Investors have also been unwinding positions because they need cash after suffering heavy losses in equity and other asset markets, analysts say.

"Investment houses and hedge funds are unwinding positions," said Dennis Wong, chief foreign exchange dealer at Hang Seng Bank.

Wong said a narrowing of the spread between short-dated Hong Kong and U.S. interbank rates in the past few days meant there was virtually no demand for U.S. dollars for arbitrage trade.

When the Hong Kong dollar hits 7.7500, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, or central bank, is forced to come in and sell Hong Kong dollars to keep the trading band intact.

Over the past few weeks it has intervened several times as the currency hit the top of the trading band. In New York trade on Monday, the HKMA injected HK$1.938 billion into the market to stem the currency's strength.

After the third injection on Tuesday afternoon, the Hong Kong dollar was still at its upper limit, trading at 7.7500/01 at 0954 GMT. (Reporting by Christina Lo and Susan Fenton) (Editing by Anne Marie Roantree)

title: WSJA(10/28) Asian Markets Dive And Europe Follows
text:
WSJA(10/28) Asian Markets Dive And Europe Follows

(From THE WALL STREET JOURNAL ASIA)

A massive selloff in Asian shares Monday highlights growing investor nervousness over emerging vulnerabilities in a region until recently considered relatively safe from crisis contagion.

Tokyo shares fell 6.4% to their lowest level in 25 years and Hong Kong's stock market fell 12.7% as fearful investors pulled out of the region's equity and currency markets. The Philippines benchmark index in Manila fell 12.3%, while Bangkok tumbled 10.5%. Shanghai fell 6.3% and Singapore lost 8.3%. Taiwan shed 4.7% and Mumbai lost 2.2%.

Only South Korea defied the trend, closing modestly higher after the central bank announced a surprise, three-quarter percentage-point rate cut.

European markets fell sharply as well Monday. Investors were watching U.S. markets to see whether the pullback would continue as investors shunned risk and moved into cash or the safest of investments.

Asia's declines, which come after a punishing day of losses Friday, signal the financial crisis that began with subprime mortgages in the U.S. has moved squarely into the heart of Asia. While exposure among the region's banks to tightening global credit have been one point of concern, the most vulnerable access point, it turns out, is Asia's dependence on exports to the weakened U.S. and European economies.

'The false premise all along has been that Asia could decouple,' said Stephen Roach, Asia chairman for Morgan Stanley. 'I think we're seeing in a global recession there is no decoupling from the powerful cross-border linkages of trade flows, capital flows, labor flows and information flows.'

Asian-Pacific currencies mostly continued to fall against the U.S. dollar. Though the Reserve Bank of Australia said it intervened Friday and Monday, the Australian dollar remains near five-year lows. Hong Kong monetary authorities intervened to keep the local currency, seen as a haven, from rising too much against the U.S. dollar, to which it is pegged.

In Japan, the Nikkei 225 Stock Average lost 486.18 points to 7162.90 as nervous investors sold shares of banks and exporters on fresh concerns over the fallout from the U.S. financial crisis and an ever-strengthening yen.

Gloom mounted over Japan's banks Monday after Mitsubishi UFJ, Japan's largest lender, said it would raise as much as 990 billion yen, or $10.7 billion, in capital through share issues within the next year. Until recently, Japan's banks appeared to be among the world's strongest.

The surging yen prompted finance chiefs from the Group of Seven leading nations to warn that recent 'excessive volatility' in the yen threatens the global economy and financial system.

The Nikkei is now at its lowest level since October 1982, when Japan was on the eve of an export-led boom that culminated in the burst of its stock-and-real-estate bubble in the early 1990s.

'It's a crisis. It's a psychological shock to think we're back to where we were almost 30 years ago' said Hisashi Takeda, a real-estate worker in central Tokyo.

Japan's economy is heavily dependent on exports for growth, making it vulnerable to currency fluctuations and economic downturns in overseas markets. In 2007, exports were responsible for 67% of Japan's GDP growth.

'More than half of growth comes from exports,' says Akira Maekawa, a senior economist for UBS Securities Japan.

In addition to concerns about exports, other fears have dealt a blow to Asian markets this month. Losses from leveraged currency positions revealed by Citic Pacific Ltd., a Hong Kong-listed conglomerated backed by Chinese state money, have made investors nervous about other similar undisclosed liabilities on corporate balance sheets.

Another trigger: the president of Argentina's decision to nationalize the country's pension funds, which raised fears that other small nations under pressure from the financial crisis might resort to extreme measures to meet their obligations. 'For the first time in a long time, we started hearing people talk about 'emerging-market contagion,'' said Steve Diggle, partner at Artradis Fund Management, a US$4 billion hedge fund in Singapore.

title: UPDATE 3-Hong Kong c.bank curbs rise in "safe haven" HK dollar
text:
(Adds quote, background)

HONG KONG, Oct 23 (Reuters) - Hong Kong's central bank intervened on Thursday for the first time in nearly a year to stem a rise in the Hong Kong dollar and keep it within official trading limits against the U.S. dollar.

Traders said funds had poured into Hong Kong banks in the past few days as the territory's sound financial system and currency peg to the U.S. dollar were seen as a safe haven, putting upward pressure on the local currency.

"Markets in general are very volatile," said Carlos Cheung, chief foreign exchange dealer at Bank of East Asia.

"Hong Kong is seen as a safe haven as neighbouring countries are quite unstable financially."

The central bank, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA), injected HK$3.877 billion (US$500 million) into the market on Thursday afternoon as the Hong Kong dollar was trading at around 7.7540 per U.S. dollar.

The currency is pegged to the U.S. dollar at 7.8, but can trade between 7.85 and 7.75. The HKMA is obliged to keep the currency in that range under an arrangement known as the convertibility undertaking.

"The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate has strengthened to near the strong side of the convertibility undertaking rate, while short-dated Hong Kong dollar interest rates rose to a premium over U.S. dollar interest rates," an HKMA spokesman told Reuters.

"These developments reflect increased demand for Hong Kong dollars. Taking into account market conditions, the HKMA operated within the convertibility zone, purchasing U.S. dollars against Hong Kong dollars," he said.

GLOBAL DOWNTURN

By late Thursday afternoon, the currency was trading at around 7.7539 to the U.S. dollar.

"It's still very near the strong side of the convertibility undertaking, so I wouldn't rule out further injections," said Frances Cheung, a strategist at Standard Chartered Bank.

The Hong Kong currency's appeal as a safe place to park money was underpinned by the U.S. dollar's rise to a two-year high against a basket of currencies on Thursday, analysts said.

Investors have pulled money out of other Asian markets in the past few days, worried about how the region will be affected by a global economic downturn.

Emerging markets generally were perceived as much more risky after it was reported that Pakistan and Hungary sought help from the International Monetary Fund and Argentina nationalized its pension system, seen as an attempt to stave off default.

Pakistan said on Thursday it had not formally asked for a loan facility from the IMF.

"Even Asian currencies with relatively sound fundamentals like the Singapore dollar <SGD=> and Taiwan dollar <TWD=TP> have been depreciating this week as fear in emerging markets has increased sharply," said Joe Lo, senior economist at Citigroup.

"Hong Kong's financial system is strong and its currency peg is very stable so it's becoming a safe haven for money in the region."

Fitch ratings agency said on Friday that Hong Kong banks are fundamentally sound and should weather challenging economic conditions.

Lo said the territory's decision last week to guarantee bank deposits may also be helping boost the Hong Kong dollar, although the impact was limited as only customer deposits are guaranteed not interbank deposits.

In offshore trade overnight, the Hong Kong dollar had hit a near one-year high of 7.7516 to the U.S. dollar.

It has stayed on the strong side of its trading band for the past two months as rising risk aversion amid the global credit crisis has discouraged arbitrage trade. Banks' reluctance to lend to each other amid the credit crisis has prompted lenders to sell U.S. dollar positions for Hong Kong dollars to boost liquidity for local operations, analysts said.

Arbitrage traders sell Hong Kong dollars for U.S. dollars to make money on the differential between U.S. and Hong Kong dollar interest rates.

On Thursday, the daily one-month Hong Kong interbank offered rate (Hibor) was fixed higher for the first time in a week at 2.92571 percent. Interbank rates had drifted slightly lower this week after action by the HKMA over the past two weeks to ease tight liquidity as banks were cautious about lending amid the global credit crisis.

The HKMA said the aggregate balance -- the sum of balances on clearing accounts maintained by banks with the HKMA -- would increase by HK$3,877 million to HK$17,958 million on Oct. 27 as a result of the fund injection. title: UPDATE: BOJ, RBA, MAS Inject Cash; Officials Soothe Markets
text:
(Adds further injections by BOJ, MAS)

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Central banks and other officials around Asia leapt into action Tuesday with either cash or soothing words to reassure the short-term borrowing and othermarkets after the U.S. House of Representatives voted down a key US$700-billion U.S. financial sector bailout package.

That decision sent the Dow Jones Industrial Average tumbling 7% overnight, taking Asian bourses and manyof the region's currencies with it Tuesday.

The Bank of Japan injected Y3.0trillion into the short-term money market in two batchesto tackle an overnight call rate that was as high as 0.80%. The central bank's target rate is 0.50%.

The BOJ has now injected Y21.1 trillion into the money market over the 10 consecutive business days since U.S. investment bank Lehman Brothers Holdings Inc. filed for bankruptcy protection.

The Reserve Bank of Australia made a much smaller net injection of A$75 million in its daily operations.

Still, that will keep the level of commercial banks' exchange settlement accounts at the central bank around A$10.7 billion, the highest since the U.S. subprime-inspired market turmoil began making the headlines in mid-2007.

Money market rates in Australia were relatively steady, with the three-month bank bill swap rate fixed Tuesday at 7.32%, unchanged from Monday. The one-month rate is down 2 basis points at 7.38%. Traders said the Monetary Authority of Singapore Tuesday injected S$1.3 billion Tuesday to tackle an overnight rate of over 1.8%. The action pushed the rate down to around 1.375% and followed an injection of an estimated S$2.5 billion Monday.

Meanwhile, others used verbal intervention to calm the local markets.

Hong Kong Monetary Authority chief Joseph Yam said he expected the interbank funding market and the foreign exchange markets to be tense after the bailout was rejected but vowed to provide liquidity to the market and to banks if necessary.

A spokesman at the Reserve Bank of New Zealand said it "has the systems in place" to cope with the current global market shakeout, although that didn't stop some analysts from speculating that the RBNZ may have to continue with aggressive rate cuts, and possibly even an emergency easing, to prevent the country from sliding into a steep recession.

And in South Korea, the Bank of Korea said it had been intervening in the swap market for a week to calm the markets and would continue to do so until the market stabilizes.

Regulators and government leaders also felt the need to weigh in, expressing dismay over the failed package and hope that there would be a rethink.

Australian Treasurer Wayne Swan said he was "disappointed" that the U.S. package failed to pass, but nevertheless emphasized the differences between the struggling U.S. financial system and Australia's system.

"Our regulators...are in constant contact with all of our deposit-taking institutions," Swan said. "The advice that we are receiving is that (the system) is in good shape."

Australian Prime Minister Kevin Rudd Tuesday urged U.S. lawmakers to reconsider the package and said friends and allies of the U.S. would push the U.S. Congress to pass the package, or similar measures later this week.

Hong Kong Financial Secretary John Tsang was more positive, saying he believed in the U.S. Congress's resolve to approve the plan, adding the rejection would severely damage global economies.

Overnight, eight central banks around the world, including the Bank of Japan, Reserve Bank of Australia and the European Central Bank, announced they were more than doubling the dollar-swap facility with the Federal Reserve to US$620 billion from US$290 billion to unclog markets scrambling to meet dollar-funding needs ahead of the quarter-end.

Japan doubled the size its swap facility with the Fed to US$120 billion while Australia tripled its facility to US$30 billion.

"A dollar-liquidity problem has been intensifying in Japan, and we need to make every effort to ease" the issue, Bank of Japan Governor Masaaki Shirakawa at a press conference overnight.

The RBA said Tuesday that it would announce in the next few days another U.S. dollar repurchase agreement operation to inject U.S. dollars into the financial system as part of the swap line expansion.

-By Karen Lane, Dow Jones Newswires; 65 6415 4043; karen.lane@dowjones.com

title: 2nd UPDATE: HKMA Injects Funds In Mkt; More To Come-Analysts
text:
(Adds analysts' comments on intervention.) 
 

HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--The Hong Kong Monetary Authority's injection of HK$1.556 billion into the interbank market Thursday is unlikely to be the last such intervention during the current global liquidity crunch, analysts said.

"Clearly, what they're doing is what everybody is doing, to provide as much liquidity as they can to the market, as the market is in such an irrational state," said J.P. Morgan analyst Claudio Piron.

Hong Kong interbank offered rates retreated from earlier highs after the HKMA announced the liquidity injection in the early afternoon. Thursday's rise was driven by strong demand for liquidity in the current credit crisis.

The one-month Hibor was last at 4.03%, down from a high of around 4.80% earlier in the session, but still up sharply from 2.22% late Wednesday.

The three-month Hibor was last at 2.75%, retreating from a high of 3.0% earlier in the session, but up from 2.16% late Wednesday.

Analysts said it was abnormal for short-dated Hibors to be higher than the long-dated counterpart.

"This implies that liquidity is extremely tight due to the credit concerns across the global markets," said Frances Cheung, fixed-income strategist at Standard Chartered Bank. "The HKMA's move is simply to ease the tight liquidity."

Cheung said a reasonable level for the one-month Hibor would be around 3%.

At 0755 GMT, the U.S. dollar was trading at HK$7.7821, down from HK$7.7838 late Wednesday.

The latest injection increases Hong Kong's aggregate balance, a measure of interbank liquidity, to HK$6.40 billion from HK$4.73 billion.

The HKMA last intervened in the market on Oct. 31, when it bought U.S. dollars to halt the Hong Kong dollar's rise.

At the time, the Hong Kong dollar had hovered near the top end of its trading band to the U.S. dollar before the HKMA stepped in to intervene.

title: UPDATE HKMA Investment Returns Hit 9 Year-high Of 11.8%
text:
(Adds comments from HKMA chief executive, exchange fund's total asset value.)   

By Chester Yung   

OF DOW JONES NEWSWIRES   

HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--The Hong Kong Monetary Authority said Monday its investment portfolio posted a nine-year high return of 11.8%, but added that such a performance could be hard to repeat this year.   

"Concerns about widening credit spreads, the profitability of financial institutions and the risks to U.S. economic growth will continue to affect sentiment," HKMA Chief Executive Joseph Yam told a news conference.   

Yam also said "unpredictable administrative measures" in mainland China can affect the investment environment.   

Yam didn't elaborate, but Hong Kong's market got a big lift in August when China said it would allow individuals in the mainland to purchase shares directly in Hong Kong, a deal that has become known as the "through train."   

Since then, there has been no word on when the program could start, stirring up much speculation about delays.   

The HKMA said Monday the Exchange Fund posted unaudited investment income of HK$142.2 billion (US$18.2 billion) last year, up from HK$103.8 billion in 2006. Net investment income in 2007 jumped to HK$132.2 billion from the previous year's HK$93.5 billion.   

The overall rate of return was 11.8%, the highest since the fund made 12.1% in 1998. The latest return was based largely on gains in local equities and bonds and compared with a return of 9.5% in 2006.   

Yam said market volatility is likely to remain high, given developments in international financial markets and the likely continued macroeconomic tightening in China. The Exchange Fund is used to manage Hong Kong's exchange rate and maintain financial stability. Its total assets stood at HK$1.42 trillion by the end of December, up from HK$1.18 trillion a year earlier.   

The fund made HK$55.8 billion, or about 40% of last year's gains, in the local stock market. It gained HK$61 billion from bonds and other investments. It generated a foreign-exchange gain of HK$18.7 billion in 2007 from its holdings in different currencies, mainly as a result of the appreciation of other currencies against the U.S. dollar. Hong Kong pegs its currency at 7.8 to the U.S. dollar.   

The Hong Kong government's share of the Exchange Fund's gains amounted to HK$27.6 billion, higher than the government's February 2007 estimate of HK$26 billion.   

Hong Kong places money from fiscal surpluses into the fund.   

Facing questions from reporters, Yam said there is no sign of massive capital outflow from Hong Kong despite a recent slide in the territory's stock market. Hong Kong blue chips added to their recent losses by plunging 5.5% Monday.   

Yam said the Hong Kong dollar has "remained stable" against the U.S. dollar.   

The HKMA is committed to keeping the local currency trading within a band of 7.75 to 7.85 to the U.S. dollar. It had to intervene five times in October when the Hong Kong dollar tested the upper limit of the band.   

-By Chester Yung, Dow Jones Newswires; 852-2802-7002; chester.yung@dowjones.com [ 21-01-08 1206GMT ]

The HKMA said Monday the Exchange Fund posted unaudited investment income of HK$142.2 billion (US$18.2 billion) last year, up from HK$103.8 billion in 2006. Net investment income in 2007 jumped to HK$132.2 billion from the previous year's HK$93.5 billion.   

The overall rate of return was 11.8%, the highest since the fund made 12.1% in 1998. The latest return was based largely on gains in local equities and bonds and compared with a return of 9.5% in 2006.   


Yam said market volatility is likely to remain high, given developments in international financial markets and the likely continued macroeconomic tightening in China.   

The Exchange Fund is used to manage Hong Kong's exchange rate and maintain financial stability. Its total assets stood at HK$1.42 trillion by the end of December, up from HK$1.18 trillion a year earlier. 
  
The fund made HK$55.8 billion, or about 40% of last year's gains, in the local stock market. It gained HK$61 billion from bonds and other investments.   It generated a foreign-exchange gain of HK$18.7 billion in 2007 from its holdings in different currencies, mainly as a result of the appreciation of other currencies against the U.S. dollar. Hong Kong pegs its currency at 7.8 to the U.S. dollar. 
   

The Hong Kong government's share of the Exchange Fund's gains amounted to HK$27.6 billion, higher than the government's February 2007 estimate of HK$26 billion. Hong Kong places money from fiscal surpluses into the fund. Facing questions from reporters, Yam said there is no sign of massive capital outflow from Hong Kong despite a recent slide in the territory's stock market. Hong Kong blue chips added to their recent losses by plunging 5.5% Monday. Yam said the Hong Kong dollar has 'remained stable' against the U.S. dollar. The HKMA is committed to keeping the local currency trading within a band of 7.75 to 7.85 to the U.S. dollar. It had to intervene five times in October when the Hong Kong dollar tested the upper limit of the band. -By Chester Yung, Dow Jones Newswires; 852-2802-7002; chester.yung@dowjones.com -0-

title: IMF urges HK to fix anomalies to guard dollar peg
text:
HONG KONG, Nov 20 (Reuters) - The International Monetary Fund has urged Hong Kong to look at ways to reduce anomalies between its money and exchange rate markets to prevent speculative pressure on the territory's currency peg.   

Hong Kong interbank rates, which typically trade below U.S. dollar rates, recently shot up partly because of fund inflows for big initial public offerings by mainland Chinese firms.   

The high interest rates, and rapid fund flows into local equities, pushed the Hong Kong dollar <HKD=> to the top of its trading band for the first time last month, prompting the Hong Kong Monetary Authority to intervene to defend the peg.   

The Hong Kong dollar is pegged at 7.8 to the U.S. dollar but since 2005 has been allowed to trade between 7.75 and 7.85   

"The authorities could consider reinforcing the link between changes in the aggregate balance and Hong Kong dollar interest rates, as well as look to improve the management of liquidity within the financial system," the IMF said in a report on Hong Kong circulated on Tuesday.   

"Doing so could help to avoid further episodic anomalies between the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate and interest rate movements, which is a potential source of market speculation about the longevity of the linked exchange rate system."   

Joseph Yam, chief executive of the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, told legislators this month that there was room to enhance the peg -- known as the linked exchange rate system -- without fundamentally changing it, but did not say how.   

Investment bank  Morgan Stanley said his remarks suggested the HKMA would look at ways to improve efficiency of the money market.   

Interbank rates were pushed up to their highest levels in six years last month as strong demand for Hong Kong dollars for IPOs tightened liquidity and as banks were cautious about lending in the wake of a global credit squeeze.   

A strong stock market pushed the currency to test its limit at 7.75 and some speculators emerged, betting the territory could abandon its link with the U.S. dollar or widen the trading band.   

Yam said the government had no intention of changing the peg or widening the band and the IMF in its report supported Hong Kong's commitment to the linked exchange rate system.   

Rates have now dropped below U.S. dollar rates and the Hong Kong dollar is back within its trading band. It was quoted at 7.7812/13 on Tuesday afternoon. (Reporting by Susan Fenton, editing by Dominic Whiting)

title: UPDATE: HK Fincl Secy: To Increase Reserves To Defend Peg
text:
(Adds more comments from Tsang, background of Exchange Fund.)   

By Jackie Cheung   

of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES   

HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--Hong Kong Financial Secretary John Tsang said Monday the government plans to gradually increase its fiscal reserves to maintain monetary and fiscal stability, giving it greater ability to defend against any attacks on the Hong Kong dollar's peg to the U.S. dollar.   

Tsang told legislators he expects the government's reserves will gradually increase to HK$587.9 billion (US$75.4 billion) in the fiscal year ended 2012, representing 30.2% of GDP, up from the current fiscal year's HK$394.7 billion, which accounts for 25.7% of GDP.   

"We have seen the speculation last week, and we expect the market to remain volatile, so we want to increase our reserves as much as possible to defend our peg," Tsang told legislators. "We shall maintain the fiscal reserves to the extent necessary to meet our needs."   

Hong Kong pegs its currency at HK$7.8 to the U.S. dollar and allows it to trade within a band of HK$7.75-HK$7.85 to the U.S. unit.   

Last week, the HKMA intervened in the currency markets five times, selling a total of HK$7.828 billion for U.S. dollars, as the local dollar reached the upper limit of its trading band on inflows of funds into Hong Kong's red-hot stock market. The HKMA had intervened twice the previous week with a smaller amount.   

The government's fiscal reserves are transferred to the Exchange Fund, which is under the management of the Hong Kong Monetary Authority and can be used to back the issuance of Hong Kong banknotes.   

According to the HKMA, the total assets of the Exchange Fund amounted to HK$1.31 trillion at the end of September, up from HK$1.14 trillion a year earlier.   

Tsang said inflation - driven by higher food prices, a weaker U.S. dollar and a vibrant stock market - will be one of his major concerns for coming years.   

He expects the composite consumer price index may rise between 1.8% and 2% this year, though he said the level isn't particularly high taking into account the better-than-expected 6.1% growth in first-half gross domestic product.   

-By Jackie Cheung, Dow Jones Newswires; 852-2802-7002; jackie.cheung@dowjones.com [ 05-11-07 1057GMT ]

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES   

HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--The Hong Kong Monetary Authority intervened twice in the currency market Wednesday, buying HK$3.875 billion worth of U.S. dollars to halt the Hong Kong dollar's rise and keep it within its allowable trading band to the U.S. unit.   

Analysts said they expect further interventions by the city's de-facto central bank in the near term amid expectations the U.S. Federal Reserve will cut its key interest rates later Wednesday.   

"I expect the intervention will typically come in a wave, rather than being one-off," said  JPMorgan analyst Claudio Piron. "We'll likely continue to see more intervention going forward."   

Under Hong Kong's currency board system, the Hong Kong dollar is pegged at 7.80 to the U.S. dollar but is allowed to trade between 7.75 and 7.85. When the Hong Kong dollar reaches the limits of its trading band, the HKMA can be expected to intervene.   

The HKMA declined to provide the level at which it intervened Wednesday, but traders said they believed it was 7.75.   

The Hong Kong dollar had hovered near the top end of its trading band to the U.S. dollar all morning Wednesday, before the HKMA stepped in first with a HK$3.1 billion intervention. Less than half an hour later, it made a HK$775 million intervention.   

Wednesday's moves follow two interventions by the HKMA last week, which were its first such actions in more than two years.

title: UPDATE 3-HK spends $1 bln easing HKD, waves off de-pegging talk
text:
(Add details, latest intervention, market comments)   

HONG KONG, Oct 31 (Reuters) - Hong Kong's central bank sold the equivalent of around US$1 billion in Hong Kong dollars on Wednesday as the local currency bumped up repeatedly against the ceiling of its trading band with the weakening U.S. dollar.   

The central bank intervened five times in three hours, selling HK$7.828 billion as it stepped up efforts to temper the strength of the local currency.   

The Hong Kong dollar has clung stubbornly to its two-year-old ceiling of 7.75 against the U.S. dollar, which hit a record low against a basket of major currencies for the fourth trading day in a row on Wednesday.   

Funds flowing into Hong Kong, plus rising import costs from the Chinese mainland, are stirring talk that the Hong Kong Monetary Authority will have to drop a two-decade-old peg against the U.S. dollar, or at least widen the local currency's wafer-thin trading band.   

Fuelling upward pressure on the currency was demand to buy shares in the initial public offering of China e-commerce firm  Alibaba.com.

The US$1.49 billion offer has attracted about US$100 billion in orders from institutions alone, sustaining inflows from outside Hong Kong into Asia's second-largest stock market.   

Traders and analysts saw little pure speculative buying. The central bank reaffirmed its commitment to the peg, adding it had no intention of lobbying Beijing at present for permission to drop the link despite talk to the contrary.   

"If there's any speculative buying, it wasn't big. The Alibaba subscriptions need Hong Kong dollars. Local interest rates are high now, but will come down after the Alibaba settlement," said Andrew Fung, head of investment and insurance at Hang Seng Bank.   

"The stock market is so hot these days."   

The local currency is pegged at 7.8 per U.S. dollar but since May 2005 has been allowed to trade between 7.75 and 7.85. Under the exchange rate mechanism, the central bank is committed to buying U.S. dollars from licensed banks in exchange for Hong Kong dollars if the spot rate hits 7.75.   

Indded, the HKMA had to intervene twice last week, selling a total of HK$1.55 billion for U.S. dollars.   

By 0938 GMT, the Hong Kong dollar was trading at 7.7500/01 against the U.S. dollar.   

RUMOURS FLY   

ING expects Hong Kong to prise the trading range wider in time, possibly at the upper limit. But economists said abandoning the peg, which stood firm through the Asian financial crisis of 1997/98 and the SARS epidemic of 2003/04, was unlikely.   

Talk of an imminent adjustment -- which includes speculation of an adjustment of the exchange rate, or a link to the Chinese yuan -- picked up in volume after government sources said central bank chief Joseph Yam would step down in 2009.   

"The government is fully committed to the maintenance of the linked exchange rate system," a central bank spokesman said, repeating comments on the peg over the past week. "We have no intention to introduce any changes to the system."   

Reuters data showed the central bank intervened on Wednesday for the first time shortly after the currency hit its ceiling at 0705 GMT, selling HK$3.1 billion worth of local currency. It followed with four other actions over the next few hours.   

Before the peg speculation re-emerged in past months, a buoyant stock market, frenzied IPO activity and a weakening U.S. dollar had already attracted funds into the city.   

"A strengthening yuan, appreciation of Asian currencies against the greenback, plus talk of Yam's departure, are all triggering talk of a change in the peg," a trader with a foreign bank said. "As the local currency holds firm, that's attracting an inflow of capital."   

Hong Kong's blue-chip Hang Seng Index has risen about 50 percent in the past two months, after China said it would let mainland individuals buy into Hong Kong stocks. Now, mounting inflation is lending weight to arguments for a peg abolition.   

Others argue that inflation has quickened this year, partly because of the rising cost of Chinese imports as the yuan climbs in value, but remains relatively moderate at below 3 percent. ($1=HK$7.750) (Additional reporting by Alison Leung)

title: UPDATE 2- Hong Kong intervenes  to defend its  currency  peg
text:
(Adds quote, details)   

HONG KONG, Oct 26 (Reuters) - Hong Kong's central bank intervened on Friday to curb strength in the Hong Kong dollar and underline its commitment to the linked exchange rate, after the currency hit its upper limit for the second time this week.   

The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) sold HK$775 million (US$100 million) for U.S. dollars after the most actively traded currency in Asia after the yen hit 7.75 <HKD=> per U.S. dollar, partly fuelled by a stock market <.HSI> rally to a record high.   

"The government is fully committed to the maintenance of the linked exchange rate system," a spokesman for the HKMA said.   

Funds flowing into Hong Kong, plus quickening inflation as Chinese import costs rise, have fuelled speculation the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) will have to drop its two-decade peg against the U.S. dollar, or at least widen the currency's trading band.   

ING Financial Markets said in a research note that it expected Hong Kong to widen the band in time, possibly only at the upper limit. But for now economists said abandoning the peg was unlikely.   

"We see no change. The HKMA's actions today agree with the principles of the currency board," said Ben Simpfendorfer, an economist at  Royal Bank of Scotland.

"There's a lot of interest at the moment in the Hong Kong dollar in particular because of a buoyant equity market. We think the peg is credible and it makes no sense to change it."   

Under the currency board system, the Hong Kong dollar can trade in a range of 7.75-7.85 per dollar, around a peg of 7.8. The HKMA is committed to buy U.S. dollars for Hong Kong dollars if the spot rate hits 7.75.   

Real time information available on Reuters page <HKMAOOC> showed the HKMA intervened at 0425 GMT. By 0649 GMT the Hong Kong dollar had pulled back to 7.7505/06 to the U.S. dollar, Reuters data showed.   

On Tuesday, the HKMA also sold HK$775 million for U.S. dollars after the currency hit 7.75. The upper limit of the trading band was only set in 2005. Previously the currency was pegged at 7.8 per dollar with a lower limit of 7.85.   

CREDIT SQUEEZE   

Although the stock market has been rallying all year, the Hong Kong dollar was held in check earlier in 2007 by an interest rate trade in the interbank market.   

The trade was based on the fact that Hong Kong interbank interest rates were lower than corresponding rates in the United States.   

That meant investors could profit by selling Hong Kong dollars for U.S. dollars to exploit the higher U.S. interbank rates. The interest rate advantage has now been lost, so fewer Hong Kong dollars are flowing out of the territory.   

Hong Kong interbank rates subsequently rose to six-year highs amid tight demand for Hong Kong dollars to fund investment in recent new stock market listings and as a global credit squeeze made lender more cautious.   

While inflation has been quickening this year, partly because of the rising cost of Chinese imports as the yuan <CNY=CFXS> steadily increases in value, economists say it remains relatively moderate at less than 3 percent.   

"At a time when Hong Kong's domestic CPI inflation trend is heading up gradually, it is perhaps not surprising that there has been renewed market concerns on the sustainability of the Hong Kong dollar peg regime,"  JP Morgan's head of China research, Frank Gong, wrote in a research note.   

But he added: "We believe the probability of any significant near-term change to the Hong Kong dollar peg regime is very low." (Additional reporting by Donny Kwok) ($1=HK$7.750)

HONG KONG, Aug 1 (Reuters) - The Hong Kong dollar <HKD=> on Wednesday hit its lowest level since it was pegged to the U.S. dollar more than two decades ago as investors fled the local stock market and reduced their exposure to Asian currencies.   

The currency slid to 7.83 to the U.S. dollarin afternoon trade after the stock market's benchmark Hang Seng Index <.HSI> plunged 3.2 percent on the day, on record turnover, as concerns grew that woes in the U.S. subprime mortgage sector were having an impact overseas. For details, click on [.HK]   

The Hong Kong dollar has been linked to the U.S. currency since 1983. It is pegged at 7.8 to the U.S. dollar but can trade between 7.75 and 7.85.   

"Funds are flowing out of Asia, including Hong Kong and that is being reflected in the Hong Kong dollar as well," said Nizam Idris, Asian foreign exchange strategist at  UBS in Singapore.   

"We're seeing a general re-rating of risk and Asian markets that have seen significant inflows are seeing a reversal of that. But Asian fundamentals are strong and once the market gets a lot more balanced fundamentals will be of some support in Asia, Hong Kong included."   

Support for the Hong Kong dollar at 7.83 appeared to be firm. However, analysts said the currency could break that level in coming weeks amid continued re-rating of investor risk appetite across Asia. They said it was unlikely to fall as low as 7.85. If it does hit that level the Hong Kong Monetary Authority would have to intervene to maintain the currency band.   

Funds have flooded into Hong Kong stocks this year, pushing the market to all-time highs, amid keen investor interest in Chinese companies and a robust Hong Kong economy, which is forecast to grow 5.5 percent this year, according to a Reuters poll.   

Hong Kong's China enterprises index <.HSCE> of Chinese companies listed on the Hong Kong exchange slid 3.9 percent on Wednesday, after plunging more than 5 percent in early afternoon trade.   

While demand for Hong Kong dollars for stock purchases has been strong this year, the currency has weakened as speculative fund flows anticipating Hong Kong would adjust its currency regime to trade more in line with China's appreciating yuan have disappeared.   

Arbitrage trade has also put pressure on the currency. As the Hong Kong dollar is pegged to the U.S. dollar and U.S. dollar interest rates are higher, investors make a profit on the interest rate spread by selling Hong Kong dollars for U.S. dollars.   

Traders said arbitrage trade was adding to the Hong Kong currency's losses on Wednesday, as investors who were unwinding risky carry trades in other Asian currencies saw Hong Kong dollar-U.S. dollar arbitrage trade as a relatively safe place to park some of their cash.

title: UPDATE:HKMA Chief Exec Yam:Not Concerned About Weakening HK$
text:
(Adds comments from Yam and strategist, and updated Hong Kong dollar level.)   

HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--Hong Kong Monetary Authority Chief Executive Joseph Yam said he isn't concerned about the fall in the Hong Kong dollar, as the currency dropped to its lowest level against the U.S. dollar in 22 years Friday.   

"In fact, because we now have a convertibility zone, I wouldn't attach any particular significance to the position of the spot exchange rate within the zone," he said in his weekly Internet column posted Thursday.   

The Hong Kong dollar plunged to a fresh 22-year low of HK$7.8263 against the U.S. dollar in early morning trading Friday on carry trade-related demand for the U.S. dollar. Investors see the Hong Kong dollar as a low-risk funding currency for carry trade as the Hong Kong-U.S. interest rate differential remains wide.   

The local unit was at HK$7.8242 at 0400 GMT Friday and is poised to trend lower as U.S. dollar demand persists, traders said.   

Standard Chartered PLC strategist David Mann said he expects the local unit to test the Hong Kong dollar's weak-side border at HK$7.85 in the next two to three months, as there is no large-scale fundraising activity to offset U.S. dollar demand for carry trade.   

In his column, however, the head of the city's de-facto central bank warned of dangers related to any sudden narrowing of the U.S.-Hong Kong rate gap.   

"If the gap closes abruptly, then firms and households and the financial system in Hong Kong might suffer from a large interest-rate shock, which is not good for financial stability," he said.   

Yam said the refinements to the local currency's peg to the U.S. dollar that were introduced two years ago have worked well so far and reiterated that there is no intention to use the Chinese yuan as the Hong Kong dollar's anchor currency.   

But Yam said it remains to be seen how the Hong Kong dollar will behave when it moves closer to the weak-side border at HK$7.85.   

He said Hong Kong's de-facto central bank has intervened only once within the HK$7.75 to HK$7.85 trading band to smooth out IPO-related interest-rate volatility.   

The HKMA intervened a week after it introduced refinement measures to the peg system on May 18, 2005 by selling HK$544 million of Hong Kong dollars in the currency market to address strong market demands for the local unit ahead of a slew of initial public offerings.   

In June 2005,  Bank of Communications Ltd. and China Cosco Holdings Ltd. raised more than US$3 billion from two large offerings.   

The Hong Kong dollar is pegged to the U.S. dollar at HK$7.80, but its trading band was widened to five Hong Kong cents below and above the peg rate on May 18, 2005 to increase the system's flexibility.   

-By Amy Or, Dow Jones Newswires; 852-2832 2335; amy.or@dowjones.com [ 25-05-07 0440GMT ]

title: HKMA says no net outflow of HK dollars since May'05
text:
HONG KONG, March 15 (Reuters) - Hong Kong has not seen any net outflow of Hong Kong dollars into foreign currencies since it widened the dollar's trading band in May 2005, the head of the Hong Kong Monetary Authority said on Thursday.  

 A recent downturn in the local stock market has raised concern that funds could leave the territory and reduce what has been ample liquidity and force interest rates to head higher.  

 Joseph Yam, chief executive of the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA), the central bank, said in a weekly column posted on the HKMA's Website  www.info.gov.hk/hkma ("http://www.info.gov.hk/hkma") that fund outflows could refer to either an outflow of funds from the Hong Kong dollar into foreign currencies or to the movement of money in any currency out of Hong Kong such as via stocks.  

 "As far as the Hong Kong dollar is concerned, there has not been any net outflow into foreign currencies since May 2005 after the introduction of refinements to the linked exchange rate system," Yam wrote.  

 The Hong Kong dollar has been pegged at 7.8 to the U.S. dollar for more than two decades. In May 2005, Hong Kong adjusted the mechanism, introducing an upper limit for the currency, at 7.75, and lowering the currency's downside to 7.85.  

 Under the mechanism the HKMA is required to intervene if the currency moves beyond the trading band by buying or selling Hong Kong dollars in exchange for U.S. dollars. However, it can also intervene by buying or selling Hong Kong dollars on a discretionary basis within the trading band.  

 The Hong Kong dollar has been weak recently, hitting an 18-year low at 7.8189 this month, but it has not broken its lower cap at 7.85. Late on Thursday it was trading at 8.8118.
