title: UPDATE 2-HKMA says has not  intervened  on HK dollar
text:
(Adds trader quote, details)  

HONG KONG, Jan 24 (Reuters) - The Hong Kong Monetary Authority said on Wednesday it has not intervened to influence the local dollar, despite suggestions to the contrary by investment bank UBS.  

 UBS suggested in a research report that the HKMA had a hand in the Hong Kong currency's recent decline to stave off upward pressure after the Chinese yuan <CNY=CFXS> overtook the Hong Kong dollar <HKD=> in value this month.  

 "The HKMA does not comment on individual reports," Hong Kong Monetary Authority spokesman Thomas Chan said in an email to Reuters.  

 "Following the introduction of the three refinements in May 2005, the Hong Kong dollar may move within the convertibility zone from 7.7500 to 7.8500," Chan added, referring to adjustments to the Hong Kong trading band in 2005.  

 "We will continue to keep a close watch over the markets and keep our finger on the pulse of the markets. We have not intervened in the Hong Kong dollar as (HKMA chief executive) Mr Yam has already said last week."  

 The Hong Kong dollar has weakened this year. In the past week it has fallen below its official peg at 7.8 to the U.S. dollar, hitting a near 17-year low at 7.8122 on Friday -- bucking expectations it would draw upward pressure after being overtaken in value by the yuan on Jan. 11.  

 "Once the renminbi started to enter 'Hong Kong airspace' the Hong Kong dollar made a sudden jump, weakening to the other end of the band, and the renminbi made a sudden jump as well, strengthening past the Hong Kong dollar at a rapid clip," UBS economist Jonathan Anderson wrote in the research report, which circulated in the past few days.  

 "This looks a lot like a Hong Kong dollar/renminbi 'squeeze play'," he wrote. "In other words, in order to minimise market speculation and volatility associated with the two exchange rates crossing each other, the HKMA and the People's Bank of China (PBOC) decide to speed up the process, the HKMA pushing the Hong Kong dollar weaker while the PBOC picks up the appreciation pace on the renminbi side."  

 TRADERS DOUBTFUL  

 Market traders attribute the Hong Kong dollar's decline to interest rate arbitrage activity and because demand for the Hong Kong currency is not as high as late last year when jumbo initial public offerings were launched on the stock exchange.  

 "I don't think there has been any irregular activity in the market as the Hong Kong dollar is trading within the convertibility range," a trader at a European bank said.  

 On Jan. 11, the yuan, also known as the renminbi, hit parity with the Hong Kong dollar at 7.8 to the U.S. dollar for the first time in 13 years and continues to appreciate.  

 The yuan was trading at 7.7738 on Wednesday afternoon. The Hong Kong dollar, which is pegged at 7.8 to the U.S. dollar but since May 2005 can trade between 7.75 and 7.85, was trading at 7.8018.  

 The Chinese currency's appreciation beyond the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate had raised speculation about whether Hong Kong would maintain its currency link with the U.S. dollar.  

 The HKMA has repeatedly stressed that it has no intention of abandoning its currency peg with the U.S. dollar and that parity with the yuan exchange rate would have no impact on currency policy.  

 Financial Secretary Henry Tang has said there is no question of linking the Hong Kong dollar with the yuan while the yuan is not a convertible currency.   (Additional reporting by Christina Lo)

title: =DJ UPDATE: HKMA Yam: No Need To  Intervene  In HK  Forex  Mkt
text:
(Updates with comments from HKMA chief executive, Exchange Fund's total asset value.) By Amy Or Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES  

HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--Hong Kong Monetary Authority Chief Executive Joseph Yam said he doesn't see the need to intervene in the local foreign-exchange market, after the Hong Kong dollar fell to a 20-month low against the U.S. currency for the second session in a row Thursday.  

The Hong Kong dollar is pegged to the U.S. dollar at HK$7.80 under the 23-year old Linked Exchange Rate System. In late Asian trade, the U.S. dollar was at HK$7.8067, up from HK$7.8036 late Wednesday, when it fell below the peg rate for the first time since May 2005.  

'So far the Hong Kong dollar hasn't deviated too far from HK$7.80...We didn't see a need to intervene in the past, and we don't see the need to do so now,' Yam said at a briefing.  

But he said the HKMA still has the discretion to smooth out volatilities in the Hong Kong dollar.  

Under reforms to Hong Kong's foreign-exchange rate system made in May 2005, the HKMA committed to keeping the Hong Kong dollar within a convertibility band of HK$7.75-HK$7.85 to the U.S. dollar, 5 HK cents either side of the peg rate.

title: HKMA's Yam: Yuan Rise Won't Have Strong Impact On HK Dlr
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--The Hong Kong dollar isn't likely to be significantly affected by the rise of the Chinese yuan, even if the Chinese currency breaches the psychologically important 7.80 level against the U.S. dollar, the head of Hong Kong's de facto central bank said Thursday.  

The USD/CNY dipped below 8.00 Monday and that had "no noticeable effect on the exchange rate of the Hong Kong dollar," Hong Kong Monetary Authority Chief Executive Joseph Yam said in his weekly Internet column.  

He said he believed this would also be the case even if the yuan passes through "another psychological level of 7.80."  

The Hong Kong dollar was at 7.7539 against the U.S. dollar in late trade Thursday, while the yuan was at 8.0180.  

Hong Kong now combines a classical currency board with active intervention in a trading band from HK$7.75 to HK$7.85, around the fixed exchange rate of HK$7.80. The upper limit on the currency, imposed last year, has helped defuse market speculation that a possible appreciation of the Chinese yuan, also known as the renminbi, would also push the Hong Kong dollar higher.  

Yam said the Hong Kong dollar would have been "a much more popular proxy for market participants to take speculative positions on the renminbi" had the measure not been implemented.  

He added the widening of the Hong Kong dollar's trading band "served to anchor exchange rate expectation at a critical moment."  

Yam said China's current account surplus wouldn't be resolved by exchange rate appreciation alone. He said China has a good opportunity to further liberalize its capital account to allow the large pool of domestic savings to seek higher risk-adjusted rates of return overseas.  

-By Amy Or, Dow Jones Newswires; 852-2832 2335; amy.or@dowjones.com

title: HK Dlr Mkts Late: HK Dlr At 4-Month High On Dlr Weakness
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--The Hong Kong dollar rose to a four-month high Monday as a broadly weak dollar and concerns Asian central banks may refrain from keeping their currencies weak sparked selling of the U.S. unit, dealers said.  

The U.S. dollar fell to HK$7.7514 in late trading from HK$7.7532 late Thursday and was down from the fixing level earlier Monday of HK$7.7522. Hong Kong was closed for a public holiday Friday. The Hong Kong dollar was at its strongest level since Jan. 11, when it also finished at HK$7.7514.  

Speculation that U.S. pressure is mounting on Japan and other Asian nations to let their currencies strengthen to calm protectionist sentiment at home and reduce the huge U.S. trade deficit sent the U.S. dollar lower, traders said. That helped send the U.S. dollar to below JPY112.00 for the first time in seven-and-a-half months.  

Selling of the U.S. dollar for the Hong Kong dollar Monday stopped shy of triggering the Hong Kong Monetary Authority's intervention level of HK$7.7500, a rate at which the central bank sells Hong Kong dollars to keep the currency peg intact.  

"The pair is fairly heavy (low) but the support band will hold," one senior trader said Monday.  

U.S. dollar/Hong Kong dollar forwards were lower on more confident expectations of the underlying future strength in the local unit, dealers said.  

The one-year contract was quoted at a 535-515 discount in late trade from a 482-472 discount late Thursday, reflecting expectations of a stronger Hong Kong dollar in a year's time compared with the current spot rate.  

Hong Kong interbank offered rates were lower, with the one-month rate easing to 3.91% from 4.02% late Thursday, as capital inflows into Hong Kong through the foreign exchange market helped add more liquidity to the interbank market, dealers said.  

The one-month Hibor has "been expensive in the past month" because of investors borrowing funds to buy into initial public offerings, including the coming US$7 billion Bank of China offer, one dealer said, but Monday's inflows helped offset that. [ 08-05-06 0850GMT ]

title: HK Dlr Mkts Late: HK Dlr Nears Cap As Inflows Continue
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--The Hong Kong dollar continued to rise against the U.S. dollar Wednesday, reaching a fresh high as investors continued to move funds into the currency to buy into big upcoming share sales.  

The U.S. dollar was quoted at HK$7.7600 Wednesday afternoon, down from HK$7.7622 Tuesday.  

It was the closest the Hong Kong dollar has come to the upper end of its permitted trading range against the U.S. dollar since the new top limit of 7.75 was implemented in May. The Hong Kong dollar's previous high was 7.7611.  

Market participants say the past week's rise in the Hong Kong dollar is due to investors preparing funds to buy into some large initial public offerings on the local bourse in coming weeks, such as China Construction Bank and the Link real estate investment trust.  

The movements don't appear to be due to pure currency speculation, and so aren't likely to draw the Hong Kong Monetary Authority to intervene in the foreign exchange market, one banker said.  

"After the HKMA issued the three refinements in May, I don't think speculators will try to push up the value of the Hong Kong dollar," said Mark Wan, vice president of treasury and markets for DBS Bank in Hong Kong.  

"If the money coming in was for speculation, I think the HKMA would do something," he said. "But I don't think they will do anything."  

U.S. dollar/Hong Kong dollar forwards were a touch lower Wednesday, but haven't moved dramatically despite the relatively large changes in the spot rate.  

The one-year contract was quoted at 138-128 points below the spot rate Wednesday, compared with a discount of 115-100 points Tuesday.  

Hong Kong interbank offered rates were also stable, apparently a sign that the funds moving in for IPO purchases aren't boosting liquidity in the interbank market. The one-year Hibor was unchanged at 3.97%.  

Yields on Hong Kong Exchange Fund notes fell, tracking the overnight moves in U.S. Treasurys after producer price index data showed little increase in inflation despite high energy prices.  

The two-year Exchange Fund note was quoted at a yield of 3.59%, down from 3.65% Tuesday, while the yield on the 10-year bond eased to 4.07% from 4.12% previously.

title: HKMA Says Market  Operations  Will Target "Anomalies"
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--Hong Kong Monetary Authority chief Joseph Yam says the body's interventions in the local foreign exchange market will mainly be aimed at resolving persistent "anomalies" in the behavior of interest rates.  

The comments by Yam, made in his weekly Internet column, are an apparent attempt to clarify the quasi-central bank's position and reassure market participants that the HKMA won't be a frequent actor in the currency market.  

Last month, the HKMA adjusted the Hong Kong dollar's long-standing peg to the U.S. dollar to take the form of a trading band from HK$7.75 to HK$7.85, and said it would conduct market operations within that range at its own discretion. The HKMA had previously taken a more passive stance, buying or selling Hong Kong dollars only when it was approached by market players.  

"I can understand the anxiety of those active in the foreign exchange market about what our stance might be within the convertibility zone," Yam wrote in his column. "It shouldn't be difficult to understand our thinking."  

While insisting that the HKMA doesn't have a specific interest rate policy, Yam said that the currency-board system implies that "in normal circumstances our interest rates track those of the U.S. dollar."  

While some interest rate volatility is normal when funds are moving into or out of Hong Kong, Yam said, "we would like also to avoid a situation where interest rate differentials become so large and persistent as to possibly jeopardize monetary and financial stability."  

Yam said he couldn't define the precise conditions that would prompt the HKMA to intervene, as the decision remains "a matter of judgment" that depends on circumstances.  

"It would be unreasonable to expect us to stand on the sidelines if credible evidence emerges of mounting instability in the market or conditions that prevent smooth interest rate adjustments," he said.  

The HKMA's shift to the current system was prompted by the persistent failure of Hong Kong interest rates to follow U.S. interest rates upward as market speculation about the appreciation of the Chinese yuan intensified.  

Since the previous arrangement didn't put an explicit limit on the appreciation of the Hong Kong dollar, market participants were unwilling to sell the currency, and push its interest rates higher, because of the possible loss if the Hong Kong dollar were to rise sharply.

title: HK dollar weakens as players cover short USD positions
text:
HONG KONG, June 1 (Reuters) - The Hong Kong dollar gave up recent gains on Wednesday, weighed down by a firmer U.S. dollar, dimming hopes of a near term Chinese yuan revaluation and a softening in short-dated money rates.  

The local currency <HKD=> weakened to a one-week low of 7.7845 per U.S. dollar at 0930 GMT from 7.7786/87 in late Asian trading on Tuesday.  

"The U.S. dollar rebound and fading expectations of a yuan revaluation soon have put pressure on Asian currencies. That prompted some players to cover short (U.S.) dollar positions," said a dealer from a European bank.  

Hong Kong dollar forwards were rangebound following the movement in spot rate, dealers said.  

The discount on one-year forwards <HKD1Y=> was trading at 245/220 pips, versus 300/270 pips earlier and Tuesday's close of 270/250 pips.  

The U.S. dollar surged to a 7-½ month highs against the euro <EUR=> ahead of a Dutch vote late on Wednesday which is expected to reject the European Union constitution, after France voted against it last weekend.  

Some traders said a raging dispute between China, United States and Europe over Chinese textile exports had reduced chances of an imminent adjustment of the Chinese yuan.  

Short-term interbank rates surrendered some of their recent gains as traders worried about possible interventions by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA), the city's central bank.  

"The HKMA stands ready to provide support if coming IPOs create pressure on the money markets," HKMA chief Joseph Yam told reporters on Tuesday.  

Interbank rates have risen in recent weeks as expected demand for IPOs put a squeeze on banks' funds.  

A spate of Chinese companies are hoping to raise about HK$60 billion from initial offering in Hong Kong in June and July.  

The mainland's largest coal producer, China Shenhua Energy Co., which plans to raise up to US$3.6 billion, will kick off its retail offering this Thursday.  

"Since three IPOs will be launched one after another and not overlap each other, we don't think it will put too much (upside) pressure on the money rates if banks make appropriate arrangements beforehand," one trader said.  

The overnight rate was quoted at 2.62-2.75 percent late on Wednesday. The two-week eased to 3.40-3.45 percent from 3.50-3.56 percent on Tuesday.

title: HK dollar edges lower in thin trade
text:
HONG KONG, May 30 (Reuters) - The Hong Kong dollar edged lower on Monday in thin trade but dealers say the underlying tone is firm on hopes of more fund flows into the city for a string of upcoming initial public offerings (IPOs).  

"There was some U.S. dollar buying in late trade from a U.S. name, however, overall trading volume for the day was thin given the London and U.S. markets are closed for a holiday," one senior trader from a local bank said.  

The trader said he expected the spot rate to move in a range between HK$7.7750, the level at which the central bank intervened last week, and HK$7.7830 which should attract some (U.S.) dollar selling for the local currency for upcoming IPOs.  

The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) intervened last Wednesday and sold HK$544 million of local currency in exchange for U.S. dollars in a bid to curb the Hong Kong dollar's advance against the greenback.  

On May 18, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) set a trading band for the Hong Kong dollar of between 7.75 and 7.85 to the U.S. dollar. The lower limit of the trading band will be phased in over five weeks, moving by 100 pips every Monday from May 23 until June 20. The authority also said it may conduct market operations within the "convertibility zone".  

Several IPOs by major Chinese companies worth about HK$60 billion are expected to list on the Hong Kong bourse in June and July, attracting foreign investment flows to the city.  

China Cosco Holdings Co. Ltd., which operates the world's seventh largest container fleet, began marketing a US$1.7 billion IPO on Monday.  

The mainland's largest coal producer China Shenhua Energy Co., which plans to raise up to US$3.6 billion, will kick off its retail offering this Thursday. The deal is set to price on June 8 and will debut on June 15.  

The local currency <HKD=> was trading at 7.7797/98 per U.S. dollar at 0902 GMT after hitting an intraday's low of 7.78, weaker than 7.7968/70 in late Asian trade on Friday.  

Hong Kong dollar forwards were trapped in narrow ranges in quiet trade, dealers said.

In the cash market, short-term interbank rates firmed slightly in afternoon trade with the two-week and one-month rates trading at 3.35-3.40 percent and 3.35-3.45 percent, respectively.  

Other interbank rates were little changed.

title: HK dollar firms as funds flow in for IPOs
text:
HONG KONG, May 27 (Reuters) - The Hong Kong dollar edged higher on Friday, bolstered by persistent fund flows into the territory ahead of a series of China-themed initial public offerings over the next two months.  

The local currency <HKD=> rose to as high as 7.7765 per U.S. dollar before slipping back to 7.7768/70 by 0856 GMT, firmer than 7.7795/96 in late Asian trade on Thursday.  

Several initial public offerings (IPOs) by major Chinese companies worth about HK$60 billion are expected to list on the Hong Kong bourse in June and July, attracting foreign investment flows to the territory.  

At the head of the IPO queue is the top mainland coal producer China Shenhua Energy Co., which plans to raise up to US$3.6 billion next week. The deal is set to price on June 8 and will debut on June 15.  

Interbank rates softened from recent highs amid a firming local currency as some banks were willing to release excess funds, dealers said.  

Some traders also attributed the decline to players adjusting positions on concern about further intervention by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA).  

The HKMA, the territory's de facto central bank, intervened on Wednesday and sold HK$544 million of local currency in exchange for U.S. dollar in a bid to curb the Hong Kong dollar's advance against the greenback.  

Interbank rates rose last week as liquidity tightened following HKMA moves to refine the exchange rate system, and as players positioned themselves for the upcoming IPOs in the stock market. Some investors withdrew funds from the territory after the HKMA announced its new measures.  

On May 18, the HKMA set a trading band for the Hong Kong dollar (HKD) of between 7.75 and 7.85 to the U.S. dollar in a move to prop up interest rates and discourge speculators using the currency to bet on a revaluation of the Chinese yuan.  

The overnight interbank rate eased to 2.70-2.80 percent late on Friday versus a recent high of 3.25 percent. The three-month rate was around 3.23-3.35 percent, down from 3.35-3.40 percent in the previous day.

title: HK Dlr Mkts Late: Hibors Up On HKD Demand Ahead Of IPOs
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--Hong Kong interbank offered rates rose further Thursday, boosted by increased demand for the local dollar ahead of several initial public offerings in coming months.  

The one-month Hibor was last quoted at 3.43%, up from 3.20% Wednesday, while the one-year Hibor rose to 3.47% from 3.35%.  

"Demand for the Hong Kong dollar has already risen on worries of inadequate liquidity once the subscription process begins for IPOs," said a trader at a local bank.  

He said he expects short-dated Hibors to remain high in the near term due to the buoyant demand, but said the demand is only temporary.  

"Rates will likely ease slightly for several weeks after the completion of the IPOs," he said.  

Among major IPOs in the next two months are those of coal producer Shenhua Energy Co., China's Bank of Communications, and COSCO Holdings Ltd., China's largest shipping firm.  

The companies are expected to raise more than HK$50 billion in total from their offerings.  

But the trader said the decline in Hibors should be limited after the share offerings. He said local rates will continue to correspond to U.S. rates after the Hong Kong Monetary Authority introduced last week a ceiling to the local dollar's exchange rate to the U.S. dollar to discourage its use as a trading proxy for the yuan.  

On the spot market, the Hong Kong dollar weakened slightly against the U.S. dollar, after the HKMA sold HK$544 million worth of the local currency Wednesday to buy U.S. dollars.  

The U.S. dollar was last quoted at HK$7.7799, up slightly from HK$7.7795 previously.  

The trader said Wednesday's intervention was "just the beginning."  

"With increasing demand for the Hong Kong dollar and continued yuan speculation, the HKMA may intervene again once the local dollar rises to HK$7.775 against the U.S. dollar," he said.  

He said intervention is also necessary to prevent Hibors from rising too quickly.  

U.S. dollar/Hong Kong dollar forwards rose, mainly on profit-taking after the currency intervention.  

"Players are taking profit as they don't expect the local dollar to be allowed to appreciate much in the near term," the trader said.  

The one-year U.S. dollar/Hong Kong dollar forward was quoted at 250-230 points below the spot rate, narrowing from 320-305 points Wednesday.  

Yields on Exchange Fund notes fell slightly, despite stronger demand for local dollar-denominated assets.  

The 10-year note was quoted at 3.64%, compared with 3.67% previously.

title: HK interbank rates remain firm on IPO-related fund demand
text:
HONG KONG, May 26 (Reuters) - Hong Kong interbank rates remained firm on Thursday morning on persistent demand for funds ahead of several large China share offerings next month.  

The overnight rate was quoted at 3.10-3.15 percent, while the one-month to six-month rates rose to 3.35-3.40 percent from 3.20-3.30 percent.

The local currency <HKD=> shuffled between 7.7780 and 7.7805 during the session. It was trading at 7.7798/7.7805 at 0310 GMT versus 7.7820/22 in late Asian trading on Wednesday.  

The three-month Hong Kong dollar forwards rose to the premium level from a discount on Wednesday.

The discount on one-year forwards <HKD1Y=> narrowed to 250/230 pips from Wednesday's close of 310/280 pips.

title: UPDATE: HKMA  Intervenes  To Damp HKD Rise A Week After Cap
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--The Hong Kong Monetary Authority sold HK$544 million Wednesday to damp the Hong Kong dollar's rise, just one week after it set a ceiling on the local unit to discourage inflows related to yuan speculation.  

Traders said strong foreign interest in coming initial public offerings also helped boost demand for the Hong Kong dollar, which traders have been buying in anticipation of a revaluation of the Chinese currency.  

Although the HKMA's introduction of new convertibility rules last week immediately drove over HK$3 billion of funds away from the territory, speculators soon took the HKMA's move as a sign it has information about an imminent yuan regime change.  

"Since China has promised more yuan flexibility over the longer term when it's ready, yuan speculation has persisted," a trader at a local bank said.  

Foreign interest in IPOs added further upward pressure to the local unit.  

Bank of Communications, China Shenhua Energy Co. and COSCO Holdings are expected to raise a total of about HK$50 billion in the coming months.  

The U.S. dollar was quoted at around HK$7.7750 Wednesday before the HKMA intervention, compared with around HK$7.7995 before the ceiling of HK$7.750 was announced.  

But traders were divided about the near term outlook for the local unit, with some betting on continued strength.  

"The rising trend of the Hong Kong dollar will likely continue, as hot money flows in for IPOs and yuan speculation," said DBS strategist Daniel Chan.  

Speculators may continue to push the Hong Kong dollar toward the HK$7.75 ceiling set by the HKMA to test how firmly it will back its words, the trader said.  

Others said they believe Wednesday's HKMA intervention, although small in size, sent a clear signal to the market that it means business.  

"The market has responded quite a bit already to the move," said Chordio Chan, head of risk treasury at Citigroup, referring to the U.S. dollar's rise to HK$7.7800 from HK$7.7750 following the HKMA action.  

In the short term, the Hong Kong dollar's rise has been capped, and should remain at current levels, unless a significant amount of hot money flows in, Chan added.  

Over the longer term, most agree the HKMA has the willingness and ability to stop the Hong Kong dollar from rising beyond the HK$7.75 cap.  

-By Raymond Tsoi, Dow Jones Newswires; 852-2802-7002; raymond.tsoi@dowjones.com

title: HK dollar trims early gains after HKMA  intervention
text:
HONG KONG, May 25 (Reuters) - The Hong Kong dollar trimmed some of its early gains on Wednesday after the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) stepped into the market in the afternoon to stem the local currency's advance against the greenback.  

The local currency <HKD=> was trading at 7.7820/22 per U.S. dollar at 0940 GMT after hitting a five-month high of 7.7750, and weaker than 7.7803/05 in late Asian trading on Tuesday.  

The HKMA, the territory's de facto central bank, sold HK$544 million of local currency in exchange for U.S. dollars. This is the first intervention by the HKMA since it set an upper limit for the HKD/USD trading band last week and is the first time since Dec. 10, 2004 that the HKMA has sold Hong Kong dollars.  

The move by the HKMA will lift the aggregate balance -- the sum of balances on clearing accounts maintained by banks with the HKMA -- to HK$1.317 billion after settlement on Friday, compared with HK$726 million on Wednesday.  

Last Wednesday, the HKMA set a trading band for the Hong Kong dollar of between 7.75 and 7.85 to the U.S. dollar. The lower limit for the Hong Kong dollar will move 100 pips every Monday, starting with a move to 7.81 on May 23, until it reaches 7.85 by June 20.  

After the announcement of the trading band by the HKMA, there was some HK$3.12 billion in fund outflows from the banking system as players closed their long Hong Kong dollar positions.  

Hong Kong interbank rates spiked higher after the sudden reduction in liquidity, spurring banks to raise their prime and saving deposit rates by 50 basis points on Monday.  

The market has also been short of liquidity after a fall in the aggregate balance last week, with some players selling U.S. dollars for the Hong Kong dollars in recent days, dealers said.  

"The U.S. dollar selling (by the banks) has sparked the HKMA intervention," said a dealer from a European bank.  

Hong Kong interbank rates softened slightly after the HKMA intervention. The overnight rate was quoted at 3.00-3.12 percent versus 3.06-3.18 percent the previous day.  

Discounts on longer-dated Hong Kong dollar forwards widened initially after the HKMA intervention but then narrowed.  

"Since market liquidity was still tight with the overnight interbank rate sustained over 3 percent, the downside for forwards would be limited," another trader said.  

The discount on one-year forwards <HKD1Y=> was at 310/280 pips versus Tuesday's close of 350/330 pips.  

There was also talk in the market that the tightening in liquidity was due to strong demand for funds ahead of China-themed initial public offerings (IPOs) in the territory.  

"Banks are preparing funding ahead of a number of big IPOs in June," said a dealer from a European bank.  

Prospective IPOs in June include China Shenhua Energy Co., which plans to raise US$3 billion, Bank of Communications, which aims to launch US$1.5 billion, and China's COSCO Holdings, which could raise up to US$1-2 billion.

title: DJ Dollar Higher In Rebound From Wednesday's Decline
text:
NEW YORK, May 19, 2005 (ODC via Comtex) --  

By Steven Vames  

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES  

The dollar is up modestly in early New York trading, rebounding as traders took Wednesday's weakness as an opportunity to buy dollars Thursday.  

The dollar had fallen Wednesday, mostly due to a report which showed soft U.S. core consumer inflation, which was seen as a sign that Federal Reserve policymakers will have no need to speed up their pace of interest rate tightening this year. Still, the Fed is expected to continue raising rates at a "measured" pace, which gives an advantage to the dollar as rates stagnate in Europe and Japan.  

Additionally, the dollar was helped by the fact that Hong Kong's introduction Wednesday of a top end to the Hong Kong dollar's trading band, and the debut Wednesday of trading for eight additional currency pairs in China, were not harbingers of an imminent revaluation of the Chinese yuan, as some had thought.  

Similarly, the Bank of Korea denied the thrust of a report in the Financial Times Wednesday that had suggested that the central bank's reserves are sufficient and that it will stop intervening in currency markets.  

The news from Hong Kong, China and Korea all help, at least temporarily, to put the issue over China's revaluation into the background. A revaluation from China is widely expected to pressure the dollar versus Asian currencies, and has been the focus of intense speculation and nervousness in markets recently.  

The dollar's overnight gains were extended early in the U.S. session Thursday after a report indicated that jobless claims fell by 20,000 to 321,000 in the week ended May 14, reversing the increases of the prior two weeks.  

The figures suggest that the labor market is continuing to strengthen, bolstering the posture of the U.S. economy versus some of its major trading partners.  

In early New York trading Thursday, the euro is at $1.2629, down from $1.2677 late Wednesday. The dollar is at Y107.35, up from Y106.86, and at CHF1.2214 from CHF1.2176. The pound is at $1.8366, from $1.8400 and the euro is at Y135.65, up from Y135.44.

title: HK dlr remains strong on Asian  currency  strength.
text:
HONG KONG, Oct 8 (Reuters) - The Hong Kong dollar remained
well above its pegged exchange rate to the U.S. dollar on
Wednesday although slightly down on the previous session, buoyed
by strength in several Asian currencies.
    The Hong Kong dollar stood at HK$7.7124/34 per U.S. dollar at
9.06 a.m. (0106 GMT) compared with its HK$7.80 pegged exchange
rate. The local unit was trading at HK$7.7105 on Tuesday
afternoon in Hong Kong.
    Dealers said the local unit strengthened to HK$7.7065
overnight, slightly weaker than the HK$7.7020 level reached last
Friday, the Hong Kong dollar's strongest level since the 1997/98
Asian financial crisis.
    The local unit had strengthened to around HK$7.50 in October
1997 as investors poured into Hong Kong dollars while regional
currencies tanked against the greenback.
    "There's still more potential for a strengthening of the Hong
Kong dollar as Asian currencies remain strong," said a dealer at
a local bank.
   


    "We're still seeing hot money flowing in as Chinese people in
Indonesia and Thailand see some concrete reasons to come here,"
the dealer said.
    The Hong Kong government has said it will give residency
status to investors who bring in HK$6.5 million and keep the
money here for seven years.
    The discount on Hong Kong dollar one-year forwards stood at
-395/-375 in early trade, from -410/-395 late on Tuesday,
pointing to market expectations of a further strengthening in the
spot Hong Kong dollar rate.
    The Singapore dollar rose to four-month peaks and the Thai
baht set three-year highs on Wednesday morning, tracking the U.S.
dollar's overnight fall to fresh lows against major currencies.
    "Whilst the move in the Hong Kong dollar is not driven by
local fundamentals, economic growth signals are becoming more
positive with domestic demand rebounding and deflation easing,"
research group 4cast said in a report.
 
    Hong Kong has suffered from about five years of deflation and
continues to experience near record unemployment.
    The Hong Kong dollar strengthened sharply against the U.S.
   

dollar late last month along with many other Asian currencies

following the Group of Seven nations' call for more flexible   

exchange rates.   

But recent moves by Beijing to help prop up the Hong Kong   

economy following massive civil protests in July have provided a   

strong incentive for investors to buy Hong Kong dollars.   

This has squeezing out other investors who had taken bets   

that the currency would depreciate over the next year or so given   

the government's large budget deficit.   

The local currency remains well above its pegged exchange   

rate despite several interventions by the Hong Kong Monetary   

Authority recently to try to bring the currency back to its fixed   

level. The government has repeatedly said it remains committed to   

maintaining the 20-year-old peg, seen as the bedrock of the

title: HK Regulator Sees No Unusual  Forex  Positions By Local Bks
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--Hong Kong's banking regulator said Wednesday that it hadn't detected any major currency speculation by local banks, despite the recent unusual strengthening of the Hong Kong dollar against the U.S. dollar.  

Though the Hong Kong currency is formally pegged at a rate of 7.80 to the U.S. dollar, it has been trading above that in the spot market since Sept. 22, thanks to widespread selling of the U.S. dollar and the fact that Hong Kong's currency board protects only against depreciation, not appreciation, of the currency.  

"There's no strong position-taking going on that we would be able to see," said William Ryback, the newly arrived deputy chief executive of the Hong Kong Monetary Authority. Banks' positions in the U.S. dollar aren't large enough to cause problems, he added.  

"They are managing their foreign currency positions how I would call normally. They're not taking more risk," Ryback said.  

The HKMA runs the territory's currency board and also supervises the banking sector. Hong Kong banks have traditionally been unwilling to speculate in the local currency for fear of antagonizing the regulator, usually leaving it to overseas banks to take major positions.  

"We aren't out there every day looking at banks' position taking," Ryback said, but added that it is unlikely that anything major would go on without the HKMA knowing about it given the "constant contact" it has with banks.  

Ryback said the HKMA has long been working on ways to help banks measure the risk of their foreign currency holdings. "We do want to make sure banks have an ongoing stress test and that we know what those results are."  

He declined to comment on the HKMA's recent interventions in the currency market to prevent the Hong Kong dollar from strengthening beyond 7.70 to the U.S. dollar, saying his primary responsibility is bank supervision.  

The Hong Kong dollar was trading around 7.7300 to the U.S. dollar late Wednesday, with the one-year forward contract at a discount of 220 to 200 pips to the spot rate.

title: FX  OPTIONS-HK dollar bid, volatility still high.
text:
SINGAPORE, Oct 7 (Reuters) - Two weeks after the sudden upward move in the Hong Kong dollar, options traders are not sure which way the currency will move next and implied volatility on the peg is near historic highs.   

 The Hong Kong dollar's sudden rise on September 22, after a Group of Seven communique on the weekend caused the yen and other Asian currencies to spurt, caught markets unawares.   

 The currency has been pegged to the U.S. dollar for two decades and had spent three years around 7.8 per U.S. dollar.   

 Traders who had positions in the forwards and options markets betting on a devaluation of the Hong Kong dollar have been unwinding ever since, but many of those positions still remain.   

 "Everyone's trying to sell out their puts and buy the calls, buy at-the-monies and vols," said one options trader, referring to the demand in the past two weeks to exit options to sell the Hong Kong dollar and in some cases reverse bets on the currency.   

 Forwards have been negative for more than a month, showing a rising premium on the HK dollar.   

 Implied volatility, a measure of expected volatility priced into options, was quoted near three percent for one-year options last week, which traders said was a historic high.   

 A few players were buying the HK dollar through options and forwards, but these trades seemed to be an inexpensive way of betting on the Chinese yuan revaluation and rises in other Asian currencies, analysts said.   

 "It is fundamentally stupid. No one really believes Hong Kong should revalue. It has massive structural problems," said James Malcolm, currency strategist with JP Morgan.   

 NO CAP ON HK DOLLAR   

 The Hong Kong Monetary Authority has been intervening, buying U.S. dollars in the market, but analysts say it is not obliged to do so under the guidelines of the Linked Exchange Rate System.   

 "HKMA has a commitment to sell (U.S.) dollars whenever spot goes to 7.80, but below 7.8 they have latitude in terms of deciding whether or not to buy dollars," said Malcolm.   

 Traders were wary of positioning for a retreat in the HK dollar back to its 7.8 peg level "because they don't know where the floor is for the spot," he said.   

 The premium on the HK dollar in forwards, which implies that a forward contract to sell the currency earns an attractive interest differential, should normally encourage traders to position for an eventual decline in the HK dollar to 7.8.   

 "Right now no one will take that risk because people are worried that spot (U.S. dollar) will go a lot lower before it goes higher," Malcolm said.   

 "What started off as constructive ambiguity has begun to make people very nervous," he said.   

 Meanwhile, the risks for an even sharper move up in the Hong Kong dollar were rising with the rate having strayed so far from the peg and remained there for over two weeks.   

 Hedge funds with loss-making positions would soon find their stop-losses triggered and would rush to buy the Hong Kong dollar, analysts said.   

 Meanwhile, the premium on the yuan in non-deliverable forwards was around record highs. One-year NDFs were quoting around 4,500 points, pricing in a nearly six percent appreciation in the yuan in a year.   

 One-year implied volatility on the yuan was quoted at 9.0/11.5 percent, a historic high.

title: HK dlr slightly weaker, remains above peg.
text:
HONG KONG, Oct 6 (Reuters) - The Hong Kong dollar, experiencing its strongest levels since the 1997/98 Asian financial crisis, weakened slightly early on Monday morning but remained well above its pegged exchange rate to the U.S. dollar.    

 "The trend for the Hong Kong dollar is going to remain strong," said a dealer at a medium-sized local bank.    

 "The G7 statement last month, the strength in other Asian currencies and the Hong Kong government's policies of encouraging more immigrants to invest here, are all creating a lot of demand for Hong Kong dollars," he said.    

 The Hong Kong dollar was trading at HK$7.7120/25 per U.S. dollar at 9.41 a.m. (0141 GMT), weaker than its late Friday level of HK$7.7059, but still far stronger than the HK$7.80 fixed exchange rate set by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority.    

 The local currency rose to a high of HK$7.7030 in overnight trade, its strongest since October 1997.    

 The U.S. dollar rose against the Japanese yen and the euro after Friday's surprisingly strong U.S. jobs data.    

 The HKMA, the territory's de facto central bank, intervened four times last week, injecting a total of more than HK$2.3 billion (US$295 million) to try to stabilise the currency.    

 Despite maintaining that the Hong Kong government remains committed to maintaining the 20-year-old peg, the HKMA has failed to bring the currency back to its pegged level.    

 "We are still seeing inflows of hot money, and as Hong Kong is the most liquid market in east Asia apart from Japan, I would expect the Hong Kong dollar to remain strong for the next couple of weeks," said a dealer at a European bank.    

 The U.S. dollar has been reeling ever since the Group of Seven major industrialised economies called for flexible exchange rates on September 20, a move interpreted as a call for Asian nations to stop propping up the dollar for the sake of their exports.    

 Hong Kong unveiled a money-for-residency programme on September 30 to woo rich foreign investors, saying it would bring in badly-needed cash to help reinvigorate the territory's struggling domestic economy.    

 Hong Kong dollar forwards remained at a deep discount despite last week's interventions, reflecting market expectations of further strengthening in the spot Hong Kong dollar rate.    

 The one-year forwards contract stood at -310/-290, slightly higher than the -360/-320 level reached late on Friday, their lowest level since August 2000.

title: UPDATE 1-HKMA  intervenes  again but HK dollar remains strong.
text:
HONG KONG, Oct 3 (Reuters) - Hong Kong's de facto central bank intervened for a fourth time in two days late on Friday to try to stabilise the territory's currency but it remained stubbornly strong against the U.S. dollar, to which it is pegged.   

"We have made another injection. We bought US$100 million," a Hong Kong Monetary Authority spokeswoman told Reuters, adding that it had sold Hong Kong dollars in the process.   

But after the latest intervention the Hong Kong dollar spot rate stood at HK$7.7059/80 at 1210 GMT, only marginally weaker than HK$7.7050 reached last week. That was its strongest level since the Asian financial crisis of 1997-98, and far stronger than its pegged exchange rate of HK$7.80 per dollar.   

Growing international pressure on Beijing to revalue its currency has also fuelled expectations that Hong Kong will move with China as the two economies become more closely integrated.   

In the latest intervention the HKMA sold HK$771 million (US$98.85 million) in local currency. It sold a total of HK$1.54 billion (US$197 million) on Friday in addition to HK$773 on Thursday.   

Despite the rise in the Hong Kong dollar, the HKMA said it remained committed to maintaining the 20-year-old currency peg.   

"(The peg) is the linchpin of Hong Kong's monetary and financial stability and an important factor in Hong Kong's economic success," the spokeswoman told Reuters by phone from a prepared statement.   

The Hong Kong dollar rose on Friday along with other Asian currencies against a weakened U.S. currency, as the non-deliverable market priced in a rise of over five percent in the Chinese yuan in the next year.   

Dealers said the rise in the yuan's one-year NDF premium was fuelled by speculation that China's policy of managing the yuan in a 8.2760/8.2800 per dollar range would be raised at this month's meeting of APEC leaders.   

Chinese yuan one-year non-deliverable forwards (NDFs) rose to a record premium of 4,200 points to the U.S. dollar on Friday.   

The Hong Kong dollar has remained strong over the past week after soaring to 7.7050 per U.S. dollar in New York. It moved up after a statement from the G7 industrial nations meeting urging exchange rate flexibility.   

Friday's intervention helped to bring Hong Kong dollar forwards and interbank rates down.   

One-year Hong Kong dollar forwards were trading around -360/-320 pips, their lowest level since August 2000, compared with -135/-125 pips late on Thursday.

title: HKMA Says Recent Strength In HK$ Due To Fund Inflows
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--The Hong Kong Monetary Authority said Friday that it had intervened in the Hong Kong dollar market and would continue to do so when appropriate.  

Confirming that it had bought US$100 million late afternoon when the U.S. dollar fell to around HK$7.7197, a spokeswoman at the HKMA said the government was committed to maintaining currency stability under the linked exchange rate.  

"We will inject liquidity as and when appropriate in order to dampen market volatility," she said. "We have no intention or plan to introduce any changes to the system, which is the linked exchange rate system."  

She said market sentiment toward Hong Kong has recently improved, resulting in an inflow of funds that has led to a stronger Hong Kong dollar.  

"(The peg) is the linchpin of Hong Kong's monetary and financial stability and an important factor in Hong Kong's economic success," she said.  

Friday's intervention by the quasi-central bank came a day after it sold HK$773 million. It was its fourth intervention in two weeks aimed at stemming the upward pressure on the local currency.  

The spot rate rebounded slightly after the intervention, and was quoted at around HK$7.7195 at 0850 GMT.  

The one-year Hong Kong dollar forward was quoted at a discount of around 240 to 230 basis points to the spot rate late Friday, compared with a discount of 140 to 130 late Thursday.

title: HKMA  Intervenes  In HK Dlr Mkt, Sells HK$772 Mln
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--The Hong Kong Monetary Authority Friday intervened in the Hong Kong dollar market for the fourth time in two weeks to stem upward pressure on the local currency.  

The quasi-central bank sold HK$772 million late afternoon when the U.S. dollar fell to around HK$7.7197. The spot rate rebounded slightly after the intervention, and was quoted at around HK$7.7195 at 0850 GMT.  

The HKMA's latest move comes after it sold HK$773 million Thursday.  

Traders expect the impact of the HKMA's action to be limited. Capital inflows and short-covering of the Hong Kong dollar will dominate the market near term, keeping downward pressure on the spot rate, they said.  

Speculation China will in future allow the yuan to appreciate against the U.S. dollar led to the upward pressure on the Hong Kong dollar, traders said.  

China and Hong Kong's economies are closely tied and both their currencies are linked to the U.S. dollar at a fixed rate.  

The discount on Hong Kong dollar forwards widened further following the HKMA's intervention.  

The increase in excess funds in the market put further downward pressure on Hong Kong interbank offered rates, widening the gap between Hibors and U.S. dollar London interbank offered rates.  

A bigger differential between Hong Kong and U.S. interest rates leads to a widening of the discounts on forwards.  

The one-year forward was quoted at a discount of around 240 to 230 basis points to the spot rate late Friday, compared with a discount of 140 to 130 late Thursday.

title: HK Dlr Mkts Late: Speculation Widens Discount On HKD Fwds
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--The discount on Hong Kong dollar forwards widened sharply Thursday, amid renewed speculation that China and Hong Kong may in future release their grip on their respective fixed exchange rates and let their currencies appreciate against the U.S. dollar.  

The benchmark one-year forward was trading at 140 to 130 below the spot rate late Thursday, compared with a discount of 85 to 75 on Tuesday.  

The market was closed Wednesday for the National Day holiday.  

After trading at a premium to the spot rate for the last couple of years, forwards suddenly switched to a discount last week as traders unwound long-standing positions that hedged against the depreciation of the Hong Kong dollar.  

The sharper discount in Hong Kong dollar forwards was linked to similar moves in the offshore nondeliverable forward market for the Chinese yuan, where the one-year forwards were quoted at a discount of around 3850 to the spot rate Thursday, compared with a discount of 3500 to 3600 last week.  

Though it wasn't clear what sparked the renewed speculation, traders said the discount on yuan nondeliverable forwards is now likely to test 4000 in the next few days. "It won't go much below that. It's a critical psychological level," said one trader.  

That in turn could push the discount on the one-year Hong Kong dollar forward below 200, another trader said, arguing that fund flows into Hong Kong and the U.S. dollar's weakness against the yen and other Asian currencies are also contributing factors.  

The spot exchange rate for the Hong Kong dollar was also under pressure Thursday, with the U.S. dollar/Hong Kong dollar rate falling to 7.7375 late Thursday compared with 7.7440 Tuesday.  

However, the rate rebounded from an intraday low of around HK$7.7335 after the Hong Kong Monetary Authority intervened to sell HK$387 million to prevent its currency from rising further against the U.S. dollar.  

Analysts had expected such interventions since the spot rate diverged from the official peg rate of 7.80 last week, though it is still unclear how long it will take to get back to return to that level.  

"It's a matter of when people get tired of speculating on appreciation," one trader said. "People really don't think the Hong Kong government will change the peg."  

Hong Kong interbank offered rates, already lower early in the day due to the falling forwards, declined further after the HKMA intervention pushed more funds into the market. The one-month Hibor was quoted at 0.50% compared with 0.62% Tuesday, and the one-year Hibor was at 1.03% as against 1.18% previously.  

"We think Hibors of three-month and shorter tenors could decline further to levels closer to zero in the coming weeks," Citigroup economist Joe Lo wrote in a report this week, citing fund inflows and more expected interventions by the HKMA.  

Yields on long-dated Hong Kong exchange fund notes declined, tracking lower yields on the benchmark 10-year U.S. Treasury. The two-year note was trading at 1.26%, compared with 1.40% Tuesday, and the 10-year note was at 4.17%, compared with 4.24% previously.

title: HKMA  Intervenes  In HK Dollar Market, Injects HK$387 Mln
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--The Hong Kong Monetary Authority intervened in the Hong Kong dollar market Thursday selling HK$387 million to stop the currency from rising further amid speculation of an appreciation against the U.S. dollar.  

The quasi-central bank reported its sales of the Hong Kong dollar when the U.S. dollar/Hong Kong dollar spot rate hit an intraday low of around HK$7.7335.  

The spot rate rebounded moderately after the intervention. The U.S. dollar was quoted at HK$7.7375 around 0810 GMT, compared with HK$7.7440 Tuesday.  

The market was closed Wednesday for a public holiday.  

The HKMA also bought about US$60 million last week to calm the effects of market speculation.  

"The intervention triggered some short-covering of the U.S. dollar, which may keep a lid on the Hong Kong dollar in the near term," one trader said.  

Still, the spot rate is expected to remain below the level of HK$7.80 at which the Hong Kong dollar is pegged to the U.S. dollar in coming weeks, traders said.  

Hong Kong interbank offered rates fell after the injection as the market was flooded with excess funds.  

The Overnight Hibor fell to 0.25%, compared with 0.60% Tuesday.  

The HKMA is obliged to buy the Hong Kong dollar from banks at the peg rate, which essentially puts a floor on the Hong Kong dollar's level against the U.S. dollar.  

However the convertibility undertaking is one-sided, which means intervention to sell the Hong Kong dollar is at the HKMA's discretion. Therefore, theoretically there is no ceiling for the Hong Kong dollar's value.  

"The intervention showed the HKMA isn't willing to tolerate a large deviation from the peg rate, which helped to calm down the market a bit," the trader said. "But, given the strong local equities, there could be more equity-driven fund inflows, keeping upward pressure on the Hong Kong dollar."  

The discount on the one-year yuan nondeliverable forward also widened Thursday to around 3800 on renewed speculation the yuan may be allowed to appreciate.  

This implies a more than 4% appreciation in the yuan against the U.S. dollar over the next 12 months, traders said. "It may break through 4000 in the next couple of days," one noted.  

Others doubted whether such a deep discount is sustainable, but a move to 4000 would almost certainly cause discounts on Hong Kong dollar forwards to widen further.  

The one-year Hong Kong dollar forward was quoted at a discount of 140 to 130 late Tuesday, tracking the movement in the spot rate and the yuan NDFs, compared with a discount of 85 to 75 Tuesday.

title: Brave New World for the Hong Kong Dollar.
text:
ING Financial Markets recommends long positions in the SAR's currency

HONG KONG, Sept. 30 /XFNHK/ - ING Financial Markets (ING) today predicted that the Hong Kong Dollar is set to experience a period of buying pressure as currency investors rebalance their market positions. The improving economic environment and calls from G7 for Asia to allow undervalued exchange rates to appreciate will lead to a scaling back of entrenched long U.S. Dollar, short Hong Kong Dollar positions, ING believes.  

ING forecasts that the Hong Kong Dollar one-year forward will see increased buying in the market and will trade to -200 pips from its present level of -60 pips, which would imply a spot exchange rate in one year of HK$7.73 to the U.S. Dollar.  

This dramatic shift in investors' positions comes as the long-standing reasons for traditionally selling the Hong Kong Dollar have been replaced by arguments to buy the currency. The US administration's tacit acceptance of the end of the strong dollar policy has reversed one of the principal arguments for bearishness. The market also is now selling down the U.S. Dollar to buy Yen, as investors sense that the current upswing in the Japanese market may be powerful enough to stem deflation and enable the banks to end their struggle with bad loans. The upward pressure on the Yen has transmitted like pressure to the rest of Asia. In addition, China can also no longer be considered a reason to sell the Hong Kong Dollar. The markets appear to be indicating a four per cent appreciation in the Renminbi over the next twelve months, given the one-year non-deliverable forward price, which currently stands at RMB7.947.  

Tim Condon, Chief Economist, Asia stated: "The domestic arguments for a weaker Hong Kong dollar are also receding as people move on from the low-point in March and April of this year and the SARS crisis. We see the domestic economy rebounding through a tourism-led recovery, driving GDP forecasts for 2004 and 2005 upwards, with consumption snapping back as optimism over the future returns. Investors are seeing that there is two-way risk in the Hong Kong Dollar and are looking to scale back their short positions."  

ING forecasts that Hong Kong's GDP will reach five per cent in both 2004 and 2005.  

The prediction that the Hong Kong Dollar faces upside pressure, rather than only downside pressure, comes as the Hong Kong Monetary Authority intervened in the currency markets last week, after the Hong Kong Dollar strengthened to a six-year high of 7.7050 against the U.S. Dollar. ING believes that the Hong Kong Monetary Authority sought to stabilise the spot FX market in the face of snowballing U.S. Dollar selling pressure. ING foresees that the forward discount on the Hong Kong Dollar price will continue to widen as investors and risk managers rebalance their positions in light their new appreciation of the Hong Kong Dollar.

title: HK$ Gain Sign Of Confidence But Appreciation Temporary
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--The Hong Kong dollar's recent surge against the U.S. dollar - the biggest since the 1997 Asian financial crisis - sent traders covering their short positions in panicky trade this week, but their reaction may be overdone.  

Many market observers considered the Hong Kong dollar's sharp gains to be no more than a blip as there has been no sudden improvement in the city's economic fundamentals to justify such an appreciation.  

Still, many economists argue the rise can be seen as a sign of returning confidence.  

The U.S. dollar/Hong Kong dollar spot rate plunged in London and New York trade Monday, then staged a partial rebound and stabilized between HK$7.7500 and HK$7.7600, following intervention by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, which said it bought US$60 million from the market Tuesday.  

The intervention was small but effective in a market that can see hundreds of US$50 million or US$100 million trades.  

The HKMA was giving the market a clear signal that it isn't willing to tolerate a sustained deviation from 7.80, the rate at which the currency is pegged to the U.S. dollar.  

The recent gains in the Hong Kong dollar are unusual.  

"For the last 10 to 12 years we haven't seen such strong appreciative pressure on the Hong Kong dollar, especially in the spot market," Standard Chartered Economist Mike Moran said.  

Indeed, it was a dramatic reversal from the situation just a few weeks ago when most investors were still hedging against a Hong Kong dollar devaluation on worries over the city's economic weakness.  

Economists said the significance of the recent Hong Kong dollar gains is that it showed a recovery of confidence.  

"For the first time in years, the currency market is starting to believe that Hong Kong's adjustment may have come to an end, and the Hong Kong dollar may not need to depreciate," said ABN Amro Chief Asian Strategist Eddie Wong.  

The new perception of Hong Kong could trigger a sustainable inflow of liquidity back to the city, Wong said.  

"This will be hugely positive for Hong Kong, notably in its asset prices, including stocks and property," he said.  

Indeed, Hong Kong shares recorded their biggest percentage gain in nearly five months Wednesday as the Hang Seng Index rose to a 15-month high of 11295.89 and the share market recorded a trading volume of HK$19.81 billion, its biggest in three years.  

Property companies led gainers.  

Fundamental Improvements Don't Justify Appreciation  

Although most economists agreed the economy is gradually picking up and confidence is being restored, many doubted the economy is strong enough to warrant a currency appreciation after 20 years of a pegged exchange rate.  

"The domestic fundamentals are improving, but they're not great," Moran said.  

Unemployment is at a near-record high and consumer prices have fallen for 58 consecutive months.  

"We still see Hong Kong has only recently closed the appreciation (gap) against its trading partners which it suffered during the Asian financial crisis," said Barclays Bank analyst Pieter van der Schaft.  

National Australia Bank's economist, Kevin Lai, agreed the Hong Kong dollar's sharp gains won't last.  

"The city's economy is still struggling to come out of more than four and a half years of deflation, which reflects a lack of competitiveness," Lai said.  

"Yes, overall economic sentiment is improving, but not to the extent of justifying a stronger currency."  

Technical factors also played a role, traders said.  

"The market was overly pessimistic about the Hong Kong dollar previously, (and) many have hedged against or speculated on a devaluation, building up a massive demand to buy back the currency as the spot rate plunged through all major chart points," said one money trader.  

Traders also attributed the currency strength to broad speculation on Asian currency appreciation led by the Chinese yuan, following the Group of Seven's call over the weekend for more flexible exchange rates.  

"The G-7's call fueled speculation about an appreciation of the yuan. Given the close ties between China and Hong Kong, and the fact that both are linked to the U.S. dollar, the upward pressure spread to the Hong Kong dollar," the trader said.  

"But fundamentally, Hong Kong is very different from China, there is no reason why the Hong Kong dollar should appreciate if the yuan is revalued upward," he added.  

"You'll find the U.S. dollar/Hong Kong dollar spot rate gradually reverts to the more usual tight ranges," Standard Chartered's Moran said.  

-By Raymond Tsoi, Dow Jones Newswires; 852-2802-7002; raymond.tsoi@dowjones.com (John Ryan contributed to this story)

title: Asia Econ Growth On Track Even With Stronger  Currencies
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Asia is expected to remain the world's fastest growing region even if the area's currencies edge up in value after major industrial powers called over the weekend for freer currency movements.  

But a sharp drop by the dollar in the wake of the Group of Seven meeting could seriously dent the prospects for a region just emerging from the economic damage of SARS and the Iraq war, economists say.  

G7 finance ministers and central bankers, meeting in Dubai over the weekend, called for "more flexibility in exchange rates" to promote "smooth and widespread adjustments in the international financial system."  

This amounts to a challenge to Asian export powerhouses, especially G7 member Japan and China, not to sell their own currencies to foster export-led growth.  

The G7's call "is a reflection of confidence that the global (economic) growth is on track," says David Cohen, a regional economist at MMS International in Singapore.  

But if Asian governments were to let the markets set their currency levels, it would mark quite a change in dearly held policies.  

Japan has bought an estimated $100 billion for yen so this year - well above the previous full-year record - while China also regularly must buy dollars to keep the yuan pegged around CNY8.28 to a dollar. Malaysia and Hong Kong also have currency pegs, while South Korea and Taiwan intervene to keep theirs in check.  

The result in Asia has been a massive swelling of already huge foreign-exchange reserves as national authorities sell their own currencies for dollars. In the U.S., manufacturers and some lawmakers charge that artificially undervalued Asian exchange rates are flooding the world with cheap Asian goods, ramping up the U.S. trade deficit and costing American jobs.  

Although Japan agreed to the G7 call for freer currencies and a G7 finance minister said China didn't object, Tokyo, Beijing, and Seoul made clear Monday they haven't changed their plans to keep their currencies stable to prevent exports from derailing.  

But the International Monetary Fund's director for Asia-Pacific, David Burton predicted little economic damage from the dollar's decline.  

"Most of these economies are growing robustly, and many of their exchange rates in real effective terms have depreciated somewhat in recent times, so I don't think modest appreciations would have a major effect on them," Burton told Dow Jones Newswires in an interview in Dubai.  

In its semiannual World Economic Outlook last week, the IMF forecast Asia excluding Japan would grow 5.9% this year, nearly twice the global average and trimmed hardly changed from the April forecast of 6.0% despite the ravages of SARS. The IMF more than doubled its 2003 growth forecast for Japan to 2% from 0.8%.  


 
           Bank Of Japan In The Spotlight 
   

A key issue for Asian economies in the wake of the G7 statement will be whether Tokyo can let the yen rise without roiling the markets or damaging its damaging the economy.  

After a decade of stagnation, Japan's economy grew an 3.9% annualized in the second quarter - the best in the G7.  

There is room for the yen to strengthen to Y110-Y115, says Cohen at MMS International. Morgan Stanley equity strategist Naoki Kamiyama says a Y108-Y112 range is still endurable for Japan.  

The dollar, which had already sagged Y3.5 last week, plunged in early Asian trade Monday to as low as Y111.37 - its lowest level since December 2000 - from Y114.27 late Friday in New York. Around 1000 GMT the dollar was at Y112.34.  

Some traders said they thought the Bank of Japan was selling yen covertly Monday, but Tokyo appeared to have lowered its dollar target. The Finance Ministry all year has ordered the Bank of Japan to sell yen heavily to defend the dollar at Y115 - a level that finally broke Friday as G7 ministers were arriving in Dubai.  

The dollar is now below the Y115 average rate that some exporters, such as Toyota Motor Corp., are counting on for the six-month period to next March. Shares of Japanese exporters tumbled Monday, helping drive the recently rallying Nikkei 225 Stock Average down 4.2%.  

While growing, the world's second-largest economy is still not out of the woods. Its banking system is choked full of bad debts, while consumers remain reluctant to spend.  


 
          China Pressured To Break The Peg 
   

Although the G7 didn't name names, it was clearly joining U.S. Treasury Secretary John Snow in pushing China to loosen up on the yuan.  

The yuan is convertible only on the current account, and Beijing has kept it around its current level for five years.  

Speculation regime-change has dogged the dollar for weeks in the market for forward delivery against the yuan, which can be used in place of the spot market to make bets on the yuan's long-term direction. The dollar's one-year discount steepened to a record 2400 points at one stage Monday, implying expectations of the dollar falling nearly 3% to 8.0374 yuan over the next 12 months.  

But the Chinese central bank and currency regulator insisted again Monday they;re in no change to give up currency stability, saying it's an internal matter.  

Many analysts agree China likely won't budge soon.  

"The yuan won't see much movement," says Dong Tao, an economist at Credit Suisse First Boston in Hong Kong.  

The head of research at a U.S. brokerage said China's exchange rate will remain a "political issue" ahead of the U.S. presidential elections next year, and the question is whether Beijing will be able to withstand the pressure.  

An Asian central banker, who declined to be named, said China needs to "do something," but just how and when it does will remain a mystery.  

What's not a mystery is the Chinese position.  

"A stable yuan is not only good for us, it's good for our immediate neighbors and for the whole world," deputy governor of the Bank of China, Li Ruogu, said recently.  

Li acknowledged China has a big trade surplus with the U.S., but said cheap labor costs - not exchange rates - are the main reason.  

"We're committed to liberalization, but I can't give you a very clear timetable of how long it will take," Li said.  


    -By Hasan Jafri, Dow Jones Newswires; 65-6415-4151; hasan.jafri@dowjones.com   

(Benjamin Pedley in Dubai and Arran Scott in Tokyo contributed to this item.)

title: CHINA WATCH: Yuan Policy May Make Inflation Fresh Risk
text:
A Dow Jones Newswires Column 

 SHANGHAI -(Dow Jones)- China, so often accused of foisting deflation on the rest of world, itself now faces inflation risks. 

 A number of signs suggest price rises are quickly taking hold, prompting a debate framed around China's exchange rate policy. At issue is whether China is trending toward a normal, controllable pickup in prices or the kind of runaway inflation the country endured in the late 1980s and early 1990s. How intense it gets could ultimately determine whether Beijing adjusts the yuan's exchange rate upward. 

 U.S. Federal Reserve Board Chairman Alan Greenspan suggested this month China's exchange rate policy might make the economy overheat. Domestic debt traders see a similar risk, saying the central bank will need to crack down hard on credit and money supply growth to keep inflation at bay. 

 The central bank even re-engineered its monetary policy mechanism in April to better deflect inflation with a bill-issuance program that improves its footing to handle the dollar onslaught. It is also waging a verbal campaign to cool property prices and bank lending. 

 Figures bear out signs that price pressure is building. Money supply and lending have each surged over 20% in recent months, and the local bond market is discomforted that severe acute respiratory syndrome tripped the economy less than expected. 

 China's consumer price index recorded inflation each month in the first half of 2003, rising in June to 0.6% above the year-earlier level. The rebound follows years of anemic pricing, the result of ferocious competitiveness. 

 Outright deflation gripped the economy in 2002. Declines in the CPI for 11 of 12 months last year sparked global worries deflation was China's newest and most dangerous export. The International Monetary Fund's website has 143 documents linking "China" and "deflation." 

 Foreign economists tend to be skeptical of the worry about overheating, partly because the flip in sentiment has been so abrupt. Also, prices are still falling on some important products, like mobile phones and other manufactured consumer goods. 

 "We don't see enough evidence to substantiate the argument," according to a recent report by Yiping Huang, a Citigroup Inc. economist in Hong Kong. 

Currency Is Departure Point



China's currency policy is a major departure point for views on the
extent of inflation risk - an increasingly politicized and global debate
over how much the yuan's current under-valuation matters.



Many of those optimistic the money supply expansion will be easily
contained are betting Beijing will adjust rules that govern its exchange
rate regime, if not allow the currency to rise outright.



Others are saying China will increasingly challenge a textbook
economic theory that policy makers can control only one of either the
exchange rate or interest rates, not both.



Almost every dollar that enters China is exchanged into about 8.3
yuan. These new yuan are a potential ingredient in inflation, and
whether they get into the economy is critical to the issue of
overheating.



The way China is choosing to handle the new yuan currently bucks
conventional economics. To keep the yuan exchange rate unchanged, the
central bank issues short-term debt instruments to buy back the new yuan
from banks, which keeps banks from pumping it into the economy and
kindling inflation.



But the People's Bank of China doesn't give the market much power to
determine the interest rate on those bills, maintaining for itself
control over the exchange and interest rates.



The situation wasn't much of a problem until prices started to rise,
since deflation made any rate of interest worthwhile. But now, prices
are picking up - in conjunction with a huge upsurge in foreign trade and
investment during the past year that has sent U.S. dollars hurling into
China at unprecedented speed.



These factors together suggest the central bank should lift the rates
it pays on the bills used to mop up the yuan or let the currency rise.
But it isn't complying.



Fed Chairman Greenspan hinted that the unconventional lock-hold on
both interest and exchange rates is China's root problem during recent
congressional testimony, when he said the situation is something
"they'll have to address."



                       Rule Changes


Hong Kong's extraordinary US$15 billion stock market intervention in
1998 was a direct outgrowth of a failed attempt to keep the currency
fixed and interest rates low in defiance of the theory.



Speculators backed the Hong Kong Monetary Authority into a corner with
an elaborate bet it couldn't sustain the policy, and the authority
escaped only by using shock treatment on traders expecting a more
conventional reaction to their meddling, such as a devaluation.
Afterward, a bruised HKMA quickly abandoned trying to determine interest
rates, so it could focus solely on the currency peg.



Foreign economists don't doubt the conundrum on interest and exchange
rates exists for China too. But they argue China makes hash of the
theory since use of the yuan is governed by rules. It isn't fully
convertible like the Hong Kong dollar.



In effect, China has a third lever: rule changes.



If Beijing were to permit normalized exchange in the yuan, more exit
strategies for foreign investors, foreign investment for Chinese
companies in a qualified domestic institutional investor program or a
more wide-open import regime, some inflationary pressure could be offset
by the reduction in net U.S. dollar intake. A number of such steps
already have been taken, and more were outlined Friday in Hong Kong with
plans to allow more Chinese to travel overseas, and buy foreign currency
for their travels.



"Technical changes in the foreign exchange settlement mechanism and
QDII are both conceivable," although not necessarily needed now, said Ma
Qiang, head of research at the Shanghai branch of the PBOC.

title: CHINA WATCH: Yuan Policy May Make Inflation Fresh Risk
text:
A Dow Jones Newswires Column 

 SHANGHAI -(Dow Jones)- China, so often accused of foisting deflation on the rest of world, itself now faces inflation risks. 

 A number of signs suggest price rises are quickly taking hold, prompting a debate framed around China's exchange rate policy. At issue is whether China is trending toward a normal, controllable pickup in prices or the kind of runaway inflation the country endured in the late 1980s and early 1990s. How intense it gets could ultimately determine whether Beijing adjusts the yuan's exchange rate upward. 

 U.S. Federal Reserve Board Chairman Alan Greenspan suggested this month China's exchange rate policy might make the economy overheat. Domestic debt traders see a similar risk, saying the central bank will need to crack down hard on credit and money supply growth to keep inflation at bay. 

 The central bank even re-engineered its monetary policy mechanism in April to better deflect inflation with a bill-issuance program that improves its footing to handle the dollar onslaught. It is also waging a verbal campaign to cool property prices and bank lending. 

 Figures bear out signs that price pressure is building. Money supply and lending have each surged over 20% in recent months, and the local bond market is discomforted that severe acute respiratory syndrome tripped the economy less than expected. 

 China's consumer price index recorded inflation each month in the first half of 2003, rising in June to 0.6% above the year-earlier level. The rebound follows years of anemic pricing, the result of ferocious competitiveness. 

 Outright deflation gripped the economy in 2002. Declines in the CPI for 11 of 12 months last year sparked global worries deflation was China's newest and most dangerous export. The International Monetary Fund's website has 143 documents linking "China" and "deflation." 

 Foreign economists tend to be skeptical of the worry about overheating, partly because the flip in sentiment has been so abrupt. Also, prices are still falling on some important products, like mobile phones and other manufactured consumer goods. 

 "We don't see enough evidence to substantiate the argument," according to a recent report by Yiping Huang, a Citigroup Inc. economist in Hong Kong. 

Currency Is Departure Point



China's currency policy is a major departure point for views on the
extent of inflation risk - an increasingly politicized and global debate
over how much the yuan's current under-valuation matters.



Many of those optimistic the money supply expansion will be easily
contained are betting Beijing will adjust rules that govern its exchange
rate regime, if not allow the currency to rise outright.



Others are saying China will increasingly challenge a textbook
economic theory that policy makers can control only one of either the
exchange rate or interest rates, not both.



Almost every dollar that enters China is exchanged into about 8.3
yuan. These new yuan are a potential ingredient in inflation, and
whether they get into the economy is critical to the issue of
overheating.



The way China is choosing to handle the new yuan currently bucks
conventional economics. To keep the yuan exchange rate unchanged, the
central bank issues short-term debt instruments to buy back the new yuan
from banks, which keeps banks from pumping it into the economy and
kindling inflation.



But the People's Bank of China doesn't give the market much power to
determine the interest rate on those bills, maintaining for itself
control over the exchange and interest rates.



The situation wasn't much of a problem until prices started to rise,
since deflation made any rate of interest worthwhile. But now, prices
are picking up - in conjunction with a huge upsurge in foreign trade and
investment during the past year that has sent U.S. dollars hurling into
China at unprecedented speed.



These factors together suggest the central bank should lift the rates
it pays on the bills used to mop up the yuan or let the currency rise.
But it isn't complying.



Fed Chairman Greenspan hinted that the unconventional lock-hold on
both interest and exchange rates is China's root problem during recent
congressional testimony, when he said the situation is something
"they'll have to address."

Hong Kong's extraordinary US$15 billion stock market intervention in
1998 was a direct outgrowth of a failed attempt to keep the currency
fixed and interest rates low in defiance of the theory.

an elaborate bet it couldn't sustain the policy, and the authority
escaped only by using shock treatment on traders expecting a more
conventional reaction to their meddling, such as a devaluation.
Afterward, a bruised HKMA quickly abandoned trying to determine interest
rates, so it could focus solely on the currency peg.



Foreign economists don't doubt the conundrum on interest and exchange
rates exists for China too. But they argue China makes hash of the
theory since use of the yuan is governed by rules. It isn't fully
convertible like the Hong Kong dollar.



In effect, China has a third lever: rule changes.

text:
