title: China's Yuan Down On Dollar-Buying By Importers
text:
SHANGHAI -(Dow Jones)- China's yuan weakened slightly against the U.S. dollar Friday on trade-related dollar buying by importers, traders said. 

 At 0300 GMT (11:00 p.m. EDT Thursday), the dollar stood at 8.2767 yuan versus CNY8.2766 Thursday. 

 The dollar traded between CNY8.2766 and CNY8.2767, a very narrow range even by the yuan's standard. 

 "Dollar-buying from importers slightly outpaced selling from exporters and most deals were conducted at CNY8.2767," said a trader at a foreign bank in Shanghai. 

 The central bank keeps a tight watch on the currency and controls the flow of capital across the borders. Only partial convertibility of the currency on the capital account is permitted. 

 Looking forward, traders said China's healthy trade surplus would fundamentally result in exporters' dollar selling and put downward pressure on the dollar, but without any foreign exchange policy changes expected the rate is likely to remain largely unchanged. The central bank keeps the rate in a tight range, intervening in the market when necessary. 

 The Hong Kong dollar was higher at CNY1.0608 from CNY1.0607 Thursday, while the Japanese yen fell to CNY6.8852 per 100 yen from CNY6.9532. 

 The euro edged down to CNY8.0061 from CNY8.0885 Thursday.

title: Most Asian  Currencies  Dn Late; Dlr Overcomes Bearish News
text:
Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 

 SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The dollar held firm against most Asian currencies Monday despite a new round of seemingly dollar-bearish news out of the U.S. 

 Only the South Korean won and Thai baht resisted the dollar's advance to finish stronger. 

 Another down day on Wall Street Friday combined with the government's report of a wider-than-expected May trade gap set the stage for a potential dollar pullback when Asian markets opened Monday. 

 But the dollar held its ground in the region, led by solid gains against the yen. 

 The dollar's resilience in the face of the negative news suggests that market players may have simply overextended their short-dollar positions during the U.S. currency's recent slump, analysts said. 

 Until there are signs that the stock market is stabilizing and the U.S. is getting its current account deficit and corporate accounting problems under control, the dollar will have a difficult time making any sustained headway, they added. 

 The won was the big mover during Asian hours, powering its way to a 20-month high against the dollar. 

 Exporters once again were aggressive dollar sellers, keeping the won well-bid even as the main index of the local stock market fell 4.5%. 

 The dollar closed at KRW1,165.6 down from KRW1,170.6 Friday. 

 The dollar might have fallen even further if market players hadn't been concerned that the government might intervene to prop up the flagging U.S. currency, said Frank Gong, strategist at Bank of America in Hong Kong. 

 The intervention fears kept a bid under the dollar at around the KRW1,165 level, Gong said. 

 The Ministry of Finance and Economy sold KRW700 billion worth of five-year foreign exchange stabilization bonds Monday, leading players to conclude that intervention was imminent. The MOFE in the past has authorized the Bank of Korea to intervene right after the issuance of such bonds, Gong said. 

 "Watch out for intervention over the next two days," he said. 

 The Korean government is concerned about the won's appreciation - more than 14% against the dollar since mid-April - because of its negative impact on export competitiveness. 

 More than half of the 49 companies surveyed by Korea's Ministry of Commerce, Industry and Energy said they won't be able to meet their export targets for the year at the current currency exchange rate, according to a government report released Monday. 

 The baht finished modestly higher as market players digested the government's latest attempt to explain its foreign exchange policy. 

 The baht's recent appreciation to a two-year high against the dollar has fueled concerns among some exporters about the impact of the currency's strength on their competitiveness in international markets. 

 Late in Asia the dollar was trading at 40.415 baht, down from THB40.490 late Friday. 

 Commerce Minister Adisai Bodharamik expressed sympathy for exporters, saying a decline in the dollar below THB40 would hurt their competitiveness. 

 He said that even if the baht's appreciation against the dollar is in line with that of other currencies in the region, such a rise would have a "psychological effect" on exporters. 

 Adisai's comments were in contrast with recent remarks by Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra who showed little concern about the currency's strength. 

 The baht hit its two-year high last week after Thaksin predicted the dollar would soon fall below THB40. 

 The Singapore dollar tracked the yen lower in a listless session. 

 Late in Asia the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.7352, up from S$1.7301 late Friday in Asia. 

 The U.S. dollar opened about even with its Friday close, but strengthened gradually throughout the day, mirroring its rise against the yen. 

 The New Taiwan dollar finished a touch weaker in light trading. 

 The U.S. dollar ended at NT$33.028 compared with NT$33.023 Friday. Trading ranged between NT$33.044 and NT$33.002. 

 The dollar overcame an early decline against the rupiah to finish higher after local companies boosted their dollar purchases for offshore debt repayments. 

 Near the end of trading the dollar was quoted at 8,810 rupiah, up from IDR8,000 late Friday. 

 The dollar closed unchanged against the peso at PHP50.380. 

 The resolution of a political stalemate helped boost sentiment toward the currency. 

 Senator Robert Jaworski's announcement Sunday that he will support President Gloria Macapagal Arroyo effectively ended a deadlock in the battle for control of the Senate, which had threatened to paralyze the administration's economic reform program.

title: Emerging Asia  FX  - Directionless, local leads in focus.
text:
SINGAPORE, June 3 (Reuters) - The Asian currencies went 

 their own ways on Monday as uncertainty over the dollar/yen 

 direction following the recent intervention by Japanese 

 monetary authorities prompted the market to shift focuses to 

 local leads. 

     The dollar/yen recouped some lost ground after a 

 combination of factors -- the Japanese dollar-buying 

intervention, strong economic data out of the U.S., and the 

 fact that the market is getting massively short of the dollar 

 -- gave it some tail winds. 

     Some dealers estimated the intervention on Friday alone 

 could have set the Bank of Japan back by around $10 billion. 

     Most players opted to stick to local factors and were 

 reluctant to buy aggressively into the dollar's strength 

 because they were unsure of its outlook. 

     "I don't think the trouble is over for the dollar by any 

 stretch. We still have to wait for mid-June corporate results 

 to come out, and I suspect that could hurt the dollar again," 

 said Claudio Piron, currency strategist at Standard Chartered 

 in Singapore. 

 "The problem is that the economic resilience in America has 

 not been translated into corporate resilience in term of 

 profitability," he said. 

 The Singapore dollar , which tends to track the yen 

 closer than other Southeast Asian currencies, came off. It 

 hovered around 1.7870 against 1.7850 late on Friday. 

 The Indonsian rupiah , on the other hand, raked in 

 robust gains, rising to its nine-month high of 8,550 on the 

 back of buying from state banks and positive trade data. 

     Indonesia's trade surplus rose to $2.34 billion in April 

 from $2.22 billion in March and $2.20 billion in February. 

     The rupiah was barely affected by news the government 

 delayed, for the second time, a meeting on whether to proceed 

 with a planned auction of a 51 percent stake in 

 state-controlled Bank Niaga, primarily because the news broke 

 when the market was wrapping up for the day. 

 THAI BAHT FIRM 

 The baht was resilient, holding near its recent 

 highs due to support from equity inflows and increased optimism 

 about Thailand's economic outlook following encouraging April 

 data, especially the industrial production and exports growth. 

     The currency traded around 42.38 to the dollar from around 

 42.50 late on Friday. 

     Foreign investors continued to pour money into local 

 stocks. Last week alone, they bought a net 7.19 billion baht 

 ($169.75 million) worth of Thai shares. 

     May inflation eased to a 30-month low of 0.1 percent due 

 to 

 the declining cost of food, energy and cheap non-food 

 products, further fuelling speculation the central bank would 

 keep its benchmark rate unchanged at 2.00 percent later in the 

 day. 

 The Taiwan dollar closed at an 11-month high 

 despite repeated intervention by the central bank on hefty 

 dollar offers from exporters. It finished at 34.139 to the 

 dollar, the highest close since mid-June last year. 

 Dealers in Singapore said part of the reason the Taiwan 

 dollar was in demand was that it was seen as a cheap proxy for 

 long yen positions in option plays. 

     Analysts said they expected the Taiwan dollar's uptrend to 

 remain intact given the island's economic recovery. 

     Some suggested the central bank should allow the 

 undervalued currency to appreciate instead of reining in its 

 gains to subsidise traditional industries. 

     "Taiwan has in fact amassed too much in foreign reserves, 

 thanks to the CBC's consistent intervention," said Steve Xu, 

 regional economist at SG Research in Hong Kong. 

     "The most sensible policy response for the CBC now would be

title: Argentina troubles worry HK dollar, but not much.
text:
HONG KONG, Dec 21 (Reuters) - The Hong Kong dollar, the world's second-most talked about pegged currency, came under renewed pressure on Friday after Argentina's political regime collapsed under the weight of its economic problems. 

 One-year Hong Kong dollar forwards rose to 300 pips from 240 late on Thursday. The rate had been at 175 on Wednesday, before the onset of the worst riots in Argentina's history marked the beginning of the end for the country's government. 

 A rise in forward rates indicates pressure on the currency. 

 Like Hong Kong, Argentina links its currency to the U.S. dollar through a currency board system. Its troubles invariably spark currency jitters in Hong Kong. 

 Argentina's currency peg is widely expected to be on the way out following the abrupt departure of Economy Minister Domingo Cavallo on Thursday and the subsequent resignation of the country's president Fernando de la Rua. 

 Analysts say the Hong Kong dollar is still rock solid, but that doesn't mean it's irrational for traders to be cautious. 

 "I'm absolutely certain that (Hong Kong's) peg will stay," said Pieter van der Schaft, associate director, economic research, at Barclays Capital in Hong Kong. 

 "But there are some in the market that for precautionary reasons have established short positions. And that's mainly due to the small but residual risk that the peg could be abandoned." 

 HECK NO, THE PEG WON'T GO! 

 Hong Kong has no intention of letting that happen, though. 

 Financial officials have made it abundantly clear over and over again that snapping the peg would cause the territory more pain than gain. 

 The downsides from the peg are clear. 

 For one thing, it renders the Hong Kong Monetary Authority unable to conduct monetary policy independent of the U.S. Federal Reserve. 

 Because the currency can only move in a narrow band, any adjustments in the economy must be made through prices rather than foreign exchange movements. In recent years, Hong Kong has suffered from nagging deflation and falling asset prices, at least partly due to its relatively strong currency. 

 The benefits are equally clear. 

 Foreign investors in this most open of economies do not need to worry about exchange rate risk. The government, as well as most economists, agree that breaking the peg could cause massive capital outflows. 

 BUT WHAT ABOUT THE SPECULATORS? 

 It's all well and good if the authorities want to keep the peg, but what if speculators take aim at the currency? 

 They did once before, and were beaten badly. 

Hong Kong authorities in August 1998 intervened in the stock market to foil what they called a double edged attack on Hong Kong, whereby speculators put pressure on the peg in an attempt to drive up interest rates and push down stock prices, allowing them to take profits on short share positions. 

 That was at the height of the Asia crisis, and there have been no serious attacks on the peg since that time. 

 There's little in the Argentina crisis that would embolden speculators to go after Hong Kong's peg. Aside from their currency boards, highly indebted Argentina and virtually debt-free Hong Kong have little in common. 

 Hong Kong Financial Secretary Anthony Leung said investors know this. 

 "International investors and banks understand that Argentina and Hong Kong have great differences. Even though we both have a currency board system, our economic fundamentals are vastly different," Leung said in a dinner speech on Thursday. 

 But Leung also said Argentina's fate should sound a warning to Hong Kong to maintain its strong financial system and take decisive steps to deal with its budget deficit, which has widened due to the economic slowdown. 

 Economists polled by Reuters on average expect Hong Kong's economy to contract 0.2 percent this year before rebounding by about two percent in 2002. 

 YEN ALSO A TROUBLEMAKER 

 Hong Kong currency dealers said trading activity was light and moves exaggerated ahead of the Christmas holidays. 

 They also said the weaker yen was as much to blame for the fluctuations in rates as the Argentina situation. 

 The yen fell to a three-year low of 129.49 per U.S. dollar on Friday after a member of Japan's finance ministry said the yen's weakness was merely a correction of its excessive strength. 

 The yen has come under severe pressure recently on growing evidence of Japan's economic malaise. 

 "People who want to short Asian currencies because of the weak yen will go to the Hong Kong dollar market," Barclay's van der Schaft pointed out. "It's more liquid than the others." 

 (with additional reporting by Christina Lo).

title: UPDATE1-HK Exchange Fund assets HK$985.86 bln end-Oct.
text:
HONG KONG, Nov 5 (Reuters) - The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) said on Monday the Exchange Fund had total assets of HK$985.86 billion (US$126.39 billion) at the end of October versus HK$992.23 billion at the end of September. 

 Exchange Fund data issued by the territory's de facto central bank showed that during the 10 months from January to October the fund's investment income was HK$6.1 billion, reversing a HK$6.2 billion investment loss in the January-September period. 

 But after interest and expenses the fund made a net investment loss of HK$2.4 billion from January to October, versus a HK$13.9 billion loss in the January-September period. 

 Resources of the Exchange Fund are used to back the Hong Kong dollar, unless they are needed for general revenue. 

 Noting the investment income, HKMA Chief Executive Joseph Yam told legislators: "This was a positive return. We were not making a loss. We hope to be able to maintain that in the coming two months so that it won't be in the red at the year-end". 

 "But the conditions in financial markets are difficult to predict," he added, saying it was too early to predict if the fund would make a loss this year. 

 Last week, Yam said withdrawals of fiscal reserves from the Exchange Fund totalled HK$58 billion this financial year (April-March) to end-September. Yam said on Monday the government had made further withdrawals in October because of the fiscal deficit. 

 The fiscal deficit for the six months to end-September totalled HK$60.7 billion, a far cry from the HK$3 billion forecast in the fiscal 2001/02 budget unveiled in March. 

 Hong Kong Financial Secretary Antony Leung said last month he would not rule out the deficit growing to HK$100 million. 

 Of the total Exchange Fund assets at end-October, HK$894.98 billion was foreign currency assets and HK$90.88 billion Hong Kong dollar assets. 

 The fund's accumulated surplus was HK$303.325 billion at end-October, versus HK$296.252 billion at end-September. The accumulated surplus fell HK$3.8 billion during the January-October period. 

 In the same 10 months, the fund made a loss of HK$37.8 billion on Hong Kong equities and an exchange loss of HK$8.9 billion, but those losses were more than offset by a HK$52.8 billion return on bonds. 

 At end-October, the Exchange Fund's Hong Kong equities portfolio, largely amassed during a two-week market intervention in August 1998 defending the local currency, was worth HK$75.2 billion. 

 That included HK$49.3 billion slated for long term investment and HK$25.9 billion for future disposal through the sale of more Tracker Fund units. 

 The Tracker Fund was launched in November 1999 as a means of disposing of the governments stock portfolio, largely acquired during the controversial intervention. 

 As end-October, the Hong Kong equity portfolio had earned income of HK$139.7 billion from disposal and dividends. 

 (US$1=HK$7.8).

title: BOJ Matsushima: Don't Plan To Weaken Yen By  Intervention
text:
HONG KONG -(Dow Jones)- The Bank of Japan has no plan to intervene in currency markets to weaken the yen as a way to ease Japan's debilitating deflationary conditions, a senior BOJ official said Wednesday. 

 "We don't have any intention of inducing the yen weaker by maneuvering (or) by intervention in the foreign exchange market," said BOJ executive director Masayuki Matsushima. 

 In September, the BOJ intervened to drive the Japanese currency lower, selling yen for dollars and euros in a series of foreign exchange market incursions that pushed the U.S. currency above Y119 from Y116. Around 0219 GMT the dollar was trading at Y122.00. 

 The BOJ has no authority to set foreign exchange policy which is entirely controlled by the Ministry of Finance. However, Matsushima remarks suggest the BOJ remains opposed to using indirect means - such as increasing the central bank's purchases of foreign currency-denominated bonds - to cheapen the yen and help alleviate Japan's worsening deflation. 

 In any case, Matsushima said deteriorating economic conditions in Japan suggest the yen is unlikely to naturally appreciate against major currencies, indicating the Japanese monetary authorities may feel comfortable about the current dollar-yen exchange rate. 

 "The Japanese government has not targeted a fixed exchange rate," Matsushima said in a speech to the East Asia Economic Summit in Hong Kong 

 "We think the rather bleak economic prospects (mean) an appreciation of the yen at present is undermined by economic growth. There is no reason for the yen to appreciate," the BOJ official said. 

 In a semiannual report released Monday the BOJ policy board said it expects the economy to shrink by around 1% in the current financial year to next March and for deflation to accelerate. 

 Despite admitting the outlook looks dismal, the BOJ board opted to leave unchanged its current super-easy policy of maintaining private banks' current-account deposits at the BOJ "above Y6 trillion." 

 The shift to a "quantitative easing" policy last March has kept short-term interest rates anchored virtually at zero ever since. 

 Matsushima said the BOJ is resolved to ridding the economy of deflation and will maintain its current policy stance until consumer prices start rising at a rate convincingly above zero. 


"The BOJ, under the current policy framework, is firmly committed to
maintain its current extremely lax monetary posture until CPI (the
consumer price index) ceases to decline," Matsushima said.
   -By Liz Rudall and Anette Jonsson, Dow Jones Newswires;

title: Asia Markets-Plot talk hits peso, Indonesia debt raises eyebrows.
text:
HONG KONG, Oct 26 (Reuters) - Talk of a plot to destabilise 

 the Philippine government and news of a planned U.S. dollar 

 bond deal from Indonesia's biggest bank were the key trading 

 points of an otherwise lacklustre Friday in Asian asset 

 markets. 

     Philippine President Gloria Macapagal Arroyo said rumours 

 of a plot against her government had undermined the peso 

 which fell past 52 to the dollar for the first time since 

 August 13 on Thursday and closed at 52.04 on Friday.

government".

external financing, falling interest rates and a shrinking



trade surplus.

steps to strengthen the peso to at least 50 per dollar by the



end of the year.


Central bank governor Rafael Buenaventura said on Friday



the bank was not intervening in the foreign exchange market to



help the peso.

triggered broad-based buying and sent airline Cathay Pacific



 leaping 6.4 percent to just off its level of



September 11.



    The Hang Seng Index        closed higher for the third



straight session, finishing up 1.6 percent at 10,404.74.



    The index has gained six percent on the week but is still



down 31 percent this year.



    Shares of Toshiba, Japan's top chipmaker, fell 4.67 percent



to 510 yen, helping to push down the benchmark Nikkei share



average by 84.94 points or 0.78 percent.



    The close was 2.32 percent off from Thursday's intraday



high of 11,052.01, its highest level since the September 11



attacks in the United States sparked fears of global recession.



    Singapore shares gave up almost all their gains to end flat



on profit-taking ahead of the weekend, with the Straits Times



Index ending up just 0.15 percent.



    Countering the overall market, the electronics index



 jumped 3.37 percent, helped by the Nasdaq Composite



Index's 2.54 percent gain as well as post-results



relief at home.



South Korea's KOSPI ended 0.23 percent higher,



extending gains to a sixth session, helped by foreign buying in



telecom shares on upbeat earnings forecasts.



Nasdaq's rally inspired a short squeeze in Taiwan, where



the key TAIEX index ended 0.78 percent higher, its



third successive firmer close.



HSBC WINS MANDIRI DEBT MANDATE



HSBC confirmed market talk it had been appointed to explore



a dollar debt deal for PT Bank Mandiri which would mark the



nation's first foray in the dollar debt market since the Asian



financial crisis of 1997/98.



Traders said the deal is expected to be small-sized with a



five year tenor and will be seen as a benchmark of investor



confidence in President Megawati Sukarnoputri's government.



"With the Latin American risk coming off a bit, now is a



good time as any to launch a bond. But I think they will have



to pay a good deal of premium," said a senior bond trader at a



U.S.-based investment bank.



Indonesia's credibility in the international capital market



has been battered after the spectacular collapse of Asia Pulp &



Paper Co Ltd , a firm laden with $12.2 billion of



debt, earlier this year.



The broader regional dollar bond market was quiet with most



investors adopting a cautious capital preservation strategy



before the year-end.



"The market is very quiet and has a slightly weak tone. The



investors are probably weighing the impact of likely new



issues," said a senior bond dealer at a European investment



bank.

title: PRESS DIGEST - Asian Wall Street Journal - July 5.
text:
SINGAPORE, July 5 (Reuters) - The following stories were reported in Thursday's electronic version of The Asian Wall Street Journal: 

 * Sony may combine its Indian television channels with those of AOL Time Warner , making a potentially major realignment in one of Asia's largest television markets. 

 * A real-estate group with ties to Matsushita Electric has racked up more than $3 billion in debt and just reported its first loss. A finance expert has been brought in to clean up the mess. 

 * CyberWorks announced deeper-than-expected cuts for its Internet businesses, including the elimination of 40 percent of online jobs, and announced a bond issue to reduce interest payments. 

 * Cathay Pacific flights have begun to experience some delays from a go-slow campaign by pilots, but observers say Hong Kong's chief executive is hesitant to intervene. 

 * China and Japan weren't able to resolve a three-month-old trade dispute during two days of talks and agreed to hold more talks later to limit the damage to their relationship. 

 * SK Telecom pushed back its launch of 3G mobile services by up to a year from the May 2002 target, joining a growing list of cautious operators world-wide. 

 * SingTel will invest $265 million over the next 18 months to open Internet data centers throughout Asia, a move that may challenge existing independent centers. 

 * The Philippine central bank will examine banks' larger foreign-exchange transactions to ensure that currency speculation isn't behind the peso's steep decline. 

 * Australia's central bank left interest rates unchanged, indicating that its easing cycle is most likely over. The Reserve Bank of New Zealand also left rates alone. 

 * The value of Japan's merger-and-acquisition deals fell 65 percent in the first half, but closer inspection shows that asset shuffling may be rising, a study says. 

 * Asia Pulp & Paper's depositary receipts were suspended on the New York Stock Exchange as officials sought to delist them, saying they failed to meet minimum pricing criteria. 

 * Hutchison Whampoa got Europe's conditional clearance for its plan to take a stake in Europe's busiest container port, bolstering the company's presence in the container-handling business. 

 * Followers of the outlawed Falun Gong sect hanged themselves in a mass suicide at a prison camp, China and a human rights group said. But the sect claimed the inmates were tortured to death.

title: Asia Markets-Wall St shakes stocks, bonds await Argentina ripple.
text:
HONG KONG, June 19 (Reuters) - Asian asset markets failed 

 to fight through Wall Street's gloom on Tuesday, with most 

 regional equity benchmarks flat to weaker and fixed income 

 markets trading nervously in the shadow cast by Argentina's 

 flailing economy. 

     A fall of two percent on Nasdaq kept Asian stocks bowed, 

 with only Hong Kong and Malaysia strong enough to break 

 decisively into positive territory, and weighed heavily on 

 sentiment for dollar bonds which saw spreads to risk-free U.S. 

 Treasuries widen an average of 10 basis points on the day. 

    Asian currencies remained hostage to the fortunes of Japan's 

 yen which sank to one month lows against the dollar before 

 recovering sharply in late trade after central bank governor 

 Masaru Hayami said intervention was necessary if forex rates 

 move too rapidly. 

     Tokyo's Nikkei 225 stock index wiped out earlier gains to 

 end lower for the third straight session, losing 0.97 percent 

 after concerns over the financial health of debt-strapped 

 Japanese retailer Mycal Corp chilled sentiment. 

     ASIAN BOND SPREADS WIDEN 

     Asian dollar bond spreads were wider across the board in 

 thin trade with a fall on Wall Street undermining prices more 

 than confusion over a change in Argentina's currency peg. 

     Asian bonds have taken it on the chin since Nortel Networks 

 warned of a $19.2 billion second quarter loss last week sending 

 U.S. corporate bond spreads sprawling and pushing Asian 

 investors to lock in profits on benchmark paper that has 

 tightened an average of 30 basis points over the past two 

 weeks. 

     Confusion over Argentina's introduction of a special 

 exchange rate for exporters and importers sent emerging market 

 bond investors in New York scurrying for safety on Monday, but 

 near term fallout for Asian bonds were seen muted. 

     "This may make people realise that there are still risks in 

 the global financial system and people may re-evaluate some of 

 the local currencies in Asia," Brian Verlaan, head of Asian 

 fixed income research at Standard Chartered Bank in Singapore 

 said. 

     "This will ultimately, coupled with some of the economic 

 fundamentals in these countries, cause people to reassess 

 spreads, but I don't think there's an immediate knock-on 

 effect," he told Reuters Television. 

     The long end of the Philippine yield curve felt most 

 pressure with the country's 9.875 percent sovereign paper due 

 in 2019 pushing out about five basis points (bps) at the open 

 and moving 10-15 further out to be quoted at about 605 bps over 

 U.S. Treasuries in late trade. 

     At the shorter end Philippine '10s were about two bps wider 

 at Asia's open, but had widened a further five bps in late 

 trade to around 497 bps over Treasuries, according to data from 

 Reuters Fixed Income 3000. 

     The sub-investment grade Philippines offers the most 

 representative comparison to Latin American risk and is the 

 biggest Asian component in the benchmark EMBI, making the paper 

 sensitive to moves in the index, dominated by Argentina. 

     PHILIPPINE PESO SLIDES 

     The peso slid to five-month lows of 52.38 as corporates 

 scrambled to buy the dollar on the weaker yen and concerns 

 about the unsolved kidnappings in the southern Philippines. 

     "We'll take any excuse to buy the dollar. And we know the 

central bank can't afford to intervene with their small 

 reserves," a local bank dealer said. The central bank's 

 international reserves stood at $14.44 billion at end-April. 

     But others said the central bank might take the opportunity 

 to intervene given the market was heavily long of dollars. 

HONG KONG STOCKS REBOUND 

     Hong Kong stocks found late support from a technical 

 rebound after the oversold benchmark index hovered around the 

 13,000 level for most of the day. 

     The Hang Seng Index ended up 1.43 percent at 13,133.66, 

 helped by gains in the two biggest stocks HSBC Holdings and 

 China Mobile. 

     Banking giant HSBC, which had fallen five percent in the 

 past month, rose 1.35 percent to HK$94, while China's biggest 

 mobile phone operator jumped 3.32 percent to HK$40.40 after 

 shedding more than four percent on Monday. 

 China shares also rebounded in late trade with the H-share 

 and the red chip indices mostly recovering their respective two 

 percent deficits to see H-shares end up one percent and the red 

 chips close just 0.30 percent lower. 

 INDONESIA BLAST FELLS RUPIAH 

 News of a bomb blast in Jakarta and another clash between 

 police and students protesting fuel price hikes dragged the 

 rupiah to a two-week low of 11,385 per dollar. 

 Five people were wounded when a powerful bomb exploded at a 

 boarding-house in a Jakarta suburb while police fired teargas 

 to disperse 100 stone-throwing students near a university. 

 Dealers in Jakarta said dollar profit-taking by interbank 

 players and some export-related inflows beyond 11,350 capped 

 its downside. They said there was no sign of the central bank

 but players were cautious a test of 11,400 may invite 

intervention.

title: UPDATE 2-Singapore downplays M&A impact on  currency .
text:
SINGAPORE, May 16 (Reuters) - Singapore on Wednesday played down the impact an estimated outflow of up to US$14.5 billion resulting from overseas acquisitions would have on the local currency. 

 "I don't think the amounts are sufficiently large to move the Singapore dollar in a significant way," the Minister of Finance, Richard Hu, said in Parliament on Wednesday. 

 But he said the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), would take any short-term impact into account. 

 The finance minister's statement followed recent weakness in the Singapore dollar against the U.S. unit on the foreign exchange market, which traders have linked to merger and acquisition flows and market expectations of these flows. 

 Singapore Telecommunications announced in March a planned purchase of Australia's second largest telco, Cable & Wireless Optus Ltd , worth up to US$8.7 billion. 

 When asked about whether there was any change in the terms of the proposed acquisition of Optus, Hu said: "I'm not aware of any significant change." 

 SingTel, currently 78 percent owned by the government, is seeking approval from Australian authorities for its takeover of C&W Optus, which is 52-percent owned by Britain's Cable & Wireless Plc . 

 Separately, DBS Group , in which the government owns 38 percent, has mounted a bid worth up to US$5.8 billion for Hong Kong's Dao Heng Bank . 

 MAS INTERVENES TO SUPPORT SINGAPORE DOLLAR 

 The MAS, in a rare departure from a policy of no comment, confirmed to a local newspaper, the Business Times, on Wednesday that it has been selling U.S dollars in support of the weak Singapore currency. 

 "MAS confirmed in writing to BT yesterday that it sold US dollars in the market last week - a departure from its usual practice of not commenting on its actions," the paper reported on its front page on Wednesday. 

 The newspaper quoted the central bank saying: "MAS will continue to do so when necessary to offset any market impact of such corporate demand for U.S. dollar against the Sing dollar." 

 The MAS also confirmed that its policy for a modest and gradual appreciation of the Singapore dollar remains unchanged. 

 "This policy is based on our medium term assessment of the economy, not short term economic or inflation developments," the MAS said in its statement. 

 The Singapore dollar, which has lost more than four percent since the beginning of the year, edged up to 1.8125/35 0850 GMT, up from fresh 11-year lows hit last week at 1.8265. 

 OVERSEAS ACQUISITIONS OF STRATEGIC INTERESTS 

 Hu said the proposed purchases by Singapore government-linked companies of both Optus and Dao Heng Bank were long term strategic business moves. 

 "Hong Kong is clearly one market, (which) for obvious reasons, is a must for DBS since they are going to be a regional player," Hu said. 

 The government has been encouraging local firms to grow beyond the confines of the Singapore economy for some time. 

 Hu said both acquisitions were such moves, and they would enable them to tap regional opportunities and become more than Singaporean companies. 

 SingTel's expansion plans hit snags twice last year as bids for stakes in Hong Kong's C&W HKT and Malaysia's Time Engineering fell through on perception that the firm was controlled by the Singapore government. 

 In an effort to shake the perception, the eighth largest telecom firm in Asia said last month the Singapore government had given up its special share which offered veto rights over major corporate decisions. 

 Hu said the government did not interfere in the commercial decisions of government-linked firms. 

 "Their soundness (acquisitions) has to be judged over time by the performance of SingTel and DBS, and not by the immediate reaction of the stock market as reflected in their share prices." 

 Hu also defended both acquisitions which were seen too high for the price of growth. 

 "When you buy controlling shares in a large operation, generally you have to pay a substantial premium," he said, adding that the size of the premium was a judgement the management had to take and it was not in the government's interest to challenge.

title: Emerging  FX -Rangebound on yen,  intervention  fears.
text:
SINGAPORE, April 9 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were rangebound, not far from their recent lows on Monday, in the face of intervention threats and uncertainty about the near-term direction of the yen . 

 More warnings from Japanese officials against excessive exchange rate weakness kept the yen supported the firm side of 125 to the dollar for most of the day, making players wary of pushing the regionals lower. 

 But most analysts expected the dollar to move ahead again on continued safe haven flows after a brief period of consolidation. 

 "The dollar is basically in a consolidation phase and there is some uncertainty on how long it will remain in this phase. So for the time being there is some respite for other currencies," a chief dealer of a European bank said. 

 The rest of the region was also rife with talk of central bank intervention as finance officials and politicians kept up their verbal routine. 

 Korean foreign exchange authorities were spotted selling dollars via onshore banks at around 1,343.00, continuing last week's aggressive intervention. 

 However, comments by Thai officials worked the other way, taking the baht to a new 37-month low. 

 The euro managed to hold its day highs around $0.9040 amid concerns over the U.S. economy after March payrolls data released on Friday showed the steepest monthly fall in ten years. 

 THAI BAHT 

 The baht perked up after rumours swirled in the market that the central bank stepped in to prop up the currency at 45.80-45.85. 

 The central bank said earlier it was monitoring the baht closely, but reiterated the baht weakness was caused by the soft yen and other external factors. 

 Dealers said the baht fell to intraday lows of 45.85 partly due to a remark by Commerce Minister Adisai Bodharamik that a weak baht was helping exports. 

 "The market's interpretation of it was the government was willing to tolerate a weaker baht," said a Singapore dealer. 

 Meanwhile, Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra said Thailand had no plan to impose monetary controls to stem losses in the baht which hit fresh 37-month lows on Monday. 

 The one-month forward rate in the offshore market eased slightly to 30/60 satang per dollar from around 40/50 satang in the morning. 

 KOREAN WON -2 

 The won moved within a tight range, helped by a steadier yen and on dollar selling intervention by the Bank of Korea. 

 Dealers in Seoul said the central bank sold an estimated $200 million via onshore banks at 1,342.0 won in the morning and 1,343.0 in the afternoon. 

 But they scoffed at Monday's operation, which came on the back of an aggressive $400-$500 million intervention last week. 

 However, a bearish outlook for the region reinforced by weak U.S. March payrolls data and the KOSPI's fall following the Nasdaq's losses on Friday, kept sentiment depressed. 

 Analysts said the market would keep an eye on more data from the U.S. including retail sales and the producer price index for March due later in the week. 

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR 

 The Sing dollar remained under selling pressure due to the regional trend and talk of a major local bank planning to buy a bank in Hong Kong. 

 Dealers said players had bid up the dollar on reports that DBS Group , Southeast Asia's largest bank, was set to make a bid of up to HK$45 billion ($5.78 billion) for Hong Kong's Dao Heng Bank . 

 Otherwise, the market was awaiting flash data on January-March growth and the government's revised 2001 growth forecast to be released on Tuesday. Economists polled by Reuters expected the economy to grow 5.9 percent in the first quarter. 

 "The official 2001 economic growth forecast - currently at 5-7 percent - is expected to be revised downwards," said a DBS report. 

 "However, this should not have any material impact on the forex and equity markets which have largely priced in the slower growth," it said. 

 The Reuters poll produced an average forecast of 4.6 percent growth in 2001. 

 INDONESIAN RUPIAH 

 The rupiah was wedged in a narrow range, with foreign banks trimming long dollar positions and state banks buying the dollar, dealers said. 

 One Jakarta dealer said Bank Indonesia, the country's central bank, was heard entering the market to sell a small amount of dollar at 10,850. 

 The market expected a long-awaited visit by the IMF to Indonesia this week would give the ailing rupiah some reprieve. 

 The visit should pave the way for disbursement of a $400 million loan delayed by the IMF since late last year and trigger a $5.8 billion debt rescheduling deal with the Paris Club of official creditors.

 Dealers in Hong Kong said exporters sold U.S. dollars as the Taiwan dollar eased towards its session low of 32.95 fearing the central bank may not allow the currency to test the 33 level. 

 On Friday, the central bank capped the Taiwan dollar's gains at 32.90, leaving it confined to a narrow range. 

Central bank governor Perng Fai-nan said on Monday the Taiwan dollar rate should reflect changes in the international financial environment. 

 Dealers said sentiment was weighed by a fall in the TAIEX and the continued deadlock between China and the U.S. over a spy plane and its crew detained by Beijing. 

 The market will be watching for March trade balance data due on Tuesday. A Reuters poll showed an average of $759 million surplus expected for March, compared with a surplus of $1.059 billion in February.

 The peso was steady with only a few small offshore deals reported as markets in Manila were closed for the Valour Day holiday. Trade will resume on Tuesday. 

 Dealers in Singapore said a weak outlook for the yen and other regional currencies would continue to keep the peso pressured as exporters and overseas workers held back dollars.

title: Emerging  FX -Yen weighs,  central bank  fears help.
text:
SINGAPORE, April 6 (Reuters) - Asian currencies came under renewed pressure on Friday as the yen's three-day winning streak against the dollar ran into some resistance. 

 The yen stumbled as a much-awaited economic package by the Japanese ruling coalition failed to impress the market, but renewed jawboning boosted it in late trade. 

 The Finance Ministry's Haruhiko Kuroda said it was hard to justify recent moves in the dollar/yen as there had been no big change in Japan's fundamentals and that Japan would take action in currency markets if current trends continued. 

 Most regional currencies opened higher on the back of the yen's overnight gains but a reversal of those gains sparked covering of short dollar positions. 

 But central banks in Korea and Indonesia intervened while the fear of that in Singapore kept the won, rupiah and Sing dollar off recent lows. 

 With Bangkok closed for a holiday, the baht was not so lucky and slipped to a fresh 37-month low in offshore trade. 

 Analysts said central bank threats and actions could temporarily ease some pressure on the currencies but the outlook remained weak on slowing growth and exports. 

 Fresh trading cues were likely to emerge from the U.S. March employment report due at 1230 GMT. 

 Economists polled by Reuters on average expect a higher unemployment rate, up to 4.3 percent from February's 4.2 percent. They also forecast 58,000 new jobs were created outside the farm sector in March, compared with 135,000 in February. 

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR The Sing dollar kept a soft tone as the yen eased. 

 Dealers said local banks placed sizeable U.S. dollar orders in the afternoon, which pushed it down to session lows of 1.8184. 

 But the market turned wary as the Monetary Authority of Singapore was suspected to have defended that level late on Wednesday. This allowed the Sing dollar to avoid a damaging break of 1.8200 which would expose it to decade lows of 1.8230 hit on Monday. 

 But the market saw no signs of aggressive action by the authorities, which again spurred speculation the MAS had already shifted its monetary stance to neutral from a tightening bias. 

 The MAS has said it would review its monetary policy in the middle of the year. 

 Dealers said the market would focus on a revised growth forecast for 2001 and preliminary growth figures for the first quarter due for release on Tuesday. 

 The government estimates the economy will grow between five to seven percent this year, but economists suspect worsening external conditions could slow growth to as low as 4.8 percent. 

 THAI BAHT 

 Offshore players took advantage of a holiday in Bangkok to push the baht to a 37-month low of 45.72. 

 Dealers in Singapore said the dollar crawled higher in ultra-thin trade, which exaggerated the impact of relatively small deals. They added U.S. names were spotted buying up dollar/baht when the yen fell past 125. 

 "With Bangkok on holiday, that means no Bank of Thailand. So you might as well take adventage of that," said a dealer at a European bank, referring to the central bank's suspected intervention to shore up the baht earlier this week. 

 Charts showed the dollar/baht had wandered deeply into overbought territory with a reading of 84.863 on the 14-day relative strength index. 

 Offshore baht funding costs were still firm at 41/52 satang per dollar against 40/50 satang late Thursday. 

 KOREAN WON -02 

 The won was propped up by the Bank of Korea as it tried to track the yen's retreat against the dollar. 

 Dealers estimated the central bank had directly sold about $150-200 million at around 1,358 won in late morning trade, intervening again in the afternoon. 

 Both times the won rose to around its session high of 1,339.9 where importers and offshore players were seen buying dollars. 

Hong Kong dealers said the intervention, which came after weeks of verbal threats and recent state bank dollar sales, was not as aggressive as expected, given the $1.5 billion average daily turnover in the won market. 

 They said fears the central bank was probably testing the depth of the market and might come in more strongly later, kept players cautious. 

 TAIWAN DOLLAR 

 The Taiwan dollar was firmer, but did not venture very far from Thursday's close of 32.979 as the yen wavered. 

 For the past several weeks, the Taiwan dollar has been tracking the yen closely as Taiwan and Japan compete on electronics exports. 

 Consumer inflation data showed a slight 0.44 percent on-year rise in March against February's 1.02 percent fall. Analysts said the slight rise meant inflation was still benign and may provide more room for the central bank to cut rates. 

 On the Taiwan dollar NDF market, the six-month rate was at 0.560/610 and the one-year was at 0.850/900. 

 INDONESIAN RUPIAH 

 The rupiah dipped to a near four-week low of 10,930 as early dollar buying by some state and foreign banks sent local corporates scrambling for dollars. 

 Dealers in Jakarta said the central bank pumped in around $10-30 million from around 10,930 all the way to 10,850, but they added that local corporate demand for dollars was strong in the 10,750-10,800 range. 

 The market was unimpressed by news an IMF review mission would start its work in Jakarta on Wednesday as conditions of the visit had been met. 

 Dealers said the market was likely to wait for a formal resumption of IMF lending before pushing the rupiah higher. 

 However, Bank Indonesia governor Sjahril Sabirin said he expected the IMF visit to help boost sentiment in the rupiah which could give the central bank room to lower interest rates. 

 The mission's visit should pave the way for a new $400 million loan from the IMF which has been delayed since late last year due to a dispute between Jakarta and the Fund over key reforms. 

 PHILIPPINE PESO 

 The peso ended at 50.200, slightly below its Thursday close after hitting a session low of 50.50 in line with weakness in other regional currencies. 

 Dealers said oil importers and some foreign banks were seen bidding the dollar up in early trade but inflows from overseas workers ahead of a long weekend capped the peso's downside. 

 Manila's financial markets will be closed on Monday for the Day of Valour.

title: China Yuan Ends Up On Exporter Dlr Sales; Bonds Mostly Dn
text:
SHANGHAI -(Dow Jones)- China's yuan ended stronger against the dollar Thursday on exporter selling of the U.S. currency, traders said. 

 The dollar closed lower at 8.2774 yuan compared with CNY8.2778 Wednesday. 

 It traded in a narrow range between CNY8.2771 and CNY8.2778. 

 Volume shrank to US$70 million from the previous US$150 million. 

 "Dollar selling by exporters is still the primary driver of yuan trading," said a trader at Shanghai Pudong Development Bank. "We didn't see any particularly large deals conducted by the central bank." 

 China's yuan can only be converted for trading purposes and most exporters must repatriate 85% of their overseas receipts to state-owned banks. 

 The central bank, the People's Bank of China, often intervenes in the market. 

 The Hong Kong dollar rose to CNY1.0615 from CNY1.0610, and the Japanese yen dipped to CNY6.9352 per Y100 from CNY6.9764. 

 Meanwhile, government bonds closed mostly lower on profit-taking. 

 "Since bonds have been rising for four straight days, such profit-taking was expected sooner or later," said a trader at Shenyin & Wanguo Securities in Shanghai. 

 The trader added that the market remains bullish overall because there haven't been many initial public offerings in the stock market recently, so there's less of an incentive for investors to sell bonds and buy stocks instead. 

 The 1999 10-year bond retreated CNY0.28 to CNY101.71 on trade of 629,095 lots. Its yield increased to 3.28% from 3.24%. 

 The 2000 10-year floating-rate bond shed CNY0.14 to CNY103.71 on trade of 327,066 lots. 

 The only issue bucking the trend was the 1997 10-year bond, which jumped CNY0.11 to CNY138.44 on trade of 165,397 lots. Its yield slid to 3.86% from 3.87%. 

 Total transaction volume was CNY1.94 billion, below CNY2.13 billion Wednesday. 

 China's bond market is off-limits to foreign investors.

title: WRAPUP 2-Asian stocks slide, Nikkei hits 15-yr low.
text:
SINGAPORE Feb 28 (Reuters) - Tokyo led most Asian markets lower on Wednesday, with the Nikkei 225 Share Average briefly touching a 15-year low on miserable economic data at home and from the United States. 

 The index fell as far as 12,784.17, its lowest since December 10, 1985, before recovering to 12,883.54 at the close, down 1.35 percent - a 28-month low. 

 The Nikkei took its cue from overnight losses on the Nasdaq Composite Index, which fell 4.36 percent on the back of big declines in U.S. consumer confidence and home sales, raising fears the country's economy may be in worse shape than most people think. 

 Adding to the bearish tone were lower than expected figures for Japanese industrial output for January, raising the spectre of recession in the country. 

 Preliminary data released by the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry before the start of trade showed a shocking 3.9 percent month-on-month drop, much worse than a median forecast of a 0.2 percent rise in a Reuters poll of 13 economists released last week. 

 "It's a very bleak number," said Garry Evans, strategist at HSBC Securities. 

 Fibre-optic shares and high-techs - such as Nikon Corp - played a large part in the fall. 

 Furukawa Electric Co Ltd, Japan's top optical fibre maker, came under pressure after shares of JDS Uniphase Corp, the world's top supplier of fibre optic components, fell 15 percent in New York. 

 EURO MISSES OPPORTUNITY 

 On the currency markets, the euro failed to make much of the dire figures from the United States and Japan, holding around 106.65 yen and easing back to $0.9180 after an early bounce failed to clear resistance at $0.9185. 

 The yen proved remarkably resilient, thanks in large part to exporters' hedging forward receipts and the fact that Japanese markets have long discounted a return to recession and almost given up hope of a policy remedy. 

 "We can't get any gloomier," one dealer said. 

 The dollar was at 116.18 yen compared with 116.20 before the Japanese data. 

 Markets are now focused on the BOJ policy meeting taking place on Wednesday and Federal Reserve Board chairman Alan Greenspan's speech later in the day. 

 Investors are looking for signs of a more aggressive stance from both to boost the economies of their respective countries. 

 News that Greenspan would take the unusual step of altering the monetary policy testimony he delivered two weeks ago to a Senate panel as he goes before the House Finance Committee has fanned speculation in markets eager for signs the Fed will cut rates soon. 

 But few analysts see either central bank responding to the soft data immediately. 

 HSBC DRAGS 

 In Hong Kong, the benchmark Hang Seng Index was dragged lower by global banking group HSBC Holdings, which fell 3.26 percent, extending Tuesday's losses after poor earnings. 

 The index was down 1.66 percent to 14,589.17 at midday. 

 Dealers said investors sold HSBC shares on lingering concerns that a slowing U.S. economy would hurt the bank's earnings. 

 The H-share index of mainland companies listed in Hong Kong fell 4.53 percent, contrary to market expectations. 

 Investors had been expecting the index to jump in tandem with gains in B shares following the resumption of trade in the Shanghai and Shenzhen markets on Wednesday. 

 Investors shifted their funds to China's offshore oil exploration company, CNOOC Ltd, which made its Hong Kong debut on Wednesday, dealers said. 

 Shares of CNOOC Ltd, China's third largest petroleum company, closed midday at HK$6.70, up 12.6 percent from an issue price of HK$5.95 per share before brokerage fees. 

 CHINA B MARKET SOARS 

 The much-heralded reopening of China's B share market panned out as predicted by analysts with both the Shenzhen and Shanghai indices soaring near their 10 percent daily limit on minute volume. 

 It was the first trading day since February 19, when China allowed citizens with legal foreign exchange accounts to buy B shares and opened the door for a potential $75 billion in foreign exchange deposits to be invested. 

 Analysts expect a sustained rally of 30-50 percent as investors plug the valuation gap between B shares and local-currency A shares. 

 There were few sellers when trading resumed, however, and new punters could only watch with envy as existing B share investors saw nine years of patience finally pay off. 

 "If you already hold B shares, you are very lucky, but if you play the game now it's probably a fool's game," said James Cheng, of Hong Kong fund house Asia Strategic Investment Management Ltd. 

INTERVENTION PROP 

 Korean stocks held onto marginal gains, as heavy buying by investment trust management companies that had received funds from the National Pension Fund helped offset the gloomy news from abroad. 

 The National Pension Fund said last Friday it would invest 160 billion won ($128.2 million) this week in the stock market, and an undetermined amount in March. 

 An official from the pension fund said it put 160 billion won into three investment trust companies, Samsung, LG and Hyundai Investment Trust Management. 

 The presidential Blue House said earlier this month the nation's pension funds would expand their stock investments to 25 trillion won from eight trillion won. 

 The Korea Composite Stock Price Index was up 0.09 percent to 578.10 points at the close. 

 The Taiwan market was closed for Peace Memorial Day. 

 Oil prices on Wednesday were lifted from seven-week lows after weekly data from the United States showed only a small recovery in lean U.S. crude inventories. 

 U.S. light crude in electronic trade edged up 12 cents to $28.25 a barrel after industry group the American Petroleum Institute (API) said crude stocks rose a modest 2.2 million barrels in the week to February 23. 

 Wednesday's uptick interrupted a steady slide in oil prices that has seen U.S. crude fall $4.50 a barrel over the past five weeks.

title: UPDATE 2-HKMA says HK banking system robust, profits rise.
text:
HONG KONG, Jan 11 (Reuters) - The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) said on Thursday that the territory's banking sector remained robust as the economy and operating conditions improved. 

 The territory's de facto central bank also said the total assets of Hong Kong's Exchange Fund, which backs the local currency, was HK$1,020.8 billion at the end of 2000, up 1.8 percent from 1999. 

 In a presentation to legislators, the HKMA said that the pre-tax operating profits of local banks had grown 45.7 percent year-on-year in the first nine months of 2000 which represented a sharp rise compared with 15.2 percent growth in 1999. 

 "Strong growth was mainly attributed to a significant drop in bad debt charges and increases in net interest and fee income," the HKMA said. 

 Banks' asset quality had continued to improve slowly, with charges for bad debts falling 54.8 percent in the first three quarters of last year, it said. 

 The asset quality of banks' mortgage portfolio remained relatively low though the delinquency ratio rose to 1.31 percent in November versus 1.13 percent at the end of 1999. 

 Banks remained well capitalised and highly liquid, as reflected in their high capital adequacy ratio, which came in at 18.7 percent, and their liquidity ratio of 50.2 percent as of September 2000. 

 The territory's Exchange Fund recorded modest profit for 2000 though it shed HK$11.6 billion on its equity portfolio because of falls on the Hang Seng , it said. 

 The government still had HK$150.7 billion (US$19.3 billion) worth of Hong Kong stocks at the end of 2000, including stocks transferred from the Land Fund in 1998. 

 The contents of Hong Kong's equity portfolio was largely amassed when the government intervened in the stock market to fend off speculators in 1998. 

 The HKMA said it intended to keep only around HK$50 billion worth of its remaining equity portfolio in accordance with investment guidelines laid out by the Exchange Fund. It did not say when it intended to reach this level. 

 (US$ = Hk$7.8).

title: Emerging  FX  - Mixed, outlook bleak on U.S. worries.
text:
SINGAPORE, Jan 9 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were a mixed bag late Tuesday with some consolidating around recent weak levels, but overall the mood was depressed on worries about the impact a cooling U.S. economy could have on the region. 

 "Global investors are still very much focused on the majors and there is very little risk appetite for emerging markets like Asia," said Andrew Fung, head of Asia Pacific research at Rabobank. 

 Fung said weakness of the yen on top of the U.S.-led global slowdown would hit exports and growth throughout the region. 

 Morgan Stanley Dean Witter in a research report on Tuesday said Asian governments were likely to let their currencies weaken to cushion against an export downturn as the U.S. economy went into recession in the first half. 

 The U.S. investment bank warned on Monday that the U.S. economy would probably sink into recession in the first half of 2001, breaking its longest expansion in history. 

 It said the won and Taiwan dollar looked the most vulnerable, facing declines of about 10 percent before bouncing back with the U.S. recovery late in the year. 

 It said the peso, baht and rupiah would respond more to domestic politics rather than to changes in the global demand scenario, while the Singapore dollar was likely to follow the North Asian currencies. 

 The yen was steady around 115.90, off last week's 17-month lows against the dollar while profit-taking softened the euro from last week's six-month peaks. 

 THAI BAHT 

 The baht traded in a tight range of 42.79-43.00, caught between foreign investors looking to sell dollars and local corporate demand for dollars. 

 Though it briefly slipped to 43.00, dealers in Bangkok said the post-election mood was still upbeat. "We're still optimistic about a stable outcome from the elections," said a dealer at a European bank. 

 "The baht might be consolidating around these levels. We're now waiting to see who (Thai Rak Thai Party leader) Thaksin (Shinawatra) will choose as Finance Minister," he added. 

 Telecoms tycoon Thaksin won the weekend general election by a landslide, according to unofficial results. 

 However, the victory has not entirely dispelled political uncertainty in Thailand as Thaksin is awaiting a court decision that determines his immediate fate. 

 A constitutional court is expected to rule in the coming months on whether Thaksin was guilty of hiding assets. If found guilty, he would be barred from taking office for five years. 

 INDONESIAN RUPIAH 

 The rupiah mustered some strength to rise above the 9,500 level on the back of dollar selling from foreign banks in Jakarta earlier in the day. 

 Dealers in Jakarta said the dollar offers were spurred by the stronger baht and Singapore dollar, but met with dollar bids from local banks buying on behalf of corporates. 

 State banks were also spotted selling dollars, though only in small amounts. A dealer at a U.S. bank in Jakarta said volume was around $200 million by late afternoon. 

 The market was also watching Bank Indonesia's SBI note auction on Wednesday, and some dealers said they believed the bank may hold on rates after last week's rate cuts by the Federal Reserve. 

 Indonesia's chief economics minister Rizal Ramli warned on Monday against excessively high interest rates. Rates have been steadily creeping higher in recent months to shore up support for the rupiah. 

 Bank Indonesia has said it would decide this week on whether to follow the U.S. rate cut. 

 PHILIPPINE PESO 

 The peso made slow progress above the 51 per dollar mark, hovering in a tight nine-tick band on light volume of $77 million, below Monday's already thin $93 million. 

 A lack of commercial demand and wariness over the impeachment saga dampened activity, though Manila stocks did manage a solid 2.5 percent rise, with brokers even citing foreign buying of selected blue chips. 

 They said offshore investors were beginning to position for a decision on President Joseph Estrada's impeachment trial, slated to end around February 12. The prospect of lower interest rates also helped. 

 Estrada said on Tuesday economic and political stability would be restored once he was acquitted of corruption charges. 

 But in a reminder of the problems besetting the economy, Finance Secretary Jose Pardo said the budget deficit for 2000 was likely to be below 140 billion pesos, above an official estimate of 130 billion pesos made only last week. 

 The deficit for the first 11 months of 2000 was 114.38 billion pesos, dwarfing the government's original 62 billion peso target. 

 TAIWAN DOLLAR 

 The Taiwan dollar climbed on the back of rallying local equities, with investors hoping the beleaguered stock market was making a long-awaited rebound. 

 But dealers in Hong Kong noted that the central bank was in the market around the Taiwan dollar's intraday high of 32.695 to buy U.S. dollars. 

 "They were there chiefly to smooth the Taiwan dollar's appreciation," said a chief dealer at a European bank in Hong Kong. 

 Despite the central bank's intervention, the local dollar held onto most of its gains as local and foreign banks continued to unwind long dollar positions. 

 While dealers said there were still some of these positions that would likely be liquidated this week, they also noted that the Taiwan dollar had appreciated against the currencies of its regional competitors. 

 The cross rate between the Taiwan dollar and yen stood at 3.5461 at 0819 GMT, which some dealers and analysts said may be too high for the authorities' liking. 

 Moreover, Taiwan's economy is expected to show signs of slowing, as it is particularly exposed to the U.S. economy. 

 December trade data released on Monday showed import growth slowing to a one percent rise on year, largely due to a seven percent contraction on year in capital equipment imports. Analysts said this was a worrying reflection of sluggish domestic demand, and with exports growth expected to slow, Taiwan could face tougher times. 

 KOREAN WON -2 

 The Korean won firmed from early levels helped by foreign portfolio inflows, which prompted local exporters to offload their holdings. 

 But dealers said most participants in the market were reluctant to unwind dollar longs given a depressing export and growth outlook amid a slowing U.S. economy. 

 Foreign investors were net buyers of about 35 billion won worth of local shares, adding to shares worth 144 billion won they bought on Monday. 

 Dealers said a steadier yen also helped sentiment but offshore players were active in the forward market to hedge their equity investments. 

 The six-month non-deliverable forward dollar/won was at 1,255.9/57.3 from 1,260.6/62.1 earlier in the day. 

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR 

 The Singapore dollar hovered around the 1.7300 mark drawing some support from a steadier baht which kept most players cautious on going long U.S. dollars. 

 A steadier won and the Taiwan dollar also helped sentiment in the Singapore dollar. 

 "The volatility in the last few days has made local corporates a bit cautious but broadly speaking everyone in the market is looking at weaker levels for the Singapore dollar," a dealer at a U.S. bank said. 

 He said Singapore dollar's failure to convincingly break 1.7280, where local corporates were spotted buying U.S. dollars, would encourage bears. 

 He said the Singapore dollar was likely to move into a lower range of 1.7330-80 in the coming days as the post-election euphoria in the baht market settled down.

title: Emerging  FX -Plagued by economic, political demons.
text:
SINGAPORE, Jan 3 (Reuters) - Most Asian currencies dipped late Wednesday in otherwise lacklustre trading with economic and political woes lurking in the background. 

 Regional foreign exchange markets took their cue from flagging U.S. markets as further evidence emerged of a more serious than expected slowdown in the U.S. economy. 

 The U.S. National Association of Purchasing Management's index fell to 43.7 in December - its lowest level since April 1991, and well below forecasts of a 47.0 reading. 

 While Asia is vulnerable to a sharper than anticipated downturn in the U.S. economy, analysts have also said a global economic slowdown will shift the stress on regional developments. 

 And with labour unrest in Korea, a nascent banking crisis in Taiwan, and political uncertainty in the Philippines, Indonesia, and Thailand, Asia has not been looking its best lately. 

 "On the one hand, you have the weaker dollar. But on the other hand, the regional picture doesn't look so good either," said a chief dealer at a European bank in Singapore. "It's the final nail in the coffin - a weaker U.S. economy." 

 The region's largest economy, Japan, has been showing signs of distress as well, causing the yen to slip against the dollar and euro . The euro moved higher on growing optimism about Europe's economy relative to Japan and the U.S. 

 KOREAN WON -2 

 The won recovered after weakening sharply to 1,292 in early trading, with local banks selling dollars in a thin market. 

 Korea Development Bank and other state banks were among the sellers during the session, sparking speculation the authorities were behind the selling. 

 Two senior officials at the Finance Ministry expressed displeasure over the won's weakness, with one calling the recent dollar-buying "irrational" and the other threatening intervention. 

 A dealer at a European bank in Hong Kong also said a major U.S. investment bank sold U.S. dollars in options-related trade. He said the bank had been steadily selling U.S. dollars since late Tuesday, and had sold a relatively large amount around 1,290. 

 The won's weak start in the new year has largely been attributed to a waning local stock market, which has been roiled by a pessimistic economic outlook, and importer settlements. 

 Korea's financial markets have also been hurt by the slow progress of corporate reforms and recent labour unrest. 

 TAIWAN DOLLAR 

 The Taiwan dollar kept to the wrong side of 33 per dollar but fears of central bank intervention limited the downside. 

 Dealers said declines in the won and yen and worries about a slowing U.S. economy and global tech-sector demand weighed on sentiment. 

 UBS Warburg suggested players take long U.S. dollar/Taiwan dollar positions, arguing that falling exports and an ailing financial sector would weigh on the island's currency. 

 It said in a research note Taiwan's economy was in trouble from both external and domestic factors and advised clients to go long the dollar at 32.90 with a target of 35 and stops at 31.95. 

 UBS Warburg said last week's interest rate cuts suggested the central bank had decided "to engineer a controlled devaluation of Taiwan dollar as a response to worsening fundamentals". 

 It said a break above 33.194, the November 30 low, was expected to take the Taiwan dollar to the next key support of 34.851, last seen in August 1998. A breach of this level could pull the currency towards a long-term objective of 40. 

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR 

 The Singapore dollar was supported by dollar selling by some local banks related to what dealers said was local corporate investment flows. Low volumes exaggerated the move. 

 They said the Singapore dollar rose to a day high of 1.7305 from late Tuesday's 1.7351 as the inflows prompted other players to trim their long dollar positions. 

 But strong dollar demand near the lows eroded the gains. 

 "There were some investment flows and the market is still quite thin so the dollar/Sing eased," said a dealer at a European bank. 

 The rising euro, at around five-month highs against the U.S. dollar, also helped sentiment. The single currency is believed to be a significant component of the trade-weighted basket Singapore uses to manage its exchange rate. 

 But dealers said weakness of other regional currencies and the yen, also believed to have a sizeable share of the basket, were likely to cap its upside. 

 "The net weakness of the U.S. dollar on a trade weighted basis is likely to help but direction of other regional currencies will have its bearing," the dealer said. 

 INDONESIAN RUPIAH 

 The rupiah found its new year's rally short-lived, with dealers in Jakarta blaming local bank dollar purchases on behalf of corporates for Wednesday's decline. 

 It was still well off recent lows of around 9,700, which were hit in holiday-thinned offshore trade, but back the wrong side of 9,500 with foreign banks also on the bid for dollars. 

 Data released on Wednesday shows deteriorating economic picture with trade surplus shrinking to $1.52 billion in November from $2.03 billion in October as exports fall 7.5 percent and imports rise 2.9 percent. 

 Inflation rose to 9.35 percent in December compared with 9.12 percent the month before. 

 THAI BAHT 

 The baht pulled away from its overnight lows, helped by dollar profit-taking by local and foreign banks. 

 Dealers in Bangkok said the dollar had been creeping into overbought territory in a market already hugely long on dollars, but was now edging away from the overbought mark of 70 on the 14-day relative strength index, to stand at 66.2. 

 But the baht's gains were seen capped around 43.40/50, which is around the 62 percent retracement of the dollar's November 21-December 22 decline. 

 Dealers added that political uncertainty ahead of the January 6 poll still hung over the market. Front-runner Thaksin Sinawatra was indicted last week on corruption charges, and faces a five-year ban from politics if found guilty. 

 But the court proceedings could take months, possibly leaving the country in limbo if Thaksin's party wins the elections. 

 On the offshore baht forward market, the one-month forward was at -1/3 satang per dollar compared with -2.5/1.6 earlier in the day. 

 PHILIPPINE PESO 

 The peso hovered around the 51 per dollar mark posting a day high of 50.65 and a low of 51.17 as players remained wary of intervention after the central bank governor said the currency should go back soon to 49-50 range. 

 Dealers in Manila said most of the activity was interbank as other players and corporates stayed out amid uncertainty surrounding President Joseph Estrada's impeachment trial. 

 Rafael Buenaventura said volatility in the peso was "very temporary" and the exchange rate should settle in the 49-50 range where it was before the spate of bombings over the weekend. 

 He also said the central bank did not intervene in the currency market on Wednesday. 

 Buenaventura earlier said the government wanted to cut key overnight interest rates but deeper cuts were not possible because of a large fiscal deficit. 

 He said the central bank was trying to bring overnight rates to around 11-12 percent. The overnight borrowing rate now stands at 13.5 percent and the lending rate at 15.75 percent. 

 The Philippine budget deficit had overshot the projected level of 62.5 billion pesos and soared to 114.438 billion pesos as of November last year. Recent official estimates place it at around 120 billion pesos. 

 The country's Senate will hold a special session starting next week to discuss the 2001 national budget. The session has been delayed because of Estrada's impeachment trial. 

 After Senate approval, a bicameral panel would be formed to draft a final version for clearance by both houses of Congress.
