title: Emerging  FX  - Steady, but pressure building.
text:
SINGAPORE, Dec 14 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were steady early Thursday, but may come attack later in the day as concerns over U.S. economic growth overshadowed the presidential election drama. 

 While U.S. blue chips gained some ground after the Supreme Court ruled in favour of Republican George W. Bush, the Nasdaq was hit by worries over slowing growth in the technology sector. 

 The world's No. 1 personal computer maker, Compaq Computer Corp. , fell 13 percent after it issued a profit warning late Tuesday. Regional technology-driven bourses in Taiwan and Korea stand to lose the most from the Nasdaq's 3.72 percent fall. 

 However, investors are hoping that a cut in U.S. interest rates early next year might bring some cheer. U.S. retail sales data issued Wednesday showed a 0.4 percent drop in November after October's flat growth, adding to increasing evidence that the U.S. economy is slowing down. 

 The dollar stood firm against the euro and yen , which is suffering from concerns over the Japanese economy. A major Japanese newspaper Asahi Shimbun said in a report on Thursday the Economic Planning Agency would revise July-September growth to below zero from 0.2 percent. 

 Markets in Asia are also facing a raft of domestic woes on top of a depressing external environment. Investors in the Philippines have been largely sidelined during the impeachment trial of President Joseph Estrada. 

 Indonesia, which is coping with separatist movements as well as snail-paced economic reforms, has yet to ratify changes to central bank law, as the bank's governor awaits trial. The major debt restructuring case of Thai Petrochemical Industry and upcoming elections are weighing on Thai markets. 

 North Asia is suffering from its own headaches over economic growth and corporate and financial reform. Korea's largest commercial bank Kookmin Bank said early Thursday it had suspended its merger talks with Housing and Commercial Bank due to protests from labour unions. 

 TAIWAN DOLLAR 

 The Taiwan dollar was likely to come under renewed pressure as offshore players seek to test the local dollar's support despite expected central bank intervention. 

 Dealers in Hong Kong have said the general market sentiment is that the Taiwan dollar is overvalued given the weaker yen and won, as well as the numerous domestic political and economic issues weighing on Taiwan. 

 Some dealers in Singapore said both domestic and foreign players increasingly believed the central bank had no choice but to give up its dogged defence of the Taiwan dollar as it is providing the only support to the currency. 

 The bank was believed to have spent $300 million to $400 million on Wednesday in preventing the local dollar from falling past 33.10. 

 With more profit warnings from U.S. tech companies and falls on the Nasdaq and Philadelphia Semiconductor Index , Taiwan equities are expected to fall, adding more pressure to the local currency. 

 On the non-deliverable forward market, the six-month Taiwan dollar was at 0.76/84 and the one-year was at 0.91/96. 

 THAI BAHT 

 The baht moved in a narrow range, well supported around 43.65-43.70 as baht liquidity offshore tightened. 

 The one-month offshore forward rate edged up to 5.5-10.5 satang per dollar while the onshore rate of the same tenor was steady at -5.0/-0.3 satang. 

 "There's still good demand for dollars out there. But the direction of the baht would perhaps hinge largely on the liquidity," said a dealer at a U.S. bank in Singapore. 

 Meanwhile, the central bank said it hoped Thai banks would lend more to the business sector to stimulate economic growth next year. 

 However, some analysts doubt if that would happen, given the amount of bad assets carried by the sector and threats of banks having to do the second or third round of recapitalisation as the economy slows and asset quality deteriorates. 

 PHILIPPINE PESO 

 The peso was little moved in early offshore trade as uncertainty over the impeachment trial of President Joseph Estrada and ahead of Friday's central bank policy meeting kept players cautious. 

 Dealers expect the peso to move in a weak but narrow range with inflows from overseas workers limiting losses and demand for dollars from local corporates capping the upside. 

 An expected slowing of remittances from overseas workers in the second half of the month was likely to pull the peso down towards 50-50.50 to the dollar in the coming days, a dealer at a European bank in Manila said. 

 The central bank has hinted at a cut of 50-100 basis points in its key overnight borrowing and lending rates. 

 The rates have been cut twice in the past two weeks by a total of 100 basis points, after they were jacked up in October by four percentage points. 

 The overnight borrowing rate now stands at 14 percent and the lending rate at 16.25 percent. 

 Analysts say the impeachment trial and the uncertainty over its decision on the fate of Estrada could drag on well into the next year's first quarter. 

 But whatever the decision, the economy is expected to slow, further worsening its fiscal problems and keeping sentiment on the peso depressed, they said. 

 The International Monetary Fund echoed these concerns on Wednesday, saying the government urgently needed to rein in its budget deficit, which it said was likely to come in this year at double the original target. 

 It said the Philippine economy should grow by 4.0 percent this year but that growth would slow in 2001 because of political worries and a host of external and domestic economic problems. 

 The statement, also expressing worries over a swelling budget deficit, slow pace of structural reforms and foreign investment inflows, was issued at the end of the annual policy review of the Philippine economy. 

 KOREAN WON -2 

 The won gapped lower at the open mainly due to pressure from falls in local equities as well as persistent poor local sentiment over the country's economic future. 

 Renewed concerns over profits at U.S. technology companies forced the Nasdaq lower, also hitting the benchmark Korean stock index as local tech heavyweights lose ground. 

 Dealers said the market was generally more bullish on the dollar following the Supreme Court ruling that will likely result in Republican George W. Bush becoming the U.S. president. 

 They added that the market was very thin, and therefore, more subject to volatility. 

 Korea is also facing other domestic woes outside of the technology sector, whose weakness has brought forecasts of slowing exports and economic growth. 

 The government-led corporate and financial restructuring programme received a blow when Korea's largest commercial bank Kookmin Bank announced it had suspended merger talks with Housing and Commercial Bank due to increasing protests from labour unions. 

 The Bank of Korea is expected to announce measures to ease an ongoing corporate cash crunch later in the day. Dealers said they did not expect the measures to influence the spot market. 

 On the NDF market, offshore players have been buying U.S. dollars in the three-month and six-month tenors, which were both quoted at 1,194/95. 

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR 

 The Sing dollar was hovering the wrong side of 1.74 amid talk the Monetary Authority of Singapore was in the market again overnight to buy the U.S. dollar from 1.7370, pushing it to highs of around 1.7420. 

 Dealers said there was good two-way interest for the currency in early trade, but fears the MAS might be trying to prevent an appreciation of the Sing dollar against its trade-weighted basket might cap the upside. 

 The dollar has hovered near or in overbought territory last week and early this week. It is now trading in the neutral zone on the 14-day relative strength index, with a reading of 46.186. 

 "Given fear of intervention and the dollar's strength against the yen and the euro, the dollar should be well-supported against the Sing at 1.7400," said a dealer at a U.S. bank in Singapore. 

 INDONESIAN RUPIAH 

 The rupiah traded with a steadier tone in light volumes amid wariness of central bank intervention that dealers said pushed the currency up from an intraday low of around 9,550 on Wednesday. 

 A dealer at a European bank in Singapore said offshore players were already staying away from the volatile rupiah but dollar demand from importers and foreign debt repayment needs of local private firms were likely to keep it under pressure. 

 "It is onshore demand that is pushing dollar/rupiah up. It's mostly local banks who will come to buy dollars for their clients and then come to sell dollars for the central bank," he said. 

 He said several players were caught long dollars after Wednesday's intervention and were likely to cover their positions which could give the rupiah a firm tone. 

 "But eventually the dollar demand in the market will pull it down," the dealer added. 

 The rupiah's weakness comes despite a new government rule that state firms can only buy dollars from the central bank. It is estimated that state firms' average monthly dollar purchases are between $500 million to $750 million - around a third of the market's total dollar demand. 

 But analysts said outstanding private foreign debt which stood at the end of the third quarter at $68.2 billion, against Indonesia's total external debt of $143.3 billion, was enough to keep the rupiah depressed. 

 Private foreign debt repayment needs in December alone are estimated in a range of $3-$7 billion. 

 Dealers said the market will closely watch the central bank's board of governors' presentation to parliament on controversial amendments to the bank's laws expected next week. 

 A special parliamentary committee will sit through a month-long recess to deal with the amendments. Parliament resumes sitting in full around mid-January when a decision on the amendments is expected. 

 If passed, the amended laws would give parliament the power to dismiss any of the board's eight members who fail to meet certain performance standards.

title: WRAPUP 2-Asia shares mixed - Japan, HK down on Nasdaq.
text:
SINGAPORE, Dec 7 (Reuters) - Asian share markets were mixed on Thursday with Japan and Hong Kong hit by Wall Street's fall on a gloomy earnings outlook from Apple Computer but Korea and Taiwan making some headway in late trade. 

 European stock markets were also expected to weaken after the sharp reversal of sentiment on Wall Street, traders said. 

 In Tokyo, high tech stocks such as Softbank Corp and Sony Corp foundered on a setback in their Nasdaq-listed counterparts, dragging indices lower despite a firm "old economy" performance. 

 The benchmark Nikkei 225 average finished 1.14 percent lower at 14,720.36 while the broader TOPIX index slipped 0.93 percent at 1,368.17. 

 "It looks like cheaper, non-technology stocks are lending quite a bit of support to the market," said Toshihiro Koizumi, fund manager at Chuo Mitsui Asset Management. 

 "We still think technology shares will recover into the new year, but there will likely be a bit of volatility and defensives and old economy stocks will likely lend support along the way." 

 The U.S. market sank on Wednesday after Apple warned that soft holiday sales would put it in the red for the quarter. 

 The Nasdaq Composite Index fell 3.23 percent at 2,796.50 after scoring its biggest one-day rise ever the previous day when it jumped over 10 percent on speculation the U.S. central bank might soon cut interest rates. 

 In after-hours trading the Apple news continued to bite with shares of computer giant International Business Machines Corp extending losses. 

 EURO HIGHEST SINCE SEPT 22 

 The news also hit regional currency dealings, taking profit warnings from U.S. companies back to the fore of the market's focus for the Asian units. 

 The dollar was firmer against the yen in late afternoon Tokyo trade, but was off its intraday high of 110.60 yen on profit-taking and caution ahead of U.S. jobs data. The market was focusing on U.S. November nonfarm payrolls data to be released on Friday, for signs of scope of slowdown in U.S. economy. 

 The euro rose to $0.8953, the highest level since $0.9040 hit on Sept 22, when the Group of Seven (G7) industrialised countries jointly intervened to prop up the currency. 

 SEOUL, TAIWAN, AUSTRALIA RECOVERS 

Hong Kong stocks fell on Wall Street weakness and investor disappointment over prices paid for two development sites in a govenrment land auction. The Hang Seng Index lost 1.24 percent to 14,911.22 in afternoon trade. 

 Seoul tech shares were hit hard in early trading, dragging the Korea Composite Stock Price Index (KOSPI) down 0.69 percent. But the KOSPI rebounded in late trade to gain 1.14 percent to 523.78, spurred by the central bank's decision to keep call rates on hold in December. 

 The rebound buoyed hopes for a year-end rally as lower interest rates may switch money back into underperforming equities, fund managers said. But the upside was capped by overnight losses in U.S. chip and computer stocks. 

 Taiwan stocks nudged higher on bargain hunting following early losses triggered by Nasdaq's pullback and Standard and Poor's downgrade of Taiwan's economic outlook. The benchmark index ended up 0.81 percent at 5,212.73. 

 Australian shares ended mixed with resources issues taking heart from stronger commodity prices, while earnings concerns emerged elsewhere. The S&P/ASX 200 index ended just 0.9 of a point higher at 3,309.0. 

 Singapore shares were lower in afternoon trade on selling in stocks that could be affected if Morgan Stanley Capital International (MSCI) adopts a free-float system for its widely tracked indices. The Straits Times Index was down 1.16 percent to 1,952.00 by 0712 GMT. 

 Oil prices crept back above $30 per barrel as a blast of Arctic air chilled much of the United States and sent U.S. natural gas and home heating fuel prices soaring. 

 U.S. light crude futures stood at $30.26 a barrel at 0627 GMT, a rise of 41 cents from the New York settlement of $29.85.

title: HKMA Outlines Flexible Approach To HKD Strengthening
text:
HONG KONG -(Dow Jones)- The Hong Kong Monetary Authority Thursday outlined the circumstances under which it operates in the foreign exchange market when the Hong Kong dollar is strengthening. 

 According to the Exchange Fund Advisory Subcommittee on currency board operations, chaired by the HKMA Chief Executive Joseph Yam, the quasi-central bank should remain flexible in dealing with a strengthening Hong Kong dollar. 

 It said the "complex interaction of a number of different circumstances" that can trigger the selling of U.S. dollars to the HKMA - in exchange for Hong Kong dollars - "precludes" applying specific rules for intervening to stop a rise in the local currency. 

 In deciding when to act the HKMA should take account of the size of the gap between the market rate for the U.S. dollar and the HK$7.80 convertibility rate, the difference between Hong Kong dollar and U.S. dollar interest rates, and the level of the aggregate balance. 

 The convertibility rate is the rate at which it guarantees to buy Hong Kong dollars from the market, thereby putting a ceiling on any rise in the U.S. currency. 

 But when the U.S. dollar is under selling pressure and the banks come to the HKMA, the quasi-central bank can then either reject any bank's offer to sell it U.S. dollars, accept it, or "adopt a more active approach in purchasing U.S. dollars", in efforts to restore the liquidity in the aggregate balance. 

 The aggregate balance, a key measure of interbank liquidity, amounts to the balance of funds in clearing accounts maintained by the banks with the HKMA, and is an important feature of the currency board system that pegs the Hong Kong dollar to the U.S. dollar. 

 If the HKMA buys U.S. dollars from the banks, it then credits the aggregate balance with the funds. 

 EFAC stressed the "dangers" of injecting liquidity into the aggregate balance too quickly when it has dipped into a deficit, thereby giving rise to concern the HKMA is interfering with the operation of the currency board system. 


Conversely, EFAC also said acting too slowly to restore funds in the
balance can lead to unnecessarily large fluctuations in the exchange
rate and interest rates.

When the aggregate balance is in deficit due to Hong Kong dollar
selling, the lack of liquidity will force interbank interest rates up to
a point that will then spark buying of the local currency and an
eventual restoration of funds to the system.



Last month, Hong Kong's quasi-central bank rejected calls for
so-called two-way convertibility, that is, a guaranteed exchange rate
for the Hong Kong dollar both when the U.S. dollar rises or falls.



EFAC cited the speculative buying of the Hong Kong dollars, or
significant non-speculative buying, as two of the "circumstances"
against the introduction of two-way convertibility. It also cited a
sharp decline in the aggregate balance arising from a speculative
outflow of funds or large commercial selling orders of Hong Kong
dollars.

title: HKMA says recouped 60 pct of Aug '98  intervention .
text:
HONG KONG, Aug 3 (Reuters) - Hong Kong Monetary Authority Chief Executive Joseph Yam said on Thursday the government has recouped more than 60 percent of the controversial HK$118 billion it poured into Hong Kong equity markets in August 1998. 

 "As of yesterday, we have recouped HK$72.5 billion of the HK$118 billion we invested, and we still have about HK$175 billion in hand at market value - all for the good of the people of Hong Kong," Yam said in his weekly Viewpoint posted on the de facto central bank's website. 

 The government acquired most of its blue-chip equity portfolio during a controversial two-week stock market intervention to defend the Hong Kong dollar against currency speculators in August 1998. 

 It sold HK$33.3 billion worth of shares through the issue of Tracker Fund units in an initial public offering last November, and has a "tap facility" allowing mainly institutional investors to buy additional units on request. 

 The government on Wednesday invited investment banks to make proposals for another disposal, saying it would focus on share placement and exchangeable bonds. 

 About HK$48 billion of the portfolio will be retained as a long-term investment, it said. 

 Yam said on Thursday the intervention was "an unpleasant experience that I simply wish I could forget." 

 "I will probably have to carry it to my grave with mixed feelings. A firm believer in free markets being forced into market intervention can find this sort of thing traumatic," he said. 

 "It felt like an old and trusted friend turning his back on you and failing you miserably when you needed him most. It felt like discovering your comfortable home being infested with termites," he added.

title: UPDATE 1-HK Exchange Fund total assets fall 4.7 pct in 1H.
text:
HONG KONG, July 31 (Reuters) - The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) said on Monday the total assets of the Exchange Fund, which backs the local currency, fell HK$48 billion in the first half of 2000 to HK$966.4 billion at the end of June. 

 Liabilities totalled HK$680.4 billion, down from HK$723 billion at the end of December 1999, the HKMA said in a statement. 

 The accumulated surplus of the Exchange Fund, was HK$285.9 billion at the end of June, down from HK$291.3 billion at end-December, due to lower Hong Kong equity prices. 

 "The decrease in the accumulated surplus was caused by the significant fall in the prices of Hong Kong stocks held by the Exchange Fund during the period," the HKMA said. 

 "There was an evaluation loss of HK$24 billion in the Exchange Fund's equity portfolio, which more than offset the investment gains in bonds and other financial instruments held by the fund." 

 The market value of equity investments in the government's Hong Kong equity portfolio was HK$170.905 billion at end-June versus HK$218.806 billion at end-December, the HKMA said. 

 During the first half, a total of HK$23.593 billion of shares was sold under the tap facility of the Tracker Fund . 

 The government bought HK$118.1 billion worth of Hong Kong stocks in a controversial market intervention in August 1998, and disposed of HK$36.7 billion via Tracker Fund unit trusts last year. 

 TOTAL ASSETS FALL 4.6 PCT 

 The HKMA said the main reason for the decrease in the total assets of the Exchange Fund were: 

 * HK$22.1 billion redemption of bank notes issued at the end of 1999 to cope with Y2K-related demand 

 * HK$16.1 billion fall in placements by other institutions including placements from other statutory bodies and bank borrowings 

 * unwinding of Y2K contingency held by banks with the HKMA 

 * HK$5.4 billion fall in accumulated surplus. 

 "Concerns in developed economies, particularly the U.S., over inflation have led to very high volatility in financial markets, including the Hong Kong equity market, and the performance of the Exchange Fund in the first half of 2000 has been adversely affected by the net fall in the prices of Hong Kong equities during the period," said HKMA Chief Executive Joseph Yam in a statement. 

 The losses in the first half were largely recouped as the Hang Seng Index rallied by over 1,000 points in the first three weeks of July, Yam said, but also noted that the index had fallen by around 780 points since. 

 "Until the outlook for interest rates become clearer the investment environment for the rest of the year will remain uncertain and we can expect to see more ups and downs of this kind," he said. 

 The HK$966.4 billion total assets figure include assets held by the Exchange Fund's subsidiaries such as the Hong Kong Mortgage Corp. 

 Excluding subsidiaries, the Exchange Fund's assets stood at HK$956.1 billion at the end of June, up HK$21.7 billion from end-May, the HKMA said in a separate statement on Monday.

title: China Bonds End Higher On Weaker Stocks; Yuan Slips
text:
SHANGHAI -(Dow Jones)- China's government bond prices closed higher Thursday in active trade, as investors flocked to fixed-income instruments amid continued weakness among local shares, traders said. 

 The dollar resumed its climb after a one-day breather, ending at 8.2792 yuan from Wednesday's CNY8.2786 as importers came back into the market to buy more dollars. 

 The dollar hit an intraday high of CNY8.2882, which traders considered a market aberration. Trading immediately went back to the normal range without central bank intervention, traders said. 

 The Hong Kong dollar slipped to CNY1.0513 from CNY1.0613 in the last session, while the yen rose to CNY7.8711 per 100 yen from Wednesday's CNY7.7950. 

 China's yuan can only be converted on current account or trade transactions. 

Foreign exchange trading is tightly regulated, making speculation virtually impossible. 

 The bond market was rejuvenated as funds flowed back from the equity market, which is currently mired in consolidation. 

 "This makes the market liquidity back to normal level," a trader at Shenyin & Wanguo Securities in Shanghai said. 

 Due to the lack of any other investment tools, the local stock and bond markets usually move in opposite directions. 

 The new 10-year floating-rate bond gained CNY0.20 to CNY101.94 on trade of 475,511 lots, leading to an annual yield of 1.04% compared with 1.26% Wednesday. 

 The 1999 10-year bond rose CNY0.07 to CNY101.46 on trade of 393,690 lots, with its effective yield edging down to 3.44% from Wednesday's 3.45%. 

 Trading volume went up to CNY1.49 billion Thursday, as compared with CNY1.09 billion Wednesday. 

 China's bond market is off-limits to foreign investors.

title: Asian  Currencies : Ctrl Bk Knocks Won Off Post-Crisis High
text:
HONG KONG -(Dow Jones)- Aggressive central bank intervention forced the South Korean won down steeply during Asian trading Monday. 

 Dealing in other regional markets was generally quieter, although both the Philippine peso and the Indonesian rupiah were sold down to test the bottom of their recent ranges. 

 The Bank of Korea's intervention came soon after the start of trading in Seoul, which had seen the won bid up to a fresh post-crisis high, with the dollar sold down to a low of KRW1,104.10, its lowest level since late November 1997. 

 Dealers estimated that the authorities purchased between $500 million and $750 million, driving the dollar sharply higher to KRW1,116.90, its highest level in nearly two weeks. 

 The central bank's action came hard on the heels of the bank of Japan's intervention to weaken the yen, and was widely assumed by market players to be aimed at restoring the won's competitiveness relative to the Japanese currency. 

 "The specific motivation for the intervention today was the March trade numbers," said Graham Courtney, regional economist at Warburg Dillon Read in Tokyo. 

 Data released over the weekend revealed a pronounced narrowing of Korea's trade surplus, which dropped to just $382 million in March compared with $2.35 billion in the same month last year. 

 Courtney blamed the decline largely on a deterioration in Korea's terms of trade, saying that the authorities in Seoul are anxious to enhance export competitiveness while imported inflation remains subdued. 

 "As long as the terms of trade are bad, I think the government will err on the side of an undervalued currency," he said. 

 Other analysts, however, argued that the BOK's action, which was backed up by verbal intervention from the Finance Ministry, was impelled more by domestic considerations ahead of next week's National Assembly elections. 

 "Won appreciation equals a de facto monetary tightening, which is a negative for the equity market: something the government wants to avoid so close to election," said Steven Xu, regional treasury economist at Standard Chartered Bank in Hong Kong. 

 By the end of the Seoul session the dollar had eased slightly to trade at KRW1,112.30, down from its earlier high but up from KRW1,106.00 at Friday's close. 

 In other regional markets the Philippine peso dropped to its lowest level in six months during intraday trading as deteriorating sentiment toward the political outlook spurred dollar buying in the wake of weekend rumors of a possible coup attempt aimed at unseating President Estrada. 

 The dollar's rise against the peso was capped at PHP41.185, however, after the central bank threatened to intervene to support the local unit. 

 By the close the U.S. currency had retreated to PHP41.135, the same level as Friday's close, prompting some dealers to suggest that the central bank may have covertly sold dollars. 

 The rupiah also dropped to its lowest level in six months, as the dollar broke up through resistance at IDR7,650 to hit a high of IDR7,690. 

 Dealers said the U.S. currency's gains were largely driven by corporate demand for dollars in thin market conditions ahead of Tuesday's and Thursday's Indonesian holidays. 

 Late in Asia, the dollar was quoted at IDR7,685, up from IDR7,615 late Friday. 

 Markets in Singapore and Thailand were relatively quiet. Against the Singapore dollar the U.S. currency slipped to S$1.7142 from S$1.7181 late Friday. Against the baht, the dollar eased to THB37.780 from THB37.920. 

 With markets in Taipei closed Monday and Tuesday for a holiday, there was no dealing in the New Taiwan dollar.

title: Asian  Currencies :  Intervention  Blocks Taiwan Dlr Fall
text:
HONG KONG -(Dow Jones)- Massive intervention by the Taiwanese central bank blocked a potential free-fall in the New Taiwan dollar during Asian dealing Monday as market participants scrambled to sell the local currency following opposition candidate Chen Shui-bian's victory in Saturday's presidential election. 

 Trading in other Asian currencies was relatively quiet, with most finishing local hours a touch weaker against the U.S. dollar as markets priced in a rise in U.S. interest rates Tuesday, when the U.S. Federal Open Market Committee meets. 

 Dealers in Taipei described across the board demand to buy U.S. dollars as traders, investors and commercial customers sought to cover their exposure to the Taiwanese currency, afraid of heightened tensions with mainland China and domestic political instability following the weekend's poll. 

 At US$1.364 billion, trading volumes in the onshore spot market amounted to over twice the normal daily volume. Despite the pressure, the Central Bank of China - the Taiwanese central bank - held firm, selling enough U.S. dollars to cap the U.S. currency at its intraday high of NT$30.799, and driving the U.S. dollar down again before the close. 

 Drawing confidence from the central bank's determination to stamp out market volatility and prevent the U.S. dollar breaking up through NT$30.800, most participants believed the storm would soon blow over. 

 "This has all happened before," said the treasurer of one major foreign bank in Taipei. "It's the central bank's policy not to let the market panic, and I don't think we'll see any deviation from that any time soon." 

 At the close of local trading, the U.S. dollar was quoted at NT$30.791, up from NT$30.766 at Friday's close. 

 In the offshore market, rates on short-dated U.S. dollar/New Taiwan dollar non-deliverable forwards briefly spiked to a premium from a discount. 

 Toward the end of Asian trading, however, NDF rates had eased back to a discount, indicating that the market attaches no risk premium to holding New Taiwan dollars, and that players still anticipate local currency appreciation over the longer term. 

 "Watch the equity market," advised Rebecca Patterson, foreign exchange strategist at J.P. Morgan in Singapore, explaining that moves in the New Taiwan dollar correlate closely with foreign portfolio flows into Taiwanese stocks. 

 Although Taiwan's benchmark stock index fell by 2.6% Monday despite support from government funds, foreign institutions were net buyers of local equities, according to the stock exchange. 

 "It's our view that the pressure on Taiwanese equities and the New Taiwan dollar will fade fairly quickly," Patterson said, citing Taiwan's positive economic outlook and the conciliatory stance President-elect Chen has so far adopted toward Beijing. 

 In other regional markets, the South Korean won closed moderately lower following U.S. dollar purchases executed by the state-run Korea Development Bank. At the Seoul close, the dollar was at 1,118.00 won, compared with KRW1,117.30 Friday. 

 In Southeast Asia, the Singapore dollar slipped a touch in line with the local stock market as dealers pointed to market jitters over Taiwan and expectations of higher U.S. interest rates. 

 Late in Asia, the U.S. dollar was at S$1.7189, up from S$1.7125 Friday. 

 Against the Indonesian rupiah the dollar was at 7,453 rupiah, up marginally from IDR7,441 late in Asia Friday. 

 Against the Thai baht, the dollar nudged a fraction higher to THB38.005, from THB37.995 Friday, despite strong fourth quarter gross domestic product data released Monday. 

 On the Philippine Dealing System, the peso ended the session little changed, with the dollar at 40.960 pesos, compared with PHP40.963 at the previous close.

title: Asian  Currencies :Mostly Up;Verbal  Intervention  Checks Won
text:
HONG KONG -(Dow Jones)- Most Asian currencies finished local trading hours Tuesday a touch stronger against the U.S. dollar, but activity was relatively subdued and regional markets generally trendless. 

 Enthusiastic buying of the won by foreign equity investors lifted the Korean currency steeply in early trading. Within an hour of the open, heavy dollar sales had pushed the U.S. currency to an intraday low of 1,115.10 won, only just above its 13-month low of KRW1,114.00 hit last month. 

 The speed of the won's run-up proved uncomfortably fast for the Korean monetary authorities, prompting an official at the Ministry of Finance and Economy to declare that the government will not tolerate further strengthening in the won. 

 Meanwhile the Bank of Korea warned that the won's appreciation could damage the country's economy and said the central bank is prepared to act to stabilize the currency market. 

 The verbal interventions, coupled with government-backed dollar buying by the state-run Korea Development Bank, pushed the won back down from its high, but the currency still ended up on the day. 

 At the close the dollar was quoted at KRW1,118.50, down from KRW1,119.20 Monday. 

 Although Korean officials have said the government is ready to issue further tranches of won-denominated bonds to fund future foreign exchange market interventions, most market participants remain confident that the won will continue to strengthen over time. 

 Rather than attempting to reverse the local currency's upward trend, the authorities are merely trying to limit its appreciation to a manageable pace, they believe. 

 Elsewhere in the region the New Taiwan dollar ended little changed, as the central bank bought U.S. dollars to counter the upward pressure on the local currency from continued foreign fund inflows. 

 Despite a heightening of tensions with mainland China in the run-up to Taiwan's March 18 presidential election, offshore market players argue that the island's favorable economic fundamentals will support the currency over the long term. In the short term the authorities in Taipei will act to smooth any excessive market volatility, they add. 

 At the end of local trading, the U.S. dollar was quoted against the Taiwanese currency at NT$30.762, little changed from NT$30.764 the previous day. 

 In Southeast Asia the Philippine peso ended sharply lower as the local equity market index dropped 3%. The fall reflected the damage inflicted on investor confidence by an ongoing price manipulation scandal on the Manila stock exchange, which Tuesday triggered the mass resignation of the bourse's compliance staff. 

 By the close of currency dealing, the dollar had risen to 40.980 pesos, up from PHP40.900 Monday. Dealers widely expect the U.S. currency to breach the PHP41.00 mark Wednesday. 

 The Singapore dollar recovered slightly from recent lows, after the U.S. currency failed to sustain its advance above S$1.7250. Some dealers suspected the local monetary authority had sold U.S. dollars to bring the local currency back into line with its target index. 

 Toward the end of trading in Asia, the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.7213, down from S$1.7252 the day before. 

 The Thai baht also gained ground, with the U.S. dollar easing back to 38.0250 baht late in Asia, from THB38.1250 the previous day. 

 The rupiah ended Asian dealing a fraction weaker after reports that Indonesian president Abdurrahman Wahid had canceled meetings for a cardiac checkup raised fresh fears about the head of state's fragile health. A presidential spokesman denied the medical was unscheduled. 

 Towards the end of Asian dealing the dollar was trading at 7,455 rupiah, compared with IDR7,447 the day before.

title: Asian  Currencies  Mostly Range-Bound; Govt Talks Won Down
text:
HONG KONG -(Dow Jones)- A barrage of verbal interventions backed by dollar purchases executed by state-run banks took some of the recent shine off the South Korean won Tuesday, forcing the currency lower on the day. 

 Trading activity elsewhere in the region was muted, with most Asian currencies edging slightly higher in tightly range-bound markets. 

 Repeated comments from the South Korean finance ministry triggered a wave of dollar short-covering against the won Tuesday, as the Seoul authorities stressed they don't want to see a sharp rise in the local currency. 

 Officials have been engaged in a firefighting exercise to counter won appreciation since last Friday, when South Korea's newly appointed Minister of Finance and Economy Lee Hun-jai indicated that the government would in future be less inclined to intervene in the foreign exchange market to suppress the currency. 

 Lee's remarks, reported in the Korean press, sparked heavy won buying by local and international market participants which on Monday carried the won to its highest level since November 1997. 

 The rally prompted finance ministry officials to repeat warnings Tuesday morning that the government remains prepared to intervene to damp excessive market volatility. 

 Those threats were lent further weight later Tuesday by reports that Lee had said there was no sound reason for the won's abrupt appreciation. 

 "The rise in the won due to non-financial factors could spur wrong expectations and that is why the government needs to intervene," Lee was quoted as saying by Korea's Yonhap News Agency. 

 Lee's efforts to talk down the won, backed by dollar-buying from the state-run Korea Development Bank, proved effective Tuesday as market players moved to cover their short positions in the U.S. dollar. 

 By the end of local trading the dollar had been driven up to KRW1,127.00, from KRW1,121.00 at Monday's close. 

 Elsewhere in North Asia, the New Taiwan dollar ended the day flat, as U.S. dollar purchases executed by the central bank offset local currency buying by foreign investors. 

 At the Taipei close, the U.S. dollar was at NT$30.837, compared with NT$30.835 the day before. 

 Southeast Asian currencies ended local trading hours mostly a touch higher, despite an early selloff in the rupiah. 

 Sentiment toward the Indonesian currency continued to suffer from the weekend's speculation that cabinet minister General Wiranto may be given his marching orders, potentially precipitating a military coup. 

 The market's mood was further clouded by news that religious unrest had spread to the island of Lombok and reports of demonstrations by dispossessed farmers on the island of Bintan, which neighbors Singapore. 

 In response the dollar was bid up to touch IDR7,300, only to ease back again after encountering firm offers at that level. 

 With dollar-buying interest seen at levels between IDR7,150 and IDR7,200, the U.S. currency is expected to range tightly against the rupiah over the short term. 

 Late in Asia Tuesday, the dollar was quoted at IDR7,262, down slightly from IDR7,278 the previous day. 

 With little news to guide the market, trading in the Singapore dollar and Thai baht was led by activity in the rupiah Tuesday. After being bid up to a high of S$1.6750 against the Singapore currency, the U.S. dollar slipped to end Asian hours at S$1.6714, down from S$1.6742 late Monday. 

 Against the baht, the dollar eased to THB37.365, from THB37.425 the previous day. 

 In Manila, the Philippine peso bucked the regional trend, ending lower in relatively light trading. 

 At the close, the dollar was at PHP40.605, compared with PHP40.564 the day before.

text:
SINGAPORE, Dec 27 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were mostly 

 easier in late Monday trade, with activity dominated by 

 position squaring and commercial flows in thin, end-year 

 markets. 

     Holidays in Sydney and Hong Kong dampened interest further. 


    The yen	    crept higher despite repeated intervention


warnings from Japanese officials and the Bank of Japan's



decision to leave a record 4.5 trillion yen surplus in the



money market in its determination to keep overnight rates near



zero amid any build-up in Y2K pressures.



    Warnings against further yen strength were somewhat



countered by BOJ governor Masaru Hayami's comment that the



yen's rise relected increased overseas confidence in Japan's



recovery.



    KOREAN WON	     -2



    A smattering of dollar sales by exporters and dollar bids



by state-run Korea Development Bank helped confine dollar/won



to a tight trading range, with dealers expecting the mood to



remain quiet until the new year.



    But bullishness over the won persisted despite incessant



verbal and direct intervention in recent weeks, with traders



expecting an appetite for stocks to push the won above 1,110 in



the first quarter of next year.



    The central bank said it expected gross domestic product



growth to come in at 10.02 percent this year, compared with its



earlier forecast of 8.8 percent growth.



    It also cut its 2000 inflation forecast to 3.1 percent from



an earlier 3.8 percent.



    TAIWAN DOLLAR	



    The Taiwan dollar bounced to a 25-month closing high,



bolstered by active foreign inflows to the stock market and



U.S. dollar sales by exporters.



    Taipei shares gained 2.4 percent in a brisk rally fuelled



by longer-term investors, especially foreign funds.



    The cabinet said Taiwan's surplus should hit US$11.5-12



billion in 1999, exceeding the finance ministry's latest $10.5



billion forecast.



    Taiwan's index of leading indicators showed a healthy



"green" light for a second straight month, showing the effects



of a massive September earthquake had all but subsided.



    INDONESIAN RUPIAH	



    Trade in the rupiah was extremely thin with year-end



activity further slowed by concerns over Y2K.



    Dealers in Jakarta said they expected it to hover around



the 7,000 per dollar level until the end of the year.



    The market seemed to have shrugged off news of more clashes



between Christians and Moslems in Ambon at the weekend.



    More than 700 people have died since Moslem-Christian



bloodshed erupted in the Moluccas last January.



    PHILIPPINE PESO	



    The peso was easier, in line with the baht, with trade



largely driven by commercial transactions.



    A Reuters poll showed the country's GDP was expected to



grow an average 2.94 percent in 1999 and 3.97 percent in 2000



compared with government predictions for 3.0 to 3.5 percent



growth in 1999 and 4.0 to 5.0 percent in 2000.



    The economy contracted 0.5 percent in 1998.



    SINGAPORE DOLLAR	



    The Singapore dollar was barely moved but dealers said it



remained well supported by a bullish stock market and further



evidence of a pick-up in domestic growth.



    Singapore's total manufacturing output rose 18.2 percent in



November compared with the same month of 1998. The electronics



sector grew 25.5 percent year-on-year in November.



    THAI BAHT	



    The baht was slightly lower in a paper thin market as



importers bought dollars to pay their bills.



    Dealers said gains in the local stock market barely boosted



the currency because it was driven mostly by retail investors



and not foreign institutions.



    The baht is expected to move in a narrow 37.65-38.00 range

title: Asian  Currencies : Won Forced Down, Late Buying Lifts Baht
text:
HONG KONG -(Dow Jones)- Verbal intervention coupled with government-directed dollar buying forced the South Korean won lower for the second day running on Wednesday. 

 In Southeast Asia, regional currencies drifted sideways for most of the session, before a flurry of late dollar sales by market participants based in Europe pushed the Thai baht and the Indonesian rupiah up sharply to end the day higher. 

 The Korean Ministry of Finance and Economy sought to set its stamp on the day's trading in Seoul by issuing a statement minutes before the local market's open, declaring that "the won's appreciation is never desirable." 

 In recent days, the monetary authorities in Seoul have struggled to check a rapid appreciation of the won, driven by heavy trade and investment flows. 

 After the central bank intervened directly in the market Tuesday, Wednesday's verbal intervention was backed up by dollar-purchases executed by the state-run Korea Development Bank. 

 By the end of local trading in Seoul, the dollar had been driven up to close at KRW1,135.00, well above KRW1,133.30 at the end of Tuesday's session. 

 Despite the dollar's advance against the won Wednesday, the majority of market participants retained their bullish view on the Korean currency. U.S.-based J.P. Morgan, for example, was sticking to its year-end exchange rate forecast of KRW1,100. 

 "That's a very aggressive target," conceded Chia Hsin-Li, Asian foreign exchange strategist at the bank. 

 "But in the long run, the equity inflow story is still there and is still strong," she added, saying that Wednesday's selloff in Korean stocks, which saw Seoul's benchmark index plunge by nearly 4%, was due to profit-taking by local players and not to any change of heart by foreign investors. 

 The won is also being supported by South Korea's strong trade position. Over the first 11 months of the year, the country notched up a trade surplus of $21.6 billion, the Korean customs service announced Wednesday. 

 Elsewhere in North Asia, the new Taiwan dollar closed marginally weaker, with the U.S. dollar edging higher to close at NT$31.640, compared with NT$31.637 at the end of Tuesday's session. 

 In Southeast Asia, regional currencies drifted sideways for most of the day before a late flurry of buying briefly lifted the baht and the rupiah. 

 "We saw some (dollar) selling when Europe opened," explained one Singapore based broker, saying that market players in London had sold the U.S. currency against baht, rupiah and Singapore dollar. 

 "But these are very thin markets and there are no big amounts going through. This was just some (dollar) longs selling to take profits and square off their positions before the end of the year," he said. 

 By the time Asian trading ended, the dollar had lifted a little from its earlier low against the baht of THB38.4300 to trade at THB38.4650. Late Tuesday, the dollar had been quoted at THB38.5550. 

 Dealing was unaffected by the no-confidence debate in the Thai parliament, with most traders assured the government will survive unscathed. 

 News that the International Monetary Fund assistance program to Indonesia suspended in August will be superseded by a new extended program to run until November 2003 had no impact on foreign exchange dealings in Jakarta. 

 Late in the Asian day, the dollar was quoted against the rupiah at IDR7,202, down from IDR7,235 the day before. 

 Against the Singapore dollar, the U.S. currency closed at S$1.6790, flat compared with S$1.6787 the day before. 

 In Manila, the Philippine central bank's decision to raise its overnight lending rate to 12% from 11% in anticipation of increased funding demands over the new year had little effect on peso trading. 

 On the Philippine Dealing System, the dollar closed against the peso at PHP40.690, up from PHP40.665 the day before.

title: Asian  Currencies  Lose Ground As Govt Forces Won Down
text:
HONG KONG -(Dow Jones)- Central bank intervention coupled with threats of further official measures to hold down the won knocked the South Korean currency off Wednesday's two-year high during Asian trading hours Thursday. 

 Asia's other regional currencies also lost ground, but for the most part, activity elsewhere was subdued as markets wind down ahead of the year's end. 

 In a speech delivered Thursday, South Korean Minister of Finance and Economy Kang Bong-kyun said he was "deeply concerned" by the won's recent surge against the U.S. dollar and pledged fresh measures to slow the currency's rise and defend local exporters' competitiveness. 

 Kang's remarks, backed up by heavy U.S. dollar purchases executed by the Bank of Korea, were sufficient to drive the U.S. dollar up to an intraday high of 1,135 won from an opening low of KRW1,126. 

 The dollar failed to hang on to its full gains, however, as South Korean exporters and foreign investors took advantage of the currency's fall to re-enter the market and buy won. 

 Despite the Seoul government's determination to hold the won down and to preserve the international competitiveness of the country's exports, most analysts believe the authorities will have no option but to permit local currency appreciation over the medium term. 

 Allowing the currency to strengthen, and thus, counter growing inflationary pressure, will be less damaging to the domestic economy than raising interest rates, they argue. 

 "The government does not want to raise interest rates. It still wants to monetize domestic debt," said Steven Xu, regional treasury economist at Standard Chartered Bank in Hong Kong. 

 Other analysts agree, insisting the won is still set to climb further, with the dollar weakening to levels around KRW1,100 over the next month or so. 

 At Thursday's close, the dollar was quoted at KRW1,130.10, up from KRRW1,126.00 the previous day. 

 Elsewhere in the region, the New Taiwan dollar also closed lower as central bank buying continued to support the U.S. currency above Wednesday's two-year low at NT$31.550. 

 At the close of trading in Taipei, the U.S. dollar ended at NT$31.616, up from NT$31.605 at Wednesday's finish. 

 In Southeast Asia, regional currencies eased slightly in uneventful trading. 

 The rupiah was little affected by both the crisis at bank Putera, confirmation that Indonesia will seek to reschedule debts owed to commercial lenders, and by the announcement that the budget for the next fiscal year will be based on a projected exchange rate of IDR7,000 to the dollar. 

 In thin dealings due to the start of the Muslim holy month of Ramadan, trade in Indonesia was dominated by demand for dollars from local participants afraid market liquidity will deteriorate even further toward the end of the year. 

 Late in Asia the dollar was quoted against the rupiah at IDR7,235, up a touch from IDR7,220 the day before. 

 Dealing in the Thai baht was also lackluster, with the Thai Bankers' Association advising members to cease trading between Dec. 15 and Jan. 15, because of the risk of market illiquidity and settlement problems over the new year period. 

 Late in Asia Thursday, the dollar was quoted against the baht at THB38.6550, up from THB38.5600 the previous day. 

 Against the Singapore dollar the U.S. currency was at S$1.6810, up from S$1.6775. 

 The Philippine peso bucked the regional trend, rising against the U.S. dollar on expatriates' remittances despite concerns over the size of the government's fiscal deficit. 

 The U.S. currency ended the Manila session at PHP40.710, down from PHP40.740 at Wednesday's close.

title: Asian  Currencies : Won, NT$ Up Despite Govt  Intervention
text:
HONG KONG -(Dow Jones)- North Asian currencies pushed higher Thursday despite government intervention intended to preserve export competitiveness. 

 In Southeast Asia, regional currencies slipped back in quiet trading as market players covered their short positions in the U.S. dollar ahead of the month's end. 

 The release in Seoul of strong economic data for September underlined the power of Korea's economic recovery and helped drive the won higher, as the U.S. dollar dropped to close below the psychologically significant KRW1,200 mark. 

 Elsewhere the Taiwanese central bank, facing heavy trade and investment inflows, allowed the New Taiwan dollar to continue inching upward toward its highest level in two years. 

 Data released Thursday illustrated the magnitude of the upward pressure on the won, as a booming export sector brought South Korea's current account surplus for the first nine months of the year to $19.16 billion. 

 Although that figure represents a decline of 40% compared with the equivalent period last year, the surplus remains strongly won-supportive. 

 At the same time analysts interpreted the fall favorably for Korea, saying the sharp rise in imports seen in 1999 emphasizes the recovery in the domestic economy. 

 That view was supported by data showing that wholesale and retail sales were up by an impressive 14% in September, compared to the previous year. 

 Despite the fundamental upward pressure on the won, dollar buying by the authorities, which have now built up foreign currency reserves of nearly $65 billion, limited the local currency's gains. 

 At the close of trading in Seoul, the U.S. dollar was quoted at KRW1,199.70, compared with KRW1,200.60 at the end of Wednesday's session. 

 The New Taiwan dollar also edged higher Thursday, with the U.S. currency dropping to NT$31.737 in intraday trading, its lowest level since early December 1997. 

 The U.S. dollar's losses were limited by heavy buying from Taiwan's central bank, which over recent months has sought to slow the pace of the local currency's appreciation as the domestic economy picks up. 

 By Thursday's close the U.S. dollar had lifted off its earlier low to end the session at NT31.743, down from NT$31.747 the day before. 

 Despite the authorities' intervention, upward pressure on the local currency is considerable and most observers expect the New Taiwan dollar is likely to continue its measured rise over the medium term. 

 Trade and investment inflows remain strong as the Taiwanese economy has largely shrugged off the impact of September's earthquake and the recent easing of tensions with mainland China has only added to foreign investors' enthusiasm. 

 In South East Asia, the rupiah continued to slip in response to increased sniping about the makeup of Indonesia's new cabinet, which just two days previously had been hailed as an artful political compromise. 

 Toward the end of Asian trading, the U.S. dollar had climbed to 6,945 rupiah, up from IDR6,860 the day before. 

 Both the Singapore dollar and the Thai baht also fell back as dealers covered their short positions in the U.S. dollar. 

 Late in Asian trading, the U.S. currency was quoted at S$1.6691, up from S$1.6682 the previous day. 

 Against the baht, the dollar was at THB38.8150, compared with THB38.7500 on Wednesday. 

 The Philippine peso, too, lost ground, with the dollar remaining well above the PHP40.000 mark, after central bank governor Raphael Buenaventura promised a 25-basis-point cut in the central bank's key overnight borrowing rate. 

 Although Buenaventura said heavy inflows from Filipinos working overseas should support the peso, pushing the dollar back below the PHP40.000 level, some analysts were skeptical. The pattern of seasonal flows is well-known, they said, and already discounted by the foreign exchange market.

title: HK Dlr Mkts: Rates, Forwards Up Late;Demand, Tracker Fund
text:
HONG KONG -(Dow Jones)- Hong Kong interbank rates and forward premiums continued to strengthen late Thursday, with traders citing overseas demand for short-end Hong Kong dollar forwards and local preparations for the sale of the government's Tracker share fund. 

 Forward premiums of all maturities opened higher Thursday and continued to climb throughout the session. The one-month premium is 40-45 points above the spot rate from 35-40 late Wednesday, while the one-year is at 660-670 from 630-650. 

 Traders cited a number of reasons behind the move, including interest from London overnight, where players bought into the one-month in an effort to cover their short positions. 

 However, a dealer from a British bank said the interest rate squeeze may reflect typical end-of-month demand. 

 Another trader with a local bank said banks were preparing for the release of the government's HK$10 billion Hang Seng Index-tracking mutual fund by storing up liquidity, as they were unsure how much demand for the fund will drain cash from the banking system. 

 "They don't want to lend in the one- to three-month period," he said. "And that is affecting interest rates."

title: ASIA MARKETS- Currencies  firm, Wall Street soothes.
text:
SINGAPORE, Oct 25 (Reuters) - Asian stock markets were mixed 


on Monday, with Hong Kong	   , Singapore	    and Taiwan


    partly lifted by rises on Wall Street. 


    Elsewhere, Korean stocks	     ended 2.5 percent lower on
jitters over how much of Daewoo Group's		 debts would
have to be written off while Manila stocks	    fell to an



eight-month low over rising interest rates and prospects of weak



corporate earnings.



    Most regional currencies made some headway, and analysts



said further gains were likely over the longer term.



    "Asian currencies are in a consolidative phase and that's



about to end. We now expect Asian currencies to start



strengthening from here," said Chin Loo Thio, strategist at



Paribas.



HANG SENG CLIMBS, RESPONSE TO TRACKER FUND MUTED



Hong Kong stocks climbed more than two percent at one stage



but that was spurred more by Wall Street's strong performance on



Friday and activity surrounding particular blue-chips than by



any reaction to the government's marketing of its unit trust.



The government launched its much awaited Tracker Fund at



midday to help sell down a massive stock portfolio amassed



during its August market interventions last year.



    Some analysts in Hong Kong said the size and terms of the



blue-chip fund were largely within market expectations.



    The fund totals HK$10 billion and includes shares of all 33



index companies.



    Retail investors are expected to be given a minimum discount



of five percent.



    BAHT PIERCES KEY RESISTANCE BUT DOLLAR BULLS LURK



    The Thai baht	    regained the most ground in off-shore



trade, with domestic financial markets closed for a holiday.



    Analysts in Singapore said it was taking cue from the



generally firmer regional tone as well as from renewed strength



in the rupiah	   .



    Intra-day, dollar/baht slipped as U.S. banks sold dollars



but they came up against some bids from European funds around



the 38.90/95 level.



    But dealers said dollar demand was likely to prevail later



in the week, and the baht could head back towards 39.40.



    "We have seen dollar/Thai under some downward pressure in



the last few days...associated with the better picture in



Indonesia," David Simmonds, regional currency strategist at



Citibank, told Reuters Television.



    RUPIAH STICKS ON CABINET QUESTION-MARK



    The rupiah stuck to levels of around 6,800 per dollar as



investors took a wait-and-see stance towards the appointment of



a new post-election cabinet.



    Traders in Indonesia said they generally see Thursday as the



day President Abdurrahman Wahid will announce his new line-up.



    "For the rupiah, much of the profoundly good political news



of last week is rather fully priced in. Markets are generally



short U.S. dollar, long rupiah with no rush to square those



positions," Simmonds said.



"If we are to see a stronger rupiah over the next few days,



one has got to look for new trigger points like the formation of



a new cabinet. We're looking for a reasonable market-friendly



outcome there," he said.



President Wahid said at the weekend that he might take on



ministers from previous cabinets, but insisted they would have



to be honest and follow the new government's plans to promote



economic development.



Indonesia's central bank governor Syahril Sabirin said on



Monday that he saw the currency strengthening to 6,000 per



dollar at most.



SINGAPORE DOLLAR SEEN FAVOURED LONG-TERM



With the relative lack of liquidity in most regional


currencies at the moment, analysts said the Singapore dollar



 was seeing renewed interest.



"The market is liquid, with dollar/Sing enjoying quite a



bit of inflows. It's much better than the baht at the moment



after the Bank of Thailand enforced swap restrictions," said



Thio of Paribas.



Investors were eyeing the country's steady recovery from



the economic downturn, with inflation data released at the



weekend showing the consumer price index (CPI) back near



pre-crisis levels.



CPI rose 1.2 percent in the year to September, compared with



a 0.9 percent year-on-year rise in August.

title: Asia Economy Watch: HK Share Sale Won't End Controversy
text:
HONG KONG -(Dow Jones)- Whether or not they think the Hong Kong government's 1998 stock market intervention was good policy, analysts give the authorities credit for honoring a pledge to remain a silent shareholder in the city's biggest companies. 

 But the structure of a plan to dispose of shares bought during the intervention ensures that questions will continue to frustrate the government's attempts to end the controversy. 

 The government kicked off Monday a glittery marketing campaign for the first share disposals. Under the plan, the government will bundle shares into a fund designed to mirror the benchmark Hang Seng Index. The Tracker Fund of Hong Kong, or TraHK, will be tradable on the local stock market. 

 Pricing details or how much of the portfolio will be offered initially haven't been announced. 

 The government's stock buying in August, 1998, was one of the most remarkable moments of the recent global financial crisis. 

 Officials decided that buying more than US$15 billion of local equity was the only way to combat what Financial Secretary Donald Tsang Yam-kuen Monday called a "merciless and sustained attack on several fronts." 

 The move revived many of the jitters associated with the handover to Chinese rule last year. It came as such a shock that the U.S.-based Heritage Foundation threatened to strip Hong Kong of its mantle as the world's freest economy, and Nobel laureate economists said it was wrong. 

 The portfolio is now worth about US$26 billion, and, to the government's relief, the rebound has been enough to mute much of the initial criticism. 

 As part of the marketing campaign for the new fund, price discounts and other incentives are being offered to local investors. But even as the government touts the shares as affordable, the strong marketing push is likely to drive up demand and, in turn, the price of the fund. 


            Gala Marketing Push



Monday, Tsang, Hong Kong central banker Joseph Yam Chi-kwong and Ti
Liang Yang, a well-respected former judge who oversees the intervention
money, hosted a gala for investment managers and local luminaries to
announce the Oct. 25 fund sale.



They showed a slick television advertisement, noting in particular
that it should appeal to the elderly, unveiled a telephone hotline and
an Internet site and said marketing leaflets will be distributed
throughout the territory.



Asked by Dow Jones Newswires whether there is a conflict of interest
for government officials publicly endorsing one stock offering, but not
others, Yang replied, "It's a fair question." But he refused to comment
further.



Mark Machin, an executive director of Goldman Sachs (Asia) Ltd. who is
involved in the mutual fund sale, defended the government's high-powered
sales effort, saying finance ministers get "involved in marketing around
the world."



"We need to raise public awareness," said Miriam Li, a central bank
fund manager. She likened the officials' public relations efforts to the
privatization of a state-owned company, such as Australian
telecommunications company Telstra Corp. (TLS).



"You understand that ours is a special situation," she said, backing
away from suggesting the companies were ever nationalized.



             Quarterly Sales Decisions



But questions being raised about the plan go beyond marketing
strategy.



Sales will be an ongoing program and decisions on how much to offer
will be made quarterly. Li said the government will try to avoid
swamping the market by selling too much stock.



With quarterly decisions on how much of the fund to sell, the
government will likely take into account its other privatization
efforts, such as the planned initial public offer next year of its
subway operator.



Kevin Chan, an economist at Nomura International (Hong Kong) Ltd.,
said the mutual fund plan won't add new liquidity that could make the
market less volatile. It merely shifts the role of market heavyweight
away from the government and onto a fund manager.



"The first best option is to sell (the shares) directly into the
market," he said.



A Hong Kong affiliate of Boston's State Street Bank and Trust Co. will
manage the fund. Vincent Duhamel, the affiliate's chief executive,
acknowledged the sway State Street will hold over the market,
particularly when there are changes to the make-up of the Hang Seng
Index that would force the fund to buy or sell stocks that had been
added or dropped.



"This is where the skills of a passive manager come in," he said.



Compared with the government, which has steadfastly avoided
participating in corporate management since buying the shares last year
and vows to continue with the policy, State Street will show its face
more often.



The bank won't shy from voting the shares it controls when proposals
are put to investors "if we feel it is in the interest of the
shareholders," Duhamel said.



At the same time, the system's design will leave the fund manager with
very little discretion to influence the overall trading environment in
Hong Kong on most days.



Since the fund is designed to track the 33-stock Hang Seng Index,
institutional investors will have an arbitrage opportunity to exploit
any difference between the listed fund's net asset value and the prices
of underlying individual shares. This should ensure the value of one
never gets too far from the other.



Hong Kong employs the same arbitrage principle in its currency board
that ensures the Hong Kong dollar trades in lock step with the U.S.
dollar.



Machin at Goldman Sachs said there is little chance that hedge funds,
blamed for the 1998 speculation, will come back and profit from the new
arbitrage opportunities being created.



"The hedge funds will not be the market community trading these back
and forth and keeping the market honest," he said.

title: World Markets: Shares End Mixed In Europe; Hong Kong Stocks Fall 1%
text:
NEW YORK -(Dow Jones)- Shares in Europe closed mixed Monday, with trading volume thin because of holidays in the U.S. and Japan. Stock markets in Brazil and Mexico closed higher, but markets in Argentina and Canada were closed Monday. Asian stock markets ended mostly lower without Tokyo's guidance, with Hong Kong's key index falling about 1%. 

 With Tokyo financial markets closed and the Columbus Day holiday closing the U.S. Treasurys market, European investors had little inspiration despite some early modest gains on Wall Street. The Dow Jones Industrials went on to close down less than two points, but the Nasdaq Composite climbed more than 29 points to a record high. 

 On the European economic front, gross domestic product in the 11-country euro zone grew 0.5% in the second quarter of 1999, compared with the first quarter, the European Union statistical agency Eurostat said. That was an upward revision from the 0.3% growth previously reported. 

 Second-quarter GDP was up 1.6% compared with the second quarter of 1998, primarily because of a strong pickup in second-quarter exports, Eurostat said. 

 In London, the FT-SE 100 index closed up 35.4 points, or 0.6%, at 6234.8, after slipping just one point on Friday. 

 Pharmaceutical shares rose on merger speculation reignited by talk that SmithKline Beecham chief executive Jan Leschly is to retire early. SmithKline rose 38.5 pence, or 5%, to 813 pence, and Glaxo Wellcome rose 70 pence, or 4%, to 1,801 pence, despite SmithKline's denial that Leschly is leaving. Leschly was seen as the main obstacle to a deal between the pharmaceutical companies after talks broke down last year. 

 Frankfurt's Xetra DAX index of 30 blue chips slipped 4.76 points, or 0.1%, at 5414.50, after ending little changed Friday. 

 In Paris, the CAC-40 index of most actively traded French stocks edged up just 0.42 point to 4722.35 after Friday's 0.4% decline. Interest-rate concerns kept a lid on trading. 

 "We just can't seem to get away from these rate-hike fears, whether it's in the U.S. or in Europe," said Richard Morisseau, a trader at Paris brokerage Meeschaert-Rousselle. "It's making investors very wary and they're staying well out of the market." 

 Elsewhere in Europe, Zurich's Swiss Market index rose 13.50 points, or 0.2%; Madrid's IBEX-35 index ended up 37.3 points, or 0.4%; Amsterdam's AEX index rose 4.93 points, or 0.9%, and Stockholm's Swedish General index rose 19.16 points, or 0.4%. But Milan's MIBtel index declined 49 points, or 0.2%. 

 The Dow Jones Stoxx Index of 614 European companies rose 0.78 points to close at 313.15. The Dow Jones Euro Stoxx Index, which tracks 310 companies in countries that joined the single currency, closed up 0.53 at 327.75. 

 In Moscow, the benchmark RTS Index rallied 3.88 points, or 4.2%, to end at 97.19. Trading volume increased to $13.2 million from $10.5 million Friday. 

 Russian traders brushed off news about President Boris Yeltsin's brief weekend hospital stay, connected with a bout of flu. Yeltsin has been plagued with health problems since his re-election in 1996, and news of his hospitalization has become a routine event in Russia. 

 Turning to Latin America, Brazil's Bovespa index rose 25.02 points, or 0.2%, to close at 11466.35 after climbing 1.3% Friday. Trading was at a near standstill ahead of Tuesday's national holiday. 

 "There's not much to say about the market because there aren't any flows. Most people are taking advantage of Tuesday's holiday to have a four-day weekend," said a trader at Unibanco in Sao Paulo. 

 Traders said the Brazilian market is anxiously awaiting Thursday's scheduled announcement by the central bank about a package of measures to help ease consumer lending rates. Optimism about the announcement should give the market support when trading resumes on Wednesday. 

 Mexican stocks finished higher for a fourth session. The IPC index climbed 48.06 points, or 0.9%, to finish at 5331.02 after jumping 1.9% on Friday. 

 Traders said that, despite a slowdown in trading, there was significant interest from foreign investors in Mexican equities. They noted that expectations of strong third-quarter earnings were attracting foreign investors into Mexican issues, many of which are at bargain-basement prices resulting from the market's recent slump. 

 Earlier in Asia, Hong Kong's Hang Seng index fell 119.70 points, or 0.9%, to close at 12992.72, after slipping 0.78 point Friday. 

 The Hong Kong government said it will begin retail sales of its long-awaited Hong Kong Index Fund, which will track the blue-chip Hang Seng index. The mutual-fund listing is the government's first attempt to divest itself of shareholdings amassed in a mammoth market intervention last year that are worth more than 200 billion Hong Kong dollars (US$25.74 billion). 

 Banking and property stocks, which make up the bulk of the government shares, saw more selling as some investors unloaded them in anticipation that the new fund will allow investors to buy the shares at a 5% to 9% discount to current market prices, dealers said. 

 Most other Asian stock markets closed lower, with Thailand's SET Index falling 1.1% and South Korea's Kospi ending down 0.6%. But Taiwan's Weighted Price Index rose 0.7%, boosted by stength in some banking and technology shares.

HONG KONG, Sept 7 (Reuters) - US/HK forwards and Hong Kong interbank rates opened slightly easier on Tuesday, despite the settlement of a decline of HK$155 million in the aggregate balance of the banking system.



The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) forecast the balance before the discount window opened on Tuesday to be HK$748 million.



After markets closed on Monday, the HKMA announced several measures to ensure adequate banking liquidity for the turn of the millennium.



The HKMA said it would enlarge the discount window from November 15 to January 31 2000 by allowing certain instruments such as triple-A rated securities to be used as collateral, and launch term repurchase agreement facilities (repos) from December 1 1999 to January 31 2000.



The move was the first loosening of collateral requirements on discount window borowings since the HKMA ruled last year that no new issues of debt securities other than Exchange Fund bills and notes would be accepted as collateral at its discount window.



Dealers said the effect of the new measures would not be seen until closer to year-end, but they expected less upward pressure on interbank rates as a result of improved liquidity.



A dealer said the measures would not affect the direction of interbank rates, though the spread between interbank rates and Exchange Fund bills and notes could narrow.



He said Exchange Fund bills and notes were in higher demand because some banks had thought they would be needed as collateral to borrow from the discount window ahead of the millennium.



Most regional currencies were easier in early Asian trade on Tuesday as the dollar managed to erase earlier losses against the yen on buying by Japanese investors and importers.



Traders in Tokyo said the dollar was also supported by wariness over possible intervention by the Bank of Japan.

title: Asian  Currencies  Mostly Up; Intervention  Pushes NT$ Higher
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--Taiwan's central bank took advantage of the U.S. currency's overnight sell-off in the major foreign exchange markets, intervening heavily during Asian trading Tuesday to drive the New Taiwan dollar back up. 

 Other Asian regional currencies also benefited from the U.S. dollar's weakness against the yen, with the Singapore dollar and baht both rising during Asian trading. 

 The Korean won, however, was pushed down steeply to hit its lowest level in two months as heavy government-directed dollar buying by state-owned banks caught the market short of the U.S. currency. 

 Once again, however, attention was focused on the New Taiwan dollar market. The Central Bank of China - the Taiwanese central bank - took the opportunity afforded by the U.S. dollar's weakness against the yen to push the local currency back to levels it last saw a week ago, when relations between Taiwan and China turned sour. 

 "The central bank is very serious about limiting the impact of the crisis on the exchange rate," said the head of foreign exchange trading at one major foreign bank in Taipei, estimating that central bankintervention accounted for over a third of Tuesday's onshore market volume of US$530.50 million. 

 The coming days will see the authorities continuing to intervene to keep the exchange rate stable, or even to drive the U.S. currency lower should the dollar lose more ground against the yen, said the trading chief. 

 At the close of onshore dealing Tuesday, the U.S. dollar was quoted at NT$32.257, down from NT$32.332 the previous day.

title: Dollar revives in Asia after overnight mugging.
text:
SINGAPORE, July 20 (Reuters) - The dollar was looking a bit healthier by midday in Asia after an overnight shakeout which led traders to speculate on possible European Central Bank intervention and surprised them by the Bank of Japan's absence. 

 It perked up as short-term players booked profit on the yen's overnight surge to five-week highs, with traders in Asia still wary of the BOJ despite a Japanese holiday. 

 But most analysts dismissed the likelihood of the BOJ intervening in thin Singapore and Hong Kong markets. 

 "To be sure during a Tokyo holiday you could have a big impact because the market's thinner. But are you influencing the people who are going to be moving the market?" said Andrew Dermot-Fung, treasury economist at Standard Chartered. 

 "The answer has to be no... The big risk is if they intervene during a Tokyo holiday, then London comes in and says, 'Thankyou very much,' and we're back to where we were," he said. 

 The dollar stood at 118.57/60 yen at 0455 GMT against its New York close at 118.15/25 yen. The euro was at $1.0294/04 against $1.0307/12. Euro/yen was at 122.21/3.21 against 121.73. 

 Some analysts said the BOJ could also be signalling tolerance of a wider trading range for dollar/yen. 

 "Overall I think they are happy in a range of 115-125 and I think they have to be more flexible. To defend the 120 yen level in a stubborn way is difficult against the market," said Karl Broecker, head of treasury at Landesbank Baden-Wuerttemberg. 

 Broecker told Reuters Television the BOJ was likely to step in and check prices if the dollar fell below 117.50 yen, but added that this was likely to be aimed at stabilising the market. 

 Further gains in the dollar were, however, blocked by offers left by Japanese exporters and investors below 119 yen. 

 Analysts noted that the euro's overnight bounce had also removed pressure on the euro/yen exchange rate - a major source of concern for Japanese officials. 

 "Japanese exporters need to sell euro/yen more than they need to sell dollar/yen. They went into European assets at the end of last year and that really hasn't paid off," said a senior trader at a European bank. 

 The BOJ has intervened repeatedly to block the yen's rise against the dollar and euro in the past month, with much official fretting that a strong yen could smother Japan's infant recovery. 

 The euro won a reprieve overnight amid speculation the ECB had stepped in to stem the seven-month-old unit's embarrassing slide towards parity with the dollar. 

Intervention talk was fuelled by ECB Vice President Christian Noyer's comment on Monday that the euro is now being watched much more closely than before. 

 No official confirmation was available and there was also talk of large hedge fund orders in a market severely short of euros, but analysts said covert central bank action could not be ruled out. 

 "The action, if it was taken, was in a very sensitive way. Simply an open intervention would have failed and this would be a blow in the face of the ECB. But getting the market wrong-footed helped to engineer this recovery (in the euro)," said Broecker. 

 He noted that expectations of a strong German Ifo business climate index for June should also give a boost to the euro. Analysts in a Reuters poll predicted a rise in the headline western Germany index to 91.1 from 90.4 in May. 

 But few were willing to bet on the euro's rebound being more than a mild respite and dealers said its near-term prospects remained shaky. 

 "The economists are saying the ECB could hike rates soon, European growth could pick up soon, but soon is not something we trade on," said one. 

 Thio Chin Loo, strategist at Paribas, agreed that it was too early to call a reversal in the euro's overall downtrend. 

 "I wouldn't be convinced that the euro has turned around until it closes above $1.05," she said.

title: Asian  Currencies :  Intervention  Supports New Taiwan Dollar
text:

Dealers estimate that the Taiwanese authorities have now spent over $1 billion supporting the New Taiwan dollar since the cross-straits crisis over Taiwan's status erupted a week ago.
