title: Obscure Rule Changes Saved HK Dlr - Nobel Prize Winner
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--Ten months after the Hong Kong government's decision to pour $15 billion into its own stock market, the Hong Kong dollar is a picture of stability and stock prices are still rising. So the controversial approach to supporting the beleaguered currency was a success, right? 

 Not quite, says Merton Miller, a Nobel prize winning economist with the University of Chicago, who was a vocal critic of the government's stock market intervention last September. 

 Miller, who is visiting Hong Kong Monday, says Hong Kong officials instead can credit two relatively obscure, technical changes in the way the Hong Kong Monetary Authority manages its currency. Those changes, he says, helped preserve the currency's peg to the U.S. dollar at HK$7.8 for every US$1, a policy in place since 1983 that came under tremendous stress during the financial turmoil of 1997 and 1998. 

 The first, announced shortly after the September 1998 stock market intervention, was a promise to all of Hong Kong's banks that the HKMA would convert Hong Kong dollars into U.S. dollars at a rate of HK$7.75 to US$1 for the next six months. The promise removed concerns among the banks that they would face losses if the currency was devalued, and thus eased the run on the currency. 


        Free-Market Image Tarnished By Intervention


The second was a commitment to allow banks to borrow from the HKMA at
"non-prohibitive" interest rates if they became short of funds. This
policy was in direct contrast to its policy in October 1997, when HKMA
tried to punish banks for lending to hedge funds by threatening to
charge high interest rates if these banks came to the HKMA for
short-term cash.



When the government made that threat in 1997, interest rates soared as
banks scrambled for other sources of cash, and the soaring interest
rates helped to knock the stock market lower. But with the government's
promise to provide funds to the banks at more reasonable rates in 1998,
Miller says, the punishing effect of high interest rates quickly
subsided.



"The Hong Kong Monetary Authority is finally doing the right thing,"
he says.



The government argued that the stock market intervention was necessary
to keep hedge funds from selling shares and the currency at the same
time. But Miller contends, as he did last year, that all intervention
did was tarnish Hong Kong's image as a free market. And because of that,
this university professor gives the Hong Kong government a mixed grade
for its handling of the crisis.



"They flunked the mid-term," he says of the decision by policy makers
to intervene in the stock market. "The problem that I see in Hong Kong
is they're not willing anymore to let the markets tell them what the
score is."

title: Asian  Currencies  Unmoved By BOJ; Philippine Peso Drops
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--The Bank of Japan's intervention to weaken the yen barely caused a stir in Asia's regional foreign exchange markets Monday, as most other Asian currencies tracked sideways or trended only moderately lower. 

 The sole exception was the Philippine peso, which sank back as market players trimmed their long positions in the currency in response to the peso's shrinking yield spread over the U.S. dollar. 

 The yield on the Philippines' benchmark treasury bill dropped Monday to its lowest level in over 12 years, falling to 8.474%, down steeply from 13.459% at the beginning of the year. 

 "Clearly the interest rate differential is going against the peso, with local currency interest rates coming down, and U.S. dollar rates having been tightened," said David Simmonds, Asian currency strategist at Citibank in Singapore. 

 Although the factors driving peso yields lower - a declining inflation rate and buoyant exports - should be positive for the peso in the long run, in the short term the Philippine currency may be set for further weakness as traders cut back long peso carry trades. 

 "The market appears uncomfortable over whether the Philippine central bank's policy to pursue a stable exchange rate can coexist alongside its aggressive easy monetary stance, especially after the U.S. hiked rates by 25 basis points," wrote analysts at Standard Chartered Bank in a research note dated Monday. 

 By the end of local trading Monday, short covering had pushed the U.S. dollar up to finish the day at PHP38.145, up from PHP38.073 at Friday's close.

title: ASIA  FOREX  - Regional firmer, rupiah bucks trend.
text:
0900 GMT - Asian currencies ended a quiet day slightly 

 firmer as money continues to flow into regional financial 

 markets to profit from the preceived economic recovery. 

     But trading ranges were narrow as dealers feared more 

intervention, not only by the BOJ but by some of the regional 

 central banks as well, particularly in South Korea. 

     **** The yen firmed slightly, shrugging off Sakakibara's 

 comments that he was watching movements in dollar/yen and 

 euro/yen very carefully. 

     Traders said the dollar was likely to remain under pressure 

 in the absence of central bank intervention as hopes run high 

 over a Japanese economic recovery. 

     *** The Korean won firmed after some good news from rating 

 agency Fitch IBCA. 

     Fitch upgraded South Korea's long-term foreign currency

 rating to BBB from BBB-, citing the strong reassertion of the 

 country's traditional economic fundamentals. 

     The international credit rating agency said in a statement 

 it had also raised the country's short-term foreign currency

 rating to F2 from F3, in recognition of the continued build-up 

 of external liquidity, which has exceeded earlier expectations. 

 A Fitch official told Reuters Television that any future 

 upgrade would depend on what happens in the corporate and 

 banking sectors. 

 *** IMF Asia Pacific director Hubert Neiss, speaking at a 

 debt conference in Hong Kong, said he believed South Korea's 

 recent direct intervention in the foreign exchange market was 

 aimed at smoothing moves in the won. 

 *** The Thai baht was steady with the authorities attacking 

 rating agency Moody's for their report which said Thai banks 

 remained heavily insolvent. 

 Kiatchai Sopasathienpong, director of the Bank of 

 Thailand's financial institutions supervision department, said 

 Moody's negative views on Thai banks were not shared by other 

 ratings agencies, such as Standard & Poor's and Fitch IBCA. 

     "Moody's holds rather negative views of us and they have an 

 impact...the stock market was disappointed that it did not 

 upgrade Thai banks...," he said. 

     Moody's said all Thai banks remained "heavily insolvent in 

 true economic terms" though with varying outlooks. It said 

 despite the banking sector's deep capital impairment, 

 regulatory forbearance was substantial. 

 *** Thailand's Prime Minister Chuan Leekpai reaffirmed 

 official estimates of 1.0 percent GDP growth for 1999 and 3.0 

 percent for 2000. 

 Chuan said that the economy had shown clearer signs of 

 recovery following the stabilisation of the baht, a period of 

 low inflation and falling interest rates. 

 The prime minister also said inflation for 2000 was 

 estimated at 3.0 percent against a projected 0.5 percent for 

 1999. 

 *** Malaysian news agency Bernama quoted First Deputy 

 Finance Minister Wong See Wah as saying that the finance 

 ministry is looking at revising its official GDP growth 

 forecast of one percent for 1999. 

 Malaysia on Wednesday announced its GDP estimates, which 

 showed a 1.3 percent contraction in the first quarter of 1999 

 year on-year, less than the 1.6 percent recently indicated by 

 Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad. 

 The central bank said the economy had begun to rebound in 

 the past three months, and GDP would strengthen in the second 

 half of the year. 

 *** The rupiah bucked the regional trend giving up some of 

 its recent strong gains but the profit-taking came as no 

 surprise. 

 IMF Asia Pacific director Hubert Neiss said there was still 

 room for the rupiah to strengthen, which would be good for 

 confidence in Asia. 

 *** Indonesian Central Bank governor Syahril Sabirin told 

 reporters he expected month-on-month inflation in June to be 

 zero or negative, versus May inflation of minus 0.2 percent. 

 Separately, Economics minister Ginandjar Kartasasmita said 

 the government had not yet changed the assumed average exchange 

 rate for the rupiah in the state budget despite the currency's 

 rise. 

     *** Hong Kong's April retail sales fell 10 percent in value 

 year-on-year but rose one percent from March. 

     Total retail sales was a provisional HK$14.3 billion in 

 April.

title: HK Dlr Flat Midday; Strong Hibor Slows Weakening Trend

title: Asian  Currencies : Rupiah Shrugs Of BOJ To Hit 8-Mo High
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--Rupiah bulls ignored repeated dollar-supportive interventions by the Bank of Japan to bid up the Indonesian currency to its highest level in eight months during Asian trading hours Monday. 

 Other Asian markets failed to shrug off the Japanese central bank's action, as currencies across the region finished the day lower, dragged down by the BOJ's yen sales. 

 Sentiment toward Indonesian markets remained buoyant, despite a further delay to the already protracted vote count following the country's parliamentary election two weeks ago. 

 Indonesia's electoral commission admitted Monday that it will be unable to produce a final poll result until July 8, but the news did little to deter foreign investors. 

 "There is a lot of money going into the Indonesian stock market, so people are buying rupiah to buy equities," said the rupiah trader at one U.S. bank in Singapore. 

 He estimated that overseas investors had bought as much as $200 million-worth of rupiah by early Monday afternoon, encouraged by a 1% rise in the local stock index and the announcement that Bank Internasional Indonesia is planning a private stock placement to assist its recapitalization. 

 Dealers also cited weekend comments from Stanley Fischer, first deputy managing director at the International Monetary Fund, as a strong reason to buy the rupiah. 

 Addressing a press conference in Jakarta, Fisher said that the rupiah still has further room to appreciate. He even raised the possibility that the rupiah may get so strong that Bank Indonesia might buy dollars to hold the currency down. 

 "These comments are very, very positive for the rupiah," said a trader at a second U.S. bank in Singapore. 

 Fischer's remarks lent weight to last week's comments from Indonesia's senior economics minister, Ginandjar Kartasasmita, and Bank Indonesia's governor, Sjahril Sabirin, both of whom said the dollar would at fair value between IDR6,500 and IDR7,000.

title: HK Dollar Stronger Due To High Short-Term Interbank Rates
text:

 There was early buying by Singapore-based banks, traders said. 

 The Hong Kong dollar is trading at HK$7.7577 at 0330 GMT (11:30 p.m. EDT), after hitting its strongest intraday level of HK$7.7575 very early in the session. 

 While the Hong Kong currency is nearly flat from late Friday's levels, it had been expected to continue a weakening trend of the past few weeks, which has seen it bump against the Hong Kong Monetary Authority's intervention rate. 

 That rate has been weakening by one "pip" (0.0001 point) per day since April 1 and will continue to move until it reaches the official peg rate of HK$7.80 per US$1.00. 

 The treasury chief at a domestic bank said that with the overnight and one-week interbank rates at over 6% early, investors took on short-term Hong Kong dollar positions, avoiding what many had expected to be a day when the local currency weakens to HK$7.7580. 

 The quasi-central bank was seen lending in short-term money markets early Monday, taking those rates below 6%. 

 With the move into the local dollar, some investors squared long-term forward hedging positions. The six-month premium is down to 295 points over the spot rate from 320 points late Friday. The one-year premium is 1000 points, down from 1050. 

 Dealers said they're seeing some hedging in short-term forward markets, likely due to the early spot activity. But premiums haven't risen significantly. 

 Some currency investors are displaying jitters over tight liquidity in the interbank system, with a continued forecast of a negative balance in the aggregate balance of clearing accounts banks maintain with the HKMA. Until there are signs of more liquidity, they're expected to be cautious, the treasury chief said.

 However, the interest rate jitters, compounded by a rise in the 30-year U.S. Treasury yield to over 6% Friday, is leading to a rise in Hong Kong dollar forward premiums, traders said.

title: Asian  Currencies : BOJ Spoils Party For Regional Bulls
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--Massive intervention by the Bank of Japan to push the yen lower spoilt what would otherwise have been a field day for Asian regional currency bulls Monday.

 Monday's trading started on a strongly positive note for regional currencies. The admission over the weekend by Indonesia's governing Golkar party that it had lost last week's parliamentary elections, boosted the rupiah (IDR) to its highest level in six months. 

 The rupiah's climb, which saw the U.S. dollar fall to IDR7,525 in early dealing, boosted the Singapore dollar too. 

 As the U.S. dollar came under pressure against the yen, falling to a low of Y117.91 in early trading, the U.S. currency was also sold down against the Singapore dollar. title: China yuan ends steady on export hopes.
text:
SHANGHAI, June 14 (Reuters) - China's yuan closed steady on Monday, continuing to stay at high levels, on expectations that China's exports would show a recovery in May, dealers said. 

 The yuan finished at an intraday high of 8.2775, unchanged from Friday. 

 After the market closed on Monday, customs said that exports rose 4.2 percent year-on-year in May to $15.53 billion. 

 Dealers said May's year-on-year rise in exports was the first rise this year and further improvement was expected in exports in the coming months. 

 "Traders expects more foreign exchange to flow into the market in the near term," said a dealer at a foreign bank. 

 "This convinced some traders to build yuan positions, helping the yuan to stay at high levels." 

 The yuan now stands near a historical closing high of 8.2773, which was reached on December 8 last year. 

 Dealers said the yuan could undergo a correction in the next few days, but improving exports could help it resume an upturn to test the record closing high in the short term. 

 There were no signs that the central bank intervened in the tightly-controlled market on Monday, dealers said. 

 The yuan touched an intraday low of 8.2778 with most business done at 8.2776, they said. The weighted average price on Friday was 8.2777. 

 The local unit closed higher against the Japanese yen at 6.8988 to 100 yen from Friday's 6.9650. The yuan's rise followed a fall in the Japanese currency on the international market as the Bank of Japan intervened to buy dollars. 

 The yuan finished easier against the Hong Kong dollar at 1.0680 to HK$1 against 1.0670.

title: ASIA MARKETS - Investors sidelined by uncertainty.
text:
SINGAPORE, June 11 (Reuters) - Asian shares and currencies

 were mixed on Friday, although Japan's euphoria over strong GDP 

 data lent some support. 


    The dollar/yen	    volatility was seen limiting activity



in regional currency markets, as investors waited for it to



settle.



    The dollar was still bearish against the yen by late trade,



but dealers said caution over possible Bank of Japan (BOJ)


intervention was limiting dollar sales.


Hong Kong shares	    firmed more than one percent, in
line with Japan's benchmark Nikkei average	    , which



finished 0.56 percent higher at 17,198.55.



    SOUTH KOREAN SHARES AND WON CLOSE LOWER AFTER FLUCTUATIONS



    South Korea's won	    inched slightly lower against the



dollar on Friday as a series of government measures erased



earlier gains.



    Dealers said the central bank stepped in shortly before the



closing and bought about $100 million.



    The intervention came after a comment by an IMF official who



told Reuters that South Korea faced no restraints in intervening


to smooth day-to-day volatility on the local foreign exchange


market.



The central bank has intervened on each of the past two



days, buying more than $100 million on Thursday and $50 million



to $60 million on Wednesday, reflecting their concern that a



strong won would hurt exports, thereby hindering a nascent



recovery.



But Andrew Dermot Fung, regional treasury economist at



Standard Chartered Bank in Singapore, said he thought the


central bank was more worried with the pace of the won's rise,



rather than the currency's strength itself.



"There's this really strong view that as the economy



strengthens, so will the won, and inflows are gong to keep



coming back as both Korea and the rest of the region improves,"



he said.



"So it's not a case of Korea's central bank and the MOFE



(Ministry of Finance and Economy) standing in front of a train



and saying stop. In fact it's more like them saying the pace is



a bit excessive, so we'll slow it down so that the impact on



exports will be less," he said.



South Korean shares closed lower after a MOFE spokeswoman



told Reuters Television that the stock market's further rally



might lead the government to sell its shares of local commercial



banks.



"Selling the banking shares will be determined by the market



condition," spokeswoman Kang Yeoun-sun said. "When the timing is



right, depending on the KOSPI's movement, then the government



will sell the banking shares."



PHILIPPINES CENTRAL BANK TO CUT KEY OVERNIGHT RATES



The Philippine central bank said it would cut its key



overnight rates by 12.5 basis points each on Monday. The cuts



would bring down the overnight borrowing rate to 9.5 percent and



the overnight lending to 11.5 percent.



The move, aimed at spurring banks to lend and boost economic



recovery, would be the 17th cut this year in overnight rates for



a total of 387.5 basis points.



TAIWAN DOLLAR POSTS FOUR-MONTH HIGH



The Taiwan dollar	  posted its fifth consecutive gain,



notching a four-month closing high as the weakening U.S. dollar



overseas showed few signs of a recovery.



Turnover was active at $497.5 million on the main market.



The central bank said on Thursday that the local currency's



recent appreciation reflected international trends such as the



rise in yen and other regionals. It also pledged to respect



market forces.



INDONESIAN RUPIAH STEADY, TONE CAUTIOUS



The Indonesian rupiah	  was steady in thin trade, with



relief over the lack of election-related violence wearing as



attention moved to the slowness of vote-counting.



One foreign bank dealer said the rupiah was still cautious



and would remain trading in a tight range, as uncertainty was



considered too high by speculative players.

title: HK Dollar Slightly Weaker Midday; Near  Intervention  Level
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--The Hong Kong dollar is slightly weaker against the U.S. dollar midday Tuesday, hovering near a key intervention level, but market participants say the local currency will remain stuck in its current tight trading band for the time being. 

 Sustained, but moderate, selling of the Hong Kong dollar for U.S. dollars over the past few sessions is keeping the local unit within a few pips of Tuesday's HK$7.7569 intervention rate. But stability reigns in local money markets, and traders are ruling out any breach of the rate at which the Hong Kong Monetary Authority has pledged to step into the market to support its local currency. 

 Around 0300 GMT (11:00 p.m. Monday EDT), the Hong Kong dollar is quoted at HK$7.7568 to the U.S. dollar, slightly weaker than the HK$7.7564 seen late Monday. 

 A total of HK$566 million will leave Hong Kong's banking system Tuesday, having been sold for U.S. dollars Friday. A further HK$543 million will depart Thursday, as a result of transactions conducted early Tuesday under Hong Kong's T+2 settlement system. 

 But the selling has had little impact on local interbank rates, which automatically rise on any substantial outflow of local currency, because of the operations of Hong Kong's currency-board system. The volatile overnight Hong Kong interbank offered rate is quoted 4.75% midday Tuesday, up from 4.375% late Monday. 

 And the forward market is also decidedly calm Tuesday, with longer-term premiums declining, indicating increased confidence in the local currency and the view that interest rates might not be moving higher. The one-year premium is quoted at 950 points midday Tuesday, down from 975 points late Monday, on what a trader at a local bank said was some houses unwinding long U.S. dollar positions. The six-month premium is quoted at 250 points, down from 275 points. 

 That's putting traders at ease over the outflows, with most expecting the Hong Kong dollar to remain in its current range just below the intervention rate, barring any major additional selling of the currency.

title: HK Dlr Near  Intervention  Rate Midday On Funds Outflow

title: HK Dollar Steady Midday; Fwd Premiums Fall On Pft-Taking

 Worries about Argentina abandoning its currency board caused the spot exchange rate to weaken and forward premiums to rise for most of Monday in Asia, on nervous hedging and speculation that the local dollar would weaken further over the next year.

 Other investors - seeing or hearing what the hedge funds are doing - are nervously hedging Hong Kong dollar exposure in the forward markets.

title: HK's Fincl Secretary Says HK Dlr Peg To U.S. Dlr Must Remain
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--Financial Secretary Donald Tsang said the Hong Kong dollar peg to the U.S. dollar must remain and defended the government's HK$118.1 billion intervention to defend its currency peg. 

 "Our necessary but successful adherence to the link during difficult times has proved the confidence and resilience of the Hong Kong people," Tsang said in a speech in Denmark on Tuesday. 

 Tsang said the Hong Kong Monetary Authority's intervention in the territory's stock and futures markets last August doesn't mean the government isn't committed to free markets. 

 "Our commitment to free markets should not be judged on a single, extraordinary event during an exceptional and destabilizing attack on our currency and stock markets," he said. 

 Tsang said there was clear evidence in an "unprecedented volatile external environment" of speculators "deploying a double-play strategy." 

 "There were strong signs that the markets were beginning to fail, and local confidence was in jeopardy," Tsang said. 

 That was why the government decided to intervene in the stock and futures market to squeeze out speculators attacking the Hong Kong dollar, Tsang said.

title: Hong Kong Banking Cartel Cuts Rates For 8th Time In 14 Months
text:
HONG KONG -(Dow Jones)- The local rate-setting cartel cut deposit rates for the eighth time in 14 months Friday, but bankers and analysts said the move probably won't cause a surge in Hong Kong's stock market next week. 

 The Hong Kong Association of Banks cut deposit rates one-quarter point to 3.5% at its weekly meeting, its second rate cut this month. 

 The rate cut probably will be reflected Monday in the activities of the few market participants who said they hadn't expected a rate policy move until at least the middle of May. But the probability of a rate cut had grown throughout the week, and most dealers and brokers said they had already factored such a move into their buying and selling strategies. 

 The Hong Kong dollar may face some initial pressure and interbank rates will definitely go down. If the stock market resumes its upward course, however, the effect on the Hong Kong dollar will be mitigated by a continued steady inflow of overseas funds into Hong Kong markets, bankers and analysts said. 

 The rate-setting cartel as much as signaled that the cut was its last unilateral cut before it goes back to following moves by the U.S. Federal Reserve. Hong Kong tends to follow the Fed's moves because the Hong Kong dollar is pegged to the U.S. dollar. 

 The territory's major banks immediately followed the cartel's lead Friday, announcing matching percentage cuts in their individual prime-lending rates. Most banks' best lending rates dropped to 8.25% from 8.5%. 

 Liu Jinbao, chairman of the Hong Kong Associatin of Bankers, told reporters that the cut was justified, since the continued wide spread between U.S. and Hong Kong interest rates have been acting as a drag on the domestic economy. 

 "Hong Kong's real interest rates are still very high, which is unfavorable to Hong Kong's economic recovery," Liu said. 

 Analysts said it is hard to see how Friday's rate cut could further boost a stock market that has rallied 22% this month, and is looking a touch overvalued. 

 In fact, Louie Shum, associate director of Emperor Securities Ltd., predicted that the Hang Seng Index will be hit by profit-taking by late Monday. 

 Property stocks probably will be the only major beneficiaries of the rate cut, said Alex Wong, research manager at OSK Asia Securities Ltd. 

 The stock market is trading at a premium now, and the only way it will get a major boost is through some external good news, Wong said. 

 The story is likely to be the same in the money market, traders said, where HKAB has merely played "catch-up" with the wholesale market. 

 "It (HKAB) is just ratifying what the market has done already with interbank rates," said Andrew Fung, treasurer of the Hong Kong branch of the Commonwealth Bank of Australia. Fung noted that interbank rates have eased steadily in recent weeks on expectations of another deposit rate cut. 

 Mike Powell, head of interest rates with HSBC Markets, a unit of HSBC Holdings PLC., said the spot Hong Kong dollar will weaken, but not significantly. 

 Local interbank rates are already below their U.S. counterparts in some cases, he said. "You can hold U.S. dollars and get a slight premium," Powell said, noting that inflows of hot cash in recent weeks have helped offset the effect of arbitraging into U.S. dollars. 

 At International Bank of Asia Hong Kong, Treasury Chief Davy Kwan said the weakening of local currency interest rates could lead money market investors to switch to higher-yielding U.S. dollar positions. 

 The Hong Kong dollar is likely to move closer to the Hong KongMonetary Authority's daily moving intervention rate, he said. That rate - at HK$7.7501 April 1 - is moving one point per day until it hits the official peg rate of HK$7.80 to the dollar. 


"I do not think the Hong Kong dollar will weaken much because of the
much-improved environment in Hong Kong," Kwan said. "There will be some
more hot money, enough to balance a drop."

title: HK Rate Cut Not Seen Spurring -3: Some Caught By Surprise
text:
International Bank of Asia Hong Kong Treasury Chief Davy Kwan said the weakening of local currency interest rates could lead money market investors to switch to higher-yielding U.S. dollar positions. 

 The expected weakening effect on the Hong Kong dollar will be somewhat mitigated, though, by a continued inflow of overseas money headed for the stock market because of lower interest rates, he said. 

 The Hong Kong dollar is likely to move closer to the Hong KongMonetary Authority's daily moving intervention rate, he said. That rate - at HK$7.7501 April 1 - is moving one point per day until it hits the official peg rate of HK$7.80 to the dollar. 

 "I do not think the Hong Kong dollar will weaken much because of the much-improved environment in Hong Kong," Kwan said. "There will be some more hot money, enough to balance a drop." 

 While many had expected a rate cut in the near future, and though talk of one gathered steam throughout the week, Friday's decision may have caught some off-guard. That surprise will be reflected in market activity Monday and beyond, said Kwan of the International Bank of Asia Hong Kong. 

 "On the interbank market, I think it was slightly unexpected. It came a little bit too early. Most expected a cut only in mid-May or end-May," he said. "I expect interbank rates will drop by maybe 10 (basis points) to 15 basis points." 

 And economists said the rate cut isn't a cure-all for Hong Kong's still-fragile economy. 

 "Real interest rates are still high," said Core Pacific - Yamaichi International (HK) Ltd. economist Andy Wong. He noted that real interest rates are still just below 11% - due largely to deflation of a year-on-year -2.6% as of March. 

 Wong said he doesn't see any sign of the economy recovering until late this year.

title: HK dollar remains strong, more inflows seen.
text:
HONG KONG, Dec 31 (Reuters) - The Hong Kong dollar remained
stubbornly strong against the U.S. currency on Wednesday,
shrugging off repeated interventions by the Hong Kong Monetary
Authority (HKMA) to weaken it as money for investment flows in.
    Dealers expect the local unit to hold above its pegged
exchange rate of 7.80 to the dollar for at least a couple of
months.
    "I think some investors are shunning U.S.-denominated assets
because the greenback is weak, but they need to find a way out
for their ample funds," one trader at a local bank said.
    "Investors have fixed their eyes on the Hong Kong equities
market and that's why liquidity keeps streaming into the city,"
the trader said.
    The greenback slipped to a fresh record low against the euro
on Wednesday and fell against the Japanese yen. The Hong Kong
dollar rose along with other Asian currencies.
   


    The HKMA, the territory's de facto central bank, intervened
for the sixth time in two days on Wednesday afternoon in a bid to
rein in the local currency's strength.
    It sold a total of HK$2.337 billion and bought U.S. dollars
in two separate moves on Wednesday in addition to selling
HK$1.227 billion (US$158 million) on Tuesday.
    The latest move will further boost the aggregate balance -- a
key measure of interbank liquidity -- to a new high of HK$31.841
billion on Monday.
    After the latest intervention the Hong Kong dollar exchange
rate  was trading at 7.7630/35 at 0811 GMT, only marginally
weaker than 7.7630/31 at mid-morning. It has appreciated by about

    The local unit strengthened sharply in late September to

yuan, brighter domestic economic prospects, and capital inflows.
    It has slowly retreated to the 7.76-7.77 level after numerous
interventions by the HKMA, which has sold a cumulative HK$31.336
billion since September.
 
    The HKMA has intervened at around 7.7630 recently and dealers
saw that as a support level for the U.S. dollar.
    Some dealers said strong gains in the Hong Kong stock market
and a flurry of high profile initial public offerings have
fuelled an inflow of funds and demand for the local dollar.
    Hong Kong stocks ended modestly higher on the final trading
day of 2003 on Wednesday, capping a solid 35 percent gain for the
year that snapped a three-year losing streak.
    Traders see a risk of further HKMA interventions in the near
term as a number of Chinese firms will seek listings in Hong Kong
next year that will attract more overseas investors.
    Auditing firm PricewaterhouseCoopers predicted funds raised
from Hong Kong IPOs could reach HK$100 billion (US$12.8 billion)
next year.
    "If the stock market continues to rise, the local currency is
to remain comparatively strong," said a dealer at a Japanese
bank.
    Another dealer from a European bank expects the Hong Kong
dollar to remain strong for at least three to six months.
    Hong Kong interbank interest rates fell in the face of
capital inflows and the rises in interbank liquidity. Short-term
rates traded near zero.
    The discount on the one-year Hong Kong dollar forwards

title: HKMA Sells HK$233 Mln In Latest Move To Weaken HK Dlr
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--The Hong Kong Monetary Authority sold HK$520 million in two interventions in the currency market Tuesday in its latest effort to cap the strength of the local unit.  

As with its earlier interventions, the quasi-central bank's action had little immediate effect on the market exchange rate.  

The U.S. dollar was quoted around HK$7.7637 late Tuesday, barely changed from HK$7.7640 Monday.  

"There has been little reaction to the HKMA's move, no one really cares, most people are keeping their trading activity down ahead of the (New Year) holiday," a dealer at a local bank said.  

Since late September, the Hong Kong dollar has been trading at a rate stronger than its official peg to the U.S. dollar of HK$7.80. This unusual situation has been created by a combination of foreign investment into Hong Kong assets, and speculation about an appreciation in the yuan, using the Hong Kong dollar as a proxy.  

Hong Kong's currency board system automatically prevents the local unit from weakening away from the peg rate, but there is no such provision in the system to prevent it from strengthening - only the HKMA's discretion to sell the currency in individual transactions.  

Since September, the HKMA has sold over HK$27 billion, which would buy around US$3.5 billion.  

The HKMA provides information on its market actions to financial data systems, but doesn't comment on them other than to say it acts as needed to counter market volatility.

title: HK dollar seen buoyant as shares rise, yuan eyed.
text:
SINGAPORE, Dec 22 (Reuters) - With Hong Kong's stock market strong and many investors punting on a rise in the Chinese currency, analysts expect the Hong Kong dollar to hold above its pegged minimum against the dollar for at least some months.   

A key issue is the central bank's apparent decision to leave money more freely available in the Hong Kong banking system after its periodic interventions in the foreign exchange market, making it easier for people to borrow and buy shares.   

"Hong Kong has long been a no-growth, deflationary economy," said David Simmonds, strategist at Royal Bank of Scotland in Singapore, referring to slow growth and falling consumer prices in the past 60 months.   

"All of a sudden you have got nirvana: a weak U.S. dollar, low interest rates, a hot Chinese economy, and increased willingness among investors to park cash in Hong Kong.   

"This strikes me as being as decent a combination as you can get. So why give all that up? They should keep the policy a bit flexible for now at least," he said.   

To keep its currency from strengthening too far and hurting exports, Hong Kong's central bank has, since September, bought billions of U.S. dollars. It exchanges them for Hong Kong dollars, which then sit in bank accounts, available for lending. It sold HK$16 billion ($2.1 billion) between December 12 and 19 alone.   

UNSTERILE   

Central banks normally "sterilise" that liquidity effect by selling short-term securities, taking cash back out of the system to match the inflow.   

But Hong Kong's central bank, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, has evidently not sterilised all of its currency intervention lately. Falling interest rates show that money is more freely available, propping up the share market, whose rallies have attracted people to buy more Hong Kong dollars.   

Although that has tended to push the currency a little higher, despite the intervention, analysts such as Simmonds think the scheme suits Hong Kong's economy, which could do with low interest rates and a bit of market optimism. So they reckon the currency will remain buoyant for a while yet.   

The Hong Kong dollar since late September has strengthened above the minimum rate of 7.80 per U.S. dollar that the central bank has defended since 1997. It was around 7.7650 per dollar on Monday, down from an October high of 7.6920.   

On Monday, Hong Kong's official interbank rate was 0.14955 percent, against 1.14625 in the United States.   

IPO FLOWS    


A factor pushing the currency higher has been speculation that China
would raise the value of the yuan            , in the face of trade
pressure from the United States.
   

One year yuan non-deliverable forwards , which reflect expectations of the future direction of the currency, traded on Monday at a rate suggesting a yuan at 7.83 per U.S. dollar in a year's time, from the current peg at 8.28 per dollar.   

Hong Kong dollar forwards were trading at an implied rate of 7.2 per U.S. dollar in a year's time.   

Another has been rising optimism about the Hong Kong economy, which has combined with the easy availability of money in drawing investors into the share market.   

The benchmark Hang Seng Index has climbed 50 percent from its low for the year in April, to hit highs last seen in July 2001.   

A flood of investments into large initial public offerings of shares - such as the $3.46 billion offering of China Life shares, the largest IPO this year - has further boosted Hong Kong dollar demand.   

Analysts said the central bank of the territory could have pushed the currency back to the peg if it had wanted to, because it could have fully sterilised its interventions.   

"Ideally, the way it should work is that because U.S. rates are higher, funds should be flowing out of Hong Kong and taking advantage of higher U.S. rates. But that is not happening," said Claudio Piron, strategist at Standard Chartered Bank. (US$1=HK$7.76).

title: HK Dlr Mkts Late: Hibors Down On Continued High Liquidity
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--Hong Kong interbank offered rates declined again Friday, as more money from the Hong Kong Monetary Authority's currency interventions made its way into the market, and the closing of recent initial public offerings depressed demand for funds.  

The overnight Hibor dropped to 0.25%, from 0.65% Thursday, and the one-month Hibor was down to 0.21% from 0.23% previously. Traders said further declines were possible, as the overnight rate had gone below 0.01% before the recent rush of IPOs pushed it up, and there is significant excess liquidity in the system.  

The aggregate balance, a measure of interbank liquidity, opened at HK$28.42 billion Friday.  

Before the HKMA began its sales of Hong Kong dollars to stem the strengthening of the currency, the aggregate balance was typically less than HK$1 billion. It began December at HK$11.6 billion.  

The Hong Kong dollar was little changed in the spot and forward markets.  

The discount on the benchmark one-year forward contract widened slightly to 540 to 520 below the spot rate, compared to a discount of 530 to 510 previously.  

The U.S. dollar was quoted at HK$7.7655, compared to HK$7.7645 previously. The pair have been trading recently in a range of 7.7600 to 7.7650, and the Hong Kong dollar isn't expected to weaken significantly given continued buying interest in Hong Kong assets.  

"Equity-driven inflows are likely to keep the Hong Kong dollar well-supported at the 7.77 level," one trader said.  

Yields on Hong Kong Exchange Fund notes fell, tracking changes in U.S. Treasurys driven by year-end buying to settle positions.  

The two-year EF note was quoted at 1.20%, compared to 1.21% previously, while the 10-year note fell to 4.32% from 4.38%.

title: HKMA Defends Policy Of Allowing Stronger HK Dollar
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--Though Hong Kong has kept its currency strictly pegged to the U.S. dollar for 20 years, even the biggest champion of that regime still appreciates the virtues of flexibility.  

A previously little-known quirk of the currency board system - the fact it only prevents a weakening, not a strengthening of the local currency - has allowed the market exchange rate of the Hong Kong dollar to become stronger than its peg of HK$7.80 to the U.S. dollar since late September. The pair was trading at about 7.7650 late Thursday, and has gone as low as 7.70.  

The newfound volatility in the Hong Kong dollar rate has prompted calls from some observers for the Hong Kong Monetary Authority to institute a stricter currency board system, one that would work on both the strong and weak sides of the peg.  

But the HKMA shows no sign of changing its mind, as it seems to appreciate the advantages of having that flexibility on the strong side. Rather than changing the system, it has intervened occasionally in the market, selling Hong Kong dollars and buying U.S. dollars, to keep the rate from drifting too far from the peg.  

In a report issued Thursday, the HKMA pointed out that the strengthening of the exchange was due in part to improved sentiment toward Hong Kong, and had had no ill effects on the local economy.  

"The sudden shift in market sentiment reflects improved fundamentals in Hong Kong, as well as the recent weakness of the US dollar and market speculation about an appreciation of the renminbi (or yuan)," the HKMA said in a report issued Thursday.  

"This had minimal macroeconomic implications," it said in its new Monetary and Financial Stability Report.  

What's more, the HKMA suggested, having room for the currency to appreciate has prevented local interest rates from falling even lower than they already have. Though the low interest rates help stimulate lending, they can hurt banks' profitability if they are sustained.  

"The adjustment of the exchange rate has probably also been affected by the limited room for falls in interest rates, which were already at a low level," it said. "Should the spot rate be kept close to 7.8, interest rates would have to decline much more."  

Ultimately, the HKMA concluded, the flexibility now built into the Hong Kong dollar currency board hasn't harmed investors' confidence in the system.  

"It does not appear that the absence of a convertibility undertaking on the strong side of the link has had any effect on the credibility and effectiveness of the currency board system," it said.

title: HK Dlr Mkts Late: Forwards Discount Widens On Liquidity
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--The discount on Hong Kong dollar forwards widened Thursday, as brief worries over a new SARS case in Taiwan gave way to a flood of interbank liquidity brought on by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority's recent interventions.  

The excess funds in the interbank market pushed down local interest rates, widening the gap between Hong Kong and U.S. interest rates, thus leading to a deeper discount on forwards. The benchmark one-year forward contract was quoted at 530 to 510 below the spot rate, compared with 500 to 480 Wednesday.  

Health officials in Taiwan had said Wednesday that a medical researcher had contracted SARS, or severe acute respiratory syndrome, apparently in the process of studying the disease. The news spooked investors in Taiwan and other Asian markets, and caused Hong Kong forward discounts to narrow Wednesday.  

But by Thursday they had widened again, as funds from the HKMA's recent sales of Hong Kong dollars entered the market. The aggregate balance, a measure of interbank liquidity, surged to HK$24.17 billion Wednesday, from HK$15.3 billion, and is forecast to expand further to HK$27.81 billion Thursday.  

"The focus of the market therefore shifts back to excess liquidity," one trader said.  

The HKMA sold a comparatively small HK$559 million into the market overnight Wednesday, which followed a massive HK$7.94 billion intervention Tuesday.  

Traders say the HKMA's sales, which would tend to weaken the local currency, are aimed at relieving the upward pressure from the recent big purchases of Hong Kong dollars by foreign investors interested in Hong Kong stocks.  

The U.S. dollar was, however, little moved at HK$7.7645, compared with HK$7.7638 Wednesday.  

Hong Kong interbank offered rates declined with the continued influx of liquidity from the HKMA. The one-year Hibor was quoted at 0.75%, from 0.79% Wednesday.  

Yields on Hong Kong Exchange Fund notes rose slightly, in line with similar changes in U.S. Treasurys. The two-year note was quoted at 1.21%, up from 1.19% previously. The 10-year note was unchanged at 4.38%.  

The market is still digesting the unexpected fall in U.S. consumer prices in November, which showed there is little pressure on the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates, as inflation hasn't yet taken hold.

title: FX  Asia:Investors Snap Up Blns of HK Dlrs Sold By HKMA
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--Despite the Hong Kong Monetary Authority increasing the size and frequency of its currency market interventions, the Hong Kong dollar has shown few signs of giving up its recent strength as the market easily absorbs a flood of the local currency from the HKMA.  

It seems the HKMA's strategy of upping the dosage of its interventions can't weaken the currency, but merely prevent it from strengthening further in a market dominated by persistent fund inflows attracted by investment opportunities in Hong Kong.  

"Foreign investors must have spotted some opportunities to invest or speculate in Hong Kong's financial markets or other types of assets," Hang Seng Bank senior economist Henry Tsoi said.  

"They could be positioning such trades currently, and looking to cash out over ... a few months to a year," Tsoi said, adding that a quick reversal of these inflows is unlikely as a result.  

Since the local unit strayed from its U.S. dollar peg rate of HK$7.80 in late September amid talk of yuan revaluation, the HKMA has been intervening from time to time to contain the currency's strength.  

From a usual intervention size of about US$100 million-US$200 million per day, the quasi-central bank has upped the size of its U.S. dollar purchases to about US$500 million to US$1 billion a day in recent sessions, usually in multiple transactions.  

"Through these larger and more frequent interventions, the HKMA probably wanted to show the market it is very committed to maintaining currency stability," said a foreign exchange trader with a local bank.  

As committed as the HKMA may be to the city's 20-year-old linked exchange system, foreign investors have their own objectives and trading plans.  


 
   Investors Buying HK Dlrs To Position For Investments 
   

Indeed, the Hong Kong dollar hardly budged after all these interventions in recent weeks, sticking most of the time to a narrow range between HK$7.7600 and HK$7.7650.  

"The interventions did little to boost the U.S. dollar, this probably implied there are strong fund inflows offsetting those transactions," the trader said.  

"These fund inflows could be part of efforts by foreign investors to build up their Hong Kong dollar positions for future investment in local equities and initial public offerings next year," he added.  

HKMA Chief Executive Joseph Yam attributed the recent influx of foreign funds partly to a flurry of IPO activity.  

Among recent IPOs, Great Wall Automobile Holding Co. (2333.HK) and China Life Insurance Co. (2628.HK) were two large initial share sales that attracted heavy oversubscription, tying up billions of Hong Kong dollars.  

Traders said the HKMA may have noticed significant IPO-driven fund inflows and has been acting more aggressively in the foreign exchange market to neutralize them.  

It may also be part of the HKMA's strategy to depress Hong Kong dollar interest rates through larger injections, thus reducing the local unit's attractiveness to foreigners.  

One-month Hong Kong interbank offered rates were quoted near zero, at 0.28% Wednesday afternoon.  

Still, traders doubt if lower interest rates will make much difference, as potential gains from Hong Kong dollar assets should easily make up for reduced interest return in the current bull market for shares and amid rising property prices.  


 
   Traders Raise Possibility Of Negative Rates 
   

The benchmark Hang Seng index has gained more than 40% since its near-five-year low in the spring as the city emerges from a short recession in the third quarter.  

Continued economic improvement led by tourism gains, export expansion and growth in domestic consumption is likely to preserve the attraction of Hong Kong shares for foreign investors in the coming months, analysts said.  

To a lesser extent, inflows may be attracted by the city's zero-tariff access to the China market granted under Hong Kong's trade pact with Beijing.  

"The economic sentiment has improved substantially after a series of favorable mainland polices toward Hong Kong, including the relaxed restrictions on individual travel and the Closer Economic Partnership Arrangement," Daniel Chan of DBS Bank (HK) said. Foreign investors may expect these moves to increase their opportunities to make profits in the territory.  

Still, the HKMA's recent actions imply it won't tolerate an appreciation in the local unit beyond HK$7.76 against the U.S. dollar, a resistance level for the local unit most traders expect will stay intact.  

"The HKMA seems to be very dedicated to this level," the trader said.  

"It can even introduce negative interest rates to penalize banks keeping too much of a Hong Kong dollar surplus, forcing them to convert their Hong Kong dollars into U.S. dollars."  

Although Yam said he wouldn't rule out introducing such deposit charges on banks' surplus balance in their clearing accounts with the HKMA, he doesn't yet envisage the need to do so, and he still hopes that the market will adjust itself.

title: HK Dlr Mkts Late: Forward Discounts Narrow On SARS Fears
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--Hong Kong dollar forwards discounts narrowed slightly Wednesday on concerns about the return of SARS to the region.  

Health officials in Taiwan said Wednesday a 44-year-old male medical researcher tested positive for severe acute respiratory syndrome and has been isolated at a local hospital.  

Although officials downplayed the likelihood of another outbreak of the deadly disease, stressing that this appeared to be an isolated case, local traders remained concerned SARS may return to haunt the region, including Hong Kong.  

The one-year contract was quoted at 500-480 below the spot rate, compared with 510 to 500 Tuesday.  

Further aggressive intervention by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority recently has also put upward pressure on forwards.  

The quasi-central bank sold HK$7.94 billion Tuesday, the largest amount it has sold on a single day since the currency strayed from the U.S. dollar peg rate in late September.  

SARS fears and HKMA interventions combined to push the local unit lower, although only by a small margin.  

The U.S. dollar was quoted at HK$7.7638, compared with HK$7.7627 Tuesday.  

Traders, however, expect foreign inflows to persist in the near term, as investors buy shares on the Hong Kong stock market and participate in a series of initial public offerings.  

"Such potential inflows may keep the U.S. dollar firmly capped around HK$7.77 over coming months," the trader said.  

Hong Kong interbank offered rates moved higher despite the HKMA's injections, as traders preferred to have surplus funds on hand amid the uncertainty over SARS.  

"Banks are borrowing most actively in short-dated funds up to one month," the trader said.  

The one-month Hibor was quoted at 0.28%, compared with 0.25% Tuesday.  

Long-term interbank funds were relatively steady, with the 12-month Hibor quoted at 0.79%, compared with 0.80% previously.  

Hong Kong Exchange Fund note yields were little moved.  

The 10-year EF note was quoted at 4.38%, compared with 4.39% Tuesday.

title: HKMA Sells HK Dlrs Overnight Tues; Day's Total HK$7.94B
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--The Hong Kong Monetary Authority continued to sell Hong Kong dollars in the currency market during London and New York trading hours Tuesday, in its heaviest day of market activity yet as it worked to keep the Hong Kong dollar from strengthening.  

The HKMA sold HK$4.04 billion during Hong Kong trading hours Tuesday. But according to figures provided to financial data systems, it went on to sell HK$3.9 billion more after hours, bringing the total to HK$7.94 billion in the day - buying more than US$1 billion.  

The spot exchange rate was little moved early Wednesday, with the U.S. dollar quoted at HK$7.7628. That implies that the HKMA's actions are simply neutralizing massive purchases of Hong Kong dollars by others, for instance by subscribers to a recent US$1.9 billion share placement by BOC Hong Kong (Holdings) Ltd. (2388.HK).  

Hong Kong's currency board system automatically prevents the local unit from weakening away from the peg rate, but there is no such provision in the system to prevent it from strengthening - only the HKMA's discretion to sell the currency in individual transactions.  

Since late September, the Hong Kong dollar has been trading at a rate stronger than its official peg to the U.S. dollar of HK$7.80. That unusual situation has been driven by a combination of strong flows of foreign investment into Hong Kong assets, and speculation on the possible appreciation of the Chinese yuan, using the Hong Kong dollar as a proxy.  

The HKMA has been intervening occasionally in the markets since then to prevent further strengthening of the Hong Kong dollar, usually to keep the U.S. dollar from falling below HK$7.76. It has so far sold a total of HK$26.48 billion, buying about US$3.4 billion.  

-By Andrew Batson, Dow Jones Newswires; 852-2802-7002; andrew.batson@dowjones.com

title: HKMA Sells HK$1.32 Bln In Latest Move To Weaken HK Dlr
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--The Hong Kong Monetary Authority sold another HK$1.32 billion in the currency markets Tuesday, buying about US$170 million, continuing its unusually active recent streak of market interventions.  

The HKMA, which acts as the city's central bank and implementer of its currency board system, sold HK$4.57 billion Monday and HK$2.96 billion Friday in similar interventions intended to weaken the local unit against the U.S. dollar.  

But the currency's spot exchange rate appeared largely unaffected by the latest sale. The U.S. dollar was quoted around HK$7.7630 Tuesday afternoon, roughly the same level it has been at during the previous interventions Friday and Monday.  

Hong Kong's currency board system automatically prevents the local unit from weakening away from the peg rate, but there is no such provision in the system to prevent it from strengthening - only the HKMA's discretion to sell the currency in individual transactions.  

Since late September, the Hong Kong dollar has been trading at a rate stronger than its official peg to the U.S. dollar of HK$7.80, an unusual situation driven by a combination of flows of foreign investment into Hong Kong assets, and speculation on the possible appreciation of the yuan, using the Hong Kong dollar as a proxy.  

-By Andrew Batson, Dow Jones Newswires; 852-2802-7002; andrew.batson@dowjones.com

title: HKMA Sells HK$3.07B More Overnight; Monday Total HK$4.57B
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--The Hong Kong Monetary Authority sold an additional HK$3.07 billion into the currency markets during London and New York trading hours Monday, capping its largest single day of interventions since the Hong Kong dollar first strengthened above its peg in September.  

The sales of Hong Kong dollars, and purchases of U.S. dollars, are intended to prevent the local currency from strengthening further against the U.S. dollar. Added to the HK$1.5 billion the HKMA sold during Hong Kong trading hours Monday, the day's total comes to HK$4.57 billion, buying about US$590 million.  

Yet the additional sales Monday, like an earlier round of large sales Friday, had little obvious effect on the market exchange rate. The U.S. dollar was quoted around HK$7.7630 early Tuesday, the same level it was trading at for most of Monday.  

Since late September, the Hong Kong dollar has been trading at a rate stronger than its official peg to the U.S. dollar of HK$7.80, an unusual situation driven by a combination of flows of foreign investment into Hong Kong assets, and speculation on the possible appreciation of the yuan, using the Hong Kong dollar as a proxy.  

Hong Kong's currency board system automatically prevents the local unit from weakening away from the peg rate, but there is no such provision in the system to prevent it from strengthening - only the HKMA's discretion to sell the currency in individual transactions.  

The latest interventions bring the HKMA's Hong Kong dollar sales since the September strengthening of the currency to a grand total of HK$18.54 billion, which would buy just under US$2.4 billion.  

The HKMA provides information on its market actions to financial data systems, but doesn't comment on them other than to say it acts as needed to counter market volatility.

title: WRAP: HKMA Sells HK$4.04 Bln In  Interventions  Tuesday
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--The Hong Kong Monetary Authority Tuesday sold a total of HK$4.04 billion, buying around US$520 million, in several transactions aimed at easing any possible gain in the Hong Kong dollar against the U.S. dollar.  

The sales continue what has been an unusually active few days for the HKMA, which acts as the city's central bank and implementer of its currency board system. It sold HK$4.57 billion Monday and HK$2.96 billion last Friday.  

"The HKMA might have detected some significant fund inflows and has therefore been selling the Hong Kong dollar in sizable amounts to keep it from rising too much above the peg rate of HK$7.80," a trader said.  

In response to Tuesday's interventions, the Hong Kong dollar weakened very slightly. Late in the Hong Kong trading day, the U.S. dollar was quoted at HK$7.7635, compared with HK$7.7627 earlier.  

Market participants suspect the recent HKMA sales were largely absorbed by foreign investors buying Hong Kong dollars, for instance to participate in local initial public offerings.  

Hong Kong's currency board system automatically prevents the local unit from weakening away from the peg rate, but there is no such provision in the system to prevent it from strengthening - only the HKMA's discretion to sell the currency in individual transactions.  

Since late September, the Hong Kong dollar has been trading at a rate stronger than its official peg to the U.S. dollar of HK$7.80. That unusual situation has been driven by a combination of strong flows of foreign investment into Hong Kong assets, and speculation on the possible appreciation of the Chinese yuan, using the Hong Kong dollar as a proxy.  

So as it has this week, the HKMA has been acting occasionally to do what it calls preventing market volatility. It has sold a total of HK$22.58 billion since September, including Tuesday's sales, buying about US$2.9 billion.  

Yet most market participants don't anticipate a return to the peg rate until the fund inflows to Hong Kong, which have been supporting the stronger currency, reverse.  

In the meantime, the HKMA's sales of currency have been adding huge amounts of liquidity to an already flush interbank market, pushing down local interest rates. The one-year Hong Kong interbank offered rate, or Hibor, was quoted at 0.80% late Tuesday, down from 0.98% in the middle of last week.  

-By Andrew Batson and Raymond Tsoi, Dow Jones Newswires; 852-2802-7002; andrew.batson@dowjones.com

title: HKMA Sells HK$2.14 Bln More In Latest  Intervention
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--The Hong Kong Monetary Authority sold an additional HK$2.14 billion in the currency markets Tuesday afternoon, buying about US$275 million, in its latest intervention to weaken the Hong Kong dollar against its U.S. counterpart.  

Combined with earlier sales Monday, the HKMA's latest move brings its total sales for the day to HK$3.26 billion, which would buy about US$420 million.  

But the currency's spot exchange rate remained largely unaffected by the HKMA's increasing activity. The U.S. dollar was quoted around HK$7.7627 Tuesday afternoon, roughly the level it was at earlier Tuesday and Monday.  

Hong Kong's currency board system automatically prevents the local unit from weakening away from the peg rate, but there is no such provision in the system to prevent it from strengthening - only the HKMA's discretion to sell the currency in individual transactions.

title: WRAP: HKMA Sells HK$1.5 Bln In 2nd Day Of  Interventions
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--The Hong Kong Monetary Authority sold Hong Kong dollars and bought U.S. dollars again Monday, in a renewed bout of market interventions intended to keep the local currency from strengthening against its U.S. counterpart.  

The HKMA, which acts as the city's central bank and implementer of its currency board system, sold a total of HK$1.5 billion Monday afternoon in a series of transactions, buying about US$190 million. The latest round of interventions follows several sales Friday that totaled HK$2.96 billion, which bought around US$380 million.  

Yet Monday's sales, like the previous ones, appeared to have little immediate effect on the Hong Kong dollar's exchange rate. The U.S. dollar was quoted around HK$7.7630 for most of Friday and Monday.  

The HKMA has previously acted to prevent the U.S. dollar from falling below HK$7.76, but that didn't seem to be a major issue recently with the local currency markets quiet.  

"It's very difficult for us to understand their thinking," a Hong Kong-based currency trader said. "There hasn't been much fluctuation in the rate recently."  

"The lack of movement in the spot market may imply there are fund inflows offsetting the HKMA's intervention," another trader with a local bank said.  

Since late September, the Hong Kong dollar has been trading at a rate stronger than its official peg to the U.S. dollar of HK$7.80, an unusual situation driven by a combination of flows of foreign investment into Hong Kong assets, and speculation on the possible appreciation of the yuan, using the Hong Kong dollar as a proxy.  

Most market participants don't anticipate a return to the peg rate until the fund inflows to Hong Kong, which have been supporting the stronger currency, reverse.  

There is no immediate sign that will happen, especially given the recent wave of highly popular initial public offerings from China-related companies such as China Life Insurance Co.  

So rather than actively work to return the Hong Kong dollar to its peg rate, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority has intervened occasionally in the market to keep the local currency from strengthening too far away from the peg.  

Hong Kong's currency board system automatically prevents the local unit from weakening away from the peg rate, but there is no such provision in the system to prevent it from strengthening - only the HKMA's discretion to sell the currency in individual transactions.  

Friday's and Monday's sales bring the HKMA's total sales since the September strengthening of the currency to HK$15.48 billion, which would buy just under US$2 billion.  

The HKMA provides information on its market actions to financial data systems, but doesn't comment on them other than to say it acts as needed to counter market volatility.  

-By Andrew Batson and Raymond Tsoi, Dow Jones Newswires; 852-2802-7002; andrew.batson@dowjones.com  

-Edited by Andrew Bullard

title: HK Dlr Mkts Late: HK Dlr Flat After HKMA  Intervention
text:

title: HKMA Sells HK$156 Mln More In Additional  Intervention
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--The Hong Kong Monetary Authority sold an additional HK$156 million Friday afternoon, buying about US$20 million, in its second transaction of the day to weaken the Hong Kong dollar.  

The sale brings the day's total intervention to HK$932 million, according to data provided by the HKMA to financial information systems.  

Yet Friday's second sale, like the first, didn't have a dramatic effect on the currency's level. After the transaction, the U.S. dollar was quoted at HK$7.7639, up from HK$7.7630 earlier in the day.  

The Hong Kong dollar's spot exchange rate has been stronger than its peg rate of HK$7.80 to the U.S. dollar since late September.  

Hong Kong's currency board system automatically prevents the local unit from weakening away from the peg rate, but there is no such system to prevent it from strengthening.  

The HKMA has been using occasional sales of Hong Kong dollars to ease the local unit's recent strength, although it hasn't actively tried to force a return to the peg rate.

title: HKMA Sells HK$776 Mln In Latest Move To Weaken  Currency
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--The Hong Kong Monetary Authority Friday sold HK$776 million, buying about US$100 million, in a currency transaction intended to weaken the local unit against the U.S. dollar.  

The intervention happened when the U.S. dollar was trading around HK$7.7630. A currency trader said the intervention didn't have a major impact on the market, with little change in the spot rate after the sale.  

It wasn't immediately clear why the HKMA chose to make the sale at that level. In the past it has intervened around the HK$7.76 level.  

The Hong Kong dollar's spot exchange rate has been stronger than its peg rate of HK$7.80 to the U.S. dollar since late September, an unusual situation driven by a combination of strong foreign investor interest in Hong Kong's stock and property markets, and speculation on the possible appreciation of the Chinese yuan, using the Hong Kong dollar as a proxy.  

Most market participants don't anticipate a return to the peg rate until the strong fund inflows to Hong Kong, which have been supporting the stronger currency, reverse. And there is no immediate sign that will happen, especially given the recent wave of highly popular initial public offerings from China-related companies.  

Rather than actively work to return the Hong Kong dollar to its peg rate, the HKMA has intervened occasionally in the market to keep it from strengthening too far away from the peg.

title: HKMA Advisory Group: No Need To Change HK  Currency  Board
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--The recent strengthening of the Hong Kong dollar away from its peg to the U.S. dollar doesn't create a need for any changes to the city's 20-year-old currency board system, advisers to Hong Kong's quasi-central bank said.  

The Exchange Fund Advisory Committee's subcommittee on currency board operations said in a meeting last month that the Hong Kong Monetary Authority's recent use of interventions to "dampen excessive market volatility" in the local currency were "appropriate." Systemic changes aren't necessary, it said.  

Under Hong Kong's currency board system, the HKMA is obliged to buy the Hong Kong dollar from banks at the peg rate of HK$7.80 to the U.S. dollar, an automatic mechanism that prevents the Hong Kong dollar from weakening against the U.S. dollar. However the HKMA has no obligation to sell the Hong Kong dollar at that rate, so the currency can become stronger than the peg.  

Since the Hong Kong dollar first strengthened away from the peg rate on Sept. 22, the HKMA has bought more than US$1 billion in a series of market interventions, usually timed to keep the Hong Kong dollar from strengthening beyond HK$7.76 to the U.S. dollar.  

Now that the Hong Kong dollar has spent an extended period trading away from the peg, some economists and market participants have criticized the one-sided currency board for introducing uncertainty into the territory's exchange rate regime.  

Current and former HKMA officials have said, however, they prefer to maintain the flexibility on defending the strong side of the peg that the current system gives them.  

The advisory committee found no ill effects from the stronger currency.  

"Members observed that the impact of the strengthening of the dollar on the real economy had been minimal," the report of the committee's meeting said. "It appeared that the concerns in the market about deflation, the budget deficit and unemployment had for the time being subsided."  

The committee's meeting was held Nov. 7, but the record of its discussions wasn't released by the HKMA until late Thursday.  

-By Andrew Batson, Dow Jones Newswires; 852-2802-7002; andrew.batson@dowjones.com

title: Asia Bonds-Hong Kong markets challenge ties with U.S.
text:
SINGAPORE, Nov 21 (Reuters) - An unusual combination of factors has driven short term interest rates in Hong Kong well below their U.S. peers, challenging the convention that the territory's currency peg should mean interest rates are the same.   

Analysts and traders say, however, arbitrageurs are unlikely to close the gap in the short term because of heavy investment flows into Hong Kong, the gateway to China. The peg should survive the test in the long run, they add.   

Hong Kong's dollar currency has been pegged to the U.S. dollar for 20 years and the currency board arrangement that supports the peg requires that interest rates move in parallel.   

But the Hong Kong dollar has spent the last two months on the stronger side of its pegged level at 7.8 per U.S. dollar.   

Overnight rates in Hong Kong are at historic lows and quoting under two basis points, and the spread between one-month swap rates in the United States and Hong Kong has widened to 105 basis point from eight in late-September.   

There is no divergence in the longer tenors, suggesting markets do not expect the HK dollar's strength to last.   

Ten-year swaps are around 4.6 percent both in Hong Kong and the United States, propped up by expectations of an economic rebound.   

"You have a situation in Hong Kong where you have zero interest rates at the short end and, at the same time, the long end is trying to price in U.S. policy tightening towards the end of the next year," said Simon Klassen, fixed income analyst with JP Morgan.   

"There is an extra 100 basis points between the Hong Kong and the United States,"   

In an ideal situation, such an interest differential would give rise to arbitrage trades, in which investors would exchange their HK dollars for U.S. dollars to earn the higher U.S. yields.   

But, foreign money is pouring into Hong Kong for investment in property and in equities, especially Chinese stocks, and for speculation on revaluations in the Chinese yuan.   

In addition, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority has been intervening to try and weaken the HK dollar back towards its 7.8 peg. It has injected nearly HK$11 billion since September.   

"All those inflows are just getting focused at the short end and have pushed down rates to very low levels," Klassen said.   

"There is a natural arbitrage that says that you should be borrowing in HK dollars and investing in the U.S., but that's not the way the flows are and no one's prepared to arbitrage."   

STILL STABLE   

Mike Moran, economist at Standard Chartered Bank, said this did not mean the currency board arrangement was at any risk. Policy rates, with Hong Kong's base rate at 2.5 percent, were still unchanged, he said.   

HKMA chief Joseph Yam said last week he did not mind the decline in rates given Hong Kong was still mired in deflation.   

Other analysts agreed that short-term currency moves could lead to a temporary disconnect between Hong Kong and U.S. yields.   

"At the very short end there can be a temporary decoupling of rates," said Bert Gochet, interest rates strategist with UBS.   

"If in the next one year the HK dollar can appreciate or move around in a one percent band, then it means interest rates can be different from the U.S. rates by one percent," he said.   

But long term yields in the HK$120 billion exchange fund notes and bills market are rising, reflecting the newfound optimism over U.S. growth and yields.   

"In the long run, people will expect the peg to hold at 7.8 and so the long end of the curve cannot differentiate. So you get a steep curve," Gochet said.

title: UPDATE 1-HK's fin sec says no barrier to more HK$ sales.
text:
HONG KONG, Nov 20 (Reuters) - Hong Kong's Financial Secretary Henry Tang said on Thursday the government would not hesitate to sink more money into the market to stabilise the local currency against the greenback.   

"We will continue to monitor the situation. If necessary we will continue to inject further liquidity into the market," Tang told reporters on the sidelines of a luncheon.   

Tang made the comments when asked if the government would consider setting a ceiling on the strength of the local currency, which has been pegged at HK$7.80 per U.S. dollar for twenty years.   

The Hong Kong Monetary Authority has been intervening in the money market since September to weaken the local dollar following an unusual appreciation of the currency against the U.S. dollar after calls by industrialised nations for more flexible exchange rates.   

Inflows of funds for upcoming initial public offerings and speculation over a possible future revaluation of the Chinese yuan currency have been cited by analysts as reasons for the local currency's strength.   

The appreciation comes despite the fact that the Hong Kong government is facing a record budget deficit this year and with the local economy only showing a modest recovery.   

From its pegged exchange rate of HK$7.80 per U.S. dollar, the Hong Kong dollar firmed to about HK$7.70 in late September, triggering interventions by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority.   

The currency then gradually headed back towards its peg rate until last week when it strengthened to HK$7.73 per dollar, drawing the HKMA into its latest round of liquidity injections.   

The local unit weakened slightly following Tang's comments to HK$7.7591/01 per dollar from its morning level of 7.7585/95.   

The HKMA's interventions from September 25 to date amount to nearly HK$11 billion (US$1.4 billion). Traders say the intervention is becoming less effective due to persistent bearishness on the U.S. dollar.   

The HKMA, the territory's de facto central bank, has intervened in the market seven times so far this week and bought a total of US$337 million. It is obligated to defend the Hong Kong dollar from weakening below its HK$7.80 peg with the U.S. dollar but has no mandate to stop it from strengthening above that level.

title: HK Fincl Secy:  Forex Intervention  Will Continue If Needed
text:
Hong Kong (Dow Jones)--Hong Kong Financial Secretary Henry Tang said the government won't hesitate to intervene in the foreign exchange market if needed.  

"If necessary, we will continue to intervene," Tang told reporters Thursday.  

Tang said the recent strength of the local unit reflects rising confidence in the city's economy.  

The strong demand for the Hong Kong dollar was also due to diminishing concerns that the currency will be devalued, Tang added. However, "there is no reason at all to change the (U.S. dollar) peg."  

Hong Kong dollar forwards, a barometer of the level of confidence in the city's currency peg, mostly traded at a premium to the spot market in recent years, as the city faced a prolonged period of economic weakness marked by rising unemployment and deepening deflation.  

But market sentiment started to turn around as Hong Kong's economy began showing signs of recovery, boosted by a revival in tourism and business opportunities from its trade pact with China.  

In late September, heavy selling of the U.S. dollar against Asian currencies triggered a sharp rise of the Hong Kong dollar above the HK$7.80 peg rate, pushing the one-year forwards to trade at a discount from a premium.  

The slide of the U.S. dollar prompted a series of interventions from the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, which has been fighting to preserve the Hong Kong dollar peg. In the past two weeks, the HKMA bought US$937 million in the spot market.  

But the HKMA intervention has had little effect on the U.S. dollar, barely keeping it around 7.76, which is believed to be the quasi-central bank's target level.  

Traders expect the strength of the local unit to persist in the near term as the recovering economy and local equities continue to attract foreign funds.  

The U.S. dollar's general slide against most currencies and the intensifying trade dispute between the U.S. and China will also keep upward pressure on the Hong Kong dollar.

    The HKMA is obligated to defend the Hong Kong dollar from
weakening below its HK$7.80 peg with the U.S. dollar but has no
mandate to stop it from strengthening above that level.
    The HKMA, the territory's de facto central bank, sold a total
of HK$1.163 million (US$150 million) on Wednesday.
   


 This is the
fifth time in two days that the HKMA has intervened in the market
according to information it publishes daily on Reuters screens
 .
 
    It also sold a total of HK$1.318 billion (US$170 million) on
Tuesday during London and New York trading hours.
    As a result, the aggregate balance, a key measure of
   

interbank liquidity, will increase to HK$11.402 billion on   

Friday. This will push local interbank rates lower and force the   

discount on Hong Kong dollar forwards even wider.   

"People had accumulated a lot of U.S. dollars against the   

local unit in arbitrage trades in the past. As the U.S. dollar   

weakens, those who have burnt their figures are rushing to sell   

U.S. dollars to liquidate their positions," said a dealer from a   

French bank.   

Some dealers said banks in Hong Kong had become cautious   

about the size of their short term U.S. dollar holdings due to   

the greenback's recent weakness and the volatility of the local   

unit, which has been strengthening since late September.   

"I think many banks in Hong Kong have given instructions to   

traders to limit the size of U.S. dollar holdings to control   

currency risk," said another dealer from a European bank.   

The U.S. dollar fell against the euro on Wednesday after   

Washington said it would impose import quotas on Chinese   

textiles, fuelling fears of protectionism that could undermine   

the U.S. economic recovery.    


 
    Dealers also said investors were reluctant to buy U.S.
dollars against the local unit in arbitrage.
    "As the interest rate differential between U.S. dollar and
   

Hong Kong dollar is only one percentage point, there is in fact   

not much of an incentive for people to buy U.S. dollar," one   

dealer said.   

The discount on one-year Hong Kong dollar forwards   

broke key support at 400 pips and deepened to a fresh low of   

480/460 pips by late afternoon versus 385 pips late on Tuesday.
