title: HK dollar defies fundamentals, stays strong.
text:
SINGAPORE, Nov 19 (Reuters) - Braving heavy central bank intervention and an unhealthy economic backdrop, the Hong Kong dollar has surprised markets by straying from a pegged exchange rate and remaining firm for two months.  

And now, surging fund flows into domestic money markets have driven short-term interest rates to historic lows and are helping keep the currency strong, both in the spot and forward markets.  

Throw in expectations of an appreciation in the tightly managed Chinese renminbi and traders think there is a case for a higher Hong Kong dollar.  

The HK dollar was quoted around 7.75 per dollar on Wednesday. The two-decade old peg spiked from a fixed level of 7.8 per U.S. dollar in late September after a Group of Seven communique on currency policies caused the U.S. dollar to slide.  

Forwards moved into deeper discounts on the U.S. dollar, with the one-year Hong Kong dollar priced at 7.35 on Wednesday.  

"The key driver is that there is still a lot of liquidity in Hong Kong that is keeping onshore rates very, very low and that clearly has been driving forwards lower," said Mike Moran, global markets economist with Standard Chartered Bank.  

"As a secondary factor, what is happening in China and what is happening to the broader economy is also driving people to take a position on the Hong Kong dollar as well as the renminbi."  

"The discount in the forwards isn't necessarily a reflection that people expect the HK dollar to be very strong in the future," he said.  

Fundamentally, there is little to support any bullishness. Hong Kong is barely recovering from its third recession in six years, unemployment remains high and deflationary pressures have dogged the economy for five years.  

LIQUIDITY SWELLS  

Liquidity has been rising as foreign money betting on stocks and on a yuan revaluation poured into the territory.  

The stock market is up nearly eight percent in two months. According to Nomura International's data, foreigners have invested over $400 million so far this year in Hong Kong stocks.  

Those flows pale in comparison with the funds the Hong Kong Monetary Authority has been injecting through its U.S. dollar-buying intervention to rein in the rising currency.  

An asymmetry in the Hong Kong currency board arrangement has the HKMA strictly defending its currency from a decline beyond 7.8 but it is not obliged to stop the HK dollar from rising.  

The HK dollar has not moved back to the 7.8 peg level, but inter-bank liquidity has doubled in a week to over HK$10 billion.  

Short-term rates have moved Japan-style to near zero, and that keeps currency forwards at their lows.  

CONVOLUTED  

Trading in the HK dollar has been full of twists and turns.  

For over a year markets were betting the currency would weaken to converge with the yuan, as the latter appreciated from its nearly pegged levels around 8.3 per dollar.  

At the peak of the frenzied speculation, when the yuan was seen rising seven percent in a year, the bets on the HK dollar were reversed to factor in a higher currency.  

Now, despite the United States imposing quotas on Chinese garments, markets expect the yuan will appreciate just about four percent in a year if its trading band is widened.  

They have not scaled back their bullishness on the HK dollar markets. Few are buying U.S. dollars, even though they expect the HK dollar will eventually decline to 7.8 and they earn an interest rate differential on such trades.  

"The risk is that there is a larger deviation to the downside and the HKMA has not been particularly effective in stemming that," said James Malcolm, currency strategist with JP Morgan.  

"No one is sure where the floor is in U.S.dollar/HK dollar because there are still some positions outstanding and some flows into the market. None of the dealers want to take the risk of buying U.S. dollars, which is why the forwards are this way."

title: HKMA Sells Additional HK$82 Mln In Latest  Intervention
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--The Hong Kong Monetary Authority sold an additional HK$82 million, buying approximately US$10 million, in its third intervention of the day Wednesday.

title: HK Dlr Mkts Late: HK Dlr Stronger On Global US Dlr Sales
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--The Hong Kong dollar strengthened in the spot and forwards markets Wednesday, in response to heavy selling of the U.S. dollar against major global currencies.  

The U.S. dollar was quoted around HK$7.7555, down from HK$7.7610 Tuesday. The benchmark one-year Hong Kong dollar forward was quoted at 480 to 460 below the spot rate, much deeper than the 390 to 375 discount Tuesday.  

"We see some relocation of money from the U.S. into higher yielding markets," a trader said.  

The drop in the spot rate below the HK$7.76 level triggered another round of overnight interventions by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority. The HKMA sold a total of HK$1.32 billion in three transactions, buying U.S. dollars at an exchange rate estimated around HK$7.7530. The HKMA has been active in the market in the past week, usually moving when the U.S. dollar falls below HK$7.76.  

The effectiveness of the HKMA's latest interventions seems to be waning, as the U.S. dollar didn't move back above HK$7.76. Still, traders suggested the U.S. dollar would have traded even weaker against the Hong Kong dollar without them.  

"Once they (the HKMA) start taking action, they can't stop. If they did, the spot rate would really slide," the trader said.  

The latest sale by the HKMA added further liquidity to an interbank market already swimming in surplus cash, helping to further push down Hong Kong interbank offered rates.  

The three-month Hibor fell to 0.13%, from 0.19% Tuesday, while the one-year Hibor dropped to 0.87%, from 0.93% previously.  

Traders said rates were likely to keep falling until funds start moving out of Hong Kong. The strong performance of the local stock market has attracted many investors, while others are speculating on an appreciation of the currency.  

Yields on Hong Kong exchange fund notes fell, after the U.S. issued data showing slow inflation, and an official from the Federal Reserve repeated the central bank's disinclination to raise U.S. interest rates in the short term.  

The yield on the two-year EF note was quoted at 1.24%, from 1.36% Tuesday, while the 10-year note was down to 4.15%, from 4.26% previously.

title: HKMA Moves To Curb HK Dollar Rise Becoming Less Effective
text:
Hong Kong(Dow Jones)--The Hong Kong Monetary Authority intervened in the foreign exchange market again late Tuesday in a bid to prevent the U.S. dollar from weakening against the local unit, but the effectiveness of the quasi-central bank's interventionist moves appears to be waning.  

The HKMA doesn't normally comment on its market activities, but does provide information on its transactions to financial data systems, which show it sold HK$1,318 million, equivalent to buying around US$170 million.  

The HKMA sold about HK$4.66 billion last week.  

Traders said the U.S. dollar's general slide against major currencies led to a fall in the U.S. dollar against the Hong Kong dollar overnight, and prompted three rounds of intervention by the HKMA. A money trader estimated the transactions were executed at an average exchange rate of HK$7.7530.  

The HKMA's latest intervention, however, hasn't been entirely effective in curbing the appreciation of the Hong Kong dollar: the U.S. dollar was being quoted at HK$7.7555 Wednesday morning, lower than its level of HK$7.7610 Tuesday afternoon.  

The belief in the market is that the HKMA is aiming to keep the U.S. dollar from dipping much below HK$7.76.  

"Market sentiment is against the U.S. dollar, given its general slide against most currencies," the money trader said.  

Traders were also concerned an intensifying trade dispute between the U.S. and mainland China could lead to a resurgence in political pressure for a yuan revaluation.  

Since the Chinese currency isn't freely tradable, market participants often use the Hong Kong dollar as a proxy for the yuan given the close economic relationship between the territory and mainland China, even though the currencies have no real ties.  

"Despite the HKMA's clear commitment to keeping the peg, and significantly higher U.S. dollar interest rates than Hong Kong dollar interest rates, market participants remain reluctant to long the U.S. dollar," the trader noted.  

The Hong Kong dollar strayed from the HK$7.80 peg rate Sept. 22, when there was heavy selling of the U.S. dollar against Asian currencies. The U.S. dollar was quoted as low as HK$7.71 in the immediate aftermath, but then rebounded to around HK$7.77 before coming under selling pressure again recently.  

The HKMA's repeated sales of Hong Kong dollars have flooded the interbank market with surplus funds. The aggregate balance, a key measure of interbank surplus liquidity, will rise to over HK$10 billion Thursday when the HKMA's latest transactions settle.  

The excess liquidity has depressed Hong Kong interest rates and pushed the discounts on Hong Kong dollar forwards to their deepest levels since forwards moved from a premium to a discount late September.  

The one-year forward was quoted at a discount of 450-440 to the spot rate Wednesday morning, compared with a discount of 390-375 Tuesday afternoon.  

"Forwards are likely to remain at a deep discount unless there are major outflows, but that seems unlikely in the near term," the trader said.  

-By Raymond Tsoi, Dow Jones Newswires; 852-2802-7002; raymond.tsoi@dowjones.com

HONG KONG, Nov 19 (Reuters) - The Hong Kong dollar remained

title: HK Dlr Mkts Late: Hibors Fall Again On Growing Liquidity
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--Hong Kong interbank offered rates declined again Tuesday on fresh inflows of liquidity that resulted from the Hong Kong Monetary Authority's currency market interventions last week.   

The one-year Hibor was quoted at 0.93%, down from 0.98% Monday, while the three-month Hibor declined to 0.19% from 0.23%.   

"Low Hibors will likely continue until the end of this year," a trader said.   

The main indicator of surplus interbank liquidity, the aggregate balance, opened at HK$8.19 billion Tuesday, up from HK$5.9 billion late last week - already an unusually high level.   

The HKMA's sales last week of Hong Kong dollars, aimed at keeping the U.S. dollar from weakening below the HK$7.76 level, totaled about HK$4.66 billion.   

In another sign of excess liquidity, Tuesday's regular auction of short-dated Exchange Fund bills also drew an average accepted yield of -0.01% for the one-month bill.   

A negative yield, meaning that the price paid for the bond is higher than its return, usually makes financial sense for an investor only if rates are expected to fall further.   

Traders also noted that market makers are required to participate in the HKMA's auction, helping push the yield into the negative. "They bid for the shortest tenor to minimize the risk, while still fulfilling the tender participation requirement," a trader said.   

Yields on longer-dated Exchange Fund notes rose somewhat slightly, in line with U.S. Treasurys, on profit-taking, traders said. The two-year note was quoted at 1.36%, up from 1.31% Monday, while the 10-year note rose to 4.26%.   

The Hong Kong dollar was little moved in the spot and forward markets. The U.S. dollar was quoted at HK$7.7610, compared with HK$7.7593 Monday. Traders said the HKMA's interventions last week had established clear support at the HK$7.76 level.   

The discount on Hong Kong dollar forwards remained wide, reflecting the wide interest rate gap between Hong Kong and the U.S. The one-year forward contract was quoted at 390 to 375 below the spot rate, compared with 390 to 380 Monday.   

Widely anticipated news that Hong Kong banks would be allowed to offer services in the Chinese yuan, or renminbi, had little impact on the bond or currency markets. "It's not a big liberalization," another trader said.   

Hong Kong Chief Executive Tung Chee-hwa said Tuesday that all locally licensed banks will be permitted to offer basic financial services denominated in yuan to retail customers beginning next year.

title: HK dlr range trades, forwards discount widens.
text:
HONG KONG, Nov 17 (Reuters) - The Hong Kong dollar was
rangebound on Monday on cautious sentiment after a series of
interventions by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) last
week.
    The local unit shuffled between 7.7580-7.76 for most of the
day. It was trading at 7.7590 to the dollar at 0925 GMT,
compared with 7.7578/98 at 0917 GMT on Friday.

So investors are more cautious," a dealer at a European bank
said, explaining the range trading.
    The HKMA, the territory's de facto central bank, bought
US$600 million last week against the HK dollar to show its
commitment to exchange rate stability. The local currency has
been strengthening over recent weeks.
    The aggregate balance, a key measure of interbank
liquidity, will expand to HK$8.966 billion on Tuesday -- the
highest level since November 1998. High liquidity pushes
interbank rates down.

interbank rates low to encourage banks to buy U.S. dollars
against the local units in arbitrage. A long time ago, say in
1987, such arbitrage was seen lucrative as U.S. interest rates

as the U.S. interest rates are so low, investors see artibrage
as less attractive," another dealer said.
    The interest rate differential between the Hong Kong dollar
and the U.S. dollar was around one full percentage point at
present, the dealer added.
 
    He expected the spot rate to move between 7.75-7.77 to the
dollar in the near term.
    Traders see a risk of further HKMA intervention in the near
   

term, which will push local interbank rates down further -   

short term rates are already close to zero - and widen the   

discount on Hong Kong dollar forwards.

Friday.

title: HKMA Sells HK$776 Mln In Latest Move To Weaken HK Dlr
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--The Hong Kong Monetary Authority Friday sold HK$776 million into the market in its latest move to stem the strengthening of the Hong Kong dollar.  

A foreign exchange trader said Friday's sale, the latest in a series of moves by the HKMA this week, took place when the U.S. dollar was quoted around HK$7.7575.  

The sales this week have convinced the market the HKMA won't permit the U.S. dollar to fall below the HK$7.76 level.  

"7.76 is already the alert level for the HKMA. Each time we break this level, they come in and intervene," the trader said.  

The HKMA has sold Hong Kong dollars into the market every day this week, in its most active series of interventions since late September, when the Hong Kong dollar's exchange rate has been stronger than the peg rate of HK$7.80 to the U.S. dollar.  

The latest transaction brings the HKMA's total intervention this week to about HK$4.7 billion, or around US$600 million.  

The repeated injections of cash into the system have pushed down interest rates, already extremely low, and demonstrated the HKMA's commitment to the city's 20-year-old currency peg.  

But as the repeated strengthening of the Hong Kong dollar shows, traders remain reluctant to buy the U.S. dollar, given its weakness against other major currencies.  

"This afternoon there wasn't enough liquidity, and a few traders were able to push the rate from 7.7620 to as low as 7.7520 in just a minute," the foreign exchange trader said. "So the HKMA move was widely expected by traders."  

The latest intervention, however, wasn't able to keep the U.S. dollar above the HK$7.76 level. Late Friday afternoon, after the HKMA sale, the U.S. dollar was quoted around HK$7.7580, compared with HK$7.7620 earlier in the day.

title: HKMA Late Thursday Action Brings Week's Sales To HK$3.9B

That strength has been driven by large inflows of speculative money into Hong Kong, betting on the local stock markets and a possible appreciation in the Chinese yuan.

title: HK dlr ends up despite  intervention , seen strong.
text:
HONG KONG, Nov 14 (Reuters) - The Hong Kong dollar ended the
week above its pegged exchange rate to the U.S. dollar despite a

central bank to try to weaken it.
 
    Analysts and dealers said they expect the local unit's
strength to persist over the next week at least.
    "Eventually the Hong Kong dollar will move back towards the
HK$7.77 level, but not for now," said a dealer at a European bank
in Hong Kong.
    Continuing demand for Hong Kong dollars for upcoming share
  

issues and ongoing speculation that China may eventually revalue  

its yuan currency have kept the Hong Kong unit firm in recent  

months.  

The Hong Kong dollar was trading at 7.7578/98 per U.S.

7.7628/38, and firmer than HK$7.7655/60 at the close of Hong Kong  

trade on Thursday. It had strengthened to 7.7380/90 in London on  

Monday.  

The Hong Kong dollar had firmed to about HK$7.70 late in  

September compared with its pegged exchange rate of HK$7.80  

following calls by industrialised nations for more flexible  

exchange rates in Asia.  

The HKMA intervened late on Friday for the seventh time this  

week, buying about US$100 million in addition to the US$500  

million it bought earlier in the week. The move caused a brief  

weakening in the local currency before it firmed up again.  

The discount on the one-year Hong Kong dollar forwards  

contract stood at 360/350 pips from the morning's -330/-310 pips  

level, and from -320/-300 late on Thursday.  

The widening discount implies that the market expects the  

local unit to remain firm in coming sessions. Analysts said there  

was no limit to how much Hong Kong dollars the HKMA could sell.  

"As long as the HKMA's sales and issuance of Hong Kong  

dollars are backed by U.S. dollars, and if they sell Hong Kong  

dollars and credit the clearing accounts of banks, it's OK. All  

this Hong Kong dollar printing is 100 percent backed by U.S.  

dollars," said Eddie Wong, chief strategist for Asia at ABN AMRO  

in Hong Kong.  

"The concern is that surplus liquidity will continue to flood  

into the clearing accounts of the banks and Hong Kong interbank  

rates could become zero," he added.  

"What the HKMA might do is to issue Exchange Fund bills to  

mop up the surplus funds in the banks if necessary, and that  

would make the issuing of Hong Kong dollars even more  

open-ended," Wong said.  

The Hong Kong Monetary Authority said on Thursday it would be  

happy to keep Hong Kong dollar interbank rates lower than those  

for the U.S. dollar as this would help to encourage consumption.  

"The HKMA is preparing the public for significant injections  

of liquidity," said James Malcolm, currency strategist at JP  

Morgan Chase in Singapore.  

"The whole point of having a lot of liquidity sloshing around  

the system is to make the opportunity cost of not buying U.S.  

dollars increasingly high," Malcolm said.  

Overnight Hong Kong dollar interbank rates have fallen to  

nearly zero since late September when the Hong Kong dollar staged  

its highly unusual appreciation against the U.S. dollar, driven  

by speculation that the Chinese yuan could be revalued following  

intense pressure from industrialised nations.  

This has left Hong Kong dollar interest rates about one full  

percentage point below those for the U.S. dollar. Under the  

territory's 20-year-old currency board regime, the HKMA is tasked  

with maintaining the stability of the Hong Kong dollar.  

While it is obliged to defend the local currency from  

weakening below the HK$7.80 per dollar level, it is not mandated  

to prevent it from strengthening above that level, as long as the  

exchange rate is kept relatively stable.

title: HK Dlr Mkts Late: HK$ Eases After HKMA  Intervenes  Again
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--The Hong Kong dollar weakened further Thursday after the Hong Kong Monetary Authority intervened again in the market to strengthen the U.S. dollar.  

"The HKMA has shown a very aggressive stance in recent interventions," one trader said. "It has indicated clearly excessive strength of the currency won't be tolerated."  

The quasi-central bank sold an additional HK$777 million Thursday to push up the U.S. dollar, after having injected over HK$2.3 billion in the previous three days.  

The U.S. dollar rose gradually after the intervention and was quoted at HK$7.7665 late Thursday, up from HK$7.7630 Wednesday.  

Traders said the HKMA could sell the local unit again in coming weeks to help the U.S. dollar gradually move back toward the HK$7.80 peg rate.  

"Potential interventions from the HKMA may deter traders from selling the U.S. dollar, which will keep it well supported around HK$7.760 in the near term," the trader said.  

Discounts on Hong Kong dollar forwards narrowed following the HKMA's move, which was seen as a strong signal the city's U.S. dollar peg will be kept intact over the long term.  

The one-year contract was quoted at a discount of 320-300 to the spot rate, compared with 370-350 Wednesday.  

Long-dated Hong Kong interbank offered rates edged higher amid stronger borrowing interest from foreign banks, as the rates were considered cheap relative to comparable U.S. dollar London interbank offered rates.  

The one-year Hibor was quoted at 1.14%, up from 1.08% Wednesday.  

"Foreign banks are quite keen to borrow longer term funds, especially the one year," the trader said.  

If there is little chance of the Hong Kong dollar appreciating, the one-year Hibor can't justify trading at more than 40 basis points below the one-year U.S. dollar Libor, traders said, adding that an upward bias is therefore likely to persist.  

Hong Kong Exchange Fund note yields barely moved. The yield on the 10-year bond was 4.50%, the same as Wednesday.

title: UPDATE 1-HKMA has no qualms keeping HK$ interest rates low.
text:
HONG KONG, Nov 13 (Reuters) - The Hong Kong Monetary Authority would be happy to keep Hong Kong dollar interbank rates lower than those for the U.S. dollar as this would help to encourage consumption, the territory's de facto central bank said on Thursday.   

"With continuing deflation... we do not mind seeing Hong Kong dollar interest rates being kept low, and lower than U.S. dollar interest rates," HKMA chief Joseph Yam said in his weekly column published on the HKMA's Web site.   

Overnight Hong Kong dollar interbank rates have fallen to nearly zero since late September when the Hong Kong dollar staged a highly unusual appreciation against the U.S. dollar, driven by speculation that the Chinese yuan could be revalued following intense pressure from industrialised nations.   

This has left Hong Kong dollar interest rates about one full percentage point below those for the U.S. dollar.   

"Low interest rates will hopefully encourage consumption and credit expansion, and help stabilise and perhaps inflate asset prices and the economy," Yam said.   

Hong Kong has suffered from five years of deflation, which has sapped companies' profitability and driven up unemployment to record levels.   

While deflation and unemployment have improved slightly over recent months, they remain significant barriers to sustainable economic growth over the next few years.   

The drop in Hong Kong dollar interest rates has been a result of numerous interventions by the HKMA to sell Hong Kong dollars and buy U.S. dollars to stabilise the local unit.   

The Hong Kong dollar firmed to about HK$7.70 late in September compared with its pegged exchange rate of HK$7.80.   

Under the territory's 20-year-old currency board regime, the HKMA is tasked with maintaining the stability of the Hong Kong dollar.   

While it is obliged to defend the local currency from weakening below the HK$7.80 per dollar level, it is not mandated to prevent it from strengthening above that level, as long as the exchange rate is kept relatively stable.   

The HKMA has bought a total of US$400 million against the local unit this week.   

As a result, the aggregate balance, a key measure of interbank liquidity, will expand to HK$7.4 billion on November 17 from HK$5.8 billion on Thursday.   

The Hong Kong dollar was little moved against the greenback on Thursday following the intervention, trading at HK$7.7640/50 per U.S. dollar late on Thursday compared with the previous day's Hong Kong close, despite weakening shortly after the HKMA's latest move.

title: WRAP: HKMA Again Moves To Weaken Hong Kong Dollar Rate
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--The Hong Kong Monetary Authority on Wednesday again sold Hong Kong dollars, and bought U.S. dollars, giving fresh impetus to the weakening of the Hong Kong dollar's exchange rate, already under way after its sales earlier this week.  

In its latest transaction, the HKMA sold HK$776 million, buying about US$100 million, apparently during the lunch hour Wednesday. The move had its desired effect, moving up the exchange rate: the U.S. dollar was quoted around HK$7.7630 late Wednesday, after the injection, compared with around HK$7.7540 Tuesday.  

Yet even before the HKMA's intervention Wednesday, the U.S. dollar was falling against the Hong Kong dollar, after the HKMA sold HK$1.55 billion in two transactions earlier this week.  

"It seems the government is quite aggressive in the U.S. dollar market right now," a foreign exchange trader said.  

"It doesn't want very much volatility in the market."  

The Hong Kong dollar's spot exchange rate has been stronger than its peg rate of HK$7.80 to the U.S. dollar since late September, an unusual situation that has been driven by a combination of strong foreign investor interest in Hong Kong's stock and property markets, and speculation on the possible appreciation of the Chinese yuan, using the Hong Kong dollar as a proxy.  

Since the Chinese currency isn't freely tradable, market participants often use the Hong Kong dollar as the closest available equivalent, even though the Hong Kong dollar's link to the U.S. dollar means there is no real tie to the yuan.  

Though the spot rate has been gradually weakening back toward the peg level over the past month, generally trading between HK$7.75 and HK$7.77, the HKMA's latest sales were sparked by a sudden strengthening of the local currency late Monday.  

"We think the much more active interbank market has played a significant role in the latest Hong Kong dollar rally, as two large back-to-back IPOs from China have started trading and frozen proceeds have returned to the money market," Credit Suisse First Boston economists wrote in a research note.  

Last week, PICC Property & Casualty Co. (2328.HK) debuted on the Hong Kong stock exchange after an initial public offering that raised HK$5.41 billion, and China Resources Power Holdings (0836.HK) started trading Wednesday after a HK$2.58 billion share sale.  

The HKMA's injection of new funds into the banking system helped push down local interest rates, which were already near zero. The one-month Hong Kong interbank offered rate, or Hibor, was quoted at 0.05%, down from 0.10% Tuesday.  

Theoretically, the low interest rates should also contribute to the weakening of the Hong Kong back toward the peg rate, as they encourage investors to move out of the Hong Kong dollar and seek higher returns elsewhere.  

Under Hong Kong's currency board system, the HKMA is obliged to buy the Hong Kong dollar from banks at the peg rate, which essentially puts a floor on the Hong Kong dollar's exchange rate against the U.S. dollar.  

However, the HKMA, which acts as the territory's central bank, has no such obligation to sell the Hong Kong dollar at the peg rate, meaning there is no automatic mechanism to prevent the exchange rate from becoming stronger than the peg rate.  

Such sales are only made at the HKMA's discretion. The HKMA doesn't provide guidelines as to when it might be willing to sell the Hong Kong dollar, saying only that it acts as needed to counter market volatility.

title: WRAP: HKMA Sells HK$1.5 Bln As HK Dlr Strengthens Again
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--Facing a surge in selling of the U.S. dollar against the Hong Kong dollar, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority once again intervened in the currency markets in an attempt to prevent the local unit from strengthening further.  

Though the HKMA doesn't comment on its market activities, it does provide information on its transactions to financial data systems. Those show it sold HK$1.5 billion, in two transactions of HK$775 million each, equivalent to buying around US$200 million.  

A trader in Hong Kong said Tuesday the first sale happened when the U.S. dollar fell to around HK$7.73. It came amid heavy selling of the U.S. dollar after the Hong Kong market closed Monday, and was later followed by the second sale. The U.S. dollar had been trading between HK$7.76 and HK$7.77 over the last few days before the sell-off.  

"The sale of the U.S. dollar for the Hong Kong dollar was rumored to have been initiated by a U.S. house, which could be related to upcoming IPO activities," a money trader said. "But it could also just have been profit-taking of U.S. dollar positions after it failed to break the resistance at HK$7.77."  

Under Hong Kong's currency board system, the HKMA is obliged to buy the Hong Kong dollar from banks at the peg rate of HK$7.80 to the U.S. dollar, which essentially puts a floor on the Hong Kong dollar's exchange rate against the U.S. dollar.  

However, the HKMA, which acts as the territory's central bank, has no such obligation to sell the Hong Kong dollar at the peg rate, meaning there is no automatic mechanism to prevent the exchange rate from becoming stronger than the peg rate.  

Such sales are only made at the HKMA's discretion. The HKMA doesn't provide guidelines as to when it might be willing to sell the Hong Kong dollar, saying only that it acts as needed to counter market volatility.  

The Hong Kong dollar strengthened from the peg rate Sept. 22, when there was heavy selling of the U.S. dollar against Asian currencies. The U.S. dollar was quoted as low as HK$7.71 in the immediate aftermath, but since then its exchange rate with the Hong Kong dollar has moved gradually back up toward the peg rate.  

The HKMA has sold Hong Kong dollars occasionally since then, though analysts say it hasn't been trying to actively guide the spot rate back to the peg rate. Rather, it has acted only intermittently to keep the rate from going below a certain level.  

The HKMA's move did have some effect on the market: the U.S. dollar was quoted around HK$7.7525 early Tuesday afternoon, compared with HK$7.7480 earlier in the day, though the rate is still down compared with HK$7.7695 Monday afternoon.

text:

U.S. Treasury report," said a dealer at a local bank.
    But the dealer added that some profit taking took place when

struggled between 7.7630-50 in the afternoon.
    At 0912 GMT, the Hong Kong dollar was trading at 7.7660,

expected to creep back towards the peg rate in the near term,
dealers said.

the territory's de facto central bank and repeated statements   

from China rebuffing U.S. pressure for a yuan revaluation.   

"The U.S. GDP figures were strong and if the unemployment

its fastest pace in almost 20 years.   

A strong recovery in the United States is expected to boost   

Hong Kong's own. The United States is the territory's second   

largest trading partner.   

Meanwhile, Snow told the U.S. Senate Banking Committee that   

the Treasury was actively urging China to end its decade-old   

practice of pegging its yuan currency at about 8.28 to the U.S.   

dollar.    


 
    But he resisted the idea of setting a deadline for China
because of the effect that would have on currency markets.

title: HK Dlr Mkts Late: HK$, Forwards Steady After Yam Remarks
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--Hong Kong dollar forwards and the local currency's spot rate were little changed Wednesday as remarks by the city's quasi central banker that he had a "relaxed attitude" about the Hong Kong dollar's recent appreciation had little impact on currency markets.  

The USD/HKD spot exchange rate moved a touch lower, to around 7.7440 Wednesday from 7.7480 Tuesday. The benchmark one-year forward contract was also largely unchanged, at a discount of 175 to 165 to the spot rate.  

Monetary Authority Chief Executive Joseph Yam said in a speech late Tuesday: "Our somewhat relaxed attitude toward small deviations in the exchange rate on the strong side of 7.80 does not mean that we are any less committed to maintaining the link."  

"It's difficult to pin anything on Yam's speech," a trader said, noting that the USD/HKD spot rate actually went down despite the HKMA's sale of HK$969 million yesterday.  

The trader said he didn't expect the USD/HKD rate to rise above 7.75 in the near term, arguing that there are still many market participants long in U.S. dollars who haven't been able to completely liquidate their positions following the recent strengthening of the Hong Kong dollar.  

The injection of new liquidity by the HKMA helped depress already low Hong Kong interbank offered rates. The three-month Hibor was quoted at 0.43%, compared with 0.49% Tuesday.  

With Hong Kong dollar interest rates now, unusually, below their U.S. dollar counterparts, Citigroup economist Joe Lo issued a report predicting they would converge in two to three months.  

He estimated that would be the amount of time it would take for excess liquidity to drain out of the system and for currency markets to ease their speculation over an upward revaluation of the Chinese yuan, which is also creating appreciation pressure on the Hong Kong dollar.  

The greater liquidity brought on by the HKMA's intervention also helped prompt more buying interest in short-term Hong Kong Exchange Fund bills by banks. Another trader said the three-month note yield was quoted as low as 0.01%.  

There was less activity in longer-dated Exchange Fund notes, though there was some interest in the two-year note, whose yield declined slightly to 1.21%. The yield on the 10-year note rose to 4.47% in response to investors switching out of U.S. Treasurys and into U.S. stocks.

title: WRAP: HKMA Relaxed About Stronger HK Dollar, Firm On Peg
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--The Hong Kong Monetary Authority said it sees no threat to the territory's 20-year-old currency peg, which links the Hong Kong dollar to the U.S. dollar, from the local currency's strengthening in recent weeks above the fixed rate of 7.80.  

"Our somewhat relaxed attitude toward small deviations in the exchange rate on the strong side of 7.80 does not mean that we are any less committed to maintaining the link," said HKMA chief executive Joseph Yam in a speech Tuesday evening.  

"There is an effective mechanism for us to ensure that these fluctuations are not so large as to undermine credibility and confidence in the link," he said.  

In separate remarks to reporters earlier Tuesday, Yam said that the HKMA's priority in this unusual situation isn't targeting a particular exchange rate, but rather maintaining the overall confidence of investors and the public in the peg system.  

While Hong Kong's currency board system has an automatic mechanism to prevent depreciation of the currency, it doesn't have any such arrangement to prevent appreciation. In order to weaken the currency, the HKMA must make transactions, at its discretion, in which it sells the Hong Kong dollar and buys the U.S. dollar.  

In fact, though Yam didn't allude to it, the HKMA did so Tuesday, selling HK$969 million into the market when the currency was near the 7.75 level. But that move and Yam's comments had little effect on the spot exchange rate, and the Hong Kong dollar strengthened to around 7.7440 Wednesday.  

The HKMA has intervened to sell Hong Kong dollars and buy U.S. dollars on four days since the USD/HKD exchange rate dropped below 7.80 on Sept. 22, injecting a total of HK$3.75 billion into the market.  

"Minor fluctuations in the market exchange rate on the strong side of the link are a feature of our monetary system, and they are nothing to get too excited about," Yam said in his speech, a written copy of which was provided by the government.  

Not everyone agrees. Michael Spencer, an economist at Deutsche Bank, argues that by permitting a stronger currency, the HKMA has changed the rules of the game. "The understanding was that the currency was fixed at 7.8. We're clearly no longer in the same regime we were three weeks ago," he said.  

Of course, such complaints can be dismissed as sour grapes from those who had been speculating on a future depreciation of the Hong Kong dollar, and got caught out when the spot exchange rate unexpectedly strengthened in response to speculation about appreciation of the Chinese yuan and by selling of the U.S. dollar.  

Since that happened on Sept. 22, analysts say the HKMA has indeed been "relaxed" about returning the exchange rate to 7.80, as its sales haven't been big or frequent enough to give the rate much of a push back toward 7.80. They note that a stronger currency helps keep down interest rates, and also contributes to the recent increased optimism about Hong Kong's economic prospects.  

Other critics have pointed out that Hong Kong has endured years of deflation in order to bring its prices down to more competitive levels, an achievement that could be threatened if the stronger currency continues. Yam, however, downplayed the significance of a slightly stronger Hong Kong dollar, saying it was outweighed by the broader weakness of the U.S. dollar.  

"An orderly depreciation of the U.S. (dollar) against other currencies is in Hong Kong's interests," Yam said in the speech. "Because Hong Kong's currency is linked to the U.S. dollar, Hong Kong also becomes more competitive."  

"This larger point may have been overlooked in all of the fuss about the somewhat less significant strengthening of the Hong Kong dollar against the U.S. dollar," he said.  

-By Andrew Batson, Dow Jones Newswires; 852-2802-7002; andrew.batson@dowjones.com

title: HK dlr remains strong despite HKMA  intervention .
text:
HONG KONG, Oct 15 (Reuters) - The Hong Kong dollar was
slightly firmer against the greenback on Wednesday morning
despite the Hong Kong Monetary Authority's (HKMA) move on Tuesday
to buy U.S. dollars against the local unit.
 
    "I think the market will continue to trade in a wider range
as there is no upper limit on HKD strength," one dealer said.
    At 0238 GMT, the local unit was trading at 7.7415 per U.S.
dollar, compared with Tuesday's 7.75 and still well above its
HK$7.80 pegged exchange rate.
    The Hong Kong dollar has been trading above its linked
   

exchange rate since late last month after Asian currencies

strengthened following a call by G7 industrial nations for more   

flexible exchange rates.   

The HKMA has now intervened six times within a four-week   

period, injecting a total of HK$3.751 billion into the aggregate   

balance. The territory's de facto central bank is forecasting the   

aggregate balance - a key measure of interbank liquidity - to   

rise to HK$4.166 billion at settlement on Thursday.   

The HKMA is obligated to defend the Hong Kong dollar from   

weakening below HK$7.80, but has no mandate to stop it from   

strengthening above that level.   

The discount on Hong Kong dollar forwards widened, tracking   

the movement in the spot rate and supported by an expansion in   

the aggregate balance.    


 
    One-year forwards          were trading at around -200/-180
pips, versus -155/-125 pips late on Tuesday.
    The market is also looking ahead to U.S. President George W.
   

Bush's trip to Asia, beginning this week. He is expected to press

text:
Hong Kong, Oct 15 (Reuters) - These are some of the leading stories in Hong Kong newspapers on Wednesday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

title: HK Dlr Mkts Late: HK$ Dn As HKMA Move Has Mixed Results

Late Tuesday, the U.S. dollar was quoted around HK$7.7500, near the level at which traders said the HKMA had intervened to sell Hong Kong dollars and buy U.S. dollars. Traders said position adjustment ahead of the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation forum summit narrowed the yuan non-deliverable forwards discount, which pushed Hong Kong dollar forwards higher.  

"The tightening of the one-year yuan NDF discount back to below the 4000 key level spurred waves of profit-taking in Hong Kong dollar forwards," a trader said.  

Traders, however, expect further upside for forwards to be firmly capped given the excess liquidity in the interbank market after recent equity-driven inflows and injections from the Hong Kong Monetary Authority.  

Hong Kong interbank offered rates rose as the Hong Kong dollar weakened, The one-month Hibor was quoted at 0.32%, compared with 0.21% Monday. However, the overnight Hibor fell to 0.04% because of the HKMA's injection of liquidity through its intervention.  

Hong Kong Exchange Fund note yields rose marginally as recent strength in local shares continued to spur funds to switch into equities and out of bonds.  

The two-year EF note was quoted at 1.21%, compared with 1.17% Monday. The 10-year EF note was quoted at 4.46%, up from 4.40% previously.  

"If the Hang Seng Index stays firmly above 12,000 points, we may see more switching into shares and therefore a continued upward bias of bond yields," the trader said.

title: HKMA's Yam: Will  Intervene  To Maintain Confidence In Peg
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--Hong Kong's quasi central bank will intervene in the currency markets if it is necessary to maintain the confidence of the markets and the public in the Hong Kong dollar's peg to the U.S. dollar, Hong Kong Monetary Authority chief executive Joseph Yam said Tuesday.  

"Our responsibility is to maintain the stability of the exchange rate and observe the sentiment of the market. We will act accordingly and respond to the market sentiment," he told reporters.  

"We can't tolerate any deviation which is big enough to undermine confidence in the system. Then we will respond to the market," he said.  

Yam wouldn't discuss any specific interventions in the Hong Kong dollar market, including today's when the HKMA sold HK$969 million, or indicate a specific level of the currency that it would try to defend.  

The peg system has come under an unusual challenge recently, as the Hong Kong dollar has spent weeks trading above its pegged rate of 7.80 to the U.S. dollar. The currency board system has an automatic mechanism to prevent devaluation, but any move to prevent appreciation must be through discretionary sales, or interventions, by the HKMA.  

That recent deviation from the pegged rate has caused some questioning of the currency board system, though officials have reiterated that there has been no actual change in currency policy, only a change in market sentiment.  

Asked repeatedly about the HKMA's plans for interventions to bring the currency back to its 7.80 peg, Yam emphasized that its actions wouldn't be driven by specific numerical targets, but by the desire to maintain overall confidence in the peg.  

"It all depends on the market sentiment. If they are comfortable and are not questioning the credibility of the system, then we will leave the market to work it out," Yam said.  

Yam's remarks came at a briefing on the currency peg to mark its twentieth anniversary, which falls on Friday. He also repeated the HKMA's standard insistence that it has no intention of abandoning the linked exchange rate system.  

"We surely need it," he said. "For the past 20 years, the system has made a great contribution to Hong Kong's stability and prosperity. In a market where there is free flow of capital, an exchange rate peg will help businesses to defend against volatility."  

The HKMA acts as Hong Kong's central bank, but it isn't an independent one. Yam noted that he and the HKMA report to Financial Secretary Henry Tang, who would be the one who would make any policy decision to continue, change or abandon the peg system.  

-By Andrew Batson and Loretta Ng, Dow Jones Newswires; 852-2802-7002; andrew.batson@dowjones.com

title: HKMA  Interveness  In HK Dollar Mkt, Sells HK$969 Million
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--The Hong Kong Monetary Authority on Tuesday again intervened in the local currency market, buying U.S. dollars and selling Hong Kong dollars in an attempt to bring the currency closer to its peg rate of 7.80.  

"The result wasn't ideal. The rate actually went down," a currency trader said, noting that the HKMA's sales were made when the U.S. dollar/HK dollar spot rate was at around 7.75, but that it had actually declined after the intervention.  

The U.S. dollar was quoted at around HK$7.7480 at 0745 GMT. Since Sept. 22, the Hong Kong dollar has been trading above its pegged rate of 7.80 to the U.S. dollar.  

The sales were made in two separate transactions about ten to fifteen minutes apart, the trader said. They totaled HK$969 million, according to HKMA data distributed to financial information terminals.  

It wasn't immediately clear what triggered the intervention, and the HKMA normally doesn't comment on its market activities.  

The HKMA's previous interventions, during the past weeks when the Hong Kong dollar has been stronger than the peg rate, have been at around 7.70 or 7.73, higher than the today's level.  

Traders have also said that volatility in the Hong Kong dollar market had been easing in recent days, with most expecting the currency to stabilize and trade within a tight range of 7.72 to 7.74 in coming weeks.  

The HKMA, which acts as Hong Kong's central bank, is obliged to buy the Hong Kong dollar from banks at the peg rate, which essentially puts a floor on the Hong Kong dollar's level against the U.S. dollar.  

However, the convertibility undertaking is one-sided, which means that selling the Hong Kong dollar is at the HKMA's discretion. Therefore there is theoretically no ceiling for the Hong Kong dollar's value.  

-By Andrew Batson, Dow Jones Newswires; 852-2802-7002; andrew.batson@dowjones.com

title: UPDATE 1-HKMA  intervenes  again on dollar.
text:
HONG KONG, Oct 14 (Reuters) - The Hong Kong Monetary Authority bought US$125 million and sold HK$969 million on Tuesday afternoon - the sixth time in less than four weeks that the de facto central bank has stepped into the spot currency market since the local dollar suddenly climbed.    

 "The figure reflected banks selling U.S. dollars to us. We have been selling Hong Kong dollars. Banks approached us to do it," the spokesman told Reuters. The spot rate briefly weakened to HK$7.75 to the U.S. dollar after the injection but then firmed back to HK$7.7464 as of 0738 GMT, and remained well below the local dollar's official pegged exchange rate of 7.8 to the U.S. dollar.    

 The Hong Kong dollar shot up to HK$7.7050 in late September, its strongest level since the Asian financial crisis of 1997-98, on growing signs that its long ailing economy was recovering.    

 Mounting international pressure on Beijing to revalue its currency has also fuelled expectations that Hong Kong's currency will icreasingly move in tune with China's as the two economies become more closely integrated.    

 Despite repeated HKMA interventions the currency has remained stubbornly strong, though many dealers expect it will slowly drift back to the pegged level over time.    

 The HKMA has repeatedly said it remained committed to maintaining the 20-year-old currency peg, which has often been described as a pillar of the former British colony's economy.    

 The Hong Kong dollar moved up last month after a statement from the G7 industrial nations meeting urging exchange rate flexibility.

title: HK dlr weakens in afternoon trade on profit taking.
text:
HONG KONG, Oct 8 (Reuters) - The Hong Kong dollar weakened
sharply on Wednesday afternoon, heading back towards its pegged
exchange rate to the U.S. dollar, as some dealers took profits
after a highly unusual strengthening two weeks ago.
    The local unit was trading at HK$7.7427/37 per U.S. dollar at
5.39 p.m. (0939 GMT) compared to the morning's HK$7.7124 level,
but remained well above its HK$7.80 pegged exchange rate.
    Four interventions by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority last
week and fears of more by the de facto central bank to stabilise
the spot rate may have convinced some traders to sqaure Hong Kong
dollar positions.
    Many traders had expected its rare show of strength to be
short-lived. Although the territory's economy is showing signs of
picking up, the rebound has been patchy.
    "This move could just be profit taking by some people who had
long Hong Kong dollar positions at the HK$7.78 level.
   


 After it
strengthened to around HK$7.71, they may have decided to just
take profits," said Eddie Wong, chief strategist for Asia at ABN
AMRO.
    The Hong Kong dollar climbed to HK$7.7020 last Friday, its
strongest level since the 1997/98 Asian financial crisis,
triggered by a call by industrialised countries for more flexible
exchange rates, strong fund inflows into the surging stock market
 and by hopes that the long ailing economy was in a sustainable
recovery.
    The discount on Hong Kong dollar forwards sharply narrowed on
Wednesday afternoon, suggesting that investors are betting that
the local currency will not appreciate by as much as they were
expecting it to earlier in the day.
 
    The one-year Hong Kong dollar forwards narrowed to -180/-160
late on Wednesday from -410/-395 late on Tuesday.
    "There was some outright purchases from fund houses in the
spot and forwards markets," one trader said.
    "Some investors booked profits after the one-year forwards
fell to a discount of -400. A narrowing in discount of yuan NDFs
also helped the market," the dealer added.
     Hong Kong dollar forwards had been moving toward a discount
   

when the local currency suddenly rose on September 22, after a   

statement from the Group of Seven industrial nations urging   

exchange rate flexibility.   

Forwards fell into a deeper discount early on Tuesday in   

tandem with yuan NDFs on persistent speculation of a revaluation   

of the Chinese yuan.   

"Market jitters alleviated as Chinese Premier Wen Jiabao said   

China would keep its yuan exchange rate stable," another dealer   

from a European bank said.    


 
    One-year yuan NDFs           were dealt at -4,500 points
compared with -5,300 points late on Tuesday.
    China manages the yuan in a 8.27-8.28 per dollar range, which
   

other countries have criticised as too weak, saying it gives   

China an unfair trade advantage. Hong Kong's economy is   

increasingly integrated with mainland China's.   

Dealers said speculation on a move in the yuan has   

intensified ahead of the APEC leaders summit in Bangkok later   

this month, in which the region's currency policies, especially   

those of China, are expected to be raised.    


 
    The sharp correction in the spot and forwards markets pushed
up interbank rates.
    The three- and six-month interbank rates were bid at 0.37 and
0.50 percent respectively in late afternoon, compared with 0.21

title: FOCUS - HKMA says  currency  board to stay, banks safe.
text:
LONDON, Sept 1 (Reuters) - Hong Kong is determined to keep its currency board system and will continue to defend its U.S. dollar currency peg against speculative attack, the deputy head of the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) said on Tuesday. 

 HKMA deputy chief executive David Carse said he saw no threat to the solvency of Hong Kong's banks despite a sharp fall in profits in the first quarter of 1998. 

 "We remain determined to maintain the currency board system and the current link between the Hong Kong dollar and the U.S. dollar," Carse said in a briefing to a mainly banking audience in London. "There is absolutely no question about that." 

 Abandoning the currency board system, under which the territory's local monetary base must be matched by foreign currency reserves, would provoke huge capital flight, he said. 

 "We are prepared to accept the pain that a currency board system imposes," he said. 

 Under the currency board, interest rates automatically rise if demand for Hong Kong dollars falls. This in turn cramps economic growth and hits property and stock market prices. 

 Carse said the Hong Kong dollar, pegged at 7.8 to the U.S. unit since 1983, had suffered four distinct waves of speculative attack since October 1997 as financial crisis gripped Asia. 

 This had led to extreme interest rate volatility and a higher country risk premium for Hong Hong, with the margin of the one-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR) over the one-month U.S. dollar London Interbank Offered Rate (LIBOR) averaging more than 200 percentage points since mid-1997, he said. 

 In the most recent attack, investors sold short Hong Kong stocks and offloaded Hong Kong dollars in a deliberate ploy to force up interest rates and thus push share prices lower. 

 The HKMA has responded by buying stocks and futures contracts to try to thwart the speculators, spending an estimated HK$100 billion ($12.8 billion) or more. 

 The Hang Seng Index lost just under three percent of its value on Tuesday to close at 7,062.47, compared with a high of around 16,800 points in August 1997. 

 The HKMA had not intervened on the stock and futures markets on Monday or Tuesday, but was willing to repeat such action if needed, Carse said. 

 "We will come back into the market if it is necessary in order to frustrate this kind of speculation, but we're not going to put any figures on it," he said. 

 "We don't believe it's a breach of Hong Kong's free market and non-interventionist principles. If anything, our markets have been too free and too easily exploited by people who are not prepared to play by the rules of the game." 

 Hong Kong's futures exchange on Saturday announced new rules that would penalise holders of large long and short positions. 

 Although Hong Kong's banking sector was suffering badly from flat lending volumes, lower interest margins and a rise in bad debts, it was still in better shape than banks in other crisis-hit Asian countries such as Indonesia or Thailand, Carse said. 

 Hong Kong banks' profits fell by an average of 25 to 30 percent in the first half of 1998, but all remained in profit, he said. 

 Non-performing loans rose sharply to 2.97 percent of the total at the end of June from 1.8 percent at the end of December 1997, he said. 

 "Obviously problem loans are rising in Hong Kong...(but) while asset quality is clearly deteriorating it is not collapsing as it has done in the rest of the region," he said. 

 "The banks remain highly capitalised and liquid. What we're facing is a profitability issue, not a solvency issue. The banks have the strength to manage their way through the current difficulties." ((London Newsroom +44 171 542 6414, fax 583 7239, uk.emergingmarkets.news@reuters.com)).

title: HK stocks braced for sharp fall after Wall St drop.
text:
HONG KONG, Sept 1 (Reuters) - Hong Kong stocks are braced for another sharp slide on Tuesday as the market faces the aftermath of a dramatic fall on Wall Street possibly without any support from government buying, brokers said. 

 "We have a dual scenario. One has the Hong Kong Monetary Authority coming in and keeping the market relatively stable and the other has market forces just playing around with it," said Kent Rossiter, institutional sales manager at Nikko Securities. 

 "I am kind of tempted to say that despite the fact that at some point I do think the HKMA is going to come back in, they should be less concerned about the level of the market as with the pressure on the (Hong Kong) dollar," he said. 

 The Dow industrials suffered their second-largest point loss overnight, tumbling 512.61 points, or 6.37 percent, to 7,539.07 points, rattled by worries about the global economy. 

 Following the drop, the Nikkei 225 was down 378 points, or 2.68 percent, at 13,730 on Tuesday morning. 

 The Hong Kong market is vulnerable to a sharp correction, having been bolstered by government intervention over the last two weeks. Some brokers expect the Hang Seng Index to return to pre-intervention levels of about 6,500 points. 

 "Hong Kong could certainly visit the underside of 7,000 today," said Rossiter. 

 As the government retreated from the market on Monday, the Hang Seng Index plummeted 554.70 points, or 7.08 percent, to close at 7,275.04. 

 "It will be down again two or three hundred points," said Geoff Galbraith, vice president institutional sales at DBS Securities. 

 Adding to the bad news, Standard & Poor's on Monday lowered Hong Kong's long-term foreign currency sovereign credit rating to A from A-plus and cut Hong Kong's short-term foreign currency rating to A-1 from A-1 plus. 

 It said the downgrades reflected a decline in Hong Kong's financial flexibility due to the growing domestic impact of East Asia's recession, which was likely to persist through 1999, as well as the large official purchases in the local equity and futures markets. 

 But Galbraith expected an orderly decline on Tuesday since investors had taken advantage of massive government intervention on Friday to sell their holdings which would reduce further selling pressure. "All the people in the short term have sold already so there is not going to be too much volume," he said.

title: WRAP: Volatile Mkts, Govt  Intervention  Raise Concern In HK
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--The Hang Seng Index was rattled by the collapse of share prices worldwide, including a severe decline on Wall Street overnight, and news that Standard & Poor's had downgraded Hong Kong's sovereign rating. 

 But a wave of short-covering in the stock and stock futures market - some of it believed to have been generated by the government - kept the benchmark index from diving to new lows Tuesday and helped ease a fall in September Hang Seng Index futures. 

 The benchmark Hang Seng Index fell only 212.57 points, or 2.9%, to close at 7062.47 in a volatile session. It moved between 6982.43 and 7306.40 points Tuesday. The September Hang Seng futures contract closed at 6810, down 190 points, narrowing its even steeper discount from just a few days ago. 

 Analysts said Tuesday's market activity indicated the government seems to be winning its war against speculators, as open interest in the futures markets has been falling in the past few days. But many continue to criticize the government's intervention, saying Hong Kong markets are no longer free. 

 Late Tuesday afternoon, money market dealers said the overnight Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate fell sharply to 6% from 19% earlier in the day amid signs of government intervention. Dealers said Hongkong & Shanghai Banking Corp. was pumping liquidity in the market on behalf of the government to drive rates lower and take pressure off the spot Hong Kong dollar and the local currency peg. 

 Neither the quasi-central bank nor Hongkong Bank would comment on market activities.

title: China/HKMA-2: Reiterates Support For HK's Stk Mkt Measures
text:
BEIJING (Dow Jones)--China is fully supportive of the Hong KongMonetary Authority's recent market intervention, said Zhu Bangzao, spokesman of the Chinese Foreign Ministry. 

 He told reporters Tuesday that Hong Kong has autonomy in financial affairs but that "the Chinese government has reiterated on many occasions that it supports Hong Kong's effort to safeguard its stock market." 

 Authorities in Hong Kong have directed government buying of stocks, stock futures and the local currency in recent weeks to drive out speculators. title: Mkt Yawns/HK Downgrade -2: Govt Hits Back At Criticism
text:
S&P joined the chorus of criticism leveled at the Hong Kong Monetary Authority for using the territory's foreign exchange reserves to intervene in local stock and futures markets. 

 "Intervention by the HKMA in the stock market last week changes the mix of financial assets backing the Hong Kong dollar. By some estimates, the HKMA has already spent up to US$15 billion buying shares and futures as part of an increasingly complex, and risky, strategy to deter speculative pressure on the currency," S&P said. 

 "As bearish sentiment against the Hong Kong dollar shows no signs of abating, further share purchases could follow. Once these operations cease, however, HKMA's portfolio likely will suffer significant losses unless the downward trend in global equity prices is reversed," the ratings agency added. 

 The government, for its part, said in a statement that it "does not find S&P's decision to downgrade the credit ratings of Hong Kong justified." 

 "Government's intervention into the stocks and futures markets is to deter manipulation in these markets by speculators who are attacking the Hong Kong dollar at the same time," it added. 

 Debt market players say it's still a bad strategy. 

 "Now, everything the government is doing is wrong," said a Hong Kong-based trader who, like most of his colleagues, requested anonymity when commenting on the government's recent activity.

title: Hong Kong Alters Strategy In Its Battle With Speculators
text:
NEW YORK -(Dow Jones)- Adding a new wrinkle to the Hong Kong government's high-profile battle against speculators who are trying to force a devaluation of the Hong Kong dollar, the government elected not to intervene in the stock and futures markets Monday. 

 Instead, the government introduced restrictions over the weekend on certain types of currency and futures trading, mostly in the areas of short-selling and stock borrowing. With the new measures, speculators suddenly found it more expensive to bet against Hong Kong markets. 

 Meanwhile Monday, Standard & Poor's lowered its credit and currency ratings for the former British colony. The new ratings - to single-A/A-1 from single-A-plus/A-1-plus for Hong Kong's short-term and long-term debt and to single-A-plus/A-1 from double-A-minus/A-1-plus on the Hong Kong dollar - reflect the growing domestic impact of the Asian financial crisis and the government's recent activity in local equity and futures markets, S&P said. 

 Under new rules governing the futures exchange, market players will have to come up with more cash when buying or selling more than 10,000 futures contracts. In addition, members will have to report and identify anyone holding 250 contracts or more. Previously, the reporting level had been 500 contracts, and market players could remain anonymous. 

 For the past two weeks, the Hong Kong government used foreign-exchange reserves to buy stocks and futures in addition to propping up the Hong Kong dollar as part of a complex defense against speculators who want to sever the local currency's link to the U.S. dollar. The government - through the Hong Kong Monetary Authority - spent billions of dollars worth of foreign-exchange reserves to buy blue-chip stocks, Hang Seng Index futures and the local currency. Many estimate the government spent as much as 110 billion Hong Kong dollars ($14.19 billion) in the two weeks. 

 However, analysts said the action exposed the currency market's vulnerabilities. Critics say the move has provided speculators with exactly the kind of tactical information they need to try something new. And there was even louder criticism for the cost of the effort. Traders estimate that firms acting for the government spent about $9 billion Friday buying mostly blue-chip stocks, attempting to overcome the global tide of falling markets. Altogether, the government has spent as much as 20% of its hard-currency reserves to protect the currency. 

 Because Hong Kong's currency is tethered to the U.S. dollar under a modified version of a currency board, interest rates will rise when the Hong Kong dollar is sold. So the recent speculative attacks on the currency have put pressure on the Hong Kong stock market. 

 Armed with the knowledge that higher rates will hurt the stock market, speculators have first sold short stock futures and then sold Hong Kong dollars. Selling short involves the sale of borrowed shares or currency. The speculators profit by buying back their stock futures at a lower price to repay the lender, after the currency's decline sparks a rise in interest rates and a decline in the stock market. 

 Because the goverment sat out Monday's session, the Hang Seng fell 554.70 points, or 7.1%, to close at 7275.04. 

 The decision to not intervene is noteworthy because Hong Kong financial secretary Donald Tsang Yam-kuen last week hinted the government would continue the buying. And Tung Chee-hwa, the territory's chief executive, on Friday suggested that China might contribute its reserves to the expanding struggle. Wang Zuebing, chairman of the state-owned Bank of China, said he supported Hong Kong's intervention. 

 The battle in Hong Kong's financial markets underscores a deepening slump in this business capital's economy. Friday, officials said the economy contracted 5% during the second quarter, the worst-ever recorded quarterly decline, and one that made it official that Hong Kong is in a recession. Government economists predicted the economy will shrink 4% for the year, which would be the first annual decline since at least 1961, the year Hong Kong began keeping economic statistics.

title: ASIA  FOREX  - Regionals withstand stronger dollar.
text:
0925 GMT - Asian regional currencies were mostly steady as 

 the dollar remained capped below 142 yen after rising on news 

 that North Korea had fired a missile into the Sea of Japan. 

     The dollar rebounded sharply from a nine-month low of 1.73 

 marks ahead of the Russian Duma's debate on the nomination of 

 Viktor Chernomyrdin as Prime Minister, due to begin at 1100 

 GMT. 

 President Boris Yeltsin's parliamentary envoy said Russia's 

 lower house of parliament was likely to reject Chernomyrdin's 

 confirmation vote. 

 The dollar had earlier come under heavy pressure against 

 the mark and Swiss franc as operators bailed out of long 

 positions amid signs Russia's leaders might be able to reach a 

 compromise, which would allow the government to deal with the 

 stricken economy. 

 *** But regional markets were more focused on a steep seven 

 percent drop in Hong Kong's blue chip Hang Seng Index and 

 Malaysia's planned measures to cope with its first recession in 

 13 years. 

 The ringgit was well off its lows in thin offshore trade, 

 with Malaysian markets closed for the National Day holiday, and 

 overseas players speculating on the possible imposition of some 

 form of capital controls. 

 The Kuala Lumpur Stock Exchange called a news conference 

 for 0900 GMT and government officials said a special cabinet 

 meeting would be held on Tuesday morning to discuss economic 

 measures. 

 Rumours swirling through forex markets ranged from 

 speculation Malaysia might impose a two-tier foreign exchange

 system to renewed talk Finance Minister Anwar Ibrahim planned 

 to resign. 

 The official Bernama news agency quoted Anwar as denying 

 that he was tendering his resignation or that he would resign 

 on Friday. 

 *** Hong Kong's stock market ended sharply lower as the 

 government retreated somewhat from its recent aggressive 

interventions. 

 But the Hong Kong dollar firmed in both spot and forward 

 markets as the overnight interbank rate jumped on a sharp 

 increase in demand for short-term funds after the Hong Kong 

 Futures Exchange said it would levy a margin surcharge. 

 On Saturday, the HKFE imposed a 150 percent margin 

 surcharge on large Hang Seng futures positions above 10,000 

 contracts. 

 *** In Thailand, the baht was off its lows, with traders 

 brushing off news that the country's trade surplus narrowed to 

 $928 million in June from $949 million in May, and compared 

 with a $920 million deficit in June last year. 

     Imports were down a massive 35.9 percent year-on-year, 

 while exports dipped some three percent. 

     The current account surplus narrowed to a preliminary $853 

 million in June from $1.01 billion in May and a $870 million 

 deficit last June. 

     *** The Korean won weakened on heavy corporate dollar 

 demand ahead of import settlements early next month, with 

 dealers shrugging off the central bank's announcement that it 

 would cut the rediscount rate by 200 basis points to three 

 percent in a bid to boost the economy. 

 Dealers said the impact of the North Korean missile news 

 was limited, as were growing expectations that an international 

 auction for ailing Kia Motors and sister firm Asia Motors would 

 be cancelled after bidders demanded better terms on the firms' 

 mountains of debt. 

 *** The Singapore dollar briefly fell to the wrong side of 

 1.78 to the U.S. dollar following a local newspaper report 

 quoting eight private-sector forecasters saying it could drop 

 as low as 1.85 by year-end. 

 Dealers said the Sing dollar was likely to remain under 

 pressure from a perception that Singapore authorities might be 

 willing to tolerate further weakness in the domestic dollar and 

 fears oil-rich Brunei, which pegs its dollar to the Sing, might 

 be facing financial difficulty.

title: Taiwan says won't tap reserves to shore up stocks.
text:
TAIPEI, Aug 31 (Reuters) - Taiwan's central bank on Monday again ruled out using foreign exchange reserves to shore up the stock market, saying the island's mountainous reserves could be mobilised only to defend the currency. 

 "It's unlikely we would use our foreign exchange reserves to hold the stock market despite its recent declines," bank vice governor Hsu Yi-hsiung said after the financial markets closed. 

 Hsu spoke in response to unconfirmed media reports that funds linked to U.S. financer George Soros had turned to Taiwan after being rebuffed in Hong Kong, where the government has supported the stock market with a huge buying campaign. 

 Hsu said Taiwan's financial system differed from that of Hong Kong and that the island's reserves would be used only in the foreign exchange market. 

 Taiwan's foreign exchange stockpile, ranking among the world's 10 largest, stood at US$83.607 at the end of July. 

 Hong Kong is thought to have used one-seventh of its US$90 billion-plus hoard of reserves and land funds in a blistering and uncharacteristic defence of its stock market. 

 Hong Kong financial officials said the defence aimed to thwart speculative international funds from manipulating the stock market to undermine the Hong Kong dollar. 

 State intervention to protect Taiwan's stock market is an open secret, and Hsu declined to specify how this is done. 

 Brokers say Taipei typically deploys major funds under its control, including pension and labour insurance funds, to buy stocks in the face of what its officials deem unwarranted selling. 

 The most conspicuous recent example came in early 1996 when intimidating war games and missile tests mounted by Taiwan's arch rival, communist China, sent Taiwan investors fleeing the stock market and currency for the safety of U.S. dollars. 

 The central bank rolled out Taiwan's reserves to defend the Taiwan dollar, but the finance ministry and other organs set up separate emergency funds that were deployed to keep a floor under the sagging stock market. 

 Since Asia's financial crisis erupted in mid-1997, Taiwan's index has fallen some 27 percent and state-linked buying became active in the past week as it has tumbled to 22-month lows. 

 Shock over Hong Kong's seven percent tumble on Monday sent Taiwan's index for a 2.76 percent slide to 6,550.11, its lowest close since October 1996. 

 Hsu said it was relatively unlikely for international speculators to attack Taiwan given its stronger economic fundamentals and floating exchange rate. 

Central bank foreign exchange director Chou Ah-ting said on Monday he was confident international speculators would find little quarter to attack Taiwan's markets. 

 "Don't be scared by Soros. The central bank does not fear him," Chou said. 

 Chou said central bank checks found no obvious presence of funds controlled by Soros or other funds in Taiwan's forex market - despite rumours to this effect. 

 In any case, they were unwelcome in Taiwan, he said. 

 "The central bank will stringently monitor the foreign exchange market so that such speculators will find no quarter to operate here," Chou said. ((Taipei newsroom, +886 2 2508-0815 fax +886 2 2508-0204, taipei.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: China says would help HK defend  currency  if asked.
text:
BEIJING, Aug 31 (Reuters) - A Chinese central bank official said on Monday Beijing would help Hong Kong defend its currency against speculators only if requested, but declined to say if assistance had already been offered. 

 "The Chinese government will help to stabilise the Hong Kong dollar only at the request of the Hong Kong government," said a spokesman for the People's Bank of China, the central bank. 

 The spokesman declined to comment when asked if Beijing had joined the Hong Kong government's unprecedented effort to defeat speculators through market intervention. 

 China's foreign exchange reserves of $140 billion could be a crucial weapon in the fight to defend the Hong Kong currency's peg with the U.S. dollar. 

 Rumours have been swirling around Hong Kong markets that Beijing may have committed some of its cash to help the territory's government, which is thought to have spent more than HK$100 billion ($12.8 billion) over the past two weeks buying stocks and futures contracts to thwart speculators. 

 A second central bank official said China had been helping Hong Kong support its currency against the biggest threat since the peg was introduced in 1983, but not through direct intervention in the markets. 

 Beijing's aid took the form of expanding credit to Hong Kong companies through branches of Chinese state-owned banks in the territory, where they are significant players. 

 "China began to take part in the campaign to jointly defend the Hong Kong dollar at the end of last year," said the official, who spoke on condition of anonymity. 

 "Hong Kong's economy has been severely hit by the Asian financial crisis and its currency is also under heavy attack, but it still appears stable," he said. 

 Li Guobin, a top economist with the State Council Information Centre, said Beijing's pledge not to devalue its yuan was already a big prop for Hong Kong's currency and would stay that way because a stable yuan was in China's interest. 

 "There shouldn't be a problem of yuan devaluation before the year 2000," he told Reuters. 

 Asked whether the Hong Kong government needed help from Beijing, Li said: "The Hong Kong government is fully capable of handling its own problem." 

 However, he added: "Premier Zhu Rongji has made it clear that Beijing would help Hong Kong at the request of the Hong Kong government." 

 China regained sovereignty over Hong Kong on July 1, 1997, and is committed to allowing the former British colony a high degree of autonomy under a policy of "one country, two systems". 

 However, a collapse of economic confidence in the capitalist enclave would be a serious blow to China's prestige. 

 Li said the fate of the Hong Kong dollar, the only Asian currency beside the Chinese yuan to withstand the region's financial meltdown, was in the hands of Hong Kong's people. 

 "I don't think the Hong Kong dollar will devalue unless Hong Kongers dump Hong Kong dollars," he said. 

 Li said the Hong Kong government and Hong Kong-based enterprises, the main holders of Hong Kong dollars, would not sell Hong Kong dollars at the moment because devaluation was not in their interest. 

 In comments carried by official media on Sunday, Li lashed out at international fund companies attacking the Hong Kong currency, calling them "liars with an axe to grind". 

 (US$1=HK$7.8).

title: Credit Suisse/HK$ Overvalued -2: No Recovery For 3 Years
text:
"I see no recovery, at least in the next three years," Tao said. 

 Unemployment will climb to 7.0% this year and 9.0% next year, he said. 

 Removing the Hong Kong dollar from circulation and exchanging it at a fixed value for U.S. dollars is both practicable and advisable for Hong Kong. 

 "This is probably the neatest way for Hong Kong to get out of trouble," he said. 

 Tao said he has presented his report to a wide range of investors in recent weeks, and "they all listened very carefully." 

 He said Credit Suisse First Boston is also trying to present the ideas in the report to the government, which has been intervening heavily in markets in recent weeks to defend the Hong Kong dollar peg. 

 He said he would hope the government would exchange Hong Kong dollars for the U.S. dollar at the current peg rate of HK$7.80 per U.S. dollar. Interest rates would fall to levels comparable to U.S. interest rates, though with a slight Hong Kong premium attached. 

 The idea of dollarization is that it would remove one variable and stress point slowing Hong Kong's recovery - currency risk - Tao said. 

 With the U.S. dollar in circulation, investors and the government would only have to worry about asset values. 

 Tao said he would recommend a move to dollarize the economy over the next 24 months, but that any move would have to be initiated by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority. 

 Were the economy to be dollarized, the HKMA would lose much of the power it now wields, Tao noted.
