title: HK Early Hibor Edges Dn, Banks Await Govt  Intervention
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--Shorter-term Hong Kong interbank rates have edged only slightly lower early Monday from the previous session as banks wait to see if the Hong Kong government will repeat last week's aggressive market intervention. 

 Longer-term rates, however, are creeping upward on borrowing from corporates, money market dealers said, while one dealer with a major foreign institution attributed the increased Hong Kong dollar borrowing to large investment banks. 

 The volatile overnight Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate is quoted between 18-19%, down a touch from 20% late Friday; the benchmark three-month rate is 15-16%, from last Friday's 16%. 

 Bankers said that short-term rates will likely remain at high levels in quiet trading as banks keep lending to a minimum as they wait to see whether the government will return to the markets. They're also nervously eying the Hang Seng Index, which has plunged by more than 400 points so far Monday, without government intervention to support it. 

 Lending in the six-month and one-year money markets is more active on investment bank borrowing, said the dealer. However, another money market dealer with a European bank described the longer-term borrowing as normal corporate activity. 

 The six-month Hibor is quoted at 16.5%, compared with 14% late Friday. The one-year rate is quoted at 13.5%, from 13% Friday. 

 On Friday, the government is believed to have spent up to HK$70.0 billion and billions more in the two weeks before that, to thwart currency speculators. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority hasn't pumped liquidity into extremely tight money markets in several weeks, in order to avoid giving banks money to fund speculators. 

 Early Monday, the Hong Kong dollar is quoted at HK$7.7435 per U.S. dollar, stronger than the HK$7.7495 recorded late Friday. 

 It's unclear whether banks will ease lending in the short-term or whether the activity in longer-term money markets will continue, dealers said. 

 "It really depends on the government," said a Treasury head with a foreign bank. "I can't predict (interbank) rates."

title: Hong Kong stock market war far from over - analysts.
text:
HONG KONG, Aug 28 (Reuters) - The Hong Kong government claimed victory on Friday in its battle against speculators but analysts said the war was not finished yet. 

 "This battle is far from over," Peter Perkins, regional equity strategist at Daiwa Institute of Research told Reuters Television. 

 "We are going to wake up Monday morning and the speculators or purported speculators and the government are still going to be going at it." 

 The Hang Seng Index dropped 93.23 points, or 1.18 percent, on Friday to end at 7,829.74. 

 Turnover reached a record HK$79.0 billion ($10.5 billion), trouncing the previous high of HK$46.02 billion set on August 29, 1997, as the government continued its aggressive buying spree. 

 The blue chip index has risen 17.56 percent since the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) started to buy stocks and index futures on August 14 to fend off currency speculators. 

 Brokers estimated the government has spent more than HK$100 billion in the past two weeks, using its ammunition to drive out speculators ahead of the expiry of the August Hang Seng Index futures contract on Friday. 

 "We have frustrated their plan," said Financial Secretary Donald Tsang. 

 But speculators were still on the warpath, analysts said. 

 The government was successful in squeezing some speculators by widening the gap between the August and September futures contracts, making it costly to roll over positions. 

 The HKMA was also seen tightening money market liquidity to make borrowing more costly. 

 But some investors were still betting that the market would sink to lower depths after the August futures expiry, doubting the government's ability to hold up the index, analysts said. 

 Some bears had rolled over their short positions in the August contract into September despite high costs and short selling on individual stocks amounted to HK$7.26 billion on Friday, compared to an already high HK$1.73 billion on Thursday. 

 But analysts raised a warning finger, saying the government was likely to do the unexpected to keep speculators on their toes. On Monday, the wide gap between the cash and futures market was expected to shrink to prevent heavy arbitrage. 

 The September contract closed on Friday at a hefty discount to the cash market, shedding 400 points to 7,210. 

 "Either the cash market comes down or the futures contract goes up, but either way there will be a narrowing of that spread," said Steven Thompson, chief analyst at Nikko Research Center. He said the government would probably cover some of its short positions in the September contract to drive up futures. 

 However, its actions had already inflated the Hang Seng Index to artificial levels which did not reflect the poor state of the local economy, analysts said. 

 "They are clearly being blown off course by problems we are seeing around the world," Mark Simpson, head of Hong Kong research at Nomura International, told Reuters Television. 

 "It is a bit of a living nightmare for both investors and the government at this point," he added. 

 The government said on Friday it was prepared to take further action in the stock and futures market and would follow its heavy intervention with policy measures to enhance Hong Kong's resilience to speculative attacks. 

 "We did not mount the market operations announced a fortnight ago in haste. They were part of an overall strategy to strengthen our financial markets," Tsang told a news conference. 

 "These measures should reduce the need of market intervention once they have been put in place firmly."

title: HK  intervention  hurts rather than helps peg system.
text:
HONG KONG, Aug 28 (Reuters) - The Hong Kong government's intervention in the territory's stock and futures market may imperil the very system it seeks to save - the currency board. 

 "It seems to me that the government's action is evidence of its increasing fears about the consequences of keeping the peg," said Richard Margolis, first vice president, equity research, at Merrill Lynch (Asia Pacific). 

 In the past, authorities' "balance of fear" between the risks of keeping the peg and letting it go clearly was on the side of maintaining the link. 

 "What they've done seems to suggest that the calculation is no longer as solid as it was. And if this process continues, it may be they are moving towards a stage in which the balance would shift in favour of letting (the peg) go," he said. 

 Since 1983, the Hong Kong dollar has been linked to the U.S. dollar at HK$7.8 per US$1 through a currency board system. 

 Repeated speculative attacks on the currency against the backdrop of Asia's financial crisis have kept interest rates at punishingly high levels over the past year. 

 Higher interest rates have sent asset prices reeling. 

 By August 13, the blue-chip Hang Seng Index had fallen almost 60 percent from its peak in August 1997. 

 On August 14, the government took action against what it called a "double play" game by speculators - who had sold the currency not because Hong Kong was fundamentally weak or even because they had a perverse desire to break the peg - but to take advantage of the currency board system. 

 Under the currency board, pressures for a weaker Hong Kong dollar automatically cause rates to increase and vice versa. 

 By selling the currency, speculators could be sure interest rates would rise and could be fairly certain share prices would fall, which meant easy profits on short stock positions. 

 Analysts initially greeted the move with scepticism and the view has become increasingly negative as the days go by. 

 "The idea behind this was to take some of the pressure off interest rates because they regarded some of the pressure to be unjustified and caused by speculators, and on that basis (Hong Kong authorities) haven't succeeded," Margolis said. 

 "And if you arrive at the conclusion that what you are doing is worse than than allowing the existing mechanism to do its job, then it is best to leave the existing mechanism alone." 

 Hong Kong's leaders have said over and over again that the currency peg was a pillar of strength in a weakened Asia and that it would be maintained, even if higher interest rates resulted in painfully lower asset prices. 

 But now the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) is propping up share prices, while also intervening heavily in the money markets to squeeze speculators needing to fund short positions. 

 Last month, the HKMA bypassed the currency board system by purchasing Hong Kong dollars for the treasury to fund a fiscal shortfall. The action was perfectly legitimate, but nevertheless raised questions about the monetary authority's motives. 

 "The strategy they are pursuing basically takes the peg off autopilot and makes the credibility of the peg a function of the intervention abilities of the HKMA, rather than a system that is self-enforcing and self-sustaining," said Cliff Tan, foreign exchange strategist at Warburg Dillon Read. 

 Lehman Brothers economist Rob Subbaraman said the stock market intervention set a bad precedent. "It's not how a currency board was meant to operate," he said. 

 "Either the HKMA is geared on punishing speculators and that's its pure motive. Or it can be a sign that the HKMA is becoming desperate," Subbaraman said. 

 "The economy is weakening and they can't afford to put up interest rates and let the currency board operate fully because they are afraid if the stock market falls, it could cause the banks to get into trouble. And of course the ultimate way for the peg to be unravelled is through a banking crisis," he said. 

 In the end, the action would raise Hong Kong's risk premium because of uncertainty about whether the government would intervene. And that would not be good for the peg. 

 One economist at a European investment bank said that before the intervention he believed the peg was sufficiently de-politicised to be self-sustaining. But that has changed. 

 "Now when I get up in the morning, I won't be saying that the Hong Kong dollar is foolproof. I'll be thinking, what is going on externally? What's happening in the domestic economy? And are these things pushing enough of the HKMA's buttons that they will actually break the peg?"

title: HK  intervention  not a factor in credit review - S&P.
text:
HONG KONG, Aug 27 (Reuters) - Rating agency Standard and Poor's Corp said on Thursday Hong Kong's intervention in the equity cash and futures markets was not having a significant impact on its review of the territory's credit rating. 

 S&P Managing Director for Hong Kong Paul Coughlin said depressed conditions in the Asian region and their effect on the Hong Kong economy through its U.S. dollar-linked exchange rate were more likely to lead to a downgrade than the actions of the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA). 

 "If the conditions in the region persist, you would expect the disinflation to be transmitted through the peg into the Hong Kong economy," Coughlin said in an interview aired on Reuters Television on Thursday. 

 "What the Hong Kong Monetary Authority is doing now doesn't affect that one way or another," he said. 

 The HKMA began intervening in the equity cash and futures markets on August 14 in an effort to force speculators to abandon short stock positions. 

 Its action has drawn heavy criticism from market participants who fear the new interventionist stance has scared away genuine investment in the battered markets of Hong Kong. 

 S&P's Coughlin said the agency was more concerned with the big picture than daily market operations. 

 "I don't think we necessarily get overly focused or overly sort of fixated on a single tactic," he said. 

 Disinflation, a slowing down of the rate at which prices increase, has been evident in Hong Kong, where consumer prices are rising at the slowest rate in 12 years. 

 Meanwhile, Hong Kong asset prices are crumbling, with both property and share prices off about 50 percent from 1997 peaks. 

 And Coughlin warned that as disinflation moved more deeply through the economy affecting nominal wages, then "the capacity (of people) to repay loans to the banks themselves could be more significantly impacted," causing greater stress in the financial sector, he said. 

 Coughlin said the Hong Kong dollar's linked exchange rate with the U.S. dollar could be the key conduit of disinflation. 

 As pressures on the currency mount, interest rates automatically rise through the currency board system, dampening economic growth and keeping price increases at bay. 

 He said S&P is examining "to what extent the peg and its effect are fundamentally undermining the considerable strengths of Hong Kong's corporate and banking sectors." 

 S&P put Hong Kong on CreditWatch with negative implications on June 22.

title: Asia Crisis At A Glance:Tokyo Stks Plunge On Global Worries
text:

As Hong Kong's government continues its intervention, it has targeted a wider range of stocks to include all the blue-chip constituents of the Hang Seng Index, traders said.

title: Economists Warn HK$ Peg In Danger If  Intervention  Continues
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--The Hong Kong dollar peg's days are numbered if the government continues to intervene in local markets, more and more economists warn. 

 As recently as a year ago, it was sacrilegious here to discuss the fall of Hong Kong's currency board. Last October, legislator and businessman James Tien Pei-chun was castigated by the government and, under pressure from fellow business people, retracted suggestions that it was time to rethink the peg. 

 But the government's repeated intervention in local currency and stock markets has caused a massive change in local sentiment, with many analysts now talking openly about the peg's imminent downfall. 

 "The peg's a goner," says Christopher Wood, a global and Asian strategist at Santander Investment Securities Asia Ltd. in Hong Kong. "My view is that it's likely to go by the end of the year." 

 Many economists say the demise of the 15-year-old U.S. dollar link is being hastened every time the Hong Kong Monetary Authority spends money in the stock, stock futures and foreign exchange markets to defend it. They argue that intervening in Hong Kong's markets is counter-productive because it prevents the currency board system from functioning properly. 

 Some even speculate that Hong Kong Chief Executive Tung Chee-hwa will use an Oct. 15 policy speech to unveil a new currency arrangement, despite the government's repeated statements that it will defend the peg at nearly any cost. 

 Jim Mellon, chairman of hedge fund specialist Regent Pacific Holdings (H.RPG), says the peg could go before the end of the year, with a devaluation of the Chinese yuan acting as a catalyst for its demise. Although he says the latest market intervention has succeeded in driving away speculators, he warns intervention doesn't solve some basic problems Hong Kong is experiencing. 

 The essence of a currency board is a governmental surrender of monetary control, letting markets determine interest rates, Wood notes. If speculators sell the currency, interest rates rise and asset prices fall, eventually attracting buyers back into the currency.

title: Barclays Capital urges caution on HK firms' bonds.
text:
HONG KONG, Aug 26 (Reuters) - Barclays Capital said on Wednesday it was reversing its earlier positive stance toward bond issues of Hong Kong firms and urging investors to refrain from entering the market. 

 "Many Hong Kong bonds appear cheap based on their apparent creditworthiness," Barclays said in a report. 

 "The recent moves from the HKMA (Hong Kong Monetary Authority) and trends in emerging markets in general, though, skew the probabilities toward further widening of bond spreads," it said. 

 Offshore bonds of Hong Kong issuers were investment grade but nevertheless had been trading as if they were at a high risk of default, Barclays said. 

 For example, Wharf Holdings BBB-plus/Baa3 rated bond due in March 2003 was trading at 900 basis points over comparable U.S. Treasuries. 

 Hutchison Whampoa's Single-A/A3 bond due August 2007 was trading at 425 basis points over the benchmark. 

 "Many Hong Kong companies remain strong credits and can withstand severe downturns in the economy. However, fundamentals do not appear to matter at the moment," Barclays said. 

 Despite the Hong Kong government's recent efforts to deter attacks on the currency by intervening in stock, futures and curency markets, further currency attacks were likely, it said 

 "Recent events in Russia and growing pressure on Venezuela's bolivar will encourage currency speculators that the Hong Kong dollar too is a vulnerable target," Barclays said. 

 "Some even see the HKMA's recent actions as 'desperate', signalling increased prospects of a weaker currency," it said. 

 If pressure continues on the Hong Kong dollar, interest rates would remain high, slowing the economy further and making local currency debt more difficult to service. 

 This would hurt most Hong Kong issuers, which in turn could face further spread widening on their offshore bonds. 

 Bonds also were likely to suffer once the HKMA stopped supporting the stock market because of the strong relationship between Hong Kong stocks and bonds. 

 "The HKMA cannot intervene in the stock market ad infinitum. Therefore, there is a danger that when it does stop supporting the stock market, the index could slump, irrespective of the currency and interest rates," Barclays said. 

 Barclays said the first step in a sustained contraction in Hong Kong bond spreads would be the perception of greater currency certainty. The second would be falling interest rates. 

 If currency attacks abate, Hong Kong's currency board would ensure that interest rates fell, Barlclays said. 

 If the peg were abandoned, short-term rates might initially spike to offset capital flows, but would ease several months later, it said. 

 "We believe when currency and interest rate views stabilise, it will provide attractive entry levels for the top Hong Kong credits with only limited downside risk," it said.

title: AWSJ: HKMA  Intervention  Creates Ripples: Fund Managers
text:
From Thursday's Asian Wall Street Journal 


   By Laurie Lande


 HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--As the Hong Kong Monetary Authority continues buying blue-chip stocks to ward off currency speculators, some local fund managers say they'd rather stay away from these shares than guess where the HKMA is going to jump in next. 

 "It really is a guessing game," says Nick Cringle, senior fund manager at Coutts Bank. "The trend we've seen this week is that they (the HKMA) rotate among batches of stocks for intervention. It makes it difficult for fund managers to decide where there are good buys." As a result, while managers may do some selective buying, there "isn't a huge amount of buying and selling going on." 

 Giampaolo Guarnieri, director of Asia Pacific Equities at Salomon Smith Barney, also says he's trying to stay on the sidelines as long as the government's intervention continues. 

 "We've been cutting our exposure to Hong Kong," he says. "We had started to buy blue chips the week before they intervened. But I'm happy to give away some of my blue chips if there is a willing buyer, and there is - the HKMA." 

 A fair number of fund managers appear to be following this strategy. Notes Terence Mahoney, managing director at TCW Asia, the Asian arm of U.S.-based TCW Funds Management Inc.: "A lot of people were looking to buy the Hang Seng (Index) at the 6000 level, but now that the index is higher, they'll be looking to lighten their load and make a profit," he says. On Wednesday, the index fell 55.69 points to 7834.40. 

 "We're not making any aggressive moves at the moment," adds Henry Tse, investment manager at Indocam Asia Asset Management, which specializes in Hong Kong and China funds. "If prices rise, and we feel certain stocks are overvalued, that may trigger some selling, but there's no point in being too aggressive at this stage as the market could go even higher." 

 Small fund managers are even more likely to stay on the sidelines rather than gamble on where the HKMA will intervene next. Notes Henry Lee, manager at Hendale Asia, "Smaller funds have to be careful ... you end up pushed to the sidelines." 

 A main reason for some managers staying out is the difficulty of making accurate stock valuations in an environment in which government intervention - rather than a company's fundamentals - is moving stock prices. 

 "Traditional analysis may not work in this type of environment, where intervention is distorting the value of blue chips," explains Tse of Indocam.

title: Intervention  no departure from HK principles-Yam.
text:
HONG KONG, Aug 24 (Reuters) - Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) chief Joseph Yam said on Monday there was no contradiction in the government becoming a market player if such intervention was for the good of the economy. 

 In an article in the South China Morning Post, Yam defended the government's intervention in the stock and futures markets this month by citing examples when the government had intervened in the past. 

 "In the monetary and financial systems, there is significant intervention in the form of the regulation of financial markets and the supervision of financial institution," Yam said. 

 "Indeed there are many examples of intervention," he said. 

 The article was the latest to be published in foreign and local newspapers explaining why the government had asked the HKMA to intervene in stock and futures markets to deter speculators. 

 Yam invoked statements by Hong Kong's former financial secretary, Sir Philip Haddon-Cave. 

 Haddon-Cave argued in the late 1970s that intervention was sometimes necessary because "imperfections in the operation of the market mechanism (may lead) to economic inefficiency". 

 Yam said: "Consistent with Sir Philip's view that interventionism should be 'relevant to the maintenance of the economic stability in Hong Kong', and with Exchange Fund Advisory Committee backing, Financial Secretary Donald Tsang made the order to intervene in the free play of market forces." 

 Yam thumbed his nose at critics of the government's action and indicated that speculators were up against an administration that was "run by people who have put Hong Kong on the map as the freest economy in the world". 

 "It is so easy to wave the banner of free markets and condemn any government intervention, and be seen to be righteous and knowledgeable; notwithstanding that the government concerned has been so successfully running the freest economy in the world," Yam said. 

 "But we must be humble and thank those wanting to lecture us on free markets, if only for the purpose of keeping us on our toes," he said in the article punctuated with sarcasm. 

 Yam repeated Hong Kong's resolve at keeping its exchange rate linked with the U.S. dollar. "This resolve has never been stronger," he said. 

 "As the financial storm in this region spreads to almost everywhere now, and with increased intensity, the discipline of currency board arrangements of our linked exchange rate system is our best safeguard for our long term prosperity and stability."

title: ANALYSIS - Govt action in Asia rings alarms.
text:
By Valerie Lee SINGAPORE, Aug 23 (Reuters) - The intervention by some Asian governments to support their stock markets and fend off speculators has received the thumbs-down from most analysts, who say governments should keep clear of markets or risk getting their fingers burned. 

 Investors gave a clear signal late last week, taking profit after sharp rallies in markets in Kuala Lumpur, Hong Kong and Taiwan earlier in the week on talk of official intervention. 

 At the close of trade on Friday, several Asian markets had surrendered the week's gains with Malaysia's key Composite Index tumbling 7.69 percent as investors cashed out. 

 "Obviously, investors will be disappointed because they hate surprise elements and if the governments try to manage the market it is not taken very positively," said Nilesh Jasani, a regional strategist with SG Securities in Singapore. "The alarm bells always go off a bit when you hear about governments propping up the markets because you are never quite sure where the real floor is," said Peter Douglas, Director of Aberdeen Asset Management in Singapore. 

 Analysts said government-backed buying of shares would bring out sellers eager to liquidate their holdings at the expense of the regional authorities. It could also hurt the long-term investor outlook for the markets involved, as risk premiums for these markets would rise, they added. 

 "What is more, you are not addressing the real issues, you are just swirling money around in the economy," said Kevin Gin, a director with Kleinwort Benson Securities. "It's taking money from out of one pocket and putting it into another," he said. 

 In recent weeks, several Asian governments either stepped into their battered share markets as buyers or announced their intention to use public funds to stimulate markets that are drastically weaker than they were before the Asian financial crisis flared up a year ago. Hong Kong started things, repeatedly intervening in stocks and future markets after leader Tung Chee-hwa said the government would step in if speculators attacked the Hong Kong dollar and pushed interest rates higher while holding short stock positions. 

 In Malaysia, Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad said last week that a fund that subsidises the annual pilgrimages of Malaysian Muslims to Saudi Arabia might intervene to buy shares on behalf of the government. 

 Malaysian Deputy Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said the huge Employees' Pension Fund (EPF), could also step in. 

 Taiwan also said its securities watchdog, the Securities and Futures Commission, was drafting various proposals to stabilise the stock market. 

 Investors said the Hong Kong intervention might succeed as the government was not committed to defending a specific level on the key Hang Seng share index. But the win would not come without a price. "It is not coming cheap. What it means is that the government is not going through the mechanism of the currency board," said a European investment house strategist, who declined to be named. 

 "It is going outside it, which means that risk premiums on Hong Kong in future will go up," he said, adding that the country's reputation as perhaps the freest financial market in Asia had been compromised. 

 Another issue was also whether or not the regional authorities had deep enough pockets to sustain their support of the markets as sellers continue to emerge, analysts said. 

 "...the market will cap any artificially generated boost to the asset markets," London-based research house I.D.E.A. said in its regional markets focus on Friday. 

 "In the near-term, some caution may be evident in shorting the indices and the currencies but over a longer time frame (bearish) fundamentals are seen winning through," it said. 

 But at least one investor said regional authorities were entitled to take protective measures. 

 "A government has a social objective at the end of the day. If you are a government, you have been elected, you have a social objective and if investors are getting unreasonable you have to act," said Jean Paolo Guarnieri, a director with Salomon Brothers Asset Management in Hong Kong. 

 "All this excitement from investors against the government intervention is a little bit naive. When you deal in foreign exchange markets around the world, for example, the central bank is always there....the objective of the central bank is not always mercantile," he said.

title: FUND VIEW - Hong Kong cannot turn back Asian tide.
text:
HONG KONG, Aug 23 (Reuters) - Government interventions in the stock market have provided some support for Hong Kong's battered shares, but such moves are no long-term solution to economic woes plaguing the territory and the region, financial analysts said. 

 The government bought shares last week in a bid to foil speculators, pushing up the Hang Seng index and cheering markets in some other beleaguered Asian centres. 

 But the joy was largely short lived as many investors, unsettled by growing weakness in overseas markets, took advantage of the rally to sell their shares and book profits. 

 Hong Kong is expected to renew its battles with speculators this week as it tries to bolster sentiment amid a slew of economic data expected to confirm it is in recession. 

 But analysts said interventions by the territory's government alone could not turn back the Asian tide, despite tough words from Hong Kong Monetary Authority boss Joseph Yam. 

 Yam was correct when he said Asian market declines were an over-reaction that bore no relation to any reasonable assessment of Asia's prospects, said Don Hanna, economist at Goldman Sachs. 

 "But Hong Kong, in itself, can't do much about that," Hanna said. 

 Global markets are showing every sign of becoming more unstable as the Asian crisis drags on, adding to the bearishness in the region, analysts said. 

 Last week, Wall Street started to wobble as some Latin American currencies looked vulnerable and Russia grappled with financial crisis. 

 "I think the government was absolutely right to get involved. Given the peg, they couldn't do anything else," said Chris Tinker, head of regional economics at ING Barings. 

 The Hong Kong dollar is the last currency in Asia linked to the U.S. dollar and the government has vowed to defend the peg. 

 Some speculators are believed to be attacking the dollar in order to reap profits on stocks. 

 They sell stocks and then move to attack the currency. When banks raise interest rates to defend the dollar, corporate profit outlooks and stock prices usually fall. Speculators can then buy back the shares at a much lower price. Hong Kong is now poised for battle with the speculators, with the nearest Hang Seng index futures contract due to expire at the end of the week. 

 It is an important battle, given the uncertainty shaking global markets. There are widespread fears that a break of the Hong Kong dollar peg - considered impossible unless the local populace loses all confidence and switches deposits into other currencies - could have worldwide implications. 

 Ultimately, however, underlying issues such as debt must be addressed to quell Asia's economic turmoil, analysts said. 

 The only solution to Asia's problems and the growing volatility in global emerging markets is a write-down of Asian debt by global banks, said Chris Tinker, head of regional economics at ING Barings. 

 "The counterparties that have to admit culpability here are the banks," Tinker said. "Banks have to accept responsibility." 

 Tinker said the failure of global banks to take the hit on the Asian crisis had kept risk premiums high and prevented Asia from attracting the capital it needed to stabilise. 

 "By failing to write down debt and therefore maintaining the risk premium demanded on Asian assets, they are preventing the opportunity cost of investment in Asia from falling," he said. 

 That has reduced net capital inflows into Asian markets and sustained volatility caused by reduced liquidity, Tinker said. 

 For as long as the banks refuse to admit culpability for the bad lending decisions that produced the Asian crisis, Asia will remain a source of global instability, he said. 

 "The issue isn't whether or not capital markets or financial markets are more volatile, the issue is what you can do about it and whose responsibility it is," Hanna said.

title: Hong Kong  Stocks Fall 3% As Government Halts Market  Intervention
text:
HONG KONG -(Dow Jones)- Hong Kong shares snapped a two-day winning streak to close lower almost 3% Friday, as investors cashed in on recent gains and the Hong Kong government took a breather from its high-profile intervention to prop up local share prices. 

 The blue-chip Hang Seng index fell 214.92 points, or 2.8%, to end at 7527.61, after jumping 16% in the past four sessions on government buying of selected blue chips. Thursday, it rose 119.95 points, or 1.6%. 

 Trading volume shrank to HK$4.97 billion from Thursday's HK$7.03 billion. The broader All Ordinaries index shed 73.64 points to close at 3355.29. 

 "There's some profit-taking today (Friday), and some people are squaring their positions before the weekend," said Andrew To, dealing director at AMB Securities HK Ltd. 

 The Hong Kong government had been using foreign-exchange reserves to buy stocks and futures in addition to propping up the Hong Kong dollar as part of a complex defense against speculators who want to sever the local currency's link to the U.S. dollar. The government - through the Hong Kong Monetary Authority - had been spending foreign-exchange reserves to buy blue-chip stocks, Hang Seng index futures and the local currency. 

 Two traders from local brokerage houses who declined to be named said they suspected the government also unloaded some shares Friday, pocketing some profits and saving ammunition for the battle with hedge funds next week when the August index futures contract expires. 

 Meanwhile, a weakening yen drove up local interbank rates and soured buying interest in equity market, said a trader with a local brokerage firm. 

 The volatile overnight Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate edged up to 9.00% late Friday from 8.875% late Thursday, while the three-month rate climbed to 10.50% from 10.125% late Thursday. 

 A sharp sell-off in the futures market also helped to drag down the underlying index, said the trader with the local brokerage house. 

 The August Hang Seng index futures contract fell 400 points to end at 7390, a 137-point discount to the cash market. Around 21,648 contracts changed hands. 

 The number of open interest for both August and September reached 103,299. It has been closely watched by market participants since the government declared an all-out war against speculators in equity and equity derivative markets last Friday. 

 Major blue-chip stocks led the across-the-board decline Friday, after recording hefty gains in recent sessions. 

 British bank giant HSBC Holdings PLC topped the most-active list, shedding HK$6.00 to HK$165.00 amid volume valued at HK$1.10 billion. 

 Other actively-traded stocks included China Telecom (Hong Kong) Ltd., which lost 95 cents to HK$10.40; Conglomerate Hutchison Whampoa Ltd., down 90 cents to HK$38.00; and Hong Kong Telecommunications Ltd., shedding 15 cents to HK$14.85. 

 Major developers' shares also took a beating. Cheung Kong (Holdings) Ltd. lost 60 cents to HK$33.00 while Sun Hung Kai Properties Ltd. edged down 10 cents to HK$25.05. Conglomerate Swire Pacific Ltd. shed HK$1.45 to HK$22.35. 

 China-related shares fared no better, with the red-chip and H share indexes falling 3.3% and 2.9%, respectively, to end at 629.44 and 284.87. Red chips are Hong Kong-listed companies backed by mainland government entities while H shares are Chinese state-owned enterprises listed in the territory. Conglomerate China Resources Enterprise Ltd. fell 30 cents to HK$5.40; Mainland toll road operator Jiangsu Expressway Co. lost 13%, or 19 cents, to HK$1.27. 

 Elsewhere, Cheung Kong Infrastructure Holdings Ltd. bucked the trend to close up 35 cents at HK$13.90, after reporting Thursday that net profit rose 20% to HK$1.23 billion in the first half ended June 30 from the same period a year earlier. Its competitor, New World Infrastructure Ltd., however, was among the top losers in percentage terms, falling 11%, or 65 cents, to HK$5.05. 

 Traders predicted more volatility in the market next week when the government is expected to resume its war against the hedge funds. "The battle is going to be very fierce," warned one trader with an Asian brokerage house.

title: HKMA's Yam defends share market  intervention .
text:
HONG KONG, Aug 20 (Reuters) - Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) chief Joseph Yam on Thursday defended the government's intervention in the stock market and called on the world's financial leaders to consider that markets could be wrong. 

 Last Friday, Financial Secretary Donald Tsang said the government had asked the HKMA to intervene in the stock and futures markets to deter currency manipulation by speculators that had built up short positions in Hang Seng Index futures. 

 The intervention is believed to have continued each trading day since Friday and has helped to drive up the stock market by more than 14 percent since last Thursday's close. 

 In a lengthy letter to the Asian Wall Street Journal, Yam said there had been "quiet support" for Tsang's decision as well as "vehement criticism" on grounds the action violated Hong Kong's free market philosophy and demonstrated the government's unwillingness to suffer the pain of economic adjustment under the currency board system. 

 Yam said the criticism was misplaced. 

 He reiterated that the government had no objection to anyone, including hedge funds, taking short positions in stock index futures and reaping the benefits of Hong Kong's asset price adjustment. 

 But he said it was clear that speculators were engaged in a "double play" of currency manipulation with the specific aim of pushing stock prices lower, with no regard to the asset adjustments that had already taken place. 

 "This presents serious risks of markets overshooting, with asset markets ratcheting down on every occasion the manipulators engage in this activity," said Yam. 

 Yam said the rising Hong Kong dollar interest rate risk premium had been unfairly attributed to fears the government would discard the currency board system, when in fact a large portion of the premium was caused by the manipulators' actions. 

 "I do not know how many times we expressed the view that we have to stick it out and bear the inevitable pain, and that a fixed exchange rate under our currency board system is the best option for Hong Kong," Yam said. 

 "But it is unfair to ask the community to put up with excessive pain inflicted on it by those engaged in this double play of the currency and stock futures markets," he said. 

 Yam said the government had agonized over the decision to intervene. "We were acutely aware of the possibility of our action being misunderstood," he said. 

 Yam said the government's resolve in adhering to the currency board system had "never been stronger," saying there was no other alternative for Hong Kong. 

 "Financial liberalisation and the globalisation of financial markets has left little scope for a small open economy to pursue flexible exchange rates," he said, adding that allowing the currency to float was not even a viable long-term alternative. 

 Yam said the government had not departed from strict observance of the monetary rule of the currency board despite the HKMA's recent buying of Hong Kong dollars for the treasury. 

 "Adherence to monetary rule does not preclude the government funding a budget deficit by drawing down its fiscal reserves that are held in foreign assets in the Exchange Fund," he said. 

 It also did not "preclude a portfolio shift outside the balance sheet of the currency board from other assets into Hong Kong stocks for whatever purposes considered to be in the best interests of Hong Kong," Yam said. 

 Yam also called into question the accepted wisdom that markets cannot be wrong and that governments generally are wrong. If this were always the case, he said, "why are we witnessing the emerging markets shaking themselves to bits?" 

 "If emerging markets continue to devalue their currencies, which some commentators still suggest is inevitable, the costs will be borne either through massive deflation in the developing world or bubbles in the developed markets, or both," he said. 

 Yam said there was a need to get a message to industrialised nations that abstaining from intervention to maintain global financial market stability, especially currency stability, may no longer be a viable option. 

 Yam's comments appeared on the paper's editorial page.

title: HK Tung -4: Says "HK People Will Bear This Pain"
text:
"We need a breathing spell," where interest rates may be a bit high but are predictable, Tung said, explaining the government's meddling in local markets. 

 Tung also defended the government's decision to protect the Hong Kong dollar's peg to the U.S. currency. 

 "A stable currency environment is important to a small economy like Hong Kong's," Tung said, though he conceded that maintaining the peg will come at a heavy price, including high interest rates and a sharp correction in asset prices. 

 "Asset prices needed a correction anyway," to be competitive, Tung said. "Rates may be high but at least they're stable and predictable."

title: HKMA Says Fight Against Speculators To Drag On - Report
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--The territory's quasi-central bank expects to maintain its pressure on speculators for a long time, a local newspaper reported Thursday. 

 "We will continue these actions until the speculators have completely left the Hong Kong market," the South China Morning Post quoted Hong Kong Monetary Authority chief executive Joseph Yam as saying. 

 "We (the HKMA) have to continue to intervene in the stock and futures markets until the speculators have wound up their short positions," Yam was quoted as saying.

 The newspaper quoted Yam as warning that the clash with speculators targeting the local currency unit by shorting the HSI would be "a long-term battle".

title: Hong Kong  Stocks Gain 1.6% Amid Continued Government  Intervention
text:
HONG KONG -(Dow Jones)- Hong Kong shares closed almost 2% higher Thursday amid the government's continued intervention in the market. 

 The blue-chip Hang Seng index rose 119.95 points, or 1.6%, to 7742.53, adding to Wednesday's 411.66-point gain. 

 The Hang Seng index has soared 16% in the past four trading days since last Friday. The market was closed for a holiday Monday. 

 Propelled by heavy short-covering of blue chips, market volume swelled to HK$7.03 billion from Wednesday's HK$6.94 billion. The broader All Ordinaries index gained 47.19 points to 3428.93. 

 "It was mostly futures-led" buying, said Jerry Pang, equity salesman at HSBC Securities Asia Ltd. 

 The Hong Kong government has been using foreign-exchange reserves to buy stocks and futures in addition to propping up the Hong Kong dollar as part of a complex defense against speculators who want to sever the local currency's link to the U.S. dollar. 

 The government - through the Hong Kong Monetary Authority - has been spending foreign-exchange reserves to buy blue-chip stocks, Hang Seng index futures and the local currency. 

 Because Hong Kong's currency is tethered to the U.S. dollar under a modified version of a currency board, interest rates will rise when the Hong Kong dollar is sold. The recent speculative attacks on the currency have triggered massive selling in the Hong Kong stock market. 

 Armed with the knowledge that higher rates will hurt the stock market, speculators have first sold short stock futures and then sold Hong Kong dollars. Selling short involves the sale of borrowed shares or currency. The speculators profit by buying back their stock futures at a lower price, after the currency's decline sparks a rise in interest rates and a decline in the stock market. 

 Investors holding short positions have been forced to scramble to cover their positions as the index rises. As there are rumors that the government will continue to drive the index above 8000, investors short in the futures market rushed to square their positions before incurring further losses, analysts said. 

 "Most buying in the cash market was genuine buying," as opposed to government intervention, Pang said. 

 The yen has also strengthened to around 142.75 yen per U.S. dollar late Thursday, which has been positive for market sentiment, analysts added. 

 After rallying considerably in recent sessions, the Hang Seng index started to consolidate Thursday and some profit-taking emerged around the 7800-point level, which erased some of the index's gains earlier in the session, Pang said. 

 The August Hang Seng Index futures contract rose 125 points from the previous session to 7790. The derivative was trading at a premium to the cash market. 

 HSBC Holdings PLC, the day's most active stock, was up HK$3.50, or 2.1%, to HK$171.00. 

 Shares of conglomerate Hutchison Whampoa Ltd. added 90 cents to HK$38.90, while its parent, Cheung Kong (Holdings) Ltd., was flat at HK$33.60. 

 Shares of two utility giants also rose. China Telecom (Hong Kong) Ltd. gained 25 cents to HK$11.35 and Hong Kong Telecommunications Ltd. rose 30 cents to HK$15.00. 

 A stronger yen helped to relieve pressure for a yuan devaluation, which in turn boosted China-linked shares. The red-chip index was ahead 5.9% and the H-share index climbed 6.3%. Red chips are companies incorporated in Hong Kong but usually controlled by Chinese government entities, with their main operations in China. H-shares are stock of Chinese state-owned enterprises listed in Hong Kong. 

 Market players predict the government will continue to fiddle with the stock market in the near future as it continues its battle to squeeze speculators out of the currency and stock futures markets. 

 "They (government officials) will keep on intervening until the end of August," said Alan Hutcheson, research director of Pacific Challenge Securities Ltd. 

 Pang noted that the market "will be highly volatile next week before the futures expiry" next Thursday. He predicted the Hang Seng index will trade in the 7000-8000 region.

title: FOCUS-Malaysia explores ways of shoring up shares.
text:
KUALA LUMPUR, Aug 18 (Reuters) - Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad said on Tuesday the government was considering supporting the ailing stock market by buying shares and barring banks from selling stock. 

 Mahathir told reporters in the capital that money from a government-run fund for Moslem pilgrims might also be used to shore up the stock market, which slumped to a new 10-year low on Tuesday. 

 He also said that the government was considering cutting taxes. 

 "It's quite difficult to raise taxes during these trying times. In fact we should lower taxes," he said. 

 Mahathir, who relishes verbal combat, earlier on Tuesday told a workers' rally that speculative attacks on currencies of emerging markets had reached a dangerous level and might prompt countries to retaliate. 

 He said, apparently in jest, that he feared attacks on the rouble might tempt Russia to use its nuclear weapons. 

 "The attacks by currency traders have reached a dangerous stage and are totally irresponsible," he said in a speech. 

 "I worry if the attacks continue on emerging markets, it may hit countries that have the capability to fight back. I worry, for example, if Russia continued to be pressured and they have nuclear bombs, then they may want to drop the bombs on those who attack them," he said, prompting laughter from some listeners. 

 "For us, we will continue to defend our country. We do not have atomic bombs or nuclear bombs. But I'm confident Malaysians can fend off all attacks mounted by any quarter." 

 Malaysia's stock market and currency have fallen sharply since the start of Asia's economic crisis in July 1997, and Mahathir has repeatedly blamed foreign currency traders. 

 Earlier on Tuesday, the Kuala Lumpur Stock Exchange's benchmark index, which has dropped by more than 70 percent since July 1997, fell to a new 10-year low of 312.90. 

 The index ended the day barely changed at 315.66 after Mahathir's comments. But the ringgit currency was not impressed, closing the day slightly lower at 4.23 to a dollar against Monday's finish of 4.22. 

 Analysts said any moratorium on the sale of shares by banks could hammer bank stocks and in the long run lead to an increase in banks' sour loans. 

 The proposal would mean banks which are holding onto shares as loan collateral might no longer be able to force the sale of the shares if the loan was in default, said markets consultancy firm S&P's MMS International in Singapore. 

 "If this is the case, it could trigger additional investor fright, as the move would essentially mean that corporate risk is now transferred to the banking sector, which may well cause the collapse of more banks under a mountain of 'uncollectible' bad debts," it said. 

 There were also questions about how the government planned to finance market intervention. 

 Mahathir said Malaysia and other countries whose currencies had been driven down by speculators had to take measures to protect their economies. 

 In Hong Kong, for example, the territorial government had to step into the market to buy shares but it was accused of interfering with free market, he said. 

 "You look at other countries, Hong Kong for example. There are some specific measures and of course they will get attacked by the foreign media and the others," he said. 

 The Hong Kong Monetary Authority intervened in the stock and futures market on Friday to support sagging prices.

title: ASIA MARKETS - Firm yen props regional  currencies .
text:
SINGAPORE, Aug 18 (Reuters) - Asian regional currencies were mostly firmer on Tuesday as the yen remained well capped at the 146 level on fears of intervention by the Bank of Japan. 

 Finance Minister Kiichi Miyazawa said earlier that Japan was always ready to intervene in the currency market to support the yen. 

 Dollar/yen rose to a high of 146.44 but lost steam as traders were unwilling to go long on dollars above 146 yen. 

 But regional stocks were mostly weaker as support from Wall Street's overnight rally gave way to lingering worries over Russia's woes. 

 Dealers said Russia's de facto devaluation of the rouble on Monday could put to the test China's commitment to maintain the value of the yuan and the Hong Kong Monetary Authority's (HKMA) will to maintain the Hong Kong dollar peg. 

 NIKKEI REBOUND ON WALL STREET'S RALLY, SHRUG OFF RUSSIA 

 Japan's Nikkei index broke through the psychologically important 15,000 level on a technical rebound following Wall Street's overnight rally. 

 The key 225-share Nikkei average put on 1.82 percent to end at 15,063.79. 

 HANG SENG EASE BUT DOWNSIDE SEEN LIMITED 

 In Hong Kong, stocks slipped in cautious trade after Friday's unprecedented intervention by the HKMA. 

 The move was to punish speculators who had been playing off attacks on the local dollar to drive up interest rates and corresponding falls in the stock markets. 

 But dealers said continued short-covering and gains in Wall Street and the Nikkei helped avert a heavy selloff that many were expecting. 

 The HKMA declined to comment earlier on whether it had intervened in the market again to fend off currency speculators. 

Hong Kong's provisional May-July unemployment rose to 4.8 percent from a revised 4.4 percent for the April-June period. 

 RINGGIT SLIPS IN LATE TRADE 

 The ringgit lost early gains and prospects for further upside looked poor as interest rates in Malaysia move even lower in a bid to stimulate the economy. 

 The National Economic Action Council said that recent cuts in the central Bank Negara's three-month intervention rate would allow commercial banks to cut their base lending rates. 

 The country's largest banks cut interest rates on Monday, following subdued inflation data and other indicators which pointed to a sharp slowdown in domestic demand. 

 The KLSE was little changed but looked sickly on the weak ringgit and uncertainty over the government's economic strategy. 

 Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad said on Tuesday that the government was considering buying shares to support the ailing stock market. 

 Mahathir also told reporters the government was studying the possibility of following Taiwan's example and placing a moratorium on the sale of shares by banks. 

 KOSPI DIVES IN EARLY TRADE BUT WON KEEP FIRM 

 In Korea, the won was slightly firmer but the stock market dived around four percent in early business before recovering slightly. 

 Traders said it was just a case of Seoul playing catch-up because the market had already closed when news of the effective Russian devaluation hit the wires. 

 But there were also continued worries about the standoff at Hyundai's plant in Ulsan where workers and their families remained camped inside and thousands of riot police gathered outside. 

 Banking stocks were also pressuring the broader market as traders feared more capital reductions due to restructuring. 

 THAI BAHT UP ON IMPROVED SENTIMENT 

 The baht continued to strengthen with sentiment still being helped by the recent package to rescue ailing domestic banks. 

 Traders said the market was also keeping an eye on Thailand's fifth letter of intent with the IMF which is expected to be finalised soon and presented to the cabinet next week. 

 The payout of $450 million from the IMF sponsored $17.2 billion rescue package would be made available shortly after that. 

 But things were less rosy on the sovereign debt side. 

 Thailand said on Monday it would delay floating the first tranche of of its planned 5.0 billion dollars of government bonds. 

 Thai stocks fared better as investors bought back bank stocks after they were heavily sold in the previous session on concerns over Russia's problems. 

 RUPIAH SURGES AS RIOT FEARS FADE 

 The rupiah surged more than four percent in early trade as fears of rioting on Indoneisa's Independence on Monday faded. 

 The market was slightly bullish given the large amount of aid dollars due to flow into Indonesia in the coming months. 

 These dollars would be converted into rupiah for spending on infrastructure and other projects and dealers said that should support the currency. 

 But Jakarta stocks suffered as the rupiah rose. The fall in blue-chips including dual-listed Telkom and Indosat pulled down the main index. 

 Traders said the rupiah's strength made dual-listed shares relatively more expensive than their overseas counterpart causing arbitrage selling. 

 STI HITS FRESH 10-YEAR LOW 

 In Singapore, the local dollar and Straits Times Index registered losses on fears of speculative attacks on the local dollar. 

 Dealers said there was talk that hedge funds wanted to sell Singapore stocks and the Singapore dollar after Hong Kong made clear it would not tolerate any short selling there.

title: Hong Kong stocks open with moderate gains.
text:
HONG KONG, Aug 18 (Reuters) - Hong Kong stocks opened moderately higher on Tuesday, with major blue chips holding on to the heavy gains made on Friday after the government intervened in the stock and futures market. 

 The Hang Seng Index rose 22.06 points, or 0.31 percent, at the opening to 7,246.75. 

 However, the blue chip index soon lost its gains to trade down five points, or 0.07 percent, at 7,219 in early trade. 

 Brokers said the market was cautiously watching to see whether speculators had backed off following the Hong Kong Monetary Authority's intervention in the stock market on Friday and weighing the possibility of further intervention. 

 The HKMA declined to comment on Tuesday whether it was intervening in the stock market. 

 "This is going to be a choppy week. It is not over yet," said Howard Gorges, a director at South China Brokerage. 

 "Market movements will depend on what degree the speculators try to test the market by perhaps starting to short again and to what extent they feel they should start locking in profits. It will also depend on the extent the government is prepared to put a squeeze on them," he said. 

Intervention in the market pushed the Hang Seng Index up 8.47 percent on Friday as the government tried to fend off currency speculators. The market was closed on Monday for a public holiday. 

 A de facto devaluation of the Russian rouble on Monday added to concerns about the Hong Kong dollar, pushing interbank rates higher on Tuesday. 

 The overnight rate rose to 8.25-8.75 percent at the opening compared with a close of 7.50-8.00 percent on Friday and the benchmark three-month interbank rate rose to 11.10-11.62 percent compared with 10.50-11.00 percent. 

 "It is not a helpful factor to have in the background although Russia is a long way away," said Gorges. 

 Brokers said another reason to stay on the sidelines was unemployment data for May to July due at 1600 local time (0800 GMT). Economists said the jobless rate could rise to between 4.8 percent and 6.0 percent compared with the 15-year high of 4.5 percent in the April to June period. 

 "The unemployment rate is expected to be at 4.8 percent but the situation is deteriorating as we hear of layoffs almost every day," said Alan Pau, associate director at South China Securities. 

 He said trading was focused on several major blue chips with most of the buying seen in HSBC Holdings Plc . The stock, which went ex-dividend, was up HK$1.386, or 0.89 percent, at HK$156.50. 

 "There is possibly some short covering," said Geoff Galbraith, vice president institutional sales at DBS Securities. 

 "But I think the market should drift off because it was up too much on Friday and the fundamentals are still the same." 

 In the futures market, the August contract on the Hang Seng Index was up 10 points at 7,220 but the September contract fell 10 points to 7,240. 

 Among the major blue chips, Cheung Kong  rose HK$0.10 to HK$32.10 and Sun Hung Kai Properties  added HK$0.10 to HK$24.10. 

 But Hang Seng Bank  fell HK$0.60 to HK$39.40. 

 The red chip Hang Seng China-Affiliated Corporations Index was down 20 points, or 3.19 percent, at 596 and the H-share index lost nine points, or 3.25 percent, to 276. 

 Market turnover was HK$1.63 billion after the first hour of trade.

title: JGBs weaker midday Tokyo as stocks rebound.
text:
TOKYO, Aug 18 (Reuters) - Key September 10-year Japanese government bond futures were weaker by midday on Tuesday due to a sharp rise in Tokyo share prices, traders said. 

 Euroyen futures were also firmer due to a rise in banking-sector shares, but trade was light, as traders looked to moves in the Hong Kong stock market for clues to direction. 

 "Hong Kong shares rose on Friday due to government intervention, and there is concern about whether such rises can be sustained," a trader for a foreign brokerage said. 

 The Hong Kong stock market, which was closed on Monday for a holiday, resumed trade on Tuesday. 

 The Hang Seng Index, which soared 8.47 percent to close at 7,224.69 points on Friday as the Hong Kong Monetary Authority intervened in the stock market to fend off currency speculators, opened at 7,246.75 points on Tuesday. 

 A fall in the Hang Seng could undermine the firmness of Tokyo share prices, which were cheered by overnight gains in U.S. stocks, traders said. 

 September JGB futures stood at 134.33 by midday, down from Monday's close of 134.38. Turnover was a light 17,776 lots. 

 Key 182nd 10-year JGB yield stood at 1.160 percent as of 0206 GMT, up from Monday's close of 1.150 percent. 

 Traders said bond and stock prices were likely to move in inverse relation to each other as long as short-term rates remained stable. 

 But they said extreme falls in share prices may raise concern about rises in money rates and profit-taking in bonds. 

 "If share prices fall too sharply, to say around the 14,500 to 14,000 points, concern about profit-taking in bonds may be heightened," said a trader for a city bank's securities unit. 

 In the Tokyo stock market, the key Nikkei 225 average stood at 15,091.81 at midday, up 2.01 percent or 297.15 from Monday's close. 

 Key March euroyen futures stood at 99.26 as of 0209 GMT, up from Monday's settlement of 99.24. 

 Some traders said euroyen futures were supported by reports by Kyodo news agency and Yomiuri Shimbun on Monday saying the government will use public funds to facilitate a merger between the Long-Term Credit Bank of Japan and Sumitomo Trust. 

 Finance Minister Kiichi Miyazawa said on Tuesday there was no truth in the reports that the government had decided on such use of public funds. 

 The Bank of Japan left a fund surplus of 1.2 trillion yen at 0020 GMT. Key call money stood at 0.35 percent as of 0214 GMT, down from Monday's weighted average of 0.41 percent. ((Tokyo Treasury Desk +81-3 5473 3748 tokyo.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: HK stocks end slightly down, seeking direction.
text:
HONG KONG, Aug 18 (Reuters) - Hong Kong stocks closed Tuesday slightly lower with investors seeking direction after the dust settled from the government's intervention in the stock and futures market on Friday, brokers said. 

 The Hang Seng Index dipped 13.77 points, or 0.19 percent, to finish at 7,210.92 after surging 8.47 percent on Friday. 

 "Most investors just don't know what to do at the moment because it is the first time the goverment has intervened in the market," said Ricky Tam, senior research analyst at Delta Asia Securities. 

 Brokers said the government may have been back in the market buying stocks on Tuesday, although less aggressively than on Friday. 

 "The strategy is different today," said Glenn Lesko, head of sales trading at ABN-Amro Hoare Govett Asia Securities. 

 "They (the government) are not coming in to ramp it, they are only coming in to support it." 

 The Hong Kong Monetary Authority declined to comment on Tuesday on whether it was intervening in the market. 

 "Intervention in the securities and futures markets can only be considered and will only be considered when there is a corresponding 'play', if you like, on the currency side," said Hong Kong Financial Services Secretary Rafael Hui. 

 The government intervened on Friday to fend off currency speculators. 

 Brokers expected the market to remain volatile in the near term. 

 "I think the market could actually climb higher in the days ahead," said Andrew Fernow, Vickers Ballas director of research. 

 "But then it may at certain levels be ripe for another selloff because of the tendendcy to take profits at higher levels, and also you are giving speculators another opportunity to establish short positions at higher levels." 

 Fernow believed the upside of the blue chip index was found at around 8,000, but added: 

 "We are still looking at the possibility of new lows being hit this year which would mean below 6,500." 

 Futures ended at a slight premium to the spot market. The August Hang Seng Index futures contract gained five points to 7,215 while the September contract was down 15 points at 7,235.

title: HK stocks set for fall after govt  intervention .
text:
HONG KONG, Aug 18 (Reuters) - Hong Kong stocks are expected on Tuesday to give back some of the government-induced gains made last Friday with investors viewing intervention by the HKMA in the stock and futures markets negatively, brokers said. 

 With speculators still circling the Hong Kong dollar and the devaluation of the Russian rouble heightening jitters about the stability of the local currency, the Hang Seng Index may get little help from overnight gains on Wall Street, they said. 

 "The government intervention is a bad thing that will dampen investor interest in Hong Kong because it adds policy risk to the market," said Alex Wong, research manager at OSK Asia Securities. 

 "Because the market is so volatile, investors will be facing big risks at the present level and in the present situation."

title: HK stocks end morning weak but losses limited.
text:
HONG KONG, Aug 18 (Reuters) - Hong Kong stocks ended the morning weak on Tuesday as analysts viewed the hefty gains sparked by government intervention on Friday as unsustainable amid Hong Kong's weak economic fundamentals. 

 However, last week's stock and futures buying by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority prompted continued short-covering, while gains on Wall Street and in Tokyo also helped to avert the heavy selloff some were expecting on Tuesday, brokers said. 

 The Hang Seng Index closed the morning down 19.23 points, or 0.27 percent, at 7,205.46 points after rallying 8.47 percent on Friday. Turnover was HK$2.96 billion compared with HK$4.80 billion at Friday's midsession. 

 "There are so many variables now at play so the market is in a state of confusion," said Robert Sassoon, head of research at SG Securities. 

 "I don't know whether the government is still continuing to purchase although they have certainly indicated that they will continue, but in the long run it should not have any impact at all. Market forces always prevail in the end," he said. 

 The Hong Kong Monetary Authority declined to comment on Tuesday on whether it was intervening in the market after it intervened on Friday in the stock and futures market to fend off currency speculators. 

 "It will be up to the Hong Kong Monetary Authority to decide what will be the appropriate action for today, if any," Hong Kong Financial Services Secretary Rafael Hui said in a statement. 

 "Intervention in the securities and futures markets can only be considered and will only be considered when there is a corresponding 'play', if you like, on the currency side." 

 Steven Thompson, chief analyst at Nikko Research Center, said the government's actions on Friday smacked of desperation. 

 Once the short-sellers had unwound some of their positions in the futures market, they would rebuild them, he said. 

 "We have had a gradual accumulation of these shorts. If they continue to unwind, they will build new positions again from a much lower base so this will put even more downward pressure on the index," said Thompson. 

 In the futures market, the August contract on the Hang Seng Index was down 35 points at 7,175 and the September contract fell 40 points to 7,210. 

 Thompson said the Hang Seng Index could still resume its sharp downtrend, possibly testing 6,000 points. 

 "Right now we think the economy is contracting by about six percent. It is a very steep recession relative to our recent history and we should be taking into account that fundamental fact," he said. 

 More bad news on the economy was expected on Tuesday with the government set to release May to July unemployment statistics at 1600 local time (0800 GMT). 

 Economists expect the jobless rate to rise to between 4.8 percent and 6.0 percent compared with a rate of 4.5 percent in the April to June period. 

 Analysts said the impact of Monday's devaluation of the Russian rouble had been limited with a public holiday in Hong Kong on Monday allowing investors to digest the news. 

 "Perhaps it was fortunate that we had a day to think about it before opening. If we had been open yesterday it might have had some effect," said Thompson. 

 However, the devaluation pushed local interbank rates higher. The overnight rate was at 8.50-8.62 percent compared with a close of 7.50-8.00 on Friday and the three month interbank rate was at 11.50-12.00 percent compared with 10.50-11.00 percent on Friday. 

 Analysts said gains on Wall Street and in Tokyo helped limit stock market losses on Tuesday. The Dow industrials rose 149.85 points, or 1.78 percent, to close at 8,574.85 overnight while in Tokyo, the Nikkei 225 was up 230 points or 1.55 percent, at 15,025. 

 Shares in HSBC Holdings Plc  rose HK$0.886, or 0.57 percent, to HK$156.00 but subsidiary Hang Seng Bank Ltd  fell HK$1.20, or 3.00 percent, to HK$38.80. 

 In the property sector, Cheung Kong  gained HK$0.10 to HK$32.10 and Sun Hung Kai Properties Ltd  added HK$0.10 to HK$24.10. 

 China plays fell sharply, hurt by devastating floods in China and the devaluation of the Russian rouble. 

 The red chip Hang Seng China-Affiliated Corporations Index ended the morning down 33.18 points, or 5.39 percent, at 582.39 and the H-share index tumbled 15.93 points, or 5.58 percent, at 269.53.

HONG KONG, Aug 18 (Reuters) - US/HK forwards ended sharply higher on Tuesday despite last Friday's government intervention in the stock and future market to fend off speculative attacks on the Hong Kong dollar.



Dealers attributed the higher rates to the Russian rouble devaluation which took regional currency markets by surprise on Monday.



"Since the (Hong Kong) financial market was closed on Monday, the market just started to feel the pain only today," a dealer said.



But other regional currencies' reaction to Russia has been subdued after they tumbled on Monday.



Many bankers had hoped to unload some of their Hong Kong dollar funds accumulated last week as the expected major speculative attack on the Hong Kong dollar during the weekend did not materialise, dealers said.



But many of these banks had held back as a result of Monday's rouble devaluation, they said.



"Banks were not very eager lending money today," said Stephen Yau, treasurer at ING Baring in Hong Kong.



Dealers said rates above one-month would stay firm in double digits in the near term, with the rouble devaluation outweighing the effect of last Friday's government intervention to ward off a speculative attack on the Hong Kong dollar.



They said rates could have gone higher on Tuesday without the intervention.



"If the Hong Kong government had not intervened last Friday, and if we still had a rouble devaluation yesterday, the Hang Seng Index would probably have plunged below 6,000 today and local interbank rates might have risen to 15 percent," said Peter Mak, treasurer at Belgian Bank in Hong Kong.



In the local forward market, trading was thin with moderate position-squaring, which indicated that most key players had not unwound their long dollar positions despite the government's intervention in the stock and future markets last Friday, dealers said.



China-backed banks were heard selling dollar forwards.



"But they were offering forwards to a selected group of banks. Some banks suspected of being involved in speculative attacks against the Hong Kong dollar were heard to be not on their list," a dealer at a major bank said.



The interbank rate yield curve has shifted up, helping to buoy the Hong Kong dollar spot.



The overnight rate was trading at two percentage points over the offer rate for the discount window at the Hong Kong Monetary Authority.



Some said the yield curve would become flatter, as higher longer-dated rates would continue to fuel upward pressure on short term rates.



A treasurer said the overnight rate could hope to resume a downward bias, given the continued existence of the discount window.

HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--Hong Kong's acting financial secretary reiterated on Tuesday that the government would intervene to prop up the territory's equity market only if there was a corresponding speculative "play" on the currency as well. 

 "What I can say is as the Government has clearly stated last Friday, intervention in the securities and futures markets can only be considered and will only be considered when there is a corresponding play, if you like, on the currency side," said secretary for financial services Rafael Hui Tuesday. Hui is serving as acting financial secretary in the absence of Donald Tsang Yam-kuen. 

 Last Friday, the Hong Kong government announced its first-ever intervention in the stock and stock futures market and continued buying of the local currency in the spot foreign exchange market to fend off speculators. 

 The government said it's not opposed to speculators short-selling Hang Seng Index Futures or selling the local currency short in the forward foreign market, but won't tolerate the two in concert because it puts a strain on the Hong Kong dollar peg. 

 Hui said the government's intention was to fend off speculators and not to support the territory's flagging stock market. He added that further interventions would depend on the territory's quasi-central bank's view of the market.

title: Hong Kong ready to lock horns with speculators.
text:
HONG KONG, Aug 17 (Reuters) - Hong Kong, sagging under a host of economic woes, is poised for a long, drawn-out battle with international speculators to protect the local dollar and its 15-year-old linked exchange-rate system. 

 Joseph Yam, head of Hong Kong's Monetary Authority (HKMA), said on Monday the territory was willing to lock horns with the international players who have attacked Hong Kong markets. 

 In a letter to London's Financial Times newspaper, he said the government would step back from intervention in the stock and futures markets only when speculative manipulation of the Hong Kong dollar stopped. 

 The Hong Kong dollar has been pegged at HK$7.8 to the U.S. dollar since 1983. 

 "Meanwhile we shall act to deter currency manipulators," he wrote. "We do object to people manipulating our currency to engineer extreme conditions in the interbank market and high interest rates to make profits in the short positions in stock index futures." 

 The government took the unprecedented step on Friday of buying local stocks and futures to hit back at speculators, whom it accused of trying to break the Hong Kong dollar peg. 

 After a day of government buying, the blue chip Hang Seng Index closed up 8.47 percent on Friday at 7,224.69 points. It had been at five-year lows during the week. 

 Yam and other officials said the aim of the intervention was to punish speculators who had been playing off attacks on the local dollar to drive up interest rates and corresponding falls in the stock market. 

 Market players who had short-sold the Hong Kong stock market - that is, borrowed stock and sold it in anticipation of later buying it back cheaper - may have lost heavily when the government drove prices higher. 

 The government move provoked some applause but also a great deal of criticism by those who saw it as an unjustifiable break in a long-standing free-market policy. 

 An editorial on Monday in the respected Hong Kong Economic Journal questioned the government's move. 

 "Speculators are using a range of tactics to profit from Hong Kong's problems. Whatever measure the Hong Kong government takes, whether it is to buy the Hong Kong dollar or buy Hong Kong stocks, will only hurt some of the speculators, but others will profit," the newspaper said. 

 By amassing stocks and futures during such volatile times the government would only put Hong Kong reserves at risk, it added. 

 "The government, having bought so many stocks and futures, could make itself more vulnerable given the volatility in the stock and futures market." 

 Hong Kong had US$96.5 billion in foreign currency reserves at end June. Officials have declined to say how much was spent in the last week protecting the local currency. 

 And the question now is how long Hong Kong can keep up the battle, the Hong Kong Standard newspaper said in an editorial. 

 "When the market opens tomorrow, the speculators might be back in full force," it said. "Then more of our reserves will have to be commandeered to keep them at bay. Whether we can last the distance is anybody's guess." 

 It added Hong Kong had no idea how much money speculators could bring to bear in the coming attacks but the speculators knew exactly how much money Hong Kong had for a dollar defence. 

 The government's intervention surprised many people in the former British colony of 6.6 million, which returned to Chinese rule last year. 

 Shortly after Britain returned the territory to Beijing after more than 150 years of colonial rule, the new special administrative region of China was swept up in the regional economic crisis. 

 The overall economy shrank 2.8 percent in the first quarter of 1998 from a year earlier. Unemployment, already at 15-year highs, is expected to rise further when new figures are issued later this week. 

 Hong Kong residents, accustomed to years of healthy growth, are hurting. About 200 Christians joined a cruise down Victoria Harbour on Sunday to pray for divine intervention. 

 With hands held up in the air, the Christians prayed for Hong Kong leader Tung Chee-hwa to embrace their God to save the territory's battered economy.

title: HK Govt/ Intervention  -2: Editorial Says Peg's Days Numbered

The Post said Secretary for Financial Services Rafael Hui noted that the Hong Kong Monetary Authority began calling around to unspecified international bodies Friday, when the unprecedented intervention was announced. 

 He said Hong Kong wanted the international investment community to understand that the government hadn't "gone off the rails and was merely trying to prop up the market." 

 Markets reacted generally negatively to the government's intervention, and Hui said that was to have been expected. But the reaction was actually less severe than the government had foreseen. Hui told the Post the decision to intervene had been an agonizing one. 

 Government intervention was supported over the weekend by the head of Hong Kong's Real Estate Developers Association, Lo Ka-shui, who is also the managing director of large property company, Great Eagle Holdings Ltd. 

 Lo accused international speculators of "front-running" in Hong Kong's markets in an attempt to cash in by hammering the local stock market and trying to break the Hong Kong dollar's peg to the U.S. dollar. 

 "It is essential the government maintain fair play in a free market; sometimes it means not allowing excessively powerful forces to play the insider game," Lo said. 

 Separately, the Post said in an unsigned Sunday editorial that "the most popular outlook is that the peg will be abandoned within the next six to 12 months," but didn't cite its sources. 

 Publicly, currency market participants are unwilling to criticize the HKMA and the Hong Kong government and all say they believe the peg will stay. 

 But off the record, many participants say they believe the question is when, rather than whether the government will cave in to speculators and abandon the link. 

 In its editorial, the Post noted that Friday's intervention to support the peg "has done nothing to reverse the growing consensus that the peg's days are numbered."
