title: Government  Intervention  May Harm  Hong Kong 's International Image
text:
HONG KONG -- Stepping away from a longstanding commitment to unhindered markets, monetary authorities undertook a major and unprecedented intervention in Hong Kong's stock and futures markets Friday to hurt speculators who are trying to force a devaluation of the Hong Kong dollar. 

 While the move forced an 8.47% jump in the benchmark Hang Seng stock index, which closed at 7224.69 Friday, some big investors said it would do far more harm than good, denting the city's reputation as a free-market haven and raising unsustainable expectations the government will prop up the market if it comes under more severe pressure. Those perceptions could harm Hong Kong's role as an international financial center. 

 The city's top officials insisted the intervention was undertaken only to deter a particular form of speculation rather than to bolster the stock market. "The government has no intention to artificially support the stock market," the city's chief executive, Tung Chee-hwa, said. "The government will, as before, adhere strictly to our longstanding policy of nonintervention in the stock and futures markets." 

 At the same time, Mr. Tung said he would take "resolute action to reduce market distortion." His finance secretary, Donald Tsang, accused speculators of attacking Hong Kong's currency with a "whole host of improper measures," including the spreading of "vicious rumors" about a devaluation of Hong Kong's currency and the stability of its banks. 

 Government officials declined to say whether there would be more intervention this week or to reveal how much was spent in Friday's buying, which came at the end of a week that saw the Hang Seng index sink to a five-year low, almost two-thirds off its peak of a year ago. Traders estimated that the government spent between 2 billion and 3 billion Hong Kong dollars (US$258 million and US$387 million) acquiring shares in the 33 companies that compose the index as well as an undetermined amount on stock-index futures, accounting for as much as a third of the turnover Friday. 

 The intervention in the stock market was aimed at catching currency speculators where they profit in staging attacks on the currency. Messrs. Tung and Tsang said speculators took advantage of the fact that maintaining the value of the Hong Kong dollar requires the monetary authorities to increase high interest rates, which in turn decrease stock-market prices. They said speculators have entered both currency and stock markets to attack the Hong Kong dollar in order to push up local interest rates and profit from the resulting fall in share prices. The moves feed an exodus from Hong Kong-dollar investments and put additional pressure on the Hong Kong currency. 

 Hong Kong's dollar has been linked to the U.S. dollar since 1983 at a rate of about 7.8 to the U.S. dollar. It is the only freely traded currency in Asia that hasn't been devalued in the last year, and speculation against the "pet" has soared in recent months. Expectations also have risen that China, which has sovereignty over Hong Kong, might feel pressure to devalue its currency, the yuan. (Hong Kong officials said they informed Beijing of their decision to intervene in the stock market only after they had decided to do it.) 

 Authorities increased the risk of speculating to make speculators more cautious, said Donald Hanna, an economist at Goldman, Sachs & Co. By making "speculative profits more uncertain," he said, the move should "reduce the number of attacks." 

 The danger of the government's intervention Friday, market participants said, is that the move could take on a momentum of its own or be viewed by investors as presaging a generally more interventionist approach. "Even if the government believes it's taking an extraordinary measure, we're going into extraordinary times, and that might mean they have to intervene every month," said Marc Faber, a Hong Kong money manager. 

 "The government is launching a battle against the marketplace, but eventually the market will prevail," Mr. Faber added. Worse still, he contends that any form of intervention could postpone Hong Kong recovery by artificially supporting stock prices. "Like in Japan, which has supported markets for a long time," he said, "this will prolong the agony." 

 Japanese authorities began intervening in Tokyo's stock market in October 1990, when the country's Nikkei stock average had fallen by half in a single year. At first, as in Hong Kong, the index responded positively, skyrocketing 13% in a single day. That success, however, launched the government into an extended, on-again-off-again game of trying to prop up the stock market. That ultimately entailed huge costs, undermining the country's credibility in carrying out its professed goal of freeing Tokyo's capital markets from overweening regulation, and it wasn't particularly successful. 

 Less than two years after the first major manipulation, Japan's Ministry of Finance took the game to a new level by arm-twisting major insurers into buying as the Nikkei fell through 18000. Three times since then, the market has dropped to the mid-14000 level. 

 Colin Bradbury, head of sales at Jardine Fleming Securities Ltd., said that in Hong Kong, the authorities "don't understand that for international investors the one thing Hong Kong has going for it is its laissez faire system." 

 Moreover, by not allowing asset prices to move freely, the government is hampering the function of the currency board -- the system that links the Hong Kong dollar to the U.S. currency -- putting a question mark over its political commitment to hold the peg no matter what the economic cost. Government officials have been aware of those concerns. In recent weeks, officials have solicited views from foreign investors "as to how far they can go in interfering in the market," Mr. Bradbury said. 

 The success of the government's move won't be immediately clear. The stock market is closed Monday for a holiday, although currency traders will be able to deal in Singapore and elsewhere. 

 The political impact was also unclear over the weekend. "It generates a sense that government can fight back -- that it's not a one-way street," Goldman's Mr. Hanna said. 

 But Albert Ho, spokesman for the Democratic Party, Hong Kong's largest political party, said it was "unwise" and "unrealistic" for the government to try to drive currency speculators out of financial markets. "Hong Kong is a free market, and speculation is a part of life in Hong Kong," Mr. Ho said. 

 "We are fully aware that we are undergoing a very long adjustment period and adjustment will be painful," said Mr. Tung, the city's chief executive, "but we are well prepared as a community to take such pain." 

 In June, the government froze new land sales in a bid to bolster slumping property prices, and in the 1980s the government bailed out several banks and allowed the city's futures market to suspend operations during the 1987 global stock-market crash. 

 But with Friday's intevention, Hong Kong "has started down a dead-end road of interference in the market," warned the Chinese language Hong Kong Economic Journal in an editorial over the weekend.

title: WEEKAHEAD-HK stocks still hounded by  currency  risks.
text:
HONG KONG, Aug 16 (Reuters) - Hong Kong's grim fundamentals and persistent currency fears could cap any gains in the stock market this coming week and could even lead to a fall despite government intervention last week to fend off speculators. 

 The Hong Kong Monetary Authority intervened in the stock and stock futures markets last Friday amid speculation against the Hong Kong dollar, fuelling a 564.27 point, or 8.47 percent, rally in the Hang Seng Index to 7,224.69. 

 Over the week the blue chip index gained 206.28 points, or 2.9 percent after touching five-year lows during the week. The market will be closed on Monday for a public holiday. 

 Hong Kong's Chief Executive Tung Chee-hwa said on Friday the government had no intention of artificially supporting the stock market, but intervened only to foil speculators. 

 "It won't change a thing. I think they (the speculators) will come back with a vengeance," said Steven Thompson, chief analyst at Nikko Research Center. 

 He said the Hang Seng Index would slide to a low of 6,000 points within the next two to three weeks. 

 "They may have achieved a certain goal of burning these speculators, but at the same time they have probably damaged Hong Kong's reputation," said Thompson, adding some legitimate buyers may have been hurt by the government's decision. 

 The HKMA also intervened in the foreign exchange market on Friday, by selling treasury bills to buy the local dollar, and recirculating those dollars back into the banking system. 

 Analysts said the intervention could lessen confidence in the Hong Kong dollar peg to the U.S. dollar, since the government had been forced to intervene. 

 "With the HKMA coming in and buying the currency...even if they are committed to the peg, it raises the spectre that maybe they are not. And then the whole thing starts to feed upon itself," said Robert Rountree, head of research at Prudential-Bache Securities. 

 "As long as speculators and hedge funds feel the Hong Kong Monetary Authority or the authorities are anything less than totally committed to the peg, then they can push the market down as low as they want," Rountree said. 

 Alex Wong, research manager at OSK Asia Securities, said next week's upside would be limited, with the first resistance at 7,350 points and then at 7,600. 

 "The intervention will have only a short-term impact on the market, because the fundamentals are still unchanged. Interest rates are high and the yen is still weak," he said. 

 Wong said some pullback could occur as the market tested the level for another intervention. "But (the HKMA) can't keep doing this, because it has limited resources," he added. 

 Analysts said the yen's volatility would continue to put pressure on the Chinese yuan, which would weigh on sentiment toward the Hong Kong dollar peg. 

 "We need to know when the political leaders of Southeast Asian and northeast Asian economies are going to get their acts together," said Thompson. 

 "If the Japanese got their act together and sorted out their banking system promptly...we could be on the road to recovery." 

 Thompson said Hong Kong's gross domestic product contraction of 2.8 percent for the first quarter of 1998 was a major factor in the index's long-term downtrend. 

 "That obviously means all our estimates have to be revised down, causing pressure on the Hang Seng Index," he said. 

 Analysts said unemployment figures for May to July, due on Tuesday, would dampen sentiment. Economists expect the jobless rate to rise to between 4.8 percent to six percent from 4.5 percent in the three months to June. 

 More anaemic corporate results would also weigh on the market, analysts said. Cheung Kong Infrastructure Holdings Ltd  is due to release interim results on Thursday.

title: Many HK papers back government market  intervention .
text:
HONG KONG, Aug 15 (Reuters) - Hong Kong daily newspapers on Saturday voiced support for the government's intervention in the stock market on Friday, although some warned the move aimed at deflecting speculators could backfire. 

 Chinese language papers, the Apple Daily, Sing Pao, the Hong Kong Commercial Daily and the independent Ming Pao newspapers all agreed that an extraordinary move was needed to cope with an extraodinary crisis. 

 The Apple Daily warned that the government's intervention would bring side effects and noted that in effect the government had intervened in the markets and used taxpayers money to gamble. 

 On Friday, the Hong Kong government intervened in the territory's stock market for the first time, effectively supporting a flailing market but raising eyebrows over whether Hong Kong truly remained a free market. 

 The Hang Seng Index surged 8.47 percent on Friday, after hitting a five-year low on Thursday. 

 Hong Kong leaders repeatedly stressed they had not abandoned their hands-off policy in the markets, despite Friday's unprecedented action and the Hong Kong Monetary Authority's ongoing purchases of Hong Kong dollars outside the currency board. 

 The Hong Kong Commercial Daily said the move would stabilise financial markets, a cornerstone for reviving the economy. 

 Pro-China papers, the Da Tung Pao and Wen Wei Po, also supported the move, noting that the government had successfully hit back at speculators and taught them a lesson. 

 Some of the dailies were less supportive, however. 

 The Hong Kong Economic Journal disagreed with the defence. The paper pointed out the HKMA was behaving like a central bank and that intervention had upset Hong Kong's financial management principles and would have a long term effect on the market.

title: FOCUS-HK govt buys shares to foil speculators.
text:
HONG KONG, Aug 14 (Reuters) - The Hong Kong government intervened in the territory's stock market for the first time on Friday, but officials said their aim was to foil speculators, not prop up the sagging market. 

 "The government has no intention to artificially support the stock market. The measures we have taken today are directed against specifically speculative activities," Hong Kong Chief Executive Tung Chee-hwa told reporters at a hastily called news conference. 

 Earlier, a grim-looking Financial Secretary Donald Tsang announced he had asked the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) to launch "counter activities in the stock and futures market" against speculators that had attacked the Hong Kong dollar as a means to influence stock prices. 

 Officals refused to disclose how much the HKMA spent buying shares and futures contracts. 

 Last week, overseas investment houses and hedge funds sold billions of U.S. dollars worth of Hong Kong dollars in both the spot and forward markets. 

 Conventional wisdom has it that speculators are not really targetting the Hong Kong dollar when they sell it. 

 Rather, they are trying to push up rates and cause stock prices to fall, either because they already have shorted the share market or want to buy stocks at cheaper prices. 

 Tsang said that was exactly what happened in the latest attack. 

 "This would enable them to benefit from their very substantial short positions which they have accumulated in the Hang Seng Index futures market," said Tsang. 

 Tsang said the government had no evidence past attacks on the Hong Kong dollar were linked to speculation in stocks. 

 "This is the first time we've intervened in the securities market because this is the first time we have seen a double play working against us in a critical time when regional confidence is fragile, when people wish to be reassured," he told reporters. 

 The Hong Kong leaders stressed repeatedly that they had not abandoned their hands-off policy in the markets, despite today's unprecedented action and the HKMA's ongoing purchases of Hong Kong dollars outside the currency board system. 

 "Our long-standing policy of non-intervention in the stock and futures markets remain unchanged," said Tsang. 

 He said the government would only contemplate intervention when it believed movements in stock and futures markets were caused by rate hikes engineered by speculators. 

 Under the currency board system, pressures for a weaker Hong Kong dollar automatically cause interest rates to rise and vice versa. Higher rates take a toll on asset markets and the real economy. 

 While most analysts say they expect the peg to stay, government actions to stabilize property prices and boost liquidity in the banking sector have raised questions about its willingness to take the pain of plummeting asset prices. 

 The latest massive attack on the Hong Kong dollar was foiled without a surge in interest rates because the HKMA purchased the local dollar for the government treasury, skirting the currency board system and recirculating the dollars back into the banking system. 

 The treasury needed the funds to fill a shortfall, but the move nevertheless was viewed by some as a convenient tactic by the government to avoid rate rises. 

 Analysts took a jaded view of Friday's stock market intervention. 

 "It won't change a thing. I think they (the speculators) will come back with a vengeance," said Steven Thompson, chief analyst at Nikko Research Center. 

 "They may have achieved a certain goal of burning these speculators, but at the same time they have probably damaged Hong Kong's reputation," said Thompson. 

 The Hang Seng Index surged 8.47 percent to 7,224.69 on Friday after hitting a five-year low on Thursday, but Hong Kong shares traded in London fell modestly after the government's announcement. ((Hong Kong Newsroom (852) 2843-6371; Fax (852) 2845-0636

title: Tung says HK gov't moved to foil speculators.
text:
HONG KONG, Aug 14 (Reuters) - Hong Kong leader Tung Chee-hwa said his administration intervened in the stock and futures markets on Friday to foil speculators and not to support prices. 

 "The government has no intention to artificially support the stock market. The measures we have taken today are directed against specifically speculative activities," he told reporters. 

 Tung said: "We are fully aware that we are going through a very long adjustment period and the adjustment will be painful." 

 He said a healthy environment was required for our economy "to undergo effective and painful adjustment...to do so, we must have a stable interest rate environment". 

 Tung said his administration had been keeping an eye on speculators. The intervention on Friday came after careful and detailed consideration. 

 "There has been massive speculative activities in the Hong Kong money market and the stock futures market," he said. 

 Tung said Hong Kong authorities worked out their moves themselves but "obviously the central (Beijing) government knows about it". 

 "It is difficult to say whether speculative activities will continue but we will watch carefully every time and take decisive measures if needed," he added. 

 "We are doing it purely against speculative play which is linked to the currency play, and the stock and futures market, and we will do it time and time again in order to make our point," he said. 

 Joseph Yam, head of the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, told reporters at a separate briefing that it was the first time the government had intervened in the securities market. 

 He vowed to leave "no stone unturned" in the defence of the Hong Kong-U.S. dollar peg. 

 Yam said the HKMA would hold the stocks it purchased on Friday until speculators had left and then sell the stocks gradually. He added that the speculators are "still out there".

title: Hong Kong markets shrug off HK dlr options rumours.
text:
HONG KONG, Aug 14 (Reuters) - The Hong Kong dollar was rock solid and forward rates were sharply lower on Friday despite talk of potentially market-destabilising options contracts expiring next week, the first on Tuesday. 

 "It doesn't look like there is going to be an attack on the Hong Kong dollar during the weekend. Activities were mainly focused on position-squaring today," a dealer at a U.S. commercial bank said at the close of trade. 

 For weeks, traders have been saying there was a pile of derivative contracts related to the Hong Kong dollar expiring in August that could rattle local markets. 

 The most persistent - and decidedly unconfirmed - rumour was that there was an enormous call option on the Hong Kong dollar with an exercise price of HK$7.8 per US$1. 

 "The talk is that there is a knockout option maturing on Tuesday," said an analyst at a European bank. 

 "If the Hong Kong dollar fails to touch 7.8, the people that bought the option get paid a big return. If it touches 7.8, then the person that issued the option gets all the money," in the form of the option premium, he said. "That's the rumour." 

 The Hong Kong dollar was linked to the U.S. dollar at a rate of HK$7.8 per US$1 in 1983. It is permitted to trade in a narrow band around that level and typically trades on the strong side. 

 In fact, the Hong Kong dollar spot rate hasn't flirted with 7.8 since 1991 and hasn't weakened past 7.75 since mid-1993. 

 It was at 7.7490/00 at Friday's close. 

 The 7.75 level is widely seen as the intervention level for the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA), which often is noted buying modest amounts of Hong Kong dollars at that level. 

 If there is a call option on the 7.8, it would imply that the buyer of the option strongly believed that the HKMA would defend the currency, while the seller believed the opposite. 

 Traders pointed out that the peg needn't break for the option to expire without being exercised. 

 Indeed, by writing an option at 7.8, the seller was more likely betting that the HKMA could not hold the rate at the super support level of 7.75 - which would spark heavy sales, pushing the local dollar to 7.8, where there would be intense pressure through the currency board system to keep it at 7.8. 

 But few really believe that whatever options have been put on the Hong Kong dollar are that simple. More likely, they say, the parties involved also have their hands in other transactions, perhaps options on Hong Kong stock futures. 

 Traders said speculators win as long as markets fluctuate. 

 "There are a lot of rumours that hedge funds are intervening in the market to scare people off. We know the hedge funds lose money if the markets don't go crazy, and they are starting to launch rumours to cash in on their positions," said an interest rate derivatives trader at a European bank. 

 Financial Secretary Donald Tsang on Friday said the HKMA had used the Exchange Fund to intervene in Hong Kong stock and futures markets to foil speculators, a highly unusual move. He said that while the government had not abandoned its policy of non-intervention, it would act in the markets again under exceptional circumstances. 

 The Hang Seng Index surged 8.47 percent, closing at 7,224.69 

 Tsang blasted speculators for hurting the public, saying their aim was to make quick profits through the futures market. 

 Conventional wisdom is that speculators are not really targeting the Hong Kong dollar when they sell it. 

 Rather, they are trying to push up rates and cause stock prices to fall, either because they already have shorted the share market or plan to buy stocks at bargain prices. 

 Last week, overseas investment banks and hedge funds launched a massive attack on the Hong Kong dollar, selling several billion U.S. dollars worth of Hong Kong dollars in the spot and forward markets. 

 Under Hong Kong's currency board system, pressures for a weak Hong Kong dollar automatically cause rates to rise. 

 Interest rates rose in response to the attack, but by only a few hundred basis points, far less than in October 1997, when an assault on the local dollar of comparable size caused the overnight rate to soar to 300 percent. 

 The rate rise was checked because the HKMA bought Hong Kong dollars for the government treasury, not through the currency board, so the dollars were recirculated in the banking system. 

 The attack rattled Hong Kong shares, but dealers said the losses would have been much greater if rates had surged.

title: Hong Kong stocks jump after government steps in.
text:
HONG KONG (Reuters) - Hong Kong stocks soared Friday as the territory's goverment stepped into the financial markets in a bid to foil speculators. 

 The main Hang Seng Index jumped 564.27 points, or 8.5 percent, to 7,224.69. It was the ninth biggest point gain ever for the blue-chip index, which has slumped in line with the severe economic downturn afflicting Hong Kong. 

 "The Hong Kong Monetary Authority has been buying up the Hong Kong dollars by selling U.S. dollars in the market," Hong Kong Financial Secretary Donald Tsang said after the market closed. 

 The authority also intervened in the stock and futures market Friday to foil speculators, investors said. 

 Tsang said that hedge funds, private partnerships that often make speculative investments, had been selling Hong Kong dollars recently in a bid to push down stocks and profit from positions they had taken, in effect betting a drop would occur. 

 "This would enable them to benefit from their very substantial short positions which they had accumulated in the Hang Seng Index futures market," Tsang said. Short selling is selling borrowed stock in a bid to profit by buying it back later at a lower price. 

 Brokers said the market also got support from a firmer Japanese yen. 

 But brokers doubted whether the gains were sustainable given continued worries about the stability of the yen and the Chinese currency, the yuan. 

 "We are not out of the woods yet, but probably we will see some support when the market moves below 7,000," said Alex Tang, head of research at Yamaichi International. 

 Tang expected the market to trade in a range of 7,000 to 8,000 in the medium term. 

 "The market fall has been exaggerated because the hedge fund managers have been selling the equity market," said David Williamson, director at Indosuez W.I. Carr. 

 Tsang declined to detail what actions authorities took but said the government would intervene again if the Hong Kong dollar came under repeated attack. He said the government had ample reserves to defend the currency, which has been pegged at HK$7.80 to the U.S. dollar since 1983. 

 "We have total resolve and we are going through all motions to defend the linked exchange," he added. 

 Investors also eyed the Japanese yen as the U.S. dollar slipped below 145 yen.

title: HK govt to  intervene  if HK$ attacked repeatedly.
text:
HONG KONG, Aug 14 (Reuters) - Hong Kong Financial Secretary Donald Tsang said on Friday the government would intervene in the markets if the Hong Kong dollar came under repeated attack, and the government had ample resources to defend the currency. 

 The government would intervene under very specific circumstances which involved repeated attacks on the Hong Kong dollar while speculators were also present in the futures market, he told a news conference. 

 The Hong Kong Monetary Authority intervened in the stock and futures market on Friday to foil speculators. 

 Tsang declined to describe the HKMA's actions or specify the scale of the intervention but said Hong Kong had sufficient resources in its foreign exchange reserves to deal with speculative activities. 

 Tsang said Hong Kong's commitment to its currency board was "paramount". The Hong Kong dollar has been pegged to the U.S. dollar at HK$7.8 per dollar since 1983. 

 "(If) what we are dealing with is a very exceptional circumstance, then we have to deploy our foreign reserves to deal with very specific attacks on the Hong Kong dollar through a very unconventional means," Tsang said. 

 "We are not going to abandon the (currency board) system... We have total resolve and we are going through all motions to defend the linked exchange," he added.

title: HK govt buys stocks to fend off speculators.
text:
HONG KONG, Aug 14 (Reuters) - Hong Kong Financial Secretary Donald Tsang said the Hong Kong Monetary Authority had intervened in the stock and futures market on Friday to foil speculators. 

 The following is a full text of Tsang's statement: 

 "In the last few days, there has been substantial speculative selling of Hong Kong dollars by a few investment houses, acting on behalf of hedge funds. On this occasion, we believe that the speculators' aim has been to undermine the stability of the exchange value of the Hong Kong dollar and to produce sharply higher Hong Kong dollar interest rates as well as sharp falls in the stock market. This would enable them to benefit from their very substantial short positions which they had accumulated in the Hang Seng Index futures market. 

 The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) has been buying up the Hong Kong dollars by selling U.S. dollars in the market. This is in response to the Treasury's request to draw down the fiscal reserves during the current deficit season. Consequently, the speculative selling of Hong Kong dollars has not led to any tightening of Hong Kong dollar liquidity. Interest rates in the interbank market have, nevertheless, edged up, but their rise has been more moderate than would otherwise be the case. 

 I must make clear that we are not against the shorting of Hang Seng Index futures by hedge funds, or indeed by anybody. But we do not tolerate attempts by speculators to manipulate our interest rates by engineering extreme conditions in the money market so that they can benefit from the short positions they have built up in Hang Seng Index futures. With turnovers becoming significantly thinner than last year, the market is vulnerable to manipulation and has recently shown signs of becoming one of the main reasons of speculators attacking the Hong Kong dollar. Instability in the stock and futures markets may in turn undermine confidence in the currency market, thereby triggering further speculative activities. 

 In order to achieve their objectives in undermining the Hong Kong dollar, speculators have deployed a whole host of improper measures which are clear to all. These measures include spreading vicious rumours on the delinking of the Hong Kong dollar with the U.S. dollar, devaluation of (China's) Renminbi, as well as the instability of our banks which led to bank runs. We have recovered from each of these speculative attacks. We have also demonstrated our resolve in maintaining our linked exchange rate. However, the sharp rise in interest rates created by speculative attacks has clearly hurt our economy and the public at large. 

 In order to deter such manipulation, I have exercised my power under the Exchange Fund Ordinance and asked the HKMA (Hong Kong Monetary Authority) to appropriate counter activities in the stock and futures markets. The Exchange Fund Advisory Committee, which I have formally consulted, supports this course of action. Accordingly, the HKMA mounted counter activities earlier today. 

 I must emphasise that our long-standing policy of non-intervention in the stock and futures markets remain unchanged. We only contemplate intervention in very exceptional circumstances when there is sufficient reason to believe that movements in the stock and futures markets are clearly and substantially caused by corresponding movements in interest rates engineered by speculative activities against the Hong Kong sufficiently clear linkage exists between the currency play and the stock and futures market play. Under any other circumstance, the government will of course continue to adhere strictly to non-intervention."

title: London HK stocks steady in active two-way trade.
text:
LONDON, Aug 14 (Reuters) - Hong Kong stocks in London were little changed on Friday but dealers reported intense two-way trading in the blue chips ahead of a market holiday on Monday. 

 London traders were little impressed by an 8.5 percent rebound in the Hang Seng index, which was seen as the result of intervention in the stock market by the Hong Kong government rather than a change in sentiment. 

 The Hang Seng London reference index was only 3.98 points ahead at 7,228.67. 

 "The index doesn't reflect the level of activity as it has been very busy across the board, probably the busiest day for the past three months, with two-way business in all the leaders," one trader said. 

 Another noted that the market had started weaker amid fears the forex markets would take their revenge against the Hong Kong government knocking prices lower. 

 A rebound in global markets prompted a recovery in the afternoon. "We don't think this (Hong Kong) rally is sustainable and with the market shut on Monday nobody wanted to take big positions," the second dealer said. 

 Index heavyweight HSBC Holdings   was among the most active stocks and ended with a gain of HK$2.5 to HK$160.5, dragged higher mainly by a strong performance of the shares on the London Stock Exchange. 

 Other active issues included New World Development , which eased HK$0.75 to HK$8.775, and Hutchison Whampoa, up HK$0.15 from its Hong Kong close. 

 Earlier in the day, the Hang Seng index jumped 564.27 points to 7,224.68. The August future contract added 600 points to 7,210. 

 Hong Kong Financial Secretary Donald Tsang announced he had asked the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) to launch "counter activities in the stocks and futures market" against speculators who had attacked the Hong Kong dollar in order to influence stock prices. 

 Officials refused to disclose how much the HKMA spent buying shares and futures contract, but they insisted their aim was to foil speculators, not prop up the sagging market.

title: US stocks firm but off highs,  currency  fears ease.
text:
NEW YORK, Aug 14 (Reuters) - U.S. stocks were off earlier highs but still firm Friday morning, reassured by words and actions in support of Asian and Russian currencies. 

 At 1109 EDT/1509 GMT, the Dow industrials were up 67 points to 8526. Blue chips had risen nearly 100 points at the open. Almost half of the Dow's gains came from a surge in J.P. Morgan  shares on reports it may merge with a European bank. 

 Morgan was up 9-1/8 at 125-15/16. 

 "Hong Kong is moving to stabilise its markets," said Jack Shaughnessy, chief investment strategist at Advest. 

 "It is not going to sit on its hands passively and allow market forces to dictate the direction of their markets." 

 Hong Kong's Hang Seng index closed up 8.47 percent after the Hong Kong Monetary Authority intervened in the stock and futures market to foil speculators. 

 Russian share and debt markets recovered after several days of panic-stricken declines. President Boris Yeltsin soothed nerves by vowing not to devalue the rouble. 

 In Japan, vice finance minister Eisuke Sakakibara said authorities were looking for a chance to intervene in the foreign exchange market to prop up the yen. 

 "Deflationary fears are what is driving financial markets - bonds up and stocks down," Shaughnessy said. 

 The long bond was up 15/32 to yield 5.56 percent, firming with dollar/yen. 

 Among the most active stocks, shares in CIENA Corp.  and Tellabs Inc. which is buying CIENA, tumbled after CIENA warned of a shortfall in third-quarter revenues and earnings.

title: H.K. stocks soar, most other Asian markets higher.
text:
SINGAPORE (Reuters) - Stocks soared in Hong Kong on Friday after the government stepped into financial markets in a bid to foil speculators, while most other Asian markets also posted gains. 

 The yen recovered some ground against the dollar, helping to offset some of the concerns about Russia's growing financial problems. Stocks in Thailand jumped 5.5 percent and share prices also rose in Indonesia, the Philippines, South Korea and Singapore. But stocks fell in Japan. 

 Hong Kong stocks led the rally, with the main Hang Seng Index jumping 564.27 points, or 8.5 percent, to 7,224.69. It was the ninth-biggest point gain for the blue chip index, which has slumped amid the territory's recession. 

 "The Hong Kong Monetary Authority has been buying up the Hong Kong dollars by selling U.S. dollars in the market," Hong Kong Financial Secretary Donald Tsang said after the market closed. The authority also intervened in the stock and futures market Friday to foil speculators, investors said. 

 Tsang said that hedge funds, private partnerships that often make speculative investments, had been selling Hong Kong dollars recently in a bid to push down stocks and profit from positions they had taken in effect betting a drop would occur.

title: WEEKAHEAD-Hong Kong stocks still dogged by  currency .
text:
HONG KONG, Aug 16 (Reuters) - Hong Kong's grim fundamentals and persistent currency fears could cap any gains in the stock market this coming week and could even lead to a fall despite government intervention last week to fend off speculators. 

 The Hong Kong Monetary Authority intervened in the stock and stock futures markets last Friday amid speculation against the Hong Kong dollar, fuelling a 564.27 point, or 8.47 percent, rally in the Hang Seng Index to 7,224.69. 

 Over the week the blue chip index gained 206.28 points, or 2.9 percent after touching five-year lows during the week. The market will be closed on Monday for a public holiday. 

 Hong Kong's Chief Executive Tung Chee-hwa said on Friday the government had no intention of artificially supporting the stock market, but intervened only to foil speculators. 

 "It won't change a thing. I think they (the speculators) will come back with a vengeance," said Steven Thompson, chief analyst at Nikko Research Center. 

 He said the Hang Seng Index would slide to a low of 6,000 points within the next two to three weeks. 

 "They may have achieved a certain goal of burning these speculators, but at the same time they have probably damaged Hong Kong's reputation," said Thompson, adding some legitimate buyers may have been hurt by the government's decision. 

 The HKMA also intervened in the foreign exchange market on Friday, by selling treasury bills to buy the local dollar, and recirculating those dollars back into the banking system. 

 Analysts said the intervention could lessen confidence in the Hong Kong dollar peg to the U.S. dollar, since the government had been forced to intervene. 

 "With the HKMA coming in and buying the currency...even if they are committed to the peg, it raises the spectre that maybe they are not. And then the whole thing starts to feed upon itself," said Robert Rountree, head of research at Prudential-Bache Securities. 

 "As long as speculators and hedge funds feel the Hong Kong Monetary Authority or the authorities are anything less than totally committed to the peg, then they can push the market down as low as they want," Rountree said. 

 Alex Wong, research manager at OSK Asia Securities, said next week's upside would be limited, with the first resistance at 7,350 points and then at 7,600. 

 "The intervention will have only a short-term impact on the market, because the fundamentals are still unchanged. Interest rates are high and the yen is still weak," he said. 

 Wong said some pullback could occur as the market tested the level for another intervention. "But (the HKMA) can't keep doing this, because it has limited resources," he added. 

 Analysts said the yen's volatility would continue to put pressure on the Chinese yuan, which would weigh on sentiment toward the Hong Kong dollar peg. 

 "We need to know when the political leaders of Southeast Asian and northeast Asian economies are going to get their acts together," said Thompson. 

 "If the Japanese got their act together and sorted out their banking system promptly...we could be on the road to recovery." 

 Thompson said Hong Kong's gross domestic product contraction of 2.8 percent for the first quarter of 1998 was a major factor in the index's long-term downtrend. 

 "That obviously means all our estimates have to be revised down, causing pressure on the Hang Seng Index," he said. 

 Analysts said unemployment figures for May to July, due on Tuesday, would dampen sentiment. Economists expect the jobless rate to rise to between 4.8 percent to six percent from 4.5 percent in the three months to June. 

 More anaemic corporate results would also weigh on the market, analysts said. Cheung Kong Infrastructure Holdings Ltd  is due to release interim results on Thursday.

title: ANALYSIS-Profit, not peg, is target in HK$ attacks.
text:
SINGAPORE, Aug 14 (Reuters) - There has been much talk of "speculative" attacks on the Hong Kong dollar in the past year but there is more to these assaults than a single-minded attempt by the market to break the peg. 

 At times since the start of the Asia crisis pressure has developed on the Hong Kong dollar because it is basically the last pegged currency in Asia and the Hong Kong economy has suffered pretty much equally with the rest of the region. 

 When pressure develops on the spot rate, for whatever reason, many other traders pile in to trade the Hang Seng and Hong Kong dollar forwards because there is money to be made. 

 "It's a situation where it's quite easy to make money with little risk," said one Singapore based trader. "As long as you can get into the forwards at a reasonable rate you can make a good turn because when the (interest) rates start to go (up) they really go." 

 The situation develops because of the way Hong Kong's currency board works and the dramatic impact that downward pressure on the HK dollar has on interest rates and therefore the forward market premiums. 

 The Hong Kong currency, linked to the U.S. dollar since 1983 after a speculative attack, is the last tradable pegged currency in the region. It is pegged at HK$7.8 per US$1 and is permitted to float in a narrow band around that level. 

 Under the currency board system, note-issuing banks buy or sell Hong Kong dollars to the public but they are bound to undertake a reverse transaction by selling or buying Hong Kong dollars from the territory's Exchange Fund. 

 This drains, or injects, liquidity into the monetary system so downward pressure on the strong Hong Kong dollar will raise interest rates and vice-versa. 

 It is this - the fact that interest rates jump when there is pressure on the spot rate - that creates a situation where forward purchases of U.S. dollars can become extremely profitable. 

 An operator, anticipating pressure on the spot Hong Kong dollar would buy forward U.S. dollars, effectively going short of Hong Kong dollars forward. 

 The same operator would then short the Hang Seng, most probably on the futures market, because the stock market is almost bound to fall as interest rates surge. 

 By then selling spot Hong Kong dollars, along with the rest of the market, the player would see the forward premium on his U.S. dollars kick up as interest rates jumped. 

 The added bonus of being short of the stock market would boost his profits when the Hang Seng fell out of bed on the higher interest rates. 

 The long forward dollar position means the short Hong Kong dollar spot is effectively funded because money is made on the forward side. 

 The situation is unlike speculative attacks on currencies such as sterling in 1992 where traders were looking to make money purely on the extent of the fall if a devaluation is forced - which they eventually did, to the tune of 15 percent. 

 The risk of a substantial loss on the short spot position is also much less with the Hong Kong dollar than with more freely floating currencies. 

 This is because its upside is as limited by the peg system as its downside. Therefore, even if you are short of Hong Kong dollars at the time of heavy intervention to stave off a speculative attack, any loss on the upside is extremely limited. 

 "What makes the Hong Kong possible to play in this manner is the fact that it's pegged," said Chiang Yao Chye, head of Asia Pacific research at CIBC in Singapore. 

 "So even if the authorities defend the Hong Kong dollar they are not going to try and make it appreciate. If the spot appreciates you're obviously looking at losses on your spot position." 

 The economic cost of maintaining the peg can be high and the money the market is making with these forward plays is basically draining out of the Hong Kong asset markets. 

 The main cost of maintaining the peg is the hit the asset markets receive when interest rates rise as the peg comes under pressure. In Hong Kong the property market has suffered badly of late and the authorities have moved to shore up prices. 

 But analysts say that to maintain a credible commitment to the peg, authorities should be self-disciplined enough to allow asset markets to fall and take the strain. It is simply one of the costs of maintaining the peg. 

 By moving to help the property market the government is effectively showing that it does not like the impact the peg is having on the economy. 

 The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) also recently borrowed and bought Hong Kong dollars for the government treasury. 

 Because these dollars will flow back into the system as they are used to offset a fiscal deficit, the action by the HKMA is tantamount to sterilised intervention so the net impact on liquidity over time is zero. 

 "It seems to me that maybe the HKMA does not like the side-effects of maintaining the peg and some of these moves we've seen recently show that perhaps they are getting soft and unwilling to take it on the chin like they have in the past," said one Singapore analyst who preferred not to be named. 

 If these kinds of attacks on the Hong Kong peg continue, it heightens the chance that the peg will eventually break, analysts say. 

 But a Reuters poll this week showed that seven out of 10 economists believed the Hong Kong dollar would stay linked to its U.S. counterpart, with no likelihood of a future de-pegging. 

 But some have their doubts, with one thinking the peg will hold out until mid-1999, while another said the risks were high that the peg would break over the next six to 12 months. 

 "There is no reason why people think there will always be pressure on the Hong Kong dollar," CIBC's Chiang said. 

 "But if things are not going well it's an excuse and if enough people jump on the bandwagon and interest rates go high enough you make a profit anyway, whether the peg breaks or not."

title: Mkt Participants Question Role of HKMA  Intervention
text:
NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--Was it an act of desperation or an act of resolve? 

 That's what market participants were trying to decide about the unprecedented act Friday by Hong Kong's central bank to intervene in the territory's equity, futures and currency markets. 

 While the move appeared to be well-timed - coming at the end of a volatile trading week and ahead of a three-day holiday in Hong Kong - currency traders and analysts remained uncertain if the action will mean the eventual delinking of the Hong Kong dollar to its U.S. counterpart. That could further roil already skittish global markets. 

 The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA), the territory's quasi-central bank, spent an undisclosed amount of its $96.5 billion in foreign exchange reserves to buy Hang Seng's blue-chip stocks, index futures and Hong Kong dollars. 

 It was the first time ever the HKMA's foreign exchange reserves were used to buy local equities - an action as unfathomable as the U.S. Federal Reserve using its reserves to buy shares of stocks included in the Dow Jones Industrial Average. 

 "It looks kind of desperate," said Eric Nickerson, currency strategist with Bank of America in New York. "It shows that a currency board is not something they are willing to live with." 

 The Hong Kong dollar is pegged to the U.S. dollar with the HKMA effectively acting as a currency board to maintain the peg. The local currency has thus far survived the rounds of devaluation and the freefall that has touched neighboring regional currencies since the onset of last year's Asian financial crisis. 

 "When you intervene, you are showing you have problems," said Stan Shipley, senior economist with Merrill Lynch in New York.

title: Firmer dollar fails to build on gains in Europe.
text:
LONDON, Aug 13 (Reuters) - The dollar was firmer in European morning trade on Thursday, boosted by jitters about Russia's financial problems and sharp losses in Hong Kong stocks, but profit-taking knocked the U.S. unit off highs. 

 Speculation about the fate of the Russian rouble was heightened by a suggestion from international financier George Soros that the currency be devalued and pegged to the dollar or euro. 

 But a blip above 1.80 marks for the first time in a month failed to generate follow-through buying in a generally thin market, while fears of Bank of Japan (BOJ) intervention knocked the dollar off its perch above 147 yen. 

 "The escalating concern about Russia has given the dollar a boost and weakened the mark on the crossess," said Rob Miniken, chief currency strategist at Citibank in London. "But market conditions are very light, so the extent of the move might have been exaggerated." 

 The dollar eased against the mark after a senior Russian central bank official said Soros's suggestion would not solve the country's financial crisis. 

 At 0730 GMT the dollar was at 1.7895/7900 marks and 146.49/59 yen, off highs at 1.8003 and 147.18 but up from 1.7750/60 and 146.01/11 in late European trade on Wednesday. 

 The mark, vunerable to Russian jitters due to the exposure of German banks, weakened to an eight-week low against the safe-haven Swiss franc at 83.18 centimes. Sterling hit a two-week high at 2.9288 marks on general mark weakness. 

 The market became more nervous after Russian stocks extended their sharp falls on Wednesday. Jitters intensified after Russia's central bank said it would put a limit on the amount of dollars local banks can purchase in the interbank market. 

 But analysts said the mark sell-off in response to Soros' proposal, published in a letter to the Financial Times on Thursday, was likely to be short-lived. 

 "There is no huge concern that Russia's problems are going to push the mark over the edge," said Paul Meggyesi, senior currency economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in London. 

 Yet, the dollar eased off its 1.7877 mark low after Russian shares opened sharply lower on Thursday. Russia's markets RTS share trade was then suspended at 0740 GMT, according to Naufor Brokers Association. The Russian securities markets watchdog had recommended suspending share trade. Some key stocks shed 16 and 13 percent respectively at the open. 

 Against the yen the dollar eased back into the mid-146 yen area after caution set in when senior Ministry of Finance (MOF) official Eisuke Sakakibara said Japan was looking for chances to conduct yen-supportive intervention. 

 A sharp fall in Hong Kong's Hang Seng share index by 2.9 percent weighed on the yen even though it gained some support from the Nikkei's resilience as Tokyo's benchmark index closed little changed, ending an eight-session losing streak. 

 But fears that the yen's prolonged weakness could prompt central banks in other countries to reduce yen in their external reserves offset some of that support, dealers said. 

 Taiwan's central bank is trimming the yen portion of its reserves to ensure maximum returns, central bank forex department chief Chou Ah-ting said on Thursday. He declined to specify the amount of the reduction. 

 Taiwan's action followed a similar report about mainland China earlier this week. The Financial Times said on Tuesday China has sharply reduced its yen-denominated reserve holdings to protect the value of its forex reserves. 

 The market was unmoved by news that Japan's current account surplusrose 46.2 percent in June from a year ago to 1.44 trillion yen, with the trade surplus rising 25.4 percent. 

 Bank of Japan Governor Masaru Hayami said "one could say the yen was over-depreciated" given Japan's large current account surplus and that progress on financial system reform should boost the yen. U.S. retail sales data will be released at 1230 GMT, along with weekly jobless claims. Retail sales are expected to have dropped 0.8 percent in July after a 0.1 percent monthly rise in June. The expected drop is partly due to the General Motors strike, and retail sales are seen up 0.4 percent excluding auto sales. title: HKMA Sold/U.S Dlrs -2: Bks Urged To Be Prudent In Lending
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--The Hong Kong Monetary Authority late Thursday confirmed it had sold a "small amount" of U.S. dollars for Hong Kong dollars during the day, in what it called a "normal transaction." 

 The quasi-central bank said the transaction was done on behalf of the government to help it meet cash needs. An HKMA spokesman said it wasn't intervention. 

 The HKMA has described its recent activity as being related to the government's expected fiscal deficit of HK$21 billion in the current year. The HKMA manages the Hong Kong government's reserves money. 

 However, analysts aren't buying the HKMA claim and see the activity as straightforward foreign exchange market intervention to ease pressure on the Hong Kong dollar. 

 By cooling the market through intervention, the HKMA is preventing spikes in interest rates that would result because of the currency board system that Hong Kong operates, according to market participants. 

 There also are rumors in the market that some Hong Kong banks have had difficulting funding themselves on the interbank market because they have lent heavily to investment houses speculating on the dollar, the spokesman said. 

 While banks are free to make such loans, the HKMA advises them "to be very conscious of the funding and interest rate risks if they lend out sizable amounts of Hong Kong dollars without pre-funding themselves," the spokesman said. 

 In a somewhat veiled threat, the HKMA's statement reminded banks that when it lends in the market, the authority "takes into account the credit standing" of borrowers. 

 The HKMA operates a discount window as lender of last resort in the local money market, but at times has refused to deal with some banks that it suspects of funding speculators.

title: HKMA  Intervention  Leads Some To Question Peg Commitment
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--Intervention by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority in recent days has worried some analysts, who say it will slow the territory's recovery from the current turmoil and may indicate it isn't prepared to pay the price its commitment to a currency peg will exact. 

 The HKMA - Hong Kong's quasi-central bank - has acknowledged buying Hong Kong dollars three times in the currency market in the past week, most recently on Wednesday. 

 It claims it's merely selling U.S. dollars from reserves to fund an expected HK$21.4 billion budget deficit for the current fiscal year, and says the moves don't constitute intervention. 

 But the activity coincided with a build-up of speculative positions against the Hong Kong dollar in the forward market, which boosted the U.S. dollar to HK$7.7510 at one point last week, above the HK$7.7500 level where it typically steps in to cool the U.S. dollar. 

 Along with intervention, Hong Kong officials have warned they will mount a spirited defense of the currency, although they are secretive about exactly what they will do. 

 "I cannot provide details of the strategies, because when we intervene and fight against speculators, we would need some element of mystery," Financial Secretary Donald Tsang Yam-kuen said Wednesday. 

 But those threats of intervention, and talk of a mystery arsenal, worry some market participants. They say the HKMA is overstepping its role as a currency board custodian and, ironically, giving speculators who hope to break the peg a reason to stick around. 

 "You don't need a secret arsenal if a currency board works," says Desmond Supple, BZW's head of Asian currency research. "It has domestic economic implications and is particularly alarming to me. That suggests the political will is not strong enough for the currency board to work."

title: Hong Kong Intervention  Leads Some To Question  Currency  Peg
text:
HONG KONG -(Dow Jones)- Intervention by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority in recent days has worried some analysts, who say it will slow the territory's recovery from the current turmoil and may indicate it isn't prepared to pay the price its commitment to a currency peg will exact. 

 The HKMA - Hong Kong's quasi-central bank - has acknowledged buying Hong Kong dollars three times in the currency market in the past week, most recently on Wednesday. 

 It claims it's merely selling U.S. dollars from reserves to fund an expected HK$21.4 billion budget deficit for the current fiscal year, and says the moves don't constitute intervention. 

 But the activity coincided with a build-up of speculative positions against the Hong Kong dollar in the forward market, which boosted the U.S. dollar to HK$7.7510 at one point last week, above the HK$7.7500 level where it typically steps in to cool the U.S. dollar. 

 Along with intervention, Hong Kong officials have warned they will mount a spirited defense of the currency, although they are secretive about exactly what they will do. 

 "I cannot provide details of the strategies, because when we intervene and fight against speculators, we would need some element of mystery," Financial Secretary Donald Tsang Yam-kuen said Wednesday. 

 But those threats of intervention, and talk of a mystery arsenal, worry some market participants. They say the HKMA is overstepping its role as a currency board custodian and, ironically, giving speculators who hope to break the peg a reason to stick around. 

 "You don't need a secret arsenal if a currency board works," says Desmond Supple, BZW's head of Asian currency research. "It has domestic economic implications and is particularly alarming to me. That suggests the political will is not strong enough for the currency board to work." 

 Because of Hong Kong's currency board mechanism, the government has in theory given up control of monetary policy. If speculators sell the Hong Kong dollar, interest rates should rise automatically until they are high enough to attract buyers back to the currency. 

 That's why critics like Supple are questioning why the HKMA has intervened over the past week to support the currency and keep interest rates down. 

 Supple said HKMA intervention is slowing Hong Kong's economic adjustment, since interest rates aren't being allowed to rise in line with market activity. 

 To some, that indicates that the territory won't stomach the havoc temporarily high interest rates will reap on the stock and property markets. The territory's main stock index, the Hang Seng, has already fallen 17% this month and 60% since last August, while property values have dropped 40% since the start of the year. 

 With the government having suspended land sales until at least the end of the current fiscal year - another effort to help cushion the blow to the property market - it has been the Hang Seng Index that has born the brunt of asset price deflation. Several market analysts have said the index - trading at about 6600 points - is nearing its bottom. 

 When it can't get any lower, speculators who are shorting the stock index may well turn their attention back to the Hong Kong dollar, they said. 

 Still, SG Securities' Clive McDonnell said the HKMA is "caught between a rock and a hard place." He says the authority will be criticized for being too interventionist if it steps into markets to support the Hong Kong dollar, or for destroying confidence in the peg if it doesn't. 

 He also said he believes rumors of speculation in recent weeks have been overblown and it makes sense for the HKMA to buy local currency for the government at this time of year because of its funding needs. 

 And sources close to Soros Fund Management, which was blamed for a speculative move on the currency last week, said finger-pointers should point elsewhere. 

 But speculators are out there, and the government is remaining vigilant. That means interest rates will remain at high levels and the economy will continue to bear the pain of the linked exchange rate, BZW's Supple said. 

 Traders Thursday warned that there will be more battles between the government and speculators, the next perhaps Friday, ahead of a three-day weekend in Hong Kong. 

 And with each battle, the questions about how long the HKMA will be willing and able to keep the peg in place heat up. Even the staunchest believers are starting to ask themselves when, rather than whether, the government will abandon the currency board it has kept in place for 15 years. 

 "The only way you can restore Hong Kong dollar wealth is by breaking the peg, and then currency adjustments start to come into play," Supple said.

title: Remarks Show/China/Yuan -2: System's Ruthless Trade-Off
text:
Under Hong Kong's currency-board system, local interest rates rise automatically if there is a speculative attack on the Hong Kong dollar. The system is practically impregnable but it exacts a ruthless trade-off. The high interest rates quickly hurt the rest of the economy, hammering property prices, cutting corporate profits, and leading to worker layoffs. 

 "If you want the peg to remain, higher interest rates are the only way even if the economy (must) bleed," said Wu of DBS. The pain caused by rising rates has exacerbated this city's worst slowdown in more than 20 years. Many politicians have been calling for the government to find ways to defend the currency without using high interest rates. 

 In recent weeks, the Hong Kong government has been trying to damp the pain of the currency-board system by intervening in the money market and the property market. It is this activity that some observers say is a hint that Hong Kong policy makers may be unwilling to endure the pain of the dollar peg indefinitely. "They're undermining the credibility of the currency board," said Chris Wood, emerging-markets strategist at Banco Santander Investments. 

 On Wednesday, the government sold U.S. dollars to buy Hong Kong dollars, an action it took last week as well. A spokeswoman for the Hong Kong Monetary Authority declined to specify the amount of U.S. dollars sold, but said it was far less than was sold Tuesday and last week. Currency traders said the sales have kept interest rates artificially low. They also said that in recent months the Hong Kong Monetary Authority has injected funds into the interbank market to keep short-term interest rates low. 

 Financial Secretary Sir Donald Tsang said late last week the selling of U.S. dollars had helped to keep local interest rates from spiking a result, he said, "that may please a lot of people." 

 Tsang and other government officials have characterized the selling as necessary to fund a seasonal shortfall of revenue from taxes and duties. They argue it isn't a direct intervention to support the currency. A spokeswoman for the Hong Kong Monetary Authority said the authority wasn't acting to keep short-term interest rates artificially low, and continued to abide by the discipline of the currency board. 

 That's not the way some market participants see it. Wood of Banco Santander said that in addition to intervening in the interbank market, the government has also been trying to ease the pain by propping up property prices. In June, the government froze new land sales to stabilize falling property prices. Much of Hong Kong's wealth is tied up in the property market, and as Hong Kong's economy has soured, so too has public opinion of the government's handling of the economy. 

 So far, public opinion in Hong Kong is solidly behind keeping the currency peg. But Wood predicted that will change as the costs of maintaining the peg rapidly mount. Already, unemployment is at 4.2%, the worst level in more than 15 years. 

 Jim Walker, an economist at Credit Lyonnais Securities (Asia) Ltd., predicted that Hong Kong will be forced to endure "the misery of the peg," in which unemployment more than doubles and the economy contracts by 5.8% next year. In his scenario, Hong Kong might not see positive economic growth until 2001. 

 The key, observers said, is whether the government has the political will to adhere to the currency-board system. "If they stick with (the currency board), they can probably pull through as long as the Chinese leaders don't devalue the yuan," said Wu of DBS.

title: AWSJ: Remarks Show Pressures On China To Devalue Yuan
text:
From Thursday's Asian Wall Street Journal 


   By Erik Guyot and Ian Johnson


 HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--Government officials from China and Hong Kong are sending mixed messages about their willingness to bear the economic pain of defending their currencies. 

 On Wednesday, Beijing's ambassador to India said in a speech that further declines in the Japanese yen would hurt China's economy and might force a rethink of China's policy not to devalue its yuan. His comments appeared to contradict statements a day earlier by a top official from the nation's central bank, who reiterated China's commitment to maintaining its currency's level. 

 Meanwhile, in Hong Kong the government continued on Wednesday to intervene in local money markets to cushion the pain of higher interest rates caused by its exchange-rate system. That activity is leading some to question the political will of Hong Kong's government to maintain its currency-board system at all costs. 

 Wednesday's events underscore the extent to which China and Hong Kong are facing rising domestic pressures as their strong currencies hurt certain sectors of their economies. The yuan and the Hong Kong dollar are the last major currencies in Asia left standing with exchange rates fixed to the U.S. dollar, in the wake of Asia's yearlong currency crisis. 

 At a speech in New Delhi, China's Ambassador Zhou Gang said that "in my view a further depreciation of the yen would force China to have a second thinking" on whether to devalue. Economists cautioned that Zhou's comments probably didn't reflect Beijing's current thinking, but instead reiterated a previous government policy in which Chinese leaders made oblique threats to devalue the yuan if the yen continued to tumble. 

 Nevertheless, Zhou's remarks highlight the pressures on Beijing to devalue the yuan. A growing number of companies engaged in heavy industry located in China's coastal provinces have been clamoring for a devaluation, which would help them compete with cheaper products from South Korea, Taiwan and elsewhere in Asia. 

 Beijing isn't expected to devalue any time soon, since that wouldn't help China's economy many companies must also import large quantities of raw materials and foreign machinery. The yuan's decline would not only raise the cost of imports and overseas borrowings but also most likely plunge the rest of Asia into another round of currency depreciations. 

 A devaluation of the yuan would also undermine confidence in the Hong Kong government's ability to keep the Hong Kong dollar trading near its fixed rate of HK$7.8 to the U.S. dollar. Although Beijing and Hong Kong operate their currency systems independently, in the minds of many investors, the two currencies are intertwined. 

 So interconnected are the two currencies, that in recent weeks some currency speculators have been attacking the Hong Kong dollar as a way of making a proxy bet that the yuan eventually will decline in value. China's currency isn't freely traded, so currency speculators take bets that the Hong Kong dollar will tumble if the yuan depreciates. 

 In trying to ward off those speculative attacks, the Hong Kong government has been sending mixed messages as to its political will to defend the currency whatever the cost, some observers said. "They are sending a confusing signal," said Fredrich Wu, chief economist at DBS Bank in Singapore. "That's why the Hong Kong dollar is under attack."

title: AWSJ: HK Hit On Fears Of Too-Expensive Property Prices
text:
From Wednesday's Asian Wall Street Journal
   By Erik Guyot


 HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--Concerns about the Hong Kong dollar's future are roiling financial markets in the former British colony, as a new worry gets factored in: Property prices - which have already slid 40% from their 1997 peak - might not be falling nearly quickly enough. 

 On Tuesday, local interest rates soared: Hong Kong dollar overnight interest rates jumped to 8%, up from 6.5% on Monday, as speculators continued to test the currency's strength. Meanwhile, the benchmark Hang Seng Index tumbled 3.6% to its lowest level in five years. Since the beginning of August, the index has fallen 15%. 

 Through it all, the Hong Kong currency's rigid link to the U.S. dollar remained largely unbudged. The Hong Kong dollar traded in a close range around 7.75 to the U.S. dollar Tuesday, near its official rate of 7.80. 

 For the second time in two weeks, however, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority said it sold U.S. dollars, although a spokeswoman declined to say how many. She declined to characterize the sale as an intervention to support the Hong Kong dollar, saying the measure aimed to raise Hong Kong dollars to help fund a temporary deficit in the government's budget. 

 Weighing on Hong Kong's currency have been fears that China might need to devalue the yuan to boost its sagging export growth. In public comments on Tuesday, an official at China's central bank vigorously denied that it would devalue. Many investors say a fall in the value of the yuan would make the Hong Kong dollar's defense far more difficult. 

 But the Hong Kong dollar is feeling pressure as well from a problem closer to home: its troubled property market. Hong Kong property prices soared to astronomical values in recent years, only to fall sharply amid Asia's economic slowdown. But many observers say the 40% decline in the past year isn't enough to make Hong Kong competitive. And as long as Hong Kong isn't competitive economically, its currency will feel the heat. 

 "The pressure on the Hong Kong dollar will continue to mount unless the property market can adjust quickly," says Frank Gong, currency strategist at Bank of America. 

 Asia's currency crisis has made many Asian cities much more inexpensive places to do business, because of falling property prices and wilting local currencies. Meanwhile, the Hong Kong dollar stands alone as the last freely traded currency in Asia that has held its value.

title: Taiwan c.bank vows to maintain  currency  stability.
text:
TAIPEI, Aug 9 (Reuters) - Taiwan's deputy central bank governor Shea Jia-dong has vowed to maintain the Taiwan dollar's stability, saying the island would not join a race of currency depreciation, local media reported on Sunday. 

 "The central bank will do its best to maintain stability of the Taiwan dollar and will not join a competition of currency depreciation," Taiwan newspapers quoted Shea as telling U.S. finance and Federal Reserve officials in Washington on Saturday. 

 "We know what role we should play," said Shea, who was in the United States to attend the vice-ministerial level trade talks between Washington and Taipei. 

 Washington has expressed concerns over the Taiwan dollar's movement, fearing a sharp fall would add further downward pressure to Asia's already-battered currencies, local reports said. 

 The Taiwan dollar has fallen about 19 percent to the U.S. dollar since Asia's financial woes erupted in mid-1997, far below the depreciations of its regional export rivals. This is eroding Taiwan's export competitiveness. 

 In July, Taiwan exports fell 16.3 percent in July from a year earlier period to US$8.955 billion, hammered by sharply lower demand from Japan and other recession-hit Asian trade partners. 

 Shea reportedly told U.S. officials that the central bank would try to eliminate "unnecessary fluctuations" of the local currency and maintain what he called a "dynamic stability" of the Taiwan dollar. 

 The central bank has repeatedly pledged to intervene in the foreign exchange market when "seasonal, occasional and abnormal" factors emerged. 

 The Taiwan dollar closed at a seven-week low of T$34.60 on Friday, with investors seeking a safe haven in the U.S. dollar amid renewed concerns about depreciation pressure on the Hong Kong dollar and China's yuan. 

 Dealers noted the intervention by the central bank to smooth the currency's downturn but said the bank seemed prepared to tolerate wider fluctuations than it has in recent days. ((Taipei newsroom, +886 2 2508-0815 fax +886 2 2508-0204, taipei.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: HKMA's  currency  defence dilemma raises questions.
text:
HONG KONG, Aug 8 (Reuters) - Will Hong Kong be able to match last week's nimble defence of the local dollar the next time currency speculators flex their muscles amid Asia's economic gloom? economists asked on Saturday. 

 "The first time speculators attacked Hong Kong, (in October 1997) the government hiked interest rates, this time they used the buying technique, what will they do next?", said Ricky Tam, Senior Research Manager, at Delta Asia Financial Group. "I think the government and the HKMA are improving their techniques." 

 "I am quite impressed with the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA)," Tam added. 

 The territory's de-facto central bank stepped in quickly during last week's massive selling of the local currency by buying undisclosed amounts of Hong Kong dollars on behalf of the Treasury. The HKMA said it needed to fill a shortfall in government coffers. 

 "The mechanism is similar to an intervention," said George Chan, research manager at Celestial Asia Securities Holdings. 

 Since Wednesday, four U.S. investment banks as well as fund houses have been selling the Hong Kong dollar short, with several billion U.S. dollars worth of Hong Kong dollars changing hands in both spot and forward markets, dealers said on Friday. 

 The government action - not, technically an intervention - helped balance the supply and demand of Hong Kong dollars in the market and staved off the threat of a hike in interest rates. 

 The Hong Kong Monetary Authority usually relies on a currency board system, which maintains the Hong Kong dollar's link to the U.S. dollar. 

 "It was on an auto pilot system, allowing interest rates to govern the supply and demand of the Hong Kong dollar and make the adjustments," said Paul Tang, senior economist at the Bank oF East Asia. 

 The trouble is, higher interest rates shackle an already beleaguered economy and impoverished Hong Kong can hardly afford another rise in interest rates. 

 Interbank rates had risen on market jitters, but bank deposit rates had not surged, as in the past. "It shows the impact of speculation on bank deposit rates so far is not as severe...it may show that the HKMA has found a way to fend off speculators," Tang said. 

 On Friday the overnight rate hovered around eight percent, just a few percentage points over the five to six percent the overnight rate has averaged over the past few months. In comparison, last October's overnight rate soared to 300 percent. Financial Secretary Donald Tsang hastened to clarify on Friday that the government was not tossing the currency board system. 

 "I am not departing from the currency board system at all. It so happened that this is a dry month for our Treasury. Usually we go and change some of our foreign exchange into Hong Kong dollars anyway to meet our payments, which occurs this time of the year," he said. 

 Economists cautiously welcomed the move, but did not rule out future hikes in interest rates should the speculators come back. 

 Certainly the stock markets fear a hike in interest rates. On Friday the blue-chip Hang Seng Index fell 3.25 percent to 7,018. Hong Kong's troubles weighed on other Asian markets. 

 And speculators may well return - Financial Secretary Tsang said on Saturday he expected speculators to attack the Hong Kong dollar for as long as Asia remains in crisis. 

 Delta's Tam said that regardless of which method the HKMA used then, the main thing was to have enough reserves of US dollars. Unlike its unfortunate neighbours, on that front Hong Kong need not worry, with US$96.5 billion safely in the bank.
