title: Heavy HK dollar sales for third day.
text:
HONG KONG, Aug 7 (Reuters) - The Hong Kong dollar came under renewed pressure on Friday as overseas investment houses kept up their assault on the currency, traders said. 

 Since Wednesday, four U.S. investment banks as well as fund houses have been aggressively selling the Hong Kong dollar short, they said. Selling continued on Friday. 

 "The U.S.-based fund houses were aggressively buying forwards today. The size of the short sales was quite big," a dealer at a European bank said. 

 The heavy sales of Hong Kong dollars have raised fears about the resilience of the Hong Kong dollar's peg to the U.S. dollar. 

 The Hong Kong dollar is linked to the U.S. unit at a rate of HK$7.8 per US$1 and is permitted to float in a narrow band around that level. It was at HK$7.7490/00 per dollar at midday on Friday, a level viewed as key support. 

 The peg was instituted in 1983 during currency instability that accompanied early negotiations between Britain and China on Hong Kong's future. Since then, the currency has fluctuated narrowly. 

 But the local dollar has come under attack sporadically over the past year, a victim of Asia's financial crisis and Hong Kong's severe economic downturn. 

 The government on Monday said the economy contracted 2.8 percent in the first quarter of 1998, a bigger decline than the two percent forecast in May. 

 Hong Kong authorities have said the economy will worsen before it gets better and economists predict a full-year recession. 

 The poor economic prognosis, coupled with weak interim results for Hong Kong companies, has cast a pall over sentiment in the territory and left the currency open to attack, analysts said. The market was particularly vulnerable after months of worry over the weak yen, they said. 

 A sagging Chinese yuan also has accentuated fears Beijing could devalue the currency, a move that many believe could imperil the Hong Kong dollar peg. 

 Several billions of U.S. dollars worth of Hong Kong dollars have been sold over the past few days in both the spot and forward markets, dealers and analysts said. 

 In Bangkok, Thailand's deputy prime minister, Supachai Panitchpakdi, said on Friday the speculative attacks against the Hong Kong dollar were undermining regional confidence. 

 "The problem in Hong Kong is now becoming a regional problem and Thailand is concerned about it because it could affect our efforts to solve the problems that we have here," he told reporters. 

 Because the Hong Kong dollar is pegged, assaults on the currency usually are made in the forward market, where there is more room for fluctuations. Selling spot Hong Kong dollars implies fears the peg could snap soon, some analysts said. 

 By midday on Friday, the three-month forward spread had climbed to 1,400-1,500 points, well above the 650-700 points registered on Tuesday, the day before the attack began. 

 Interest rates were sharply higher. The benchmark three-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate was at an eight week high of 12.69 percent at Friday's 0330 GMT fixing compared with 11.14 percent at the same time on Thursday. 

 The one-month rate was even higher at 13.2 percent versus 11.06 percent on Thursday. 

 The intense pressure on the Hong Kong dollar has caused jitters throughout Asia. While up to now, weakness in the yen and the yuan have hurt the Hong Kong unit, the salvos against the Hong Kong dollar are now harming those currencies. 

 Hong Kong dealers said the scale of the attack over the past three days was comparable to that of October 1997, when the overnight rate ballooned to 300 percent as the territory came under the most severe speculative attack since 1983. 

 "Though turning a bit bearish, the market has remained calm and it is not as panicky as it was last October," said Andy Lim, head of money market and interest rate trading at NatWest Markets in Hong Kong. 

 "Perhaps we have all well-prepared for it. The market, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority and the Hong Kong citizen are better-equipped after repeated currency attacks over the past year," he said. 

 The HKMA has said it has recently borrowed and bought Hong Kong dollars to fund a shortfall in the government treasury, but said the purchases did not represent intervention in the market.

title: AWSJ: Stability Of HK Dollar Remains A Worry
text:
From Friday's Asian Wall Street Journal

 HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--Stock prices in Hong Kong plunged to their lowest level in 3 years over concerns about the stability of this city's currency. 

 Global investors are already actively dumping the shares and bonds of Hong Kong companies with unhedged U.S. dollar debts. "Investors are very concerned" about a possible decline in the value of the Hong Kong dollar, said Raja Visweswaran, head of fixed-income research at Bank of America Asia Ltd. "If companies can prove they have hedged themselves, then automatically they will command a premium" for their securities. 

 The blue-chip Hang Seng Index fell 2.8% Thursday, while local interest rates spiked, triggered by concerns that the continued slide in the Japanese yen might induce China to devalue its yuan, a move that is widely seen as weakening the strength of the Hong Kong dollar. 

 In trading Thursday, the Hong Kong dollar stayed in a tight range of about 7.75 Hong Kong dollars to the U.S. dollar, thanks to earlier intervention on Wednesday by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority. 

 Although the government's actions helped bring down overnight interest rates to 5.5%, from 7% late Wednesday, long-term interest rates continued to rise over concerns about the Hong Kong dollar. The key three-month interbank rate rose to 11.13% Thursday from 10.21% on Wednesday. 

 Regional money markets were also hit by worries that if the Hong Kong dollar were to fall, it could trigger another round of Asian currency depreciations. The Singapore dollar weakened to S$1.74 against the U.S. dollar, from S$1.72 on Wednesday. The Thai baht eased to 41.45 baht to the U.S. dollar, from 40.95 baht at the close of trading Wednesday. The Malaysian ringgit slid to 4.17 ringgit against the dollar, from 4.14 ringgit the previous day. 

 The Hong Kong dollar is the last freely traded Asian currency that hasn't depreciated, thanks to the government's efforts to keep the currency pegged near a rate of 7.8 Hong Kong dollars to the U.S. currency. And although Hong Kong boasts more than US$96 billion in foreign-currency reserves to defend its currency, the actions by domestic corporations in hedging their U.S.-dollar exposure could weaken the local currency.

title: HK's Yam says Q2 unlikely to improve on poor Q1.
text:
HONG KONG, July 13 (Reuters) - Hong Kong Monetary Authority chief executive Joseph Yam said on Monday that the territory's second quarter economic performance was unlikely to be an improvement over the first quarter of 1998. 

 The government has estimated that the economy contracted two percent in the first quarter. 

 Yam also said in an interview with Reuters Television that the outlook for the rest of the year could be poor as well. 

 "I don't think the second quarter was an improvement over the first at all and perhaps the third quarter may not be good either," Yam said. 

 "But quite a lot will depend on the external environment and the sentiment is so adverse at this time that we may actually see a further slowdown in the economy before we see a recovery," he said. 

 Yam noted the Hong Kong government was projecting a HK$20 billion fiscal deficit in 1998/99 compared with an HK$80 billion surplus in 1997/98 due to the slowing economy and because of increased spending to soften the pain. 

 "But the public sector of Hong Kong is actually quite small so we can't possibly be spending our way out of a recession. A lot actually depends on the external environment but the external environment is still uncertain and quite unfavorable," he said. 

 Yam said the outlook for Asia would depend largely on how successful Japan was in reflating its economy and sorting out its financial problems. 

 The defeat of Japan's ruling Liberal Democratic Party in upper house election over the weekend and the subsequent resignation of Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto might delay implementation of reforms, but would not derail the process. 

 "Of course, the political situation means these measures may be delayed a little, although I don't think there will be a change in the direction of these measures," he said. 

 Continued volatility in the yen could spur destabilising currency devaluations in the region. 

 "The sentiment is such that continued volatility in the yen could spark another round of currency devaluation in Asia and may undermine the recovery efforts in Asia," said Yam. 

 "But I hope sentiment can actually be changed by greater cooperation among the G7 or G3 countries in helping Japan in coming out of its problems. I think that is in the interest of all of us," he said. 

 Yam, who was in Tokyo for a meeting of the Bank for International Settlements, said he told the group there was a need for greater stability because instability in the yen would have serious implications for the rest of the region and the contagion effects could spread to European and American markets. 

 The HKMA chief said the authority would "absolutely not" intervene in foreign exchange markets to defend the Hong Kong dollar's peg to the U.S. dollar. 

 He said interest rates automatically rose in response to selling pressure on the Hong Kong dollar through the workings of the currency board system. 

 With "a currency board system you don't need to intervene in the market. You have some sort of convertible undertaking and if people sell Hong Kong dollars to (the HKMA) we just have to take it. We are entirely passive," he said. 

 Yam said there was no reason for China to devalue its currency, even if it failed to meet its 1998 growth target of eight percent. 

 China continued to run a balance of trade surplus, had substantial foreign reserves of US$140 billion and maintained capital controls, he said. 

 "The economy is still growing, although it may not be eight percent - I think they may be able to achieve eight percent - even if it is less than eight percent, then so what? It's still quite a significant growth rate and there is no reason for the RMB to be devalued," Yam said.

text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--The Hong Kong dollar is weaker at midday Monday, with overseas investors selling due to genuine commercial U.S. dollar need before the end of the second quarter. 

 The local currency is quoted at HK$7.7495 per U.S. dollar at 0405 GMT (12:05 a.m. EDT), weaker than the HK$7.7485 level quoted late Friday. 

 A currency dealer at a European bank said overseas investors, primarily from Japan, are exiting Hong Kong's currency and money markets to repatriate funds to Japan ahead of end of the quarter and the half-year. 

 But the dollar's rise is about over for the day, the dealer noted, with participants fearing that any more aggressive Hong Kong dollar-selling will prompt intervention by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority at HK$7.7500. 

 As such, some investors who want to remain in the Hong Kong markets longer-term are seeking U.S. dollar funding through the swaps and forward foreign exchange markets. Forward premiums opened lower than Friday's late levels, but have been climbing all morning. 

 Concerns that the Hong Kong dollar will face another speculative attack shortly before markets here close Wednesday for the one-year anniversary of the territory's return to Chinese rule have subsided. 

 The three-month forward premium is 870 points over the spot rate, compared with 900 points late Friday. The six-month premium is at 2200 ponits, flat from Friday and the one-year premium is down a touch to 5000 points from 5200 points. 

 Premiums will continue to edge higher Monday, but there won't be a nervous spike, as happened on Friday, the dealer said.

title: FOCUS-Camdessus-yen fall is "crisis within crisis".
text:
STRASBOURG, France, June 23 (Reuters) - The fall in the yen is creating a crisis within the Asian crisis, threatening growth across the region and adding to market instability, the head of the International Monetary Fund said on Tuesday. 

 "A new crisis - a crisis within the crisis - has emerged with the dramatic fall of the yen," IMF Managing Director Michel Camdessus said in a speech to the parliamentary assembly of the Council of Europe. 

 "This new development reflects a serious lack of confidence, provoked by Japan's sluggish reaction to an economic slowdown that is turning into recession and the crisis in its financial institutions." 

 Camdessus, in a far-reaching speech dealing with the causes of Asia's financial turmoil and what should be done to prevent it happening again, also urged China and Hong Kong not to devalue their currencies and said foreign exchange intervention would only work if Japan corrected its economic weaknesses. 

 "The joint interventions of the United States and Japan on the foreign exchange market... were justified, but the effect will be lasting only if Japan promptly adopts energetic measures for the rehabilitation of its banking sector, tax relief, public investment and the opening up and deregulation of its economy." 

 Last week's intervention was the first time in more than six years that the United States had stepped into foreign exchange markets to support the yen, which had been trading at eight-year lows around 146.75 to the dollar. 

 The yen climbed in response to the central bank dollar sales, although markets are now seeking evidence of concrete action by Japan to ease its financial woes. 

 Camdessus said the yen's fall could slow the recovery of other troubled Asian economies and was already adding to the instability affecting Russia and some emerging economies. 

 Russia, one of the IMF's biggest borrowers before the Asian financial crisis, is now seeking an extra $10 billion or $15 billion to ease its latest financial problems. A team of IMF experts is in Moscow to review the economy and examine the request. 

 Camdessus called on Russia to reform its tax collection system if it wanted money from the international community. 

 "International markets want to see Russia tackle what constitutes its fundamental problem, that is its tax collection system," he told a news conference after the speech. 

 Listing his priorities for the international community, Camdessus stressed the need to hold exchange rate pegs in places like China and Hong Kong and he said the two should be ready to ease fiscal policy if needed. 

 "We must help preserve the stability of exchange rates in countries whose actions may be crucial to market stability, such as China and Hong Kong, despite the negative short-term impact of the crisis on their exports and growth," he said. 

 In these countries, as in Singapore and Taiwan, there is a margin for fiscal stimulus, which should be used if needed, he said. 

 China and its Hong Kong Special Administrative Region have insisted they will not devalue. But exports have been hit by Japan's economic weakness and by problems elsewhere in Asia. 

 Camdessus also called on countries with balance of payments surpluses, including some European states, to do more to help the troubled Asian states, for example with untied loans to countries going through the adjustment process. 

 Rich countries should step up humanitarian aid and improve fiscal management to guard against further economic downturns. 

 Camdessus said last year's IMF reform programs for Thailand, Indonesia and South Korea were designed to restore investor confidence, reestablish access to international capital markets and reverse excessive currency depreciations. 

 At the news conference, he defended the IMF's recipe for economic recovery and said reforms in South Korea and Thailand, where Fund prescriptions were quickly undertaken, had started to bear fruit. 

 He said Indonesia, whose acceptance of IMF medicine has been far less willing, was only at the beginning of its road to recovery. 

 "One shouldn't think that we are dogmatic in monetary matters and are looking for the highest possible interest rates to produce high currencies," Camdessus said. 

 The IMF has been accused of rigidly relying on a one-size-fits-all approach to economic crises regardless of how they may differ from country to country. 

 "We told Korea to give itself some budgetary space to produce a greater effect on the economy without having too much impact on the exchange rate. The same thing happened in Thailand and is starting to produce results," he said. 

 "On the other hand, we are at the beginning in Indonesia. We think the currency is going to have to be brought back into balance," he said, noting that inflation in Indonesia was expected to reach 80 percent this year.

 The volatile overnight Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate is quoted at 6.00%, down from 8.00% late Friday. The three-month rate is 9.00%, down from 9.5% late Friday

title: HKMA to keep HK$14 bln in stock market-paper.
text:
HONG KONG, June 20 (Reuters) - The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) said it would not sell its portfolio of HK$14 billion invested in the local stock market when the Land Fund and Exchange Fund were merged, a local paper said on Saturday. 

 "It is obviously not a good time to sell," said HKMA chief Joseph Yam in a report by the South China Morning Post. 

 The Land Fund, now at HK$195.6 billion, was created in 1983 to hold half of the revenues from government land sales. Money in this fund can be invested in both local and regional stock markets. 

 The Land Fund lost HK$3.8 billion in value in the wake of the economic turmoil that hit the territory and neighbouring countries and has cut its exposure to equities. 

 The government has announced plans to merge the Land Fund and Exchange Fund on April 1 next year. This has created uncertainty over whether the new fund will be able to invest or not, given the potential for a conflict of interest. 

 The HK$636.6 billion Exchange Fund's statutory role is to influence the exchange value of the Hong Kong dollar, usually by intervening in the local money or forex markets to maintain currency stability. This fund may not invest in local or regional markets.

title: FOCUS-Jochimsen says Japan must act to avert crash.
text:
DUESSELDORF, Germany, June 18 (Reuters) - Bundesbank council member Reimut Jochimsen warned on Thursday that world markets could face a "big crash" if Japan fails to implement fundamental domestic reforms. 

 Jochimsen said it was vital that China and Hong Kong avoided currency devaluations, but that they would not be able to do so unless Japan can convince financial markets it is serious about reviving its economy. 

 "We must avoid a big crash," Jochimsen told a news conference. 

 He said a lack of market confidence in Japan's efforts to reform its financial system was the principal reason for the recent weakness of the yen, which on Monday fell to an eight-year low of 146.55 against the dollar. 

 The yen's drop has put pressure on China and Hong Kong to devalue in response which analysts say could spark competitive devaluations across Asia, deepening the region's crisis and heightening the risk of global market turmoil. 

 Jochimsen said Wednesday's concerted intervention by the U.S. and Japan to buy yen could pay off only if accompanied by credible reforms. "Intervention can't replace reform," Jochimsen said. 

 The yen on Thursday held on to gains made overnight in New York trading after the intervention which lifted the yen to about 137 against the U.S. dollar from about 142. The yen stood at 136.60 at 1130 GMT. 

 "It is of central importance that China maintains (the level of) its two currencies... as well as the Hong Kong dollar. They won't be able to do that if Japan merely tackles its foreign trade business," Jochimsen said. 

 Short-term stimulation packages were not sufficient but needed to be backed by longer-term policy change, he said. 

 The impact of the Asian crisis on the world economy was likely to last longer than had been assumed previously, Jochimsen said. 

 Analysts said the intervention had eased the pressure on China and Hong Kong to devalue. 

 But they added that the outlook for the yen remained completely uncertain and depended in part on the outcome of a crisis meeting in Tokyo starting Thursday between U.S. Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers and senior Japanese officials. 

 The Japanese government pledged on Thursday to move aggressively on economic and financial reform, disposing of bad loans through measures such as asset securitisation and taking steps to boost domestic demand. 

 Jochimsen said growing competition from east and southeast Asian competitors in the coming months was likely to continue limiting the scope for price increases for industrial products and raw materials. 

 "For us as a central bank that is good news," Jochimsen said. 

 He added that Germany's gross domestic product was likely to grow at a faster pace in 1998 than the 2.2 percent growth experienced in 1997. 

 Jochimsen, regarded as an interest rate "dove" on the Bundesbank's council, also said that domestic demand had significantly increased since the beginning of the year in Germany, fuelling a recovery that had previously been mainly export-driven. 

 Jochimsen is the president of the state central bank of North Rhine-Westphalia, which released a report showing that sentiment in many industries in Germany's most populous state had reached its highest level since May 1993. ((Frankfurt Newsroom +49 69 756525, frankfurt.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: CORRECTED-FOCUS-Asian leaders applaud yen  intervention .
text:
In SINGAPORE story headlined "FOCUS-Asian leaders applaud yen intervention" please read in 13th paragraph....Taiwan's state-run Central News Agency...instead of....China's state-run Central News Agency... (correcting reference). 

 A corrected story follows. 

 By Jason Szep 

 SINGAPORE, June 18 (Reuters) - Coordinated U.S.-Japan intervention to support the troubled yen won loud applause on Thursday from Asian leaders, lighting a flicker of hope in the otherwise gloomy region. 

 Official reaction was fast and most hoped fresh yen strength would help give Japan better footing to pull Asia out of its economic mess. 

 "We are glad to see that the exchange rate of the Japanese yen is picking up," said China's central bank governor Dai Xianglong. 

 He was quoted by China's official Xinhua news agency as telling Asian bankers in Beijing that a devaluation of the Chinese yuan was not necessary. 

 Other Asian leaders and central banks joined in the praise for the dollar sales, with many hoping that a firmer yen would help prevent China from abandoning promises not to devalue the yuan, a move that would push Asia's financial crisis to new depths. 

 "I am glad to see that the Japanese yen rebounded yesterday after strong intervention," Hong Kong chief executive Tung Chee-hwa Tung told reporters during a visit to New Zealand. 

 "The key is now for Japan to move forward," he said, adding that the revitalisation of the Japanese economy "will have a great deal of impact on us all". 

 Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto said he was happy with the impact of the intervention on the market. 

 "I am happy with the fact that the joint intervention was appreciated by the market," he told reporters. 

 Some dealers estimated the Bank of Japan and the New York Federal Reserve spent up to $6 billion to boost the yen, which rallied to about 136 to the dollar from about 142. The yen remained fairly steady in early Asian trade on Thursday but remained under pressure amid concerns over further interventions. 

 Stock prices surged on Wall Street and in Asia in reaction to the intervention, which also gave regional currencies a much-needed boost. 

 "The move will help stabilise Asian financial markets," said Taiwan's Finance Minister Paul Chiu. 

 "And after the foreign exchange rates stabilise, it will also be positive to our economy and financial markets," Chiu was quoted late on Wednesday by Taiwan's state-run Central News Agency as saying. 

 Some officials said the move should help take pressure off China, which has seen its exports plunge as the yen crumbled. 

 "It was especially meaningful because the recent depreciation of the yen was increasing pressure on the Chinese yuan, whose depreciation will have a strong shock throughout Asia," said a senior official at the central Bank of Korea. 

 The head of the Thai central bank's banking department, Tassana Rachatapoh, said the intervention provided some reprieve to the baht, which jumped in early trading to 40.00-41.00 per dollar from 43.00/43.12 on Wednesday. 

 "This is a move in a right direction. If the yen keeps plunging, the impact would be enormous," Tassana said. 

 "But at the end of the day, Japan will need to sort out the fundamental problems, which include the troubled financial institutions. However, we welcome the move which should help lift the sentiment near-term," she added. 

 New Zealand Prime Minister Jenny Shipley described the concerted support of the yen "helpful". 

 "Japan is such an important trading partner that whatever is happening there will affect not only our trading position, but also our currency," she said. 

 "So what has happened overnight is helpful, but I will only personally have real confidence in whether or not we are going to find our way out if we see the sorts of reforms undertaken in Japan that not only I but very many other APEC leaders have discussed on many occasions in the recent past." 

 Jean-Michel Severino, World Bank vice president for East Asia and the Pacific, who said on Tuesday that Asia was plunging into depression, described the intervention as positive. 

 "It's a very positive step forward," he told reporters in Sydney.

title: ANALYSIS-HK peg pressure eases after yen firms.
text:
HONG KONG, June 18 (Reuters) - Joint U.S.-Japan central bank intervention to support the yen has eased pressure on the Hong Kong dollar by helping interest rates stabilise, analysts said on Thursday. 

 "This has eased pressure, which will be very positive for the Hong Kong interest rate environment," said Dong Tao, economist at Credit Suisse First Boston. 

 Under Hong Kong's currency board system, the currency is linked at a rate of HK$7.78 to the U.S. dollar with full U.S. dollar backing for all Hong Kong dollars in circulation. 

 This makes the peg impossible to break - but rates move sharply higher whenever the Hong Kong dollar comes under selling pressure, inflicting severe pain on the overall economy. 

 As the yen has declined, Hong Kong rates have soared. But on Thursday, rates steadied and currency forwards fell as the yen firmed to 136.35 to the U.S. dollar compared to a high of 144.09 early on Wednesday. 

 The overnight lending rate eased to 5.75 percent on Thursday and the benchmark three-month rate was at 7.50/9.50 percent from 8.50/11.50 percent. 

Currency forwards also relaxed sharply, indicating a sharp fall in hedging activity. Forwards blew out from already high levels when the yen accelerated its fall last week. 

 A firmer tone in the yen has eased fears of another round of competitive devaluations across Asia, and the rising risk of a depreciation in the Chinese yuan. 

 Over the past few days, China has stepped up its rhetoric about the damage a weak yen would do to its trade and investment performance, and hinted at the risks of yuan instability. 

 The real economic links between Hong Kong and the mainland would make it difficult for the Hong Kong peg to hold if China devalued, analysts said. 

 "It takes the pressure off China and as goes the U.S. dollar, so goes Hong Kong," said Eric Nickerson, managing director at Bank of America in Hong Kong. 

 "A weaker U.S. dollar will take some of the pressure off Hong Kong assets to deflate," he said. 

 The overnight shift in environment has persuaded analysts that deposit rates would remain unchanged at the Hong Kong Association of Banks meeting on Friday. The bankers meet each Friday to set official deposit rates. 

 No change in deposit rates means little chance of a prime rate increase - something that will allow many people and businesses in Hong Kong to breathe a little easier. 

 Hong Kong's prime lending rate - the rate banks charge their best clients - has remained at 10 percent since March 30 with an average spread between prime and the benchmark three-month interest rate of about 100 basis points. 

 But rates have been so volatile that Nickerson said it was impossible to target the type of rate spread that might trigger a prime rate increase. 

 "In March and April we had HIBOR at 400 basis points below prime. Since May, that has diminished rather significantly. As of June we've started a spike that has put (Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate) above prime, but now we're coming down again," he said. "So the rates coming down would suggest that as pressure comes off... we're likely to go down to that 100-something below prime that we've averaged." 

 But some analysts cautioned that while the rebound in the yen had eased pressure on China's yuan, markets were still waiting for concrete action from Japan to convince them the yen was stable. 

 "The yen rose to above 137 this morning but whether it can stay at these levels will very much depend on Japan's moves in the next few days to improve its economy," said Shamus Mok, chief economist at Bank of East Asia. 

 "The intervention will only have a short-term impact in the foreign exchange market and for the longer term it seems that Japan still has no special measures that could stimulate its economy."

title: Hong Kong interest rates to rise as yen slides.
text:
HONG KONG, June 16 (Reuters) - Hong Kong interest rates were expected to continue rising on Tuesday after the yen slid through 146 to the U.S. dollar on Monday, casting a nervous pall across Asia. 

 "The yen is the dominant factor at this point," said Andy Xie, economist at Morgan Stanley Dean Witter in Hong Kong. 

Hong Kong markets were already on edge after heavy intervention in New York last weekend by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA). 

 The de facto central bank spent heavily to defend the Hong Kong dollar after it came under heavy selling pressure. 

 But U.S. dollars used in Hong Kong's defence required the withdrawal of an equivalent amount of local currency from Hong Kong's money supply, in keeping with the currency board mechanism linking Hong Kong's dollar to the U.S. dollar. 

 That tightened liquidity in the system, and added to pressure on rates. The overnight lending rate was bid at an intra-day high of 16 percent from 10 percent on Friday. 

 Rates also suffered due to a rout in the Hong Kong stock market. Investors fled, pummelling the blue chip Hang Seng index 5.72 percent weaker by the end of the day to 7,462.50. 

 These capital outflows added to the pressure on the Hong Kong dollar, assisted by unconfirmed reports that Chinese Vice Premier Li Lanqing complained about the weak yen and hinted at some shift in the official position on yuan depreciation. 

 Economists and analysts doubted the veracity of the report, which China's central bank said it was checking. But markets reacted anyway, confirming the heightened sensitivity in Asia to a possible yuan devaluation. 

 The Hong Kong dollar remained steadfast despite the gyrations in interest rates, trading in a narrow range around HK$7.7420 after the weekend's successful defence of the key HK$7.7500 level in New York. 

 But there was little relief in sight with markets closing on news that unemployment in Hong Kong hit a 15-year record high of 4.2 percent in March-May, up from 3.9 percent in February-April. 

 "If the situation continues and people are worried about the Hong Kong dollar and there is continued selling of the Hong Kong dollar on the spot, the liquidity situation will get worse," said Frank Gong, senior economist at Bank of America. 

 Gong believes the overnight rate could reach 30 percent on Tuesday. Rate direction in Hong Kong has become much clearer following the HKMA's decision to reveal the size of Hong Kong dollar movements in and out of the banking system. 

 The Hong Kong Monetary Authority's page on Reuters showed that early on Monday HK$7.2 billion was expected to leave the money supply on Tuesday but that figure fell to HK$1.46 billion by early Tuesday morning. 

 "We have a much better handle on rates between now and the next three days and it clearly indicates rates will be under pressure," said Clive MacDonnell, economist at SG Securities. 

 Liquidity seemed to ease later in the afternoon on Monday, with the overnight rate dropping back to 7.0-12 percent as higher rates attracted deposits. But currency forwards remained high, confirming market nervousness about future rate direction, and overnight had reached 13-18 percent by Tuesday morning. 

 Three-month forwards were steady at 1,630-1,830 on Tuesday morning, little changed from 1,750-1,950 at Monday's open. 

 "People are viewing that it is prudent to hedge their Hong Kong dollar positions," said MacDonnell. 

 "That may just be prudence rather than speculation, but as long as forwards are higher there will be selling of Hong Kong dollars for U.S. dollars, and that indicates further tightness in the money market."

title: HK dlr market eases after weekend's cash squeeze.
text:
HONG KONG, June 15 (Reuters) - Hong Kong short-term interbank rates spiked higher on Monday in response to a "capital outflow wedge" that started on Friday when the Hong Kong dollar touched 7.75 to the U.S. dollar. 

 "Someone has shorted the Hong Kong dollar, either because of capital outflow or to finance speculation," said Andrew Fung, head of capital markets at Commonwealth Bank of Australia. 

 Early on Monday, short-term interbank rates moved higher, with overnight rates quoted at 11.00-14.00 percent compared with 10.00-11.00 percent in late trade on Friday. 

 The three-month rate was quoted at 14.00-18.00 percent on Monday morning compared to 12.00-13.00 percent in late Friday trade. It had eased to 13.00-16.00 in early afternoon trade at 0530 GMT. 

 Tomorrow next-day rates reached as high as 15.00-25.00 percent. 

 The Hong Kong Monetary Authority is believed to have intervened at a rate of 7.75 last Friday, traders said. 

 Last Thursday the HKMA began releasing aggregate balance positions information on Reuters page HKMAOOB. 

 That showed on Monday morning that based on spot currency transactions on Friday, by Tuesday the banking system was expected to return HK$7.2 billion to the HKMA for deposit. 

 "This is a capital outflow wedge," said Fung. "There's not enough HK dollars to deliver to the HKMA." 

 By 0230GMT on Monday, the figure had fallen to HK$3.9 billion, suggesting that banks were more willing to lend and that liquidity in the Hong Kong dollar money market had eased slightly. 

 "That means that there has been some switching back into Hong Kong dollars," said a treasurer at major European bank. 

 "Actually, we have been seeing some corporates placing long term Hong Kong dollars today," he said. 

 In relative terms the amount of money being moved out of Hong Kong dollars and into U.S. dollars has grown since the last major spike in interest rates in October, traders said. 

 At that time, three-month interbank rates touched levels over 40 percent. 

 "There is a bigger amount of money being switched into U.S. dollars from the corporate side," another trader said. "I think the speculators are there, but then there is genuine demand from the corporate side to buy U.S. dollars over the past few weeks." 

 For the very short term, dealers were optimistic interest rates would fall, but not by much. 

 "Already it is down from this morning's high levels," said another European bank trader, "so I believe this may be further reduced as the day or the week goes on." 

 But some traders said if dollar-yen goes up further during the week, that may give rise to further speculators buying US against Hong Kong. 

 "There is a very fine balance right now between those who believe in the peg and those who don't," one senior trader said. - Hong Kong Newsroom (852) 2843 6345; Fax (852) 2845 0636 - Email: hongkong.newsroom@reuters.com.

HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--The Hong Kong dollar weakened and forward foreign exchange premiums rose after the Japanese yen resumed its slide, triggering fears of another round of Asian currency devaluations.

 That's dangerously close to the sensitive HK$7.7500 level, which is believed to trigger Hong Kong Monetary Authority intervention. 

 Forward foreign exchange premiums also rose, in all but the one-month maturities.

title: US/HK forwards end firmer but off highs.
text:
HONG KONG, June 11 (Reuters) - US/HK forwards ended sharply firmer but off the day's highs as the yen hovered at the weaker side of 141 to the U.S. dollar, dealers said on Thursday. 

 After opening at 850-950 points, the three-month dollar forward touched a high of 1,600-1,800 points as the yen marched closer to 142 against the greenback, but it faded back to 1,175-1,325 in late trade as the yen rebounded technically. 

 The six-month ended flat versus the open at 2,300-2,500 but higher than 1,900-2,100 at Wednesday's close. 

 The Hong Kong dollar was at HK$7.7476/86 versus HK$7.7460/70 at the open and HK$7.7483/93 per U.S. dollar at the close. 

 Dealers said they did not notice any aggressive intervention in the foreign exchange market by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA). 

 "It (HKMA) did not do much in the money market as far as today is concerned, though one of the note-issuing banks was heard offering overnight money. We don't know if it is acting on behalf of the HKMA or not," one dealer said. 

 Dealers said anticipation of a Hong Kong dollar outflow on Friday helped lift interbank rates. 

 The HKMA's page on Reuters showed a negative position of HK$4.12 billion for Friday. 

 "This is a forecast and that meant the banks collectively sold more Hong Kong dollar than the aggregate balance, and therefore there may be some tightness in the market tomorrow," a HKMA spokesman said. 

 The HKMA said on Thursday it has revised the HKMA page on Reuters to enhance the transparency of its market activities. 

 Starting Thursday, the HKMA page (HKMAOOB) provides a forecast of changes in the aggregate balance of banks' clearing accounts with the HKMA attributable to the HKMA's foreign exchange transactions. 

 The forecast will enable market participants to anticipate changes in the liquidity conditions in the interbank market, the HKMA said. 

 Local term money rates surged in early trade in response to the weak yen and Indonesian rupiah and perceived tighter interbank liquidity. 

 But rates eased later as local banks offered funds, especially at the longer end, taking advantage of the higher interest rates. 

 The overnight rate soared to 7.30-8.00 percent in early trade against its close of 7.00-8.00, but eased to 5.00-6.00 percent in late trade. 

 The three-month was quoted at 11.00-13.00 versus 12.00-12.50 at the open and Wednesday's close of 10.00-11.00 percent. The six-month was quoted at 10.50-12.50 versus 12-13 percent at the open and 10.00-11.00 at the close.

title: WRAP: HK Stks Plunge On  Currency  Fears, Tung Speech
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--Hong Kong's battered markets took another pounding Wednesday on worries over the weak yen, fears of a possible yuan devaluation and a speech by Chief Executive Tung Chee-hwa that participants viewed in a negative light. 

 Already weak in the morning on currency-related concerns, the stock market took a further hit in the afternoon, as interbank rates and forward premiums jumped after Tung pledged to defend the linked exchange rate system. 

 The pledge was taken seriously, with nervous banks tightening lending in the already tight money markets, because the spot Hong Kong dollar has weakened to a level that typically sees Hong Kong Monetary Authorityintervention. 

 After notching steady losses in morning trading, the blue-chip Hang Seng Index plummeted in the afternoon, ending down 4.9% at a three-year low of 7979.37, with overseas mutual funds dumping shares as they decreased their exposure to Hong Kong. 

 The Hong Kong dollar weakened and flirted with a key support level of HK$7.750 all day. 

 Fears of a yuan devaluation rose after People's Bank of China Governor Dai Xianglong said Tuesday that China's exports and foreign investment inflow were being hurt by the weak Japanese yen. Dai also pledged that China won't devalue. 

 Despite that pledge, lingering worries about the yuan drove Hong Kong interbank interest rates close to double digits in the morning and caused forward foreign exchange premiums to climb.

title: HK's blue chip index closes at three year low.
text:
HONG KONG, June 10 (Reuters) - Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index was knocked back to its lowest close in more than three years on Wednesday as a weak yen sent investors on a selling spree, brokers said. 

 The Hang Seng Index ended down 412.09 points, or 4.91 percent, at 7,979.37, its lowest close since March 10, 1995. The blue chip index earlier hit a low of 7,906.39, its lowest intra-day level since March 8, 1995, when it reached 7,905.75. 

 China plays were hit hard and the red chip index shed 5.08 percent to 887.41 points while H shares dived 5.60 percent to 429.81. 

 Brokers said the weak yen continued to plague the market as the U.S. dollar climbed above 141 yen in Wednesday trade. 

 China's central bank governor, Dai Xianglong, said on Tuesday the weak yen was having a severe impact on Beijing's foreign trade and brokers said the soft yen sparked concern about the strength of the Chinese yuan. 

 "Our current view is that the renminbi is relatively safe although there is a risk element of the yen," said Robert Sassoon, head of research at SG Securities. 

 "If the yen does depreciate - if it goes beyond 150 - then we will obviously review the situation." 

 Asian currencies suffered a fairly severe thrashing as markets fretted about the yen, and most other regional stock markets were hammered lower. 

 In Thailand, stocks plunged more than five percent while share prices in Seoul lost more than four percent. 

 The movement of the yen was expected to dictate market direction in the short term and investors were watching for further news from the Group of Seven meeting, brokers said. 

 U.S. Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers said senior officials from the G7 nations discussed the possible adverse effect of the yen's weakness on Wednesday and would continue to monitor developments in foreign exchange markets. 

 "I think the market is already discounting a yen at up to 145 (against the U.S. dollar)," said Percy Au-Young, sales director at DBS Securities. 

 Au-Young said a bearish scenario would give the Hang Seng Index a downside of 8,000 in the medium term but added a rebound in the yen may trigger the index to climb higher. 

 "There is a lot of value in the market but the question is what is going to trigger people to come back," Sassoon said. 

 "There should be an element of short-covering soon. The question is whether people are going to panic." 

 Sharply higher interest rates rocked sentiment and the benchmark three-month HIBOR rate rose to 9.57895 percent on Wednesday's fixing against 9.08750 percent at the same time on Tuesday. 

 The overnight rate touched as high as seven to eight percent versus 5.50-6.00 at Tuesday's close. The three-month forward jumped to 1,000-1,200 points against 640-690 at Tuesday's close. 

 The Hong Kong dollar weakened below the key support of HK$7.75 against the U.S. dollar at one point before bouncing back to HK$7.7483/93 in late trade. 

 Dealers cited rumours that the Hong Kong Monetary Authority had intervened in early trade to defend the support at 7.75. 

 Hong Kong leader Tung Chee-hwa said on Wednesday his administration was determined to keep the Hong Kong dollar's 15-year-old peg against the U.S. currency.

title: ASIA MARKETS SUMMARY-China, weak yen spark shivers.
text:
0925 GMT - The yen's persistent weakness and renewed fears of a Chinese yuan devaluation shook Asian markets on Wednesday, sending a chill through much of north Asia. 

 Signs the year-old currency crisis is entering its second stage, with several Asian economies teetering on the brink of recession, fuelled the bearish mood. 

 "It's a vicious circle at the moment and everything is just being melted into the same big Asian currency pot. I can't see any way out," a U.S. bank dealer in Singapore said. 

 YEN STILL UNDER THE GUN 

 The dollar slipped below 141 yen in late Asian trade after U.S. Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers said G7 nations had discussed the possible dangers of a weak yen and would continue to monitor foreign exchange movements. 

 But it remained well supported near the high-140 yen levels, with few traders expecting any major policy announcement from the G7 deputies meeting or any co-ordinated intervention. 

 "At the moment, it's hard for them to sell dollars aggressively against the yen because the market still wants to buy dollars," the dealer said. 

 HONG KONG MARKETS STRICKEN 

 Hong Kong shares dived on worries about the weak yen, with the blue chip Hang Seng Index losing over five percent at one point to hit a new 1998 low of 7,906.39 points. 

 The Hong Kong dollar was quoted near the key 7.75 level against the U.S. dollar amid rumours the Hong Kong Monetary Authority had intervened to buy it earlier. 

 Forward rates shot up, with three-months at 950/1,100 against 640/690 at Tuesday's close and six-months at 1,950/2,150 against 1,500/1,600. 

 Dealers said funds appeared to be positioning for another speculative attack on the Hong Kong dollar peg amid speculation the territory would be forced to de-link its currency from the U.S. dollar if China devalued the yuan. 

 Hong Kong leader Tung Chee-hwa attempted to calm investor fears, saying his administration was determined to keep the Hong Kong dollar peg. 

 Tung also said Hong Kong's administration would not intervene in the stock market. 

 YUAN FEARS RESURFACE 

 The market was spooked by comments from China's central bank governor, who warned on Tuesday that the weak yen was having a severe impact on Beijing's foreign trade. 

 The head of the People's Bank of China, Dai Xianglong, did not explicitly rule out a devaluation of the yuan in response to the tumbling yen, but he simply noted promises China had made in the past not to devalue its currency in reaction to the Asian crisis. 

 TAIWAN MARKETS BLUDGEONED 

 Taiwan's dollar skidded through a series of 11-year lows, falling as far as 35.149 to the U.S. dollar on worries about China and the weak yen. 

 Dealers said most of its support came from the central bank after it breached the 35 level, but they said the interventions were not aggressive and most expected the currency to head lower as it caught up with its counterparts in the region. 

 They said a substantial portion of the U.S. dollar demand came from offshore banks in the non-deliverable forwards market. 

 Taiwan stocks were also badly hit and lost over three percent to end at a seven-month low, prompting Finance Minister Paul Chiu to appeal for calm. 

 AUSSIE DOLLAR UNDERMINED, INDIAN RUPEE RATTLED 

 The contagion was far-reaching, with Australia's dollar spiralling towards an all-time low of $0.5710/20 and the Indian rupee trading at fresh lows of 42.40 to the dollar. 

 Analysts saw little respite before the $0.55 level for the Aussie, which is under fire from the yen's decline, renewed regional instability, weak commodity prices and a market perception Australia simply cannot afford to support the currency through higher interest rates. 

 Indian Commerce Minister Ramakrishna Hegde said the rupee's drop was a cause for concern, but added that the currency would stabilise in due course. 

 RUPIAH DRIFTS DOWN 

 The rupiah slid to lows of around 12,950 on local demand for dollars, but traders said flows remained thin and commercially driven. 

 President Habibie told Reuters in an interview the stability of the rupiah was more important than its actual level against the dollar. 

 He said a stable rupiah and low inflation were possible "if and only if" growth in the money supply was tempered. 

 But analysts said the rupiah could also be undermined by prolonged weakness in the yen, which has already eclipsed the benefits of Indonesia's foreign debt rescheduling and the IMF's plan to resume lending. 

 The market was also likely to keep a close watch on President Habibie's efforts at political reform. Habibie said he had no plans to continue as head of state after the next presidential poll, which he expected around December next year. 

 REST OF SOUTHEAST ASIA STAGGERS 

 The Singapore dollar, Malaysian ringgit and Thai baht were also hit as their stock markets each lost between three and five percent on the regional jitters. 

 The Sing dollar briefly fell through the 1.73 level against the U.S. dollar as players continued to sell it as a proxy for the region. 

 The Thai baht was the wrong side of 43.00 to the dollar, but its fall was somewhat cushioned by commercial demand for the first tranche of 50 billion baht in state-backed domestic bonds, due to be floated this week.

title: HK's Hang Seng Index ends at three year low on yen.
text:
HONG KONG, June 10 (Reuters) - Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index was knocked back to its lowest close in more than three years on Wednesday as a weak yen sent investors on a selling spree, brokers said. 

 The Hang Seng Index ended down 412.09 points, or 4.91 percent, at 7,979.37, its lowest close since March 10, 1995. 

 The blue chip index earlier hit a low of 7,906.39, its lowest intra-day level since March 8, 1995, when it reached 7,905.75. 

 China plays were hit hard and the China-Affiliated Corporations Index shed 5.08 percent to 887.41 points while H shares dived 5.60 percent to 429.81. 

 Brokers said the weak yen continued to plague the market as the U.S. dollar climbed above 141 yen in Wednesday trade. 

 China's central bank governor, Dai Xianglong, said on Tuesday the weak yen was having a severe impact on Beijing's foreign trade and brokers said the soft yen sparked concern about the strength of the Chinese yuan. 

 "Our current view is that the renminbi is relatively safe although there is a risk element of the yen," said Robert Sassoon, head of research at SG Securities. 

 "If the yen does depreciate - if it goes beyond 150 - then we will obviously review the situation." 

 Asian currencies suffered a fairly severe thrashing as markets fretted about the yen, and most other regional stock markets were hammered lower. 

 In Thailand, stocks plunged more than five percent while share prices in Seoul lost more than four percent. 

 The development of the yen was expected to dictate market direction in the short term and investors were watching for further news from the Group of Seven meeting, brokers said. 

 U.S. Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers said senior officials from the G7 nations discussed the possible adverse effect of the yen's weakness on Wednesday and would continue to monitor developments in foreign exchange markets. 

 "I think the market is already discounting a yen at up to 145 (against the U.S. dollar)," said Percy Au-Young, sales director at DBS Securities. 

 Au-Young said a bearish scenario would give the Hang Seng Index a downside of 8,000 in the medium term but added a rebound in the yen may trigger the index to climb higher. 

 "There is a lot of value in the market but the question is what is going to trigger people to come back," Sassoon said. 

 "There should be an element of short-covering soon. The question is whether people are going to panic." 

 Sharply higher interest rates rocked sentiment and the benchmark three-month HIBOR rate rose to 9.57895 percent on Wednesday's fixing against 9.08750 percent at the same time on Tuesday. 

 The overnight rate touched as high as seven to eight percent versus 5.50-6.00 at Tuesday's close. The three-month forward jumped to 1,000-1,200 points against 640-690 at Tuesday's close. 

 The Hong Kong dollar weakened below the key support of HK$7.75 against the U.S. dollar at one point before bouncing back to HK$7.7483/93 in late trade. 

 Dealers cited rumours that the Hong Kong Monetary Authority had intervened in early trade to defend the support at 7.75. 

 Hong Kong leader Tung Chee-hwa said on Wednesday his administration was determined to keep the Hong Kong dollar peg against the U.S. currency. 

 Tung said the Hong Kong dollar was under pressure due to the weak yen this week. 

 "Any deviation from our long-held philosophy of fiscal prudence will give rise to speculative attack against the Hong Kong dollar, the result of which may well be another increase in our interest rates," he said. 

 Lower futures added pressure to the market and the June Hang Seng Index contract erased 400 points to 7,960 with open interest remaining large at 80,678 contracts. The July contract finished down 370 points at 8,010. 

 Index heavyweight HSBC Holdings  accounted for more than a quarter of the Hang Seng Index point loss as it slumped HK$9.00 to HK$181.00. 

 Cheung Kong  dived HK$3.00 to HK$33.80 and Sun Hung Kai Properties eased HK$1.90 to HK$30.30. Hutchison  was off HK$2.50 at HK$34.00. 

 Investors awaited U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's testimony to Congress at 1500 GMT.

title: HK stocks sharply off at midday, shaken by yen.
text:
HONG KONG, June 10 (Reuters) - Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index sank to its lowest levels since mid-January on Wednesday morning, closing sharply lower at midsession as yen weakness and concerns about the Chinese yuan pushed prices into a tailspin. 

 The Hang Seng Index closed the morning session at 8,036.17 points, down 355.29 points, or 4.23 percent. 

 In China-related stocks, the red chip index sank even further, sliding 58.90 points, or 6.30 percent, to 876.02 while the H-share index fell 22.88 points, or 5.03 percent, to 432.42. 

 "Currencies are at the forefront of everybody's mind. The market is obviously focused on a possible devaluation of the yuan," said Steven Thompson, chief analyst at Nikko Research Center. 

 The U.S. dollar edged up against the yen in early afternoon trade in Tokyo. It was quoted at 140.83/88 yen and stop-loss dollar buying was expected to take place above 141.00 yen. 

 China's central bank governor Dai Xianglong said on Tuesday the weak Japanese yen was having a severe impact on Beijing's foreign trade. H-share companies were getting particularly hard hit as they competed with Korean and Japanese producers in heavy industries, analysts said. 

 "Obviously the weakness of the yen is a problem," said Richard Verin, head of equities trading at Credit Suisse First Boston. "There is obviously a bit of panic given some of the moves we have seen." 

 He said the selling of H shares and red chips was probably coming from local retail investors. 

 "It may be an indication that we are now getting to the stage where people are having to cut losses to generate new cash to meet whatever commitments they need to meet," said Thompson. 

 In the blue chip sector, investors were selling where there was liquidity, brokers said. 

 Swire Pacific Ltd ended the morning down HK$2.90 at HK$21.70, Cheung Kong (Holdings) Ltd fell HK$2.50 to HK$34.30 and HSBC Holdings Plc dropped HK$6.00 to HK$184.00. 

 "The market is on debt watch right now. There seem to be concerns about credit ratings at the moment," said Thompson. 

 Moody's Investors Service said this week it had placed its ratings on the debt of Swire Pacific and its guaranteed subsidiaries under review for possible downgrade. 

 Debt concerns also plagued Wharf (Holdings) Ltd which was down HK$0.70 at HK$7.60 and CITIC Pacific Ltd which fell HK$1.45 to HK$13.80. 

 Analysts said the Hang Seng Index was now heading for a new year low. It ended just above the day's low of 8,007.04 points at midsession. 

 The 1998 low stands at 7,909.13, reached on January 12. 

 Hong Kong interbank rates rose on Wednesday with the benchmark three-month HIBOR rate at 9.58 percent at the fixing compared with 9.09 percent at the same time on Tuesday. 

 The Hong Kong dollar was at 7.7495/7.7505 to the U.S. dollar. Foreign exchange dealers said there was talk the Hong Kong Monetary Authority had intervened to defend key support at 7.75. 

 Some analysts said the situation was too uncertain around the region for investors to want to bargain hunt. But others said that those who had sold at higher levels would be tempted. 

 "There may be such a bounce that investors won't have a chance to accumulate at 8,000," said Thompson. 

 The June futures contract on the Hang Seng Index ended the morning down 310 points at 8,050, after falling to a low during the morning of 7,980 points. The July contract was off 340 points at 8,040.

title: HK interbank rates jump as yen breaks 141.
text:
HONG KONG, June 10 (Reuters) - Hong Kong interbank rates rose sharply in late Wednesday trade as nervousness intensified after the yen dipped below 141 per U.S. dollar and the local stock market plunged below 8,000 levels, dealers said. 

     "The market has become rather panicky as the Japanese yen fell below 141," Toby Yuen, treasurer at Bank Brussels Lambert, said. 

     The overnight rate touched as high as seven to eight percent versus 5.87-6.37 at the open and 5.50-6.00 at Tuesday's close. 

     "But I did not notice any substantial sales against the Hong Kong dollar today," Yuen said. 

     Another senior dealer said: "As short term rates get firmer, the market gets more nervous." 

     Money market sources said they heard that some major speculators had re-emerged in the local money market taking short positions against the Hong Kong dollar. 

     Dollar forwards moved higher and more rapidly 

 than in recent days. The three-month forward was up at 

 1,000-1,200 points versus 750-800 at midday, 700-750 at the open 

 and 640-690 at Tuesday's close. 

     The six-month rose to 1,900-2,100 versus 1,700-1,850 at 

 midday, 1,550-1,700 at the open and 1,500-1,600 at the close. 

     At one point in early trade on Wednesday, the Hong Kong 

 dollar weakened below the key support of HK$7.75 per U.S. dollar 

 before bouncing back to HK$7.7483/93 (GMT 0745) in late trade. 

     Dealers cited rumours that the Hong Kong Monetary Authority

 had intervened in the foreign exchange market in early trade, 

 buying the Hong Kong dollar against the greenback and defending 

 the support at 7.75. 

     The Hong Kong Monetary Authority declined to comment on the 

 market rumour. 

     "The Hong Kong dollar is stable and we do not comment on 

 money market operations," a spokeswoman from the HKMA told 

 Reuters on Wendesday. 

     But local interbank liquidity was tighter, raising renewed 

 fear of an upward bias for interbank rates. 

     The Liquidity Adjustment Facility reversal at the Hong Kong 

Monetary Authority was quoted at HK$3.2 billion on Wednesday, 

 compared with some HK$4 billion over the past week. 

     Stephen Cheung, a director at Jardine Fleming Bank, said the 

 weakening yen would continue to provide the main direction for 

 local interbank rates. 

     "The situation is worrying. Now the interbank rates 

 (longer-dated) are trading above the prime rate," he said. 

     "But raising the prime rate seems impossible given the 

 current state of the economy," he said. 

     The three-month and the six-month were quoted in a similar 

 range of 10.00-11.00 percent in late trade versus the prime rate 

 of 10.25 percent.

title: HK Dlr Strengthens Early On Surge In Forward  Forex  Premiums
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--The Hong Kong dollar strengthened early Monday after a weak yen pushed up interbank rates in defense of the local currency and forward foreign exchange premiums surged. 

 Around 0220 GMT (10:20 p.m. Sunday EDT), the Hong Kong dollar was quoted at HK$7.7485 against the U.S. dollar, down from HK$7.7497 late Friday. 

 A local bank dealer said an unnamed institution bought Hong Kong dollars at HK$7.75 Friday offshore after the local market closed. That level is believed to be the trigger for Hong Kong Monetary Authorityintervention. 

 Forward foreign exchange premiums rose after the yen pushed through 140 yen against the U.S. dollar. 

 In the forward foreign exchange market, the one-month is quoted at 220 points from 170 late in the previous session. The three-month premium is quoted at 700 points, compared with 620 points previously. The six-month premium is quoted at 1,650 points, up from 1,450 previously. 

 The one-year premium is quoted at 3,800 points, up from 3,400 previously. In the same month last year, the one-year premium averaged 321 points, but it's still well below its peak at an average 6,014 points in January. 

 Dealers said some hedge funds are believed to be making money in the forwards, having bought in recent weeks when premiums fell. "They buy them when they're cheap and then scare people into buying them when they go up," said a treasurer with a local bank. 

 The currency weakness has pushed the three-month Hong Kong interbank rate sharply higher early Monday, hitting 9.25%, from 8.625% Friday. For more Hibor news, please refer to Dow Jones page [1085].

 The volatile overnight Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate is quoted at 5.125%, up from 4.75% late Friday, but well down on the 6.5% quoted early Monday. The three-month rate is 9.00%, down from 8.625% late Friday, but down on 9.25% early Monday.

 "Sentiment is quite bearish. We just had a limited rebound on profit-taking," said a dealer with an Australian bank. 

 Dealers don't see scope for significant further falls in local rates, while Asian currencies are being led downward by the Japanese yen, particularly not while the Hong Kong dollar is so close to HK$7.75. This is seen as a trigger point for Hong Kong Monetary Authorityintervention.

title: ASIAN EXOTICS - Ringgit, won shed gains.
text:
0515 GMT - The Malaysian ringgit slipped a bit after Singapore denied rumours it had agreed to buy land owned by Malaysia's state railway company for 30 billion ringgit. 

 * A spokesman for Singapore Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong's office told Reuters there was no truth to the reports, which surfaced in forex markets on Wednesday and contributed to the ringgit's rise. 

 * But dealers said the ringgit was relatively resilient despite the denial of the rumours and Kuala Lumpur's apparent rejection of an IMF call for higher Malaysian interest rates in its recent annual review of the economy. 

 * Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad on Wednesday defended Malaysia's stance of keeping interest rates at current levels, saying businesses were already suffering. 

 * Bank Negara Malaysia accepted bids for one-month money at an average 11.04 percent and three-month at 11.07 percent under a new competitive bidding system, aimed at increasing transparency. 

 * The Indonesian rupiah remained stuck below the 8,000 level, ignoring economic czar Ginandjar Kartasasmita's confidence-boosting comments. 

 * Ginandjar said the rupiah should regain the 6,000 per dollar level this year if economic reforms remain on track, and expressed confidence this would be the case. 

 He said fuel and electricity prices would go up in May and all subsidies, except for rice and soybeans, would be abolished by October 1 as per the IMF agreement. 

 Ginandjar also announced a 15 percent pay increase for civil servants from May 1, conceding that this did not match inflation which jumped more than 25 percent in the first quarter. 

 * Central bank governor Sjahril Sabirin said overnight that interest rates would stay high for the time being to support the rupiah. 

 * But dealers said the forward market was already pricing higher interest rates and spot rupiah was unlikely to perk up against a backdrop of continuing social tension and signs of a slowdown in IMF funding. 

 * A senior IMF official said the fund would make its next proposed $3 billion payment to Indonesia in three installments and added that the fund had misjudged the crisis in its early stage. 

 * In South Korea, the won slid from its high of 1,326 as private and state-run companies aggressively tried to hedge their dollar exposures in forward trading on a belief the equilibrium for the exchange rate was at 1,350/1,400. 

 * News of soaring inflation, yet more worrying evidence of the impact of the currency crisis, did not help the market. The producer price index soared 17.5 percent year-on-year in April, against a 3.8 percent rise the year before. The consumer price index was up 8.8 percent year-on-year in April against a 4.3 percent the year before. 

 * The central bank said April import prices fell 9.1 percent month-on-month in local currency terms, but rose 34.3 percent on a yearly basis. Export prices fell 11.7 month-on-month and rose 34.1 percent year-on-year. 

 * The Thai baht was weak as the market turned apprehensive about its recent rally amid signs the government might not want it to strengthen further. 

 * Deputy Prime Minister Supachai Panitchpakdi said overnight he was happy with an exchange rate of 40 to the dollar. 

 * "I don't see the baht continuing to strengthen from here once the buying euphoria is over. But we could see continuous (dollar) sell offers if there is more investment in Thai companies," the dealer said. 

 * A Thai newspaper reported that a government-appointed panel probing the Bank of Thailand had blamed several senior finance officials, including the current BOT governor, for the baht's plunge last year. 

 * In the Philippines, pre-election jitters undermined the peso despite the central bank's rate hikes to stem speculative pressure on the currency ahead of the May 11 poll. 

 The central raised its overnight borrowing and lending rates by 50 basis points each. 

 * The peso languished below the 40.00 per dollar level, but traders said its falls would be limited by banks' dollar sales. 

 * In north Asia, the Hong Kong dollar was higher and forwards remained firm amid tight interbank liquidity and talk of overnight intervention by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA).

title: HK stocks end sharply off in shadow of Japan, U.S.
text:
HONG KONG, April 27 (Reuters) - Hong Kong stocks slumped to a sharply weaker close on Monday as soft overseas markets eroded investors' already low confidence, brokers said. 

 The Hang Seng Index shed 286.22 points, or 2.63 percent, to end at 10,593.71 after hitting a low of 10,555.57. 

 Volume picked up to HK$6.22 billion compared with Friday's quiet HK$4.27 billion. 

 The gloomy mood was expected to prevail but some brokers said the blue chip index may be approaching more stable levels with support at 10,500. 

 "There can always be a little bit of a bounce, but it is not going to be on impressive volume," said Glenn Lesko, head of sales at ABN-Amro Hoare Govett Asia Securities. 

 "I think we are in for a very slow quarter with a downward bias. That's the way it's been so far and I don't see any major reasons for it to change." 

 Local sentiment took a beating from markets in Tokyo where the yen lost ground and the key 225-share Nikkei average ended down 2.26 percent after a government stimulus package for the economy failed to impress investors. 

 Losses on Wall Street and in London on Friday further hampered trade, brokers said. 

 Steven Thompson, chief analyst at Nikko Research Center (HK), said the weakness of Japanese markets had little direct impact on the Hong Kong market. 

 "It should have a slightly positive effect," Thompson said. 

 "The weakness in Tokyo will result in some cash coming back into fund managers' hands." 

 Thompson said there may be some concerns about the Hong Kong dollar which has been hovering near the psychologically important level of HK$7.75 to the U.S. dollar for more than a week. 

 The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) may have to intervene if the currency dropped below HK$7.75, he said. 

 Futures put pressure on the market as they continued trading at a discount. The April Hang Seng Index contract finished down 420 points at 10,430 ahead of its expiry on Wednesday. 

 Index heavyweight HSBC Holdings  led the market lower, falling HK$5.00 to HK$222.00. Hang Seng Bank  lost HK$2.50 to HK$65.75. 

 Property counters were the biggest losers and the sub-index shaved off 2.97 percent. Sun Hung Kai Properties  was down HK$1.80 at HK$47.40 and Cheung Kong  dropped HK$0.75 to HK$51.75. 

 Henderson Land  closed HK$0.70 lower at HK$34.50. 

 The company said it had sold more than 1,000 of about 1,790 flats on sale at its Dawning Views development in the New Territories over the weekend. 

 The flats were offered at an average price of between HK$3,068 and about HK$4,100 per square foot. Planned apartment sales for the rest of 1998 could generate revenue of about HK$40 billion, the company said. 

 China Everbright  was down HK$0.35 at HK$5.50 ahead of its 1997 results, due later on Monday. The consensus forecast, according to Edinburgh Financial Publishing's The Estimate Directory, is for net profit of HK$264.5 million compared with a net loss of HK$202.27 million the previous year.

title: HK Dollar Strengthens After Morning Scare Over Weak Yen
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--The Hong Kong dollar is strengthening late Friday after nervous sentiment pushed the local currency to a key support level in morning trading. 

 At 0720 GMT (2:20 a.m. EST), traders said the Hong Kong dollar was hovering between $7.7492 to $7.7493 against the U.S. dollar, stronger than $7.7496 late Thursday and $7.7499 Friday morning. 

 A trader at a local bank credited a transaction made at HK$7.7470 against the U.S. dollar in the early afternoon as the reason for the Hong Kong dollar's turnaround from weak morning levels. 

 Dealers said that although the local currency was close to HK$7.75, a level which typically triggers intervention by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, they detected no strong selling pressure to push the currency any weaker. 

 While local factors, including a subdued domestic economy and a couple of long weekends were cited as factors for the local dollar's slide in early trading, dealers said in the afternoon that they now believe it's Japan's market troubles that are overshadowing the Hong Kong market. 

 'It is basically a 'Japan problem.' Hong Kong markets just reacted to it,' said a trader at a local bank. 

 He noted once news that Moodys' Investors Service downgraded Japan's outlook to negative from stable and the yen broke through 134 in the morning , forward premiums rate in Hong Kong shot up almost immediately. 

 'Banks were worried about the spillover effect from a weak Japanese yen and so they started borrowing long-term funds to protect themselves against possible rise in interest rates,' deputy chief dealer Wong Chi-yiu at Bank of China group treasury center said.

title: US/HK forwards end sharply firmer on yen woes.
text:
HONG KONG, April 3 (Reuters) - US/HK forwards ended sharply firmer on Friday as the fall of the Japanese yen below 134 per U.S. dollar lent a bid tone to the forward rates, dealers said. 

 "The local money market was becoming uneasy as the Japanese yen broke its key support at 134 per U.S. dollar, but market participants were less panicky than they were last October," a senior dealer at one of the note-issuing banks said. 

 Stephen Cheung, a director at Jardine Fleming Bank, said: "Market sentiment was still better and the market was more stable than in January or last October." 

 The Hong Kong dollar spot managed to defend the key support of HK$7.75 per U.S. dollar partly on firmer rates as well as rumours of possible intervention by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA). 

 There was no major selling of the Hong Kong dollar on Friday, Frederic Laine, head of interest rates and derivatives trading at Credit Lyonnais, said. 

 The local currency ended slightly stronger at HK$7.7473/83 per U.S. dollar after slipping to a three-month low of HK$7.7498/01, a hair away from the key support of HK$7.75, a level that traders said would trigger intervention by the HKMA. 

 The currency opened at HK$7.7493/03 against HK$7.7490/00 at Thursday's close. 

 Dealers said at least one note-issuing bank was spotted buying Hong Kong dollar spot against the U.S. dollar and was believed to be acting on behalf of the HKMA in a bid to cap the strength of the U.S. dollar. 

 But forward rates rose more sharply as dealers took short positions against the Hong Kong dollar. 

 The three-month dollar forward posted strong gains at 360-400 points against 270-300 in early trade and 230-260 at Thursday's close. 

 The six-month was up at 950-1,000 versus 880-930 points in early trade and 775-830 at the close. 

 "The bid tone on forwards was much stronger today than over the past few weeks," a senior dealer said. 

 Dealers noted that buying orders were seen mainly from Singapore and London. 

 Local interbank rates rose partly on routine demand ahead of the long weekend. 

 The overnight rate rose to 5.6-5.87 percent versus 4.43-4.93 in early trade and 4.68-4.75 at Thursday's close. This compared with seven percent on January 6 and 300 percent on October 23 when the Hong Kong dollar came under speculative attack. 

 The one-month rose most sharply, by over 130-150 basis points to 7.06-7.18 versus 5.87-6.0 in early trade and 5.46-5.60 at the close. 

 The three-month posted a smaller 80 basis point jump, ending at 7.56-7.68 versus 7.18-7.37 and 6.75-7.00 at the close. 

 The six-month was firmer at 8.37-8.5 versus 7.75-8.12 at the open and 7.50-7.75 at the close. 

 Higher short-term rates encouraged some selling of the U.S. dollar for the Hong Kong dollar, strengthening the tone of the local currency, Jardine Fleming's Cheung said.

title: Hong Kong Bankers Association Trims Rates By A Quarter-Point
text:
HONG KONG -(Dow Jones)- The Hong Kong Association of Banks said Friday it lowered deposit rates by one-quarter percentage point to 3.75%. The cut marked the first adjustment to the benchmark short-term rates since Jan. 8, when the association reduced them by a quarter point to 4%. 

 Major banks - including Bank of China, Standard Chartered Bank and HSBC Holdings PLC's local units, Hongkong Bank and Hang Seng Bank - followed suit, trimming their prime rates to 8.5% from 8.75%, effective Monday. Changes in the association's deposit rate, a benchmark in Hong Kong, typically are followed by matching changes in individual banks' prime lending rate. 

 The banks association, which meets every Friday to discuss possible changes to the deposit rates, controls rates on savings deposits of less than one-week maturity. 

 Liu Jinbao, association chairman, said he sees room for further interest-rate reductions if both domestic and external economic conditions remain stable. Liu , who represents Bank of China's Hong Kong and Macau branch, on the Hong Kong rate-setting cartel said he expects Friday's interest-rate cut to "help the overall economy in Hong Kong" and ease pressure on banks in the city, which are engaged in a battle for mortgage business. 

 Asked if the unilateral rate cut - made by association without a corresponding move in the U.S. by the Federal Reserve Board - would fuel speculation in rallying Hong Kong stocks, Liu said the cartel had considered all factors in making its decision. Hong Kong tends to follow adjustments in the U.S. benchmark federal-funds rate because of the Hong Kong dollar's peg to the U.S. dollar at a rate of HK$7.80. 

 Liu added that the banks association supports the Hong Kong Monetary Authority's proposal to begin deregulating the local interest-rate regime. A report commissioned last year by the monetary authority, Hong Kong's de facto central bank, recommended a gradual deregulation starting after 1999. Last month, Liu said the association submitted its own proposal to the authority, but provided no details. 

 Hong Kong's currency and money markets shrugged off the lower rates, but some traders said the territory's stock market could see some profit-taking when trading resumes Monday. 

 Traders said they had been expecting the cut all week, so the spot Hong Kong dollar, money market rates and forward foreign-exchange premiums already reflected the decision by the banks association to reduce the rate on savings deposits of under one week to 3.75%. "It's pretty much expected. I think 25 basis points (one-quarter percentage point) was pretty much what the market was hoping for," said Mike Powell, head of interest rates for HSBC Markets. 

 Bankers noted that short-term money market rates have fallen steadily in the past few days, reflecting the market's confidence of another rate cut. The volatile overnight rate, which hit 5.75% last week, was quoted at 4.75% late Friday, even with the comparable U.S. benchmark rate. 

 Powell described the cut as just "official rubber-stamping of what the market has done to short-dated rates." 

 With past surprise rate cuts, the Hong Kong dollar has weakened immediately after the banks association decision, but traders noted that the currency was actually slightly higher after Friday's cut. The Hong Kong dollar was trading at HK$7.7480 immediately after the news, slightly stronger than HK$7.7491 earlier in the day and much stronger than the monetary authority's Friday intervention rate of HK$7.7509. 

 The Hong Kong dollar is expected to remain stable between HK$7.7480 and HK$7.7500 against the U.S. dollar, Commonwealth Bank of Australia treasurer Andrew Fung said. 

 Traders downplayed notions that lower interest rates would lure back speculators, who last attacked the Hong Kong dollar in August 1998, sparking monetary authority to spend HK$118.1 billion in stock and futures markets squeezing the speculators out. 

 Stock-market investors had been betting on a rate cut all week, helping lift the Hang Seng Index to its highest level in more than a year. Friday, the index jumped 186.26 points, or 1.6%, to close at 11914.10. The market is likely to dip Monday, said Michael Ng, dealing director at Sassoon Securities Ltd. "As usual, investors buy on rumors, sell on news, so the rate cut is already discounted in the market," he said. 

 Ng noted the April Hang Seng index futures contract closed at about an 89-point discount to the cash market, indicating investors are betting the market's 6.7% rise this week may be running out of steam. 

 But others aren't as willing to commit to a decline Monday in the Hang Seng index because the rally also was fueled by a huge inflow of overseas funds via large investment banks and brokers. Adrian Ngan of BNP Prime Peregrine Securities (HK) Ltd. said he's not convinced the inflow of funds from the U.S. is about to abate. 

 "U.S. institutions continue to pump money into Asian markets and that will continue," said Adrian Ngan, head of research at BNP Prime Peregrine Securities (HK) Ltd. Overseas investors expected a rate cut, he said. Ngan also said property stocks will gain from the rate-cut news, particularly ahead of the government's resumption of its land sales April 20 after a nine-month hiatus.
