title: HK Govt Silent On Alleged Futures "Front-Running" By Broker
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--The Hong Kong government Tuesday refused to say whether the Securities and Futures Commission is investigating a broker for alleged misconduct related to its attempt last year to defend the local market from a speculative attack. 

 Since last week, the government has been under pressure to comment on an unconfirmed newspaper report that alleged a futures broker used by the government bought stock index futures with prior knowledge that the central bank was about to intervene to support the market - a practice known as "front-running." 

 In response to written questions from Dow Jones Newswires, the government said the securities regulator is bound by law to keeps its investigations confidential and indicated it would not divulge information concerning SFC actions. 

 It also confirmed that the Hong Kong Monetary Authority began intervention in the Hang Seng Index futures market on Aug. 13, a day earlier than it had previously said. 

 The government didn't explain why it took nearly nine months to acknowledge the real starting date of the HKMA's two-week anti-speculative market intervention, saying only that it "did not consider it necessary to report on these preparatory details." 

 For the first time, the government said the HKMA bought 491 August Hang Seng Index futures in the last 20 minutes of trading on Aug. 13, or 1.98% of the contract turnover of the day. It did so to test market conditions as speculators sold index futures and Hong Kong dollar forwards short in a bid to test the local currency's peg to the U.S. dollar. 

 The test was also to gauge "the extent and sources of selling pressure on the trading floor of the Hong Kong Futures Exchange" and to check its command structure, internal systems and settlement procedures in preparation for a bigger battle with speculators in the days ahead.

title: Source Says Hong Kong To Sell Shares Bought For Market Support
text:
HONG KONG -(Dow Jones)- The monetary authority in Hong Kong has decided to sell off a large portion of its holdings in local companies, whose shares it bought last summer to support the Hong Kong stock market, The Nihon Keizai Shimbun reported in its Saturday morning edition, citing an unnamed senior financial official, according to Japan's Nikkei news service. 

 Hong Kong's authority hasn't yet set a deadline for the sell-off, which will involve just over HK100 billion worth of shares. The unnamed senior financial official said, "We will be extremely careful not to upset the market." 

 Last summer, the authority intervened in the stock market to deter speculative selling of Hong Kong dollars and shares of local companies. 

 Most of the shares are held in the territory's foreign-currency reserve fund. The sale would lower the fund's proportion of Hong Kong stocks to 5% of its total assets - down from the current 17%, or about HK150 billion, of the fund's total assets of around HK910 billion. 

 To ease the impact on the market, the authority will consider such measures as convertible bond issuance and stock buybacks, the senior official said.

 Most of the shares are held in the territory's foreign-currency reserve fund. The sale would lower the fund's proportion of Hong Kong stocks to 5% of its total assets - down from the current 17%, or about HK150 billion, of the fund's total assets of around HK910 billion. 

 To ease the impact on the market, the authority will consider such measures as convertible bond issuance and stock buybacks, the senior official said.

title: HKMA changes Exchange Fund asset allocations.
text:
HONG KONG, March 3 (Reuters) - The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) said on Wednesday it will cut the Exchange Fund's local equity portfolio to five percent from 17 percent as market conditions permit. 

 "The pace of re-balancing the asset mix of the Exchange Fund ... will obviously depend on market conditions and may take some time," said Joseph Yam, Chief Executive of the HKMA. 

 "The government is not in a hurry to offload the shares and is confident that the Exchange Fund will take great care in executing the disposal programme in an orderly manner without disrupting the market," he added. 

 The change is part of an overall asset reallocation strategy approved by the Exchange Fund Advisory Committee. 

 Under the new investment plan investment benchmarks have changed as follows: 

 The benchmark for bonds is now 80 percent, down from 90 percent. The benchmark for equities is 20 percent (five percent Hong Kong equities), down from 10 percent. 

 For currencies, the new target is a holding of 80 percent US$-bloc currencies, 15 percent European-bloc currencies and five percent Japanese Yen. The previous benchmark targets were 70 percent, 20 percent and 10 percent respectively. 

 The goal of the new investment mix is to preserve capital, ensure the monetary base is fully backed by highly liquid, short term U.S.-dollar denominated assets as well as maintaining enough liquidity to preserve monetary and financial stability, according to the announcement. Following the government's intervention in the Hong Kong stock market last August, the Exchange Fund acquired a portfolio of Hong Kong equities which account for about 17 percent of the fund's total assets. 

 As at December 31, 1998, assets of the fund totalled HK$910 billion. The new benchmark of a five percent allocation to Hong Kong equities means that HK$46 billion of the current HK$150 billion equity portfolio will be kept as a long term investment.

title: HK dollar bumped but not budged by Brazil jitters.
text:
HONG KONG, Jan 22 (Reuters) - The Hong Kong dollar came under modest pressure on Friday amid continued worries over Brazil, but traders and analysts said there was little sign of speculative activity against the currency peg. 

 "I don't see any signs of a speculative attack against the Hong Kong dollar today, certainly not comparable to that of last August," said Stephen Cheung, a director of Jardine Fleming Bank. 

 The Hong Kong dollar was at HK$7.7480/90 per U.S. dollar at 0720 GMT on Friday, slightly weaker than 7.7468/80 at Thursday's close. Forward rates were up modestly, more so in the longer end than the short end, while interest rates were slightly higher. 

 Hong Kong's currency peg came under intense pressure in August 1998 in what the government described as a "double play" game by hedge funds to push up interest rates by attacking the currency and then take profits on short stock positions after the share market reacted badly to higher rates. 

 The government aggressively bought stocks in controversial intervention to foil speculators that month. In September, it unveiled a seven-point plan to shore up the 15-year old currency board system which included liquidity enhancing measures and promises of greater transparency. 

 The measures have contributed greatly to maintaining the Hong Kong dollar's stability even as Brazil's currency troubles spark market jitters worldwide, traders and analysts said. 

 In the past, balances in the Hong Kong banking system could be shifted by the slightest outflow of U.S. dollars, but now a huge flow is required to cause an interest rate surge, said Craig Chan, regional treasury economist at Standard Chartered Bank. 

 Hedge funds' access to funding also has diminished in recent months, especially after the well-publicised failure of U.S. fund Long-Term Capital Management late last year. Analysts noted also that speculators don't have much to gain in Hong Kong if they, as the government has insisted, were intent last year not on breaking the peg but in busting stock prices. 

 With government intervention in the share market still a threat, speculators might think twice before selling stocks short and assaulting the local dollar. 

 "Of course, one argument against the idea of government intervention is that Hong Kong already owns a big chunk of the stock market and they've already said the intervention last year was extraordinary," said Lehman Brothers economist Rob Subbaraman. "Do they really want to intervene again?" 

 Money market traders said activity has been dominated by position-squaring and concentrated in the long end rather than the short end of the curve. 

 Chordio Chan, head of money markets at Citibank, noted that the overnight rate has been trading below the U.S. discount rate for some time, although there was a short-lived spike on Thursday on rumours the monetary authority was draining funds. 

 "But the short end still remains on the soft side, in contrast to what we saw in 1997 and 1998, when everytime there was an attack on the currency, short rates tended to surge and rise higher than the longer end, rendering a flatter curve," Chan said. "But this time, we have seen the curve flattening." 

 A Hong Kong Monetary Authority representative in New York said on Thursday the peg would stand and that Brazil's devaluation would have no impact on Hong Kong's economy. 

 Still, Brazil's difficulties are sure to keep markets in Hong Kong on edge, especially if its problems are seen spreading. 

 "Brazil could cause renewed pressure on the Hong Kong dollar for two reasons - the possibility of a global growth slowdown and a credit shock that causes risk premiums to rise," said Kate O'Donoghue, regional economist at Barclays Capital. 

 Worries about the stability of China's yuan in the face of slower world growth would also unnerve Hong Kong markets, despite Beijing's repeated vows to maintain its currency. 

 On Thursday, Argentina, which like Hong Kong has a currency board system, floated the idea of adopting the U.S. dollar, a move the government said was unrelated to Brazil's woes. 

 While dollarisation by Argentina would have little direct effect on Hong Kong, it would certainly raise anew questions about the long-term viability of a currency board, analysts said.

title: Singapore rivals Hong Kong as Asia's choice.
text:
SINGAPORE (Reuters) - It used to be a no-contest: Hong Kong was easily the place of choice to do business in Asia. 

 Singapore, swaddled by red tape and policed by a stern central bank, was a distant runner-up, a destination of necessity. 

 But more than a year into the Asian crisis, Singapore appears to have edged in front and is winning kudos from investors, credit-rating agencies, securities analysts and foreign media for having one of Asia's best-run economies and financial sectors. 

 It has at last thrown down a serious challenge to Hong Kong. 

 "Singapore has finally got it right," one managing director of a regional securities firm in Singapore said. 

 "It is not about doctrine or ideology, it is all finally driven by commercial considerations - what can we do to get your business to thrive? 

 "That is the best way to win in this game with Hong Kong," he said. 

 Some of the world's biggest companies are putting their faith in Singapore, including Caltex Petroleum Corp., which said in October it would relocate its headquarters from Dallas. It is the first multinational to establish its global head office here. 

 The fight for supremacy between Singapore and Hong Kong began last year in the securities industry. 

 Trading of Hang Seng index futures on the Singapore International Monetary Exchange marked the official start of hostilities, said I.D.E.A. senior economist Jacqueline Ong. 

 And the battle is intense, with newspapers joining the fray. 

 "Hong Kong and Singapore seem to have swapped places in the eyes of the international media," the Singapore Business Times said recently. 

 "Hong Kong, which used to be the media darling up until the handover from Britain to China, is getting uncharacteristic bad press. Singapore, on the other hand, has been getting favourable reviews." 

 The issue was costs, Ong said, and a Singapore government S$10.5 billion ($6.36 billion) package of cost-cutting measures has boosted the city state's competitiveness. 

 The centrepiece of the November package was a 50 percent cut in employer contributions to a state pension fund. Trade unions accepted the move without any apparent rancour. 

 "While both cities provide reasonably good infrastructure, it boils down to cost competitiveness," Ong said. 

 On this front, Hong Kong's policy of pegging the local currency to the U.S. dollar had become a handicap, she said. 

 I.D.E.A., a research house, made a comparative study of cost competitiveness of the two cities, and Hong Kong came up short. 

 Among other things, the study looked at wages, rent, interest costs, and utilities and service costs. 

 "Our study shows that overall cost in Singapore started to correct downwards as early as Q1 1998 ... however, costs in Hong Kong continued in an upward trajectory," Ong said in the report. 

 Assuming its currency peg remained, Hong Kong property prices and wages needed to fall further this year to compete, she added. 

 The average manager in Hong Kong earns double the salary of a Singapore manager, according to recent data from U.S. funds research company William Mercer. The average in Hong Kong was $62.80 an hour and in Singapore $30.70 an hour. 

 William Mercer said rentals for a small, two-bedroom apartment in Hong Kong averaged $6,400 a month in a "good area," compared with $2,002 for a comparable apartment in Singapore. 

 Singapore has also stolen a march on Hong Kong in reforming its financial industry in the midst of the Asian crisis. 

 Last month, Washington-based Heritage Foundation said Hong Kong could lose its position as the freest economy in the world to its arch rival Singapore. 

 In 1998, the Singapore government placed billions of dollars with private fund managers to boost the industry and issued its first 10-year bond to deepen the official debt market. 

 It made it easier for foreign entities to list Singapore-dollar shares and issue Singapore-dollar bonds, raised bank disclosure standards and encouraged bank mergers. 

 As investors lauded Singapore's move to a more open market, Hong Kong authorities intervened in their stock market and Malaysia shut its doors on investors with capital controls. 

 Singapore's central bank, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), mounted a global marketing campaign, promoting itself to investors in the United States, Europe and Asia. 

 It boasted that in 1998, 15 more foreign firms were given the status of approved overseas headquarters and finance and treasury centres in Singapore, which carries with it tax benefits. 

 They included Asea Brown Boveri, Ericsson, Hitachi, Hoechst and NCR Asia. 

 The MAS said several asset management companies - including Morgan Grenfell (Asia) Ltd., ABN-Amro Asset Management and Morgan Stanley Dean Witter Investment Management Co. - were either consolidating their management of Asian funds in Singapore or had selected it as their hub for regional asset management. 

 Russell Whitehouse, regional finance director of Guardian Insurance, which recently moved its regional base from Hong Kong to Singapore, said Singapore's location was also attractive. 

 "This was part of the region our growth was coming from," he told Reuters. He also cited the city's efficient airport and its reputation as a safe and good place to live. 

 Singapore might now have its nose in front of Hong Kong in many respects, but the contest is never over, analysts said. Some cautioned that Hong Kong was still hard on Singapore's heels. 

 (C) Reuters Limited 1999.

title: ASIA MARKETS-Regional stocks down with the Dow.
text:
HONG KONG, Dec 1 (Reuters) - Asian stocks were hit hard on 

 Tuesday by the fall on Wall Street but traders and strategists 

 were not ready just yet to call the markets a strong sell. 

Currencies traded in very narrow ranges, suggesting that 

 funds have not started to flee equities. 

     FINDING THE LIQUIDITY 

     The heaviest selling pressure began after Hong Kong's Hang 

 Seng index opened and promptly lost more than three percent of 

 its value. But dealers were not entirely convinced the region's 

 falls were the start of a major correction. 

 "This could be the start of a much needed and well earned 

 consolidation," said Miles Remington, head of institutional 

 sales at SG Asia. 

     "(But) the volumes have not really been around to 

 constitute a real sell off," he said. 

     "Hopefully, we are in the hands of other markets globally," 

 he said, echoing a view that even a 2.3 percent sell-off on 

 Wall Street could not be as bad for the market as a seven 

 percent fall in Hong Kong's GDP in the third quarter, recorded 

 on Friday. 

     "We're not seeing many investors (selling), it's mostly 

 traders taking profit," said a head trader at a European bank. 

     "Lots of books are closed already, job losses are already 

 decided, there's no need for people to step up and take new 

 positions," he said. 

     But even if a sharp correction does not come from the U.S., 

 Asian markets are not seen enjoying much foreign interest. 

     "For the next 12 months at least, the major source of new 

 liquidity for these markets will continue to be through the 

 public account," said Marshall Mays, chief strategist at Nikko 

 Securities in Hong Kong. 

 "The expectation of the real money coming from the private 

 credit sector is still a long way off," he told Reuters 

 Television on Tuesday. 

 HONG KONG TECHNICALLY NUMBER ONE 

 Hong Kong retained its place at the top of the Heritage 

 Foundation's Index of Economic Freedom for 1999, but in name 

 only. The think-tank blamed Hong Kong's intervention in its 

 stock market in August as the chief reason the territory has 

 lost out to rival Singapore in real results. 

 The 1999 index was completed on June 30. Hong Kong fell 

 from the number one spot in August when the government bought 

 HK$118 billion (US$15.2 billion) in shares to drive off 

 speculators. 

 IMF-ASSISTED NATIONS GET LETTERS IN ORDER 

 Details of IMF letters of intent with Indonesia and 

 Thailand were released while Korea moved closer to plans to 

 repay its Fund loans. 

 While few analysts saw any reason to expect a problem with 

 the disbursement of funds to Indonesia or Thailand, some 

 questioned the clarity the Indonesian letter would provide. 

 "This represents what you might call a process of examining 

 what's inside a box by sticking a series of needles into it," 

 said Mays. 

 "Each of the letters of intent is an attempt to report on 

 what has been done ... in reality, of course, the 

 accomplishments have so far substantially under-performed the 

 expectations, as one would expect with a society in such a 

 drastic depression as Indonesia is," he said. 

     Thailand's letter included a projection for a better than 

 expected one percent rise in GDP for 1999. 

     The letter also said Thai foreign reserves next year would 

 rise to $32 billion from $28 billion seen this year. 

      Meanwhile, Korea was preparing to host a group of IMF 

 officials Wednesday to discuss repayment of IMF's aid loans. 

     A finance ministry official said repayment of $2.73 billion 

 in aid loans maturing by the end of this year would be 

 discussed, as well as $2 billion coming due between January and 

 February. 

CURRENCIES QUIET - MORE RUPIAH STRENGTH EXPECTED 

Currency traders were watching the December holiday period 

 roll quietly closer, with less and less business being done on 

 the already thinned regional forex markets. 

 Traders were generally unwilling to pick a favorite trade 

 in Asian currencies, but some thought the rupiah might find 

 some more upside before the end of the year. 

 In Hong Kong, Indonesian central bank governor Syahril 

 Sabirin said the rupiah could strengthen to 7,000 or 6,500 per 

 dollar and there was more room for interest rates to ease.

title: Morgan Stanley Chairman Says U.S. Economy Will Grow 3.6% in 1998
text:
HONG KONG -(Dow Jones)- The U.S. economy will grow at a steady 3.6% rate this year and the Federal Reserve Board is likely to lower interest rates again by the year end, the chairman and chief executive officer of Morgan Stanley Dean Witter & Co. said Tuesday. 

 "Our growth forecast for this year remains basically unchanged at 3.6%," despite the "global economic contagion" in the wake of the emerging market crises in Asia, Latin America and Russia, Philip Purcell said at a business luncheon in Hong Kong. 

 Purcell predicted an economic slowdown in the U.S. next year. However, "despite the global economic woes, we're still looking for 2.3% (gross domestic product) growth in the U.S. in 1999," he added. 

 He said the Fed is breaking from the anti-inflationary policy it has held in the past 19 years as the central bank tries to respond directly to troubles in emerging markets. 

 "The main danger is still a worldwide credit crunch, and I am hopeful there will be further easing of monetary policy by year end," he said. 

 Analysts remain divided on the prospect of a rate cut ahead of the Federal Open Market Committee meeting later Tuesday. The rate-setting body will meet again in December, its last meeting this year. 

 Purcell said there are signs that the worst of the Asian crisis might be over. 

 "As far as Asia is concerned, while it's a bit early to bring on the bulls, we do think that there are a number of reasons not to be bearish," he said. 

 He said that lower interest rates in the U.S., coupled with Japan's willingness to help and sustained growth in China, will benefit other Asian countries and help keep regional currencies steady. 

 "We believe we've seen the worst of the recession in (Asia) in 1998," Purcell said, predicting that investors will start to return to the region next year. 

 He said Japan and China will be "the twin pillars on which Southeast Asia's recovery will rest." Japan needs to stick to its banking reforms, while "China, in our view, will maintain the current value of its currency," he noted. 

 Purcell said he is confident that Hong Kong will retain its status as a world-class financial center. While he didn't directly comment on the Hong Kong government's massive market intervention, he praised Financial Secretary Donald Tsang's efforts to assure international investors that the territory is committed to the free market principle. 

 "Foreign investors were shaken by the moves (taken by the Hong Kong government). Some of them were punished financially...(but) confidence is returning that (Hong Kong) is going to be a free market," Purcell said. 

 The Hong Kong government spent HK$118 billion acquiring blue-chip stocks in the last two weeks of August, in a bid to fight off international speculators and maintain stability in local equity and currency markets.

title: FOCUS - HK joins land, exchange fund assets.
text:
HONG KONG, Nov 17 (Reuters) - The Hong Kong government on Tuesday said it would merge the assets of its Land Fund with its Exchange Fund in a bid to align investment policy, reduce costs and boost returns to its fiscal reserves. 

 "With the alignment, the Land Fund will be able to enjoy the same returns achieved by the Exchange Fund, thereby allowing the Land Fund to enjoy a more steady return at reduced volatility," Treasury Secretary Denise Yue told reporters. 

 "There will also be enlarged fiscal reserves," she said. 

 Before the merger, the assets of the Land Fund, which holds the proceeds from government land sales, and the Exchange Fund, which provides backing for the Hong Kong dollar's peg to the U.S. dollar, were managed separately. 

 The Land Fund, which was 40.7 percent invested in cash at the end of September, typically earns lower returns than the more aggressive Exchange Fund while suffering more volatility. 

 The move, which was effective as of October 31, 1998, fulfilled the objective announced in February this year by Financial Secretary Donald Tsang of aligning the investment policy of the two funds by next April, Yue said. 

 Land Fund assets, which were about HK$211.4 billion as of October 31, would be placed with the Exchange Fund for the account of the Land Fund, the government said. 

 The fiscal reserves already placed with the Exchange Fund amounted to HK$203.1 billion as of October 31, it said. 

 "This is a pure and simple way to handle the fiscal reserves, including the Land Fund," said Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) chief Joseph Yam. 

 With the addition of Land Fund assets, the Exchange Fund would total HK$946 billion, he said. 

 Yam said adding HK$211 billion to the Exchange Fund might "psychologically boost" sentiment toward the Hong Kong dollar peg, but he added that currency in circulation already was covered many times over by the Exchange Fund. 

 Hong Kong's currency is linked to the U.S. dollar through a currency board system, which maintains the pegged rate of HK$7.8 per US$1 through automatic adjustments in liquidity. 

 After the merger, the Hong Kong equity portfolio previously held in the Land Fund would go to the Exchange Fund Investment Ltd (EFIL) for management in the same manner as the Hong Kong shares acquired by the Exchange Fund through the government's massive intervention in the local stock market in August. 

 EFIL was set up to manage the HK$118 billion in blue chip shares the government bought in August to fend off speculators. 

 All Hong Kong equity holdings of the Hong Kong government would, therefore, be consolidated for management by EFIL. 

 At HK$12 billion at the end of September, the size of the Land Fund's Hong Kong equity holdings is relatively small compared with the Exchange Fund stock portfolio. 

 The government has said that it has not sold any shares acquired for the Exchange Fund during the intervention, but Yam said the Land Fund may have bought or sold shares in the past couple of months as part of its normal investment operations. 

 EFIL would be asked to consider disclosing the details of the enlarged Hong Kong equity portfolio as a result of the merger, the government said. 

 The merging of Land Fund and Exchange Fund assets was not designed to facilitate equity investment by the government, but rather to streamline investment policy for the fiscal reserves, Treasury Secretary Yue said. 

 The long-term strategy on the government holdings of Hong Kong equity would be examined by the HKMA in the context of the overall review on asset allocation in the management of the Exchange Fund, the government said. 

 After the merging of its assets with the Exchange Fund, the Land Fund still would remain a separate government fund and the use of its holdings for government spending would remain subject to approval by Hong Kong's legislative council, it added.

title: SE Asian  Currencies  -4: Peso Bulls Seen Charging Wrong Way
text:
Most market participants remain bullish on the peso, saying foreign direct investment and remittances from expatriate Filipinos will bolster the currency over the coming months. According to Basu at CSFB, however, that optimism may be sorely misplaced. 

 "The Philippine peso is by far the most vulnerable currency in Asia," he said, asserting the contrarian view. 

 Basu points to a current account that is barely in balance, the high level of banks' net foreign liabilities relative to the overall size of their balance sheets, and foreign reserves, which at $7.7 billion, he describes as "puny", compared with the Philippines' levels of short term debt. 

 "The Philippines' external balances are very precariously perched and could easily be tipped over the edge," he warned. 

 The rupiah's strength on Wednesday was attributed to sales of the U.S. dollar by state banks in Jakarta. Although Bank Indonesia declared that it was not intervening in the market, traders in Singapore and Hong Kong insisted that the central bank has been active in recent days, selling the U.S. dollar to stabilize the rupiah as political tension in Indonesia mounts. Apart from the state banks, said traders, few other players dared to risk entering the market. 

 "Investors will only begin to look at the rupiah again when the process of political change is complete. Until then we won't see any sustainable inflow of foreign funds," said Fong at Nomura.

title: HK's Last Governor -3: Advocates HK Property Sector Changes
text:
Patten also hit out at Hong Kong's big property developers, calling for changes to the sector, traditionally one of the key drivers in Hong Kong's economy but which has seen property prices slump as much as 50% from last year's peak. 

 Patten said that more free-market principles are needed to be brought into play in the sector, which has been dominated by a a select number of companies and overseen by a developer-friendly government. 

 "The right approach in the long-term is more reliance on the market and less reliance on what has been portrayed as a combination of cartelization and municipalization," said Patten. 

 Patten downplayed the role of government planning, saying that civil servants, as capable as Hong Kong's are, can't outsmart the market. 

 Patten also defended the August market intervention by the Hong KongMonetary Authority, which spent HK$118.1 billion to buy up blue-chip stocks and futures to ward off speculators, leaving the government a substantial shareholder in some of Hong Kong's largest companies. 

 "I don't believe (the intervention) means that Hong Kong has abandoned its traditional faith in markets and market solutions...It's the free-market economics, not government intervention, that has transformed Hong Kong" from a low value-added to high value-added economy, he said. 

 Patten also dismissed views that China is under growing pressure to devalue its currency, the yuan, adding that a devaluation wouldn't help boost China's trade performance.

title: HK Hibor Higher Late As Mkt Eyes Forecast HK$ Outflow
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--Hong Kong interbank rates are mostly higher late Monday as the market nervously eyes a forecast HK$1.82 billion outflow from the territory's banking system later in the week. 

 Dealers say the market has been almost paralyzed by concern over the outflow, which has already been transacted, but won't be settled until Thursday under Hong Kong's T+2 settlement system. Hong Kong markets will be closed Wednesday for a public holiday. 

 "The market is empty," with almost no deals being completed, said a dealer at a local bank. He noted that bid/offer spreads have widened to around 50 basis points across the curve, reflecting the market jitters. 

 The volatile overnight Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate is quoted at 4.75%, down from 6% late in the previous session. But the benchmark three-month rate is 7%, up from 6.25% late Friday. 

 Market participants were divided as to whether the Thursday outflow, and a smaller HK$78.0 million shrinkage expected Wednesday, were due to commercial transactions or were part of an attempt by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority to prop up the local currency, which is hovering near the key level of HK$7.75 to the U.S. dollar. The HKMA is known to intervene in the market when the Hong Kong dollar hits that level in the spot market. 

 Around 0823 GMT (3:23 a.m. EST), the Hong Kong dollar is quoted at HK$7.7497 to the U.S. dollar, weaker than HK$7.7495 late Friday. 

 However, several dealers said they believed the outflows were due to commercial transactions by Japanese and other banks in Hong Kong.

title: HKMA Yam To Propose Releasing Minutes From Some Meetings
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--Hong Kong Monetary Authority Chief Executive Joseph Yam said in a speech delivered late Tuesday that he will propose releasing some of the minutes from meetings of a sub-committee on currency-board operations. 

 "I shall shortly be making a proposal to the financial secretary initially for the minutes of the sub-committee, other than those concerning market-sensitive issues, to be published, with an appropriate time lag," Yam said. 

 The group was set up to advise the Exchange Fund Advisory Committee, the de facto board of directors managing Hong Kong's reserves and currency board, on currency-board matters. 

 But the move to release the minutes isn't likely to drastically increase transparency of the inner workings of Hong Kong's monetary management, even though Yam suggested minutes of the Advisory Committee itself might be released as well at some later date. 

 Yam said that, since Hong Kong's currency board system rules out an independent monetary policy in the territory, there is little to reveal. 

 "We do not have a system whereby the HKMA has to take discretionary decisions to determine interest rates or to specify monetary targets," he said. "There has therefore not been a need for a mechanism for public scrutiny of discretionary decisions because there is nothing to scrutinize." 

 However, the HKMA has come under fire recently for manipulating interest rates and intervening directly in currency markets to support Hong Kong's currency, despite the existence of a currency-board system that is supposed to make such intervention unnecessary or even impossible. And in August, the HKMA along with the government, took the intervention another step further by buying an estimated HK$15.00 billion in local shares in an attempt to squeeze speculators out of the territory's markets.

title: HKMA Chief Says Hedge Funds In Retreat; After  Intervention
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--Hong Kong's quasi-central bank said hedge funds are in retreat after it took them on in the stock and futures market to defend its local currency. 

 "We have seen substantial unwinding of the short positions in our currency by the hedge funds, with considerable losses," Hong Kong Monetary Authority Chief Executive Joseph Yam said in a statement released late Wednesday. 

 "And with the stock market having recovered substantially from the level at which we entered the market in the middle of August, more considerable losses were incurred also in their short positions in the stock index futures," he added, defending the HKMA's August intervention in Hong Kong's stock and futures markets. 

 "Free markets don't mean that markets can be freely manipulated. They need to be fair markets as well. We've a responsibility to tackle market manipulation and avoid serious market dislocations developing," Yam said. 

 Yam said the hedge funds had lined up Hong Kong dollars in advance of their attack, so that they wouldn't be hit by penal local interest rates. 

 "This they did by swapping U.S. dollars for Hong Kong dollars..., incurring an interest cost of HK$4.0 million a day for the HK$30 billion position. But this wasn't a lot of money to them," Yam said. 

 "We had reason to believe that they had been building up and maintaining quite large short positions in the stock index futures," Yam said.

title: HK Mkt Action Confusing, Affects Argentina Peso - Analyst
text:
WASHINGTON (Dow Jones)--The sustainability of Argentina's currency board depends greatly on the ability of Hong Kong authorities to hold the line on theirs, but the Hong Kong government's recent market intervention was confusing and unorthodox, a prominent Argentine analyst said Monday. 

 "The currency board in Argentina is affected by the Hong Kong situation. Maybe we study Hong Kong more than anybody in the world," said Ricardo Lopez-Murphy, head of Argentina's Foundation for Latin American Economic Research. 

 Late in August, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority bought billions of U.S. dollars worth of local stocks and futures in order to break what it said was a "double-play" action by speculators to attack the Hong Kong dollar. 

 Lopez-Murphy said he can't see Argentine authorities taking a similar action to defend the country's peso currency. For one thing, he said speculators would be hard-pressed to profit from what they were apparently doing in Hong Kong: selling stocks, futures and the currency concurrently to profit from short positions. 

 The bigger size of Hong Kong's capital markets in relation to those of Argentina is an important difference, he said. 

 "For us, it was difficult to understand why they were buying shares," Lopez-Murphy said, adding that Hong Kong's action wasn't "orthodox" in terms of currency board operation.

title: HK Govt Foreign Reserves Could Fall To $20B - Analyst
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--The Hong Kong government may have spent as much as $3 billion dollars in the local equity and futures markets in September, according a report published by Prudential-Bache Securities (Hong Kong) Ltd. 

 The government's intervention in the markets, added to the effects of Hong Kong's recession, could cut foreign reserves to as little as $20 billion by the end of 1999, the report said. That would rattle public confidence in the economy and the Hong Kong dollar, the report warned. 

 The Hong Kong Monetary Authority declined to say if it had bought shares in September. The quasi-central bank in August bought billions of dollars in local shares in an effort to squeeze speculators out of the market. 

 Stock traders, however, have said throughout September that they saw few signs of government buying. 


Pan Ming, Prudential-Bache's equities strategist, said in the report
that the government understated its share buying in its foreign reserve
figures for August.
   The government said reserves at the end of August stood at $92.1

title: HK firms tolerant of government  intervention .
text:
HONG KONG, Sept 29 (Reuters) - Hong Kong's response to Asia's economic crisis has stirred controversy, but some businesses said they were willing to look beyond government infringement of free market principles to long-term prospects offered by China. 

 "It does not make me any less confident in Hong Kong and China and it does not make me want to move our business away. It does not make me particularly nervous," said Gary Coull, chairman of Hong Kong-based Credit Lyonnais Securities Asia. 

 "I just think you have to be aware of it," he said. 

 Government intervention in both the property and financial markets have sullied Hong Kong's free market reputation, drawing criticism at home and abroad. 

 In a two-week intervention campaign in the stock market last month, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority spent an estimated HK$100 billion (US$12.9 billion) to squeeze out "manipulators" who were active in Hong Kong's stock and currency markets. 

 The Hong Kong General Chamber of Commerce, which has about 4,000 corporate members, said while the move was unusual for Hong Kong, it did not detract from people's views on investment here and the future business climate. 

 "In reviewing exactly what happened, there was general support and sympathy because the business community is very much behind maintaining the Hong Kong dollar peg and realised that this was an emergency measure," director Eden Woon said. 

 "Hong Kong is still the most international of all Asian cities and a place where a foreign investor will find the most comfort both in terms of regulations and in terms of the ease of doing business and living. And plus the proximity of China which nobody is going to be able to duplicate," Woon said. 

 It was the stability of the Hong Kong currency which, from the trade point of view, would keep businesses here, said Edward Leung, chief economist at the Hong Kong Trade Development Council. 

 "Exchange rate stability is most important to them and Hong Kong will continue to maintain a liberal trading regime," he said. 

 Measures announced early this month to tighten regulations in the securities markets would leave Hong Kong's position as a regional hub for fund management unharmed, said Desmond Chan, chairman of the Hong Kong Investment Funds Association. 

 "What has happened lately I don't think is enough to make fund managers desert Hong Kong," said Chan, pointing to local regulations and the tax regime. 

 "Hong Kong will be a gateway to China in some future time so if someone has an eye on China's fund management industry in years to come, it may be better to have an office here." 

 The hinterland has given Hong Kong an advantage which helps offset the higher costs of doing business here compared with other countries where currencies have depreciated, SG Securities said in a recent report. 

 "We dispute the simple-minded thinking that HK has fundamentally lost its competitiveness to the point where only a currency devaluation can restore that competitiveness," it said. 

 "A regional service centre's competitiveness is NOT, repeat NOT, determined overwhelmingly by the level of its currency," the report said. 

 Mike Rowse, director of the Hong Kong government's business and services promotion unit, said businesses were not just looking at price, but also at what else was offered here. 

 "You have the banks, you have the lawyers, you have the accountants, you have the chartered secretaries, you have the whole shebang," he told Reuters in an interview. 

 While concerns about the government's recent intervention would fade away, businesses would focus on the free movement of capital, rule of law, freedom of the press and freedom of movement available in the territory, Rowse said. 

 "We have got virtually all the big things right which is why we feel slightly embittered that there has been a spillover from the places that did not get these things right," he said.

title: HK democrats say rules key in foiling speculators.
text:
HONG KONG, Sept 28 (Reuters) - Tighter regulation in Hong Kong is more effective than intervention in foiling speculative attacks against the local currency, the Democratic Party said in a news briefing on Monday. 

 Albert Ho, a spokesman for the legislature's single largest party, said concern about speculative activities by hedge funds and the recent troubles of U.S. hedge fund Long Term Capital Management should not lead to the conclusion that intervention was the correct solution. 

 Prudent regulation was more effective, he said. 

 "Regulation as a preventive measure should of course be adopted instead of direct intervention in the stock market and exchange market using speculation to counter speculation," Ho said. 

 "Direct intervention must be wrong. Even the government has acknowledged that intervention was very costly," he said. 

 The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) intervened heavily in the stock and futures exhanges in August to foil speculators it said had attacked the currency peg with the aim of pushing interest rates up and share prices down to take profits on short stock positions. 

 Under Hong Kong's currency board system, pressures for a weak Hong Kong dollar automatically cause interest rates to rise and vice versa. 

 Compelling hedge funds to conform to rules and operate more transparently and regulating short selling were possible solutions to deter speculative attacks, said Ho. 

 The party called on the HKMA to exercise a rule-based and more transparent governing system to strengthen the currency board, rather than rely on its own discretion. 

 "My conclusion is that the HKMA was too overconfident in its wisdom in exercising its administrative discretion...The HKMA was reluctant to introduce a rule-based system policy so as to increase the transparency of the system to fortify the currency board and constrain speculators," he said. 

 He criticised HKMA chief executive Joseph Yam for having too much power, saying the HKMA was operating more like a central bank than a defender of the currency board. 

 "The chief executive has extensive power, from setting up the Liquidity Adjustment Facility, issuing bonds and establishing the Mortgage Corporation to intervening in the markets using huge billions of dollars from the reserve fund," said Ho. 

 The party suggested the power of the HKMA be clearly defined by ordinance. It said the chief executive should have a set term of office and should be openly accountable. 

 The party said it viewed the seven-point plan announced by the HKMA in early September to strengthen the peg system as being a step closer to a pure currency board system. 

 While the authority's discount window was irrelevant to maintaining a currency board system, it was widely accepted by the market, the party said.

title: Hong Kong stocks close up on technical rebound.
text:
HONG KONG, Sept 22 (Reuters) - Hong Kong stocks shrugged off three straight days of declines to finish higher on Tuesday on a technical rebound triggered by firmer U.S. and Tokyo stocks, brokers said. 

 The Hang Seng Index ended up 203.28 points, or 2.84 percent, at 7,373.51, but was off the day's high of 7,438.33 points. 

 "The rally on Hong Kond stocks is mainly due to a rebound on Wall Street in late trade overnight after people found that Clinton's video tapes seemed to be not that devastating," said Alex Tang, research director at Core Pacific - Yamaichi International (HK). 

 The Dow industrials erased an 185-point early loss to close at 7,933.25, up 37.59 points, or 0.48 percent on Monday as the release of U.S. President Bill Clinton's videotaped grand jury testimony was considered less damaging to him than feared. 

 "The Hong Kong market took a plunge yesterday ahead of the U.S. market and the U.S. did not really fall a lot last night so there is a rebound today," said Frederick Tsang, director at DBS Securities. 

 Tokyo's Nikkei 225 average finished up 192.51 points, or 1.42 percent, at 13,789.81 on Tuesday. 

 But the Japanese yen weakened to 135 to the U.S. dollar in late trade, triggering light profit-taking in Hong Kong stocks, Tang said. The yen opened in Asia on Tuesday at 134.44/49. 

 "A slip on the yen fuelled concerns about the outlook of the Japanese currency since a weak yen would put renewed pressure on the Hong Kong dollar," Tang said. 

 The market was also watching the development of a political wrangling between the Japanese government and opposition parties which held up crucial financial reform bills, brokers said. 

 Utilities led the blue chip gainers with CLP Holdings  gaining HK$1.20 to HK$35.90, Hongkong Electric  up HK$1.15 at HK$26.50 and Hongkong Telecom  rising HK$0.50 to HK$14.80. 

 HSBC Holdings  also added HK$3.50 to HK$135.50. 

 Hutchison  advanced HK$1.10 to HK$36.40. Hutchison Telecom, a unit of Hutchison Whampoa Ltd, said on Tuesday it would announce a new plan for Hutchison Telecom's mobile operations at a news conference on Wednesday. 

 Hutchison Whampoa said last week it was launching a new marketing strategy to promote the group's telecommunications business, including advertising for British-based mobile phone arm Orange Plc . It declined to give more details. 

 Shangri-La Asia  jumped HK$0.65, or 15.76 percent, to close at HK$4.775. 

 September index futures added 275 points to 7,395, while the October contract rose 270 points to 7,140 and December futures added 260 points to 7,100. 

 "The September future is trading quite close to the index. I think there is some switching activity. The short sellers are covering September positions and switching into October ones," Tsang said. 

 Paliburg  fell HK$0.30, or 12.24 percent, to HK$2.15, weighed by a recent sharp price fall of Chi Cheung . Chi Cheung shares dropped 87.6 percent last Friday before a trading suspension. 

 Paliburg and Chi Cheung chairman Paul Ng formed a joint venture, Rapid Growth Holdings Ltd, to hold a 74.06 percent stake in Chi Cheung. 

 China plays were firmer. The red chip Hang Seng China-Affiliated Corporations Index added 15.88 points, or 2.21 percent, to 734.42 and the Hang Seng Chinese Enterprises Index rose 13.75 points, or 4.07 percent, to 351.44 points. 

 Brokers said Hong Kong stocks lacked direction and should move within a range of 7,000 to 7,800 with investors looking to overseas markets for trading clues. 

 "There are still investors who are confident that when the HSI corrects itself, there is still value in holding onto Hong Kong stocks," said Vivian Kwok, head of research at Sassoon Securities. 

 "There is value at 7,000. When that level is reached I think there will still be a lot of buyers," she added. 

 Brokers said there was little reaction to the Hong Kong Monetary Authority's (HKMA) announcement on Monday that foreign reserves had fallen to US$92.1 billion at end-August from US$96.5 billion at end-July. 

 The drop in reserves could be attributed to both fiscal drawdowns by the government treasury and the government's intervention in the stock and futures market, the HKMA said. 

 The authority would not reveal exactly how much was spent on intervention, citing the government's desire to keep such information from speculators. 

 But the HKMA did say US$4.4 billion of the Exchange Fund was sold on the last two trading days on August 28 and 31 to fund investment in Hong Kong stocks. Those transactions would be settled in September. 

 Market analysts said the government's heftiest purchases were made at the end of August, when turnover jumped to a record shattering HK$79 billion on August 28. 

 Brokers noted that part of the funding of the stock intervention would have come from Hong Kong dollar reserves, so it was difficult to determine how much money was spent.

title: ASIA MARKETS - Stocks jumpy, central banks active.
text:
SINGAPORE, Sept 22 (Reuters) - Major Asian stock markets cheered up on Tuesday after Wall Street shrugged off the global airing of U.S. President Bill Clinton's grand jury testimony. But traders said Asia's markets were still jumpy, especially over the implications of Japan's protracted financial crisis. Regional currencies were hurt by yen weakness, and some saw central bank intervention. 

HONG KONG STOCKS CLIMB WHILE MANILA SINKS 

Hong Kong shares saw big early gains on thin volume, prompted by Wall Street's positive response to the political developments surrounding Clinton's testimony. 

 Bell-wether stocks HSBC Holdings, Hong Kong Telecom, China Telecom and Hutchison Whampoa were heavily traded. 

 But dealers declined to attribute the buying to genuine interest and said sellers were "backing off". 

 Philippine shares were the biggest losers on Tuesday, closing 3.5 percent lower as the reality of economic malaise hit home. 

 The country is coming to grips with an increasingly bleak economic outlook, economists said. 

 The stock market was hurt by confusion over leading blue chips Philippine Long Distance Telephone, rumoured to be a foreign takeover target, and Philippine Airlines (PAL), the national airline which is set to formally close on Wednesday. 

 Most market watchers felt PAL would not be forced into liquidation and was engaged in brinkmanship with the government, which has shown reluctance to bail out the airline. 

 CENTRAL BANKS IN THE FOREX MARKET 

 Limited central bank activity was seen in some currency markets, with fears of yen-induced falls pushing a few of the regional currencies through what were seen as key levels. 

 The yen was quoted around 135 to the dollar at 0950 GMT. 

 Korean central bank authorities were seen in the foreign exchange markets, after the won threatened to fall through 1,400 to the dollar on the back of the weak yen. 

 Speculative positions built up early on the dollar's recovery sparked verbal intervention by the Bank of Korea, dealers said. 

 Thailand's central bank appeared to be looking for dollars on Tuesday as the baht weakened against the greenback, dealers said. 

 The government is still cleaning up remaining long baht positions taken in the forward market by the Bank of Thailand in the past year, traders said. 

 The Singapore dollar was supported by firmer short-term interest rates, but some said the rise was odd given the twin political concerns of Malaysia and Indonesia.

title: IMF sees risks from HK stock market  intervention .
text:
WASHINGTON, Sept 21 (Reuters) - Hong Kong's decision to intervene in its stock markets poses a number of risks, but the authorities there are competent and strongly committed to their currency board system, a senior IMF official said on Monday. 

 Charles Adams, deputy chief economist of the International Monetary Fund, said Hong Kong could face the problem of stopping intervention once it had got under way. 

 "There is a risk of propping up the market and the interventions get bigger and bigger and eventually you have to have an exit strategy," he told reporters after a news conference. 

 He noted that Hong Kong was also changing some elements of the currency board, a rigid system which pegs the Hong Kong dollar to the greenback. 

 "The political commitment to the currency board system is very very strong; they have taken incredible pains so far," he said, describing the Hong Kong authorities as "very competent people...under amazing pressure." 

 He added: "I think the bigger risk for them is that if the situation in the rest of Asia does not improve soon then the situation is going to be very tough in that part of the world." 

 The Hong Kong Monetary Authority, effectively the territory's central bank, intervened heavily in stock and futures markets last month to squeeze out speculators who had attacked the Hong Kong dollar. 

 The moves prompted speculation that the territory was softening its tough free market stance in the face of financial problems across Asia.

title: Hong Kong stocks lower in quiet morning trade.
text:
HONG KONG, Sept 17 (Reuters) - Hong Kong stocks were lower on Thursday morning in quiet trade on profit-taking after a recent rally in China plays ran out of steam, brokers said. 

 The Hang Seng Index was down 132 points, or 1.69 percent, at 7,727 points. Turnover was HK$1.09 billion. 

 "Red chips and H shares are starting to correct following a strong rally earlier this month," said Ricky Tam, senior research analyst at Delta Asia Securities. 

 The Hang Seng Chinese Enterprises Index of H shares fell 13 points, or 3.36 percent, to 370 points and the red chip index lost 20 points, or 2.45 percent to 791 points. 

 "It is natural for the sectors to head for a correction since they have risen too fast too sharply," said Peter Lai, director at OCBC Securities. 

 But the Shougang group of companies were firmer ahead of their interim results due later on Thursday. 

 Shougang International  added HK$0.015, or 4.11 percent, to HK$0.38, Shougang Technology  jumped HK$0.025, or 7.81 percent, to HK$0.345 and Shougang Grand  advanced HK$0.01, or 2.38 percent, to HK$0.43.

 "This could be a sales strategy but even Cheung Kong has to sell flats at a loss. The outlook for the property market seems to be bleak," Lai said.

title: Hong Kong  Again Defends  Intervention  Aimed At Supporting  Currency
text:
NEW YORK -(Dow Jones)- Hong Kong's Financial Secretary again defended his government's unprecedented intervention in stock and currency markets last month and former governor Christopher Patten Thursday said Hong Kong remains determined to preserve the link between the Hong Kong dollar and the U.S. dollar. 

 The Hong Kong government has accused traders of improperly manipulating both its currency and stock markets in an attempt to sever the dollar link and force a devaluation of the Hong Kong dollar. 

 The deteriorating state of the global economy made Hong Kong's campaign to support its market extremely costly. Traders estimate the government spent between $12 billion and $15 billion on shares in a two week period last month. The government - through the Hong Kong Monetary Authority - used foreign-exchange reserves to buy blue-chip stocks, Hang Seng Index futures and the local currency. 

 More recently, Hong Kong introduced restrictions on certain types of currency and futures trading. Analysts believe the actions have exposed the currency market's vulnerabilities. Critics say the moves have provided speculators with exactly the kind of tactical information they need to try something new. 

 Responding to criticism from Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan, Hong Kong Financial Secretary Donald Tsang Thursday said the intervention was justified and necessary. "We were in circumstances that we believed we had absolutely no other option," Tsang said. 

 Greenspan Wednesday said Asian economies shouldn't turn their backs on open markets. He singled out the Hong Kong government's intervention for criticism. "I don't think it can succeed," Greenspan said. "The consequences of doing that erodes some of the extraordinary credibility that the Hong Kong monetary authorities have achieved over the years." the freest market in the world." 

 "We do understand that from an idealistic position of a free market, what we did is probably rather exceptional," Tsang claimed that other members of the Fed expressed support for the intervention. 

 Meanwhile, PAtten said China won't devalue its currency, because it's not in its economic interest to do so. "As far as the Chinese currency is concerned, they've got a good deal of credit, and I think that's to a certain extent justified for what they've said about not devaluing," Patten said. Patten also said he suspects that China's "dollar indebtedness is much greater than the official figures suggest, so (a devaluation) would greatly put up the cost of that," said Patten. 

 "As far as the Hong Kong dollar is concerned, the present government will be as determined as I was when we were attacked from time to time to preserve the link with the U.S. dollar, because it's the basis of Hong Kong's demonstration of financial autonomy and independence," he said. 

 China has loudly pledged it won't devalue its currency, the yuan, or the Hong Kong dollar anytime soon. Although rumors continue to make the rounds in currency and stock markets around the world that China may devalue the yuan, the People's Bank of China a few weeks ago proclaimed China won't do so. 

 Many people fear that a devalued yuan would further batter Asia's depreciated currencies, spreading the region's economic dislocation to the West. Experts say the pledge has teeth but investors and traders were burned many times in the past year as one Asian currency after another collapsed despite assurances of stability.

title: HKMA Yam/ Forex  Reserves-2:  Intervention  Didn't Deplete Much
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--The government has enough reserves to prevent stock market manipulation and still back currency in circulation, Hong Kong Monetary Authority Chief Executive Joseph Yam said Thursday. 

 Yam told legislators that Hong Kong's reserves are "ample" and weren't depleted significantly by stock and futures market intervention in August. 

 The quasi-central bank chief, however, didn't say how much the government spent on intervention and didn't release the reserve level for August. 

 Many Hong Kong market participants believe the government spent up to US$15.0 billion of its July-end US$96.5 billion in reserves to fight off speculators in the foreign exchange, stock and futures markets.

title: Institutions fuel Hong Kong's China-play rally.
text:
HONG KONG, Sept 16 (Reuters) - A return of institutional interest in China-related shares is fuelling a powerful rally in red chips and H-shares amid optimism that China's economy will pick up and interest rates will fall, market analysts said. 

 "Fund managers are buying these stocks since China's economic environment seems to have improved slightly and there are hopes that China will cut interest rates soon," said Peter So, a China analyst at Indosuez W.I. Carr Securities. 

 He said fund managers also wanted to lower their cash positions ahead of the end of the quarter. 

 The Hang Seng Chinese Enterprises Index jumped 26.85 points, or 7.53 percent, to close at 383.33 on Wednesday and the red chip Hang Seng China-Affiliated Corporations Index added 28.20 points, or 3.60 percent, to 810.90 points. 

 The H-share and red chip indices have leapt 59.5 percent and 40.2 percent each so far this month. 

 With recent trading thin, brokers said institutional buying had easily pushed up prices. The rallies were sharp partly because the China-related sector had been oversold after foreign funds cleared out their holdings earlier this year, So said. 

 The H-share index is still 50.1 percent below its 1998 high of 767.53 points and the red chip index is 56.43 percent lower than its high of 1,860.98 points this year. 

 H-shares are the shares of China-incorporated enterprises listed in Hong Kong. Red chips are Hong Kong-based companies with mainland Chinese backing. 

 "These sectors had been sold down indiscriminately and now they are being bought up indiscriminately," said Kalina Ip, head of China research at ABN Amro Asia. 

 A strengthening yen had eased fears of a depreciation of the Chinese yuan, analysts said. 

 But Andrew Fernow, director of research at Vickers Ballas, said fundamentals had not changed and that the rallies were purely due to short covering. 

 "Be careful because I think given the breadth of the rally and the momentum, it could easily subside after the short-covering is completed. There may not be as much momentum to carry these groups of stocks much higher," he said. 

 The earnings picture for the sector was still quite disturbing, said Fernow. 

 "There are a few exceptions, like the road companies and some of the food companies, which have announced satisfactory (interim) results," he added. 

 Ip said once an interest rate cut materialised, profit taking would emerge to trim gains on the stocks with poor earnings outlooks. 

 Wang Jiachun, a researcher at China's Finance Ministry, said China had few new measures left to stimulate its slowing economy in the near term with the exception of a cut in bank interest rates, the Shanghai Securities newspaper reported last Friday. 

 He did not say that an interest rate cut was imminent but rumours have circulated in Hong Kong and China's financial markets that Beijing will soon cut bank interest rates for the third time this year. 

 So said the rally could last for a while since fund managers had not seemed to have completed their buy programmes yet. 

 "Buying does not seem to have been completed yet since the cash level of foreign funds remains high after they sold large amounts of blue chips to the government during the intervention in August," he said. 

 Brokers estimate that the Hong Kong Monetary Authority spent about US$15 billion during a two-week intervention campaign in the stock and futures markets in August to foil currency speculators.

title: HK stocks end up but off highs, China plays lead.
text:
HONG KONG, Sept 15 (Reuters) - Hong Kong stocks closed moderately higher on Tuesday, encouraged by a strong performance by China-related stocks and after Wall Street kicked off the week on a strong note, brokers said. 

 The Hang Seng Index gained 71.61 points, or 0.93 percent, to finish at 7,733.47. It earlier hit a high of 7,837.96 before running into profit-taking. 

 China plays took centre stage on Tuesday, boosted by talk about a possible Chinese interest rate cut in the near future, brokers said. 

 China's increased investment in infrastructure and reconstruction plans after floods would provide fuel to stoke China's economy in the second half of 1998, one broker said. 

 The "red chip" index added 2.79 percent to 782.70 while H shares gained 5.99 percent to 356.48. 

 Ricky Tam, senior research analyst at Delta Asia Securities, said some investors may be offloading their holdings ahead of a possible sell-off of China plays if China does deliver a rate cut. 

 Brokers expected the market to remain relatively stable the rest of the week with the focus on Wall Street and U.S. President Bill Clinton's political future. 

 Investors also waited for clues from Tokyo's stock market, which was closed on Tuesday for a holiday. 

 "If some local investors already missed this train, then they don't want to buy at this moment. They want to wait for the market to come down," Tam said. 

 Tam added foreign investors were staying on the sidelines, wary after the Hong Kong government's intervention in the financial markets last month. 

 The Hang Seng Index was expected to face resistance at 8,000 with support found at 7,500, brokers said. 

 Market focus was on the next meeting of the U.S. Federal Reserve on September 29, brokers said. Percy Au-Young, sales director at DBS Securities, said a U.S. interest rate cut may trigger a rate cut in Hong Kong. 

 "I think Hong Kong is very eager to cut its interest rates," said Au-Young. 

 Interbank rates eased on Tuesday after the Hong Kong Monetary Authority said it would hold to its undertaking to convert the local currency at HK$7.75 per U.S. dollar for at least six months. 

 The benchmark three-month HIBOR rate dropped to 10.12500 percent at Tuesday's fixing against 11.89375 percent at the same time on Monday. 

 HSBC Holdings lagged, dropping HK$3.50 to HK$147.00 after hitting a year low of HK$145.50. Brokers said the share price was weighed down by worries about the banking giant's exposure to a weakening global economy. 

 "A lot of people continue to doubt about its (HSBC Holdings') evaluations, especially after seeing European banks falling in the latest round of correction," said Au-Young. 

 Au-Young believed fair value for HSBC Holdings was currently at HK$137 to HK$142. 

 Tam said worries about HSBC Holdings' exposure to Brazil added to pressure on the stock.

title: HK London stocks ease uninspired by Hang Seng, Dow.
text:
LONDON, Sept 14 (Reuters) - Hong Kong stocks in London eased in London, failing to mirror a 1.1 percent gain in the Hang Seng overnight and uninspired by advances in overseas stock markets, dealers said. 

 "We started higher in London on the back of the rise in Hong Kong, but...there was no reason to keep the sentiment up, so we drifted off," said one dealer. 

 He said investors were waiting for the next move from the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA), which has been intervening in the market to support share prices, with a dose of scepticism. 

 "What the HKMA has done of late has created more confusion than anything else," said another trader. 

 The HKMA said on Monday it would keep its guaranteed U.S. dollar conversion rate for banks at HK$7.75 to US $1 for at least six months. 

 The move was aimed at reassuring jittery forex markets, but currency dealers in Hong Kong said they were confused rather than reassured. 

 A press report quoting HKMA chief executive Joseph Yam as saying a shift in the conversion rate to HK$7.80 would happen "suddenly" and in the "short term" had sparked a wave of Hong Kong dollar selling. 

 In London, index heavyweight HSBC Holdings  fell HK$3.0 to HK$147.5 compared with its Hong Kong close. 

 The Hang Seng index gained 83.4 points to 7,661.9. The Hang Seng London reference index eased 0.7 percent to 7,604.9. 

 The September futures contract on the index traded 100 points higher at 7,480 but still at a discount to the cash market, indicating expectations of a downside trend.

title: Singapore aims to be regional observation post.
text:
SINGAPORE, Sept 14 (Reuters) - Singapore, which is sticking firmly to its pro-market stance during the Asian crisis, wants to become a base for analysts and fund managers to observe the region, a top minister said on Monday. 

 "Singapore offers itself as a base from which analysts and fund managers can follow the region dispassionately, with neither euphoria nor panic. They will be well positioned to detect the turnabout...," Deputy Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong told fund managers and investors at an investment conference here. 

 Lee, who is also head of the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), said Singapore would maintain its fundamental approach of relying on market forces, allowing free capital flows, encouraging foreign investments and plugging into the global economy to survive the regional crisis. 

 He added Singapore's "different approach" would be noted by analysts and investors and reflected in the country's credit ratings and assessments. 

 In his speech, Lee gave an outline of the approaches taken by other Asian economies battered by the crisis, among them Thailand, South Korea, Indonesia, Malaysia and Hong Kong. 

 Lee said neighbouring Malaysia's situation contrasts with that of other countries. 

 He said Malaysia, which initially followed orthodox market-oriented policies, had rejected this "orthodox prescription." 

 "In recent weeks, the Malaysian government has decisively rejected this orthodox prescription, especially after Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad dismissed Deputy Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim and took over responsibility for the economy." 

 Lee said Malaysian central bank Bank Negara's actions to impose stringent capital controls, lower interest rates and bank reserve requirements and ease classifications for non-performing loans (NPLs) were indications the governmnent was acting in line with Mahathir's convictions. 

 He said Malaysia has set out to prove to the world "that it will succeed in restoring its economy on its own, and in its own way." 

 Lee said Thailand and South Korea were two countries following the IMF prescriptions most closely but the countries' reform and restructuring process would be "gradual and painful". 

 He said Singapore and Hong Kong were traditionally the two freest markets in the region, and Hong Kong's unprecedented intervention in the market to force up share prices was a clear indication of the country's determination to defend its currency peg. 

 Lee added that apart from adhering to its free-market policies, Singapore would also cut business costs decisively and comprehensively, and carry out economic restructuring to enhance its effectiveness as a regional and international business hub. 

 (C) Reuters Limited 1998.

title: HK Dlr Seen Supported By HKMA As Banks Use Conversion Pledge
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--The Hong Kong dollar has weakened to the Hong Kong Monetary Authority's intervention level and is being supported at HK$7.75 per U.S. dollar on steady buying by the quasi-central bank early Monday, traders said. 

 "I think our government is buying at that level," said a currency dealer at a U.S. bank. 

 Traders said they detected the outflow of about US$400.0 million Monday morning from Hong Kong foreign exchange markets, as several large international investment banks began taking advantage of the HKMA's HK$7.75 per dollar conversion guarantee offered earlier this month. 

 The currency was quoted at that level at 0300 GMT (11 p.m. EDT Sunday), weaker than late Friday's HK$7.7480, and the U.S. bank's dealer said he doesn't expect it to budge, with the HKMA believed to be buying the local currency at that level, which it called its intervention level earlier this month. The HKMA didn't have an immediate comment on its activities or the reported outflow, but typically doesn't comment on what it's doing in markets. 

 The U.S. bank's dealer said he believes one U.S. investment bank is behind the outflow, selling Hong Kong dollars at HK$7.75 on the expectation that the HKMA will adjust the conversion guarantee to HK$7.80 sometime soon. 

 "I just saw one investment (bank) keep buying the outright 'TT,'" he said. 

 The bank may have been responding to an interview with HKMA Chief Executive Joseph Yam in the Hong Kong Economic Journal Monday. Yam elaborated on comments made earlier this month when he introduced measures to strengthen the Hong Kong dollar peg, saying he would move "shortly and suddenly" to change the conversion guarantee level to HK$7.80.

title: HK Dollar Stronger Late Mon -2: No Need To Move Swiftly
text:
The HKMA said it wouldn't move swiftly to change its guaranteed conversion level, fearing that would be misinterpreted as a devaluation of the local currency. 

 The quasi-central bank also noted that it won't move until the market exchange rate is "consistently at a level stronger than HK$7.75" and that it wanted to allow time for banks to remove hedge and stop-loss orders around HK$7.75. 

 Shortly after the news of the clarification hit the market, the spot Hong Kong dollar strengthened to HK$7.7470. It had been holding at HK$7.75 due to repeated HKMA local currency buying. That's well-known in markets here, as HK$7.75 is the HKMA's self-stated intervention level. 

 As pressure eased on the Hong Kong dollar, interbank interest rates fell, along with forward foreign exchange premiums. 

 The three-month premium is 1,050 points above the spot rate, down from 1,250 points earlier Monday, but still above late Friday's 800 points. The six-month premiums is at 2,200 points, down from 2,500 points earlier in the day, but up from late Friday's 2,000 points. 

 The head of treasury at a domestic bank said market calm appeared to have been restored late in Hong Kong, but that an outflow of funds may be repeated by London traders overnight. 

 He said the HKMA bought itself some time by saying it isn't moving swiftly to change the guaranteed bank conversion rate, but that speculators may already be focusing beyond the six-month period and hedging accordingly before then as they position themselves to strain the Hong Kong dollar peg. 

 He said Hong Kong dollar selling wasn't as panicked as it was two Fridays ago, when unfounded rumors of capital control measures that would be imposed on the Hong Kong dollar sparked a scramble for banks looking to cover short customer positions.

title: HKMA's Carse says ready to  intervene .
text:
WASHINGTON, Sept 11 (Reuters) - Hong Kong Monetary Authority Deputy Chief Executive David Carse said Friday the HKMA was ready to intervene in the stock and futures markets to counter any market manipulation. 

 "If we feel that the assets markets are being manipulated then we would step in," Carse told reporters in Washington. "We do not rule out future intervention." 

 The Hong Kong government began buying stocks and futures last month, saying it wanted to foil speculative attacks on the Hong Kong dollar. 

 Earlier this month the HKMA announced measures intended to strengthen the territory's linked exchange rate system and reduce interest rate volatility. The measures included specific rules for currency conversion and moves meant to bolster liquidity. 

 Carse said the intervention was not designed to "prop up" the stock and futures markets, but rather to "squeeze speculators." 

 Carse said measures to beef up Hong Kong financial markets were not a breach of Hong Kong's free market principles. "The controls are really trying to deal with market abuses which were occurring." 

 "I would hope that the follow-up measures that we've announced, in terms of tightening up on short-selling, increasing the disclosure in both the cash market and the futures market, will reduce the need for intervention in the future," Carse said after giving a speech at a conference hosted by the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation.

title: Hong Kong to maintain  currency  board - official.
text:
WASHINGTON, Sept 11 (Reuters) - Hong Kong intends to maintain its currency board system and the current link to the U.S. dollar, Hong Kong Monetary Authority Deputy Chief Executive David Carse said on Friday. 

 "Hong Kong remains determined to maintain the currency board system and the present link between the Hong Kong dollar and U.S. dollar," Carse said in a speech to a conference here. 

 Carse defended HKMA's recent intervention in the stock and futures markets, saying it was designed to counter market manipulation and speculation. 

 He said the intervention was "not designed to prop up the stock and futures market." Carse added the intervention was "not a breach of Hong Kong's free market principles." 

 Rather, he said the HKMA was demonstrating its determination to protect the currency and stability of Hong Kong's monetary system. 

 Carse said 1998 and 1999 would be tough years for Hong Kong banks because of increased bad debt and lower operating profits. 

 "However, lower profitability in itself is not a cause for concerns in terms of systemic stability because banks remain highly capitalised and liquid," Carse said. "What we are facing is a profitability issue not a solvency issue. Banks should be able to manage there way through the current difficulties." 

 Carse said problem loans have risen as a result of the regional crisis and the slowdown in the domestic economy. 

 "However, while asset quality is getting worse, it is not collapsing," he told a Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation conference.
