title: CORRECTED - Hong Kong fight against speculators fuels jingoism.
text:
In HONG KONG story headlined "Hong Kong fight against speculators fuels jingoism" please read in sixth paragraph ....On Saturday, Rebecca Lai, acting secretary for financial services, will lead the government's third appearance this week .... instead of ....Financial Secretary Donald Tsang will appear for the third time this week (correcting name). 

 A corrected story follows. 

 By Tan Ee Lyn 

 HONG KONG, Sept 11 (Reuters) - The Hong Kong government's crusade against market speculators has become a rallying cry, fuelling a sense of nationalism once rare in this former British colony, political analysts and legislators said on Friday. 

 But some warned that such "jingoism" will harm the image of this international financial powerhouse in the long run and drive investors away. 

 Government officials "are creating an impression for the general public in Hong Kong that there are speculators that are not so bad, manipulators who are really bad and these are essentially foreign devils," said legislator Christine Loh. 

 "To divide market players into good ones and bad ones, and the bad ones are from the outside is just not what we need. I mean what impression are we creating internationally?" said Loh, head of the Citizens' Party and a former commodities trader. 

 Hong Kong has locked horns in recent weeks with what it has termed "market manipulators" who are trying to profit from attacking the U.S.-pegged Hong Kong dollar. 

 On Saturday, Rebecca Lai, acting secretary for financial services, will lead the government's third appearance this week before the legislature's Financial Affairs panel to defend the government's actions, a government spokeswoman said. 

 Since mid-August, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority has spent at least HK$100 billion (US$12.9 billion) in the local stock and futures markets to foil speculators it accused of selling off the Hong Kong dollar to drive interest rates up and stock prices down to take profits on short stock positions. 

 In the past week the government has announced 37 new measures to strengthen the Hong Kong dollar's link to the U.S. dollar and make markets less susceptible to manipulation. 

 The moves, under full glare of the local media, have been hotly debated by legislators in this week's earlier sessions with Financial Secretary Donald Tsang. 

 Many politicians have used the forum to unleash wild and colourful invectives against foreign "manipulators" - not unlike the rhetoric that Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad has used for months to denounce currency speculators. 

 James Tien of the Liberal Party referred to them as "gweilos", a Cantonese term for "foreign devils", while Chan Kam-lam of the pro-China Democratic Alliance of the Betterment of Hong Kong, slammed them as "international big crocodiles." 

 Amid the name calling, Tsang, the top general in Hong Kong's market intervention campaign, has won growing support among the territory's 6.6 million people, surveys showed. 

 A poll by the University of Hong Kong on September 7 found 54.9 percent of 548 respondents agreed with the government's recent intervention in stocks and futures, up from 37.4 percent in an earlier survey conducted on September 1. 

 Tsang's approval rating scored an all-time high of 65.1 percent in the same poll. His rating stood at 58.1 percent in August 1998 and 61.3 percent in April 1997. 

 Political analyst Lau Siu-kai said the support was because of a groundswell of "anti-speculator sentiment." 

 Legislator Margaret Ng said the support given to the government was based on "financial jingoism" and warned that it could encourage the government to do whatever it chooses. 

 "The greater the support the government can count on from the jingoists, the greater will be the difficulty for Legco (Legislative Council) to act as check and balance in holding the government to its legal restraints," Ng wrote in a commentary in the South China Morning Post on Friday. 

 As an indicator of how the international community may be reacting to Hong Kong's interventionist moves, U.S. investment house Goldman Sachs on Friday said it was cutting its Hong Kong recommendation to underweight from neutral, while lifting Singapore to overweight from underweight. 

 (C) Reuters Limited 1998.

title: HKMA's Carse/Dlr Peg -2: No Breach of Free-Mkt Tradition
text:
WASHINGTON (Dow Jones)--Hong Kong regards its recent stock-market interventions not as a breach of its vaunted free-market principles but as a signal to speculators that it will defend its currency whatever the cost, a senior central bank official said Friday. 

 David Carse, deputy chief executive of the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, told a gathering of bank supervisors here that speculative attacks on the Hong Kong dollar have driven up interest rates and caused stock prices to plummet nearly 50% over the last year. 

 But the territory's central bank has no intention of abandoning its fixed exchange-rate system, among the last of its kind in East Asia. "Hong Kong remains firmly determined to maintain the currency-board system and the link between the Hong Kong dollar and the U.S. dollar, and we're prepared to accept the pain of adjustment," he said. 

 A currency-board system requires a central bank to ensure that the total of a country's currency in circulation and banking reserves always equals the amount of its foreign reserves. Under such a system, when capital flows out of the country, interest rates automatically rise. Hong Kong's interest rates used to match U.S. rates, Carse said, but are now about two percentage points higher because of the Asian financial crisis. 

 Carse said speculators have been using a "double-play" strategy to attack that system, obligating the central bank to spend an estimated $10 billion of its foreign reserves on stock-market interventions. The strategy involves selling Hong Kong dollars and shorting Hong Kong stocks. The pressure on the dollar causes interest rates to rise and causes stock prices to fall, so speculators can make money whether or not the dollar loses value. 


"That's the reason we've been intervening in the stock and futures
market," Carse said. "The objective is not to prop up stocks and
futures....The objective is to squeeze speculators." Accordingly, the
interventions are "not a breach of Hong Kong's free-market principles,
because the objective is not to support the market per se," he said.

title: Funds wary of HK stocks, wait for dust to settle.
text:
HONG KONG, Sept 9 (Reuters) - The Hong Kong government's massive intervention in the local stock market, and subsequent plans to tighten trading rules, has left fund managers wary of the market as they wait for the dust to settle. 

 "Right now there is still a lot of confusion and difficulties in terms of long-term investors positioning themselves in Hong Kong," said John Lai, chief investment officer at Nikko Global Asset Management (Hong Kong). 

 "Long-term funds will obviously wait for a while because I think a lot of them have exited the market since the government stepped in to intervene and fundamentals are departing from stock prices," he said. 

 The government is estimated to have spent some HK$100 billion (US$12.9 billion) in the stock market last month in a two-week buying spree designed to chase out speculators who had sold the Hong Kong dollar and pushed interest rates higher while shorting the stock market to profit from falling share prices. 

 Hong Kong Financial Secretary Donald Tsang followed up this week with proposals to tighten securities rules. 

 The Hang Seng Index is up 19 percent since intervention began on August 14. On Wednesday, it closed down 283.80 points, or 3.47 percent, at 7,905.45. 

 "The market remains very volatile and when you have volatility you have caution," said Philip Hampden-Smith, chief executive officer at Manulife Funds Direct (HK) Ltd. 

 "While we have seen some good numbers coming out of the performance of the market over the last two or three days, I think the problems are by no means over." 

 Hong Kong is facing its first full-year recession on record, with the government expecting the economy to shrink by about four percent this year. Unemployment is on a rising trend. 

 Interbank rates have dropped substantially since the Hong Kong Monetary Authority implemented measures on Monday to boost liquidity in the banking system and strengthen the currency board. But the trend needs to continue before any benefits are seen with prime rates coming down, analysts said. 

 "The economic fundamentals are still far from sound and Asia is going through what I consider a very sharp recession and it is going to take at least a year or two," said Terence Mahony, managing director at TCW Asia. 

 "We are underweight and if it corrects we will probably look to act but I still think cash is king at the moment." 

 Provided interest rates remained stable, the equilibrium level for the Hang Seng Index was around 6,500 to 7,000 points and a drop to lower levels could prompt some buying, Mahony said. 

 "I would definitely be a nibbler all things being equal. I think you have to look at the external factors too." 

 Stewart Aldcroft, marketing director at Templeton Franklin Investment Services (Asia), said Hong Kong was offering good value on a five-year view but more bad news for the region could lie around the corner. 

 "The economic situation in Asia continues to remain in a very volatile state with uncertainty in many different areas so by no means can I say in any way that we have yet gone through the worst of it," he said. 

 "There are lots more things that are sitting on the horizon, many of them we probably just don't know about yet, but they keep coming up. Something turns up when you are not looking." 

 While the government has claimed victory in its fight against speculators and has taken action to make financial markets more resilient to attacks, the Hong Kong dollar may be tested again, analysts said. 

 "Any news can again trigger excuses to come back and look at our currency board arrangement," said Lai. 

 "The risk premium of Hong Kong is unlikely to come down in the near term for equity investors," he said.

title: HK Dlr Stronger Midday On U.S. Dlr Short-Selling
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--The Hong Kong dollar is a touch stronger midday Wednesday as investors sell the U.S. dollar short against the local currency in moderate amounts. 

 They're doing that because while the overnight and one-week Hong Kong interbank rates are below comparable U.S. dollar rates, longer-term local currency rates are above them, making Hong Kong dollar positions more attractive, said a currency dealer at a U.S. bank. 

 The Hong Kong dollar is trading at HK$7.7490 per US$1.00 at 0350 GMT (11:50 p.m. EDT, Tuesday), compared with HK$7.7495 late Tuesday. 

 Forward foreign exchange premiums are mostly flat, with the pick-up in Hong Kong dollar buying indicating participants are feeling better about the local currency and aren't taking on new positions. Many are closing out their hedging positions as the currency strengthens. 

 The three-month forward premium is 610 points over the spot rate, scarcely changed from 600 points late Tuesday. The six-month premium is down to 1,650 points from 1,800 points. 

 While investors continue to sell short-term Hong Kong dollars to benefit from higher U.S. dollar interest rates, market participants don't intend to push the currency up to HK$7.75, a level at which the Hong Kong Monetary Authority has said it will intervene in the market to halt the U.S. dollar's rise. 

 At the same time, short-selling of U.S. dollars in longer-term money markets is providing a push in the opposite direction and should keep the Hong Kong dollar a touch stronger from Tuesday's levels. 

 "Over one week to two weeks, people like to short the (U.S.) dollar against the Hong Kong (dollar)," the dealer said.

title: HK dlr still seen vulnerable despite near-term relief.
text:
HONG KONG, Sept 8 (Reuters) - The Hong Kong Monetary Authority's package of reforms will limit market manipulation and stabilize near-term interest rates, but bankers said Tuesday the territory may remain a juicy target for speculators. 

 "The perceptions that Hong Kong is not competitive and the perceptions that Hong Kong assets are relatively overvalued are not going away because of these measures," said Stephen Yau, treasurer at ING Barings. "Speculators may still look to attack Hong Kong on this basis." 

 The measures to strengthen Hong Kong's U.S.-linked exchange rate succeeded in holding down interest rates for the second day in a row, as the three-month benchmark interbank rate closed at 8.37 percent on Tuesday versus last Friday's 11 percent close. 

 Bankers continued to digest the HKMA's sweeping seven-point plan announced on Saturday, but said it went a long way toward boosting confidence in the territory's currency board system, which pegs the Hong Kong dollar to the U.S. dollar. 

 Two of the most important reforms were the HKMA's undertaking to convert Hong Kong dollars in licensed banks' clearing accounts to U.S. dollars at a fixed exchange rate of HK$7.75 per US$1 and the conversion of its old Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF) to a discount window. 

 The convertibility undertaking shows the HKMA's firm commitment to the peg system and gives banks a guaranteed exchange rate of HK$7.75 to US$1, said Andrew Fung, treasurer of the Commonwealth Bank of Australia. 

 "They're fully committed to the 7.75 figure," Fung said. "Speculators can't spread any rumors on the peg anymore." 

 The guaranteed rate also creates an arbitrage opportunity for banks should the Hong Kong dollar come under heavy selling pressure that weakens the market exchange rate. Since banks can always sell their Hong Kong dollars at the end of the day to the HKMA at HK$7.75 to US$1, this will encourage them to buy Hong Kong dollars in the market, helping to stabilize rates. 

 "Under these new measures, we don't have to be reliant on interest rate arbitrage to bring the exchange rate close to the official level," said Roger Luk, deputy chief executive of Hong Kong's Hang Seng Bank. "You can use the exchange rate itself." 

 But the downside of the more direct arbitrage is that the HKMA, Hong Kong's de facto central bank, may have to use more of its US$96.5 billion in foreign currency reserves to defend the local dollar, said Yau of ING Barings. 

 The new discount window will improve interbank liquidity because it does not have the same restrictions on repeated borrowings as the LAF did. Those restrictions discouraged banks from using the LAF, leading to interest rate spikes during periods of heavy selling of Hong Kong dollars. 

 HKMA officials argued that the moves make the currency board less vulnerable to speculative attacks because it is more difficult for speculators to affect interest rates, and hence the stock market by selling Hong Kong dollars. 

 The Hong Kong government launched a massive intervention in the local stock and futures markets in mid-August, aiming to foil speculators it said were attacking the local currency to drive interest rates up and stock prices down to profit from short stock positions. 

 "These measures make the speculator's life very difficult and it's very good for short term sentiment" said Commonwealth's Fung. "I dont' think specultors can succeed in the short term. In the long term, I don't know." 

 Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index has gained 12 percent over the last three trading days, advancing 112.49 points or 1.39 percent on Tuesday to close at 8,189.25 on the eased local interbank rates. 

 Hong Kong's slumping economy, Asia's continuing financial turmoil and other external factors will continue to put pressure on the currency board system, bankers said, until an economic recovery or a change in sentiment takes hold. 

 "Economic adjustment will still go on," Hang Seng's Luk said. "These measures will ensure we have more stable interest rates and narrower spreads, and that will make the adjustment easier."

title: AWSJ: HK Battles Speculators; Patten Plays Down  Intervention
text:
From Tuesday's Asian Wall Street Journal 

 By G. Bruce Knecht and Erik Guyot 

 HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--The government appears to have gained ground, at least temporarily, in its war against speculators accused of assailing the stability of local financial markets. 

 During the weekend, officials proposed several rule changes intended to make it more difficult to pressure Hong Kong's currency, stock and futures markets. Monday, as Financial Secretary Donald Tsang made his first appearance before legislators since the government's unprecedented intervention last month into the Hong Kong stock market, share prices surged. The Hang Seng Index rose 7.9% to close at 8076.76. 

 Chris Patten, the last British governor of Hong Kong, disagreed with those who claim intervention will do lasting damage to the city's reputation as a financial center. "I don't think it changes, or should change, investors' fundamental view of Hong Kong," he said by telephone in his first comments on the local economy since Britain's colonial rule ended July 1, 1997. Intervention "clearly represents a departure from the previous approach," Patten said. But he added: "Presumably the Hong Kong Monetary Authority knew this would have an impact on Hong Kong's reputation" and took that impact into consideration. 

 Patten did join the chorus criticizing the government's refusal to disclose the amount of shares it accumulated during the intervention. "Everywhere in Asia the crisis has demonstrated the need for increased transparency and more openness in economic affairs," he said. 

 The government bought shares in all 33 companies making up the Hang Seng Index, and HSBC Holdings PLC last week disclosed that Hong Kong owns 8.9% of its shares. The government says it is exempt from a local rule requiring disclosure of such holdings. "If we disclose the amount now it will only help others, not ourselves," Secretary Tsang said. 

 Patten disagreed: "It's plainly a central feature of the rule of law that everyone is subject to it." 

 Tsang also described the rule changes intended to moderate swings in interbank and other short-term interest rates by increasing liquidity in the banking system. 

 The government's moves are aimed at preventing speculators from making what officials call a "double play," in which they reap big profits by simultaneously attacking the Hong Kong dollar and selling short Hong Kong shares or futures contracts. Under Hong Kong's currency system, attacks on the Hong Kong dollar automatically push up interest rates, which slam corporate profits and share prices. In a short sale, an investor borrows stock and then sells it in the expectation that the price will fall, enabling him to buy it back more cheaply before returning it to the lender. 

 Joseph Yam, chief executive of the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, said that as a result of the new measures, speculators "would need to sell quite a lot more (Hong Kong dollars) to make interest rates go up." 

 Such mechanisms might make it harder for speculators to profit by reducing market volatility, but they don't necessarily address a more fundamental problem: the lack of confidence in the Hong Kong dollar's peg to the U.S. dollar, which has helped create a crippling credit crunch and aggravated the city's worst recession in 30 years. Tsang said the government remains committed to the 15-year-old peg that fixes the value of the Hong Kong dollar at 7.8 to the U.S. dollar. The government won't impose the kind of currency controls that were implemented by Malaysia last week, he added.

title: HK says  intervention  sparked by worst crisis since '83.
text:
HONG KONG, Sept 7 (Reuters) - Speculative attacks on the Hong Kong dollar emerged just before the government launched its massive stock market intervention last month, officials said on Monday. 

 "We knew in the second week or rather first week of August that we are dealing with a very serious crisis, almost in line with the situation we saw in October 1983, when we went into the linked exchange rate," Financial Secretary Donald Tsang told reporters at a briefing, referring to the introduction of the Hong Kong dollars' peg against the U.S. dollar. 

 The briefing following the administration's presentation to the Financial Affairs Panel of the Legislative Council on its unprecedented intervention in the stock market. 

 The financial secretary refused to tell legislators or reporters the total amount the administration spent in buying stock and index futures, but market estimates put it at more than HK$100 billion. 

 Legislative councillors will continue their review into the administration's actions on Tuesday. 

 Hong Kong pegged its currency to the dollar at a rate of HK$7.80 to the dollar in October 1983, when the pace of the local currency's year-long decline quickened and sent it plunging past the rate of nine to one. 

 Speculation against the Hong Kong dollar had been seen in the wake of adjustments in Asian currencies in 1997 and early 1998, but never on this scale, Tsang said. 

 "What we saw in the middle or early part of August was vastly different from what we had in the previous few occasions," Tsang said. 

 "There was hardly any coordination of activities during the attack of last October," Tsang said. At that time the Hang Seng Index declined sharply and activity in the Hong Kong dollar forwards market increased. 

 Interbank interest rates spiked higher briefly, but were returned to relatively normal levels with an injection of liquidity from the central bank. 

 The Hang Seng Index was still trading above the 10,000, and turnover was in the region of HK$30 billion, Tsang said, adding turnover in Hang Seng Index futures was roughly 60,000 to 70,000 contracts. 

 "The market was pretty large for currency raiders to do a double act. It was a lot more difficult." 

 The double act consists of shorting the Hong Kong dollar forcing interest rates higher while holding short positions in the stock and futures markets. 

 A build-up in open Hang Seng Index futures positions is the most obvious sign of growing bearishness on the stock market or currency or both. 

 Another attack on the currency was seen in January this year, Tsang said. But market conditions were similar to those in October and the market regained some, albeit weak, equilibrium. 

 "But what we saw in august - the Hang Seng Index had fallen to 6,600, turnover was HK$4 to HK$5.0 billion, but what was most worrying was the open interest in Hang Seng Futures had risen to 111,000. In fact, there was a jump of 10,000 within three trading days," Tsang said. 

 A pattern of speculation against the currency was seen, he said. 

 "There was a very deliberate and very calculated act which attacked us in the New York market, followed through with Sydney, then Hong Kong, then followed up in London," Tsang said. 

 "The pattern was the same day in day out." 

 In addition, the volume of Hong Kong dollars "dumped" was a much greater quantity than Hong Kong authorities had seen before. 

 Other shaky global markets, including Russia and markets in Latin America, were also adding fuel to the speculative fire. 

 "So everything put together we knew that something serious was going to happen if we sat on our hands," Tsang said. 

 On August 27, total turnover on the Hong Kong stock market rose to HK$22.97 billion and on August 28 to a record-shattering HK$79.0 billion, a very large portion of which is attributed to the government buying. 

 "It has been a very difficult decision for us and we did not want to do it and we will not want to do it again," Tsang said.

title: HK lawmakers angry at government over  intervention .
text:
HONG KONG, Sept 7 (Reuters) - Hong Kong legislators lashed out at the government on Monday for a lack of transparency and the billions of dollars spent in recent weeks in defence of the local currency's linked exchange rate. 

 At a two-hour meeting with Financial Secretary Donald Tsang, lawmakers kept up a vitriolic campaign, pressing him to disclose the amount spent and names of speculators whom the government has said were trying to drive down the Hong Kong dollar. 

 The confrontation came after the government intervened in stock and futures markets last month to foil speculators, who it said had attacked the Hong Kong dollar to drive interest rates up and stock prices down to take profits on short stock positions. Experts have estimated the government has bought more than HK$100 billion (US$12.9 billion) worth of blue chip stocks to prop up the Hang Seng index with the aim of squeezing many short sellers into covering their positions at higher costs. 

 The intervention, and particularly the amount spent, has become highly politicised during the current economic downturn and many legislators used Monday's forum to unleash their anger. 

 "You have not consulted us, you have spent billions of dollars and you won't even tell us how much you spent!" said feisty legislator Emily Lau, who heads the The Frontier party. 

 "Tell us, what if the speculators don't leave? Why on earth have we spent all that money? Have we achieved our aim? Do you think you are accounting for your actions by just saying a few words to reporters? I think it is just ludicrous," she said. 

 While the confrontation was peppered with fiery accusations and sarcasm, Tsang, in a grey suit and trademark bow-tie, kept an inscrutable expression. 

 "I thank legislator Lau for her lecture," Tsang said, drawing uproarious laughter from the chamber. 

 "But I hope legislators will be patient. When speculators leave, I will give a fuller account. If we disclose the amount now, it'll only benefit others, not ourselves," Tsang said. 

 Li Wah-ming of the popular Democratic Party pressed: "Who are these people (speculators), I'd love to know. Is it (George) Soros? Which hedge fund? We should come out in the open." 

 Tsang said: "If you want definite evidence, we won't know." He said deep-pocketed and organised speculators had been trying to attack the Hong Kong dollar in different ways, at many centres and under various fronts. 

 Cyd Ho of The Frontier party questioned if the intervention might open the way for a conflict of interest for government officials, Kong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) employees and other people whom the government might have consulted. 

 But Tsang said there were clear rules regarding business interests and matters of conflict of interest governing all civil servants and HKMA colleagues. 

 Only a few legislators were able to put questions during the meeting. The meeting is to continue on Tuesday. 

 (US$1 = HK$7.75).

title: HK govt acts to stabilise markets, hurts reputation.
text:
HONG KONG, Sept 7 (Reuters) - Hong Kong's reputation as a free market is set to take a hit by government moves to tighten securities regulations, but the stability provided by the measures is welcome after recent turbulence, analysts said. 

 "Markets should probably be left to operate on a free basis. However the problem with Hong Kong is that it is open to manipulation and in this environment speculators can have a real effect on the real economy," said Jolyon Petch, head of Hong Kong research at ING Barings. 

 "It is probably negative but in this current environment, with crisis going on all around the world, the provision of stability is probably much more important than worrying about the perception of Hong Kong as a market," he said. 

 The Hong Kong government announced plans on Monday to beef up regulations in the stock and futures markets and possibly strengthen the Chief Executive's authority over those exchanges, in a bid to reduce opportunities to manipulate those markets. 

 The move came after the Hong Kong Monetary Authority intervened heavily in the stock and futures market last month to squeeze out speculators who had attacked the Hong Kong dollar and pushed interest rates higher while holding short positions in stocks and futures to benefit from falling share prices. 

 The government proposed strict rules on short-selling, including plans to criminalise unreported short-selling. It called for more transparency in the futures market and changes to Hong Kong's clearing rules to ensure timely settlement. 

 "They are going to be fiddly and picky. That is going to do nothing to enhance our reputation," said Steven Thompson, chief analyst at Nikko Research Center. 

 "It is quite clear that the stock exchange should be a separate entity to the government." 

 But some analysts said there were rule enforcement problems in Hong Kong. Howard Gorges, a director at South China Brokerage, said regulations had been particularly lax in the areas of short-selling and futures trading. 

 "It was too free. There were too many loopholes. This is not a big enough market to be totally free," he said. 

 "If people like to short sell, then they are not going to like it. But long-term portfolio investors will probably welcome measures which increase stability and reduce manipulation." 

 Analysts said government comments about increasing the Chief Executive's authority in financial markets were vague. "It might be necessary to strengthen the power of the Chief Executive to give direction to the exchanges and clearing houses to ensure that the government can react quickly whenever public interests are under threat," the government said in a statement. 

 "In times of emergency I guess you can do whatever it takes," said Frederick Tsang, a director at DBS Securities. 

 But he said it was important for the government to leave securities bodies to operate independently. "It would be OK if the government retreated from the market and then asked the stock exchange bodies to review the rules and regulations." 

 "The impression is not so good. Things are getting complicated," Tsang added. 

 The Hang Seng Index soared 588.29 points, or 7.86 percent, to close at 8,076.76 on Monday, boosted mainly by measures announced by the HKMA over the weekend to improve liquidity in the banking system and make Hong Kong's currency board system less susceptible to manipulation. 

 "There is improved liquidity in the system and improved transparency," said Andrew Look, regional director at Prudential Portfolio Managers (Asia). 

 "But one flaw, if you have to pick on the government, is that they should have done this before they intervened in the market because if you have proper rules and regulations you probably do not intervene in the first place and ruin the good reputation of Hong Kong being a non-interventionist government."

title: HK to detail shareholdings when market stabilises.
text:
HONG KONG, Sept 7 (Reuters) - Hong Kong Financial Secretary Donald Tsang said on Monday the government would give a full account of its shareholdings accumulated during recent stock market intervention when speculators had left the market. 

 The government would set up a company under the Hong Kong Monetary Authority which would manage the Hong Kong shareholdings and avoid situations of conflict of interest, Tsang told the Financial Affairs panel of the Legislative Council. 

 The Hong Kong government began intervening in the stock market on August 14 to chase out speculators who had engaged in a double play of attacking the Hong Kong dollar and pushing interest rates higher while holding short positions in the stock market to benefit from falling share prices. 

 Tsang said the Hong Kong Monetary Authority had not been in the market since August 28. 

 "The stocks that we purchased during this period of time are very good investments. We will retreat from the market in an orderly manner after those speculators have left the market," Tsang said. 

 "We will fully report the stocks we hold to the Hong Kong people and we are also prepared to establish a company under the HKMA to manage these investments and try to avoid conflicts of interest." 

 Tsang said the professional management company would be created under the Exchange Fund as soon as possible. 

 Civil servants and HKMA employees were governed by strict rules, he told the Legislative Council meeting. 

 "There are clear rules regarding business interests and matters of conflict of interest governing all civil servants and HKMA colleagues." 

 Tsang said he was personally taking responsbility for the government's intervention. "We feel that if we did not go into the market, the result would have been unimaginable." 

 "According to professional estimates, in view of the current low turnover in the stock market, plus the pressure on Hang Seng Index futures, if the situation had continued the Hang Seng Index would have dropped 2,000 to 3,000 points in a very short period of time." 

 Tsang declined to disclose the amount the government had spent in the stock and futures markets. 

 "I hope legislators will be patient. When speculators leave I will give a fuller account... If we disclose the amount now it will only help others, not ourselves," he said. 

 The government would not support the market but could not rule out the need for future intervention, he said. 

 But Tsang added that he hoped measures detailed over the weekend to strengthen the currency board, as well as proposals announced on Monday to prevent manipulation in the stock and futures markets, would mean that future intervention could be avoided. 

 "We hope that the Hong Kong government will not need to enter this kind of commercial market again," said Tsang.

title: WEEKAHEAD - HK markets seen wary after peg measures.
text:
HONG KONG, Sept 6 (Reuters) - Hong Kong financial markets will focus this week on steps by authorities to bolster the currency peg, action analysts said may help stabilise interest rates but could also create more uncertainty. 

 "It's evidence of further uncertainty and a lack of confidence in the peg mechanism," said Andrew Ballingal, a strategist at Schroders Asia. 

 The weekend moves by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) to bolster the local dollar's link to the U.S. dollar follows recent government intervention in stocks and futures aimed at fending off speculators. 

 "(HKMA chief) Joseph Yam should listen to what Milton Friedman has to say," Ballingal said. 

 Friedman, an economist famous for his free-market, anti-government intervention theories, told the Asian Wall Street Journal on Thursday that the Hong Kong government's huge intervention in the stock market undermined the credibility of its currency system. 

 Others agreed. 

 "I believe what the government is trying to do is pursue the Singaporean model, more than anything else. We believe it is a negative thing," said one analyst who asked not to be named. 

 On Saturday the HKMA announced new measures to strengthen the territory's linked exchange rate system and reduce interest rate volatility. 

 The measures, which officials described as purification of Hong Kong's 15 year-old currency board system, included new rules for currency conversion and moves meant to bolster liquidity. 

 Analysts said that in the short term, the market expected lower interest rates. But despite the likely benefits of potentially lower interest rates to the stock market, the main issue was perception, they said. 

 "Like anything to do with markets, it's something that requires confidence, the actions of the authorities bely that," Ballingal said. 

 "It's sentiment driven, if this does not work, or if the (interest rate) volatility does not change, you will see a problem," he said. 

 Fears linger that the government may still intervene and Hong Kong's blue chips are expected to be rangebound this coming week, particularly after the futures and stock exchanges tightened regulations last week. 

 Alex Tang, research director at Core Pacific - Yamaichi International (HK), said as speculators gradually retreated from the Hong Kong market, trading could steady. 

 "Speculators are moving out from the market since they know that it is difficult to win the game as the government changes its goalposts frequently," he said. 

 The Hong Kong Futures Exchange last week imposed a special margin surcharge on Hang Seng Index futures and options positions exceeding 10,000 contracts and tightened reporting rules requiring members to disclose positions of 250 contracts instead of 500 previously. 

 It said it would also ask members to identify the holders of large positions. 

 The Hong Kong Stock Exchange also took steps last week, announcing that it would reinstate the tick rule from Monday, banning short sales of shares below the best current ask price. 

 Analysts said the moves were part of the government's efforts to enhance Hong Kong's resilience to speculative attacks, after stock market intervention in which the government is estimated to have spent some HK$120 billion (US$15 billion). 

 But the moves could reduce trading interest, analysts said. 

 "The point is why should anybody come in right now? They can't hedge their positions." said Peter Churchouse, managing director at Morgan Stanley Dean Witter Asia. 

 The blue chip index surged 169.88 points, or 2.32 percent, to close at 7,488.47 on Friday but fell 341.27 points, or 4.35 percent, over the week. 

 September index futures jumped 210 points, to close at 7,170 points on Friday, a 318 point discount to the spot index. 

 Tang said he expected the Hang Seng index to see some resistance at 7,500 to 7,800 points. "The government has a number of short positions in September futures and they will buy back futures to support the market above 7,000," he said. 

 Left to its own devices the Hang Seng Index would fall below 6,000 points over the next few weeks, said Churchouse. 

 But analysts said China plays could be the focus of trading next week following a strong rebound in H-shares and red chips on Friday as a firming yen eased pressures on the Chinese yuan. 

 The H-share index jumped 35.59 points, or 13.35 percent to 302.21 on Friday and the red chip index rose 88.88 points, or 14.95 percent, to close at 683.55. ($HK$7.75)

title: HK Legislator Criticizes Govt Financial  Interventions
text:
HONG KONG (AP)--Government intervention to prop up share prices has damaged the territory's reputation as a free-market financial center, a legislator said Sunday. 

 Independent lawmaker Emily Lau said on Radio Hong Kong that the stakes in the government intervention stretch far beyond the stock market. 

 "With financial turmoil sweeping around the world, the Hong Kong dollar is seen as one of the vulnerable candidates for the next collapse," she said. 

 Last month, the government spent 15% of its $96 billion foreign reserves on a two-week stock buying spree to lift share prices to levels where speculators suffered heavy losses. 

 The Hong Kong Monetary Authority also announced steps on Saturday to strengthen the territory's 15-year-old currency peg to the U.S. dollar. 

 Lau said the battle for the Hong Kong dollar is a "political test as well as a financial crisis." 

 She warned that as market volatility continues and the people find that little has been achieved by the intervention, they may become "restive and even angry." 

 "Loss of public confidence would endanger the currency peg to the U.S. dollar, which is the linchpin of our financial system," she added. 

 Speculators have played on the currency peg's connection to local interest rates to drive rates higher and share prices lower, in an attempt to weaken the peg, which is set at 7.80 to the U.S. dollar.

title: Hong Kong moves to stabilise rates, say analysts.
text:
HONG KONG, Sept 5 (Reuters) - Policies that the Hong Kong Monetary Authority announced on Saturday would make interest rates less volatile by allowing much greater liquidity in the banking system, analysts said. 

 "It means that interest rates in Hong Kong will be a lot less volatile...," said Stuart Gulliver, Treasurer at Hongkong Bank. 

 "They are very positive measures for Hong Kong, very positive for the stability of interest rates," Gulliver said. 

 The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) on Saturday announced seven measures it said would strengthen the system under which the Hong Kong dollar is pegged to the U.S. dollar. 

 The measures would reduce interest-rate volatility and make Hong Kong's currency board arrangements less susceptible to manipulation by speculators, HKMA chief executive Joseph Yam told reporters. 

 "These measures aim at strengthening Hong Kong's currency board arrangements and achieving an even higher degree of transparency and disclosure," he said. 

 According to a senior analyst, the authorities had identified market structures which were allowing interest rates to be squeezed higher and were addressing those points. 

 "What they seem to have done is taken a series of measures to ensure a low interest rate environment," the analyst said. 

 Interbank interest rates soared to 300 percent briefly last October at the height of a speculative attack. They have come off sharply since then, but remain at punishingly high levels. 

 At 0330 GMT on Friday, the benchmark three-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates was 10.75 percent. 

 Gulliver said the new measures could widen the aggregate balance in Hong Kong's banking system from its current pool of about HK$2 billion to potentially over HK$40 billion. 

 In the past few weeks the aggregate balance has been HK$1.87 billion, which bankers say is tight. 

 Gulliver said the small size of that pool had made it relatively easy for market players to manipulate Hong Kong's interest rates. 

 Under the currency board system, sales of Hong Kong dollars for foreign currency automatically drain that pool of money and, thereby, push up interest rates - and usually cause a fall in the stock market. 

 Under the new system, the aggregate balance is increased to a potential HK$40 billion, making it harder to dent Hong Kong's liquidity and therefore harder to force interest rates up. 

 "The danger of it is, clearly someone could build up a short position of HK$40 billion," Gulliver said. 

 But he said that disclosure measures would ensure that those holding steep positions were known. 

 The moves effectively set a base rate which forms a cap for the overnight rate, the senior analyst said. 

 "In the short term, there is an expectation of lower interest rates," he said. 

 "Anyone who has sold Hong Kong dollars in the forward markets will want to buy that in. It will bring liquidity back into the market," he said. 

 Speculative pressure on the Hong Kong dollar sparked massive, unprecedented government intervention in the stock and futures markets in the past month. 

 The Hong Kong government is estimated to have spent about HK$120 billion (US$15 billion) on shares last month to boost prices and squeeze out short sellers. 

 Gulliver said the HKMA had consulted the International Monetary Fund before implementing these measures. It had also been advised by the Bank of England.

title: FOCUS-HKMA unveils moves to strengthen HK dlr peg.
text:
HONG KONG, Sept 5 (Reuters) - The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) on Saturday unveiled a series of new measures to strengthen the territory's linked exchange rate system and reduce interest rate volatility. 

 The measures, which officials described as a purification of Hong Kong's currency board system, included new rules for currency conversion and moves meant to bolster liquidity. 

 "These measures aim at strengthening Hong Kong's currency board arrangements and achieving an even higher degree of transparency and disclosure," HKMA chief executive Joseph Yam told a news conference. 

 The measures would make Hong Kong's 15-year-old currency board system, which pegs the Hong Kong dollar to the U.S. dollar, less susceptible to manipulation and could reduce the need for government stock market intervention, he said. 

 The Hong Kong government intervened heavily in the stock and futures markets in August to foil speculators who had attacked the Hong Kong dollar with the aim of driving interest rates up and stock prices down to take profits on short stock positions. 

 As part of its new measures, the HKMA replaced its Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF) with a discount window with a single Base Rate rather than a bid-offer spread used under the LAF, reducing the authority's discretion to affect rates. 

 The HKMA removed most restrictions on repeated borrowings from the discount window. 

 The restrictions were put in place last year to make it more difficult for speculators to fund attacks on the Hong Kong dollar but had the unwanted effect of squeezing liquidity as banks avoided the LAF for fear of being penalised. 

 The HKMA said no new issues of paper other than government Exchange Fund bills and notes backed by foreign reserves would be accepted as collateral at the discount window. Currently, some other highly rated debt securities are eligible. 

 Allowing freer access to day-end liquidity through the use of the Exchange Fund paper fully backed by foreign reserves would dampen interest rate volatility without departing from the discipline of the currency board arrangement, the HKMA said. 

 To that end, the authority said it would issue new Exchange Fund paper only when there was an inflow of of funds, assuring that all new paper would be fully backed by foreign reserves. 

 Yam said the measures would make it much more difficult for speculators to attack the Hong Kong dollar. 

 Liquidity as represented by the aggregate balance in the banking system currently is less than HK$2 billion, making it easy for speculators to boost interest rates with small outlays. 

 With some HK$96 billion of Exchange Fund paper outstanding, liquidity is potentially much greater, Yam said. 

 "Speculators would probably need to short about HK$30 billion before interest rates go sharply higher, sending the stock market down," he said. 

 The HKMA will publish a Base Rate every day starting from Monday. The rate would be market sensitive, but the methodology for determining the rate still needed to be honed, Yam said. 

 He suggested an average of the overnight and one-month Hong Kong interbank rates might be used as a reference initially. 

 The authority said it stood ready to convert Hong Kong dollars in the clearing accounts of licensed banks into U.S. dollars at a fixed exchange rate of HK$7.75 per dollar. 

 The move "purified" the system because by currency board rules, aggregate balances as one of the liabilities of the currency board should be transferable into U.S. dollars. 

 "The rules of the currency board say that you have to convert your liabilities into U.S. dollars," Yam said. 

 The authority chose 7.75, rather than the peg rate of 7.78, because it was closer to the current market level and has been an intervention point for the HKMA. 

 The Hong Kong dollar was linked to the U.S. dollar at a rate of HK$7.8 per US$1 in 1983. It is permitted to trade in a narrow band around that level and typically trades on the strong side. 

 "If all of a sudden when the market rate is near 7.75, you remove that support to 7.78, then all these stop losses will be triggered and there will be volatility," said Yam. 

 The HKMA intended to change its convertibility undertaking to 7.80 when the spot rate strengthened, he said.

title: FOCUS - Hong Kong beefs up  currency  board system.
text:
HONG KONG, Sept 5 (Reuters) - The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) on Saturday announced measures intended to strengthen the territory's linked exchange rate system and reduce interest rate volatility. 

 The measures, which officials described as a "purification," of Hong Kong's currency board system, included specific rules for currency conversion and moves meant to bolster liquidity. 

 HKMA chief executive Joseph Yam told a news conference that the measures would make Hong Kong's currency board arrangements less susceptible to manipulation by speculators. 

 "These measures aim at strengthening Hong Kong's currency board arrangements and achieving an even higher degree of transparency and disclosure," Yam said. 

 "They will enhance the robustness of Hong Kong's monetary arangement, characterised by the linked exchange rate system." he added. "They should also help to reduce excessive volatility in interest rates." 

 Hong Kong has pegged its currency to the U.S. dollar at a rate of US$7.8 to per U.S. dollar since 1983. Last month, the Hong Kong government began a market intervention aimed at foiling speculators it accused of pressuring the local dollar to push up interest rates, drive down stock prices and profit from short positions in stocks and futures. 

 In one of the most important measures, the HKMA said it would provide a clear undertaking to all licensed banks in Hong Kong to convert Hong Kong dollars in their clearing accounts into U.S. dollars at the fixed exchange rate of HK$7.75 per U.S. dollar. 

 The move makes explicit the HKMA's persistent intervention in the money markets at that rate and was meant to clearly demonstrate the authority's commitment to the peg system. 

 The HKMA added that the government remained fully commited to the linked exchange rate system and "strongly reiterates that there will be no foreign exchange controls" in Hong Kong. 

 In addition to the seven measures, the HKMA said it would work toward producing an Exchange Fund balance sheet showing currency board operations and have this published as frequently as is technically feasible. 

 The HKMA said its intention was to move the convertibility rate to HK$7.80 when market circumstances permit. Adopting that rate now would cause market volatility because the local dollar has been trading around HK$7.75 for some time. 

 The authority also replaced its Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF) with a discount window with a base rate to be determined from time to time by the HKMA. 

 Major Hong Kong banks reacted positively to the announcements, saying they would reduce financial market volatility. 

 "These are sensible measure which strengthen the Currency Board arrangements in Hong Kong and should have a stabilising effect on the foreign exchange and money markets, said Mervyn Davies, a group executive director for Standard Chartered Bank. 

 (C) Reuters Limited 1998.

title: HKMA to hold news conference at 0315 GMT.
text:
HONG KONG, Sept 5 (Reuters) - The Hong Kong Monetary Authority announced it would hold a news conference chaired by its chief executive Joseph Yam at 11:15 a.m (0315 GMT) on Saturday, following a meeting with banks. 

 "The press conference will address the strengthening of currency board arrangements in Hong Kong," an HKMA spokeswoman said. "The press conference will take place after the HKMA meets with banks." 

 The HKMA has invited banks to a Saturday morning meeting in Hong Kong to discuss "recent market developments," an HKMA spokesman in New York said on Friday. 

 He ruled out the possibility of foreign exchange controls. The Hong Kong government is estimated to have spent about HK$120 billion (US$15 billion) last month as it boosted share prices to squeeze out short sellers. 

 The government intervention, which officials have argued was aimed at protecting the Hong Kong dollar, sent shock waves around the world. 

 The Financial Affairs panel of the Legislative Council is due to meet on Monday to question the government about recent massive intervention in the stock and futures markets. The government has said it will use the occasion to detail how it plans to make those markets less vulnerable to manipulation.

title: HKMA/7 Steps -3:Cites "Worst Fincl Turmoil" In Asia History
text:
Banks will be allowed greater access to the revamped discount window, and the overnight bid rate, currently set at 4.00%, will be removed in favor of a multi-tiered discount rate, the HKMA said. The discount rate will be set daily. 

 In addition, all Hong Kong Exchange Fund bills and notes will be fully backed by reserves, to insure that they do not alter the total HK dollar money supply. 

 The HKMA uses the bills and notes to adjust liquidity in local money markets. 

 The quasi-central bank said it reserves the right to continue to intervene in Hong Kong's money markets, but added that the intervention would be "to dampen extreme conditions" in the market. 

 A HKMA official said the steps are necessary in the face of "the worst financial turmoil in the history of Asia." 

 They were created by an HKMA sub-committee on currency board operations chaired by Chief Executive Joseph Yam and including other HKMA officials, bankers and academics. 

 Banks were warned again Saturday against market manipulation. The HKMA has said in the past that banks which support speculative activities in Hong Kong's currency risk sanctions. 

 But the HKMA also responded to criticism of its own activities, saying that it will increase transparency by releasing more frequent updates on the balance of its foreign exchange reserves.

title: Hong Kong poised to review financial market rules.
text:
HONG KONG, Sept 4 (Reuters) - Measures to beef up Hong Kong financial markets, prevent excessive speculation in stocks and futures and protect the local dollar will top the agenda at a meeting between the administration and legislators on Monday. 

 Financial Secretary Donald Tsang will face legislators at the meeting of the legislature's Financial Affairs Panel, an aide to panel chairman Ambrose Lau said on Friday. 

 "There are three items on the agenda. Government intervention, the SFC (Securities and Futures Commission) report and insider dealing," the aide said. 

 Legislators have said they would question Tsang over the government's recent huge intervention in the stock market and criticise the government's use of an estimated HK$100 billion or more of its foreign exchanges reserves. 

 Tsang was widely expected to use the session to propose new measures to safeguard the health of Hong Kong financial markets and limit excessive speculation. 

 The government intervention, which officials have argued was aimed at protecting the Hong Kong dollar, sent shockwaves around the world and caused deep concern in Hong Kong. 

 Analysts said the administration would need legislators' support in possible rule changes concerning the Hong Kong dollar forwards market, strengthening of the currency board, circuit breakers for the stock and futures markets and closer monitoring of Hang Seng Index futures trade. 

 However, experts warned against overly draconian measures, especially those governing short selling. 

 "It will just drive the business offshore anyway," executive director Nicholas Clement-Jones at SBC Warburg Dillon Read said. 

 Short selling of Hong Kong listed stocks was not permitted until 1993, but was often done outside Hong Kong or over-the-counter. 

 "I don't think that we need a radical overhaul of the way this town does business and the regulatory regime under which that business is conducted," Clement-Jones said. 

 The Stock Exchange of Hong Kong and the Hong Kong Futures Exchange said on Friday they were not aware of the content of the government's Monday presentation and had not been asked by the government to make changes to any of their rules. 

 Both exchanges have made small but important changes since trading on August 27 and 28 when huge government intervention in the stock and futures markets raised turnover on the stock exchange to HK$22.97 billion and a record HK$79.00 billion respectively. 

 Last Saturday, the futures exchange announced increases in the cost of holding large open positions in Hang Seng Index futures, a favourite investment instrument of hedge funds. 

 It imposed a special margin surcharge of 150 percent on all Hang Seng Index futures and options positions exceeding 10,000 contracts from the close of trading on Tuesday, September 1. 

 The stock exchange council on Wednesday said it would reinstate the uptick rule on short selling and require short sales to be made at the best current ask price. 

 While the battle has been expressly aimed at protecting the Hong Kong dollar, it has sparked heated rows in Hong Kong. 

 Hong Kong Monetary Authority chief executive Joseph Yam has criticised the Hongkong Securities Clearing Co Ltd for extending a grace period to brokers who could not settle trades transacted on Thursday and Friday, some of whom were suspected to have been involved in illegal short selling. 

 By giving the grace period, the clearing house was seen in some quarters as having scuppered the authority's aim to hurt speculators by forcing them to pay the highest market prices or high borrowing rates for stock lending. 

 The clearing company said it regularly allowed a grace period of one and sometimes two days to brokers and international funds who were unable to retrieve stock from the depth of a custodian banks' vaults in the permitted two days after a transaction. 

 (C) Reuters Limited 1998.

title: Moody's Says It May Lower Debt Ratings For China, Hong Kong
text:
NEW YORK -(Dow Jones)- Moody's Investors Service Inc. Friday said it is reviewing for a possible downgrade its credit ratings on the foreign debt of China and Hong Kong, citing doubts about recent efforts to prop up the value of their currencies and economic weakness in general. 

 Moody's said China's single-A-1 long-term debt rating and the Baa-2 rating for the country's four state-owned banks are at risk of a downgrade. Single-A-1 in Moody's system is middle investment grade, while Baa-2 is two notches above "junk" status. 

 "Today's action was prompted by mounting pressures on China's external position from export weakness and declining foreign direct investment, both of which are important sources of economic growth in China," Moody's said. 

 Moody's said it will consider how much support the banks enjoy from the government. Earlier this week, Moody's cut ratings on China's big state-owned investment companies because it sees less support from the government. 

 The agency is also looking at Hong Kong's long-term single-A-1 rating, citing Hong Kong's status as part of China and trade ties with the mainland. In particular, Moody's is concerned about whether the Chinese yuan will be devalued and confidence in the Hong Kong dollar's link to the U.S. dollar. However, Moody's offered no prediction about whether the yuan will be devalued. 

 Moody's noted China's "sizable official foreign-exchange reserves and current account surplus" but spoke of a "continued deep slump in regional economic and trade performance as well as in a retrenchment of global capital market funds for emerging markets in general." Moody's said it is uncertain whether China's effort to sustain economic growth and minimize unemployment will "complicate" the country's "enormous task" of reforming its state-owned enterprises. 

 China's usually quiet central bank has made loud pledges in recent weeks that it won't devalue the yuan anytime soon. But rumors continue to make the rounds in currency and stock markets around the world that China will do so. Many people fear that a devalued yuan would further batter Asia's depreciated currencies, spreading the region's economic dislocation further West. Experts say the pledge appears to have teeth but investors and traders were burned many times in the past year as one Asian currency after another collapsed despite assurances of stability. 

 The devaluation rumors have stepped up in recent weeks because of a slowing Chinese economy and weak yen, accompanied by black-market prices for the yuan plunging to depths not seen since Beijing last devalued the currency in early 1994. China's central bank has been adjusting interest rates to prop up the yuan and the Hong Kong dollar, the only two major currencies in Asia to have so far escaped devaluation in the region's economic crisis. 

 Hong Kong has been hurt by the region's financial-markets turbulence and by speculation in the local currency, Moody's said. Confidence in the Hong Kong dollar's "peg" is also being hurt by uncertainty over the yuan. "Together, these factors are causing the most serious economic downturn in Hong Kong's recent history, bringing about a deterioration in Hong Kong's traditionally strong government financial position," Moody's said. 

 Moody's also expects to see a "significant drop" in Hong Kong's reserves after the territory spent billions in recent weeks to prop up the value of its currency and stock markets. "Interventions in the future could weaken the foreign asset position further," Moody's said. 

 The Hong Kong Monetary Authority said Friday that it will conduct a series of briefings Saturday to announce a reinforcement of the Hong Kong dollar's peg to the U.S. dollar. "This is to announce various measures we have derived to strengthen the currency board system," a spokesman for the monetary authority said. He added that there was "absolutely" no thought of Hong Kong abandoning the currency board system, widening the Hong Kong dollar's trading range or changing its parity against the U.S. dollar. 

 Moody's will also review the ratings of several Hong Kong financial institutions for possible downgrade. "Pressures on the currency are expected to keep interest rates high, putting pressures on interest margins and eventually on borrowers," Moody's said. 

 Lost in much of the talk about a possible yuan devaluation is the potential impact on Hong Kong, a major trade center in Asia that was returned to Chinese rule last year. Some experts think a yuan devaluation would mean the end of Hong Kong as a financial center. 

 Many analysts stress that fundamentals in China - however weak - haven't changed all that much in recent weeks. They also point to the fact that China's currency is convertible only for trade in goods and services, or what's called the current account. It can't be exchanged under the capital, or investment, account, meaning speculators can't trade it solely for profit. 

Hong Kong's intervention threw another wrench into the works. For two weeks, the Hong Kong government waged a battle against speculators who have tried to force a devaluation of the Hong Kong dollar. The government abruptly withdrawed from the effort this week, triggering a sharp drop in Hong Kong's stock market. 

 The deteriorating state of the global economy made Hong Kong's campaign to support its markets extremely costly. Traders estimate the government spent between $12 billion and $15 billion on shares in the effort - more than half of that in an extraordinary buying spree last Friday. Even with its vast foreign exchange fund - worth roughly $97 billion - most analysts said Hong Kong can't afford such a battle for more than a few weeks. 

 Experts are now focusing on how Hong Kong officials plan to extricate themselves from the standoff. The government spent this week penning in its foes with new regulations. With the rule changes, it is now more expensive to attack the market by short-selling and more difficult to accumulate big positions secretly. The new rules, while not onerous by the standards of U.S. and U.K. markets, are a big change for Hong Kong, long considered one of least-regulated large markets. 

 In fact, the past few weeks were so strange that investors largely ignored bad news from credit-rating agencies. On Monday, Standard & Poor's downgraded the territory's foreign debt rating and its short-term local currency rating.
