title: ASIA FOCUS - Chronology of Asia's financial crisis.
text:
SINGAPORE, Sept 3 (Reuters) - The following is a chronology of Asia's financial crisis. 

 1997 

 Jan 23 - Leading South Korean steel maker Hanbo Steel Corp defaults on loans, the first of a string of major corporate failures in 1997. 

 May 14-15 - Thailand's baht currency comes under attack by speculators who decided Thailand's slowing economy and political instability meant it was time to sell. Thailand and Singapore jointly intervene to defend the baht. 

 The Philippines is affected. The central bank raises the overnight rate to 13 percent and dumps dollars. 

 June 19 - Amnuay Viravan, staunchly against devaluing the baht, resigns as Thai finance minister. Resignation has immediate impact in the Philippines, where the overnight deposit rate rises to 15 percent. 

 June 27 - Thai central bank suspends operations of 16 cash-strapped finance companies and orders them to submit merger or consolidation plans. 

 June 30 - Thai Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh assures the nation in a televised address there will be no devaluation of the baht. 

 July 2 - After a failed defence of the Thai baht, Bangkok floats its currency and calls on the IMF for "technical assistance". 

 The baht is effectively devalued by about 15-20 percent. 

 July 8 - Malaysia's central Bank Negara has to intervene aggressively to defend the ringgit. 

 In Indonesia, the rupiah starts to crumble. 

 July 14 - The IMF offers the Philippines almost $1.1 billion in financial support. 

 July 24 - Asian currency meltdown. The rupiah, baht, ringgit and peso slump as confidence in the region deteriorates. 

 August 11 - In Tokyo, the IMF unveils a rescue package for Thailand including loans of $16 billion from the IMF and Asian nations. 

 August 14 - Indonesia abolishes its system of a managed exchange rate. The rupiah plunges. 

 August 20 - IMF approves a $3.9 billion credit for Thailand. Brunei later adds $500 million to the bail-out package, bringing it to $17.2 billion. 

 Sept 20 - Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad tells delegates of IMF/World Bank conference in Hong Kong that currency trading is immoral. 

 Oct 8 - Indonesia says it will ask the IMF for financial assistance. 

 Oct 20-23 - The Hong Kong stock market suffers its heaviest drubbing ever, shedding nearly a quarter of its value in four days on uncertainty over the Hong Kong dollar. 

 Around this time the South Korean won also begins to slump in value. 

 Oct 27 - Asian jitters spill over on to world stock markets. The Dow plunges 554 points, its largest single-day point loss ever. 

 Oct 31 - Indonesia's IMF package is unveiled. It provides for as much as $40 billion in aid, although the front-line defence is $23 billion. 

 Nov 1 - Indonesia shuts down 16 troubled banks. 

 Nov 5 - IMF approves a $10 billion loan for Indonesia as part of the massive international package. 

 Nov 17 - Korea abandons its defence of the won, which rapidly falls to 1,000 to the dollar. 

 Dec 4 - IMF approves a $21 billion loan for South Korea, part of a bail-out package that will total nearly $60 billion. 

 Dec 8 - Thailand closes 56 of 58 previously suspended finance companies. 

 1998 

 Jan 8 - Representatives of the IMF and South Korea agree to a 90-day rollover of short-term debt. 

 Jan 12 - Peregrine, one of Asia's largest independent investment banks, collapses under a mountain of bad loans to Indonesian borrowers. Shares fall sharply in Hong Kong, China and Singapore. 

 Jan 15 - IMF managing director Michel Camdessus and President Suharto sign an agreement strengthening economic reforms. 

 Jan 22 - The rupiah collapses. It is dealt at 17,000 to the dollar at one stage. Bank Indonesia intervenes and drives the currency back to end at 11,800. 

 Jan 27 - Indonesia announces a temporary freeze on debt servicing. 

 Jan 28 - International creditor banks and the South Korean government say they have agreed on a plan to exchange $24 billion of short-term debt for new loans maturing in one, two and three years. 

 Jan 30 - U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan warns Asia's financial crisis could spread. 

 Feb 14 - The IMF threatens to cut off the bail-out fund for Indonesia over its plans to introduce a currency board. 

 Feb 26 - Indonesia's borrowers and lenders begin negotiations on rescheduling at least $70 billion in private off-shore debt. 

 March 1 - Indonesian President Suharto says reforms prescribed by the IMF have not worked. 

 March 4 - The IMF approves release of the third tranche payment from Thailand's package and commends the Thai government for its economic reforms. 

 March 6 - IMF says its board will not discuss Indonesia's economic reform programme before April, effectively delaying a $3 billion payment initially expected by March 15. 

 March 23 - Indonesia nearly doubles interest rates to boost the rupiah and control inflation. 

 April 1 - Japan begins steps aimed at liberalising its financial markets to make them "free, fair and global" by 2001. Tokyo share prices fall, the yen dips and Japan's central bank governor pronounces every economic indicator bad. 

 April 2 - The chairman of electronics giant Sony, Norio Ohga, says the Japanese economy is on the verge of collapse. 

 April 3 - U.S. ratings agency Moody's lowers its outlook on Japan's sovereign debt to negative from stable. Asian currencies fall sharply on the news. 

 May 7 - Fears that riots in the Indonesian city of Medan will spill over into a wider social crisis send regional stocks into retreat. 

 May 11 - India stuns the world with announcement of three underground nuclear tests. Pakistan stocks tumble 3.52 percent while India's National Stock Exchange index slides 2.55 percent. 

 May 13 - The United States imposes economic sanctions on India and Japan suspends some loans. 

 May 14 - Mobs rampage through Jakarta and students demand Suharto's resignation. Indonesia's worsening crisis takes centre-stage for Asian markets, several of which suffer sharp losses. 

 May 15 - Suharto returns home from a Group of 15 summit in Egypt amid signs he is losing his 32-year grip on power. 

 May 21 - Suharto steps down under strong pressure and is succeeded by former deputy president B.J. Habibie. Markets enjoy a limited rally. Jakarta stocks surge more than three percent. 

 May 25 - South Korean shares plummet 6.78 percent despite a lifting of foreign ownership limits on stocks. Most other Asian markets shrug off Seoul's fall. 

 May 26 - Seoul's KOSPI share index continues to dive, losing a further six percent, hurt by a looming recession and labour unrest. 

 May 27 - Asian markets are hammered as the yen falls against the dollar and amid mounting fears of economic recession. Hong Kong stocks plunge more than five percent after Chief Executive Tung Chee-hwa warns of possible recession. 

 May 28 - Pakistan conducts nuclear tests. 

 May 29 - The dollar rockets to a seven-year high of 139 yen on fears of a possible nuclear arms race in Asia and after news that Japan's unemployment rate hit 4.1 percent in April, its highest level since the end of World War Two. 

 Recession looms in much of Asia. Hong Kong reports that its gross domestic product contracted two percent in first quarter of 1998. About the same time Indonesia and Malaysia also report their economies contracted in the first quarter. 

 June 1 - Pakistani stocks plunge 12.38 percent as traders get their first chance to react to sanctions imposed after the country's nuclear tests. Asian markets are hit as nuclear tension adds to a cocktail of domestic problems. 

 June 5 - International lenders and Indonesian companies reach a deal to reschedule the country's massive corporate debt. 

 June 8 - The yen falls past 140 to the dollar, sending a shudder through Asian markets. Signs that Japan and other leading economies are unlikely to intervene to support the unit sap confidence further. 

 June 10 - China's central bank governor warns that the weak yen is having a severe impact on Beijing's foreign trade, raising fears that China may devalue its yuan currency. Markets across Asia tumble, led by a near five percent fall on Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index. 

 In Taiwan, the local dollar hits new 11-year lows and the Australian dollar plummets past 59 U.S. cents. 

 June 11 - U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin all but rules out the possibility of joint intervention by major industrial powers to bolster the yen. He says the weak yen reflects the state of the Japanese economy. 

 June 12 - Economic Planning Agency says Japan's gross domestic product fell by an annualised rate of 5.3 percent in the first quarter, signalling recession. The yen dives towards 145 to the dollar as hopes fade of official intervention. 

 June 17 - The U.S. joins Japan in selling the dollar in favour of the yen. 

 The action takes markets by surprise and the yen rises to a high of around 134 at one stage from a level of some 142.50 prior to the intervention. 

 June 19 - U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin tells Reuters he is not expecting high level meetings in Tokyo to produce specific new action plans on the economy. His statements put further pressure on the yen. 

 June 20 - Top finance officials from the Group of Seven meet in Tokyo and vow to cooperate as appropriate in the currency markets. 

 June 23 - IMF Managing Director Michel Camdessus calls the yen fall a "crisis within the crisis". 

 June 25 - Indonesia and the IMF sign another letter of intent - the fourth. The letter says that Indonesian GDP is expected to contract by at least 10 percent in 1998 and says the rupiah will stabilise at around 10,000 by the last quarter of 1998. 

 June 26 - Malaysia cuts bank statutory reserve requirements to eight percent from 10 percent. 

 June 29 - For the first time, South Korea closes banks, shutting five ailing operations in a major step towards meeting the mandate of the massive IMF rescue package. 

 July 2 - World Bank approves $1 billion loan disbursement to Indonesia, another $6 billion to arrive from international donors. 

 Japan Prime Minister Hashimoto and the ruling Liberal Democratic Party agree to adopt bridge bank system to tackle the country's massive bad loans. 

 July 4 - Foreign Minister Keizo Obuchi hints at permanent tax cuts. 

 July 8 - Hashimoto vows to seek permanent tax cuts and an overhaul of the tax system, but reveals no details. 

 July 9 - South Korea announces its intention to double this year's budget deficit in a bid to stimulate the economy. 

 July 12 - The ruling LDP is trounced in Upper House elections, winning only 44 seats, well short of a majority and 17 less than the 61 it had held prior to the election. 

 South Korea's Financial Supervisory Commission imposes involuntary restructuring on conglomerates, or chaebols, directing eight banks to pick about 16 chaebols for the exercise. 

 July 13 - PM Hashimoto announces his resignation and cancels planned official visits to France and the United States. 

 July 14 - Tens of thousands of South Korean workers down tools to protest against wage cuts and layoffs, part of the massive corporate restructuring programme. 

 July 15 - IMF approves immediate $1 billion loan payment to Indonesia. 

 July 16 - Striking Korean workers return to work, but warn of further protests if necessary. 

 Indonesia revises 98/99 budget to reflect the deteriorating economy, assuming a rupiah/dlr rate of 10,600. 

 Foreign governments announce their agreement to reschedule the country's $54.4 billion in sovereign debt. 

 July 20 - Protests begin at Hyundai's factory in Ulsan, striking workers pitch tents. 

 July 23 - Record 7.0 percent unemployment in South Korea, with more than 1.5 million unemployed. 

 July 24 - Obuchi wins 225 votes out of 411 in LDP voting to become LDP president and, almost certainly, prime minister. 

 July 29 - Moody's Investors Service warned that it may downgrade credit ratings of Thai banks due to poor results. 

 July 30 - Parliament formally names Obuchi prime minister; he then announces his new cabinet. 

 August 3 - Thailand unveils 25 point plan to salvage its economy at the start of two weeks of talks with the IMF. The plan includes measures to create jobs and stimulate the economy, and is later endorsed by the IMF. 

 Indonesia launches debt rescheduling agency to aid the country's debt-ridden companies. 

 August 6 - New Japanese prime minister Obuchi announces a plan to vary tax cuts according to existing tax brackets, and says he will ask parliament to approve cuts worth more than six trillion yen ($41.3 billion). 

 August 14 - The Hong Kong government intervenes in the local stock market, buying stocks to squeeze out investors accused of playing the currency and interest rates against the stock market. The Hang Seng Index soars 8.47 percent. 

 August 17 - Russia effectively devalues the rouble and declares a 90-day moratorium on some foreign debt. The next day, Asian markets slide. 

 Thousands of Hyundai Motor workers rally near the South Korean company's main factory complex in Ulsan, suspending production in protest over layoffs. Police stand ready for action. 

 August 25 - Hyundai workers return to work after a union-brokered agreement to limit number of layoffs. 

 August 26 - IMF approves $1 billion loan to Indonesia. 

 August 31 - Wall Street suffers its second-largest point loss in history, plunging 6.37 percent and sparking another series of stock market routs in Asia. 

 IMF approves $900 million loan payment to South Korea. 

 Sept 1 - Malaysia imposes new foreign exchange controls to contain speculation and restrict capital flows. The IMF warns that the move may undermine investor confidence. 

 Sept 2 - Malaysia announces that the ringgit will be fixed at 3.80 to the dollar indefinitely. 

 Wall Street stages its second-largest comeback in history, sparking off a rally in Asian markets. 

 Deputy Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim is sacked. Police state that Anwar is under investigation over allegations made in a banned book, "Fifty Reasons Why Anwar Cannot Become Prime Minister". 

 Sept 3 - South Korean riot police storm plants owned by Mando Machinery Corp., the country's largest auto-parts producer, to end a strike over planned mass layoffs. 

 (C) Reuters Limited 1998.

title: ASIA MARKETS - Wall St helps, Malaysia confounds.
text:
SINGAPORE, Sept 2 (Reuters) - Wall Street's strong 

 overnight rebound and Malaysia's moves to effectively kill 

 offshore ringgit trading dominated activity in Asian markets on 

 Wednesday. 

     The dollar was off its earlier highs against the yen and 

 mark on profit-taking and dealers said it was likely to make 

 slow progress as markets worldwide scrutinised Wall Street for 

 cues, while keeping an eye on Russia's woes. 

     MALAYSIA MOVES CONFOUND MARKETS 

     Utter confusion over the implication of Malaysia's newly 

 announced currency and capital controls characterised trading 

 in the ringgit and Kuala Lumpur stock market. 

     Dealers said offshore trading in spot and forward ringgit 

 had ground to a halt as banks tried to sort out how to settle 

 previous transactions. 

     Bank Negara's statement that all transactions executed 

 before September would have to be settled by September 4 did 

 not address the problem of forward contracts. 

     The central bank later said it was extending the deadline 

 to September 9. 

     Bank Negara also fixed the exchange rate at 3.80 to the 

 dollar, effective immediately, for an indefinite period. 

     Dealers said any actual trade in the ringgit on Wednesday 

 was commercially driven and confined to banks in Malaysia. 

     Offshore trading of the ringgit dried up, especially in 

 Singapore, its main centre, and there was talk that banks were 

 meeting local authorities to work out a settlement procedure. 

     While Malaysia's actions do seem likely to guarantee a 

 stable ringgit, analysts and fund managers said foreign 

 investors were taking a dim view of what amounted to a retreat 

 from the world economy. 

 "What's happening in Malaysia actually scares investors 

 off. It shows governments can turn around and change their 

 policies very quickly and there are no reassurances for 

 investors," said Slavia Cheong, investment manager at Aberdeen 

 Asset Management in Singapore. 

 The KLSE stock index staged a sharp rebound, bouncing over 

 12 percent, from Tuesday's 13 percent plunge as investors 

 scrambled to cover short stock positions amid confusion over 

 the new trading curbs. 

 The stock exchange clarified that the new rules did not 

 impose a one-year moratorium on the sale of shares, but 

 proceeds from such sales would have to be kept in Malaysia for 

 at least one year. 

 REST OF ASIA RESISTS MALAYSIA'S EXAMPLE 

 Other Southeast Asian currencies rose as investors closed 

 out short positions amid worries that more governments in the 

 region might go the same way as Malaysia. 

 The Singapore dollar, which along with the ringgit had been 

 among the most liquid of the regional currencies, was off its 

 highs in late trade after jumping sharply on long U.S. dollar 

 liquidations by hedge funds. 

 But most governments appeared keen on distancing themselves 

 from Malaysia's decision, spurring some short-covering of the 

 U.S. dollar in late trade. 

 Indonesia's top economics minister Ginandjar Kartasasmita 

 said his country would stick to a free foreign exchange system 

 while continuing to monitor developments in Malaysia. 

 Thai central bank governor Chatu Mongol Sonakul said it was 

 not planning to follow Malaysia's example as the situation in 

 Thailand had stabilised and introducing new controls would do 

 more harm than good. 

 The central bank said Thailand's outstanding foreign debt 

 at the end of June was $88.1 billion and about 68 percent of 

 total debt is long-term. 

 HONG KONG STOCKS GAIN, INTERBANK RATES DROP 

 Hong Kong's blue chip index briefly climbed above the key 

 7,500 barrier on short-covering fuelled by Wall Street's 

 rebound, a firmer yen and lower interbank rates. 

 But brokers said the Hong Kong Monetary Authority's recent 

 aggressive interventions to squeeze speculators out of stock 

 and futures markets had sparked some concern about the 

 territory's free market mechanism, especially in the light of 

 Malaysia's moves. 

 HKMA deputy chief executive David Carse said overnight in 

 London the authority had not intervened in stock and futures 

 markets on Monday and Tuesday, but was willing to do so again 

 if necessary. 

 PHILIPPINES PESO UNIMPRESSED BY REMOVAL OF LIMIT 

 The peso was unable to sustain early gains despite the 

 Philippine Monetary Board's removal of a limit that allowed 

 banks to sell dollars worth up to 20 percent of their capital. 

 The Board retained a five percent limit on overbought 

 dollar positions, and a central bank official said the removal 

 of the oversold ceiling would give an added boost to the peso's 

 recent uptrend. 

     But bankers said the ruling was academic since the dollar

title: HK  intervention  hastens re-peg need - WI Carr.
text:
HONG KONG, Sept 2 (Reuters) - The Hong Kong government's intervention in the local stock market has intensified the need for a currency devaluation, Michael Taylor, chief economist at Indosuez W.I. Carr Securities, said on Wednesday. 

 Taylor said he did not expect a devaluation in Hong Kong before one in mainland China, which was most likely early next year. 

 The Hong Kong Monetary Authority recently moved to defend the local currency from speculators by spending an estimated HK$100 billion ($12.8 billion) on stocks and futures contracts. 

 "Having forfeited the assumption of transparency, Hong Kong will have to reconstruct without the cash that was attracted to the promise of that transparency," Taylor said in a statement. 

 "Even under the best scenarios Hong Kong dollar assets and Hong Kong dollar debt will now be priced accordingly. There is a relationship between the amount of creditability blown in the defence, and the level to which asset prices must adjust," he said. 

 Speaking to reporters, Taylor said Hong Kong asset prices were sure to fall further with deflationary forces taking hold the world over. Under current conditions, the pace of the fall was likely to be quite intense. 

 He said there was little chance Hong Kong interest rates would decline. The flight of foreign capital had kept, and would keep, interbank rates high, and local banks would be forced to raise retail lending rates because they could not endure painfully tight margins forever. 

 For the government, the best move would be to devalue the Hong Kong dollar either by re-pegging it straight away at a weaker rate or letting it float for a while to find a level and then re-pegging it. 

 "We expect that Hong Kong will be taking some of the adjustment through the currency," he said. 

 The Hong Kong dollar has been linked to the U.S. dollar at a rate of HK$7.8 since 1983 and is permitted to float in a narrow band around that level. 

 Taylor said the goverment should devalue "the sooner the better". He said the government was likely to delay such a move until pressures on the economy became severe. 

 "Despite the fact that the government buying of the stock market appears to have stopped, devaluation in the very near term is probably not going to happen, and will not happen until it is forced by the very intensity of deflationary forces at work," he said. 

 Taylor said he expected Hong Kong would wait for China to devalue, which it would do soon to help to support its reform programme in a continuing deflationary environment. 

 In an August research report, Indosuez W.I. Carr predicted China would devalue its currency by 20 percent around the turn of the year. 

 "My own expectation is that Hong Kong will wait for China's devaluation. I therefore expect the devaluation of the Hong Kong dollar before Chinese New Year (February 1999)," said Taylor. 

 Worries about the contagion effects of a Hong Kong dollar devaluation were exaggerated as were concerns about the effect on the territory's banking sector. 

 Taylor declined to estimate what would be a proper level for the Hong Kong dollar, saying it would depend on the level of confidence in the market. 

 "What level the currency goes to depends on what it takes to regain confidence in Hong Kong," he said. 

 Taylor rejected the idea of dollarising the Hong Kong economy, saying it "would sound an immediate death knell for local Hong Kong banks".

title: HK gov't blasts S&P cut, analysts take other view.
text:
HONG KONG, Sept 1 (Reuters) - The Hong Kong government on Tuesday called unfair the territory's downgrade by Standard & Poor's Corp but analysts said the cut was hardly surprising. 

 "The government does not find S&P's decision to downgrade the credit ratings of Hong Kong justified," the government said. 

 S&P cut the long-and short-term foreign currency sovereign ratings of Hong Kong to Single-A/A-1 from A-plus/A-1-plus. 

 It also cut Hong Kong's long-and short-term local currency ratings to A-plus/A-1 from AA-minus/A-1-plus. 

 S&P said the downgrades reflected a decline in Hong Kong's financial flexibility due to the growing domestic impact of East Asia's recession, as well as the large official purchases in the local equity and futures markets. 

 The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) has been aggressively buying shares to foil speculators that had shorted the stock market and then attacked the Hong Kong dollar with the aim of pushing interest rates up and stock prices down. 

 In its objection to S&P's action, the government said its intervention was meant to deter manipulation, not support stocks. 

 But S&P managing director for Asia Paul Coughlin said it was not the intervention itself that was causing the rating agency concern, but rather what it said about the state of Hong Kong's economy and what it might mean for its future stability. 

 "We are not necessarily saying the intervention was the wrong thing to do. We are saying that the margin of safety has been eroded, increasing Hong Kong's risk," said Coughlin. 

 S&P noted in its ratings statement that by some estimates the government had spent up to US$15 billion buying shares and futures "as part of an increasingly complex and risky strategy to deter speculative pressures." 

 The intervention was likely to have some effect on foreign reserves, although the exact impact was not yet clear. 

 And even if the government stopped intervening, the HKMA's portfolio was likely to suffer significant losses unless the global trend of falling equity prices was reversed, S&P said. 

 HKMA assets backing the local dollar would fall in any case as funds were diverted to the treasury to finance a fiscal gap. 

 Bear Stearns sovereign analyst John Seel said the worry with the intervention was not the money spent, but what it said about Hong Kong. 

 "The important thing...is the fact that Hong Kong is becoming less transparent and the market mechanism is not being able to act as freely as it had in the past," he said. 

 Even more troublesome for Hong Kong were the stresses affecting the financial sector, S&P said. 

 Lehman Brothers economist Rob Subbaraman said S&P's concerns were valid. "In an economy contracting five percent there will be corporate failures and it will affect the banking sector, though how severely is an open question," he said. 

 The Hong Kong government on Friday estimated economic activity had fallen by about five percent in the second quarter of 1998 and forecast a full-year fall of around four percent. 

 Even after the intervention, the HKMA would have ample reserves to back the currency board, but problems could arise if the financial system were to weaken seriously, Subbaraman said. 

 "The risk is that if some banks..did develop problems and there were runs on banks, the currency board could fall apart because the Exchange Fund does not have enough money to cover all deposits," said Subbaraman. 

 In July, before the stock market intervention, Hong Kong's foreign reserves were US$96.5 billion, eight times the currency in circulation and about 44 percent of M3, the broadest measure of money supply. 

 Bonds of Hong Kong entities showed little reaction to the S&P news, but analysts noted that the bonds had been trading more like BB than Single-A credits for some time. 

 Spreads widened just slightly, said Chris Francis, head of credit research at Merrill Lynch in Hong Kong. 

 "In the past few weeks, Asian spreads have been much more affected by external events, such as Russia, than anything going on in the region," he said.

title: Economist Friedman Says  Hong Kong  Erred Badly In Market  Intervention
text:
HONG KONG -(Dow Jones)- Nobel Laureate Milton Friedman Wednesday declared that "all bets are off" as to whether Hong Kong can keep its currency pegged to the U.S. dollar. 

 Friedman, one of the best-known champions of Hong Kong's free-market system, also blasted the Hong Kong government's recent stock market intervention as "insane." 

 In a telephone interview from his home in San Francisco, he said that "if the Hong Kong government wants to restore its system, it should announce that it made a mistake and immediately sell off whatever stocks it purchased." 

 Friedman's criticism adds to a growing chorus of concern over the Hong Kong government's decision to buy stocks as an indirect means of deterring currency speculators. 

 The 1976 winner of the Nobel Prize in economics for his contributions to monetary theory, Friedman is famed for his statement that to see "how the free market really works, Hong Kong is the place to go." 

 The Hong Kong Monetary Authority - the city's de facto central bank - has spent an estimated US$15 billion to deter currency speculators from what it calls unfair attacks on the Hong Kong dollar. 

 Under Hong Kong's currency-board system, when speculators sell the Hong Kong dollar, this automatically pushes up local interest rates. Those higher interest rates eventually attract some investors to buy Hong Kong dollars, bolstering the currency. But steeper borrowing costs also slam the economy and share prices. 

 Speculators, say government officials, have been reaping huge profits by short-selling stocks - borrowing stock and selling it on the expectation that the price would fall - and then replacing the borrowed stock at a profit. The government's efforts to push up the stock market, say officials, have prevented speculators from making money and kept them at bay. 

 Friedman said the government's involvement in the stock market was totally unnecessary and counterproductive for the defense of Hong Kong's currency. The economist said that if the government let the currency board function properly, the automatic rise in interest rates would be sufficient to keep the currency impervious to all speculative assaults. 

 "If they continued to operate the system as it was set up in 1983, it would be as sound as the Rock of Gibraltar," Friedman said. 

 A spokesman from the Hong Kong Monetary Authority declined to comment on Friedman's remarks.

title: HK Dollar Stronger Late; HKMA  Intervention  Rumors Continue
text:
HONG KONG (AP-Dow Jones)--The Hong Kong dollar is stronger in late Asian trading Thursday, following unconfirmed rumors that the Hong Kong Monetary Authority has acted to stabilize the currency. 

 The Monetary Authority declined to comment on its activities Thursday, but the head of treasury at a domestic bank said rumors that it had sold an amount of under US$100.0 million at HK$7.7470 early Thursday were enough to cause banks to sell the U.S. currency on the spot market and drop the dollar as low as HK$7.7425. 

 The U.S. dollar is quoted at HK$7.7443 at 0756 GMT (3:56 a.m. EDT), down from HK$7.7475 around the same time Wednesday. 

 Rumors of Monetary Authority activity were touched off by a renewed burst of activity in the forwards market, where concerns about the Thai baht led banks to seek long-term funding to hedge their Hong Kong exposure, said a money markets chief at a U.S. bank. 

 The one-year U.S. dollar premium shot up to 1200.0 points from 500.0-900.0 points on Wednesday. It is at 1100.0 points at 0756 GMT. 

 Thursday's rise also takes the premium investors are willing to pay above the 900.0-point level recorded Monday, when pressure on the rupiah generated frenzied forward market activity. Those levels indicate participants expect the Hong Kong dollar to weaken significantly to HK$7.8643 over the next year. 

 Most buyers are interested in the two-month to six-month forwards Thursday, a period indicating they expect market volatility to continue for some time to come, said a currency analyst with a European bank. 

 Like Monday, money market liquidity tightened, pushing all rates higher and prompting further talk that the Monetary Authority is draining liquidity.

title: HK$ Bonds Mixed On HK Dollar Weakness, U.S. Treasury Rally
text:
HONG KONG (AP-Dow Jones)--Hong Kong dollar bond prices were mixed in late trading Wednesday, weighed down on one end by more fears of currency intervention, and buoyed on the other by an overnight rally in U.S. Treasurys, traders said. 

 Short-term bills endured another session of selling, especially in the afternoon, as fears intensifed that the Hong Kong Monetary Authority could intervene to support the local currency. 

 'People are just worried about the Hong Kong dollar being challenged by American funds. That's why bill (prices) went down 40 to 50 ticks,' a trader at a U.S. brokerage house said. 'But the longer-period bonds remain unchanged.' 

 Late Wednesday, the one-week Exchange Fund bill yield rose to 6.48% from 6.34% Tuesday. The 10-year Exchange Fund bond yield fell to 6.78%, compared with 6.99% Tuesday. 

 The U.S. dollar is quoted at HK$7.7475, up from HK$7.7458 Tuesday. 

 A depreciating Hong Kong dollar drives investors out of the bond markets on fears the value of their assets will be significantly eroded. However, the activity usually centers around bills, which are much more sensitive to short-term volatility.

title: Asian  currency  blight unsettles Hong Kong.
text:
HONG KONG, July 21 (Reuter) - Persistent contagion throughout Southeast Asian currency markets unsettled the Hong Kong dollar on Monday but most analysts still knocked down any suggestion of speculative weakness. 

 "I don't think the Hong Kong dollar is likely to fall prey to speculators," said Dong Tao, economist at Schroder Securities in Hong Kong. 

 Short-term interest rates soared and currency forwards widened in Hong Kong after speculators attacked the Indonesian rupiah, a currency that had seemed immune to speculation swirling through the region this month. 

 As heavy speculative selling pushed the rupiah to a new record low of 2,655 to the U.S. dollar, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, the territory's de facto central bank, intervened to support the Hong Kong dollar spot rate. 

 The intervention lifted the Hong Kong dollar within a safe distance of the key psychological level of HK$7.7500. At 0500 GMT, the Hong Kong dollar was back on firmer ground, trading at HK$7.7470/80 and well-linked to its 14-year-old fixed rate of HK$7.80 to the U.S. dollar. 

 Traders said any break of the HK$7.7500 level could signal a sharp slide, which was why the HKMA was determined to defend it. 

 But traders were tense. 

 "Everyone is nervous," one dealer said. "Yes, definitely, everyone is nervous." 

 Speculators have already forced a depreciation of the Thai baht and Philippine peso, and currencies are jittery in Malaysia and even Singapore, long considered a safe haven. 

 The Malaysian ringgit was still weak on Monday after hitting a 38-month low in London on Friday, while the Philippines central bank was forced to intervene yet again to support its battered peso on Monday, which was trading at 28.35 to the U.S. dollar compared with pre-July 11 depreciation levels of 26. 

 The Thai baht, now trading at about 30.35 to the U.S. dollar compared to pre-July 2 depreciation level of 25, was sluggish with most of the domestic market on holiday. 

 In Hong Kong, currency forwards widened to 210 in the three-month and 400 in the six-month from more usual levels in the single digits, and money market rates soared. 

 The overnight rate climbed to 6.37 percent, while the one-week Exchange Fund bill yield reached 6.53 percent compared with 5.31 percent last week. 

 Spreads to corresponding U.S. government paper widened sharply. 

 Despite the tension, analysts remained confident that the Hong Kong dollar would remain an island of stability in a sea of currency turmoil. 

 "Hong Kong's fundamentals are much stronger than many of the Southeast Asian economies. Hong Kong's foreign exchange reserves are huge even without added support from China," Tao said. 

 Hong Kong holds at least US$63 billion in foreign exchange reserves while China, which has promised to defend the Hong Kong dollar if it comes under attack, has a cache of US$121 billion. 

 HKMA chief executive Joseph Yam has issued repeated warnings to speculators never to attack the Hong Kong dollar. 

 The territory's vast reserves and strong economic fundamentals set Hong Kong apart from some of the most troubled Asian nations now battling currency speculators, as does Yam's market credibility and that of the institution he controls. 

 But confidence is key in this situation and, following weakness in the Singapore dollar, there are signs of eroding confidence in Hong Kong. 

 "I think (Yam's) message has been heard but because of the hectic happenings in the regional currency markets investors might be just too nervous to take notice of what Mr. Yam has to say," the dealer said.

text:
While the territory took time off commemorate the change in sovereignty, Thai authorities allowed their currency, the baht, to float on Wednesday, abandoning a 13-year basket arrangement in the face of increasing pressure from international markets. 

 The impact of the Thai move on the Hong Kong dollar was slight and on balance positive, as some investors switched to the Hong Kong dollar, which officials assure will continue being pegged to the U.S. dollar at HK$7.80 for some time to come. 

 A currency trader with a British investment bank said that some in the market are switching to the Hong Kong currency because of its safe haven reputation in the region, but overall the effect has been minimal. 

 In late trading Thursday, the U.S. dollar was slightly lower against the Hong Kong currency. quoted at HK$7.7440, compared with Friday afternoon's HK$7.7480. 

 The latest currency-peg assurance came Thursday from Hong Kong's top financial official, who said that Hong Kong's de facto central bank, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, hasn't yet resorted to intervention in the foreign exchange markets to influence the Hong Kong dollar rate. 

 Financial Secretary Donald Tsang Yam-kuen said, 'I do not see the threat at all, and there is no question whatsoever that I am going to even consider changing the link.' 

 Tsang added at a briefing for reporters that 'we are watching the developments with great interest. As far as the Hong Kong dollar is concerned, it is rock solid. The Hong Kong government has not been in the market. The Hong Kong dollar is still trading on the strong side of the link.' 

 Tsang wouldn't discuss if the Hong Kong Monetary Authority was asked by the Bank of Thailand to exercise an existing repurchase agreement that could help it raise cash.

HONG KONG (AP-Dow Jones)--The Hong Kong dollar is stronger Wednesday on U.S. dollar profit-taking that began during the previous session. 

 The U.S. dollar has traded tightly between HK$7.7350 and HK$7.7365 so far Wednesday. It is trading at HK$7.7456 at 0405 GMT (12:05 a.m. EDT), down from HK$7.7477 around the same time Tuesday. 

 As Hong Kong dollar interest rates fell last week and earlier this week, the U.S. dollar began to climb, rising from HK$7.7410 last week to a high of HK$7.7483 Tuesday. 

 At that level, however, it ran out of steam because Hong Kong dollar rates stopped their slide. In addition, participants feared intervention by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority if the dollar reached HK$7.7500. 

 Profit-taking began, dropping the currency below HK$7.7460 late Tuesday, mostly outside of the Hong Kong trading center. The profit-taking is continuing on a smaller scale so far Wednesday, said a currency dealer at a domestic bank. 

 She said the U.S. dollar probably won't fall below HK$7.7450 Wednesday and that buying interest may resume, taking the currency as high as HK$7.7470.

The firm's Richard Margolis added that he thinks hedge funds and other would-be speculators have subscribed to that opinion too, even if economists such as Rabushka and Nobel laureate Milton Friedman don't. 

 'I suspect there is more good than bad' in the peg and that doing away with it is 'simply too big of a risk to take,' said T.C. Chan, head of commercial and investment banking in Hong Kong at Citibank N.A. 'I think by and large people believe in the peg, at least in the short term, at least the next two years.' 

 The HKMA stresses that the Basic Law promises the Hong Kong dollar will be around for 50 years. Asked about the chance for convergence of the Chinese and Hong Kong monetary systems, the HKMA Chief Yam usually responds: 'not in my lifetime.' 

 But the Hong Kong central bank does permit some unspecified leeway in the Hong Kong dollar's market value, generally believed to be 1.0% on either side of peg, or about HK$7.7250 to HK$7.8780. 

 Merrill Lynch data show the market expects less than that amount of movement over two years, although the most pessimistic forecast is for a 10% drop to HK$8.6000. 'But that's right out on a limb,' said analyst Margolis. 'The consensus is for a negligible movement.' 

 On Thursday, the U.S. currency was around HK$7.7430. 

 Rarely dipping into the hefty foreign exchange balance under its control, the HKMA uses interest rates to keep the currency rate smooth day-to-day, draining or adding funds from the banking system as needed. In any case, the Hong Kong foreign exchange market is affected a lot more often by new share offerings than any speculation about the peg. On the most active days, the HKMA does 'check' with dealers to make them make them aware of its vigilance, though evidence of actual intervention is hard to find. 

 Public confidence in the Hong Kong dollar is the most crucial element for it to maintain its value, as was shown during the emergency of 1983 when the U.S. dollar peg had to be established in order to restore local trust.

title: FOCUS - Hong Kong falls prey to Asia  currency  panic.
text:
HONG KONG, May 16 (Reuter) - Asian currency panic filtered through the Hong Kong money market on Friday, sending interest rates skywards while currency forwards soared. 

 But the Hong Kong dollar remained rock solid in steady two-way trade, ignoring the ruckus just 46 days before this British colony reverts to Chinese control. 

 The Hong Kong dollar closed at HK$7.7385 on Friday, flat against Thursday's close and well within its unofficial trading band of one percent either side of an enforced peg of HK$7.80 to the U.S. dollar. 

 "I don't think there's a problem in Hong Kong but there's a lot of currency turmoil in Asia and there aren't many countries that aren't affected by it," said Daniel Hemmant, Asian exotic currency fund manager at Guinness Flight Asia Ltd. 

 Speculative concern about the Thai baht and Malaysian ringgit sparked sudden rate action in Hong Kong when Malaysia's central bank denied publicly that it had ordered banks to cease ringgit swap, or forward, transactions with foreign banks. 

 Hong Kong currency forwards suddenly blew out to 65 in the three-month and 100 in the six-month from more usual levels of 15 and 40 respectively, widening further in afternoon trade. 

 Rates also skyrocketed, responding to a sudden 100-basis point rise in the overnight rate to 6.50 percent. 

 The one-week Exchange Fund bill yield closed at 6.16 percent while the two-year spread to the U.S. treasury -- considered a benchmark in Hong Kong's young and thinly-traded market -- gaped to 107 points from a more usual 30. 

 Dealers reported intervention by the territory's de facto central bank, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, but it appeared to have little effect at calming the market. 

 "The market is very nervous," one dealer said at the close. "People are concerned there will be more attacks on the Malaysian ringgit and that they will succeed. If that happens, it won't be good for Hong Kong." 

 But analysts said the market action in Hong Kong was a predictable knee-jerk reaction to currency turmoil in Thailand and Malaysia, where poor economic fundamentals attracted the attention of hedge funds from overseas. 

 "Basically this is a knee-jerk move rather than a fundamentally-based move and it'll snap back fairly quickly," said Callum Henderson, currency analyst at MMS International. 

 Dealers seemed confident about the Hong Kong dollar, long considered a possible target for speculators on uncertainty associated with the switch to Chinese sovereignty on July 1. 

Foreign exchange reserves of US$63.4 billion at the end of March and Hong Kong's sturdy fiscal and economic position were powerful disincentives to speculators tempted by the infectious spread of currency weakness throughout the region, dealers said. 

 "Who dares to touch us? Not even (George) Soros dares to touch us. Everything is well prepared," one dealer said, referring to the hedge fund speculator who forced sterling out of the European exchange rate mechanism in 1992. 

 Hong Kong's situation is very different from Thailand, which is weighed under with bad debt, or Malaysia, which suffers from a wide current account deficit, he said.

title: China, HK central banks to continue to cooperate.
text:
HONG KONG, March 7 (Reuter) - China will continue to cooperate with Hong Kong's de facto central bank to assure financial stability, Chen Yuan, deputy governor of the Peoples' Bank of China, said on Friday. 

 "We will continue to cooperate with the Hong Kong Monetary Authority because we are mutually dependent on each other. That cooperation will last for many, many years," Chen told Reuters Financial Television in an interview. 

 The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) carries out most of the functions of a central bank -- focusing on protecting the Hong Kong dollar's peg to the U.S. dollar and banking supervision. The Peoples' Bank of China is China's central bank. 

 "We hope that our joint efforts to keep the market stable and the currency stable will turn out to be very successful," Chen said. 

 Hong Kong reverts to China on July 1 after more than 150 year of British colonial rule. 

 Under the "one country, two systems" scenario to be enshrined in the Sino-British treaty governing the handover, China and Hong Kong will maintain separate monetary systems. 

 China and Hong Kong have signed a bilateral repurchase agreement pact to provide liquidity in times of currency instability. 

 But Chen said cooperation between the two monetary authorities was otherwise informal. 

 "We don't have any specific instrument to use between us other than the repo agreement, but we already keep very close contact," he said, adding "that is the most efficient way to cooperate on market disturbances." 

 For example, "recently the Hong Kong Monetary Authority had a market intervention to stabilise the exchange rate, and in the morning I got a phone call from (HKMA chief executive) Joseph Yam to apprise me of the situation," said Chen. 

 Chen said China had no plans in place to "bail out" Hong Kong markets in the event of a crisis, but stressed that he did not anticipate such a need. 

 The Bank of England stepped in to help stabilise the Hong Kong dollar in 1983 when jitters about the impending handover sent what was then a free floating currency tumbling, Hong Kong government officials have said. 

 Shortly afterwards, Hong Kong pegged its dollar to the U.S. unit, a peg that has held firm since. The following year, British and Chinese negotiators signed a treaty governing the handover which served to allay some uncertainty.

title: HK Central Banker Yam Says HKMA Needs Political Autonomy
text:
HONG KONG (AP-Dow Jones)--Any changes that affect the Hong Kong Monetary Authority once China takes control of the territory must leave the quasi central bank free from political intervention, according to Hong Kong central banker Joseph Yam Chi-kwong. 

 His mandate is to ensure currency stability, said the Monetary Authority chief executive during an interview with AP-Dow Jones this week. And Yam said he thinks that the authority's role in regulating banks and developing market infrastructure helps in realizing that goal. 

 The central banker - always strident in his support for the local currency's peg to the U.S. dollar - acknowledged that he failed last month to persuade one of its biggest critics, Nobel Laureate Milton Friedman, that the link will be kept indefinitely after the political changeover on July 1. Yam also said the authority's ability to manipulate interbank liquidity means the Hong Kong system isn't a perfect example of a currency board, although that characteristic works in the territory's best interest. 

 Meanwhile, Yam indicated he is willing to see his reporting responsibility shift to the top official in the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region government, and for the territory's HK$111.21 billion land fund to managed separately from the US$65.9 billion in foreign reserves invested by the Monetary Authority. 

 The 48-year-old, who owns race horses named 'Insider' and 'Inner Circle,' and is clearly comfortable being one of Asia's key economic policy makers, also said he is a family man who is most satisfied tackling 'technical problems.' 

 Yam said he is aware of a danger of 'staying too long,' but wants to remain Hong Kong's central banker long after the transition in order to 'launch' the arrangements he has negotiated in recent years with the Chinese authorities. He said he could envisage taking an advisory role on the mainland sometime in the future.

title: Intervention  Or Not, Few Doubt China Commitment To HK Dlr
text:
HONG KONG (AP-Dow Jones)--Deng Xiaoping won't realize his dream of visiting Hong Kong, but some participants said his spirit was felt in the currency market Thursday as Chinese and Hong Kong authorities worked hand-in-hand to keep the territory stable. 

Currency trading was volatile, but not nearly as earthshaking as had been expected in the first Asian trading session following the death of China's paramount leader and architect of the 'one country, two systems' plan for Hong Kong. 

 And after an initial upward hiccup by the U.S. dollar to HK$7.7500 in New York, it was the U.S. currency that lost ground when Asian trading got underway. It dropped steadily to HK$7.7389 late Thursday. It is at HK$7.7415 at 0946 GMT.

 Whatever the case, all agree that relative calm prevailed in Hong Kong's currency market Thursday after an early burst of confusion, indicating investors felt there was little to fear from Deng's death. 

 Money market activity, valued at HK$29.22 billion, was actually below the HK$32.24 billion recorded Wednesday. 

 'This had been discounted in the market,' said Horace Fan, treasury chief at Hong Kong's Wing On Bank Ltd., noting that rumors have persisted for years and were particularly strong over the past week. 'People realize that Deng Xiaoping's passing away is not a big thing.'

title: U.S. dlr weaker, Hong Kong money fully recovered.
text:
HONG KONG, Feb 20 (Reuter) - The U.S. dollar slipped in a busy Hong Kong trading session on Thursday, but dealers said the weakness had nothing to do with the overnight death of paramount leader Deng Xiaoping. 

 "People are buying the yen on the Nikkei, which was much stronger," said one dealer. 

 The Tokyo stock market's Nikkei 225 index closed 452.59 points higher at 19,051.71 on Thursday. 

 The U.S. dollar stood at 123.60 late in Hong Kong, sharply weaker than early morning highs around 124.60 yen, with repeated tests of the 123.45 level expected. 

 Stop loss orders were reported at 123.30. 

 The U.S. dollar was also softer against the German mark at 1.686 marks late Thursday. 

 But Hong Kong money firmed sharply, discounting concern about Deng's death. 

 "Basically, the players have now discounted the news," said one analyst. "When the news finally came out, the Hong Kong dollar rose rather than fell." 

 The unit was trading at HK$7.7400 late on Thursday after attempting a break of the HK$7.7500 level earlier in the week when fears of Deng's demise filtered through the market. 

 Reports surfaced on Thursday of intervention by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority via central banks in England and China to keep the unit below the HK$7.7500 level. 

 "We heard U.K. banks and Chinese banks were the main sellers this morning. A lot of traders suspect they were selling on behalf of the HKMA or the central bank of China," she said. 

 The territory's de facto bank was also witnessed buying 10-year Exchange Fund Notes this morning to keep the market steady when the news of Deng's death broke. 

 "All the dealers suspect the HKMA was doing this because they were all sidelined," she said. 

Currency forwards, or swaps, narrowed back to more usual ranges of eight basis points in the three-month and 30 basis points in the six-month after widening earlier in the week.

title: HK dollar at two-year low, but raising few fears.
text:
HONG KONG, Feb 5 (Reuter) - The Hong Kong dollar was mired at two-year lows against the U.S. dollar on Wednesday, but analysts said there was little cause for concern as the slump was partly linked to seasonal factors and was losing momentum. 

 Hong Kong's dollar was stuck at 7.7496/06 to the U.S. unit on Wednesday, its weakest level since January 1995 following the Mexican peso crisis when it dropped to around HK$7.77. 

 The rate is pegged at HK$7.8 to the dollar but has tended to trade between HK$7.73 and HK$7.74 for the past few years. 

 The T.T. -- or telegraphic transfer, as the U.S. dollar-Hong Kong dollar exchange rate is called -- started to rise around January 20 and soared above 7.74 on January 23. 

 Analysts attributed its strength to keen demand for the U.S. dollar from corporate players, funds switching out of local stocks to other regional bourses, and note-issuing banks ahead of the Chinese New Year holidays which start on Thursday. 

 "(Note-issuing) banks print notes ahead of Chinese New Year every year," said Standard Chartered Bank treasurer Stanley Wong. "The banks need to buy U.S. dollars from the market." 

 Hong Kong's three note-issuing banks must have U.S. dollars on hand before they issue the equivalent in local dollar notes. 

 There is usually a surge in demand for bank notes ahead of Chinese New Year when people withdraw more than normal amounts of cash to buy goods and gifts for the festival and to give traditional envelopes of "lucky money". 

 Chase Manhattan Bank foreign exchange manager Tony Cheung said the local unit lost ground as some fund managers switched out of the Hong Kong stock market. 

 "Some funds are flowing out of Hong Kong stocks into other regional markets," Cheung said. 

 Wong said the T.T. did not rise as notably this time last year when only the Chinese New Year factor was in play. 

 "Some corporate players started to buy the U.S. dollar in greater amounts at a T.T. above 7.74 after they had waited in vain for the U.S. dollar to fall to lower levels," he said. 

 A banker at a regional institution said that with no visible intervention from the territory's de factor central bank, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA), some traders were testing the authority to see where it might intervene. 

 That put further pressure on the Hong Kong dollar, he said. 

 "It seems that the HKMA is quite willing to let the Hong Kong dollar have a wider trading band. They seem to be quite comfortable with the Hong Kong dollar at 7.75 (and) willing to let the dollar float outside the 7.73 to 7.74 range," he said. 

 He saw the HKMA moves as a good policy since too rigid a band would make it more difficult for it to defend the local dollar in case of attack. 

 HKMA officials were not immediately available to comment. 

 The authority has frequently warned speculators against using any uncertainty ahead of Hong Kong's handover to China on July 1 as an opportunity to take a run at the local dollar, pointing to the territory's US$63.8 billion in foreign reserves. 

 Analysts and traders said the Hong Kong dollar's fall had decelerated this week compared to last week, and would gradually reverse course. 

 "The T.T. rise has slowed down in the past few days after rising quite a lot last Thursday and Friday," Wong said. "After the Chinese New Year, it will be back to 7.7450." 

 Chase Manhattan's Cheung said: "We think it will stand at 7.7490/00 for a while and then fall back."

title: HK Dollar Stronger On  Central Bank Intervention  Concerns
text:

title: HK Dollar Unchanged In Quiet Post-Holiday Trading
text:
HONG KONG (AP-Dow Jones)--The Hong Kong dollar is unchanged Tuesday in quiet trading after a holiday weekend, with no direction from also steady local interest rates, bond yields and stock market. 

 Around 0445 GMT, the U.S. dollar is quoted at $7.7322 (Hong Kong), unchanged from around the same time Friday. 

 The Hong Kong market was closed Monday for a holiday. 

 Traders say there is a lot of cash liquidity in the Hong Kong dollar money markets, which has contributed to the stability of the local currency in recent weeks. 

 The U.S. dollar has hovered closely around the HK$7.7320 level for several weeks and is likely to continue to do so this week, dealers said. 

 'It's rather quiet (Tuesday). We've heard of some money flowing in, on stock market speculation, and some interest in selling U.S. dollars and buying Hong Kong dollars,' said the head of money markets at a large local bank. 'So last week, the HKMA (Hong Kong Monetary Authority) intervened and was buying U.S. dollars, to keep the Hong Kong dollar steady.' 

 But so far this week, the market has been mostly unchanged, he added, with no activity reported from the HKMA. 

 At the midday close, the Hang Seng index was up a meager 0.09 points to 12510.14 points.

title: Japan signs repo pacts with seven Asian nations.
text:
TOKYO, April 25 (Reuter) - Japan banded together with seven Asian partners on Thursday in a drive to provide liquidity and help stabilise foreign exchange markets in the region. 

 Japan's monetary authorities said they had signed a set of bilateral accords called repurchase agreements, or "repo pacts", with Australia, Hong Kong, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore and Thailand, that went into effect on Thursday. 

 The pacts give participants access to immediate cash -- for use to defend their currencies against excessive volatility -- by selling their holdings of U.S. government securities to a pact partner on a temporary basis with a promise to buy them back later. 

 Asian countries began mulling such arrangements after the 1994 Mexican peso crisis raised the spectre of similar speculative attacks on currencies in the fast-growing Asian economies. 

 The dollar jumped after the announcement, trading at just above 107 yen in Tokyo mid-afternoon trade after closing at around 106.56 yen in New York on Wednesday. 

 But currency dealers said that while the pacts would certainly provide some support for the dollar in the short term, they were unlikely to be a long-term factor. 

 "For now, its greatest value is to emphasise the cooperative relationship between Asian monetary authorities," one dealer said. 

 A Finance Ministry official told reporters the arrangements were meant to increase cooperation and were not specifically aimed at boosting the dollar. 

 In November, Australia, Hong Kong, Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand -- mindful of the potential economic damage that currency volatility can inflict -- signed similar agreements. 

 The Philippine central bank then said it would do so with Indonesia and Singapore, adding to the bilateral accords it forged last year with Hong Kong, Malaysia and Thailand. 

 In February, the Finance Ministry unveiled a pact allowing Japan's central bank to ask its counterparts in Singapore and Hong Kong to intervene on its behalf in dollar/yen trade in their markets, a move that some in the ministry were keen to portray as a step toward closer Asian currency cooperation. 

 Japan's Finance Ministry said in its statement announcing the pacts on Thursday that Japan's monetary authorities believed the latest moves would "further enhance mutual cooperation amongst Asian monetary authorities". 

 Japanese officials have said regional currency mechanisms like the repurchase pacts would be useful supplements to the leading role played by Washington and Tokyo in stabilising the key dollar/yen exchange rate and to that played by the Group of Seven leading industrialised nations.

title: Japan  currency  pact amounts to little - analysts.
text:
LONDON, Feb 20 (Reuter) - Hong Kong and Singapore's agreement to intervene on the Bank of Japan's behalf is of limited significance and will only lend modest support to the dollar, financial analysts said on Tuesday. 

 "There is little exceptional or substantive in this agreement," said Avinash Persaud, head of currency research at J.P. Morgan. 

 "The Asian central banks have not agreed to use their own reserves to support the Bank of Japan but merely to act on its behalf," he added. 

 He also noted that Japan already has similar agreements with a host of other central banks, including the Federal Reserve, but this did not stop dollar/yen falling below 100.00 last year. 

 But the announcement of the agreement -- coming as it did alongside aggressive BoJ intervention -- did give the dollar a boost, pushing it up two and half pfennigs/yen to around 1.4600 marks and 106.50 yen. 

 "The timing of the announcement was impeccable. Not only was it a holiday but it was when the dollar had fallen to 103-yen and at a time when the market had the potential to move the most," said Jiro Nagato, senior dealer at Sumitomo Bank. 

 Even if the timing of the announcement was aimed at giving dollar/yen a bit of a boost, the Bank of Japan itself was pouring cold water on the idea that the pact was aimed to rein in the yen. 

 A BoJ spokesman said Japan started discussions with Singapore and Hong Kong last year and the decision about the timing of the announcement was made last week and was regardless of market conditions. 

 Analysts said the impact of the BoJ buying and the pact was probably greater than it otherwise would have been because it had got the market speculating about G7 dollar intervention. 

 "Possibly one difference that BoJ intervention through Singapore or Hong Kong will have from intervention through the Bundesbank or Fed is disclosure," said Steve Barrow, economist at Chemical Bank. 

 He said very often when the BoJ intervenes through a G7 central bank the central bank involved is keen to tell the market that it is acting on behalf of the BoJ. 

 "Whether this will be the case when the BoJ go through Singapore or Hong Kong remains to be seen," he said. "If they keep quiet it might keep the market guessing and possibly make the intervention more effective." 

 There was certainly more talk of G7 intervention in the European market on Tuesday with traders speculating about the likelihood of a show of strength. 

 "They missed a golden opportunity late last week to get the dollar higher and now we are in a new lower trading range it will be more difficult to get it higher if they want to," said one trader. 

 "Maybe they will and maybe they won't. It's a tough one to call but people are ready for it and it's been the main topic of conversation in the dealing room this morning," she added. 

 Aside from possible intervention, the market will be closely watching Fed chairman Alan Greenspan's Humphrey-Hawkins testimony to congress. 

 His report on the current state of the U.S. economy is due to start at 1500 GMT and given the current confusion about growth his words will be carefully picked over. 

 "Greenspan cannot be too downbeat about growth prospects but he is sensitive to market concerns and may therefore seek to offer encouragement to easing hopes by again highlighting the real economy's current sluggishness," said Tim Fox, currency economist at Credit Suisse. 

 At 1140 GMT the dollar was 105.68/73 yen and 1.4510/15 marks, having drifted down gently from 106.08/17 and 1.4561/67 at the European opening. 

 It closed on Monday after a quiet session, with most of Asia and the U.S. on holiday, at 103.80/85 yen and 1.4428/38 marks.

title: HK dollar vulnerable to speculation -- Schroders.
text:
HONG KONG, Aug 23 (Reuter) - The possibility of a run on the Hong Kong dollar by speculators is higher than the government thinks, Schroder Securities economist Dong Tao said in a recent report. 

 "We believe there are many factors which place Hong Kong under speculators' scrutiny, even if it is not the weakest economy in the world," he said. 

 Some of these include a weakening economy in which the currency is fixed to a bigger and rebounding economy and the 1997 handover to China with its uncertainties. Since 1983, the Hong Kong dollar has been pegged at 7.8 to the U.S. dollar. 

 Regarding Hong Kong's fundamentals, Tao said the gross domestic product growth gap between the colony and the U.S. is shrinking while the inflation gap remains wide. 

 "More importantly, Hong Kong's balance of goods and services is forecast to turn to a deficit in 1996 for the first time since the introduction of the peg system," he said in a telephone interview. 

 He said the Hong Kong government argues that because Hong Kong does not have the weakest economy in the world, its currency is not a likely target for speculators. 

 "We feel the possibility of some speculation against the Hong Kong dollar is a lot bigger than the government claims," Tao said. 

 He said reasons why Hong Kong might be a target include the fact that Hong Kong residents can easily switch between local currency and foreign currency accounts, with very low transaction costs. 

 Also, while the Hong Kong Monetary Authority has an estimated US$53 billion in foreign reserves with which to defend the currency, the colony's defacto central bank has limited connections with other major central banks. 

 The HKMA's limited contacts with other central banks would make any effort at joint intervention to stem a run on the Hong Kong dollar difficult and slow "if in fact any support would arrive at all," he said. 

 In addition, Tao said a remote but real threat exists of externally generated "panic" selling of the Hong Kong dollar, for example as the result of unexpected political upheaval in China. 

 Despite these issues, he said the currency is likely to remain stable, particularly given the HKMA's large foreign currency cushion. 

 In his report, Tao said if a run on the Hong Kong dollar were to occur, there is a 75 percent chance the HKMA would successfully defend the currency by using its reserves. 

 The other possibility is that the speculation would trigger capital outflows by local and international fund managers, forcing the HKMA to raise short-term interest rates. 

 If higher rates did not stem the run, the HKMA would either re-peg the currency to the U.S. dollar, to a basket of currencies, to the yuan or let it float freely. 

 Tao said a re-peg to the U.S. dollar is the most likely outcome.--Hong Kong newsroom, (852) 2843-6441

title: Bankers say HK's Bank of China mulling CD issue.
text:
HONG KONG, Feb 8 (Reuter) - Banking sources said the Bank of China (BoC) in Hong Kong is considering a certificate of deposit (CD) issue but is concerned about the immaturity and general slack condition of the market here. 

 "The local CD market is not perfect and there are still a lot of defects," a banker close to the BoC, China's state-owned foreign currency bank, said. 

 "The BoC cannot issue CDs just because it want to have such an issue in the market," he added. 

 Banking sources said the BoC would make a decision next week on whether to issue the CDs. 

 They said market rumours suggested the bank was looking at an issue of up to HK$3.0 billion. 

 "There are internal discussions about the possibility of a CD issue but no decision has yet been made," the banker said. 

 He said there was no urgent need for the BoC to make a CD issue because its deposits exceeded loans. It would therefore have to decide on how to use any funds raised from such issues. 

 The BoC has not issued any CDs since November 1986 when its Macau branch launched a HK$100 million 5-year fixed rate CD. 

 In comparison with products such as equities, the secondary market for CDs is inactive. Only a limited number of banks participate in the CD market. 

 "If there was a better market, the BoC would have issued CDs last year," the banker said. 

 The response to ABN Amro Bank's HK$1.0 billion 5-year floating rate CD issue last month was thin, bankers said. 

 Only five banks participated, taking 39 percent of the issue leaving the four arrangers with HK$152.5 million each, they said. 

 Some bankers attributed the tepid response to pricing, which was set before the recent squeeze in the interbank market when the Hong Kong Monetary Authority intervened from January 12 to protect the Hong Kong dollar and pushed short-term interbank rates to over 10 percent. 

 Rates moved down to around six percent in late January. 

 An arranger for a Citibank Floating Rate CD (FRCD) issue said the syndication of its HK$1.0 billion three- and five-year Floating Rate CDs had been extended for three more working days to February 15. 

 "It is normal that banks would take a more conservative approach after making substantial losses during the squeeze," a local banker said. 

 "They are still licking their wounds," he said. 

 An arranger for Generale Belgian Bank's current HK$1.0 billion issue said response to the issue was relatively slow. Allocation is expected on Monday. He attributed the slow response to a lack of appetite after several recent issues. 

 Hong Kong dollar-denominated capital market issues, mostly FRCDs, flooded the market last year, amounting to HK$55 billion, a 285 percent increase on the year. 

 Among them were the Hongkong and Shanghai Bank's three-year FRCD which raised HK$3.2 billion last September, followed by Hang Seng Bank's three-year HK$2.1 billion issue and Standard Chartered Bank's five-year HK$2.5 billion issue. 

 The Bank of East Asia also issued a HK$1.0 billion step-up bond arranged by Merrill Lynch. 

 "People will now think twice about whether it is sensible to acquire that many long-term facilities," the local banker said.

title: HK dollar barely moves after local rate hike.
text:
HONG KONG, Feb 2 (Reuter) - The Hong Kong dollar, which has come under speculative attack recently, barely moved after the Monetary Authority raised interest rates on Thursday morning in line with Wednesday's hikes in U.S. rates. 

 Acting on a public holiday, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, the colony's de facto central bank, raised the Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF) rate or discount window by 0.5 percentage point, keeping pace with the rise in U.S. rates. 

 It was the fourth rise in rates in the past year by the Monetary Authority, whose main objective is to maintain currency stability. 

 Though Hong Kong banks were officially closed for the three day Lunar New Year festivities, there has been some trading in Hong Kong dollars, said dealers working during the break. 

 The Hong Kong dollar was quoted on Thursday afternoon at HK$7.7320/40 to the U.S. dollar, little changed from HK$7.7315/35 on Monday ahead of the three-day holiday. 

 In mid January, the Hong Kong dollar was attacked when investors feared that all emerging markets could be unhinged by a Mexican-peso style financial crisis. 

 The Monetary Authority forced up interbank rates on at least three occasions to stem the colony's currency outflow. 

 The intervention raised the Hong Kong dollar from an 18-month intra-day low of HK$7.7721. 

 Hong Kong's interest rates must track U.S. rates in order to maintain the local currency's peg to the U.S. dollar. 

 The Monetary Authority said it increased the LAF by 0.5 percentage point effective immediately. 

 The LAF bid and offer rates were raised to 4.25 percent and 6.25 percent, from 3.75 percent and 5.75 percent. 

 Hong Kong rates were previously raised on November 16, 1994.

title: HK  Central Bank  Declares  Currency  Stability: Amplifier
text:
by JAMES T. AREDDY 

 HONG KONG (AP-DJ)--Central bankers at the Hong Kong Monetary Authority on Friday claimed success in stabilizing the Hong Kong dollar after they faced down speculators for the second straight day. 

 With the Hong Kong dollar securely pegged to the U.S. dollar, no one seriously expects a breakdown in the system. 

 Nevertheless, at least in the short-term, currency turbulence will continue to haunt Hong Kong and other Asian countries, and the Monetary Authority will be forced back into the market, according to traders and economists. 

 The results of Friday's heavy-handed intervention in Hong Kong's money market - double-digit money market interest rates and a resurgent currency - burned speculators who sold the Hong Kong dollar short, participants agree. 

 Other Hong Kong dollar markets were also upset by the uncertainty surrounding the currency Friday. Some well-known bond brokers, for example, refused to quote prices on local currency debt because 'people don't know how to quote' in such a roller-coaster market, said Virginia Poon, Chase Manhattan Asia Ltd.'s head of Asian syndications. 

 The fact that the central bank could reverse its tight stance in Hong Kong's money markets by late Friday underscored the success of the Monetary Authority's actions, said Julia Leung, a spokeswoman for the quasi-central bank. 

 Standard Chartered Bank General Manager Ian Wilson said he hopes the market understands that the Monetary Authority is 'prepared to safeguard the Hong Kong currency.' 

 However, he added, 'who can say what is in a speculator's mind? I imagine if they see an opportunity they will try to gain from it.'

title: Hong Kong intervenes  to stabilise  currency .
text:
HONG KONG, Jan 12 (Reuter) - Hong Kong's monetary authorities intervened in the local currency markets during trading on Thursday which saw the Hong Kong dollar hit an 18-month intra-day low. 

 The Hong Kong dollar, which is officially pegged to the U.S. dollar at 7.8 normally trades in an extremely tight range stronger than the peg rate. 

 It has traded at the 7.75-76 level during most of this week, but sank to 7.7721 on Thursday afternoon. 

 It closed at 7.7710/40, but recovered slightly in European trading. 

 "This is the first time in two years that the local dollar fluctuated wildly," a Hong Kong dealer said. 

 Hong Kong's de facto central bank, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA), stepped in Thursday morning by withdrawing a total of HK$5.42 billion ($690 million) from the banking system. 

 It added funds again in the afternoon, leaving net withdrawls of HK$659 million ($84 million). 

 "With the easing of the Hong Kong dollar rate, we find it necessary to move the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate closer to the LAF (Liquidity Adjustment Facility) offer rate," said a HKMA spokeswoman. 

 "This means the authority is standing out to defend the Hong Kong dollar," said a dealer with a European bank. 

 Analysts said the Hong Kong government's policy was to avoid speculative movements in the dollar's rate, and this is why it intervened. 

 "These are strong gestures from the HKMA but it doesn't cap the market immediately...it takes the market some time, maybe a week or two (before the HKMA's actions take effect)," said Davy Kwan, first vice president at the International Bank of Asia. 

 Brokers and analysts said the local currency has weakened on a combination of speculation, pre-Lunar New Year seasonal demand and an outflow of foreign capital following poor stock market performance. 

 Hong Kong's blue-chip Hang Seng has fallen 772.99 points or 9.4 percent since the beginning of the year. It has also dropped more than a third from its peak during 1994. 

 "A lot of hot money has been flowing out of Hong Kong so some banks are quite short of U.S. dollars," said a dealer with an American bank.

title: HK dollar brushes against key support at HK$7.75.
text:
HONG KONG, April 3 (Reuters) - The Hong Kong dollar brushed against the key support level of 7.75 per U.S. dollar in early Friday trade, a level that dealers say would trigger intervention by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA). 

 "The Hong Kong dollar is stable and we do not comment on money market operations," said a spokeswomen at the HKMA. 

 "At least one foreign exchange deal was transacted at HK$7.75 per U.S. dollar, but there is no major break below that level" a senior dealer at a major bank said. 

 The Hong Kong dollar was quoted at HK$7.7498/01 per U.S. dollar at 0230 GMT, slightly weaker than HK$7.7493/03 at the open and HK$7.7490/00 at Friday's close. 

 The three-month rose by at least 50 points to 270-300 points at 0225 GMT versus 220-270 at the open and 230-260 at Thursday's close. 

 The six-month was up at 880-930 points versus 750-800 points at the open and 775-830 at the close. 

 "The local money market was becoming uneasy as the Japanese yen broke its key support at 134 per U.S. dollar, but market participants were less panicky than they were last October," another senior dealer at a note-issuing bank said. 

 "There is no major selling of the Hong Kong dollar spot," he said. 

 Dealers said that while they saw bids on forwards rising, as more participants took a short position against the Hong Kong dollar on fear of a spillover effect from the yen, the upside on dollar forwards would be capped by increasing offers on profit-taking. 

 "Many players who had gone long in forwards a few weeks ago, as forwards rates plunged to pre-Asian crisis levels, are looking for an opportunity to cover their positions," a dealer said. 

 Frederic Laine, head of interest rate and derivative trading at Credit Lyonnais, said he believed forwards would be range-bound and he did not see any major selling on the Hong Kong dollar spot. 

 Dealers said they heard that more than one note-issuing bank was on the bid side of the Hong Kong dollar spot and was believed to be acting on behalf of the Hong Kong Monetary Authority in a bid to cap the strength of the U.S. dollar. 

 Local term money rates were moderately firmer across the board partly on routine demand ahead of a long weekend. 

 Hong Kong financial markets will be closed on April 6 for a public holiday and will reopen from April 7-9 before closing again on April 10 and 13 for the Easter holidays. 

 "Interbank liqudity was tighter than yesterday but still abundant especially at the short end," a dealer said. 

 Overnight rates remained below five percent, quoted at 4.43-4.93 percent versus 4.68-4.75 at Thursday's close. 

 The one-month was moderately firmer at 5.87-6.0 versus 5.46-5.60 at the close. 

 The three-month was higher at 7.18-7.37 versus 6.75-7.00 at the close. The six-month was firmer at 7.75-8.12 versus 7.50-7.75 at the close. 

 Dealers said they were waiting for Europe and New York to start trading later on Friday for clues on market direction. 

 "Forward rates could firm up once London starts trading, as overseas traders tend to have a bearish view on the Hong Kong dollar," a dealer said. 

 But they said banks in Hong Kong were increasingly cautious about lending large amounts of Hong Kong dollars to speculators to fund positions on fears of being penalised by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority. 

 The HKMA said in October it would levy penal rates on banks that repeatedly borrowed from its Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF) or discount window on views that these funds would be used to fund speculative attacks on the currency.
