text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--The Hong Kong dollar is slightly lower in early trade, but is under pressure from falling interbank rates and close to a key support level, traders said. 

 Around 0230 GMT (9:30 p.m. EST), the Hong Kong dollar is quoted at HK$7.7486 against the U.S. dollar, slightly lower than HK$7.7488 late Thursday. 

 The Hong Kong dollar has traded in a narrow range of HK$7.7485 and HK$7.7488 so far Friday. 

 Traders said they're waiting to see if the Hong Kong dollar spot rate pushes close to HK$7.7500, believed to be an intervention point for the Hong Kong Monetary Authority. The HKMA declined to comment on whether it's an intervention point. 

 They said the HKMA was in a difficult position - trying to bring down interbank rates to pre-currency crisis levels without eroding the Hong Kong dollar. 

 'Traders are asking, `will the HKMA be there' (at HK$7.75)?' said one dealer with a local bank. 'What can it do? It's trying to bring (interbank) rates down while protecting the Hong Kong dollar.' 

 The volatile overnight Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates is quoted at 4.00%, compared with 4.125% late during the previous session. The three-month rate is 6.375%, down from 6.50% late Thursday.

title: HK Dollar Weakens, Edging Closer To  Intervention  Level
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--The Hong Kong dollar was weaker late Thursday on steady low interbank market rates. 

 Dealers cited more buying activities on the forward currency market. 

 Around 0845 GMT (3:45 a.m. EST), the Hong Kong dollar was quoted at HK$7.7488 against the U.S. dollar, weaker than HK$7.7478 late Wednesday. The Hong Kong dollar traded in a range of HK$7.7472 and HK$7.7488 Thursday. 

 The Hong Kong dollar rate is edging slowly closer to the level at which the Hong Kong Monetary Authority is likely to intervene, generally believed to be HK$7.7500. 'So there is no incentive to trade the spot market because Hong Kong dollar can't get any weaker,' a dealer at a local bank said. 

 While the spot market trading is thin, there's more activity in the forward market. Dealers said the low premiums have attracted some buyers. 

 'It is better to buy in the forward market so as to profit from any likely increases in forward premiums,' a dealer at a U.S. bank said. 

 The one-month premium has now been sitting below 10 points for most of the week, after ending January at 106 points, while the three-month premium is under 200 points, after closing January at 1339 points. 

 The one-month premium is at nine points, up from five points late Wednesday. The three-month premium is at 180 points, unchanged. The six-month premium is at 790 points, up from 780 points, and the one-year is unchanged at 2400 points. 

 The overnight Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates is quoted at 4.125%, unchanged from Wednesday, while the three-month rate is at 6.5%, also unchanged.

title: HK Dollar Stable Despite Rupiah's Tumble; Forwards Ease
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--The Hong Kong dollar remained stable Monday morning despite concern over the Indonesia rupiah's fall after the International Monetary Fund's decision to delay disbursing assistance funds. 

 Around 0415 GMT (11:15 p.m. EST Sunday), the Hong Kong dollar is quoted by the Bank of China at HK$7.7440 per U.S. dollar, weakened mildly from 7.7437 last Friday. 

 The U.S. unit has traded in a range of HK$7.7428 and HK$7.7450 so far Monday. 

 The local currency started at HK$7.7428 early before weakening to HK$7.7440 per U.S. dollar. 

 'There was initial concern over the rupiah's fall against the U.S. dollar but it was subsequently digested,' a dealer at a Chinese bank said. 

 At 0237 GMT (9:37 p.m. EST), the rupiah was trading at 11,550 rupiah (IDR) to the U.S dollar, lower than its close last week at IDR10,900. 

 The present level of the Hong Kong dollar is expected to be sustainable as the overnight rate of 4.5% commands a premium of 1.0 percentage point over the U.S. dollar. 

 The interest rate differential has encouraged arbitrage activities, as the two currencies are pegged. 

 The arbitrage is likely to stop as the local currency edges close to HK$7.7500 per U.S. dollar, a level that is believed would trigger the Hong Kong central bank's intervention. 

 In the forward foreign exchange market, the one-month premium is quoted at 85 points, down from 110 points previously. The three-month premium is quoted at 460 points, compared with 530 points late during the previous session. 

 'There were a couple of big-name banks lending in the market, pulling down the forward premiums,' the dealer said.

title: HK Dollar Down Midday On Falling Rates, Indonesia Worries
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--The Hong Kong dollar is continuing its move to weaker levels Thursday as interbank rates remain soft and investors display renewed concerns about Indonesia's political and financial situation. 

 The U.S. dollar, also locally called the 'TT,' has pushed up above HK$7.7450 and is quoted at HK$7.7453 at 0335 GMT (10:35 p.m. EST, Wednesday). It was quoted at HK$7.7435 late Wednesday. 

 'As interest rates have moved lower, driving the 'TT' up a little bit, and there is still concern on the Asian currencies. There's the question of whether Asian currencies can recover from this crisis,' said a currency dealer at a European bank. 

 The dealer said arbitrage opportunities have all but disappeared as interbank rates have fallen this week, meaning the Hong Kong dollar has lost its luster. 

 Concerns that Indonesia will lose its International Monetary Fund bailout package if it proceeds with plans to introduce a currency board have also sparked a move into the U.S. dollar, the dealer said. 

 But forward foreign exchange premiums, usually the first signal of investor jitters in local currency, are nearly flat. They typically shoot up as investors rush to hedge local currency exposure. The one-month premium is quoted at 70 points, compared with 60 points late Wednesday, the three-month at 470 points from 480 points and the six-month at 1350 points from 1400 points. 

 The dealer said the U.S. dollar could test highs of HK$7.7480 later Thursday, but that investors will ease off as the dollar approaches HK$7.7500 on the belief that the Hong Kong Monetary Authority would intervene at that level.

title: FUND VIEW-Caution urged on Jakarta  currency  board.
text:
HONG KONG, Feb 15 (Reuters) - Asian fund managers have expressed a high degree of scepticism over proposals by Indonesia to introduce a currency board mechanism. 

 They said Indonesia needed confidence rather than a new monetary system to shore up the rupiah, now trading at 8,000 to the U.S. dollar after hitting a record low of 17,000 last month. 

 "Re-establishing confidence is of critical importance," said Marshall Mays, chief strategist at Nikko Securities. 

 Tough action to clean up rotten banks, proof that nepotism and corruption were things of the past and concrete steps to solve Indonesia's huge private sector debt problem were the only possible routes to a return in confidence, fund managers said. 

 "The real issue in Indonesia is how do we really progress, move forward on these issues, and I don't think they can be solved just by a different exchange rate mechanism," said Eugene Chung, chief Asian investment strategist at SBC Warburg. 

 Politics remained the key, the strategists said. 

 President Suharto appears to be backing a currency board as a quicker method of raising the value of the rupiah currency in a bid to bring down prices and help resolve the debt issue. 

 Some critics say vested interests in Indonesia see a pegged rupiah as a way of protecting their assets. 

 "It's hugely popular with the crowd in charge right now because they have a hope they can hold onto their goodies, where if they have to give up monopolies, do the right thing and restructure the system, they would suffer," said Mays. 

 A currency board would fix the rupiah to an external currency such as the U.S. dollar or Japanese yen, with full cash-backing for the amount of rupiah in circulation. 

 In theory, the Indonesian central bank would then forfeit control over monetary policy to the United States or Japan, implying lower rates along with a stable rupiah. 

 In practice, Asia's experience with fixed exchange rates has demonstrated investors' insistence on country risk premiums over and above the rates applied to the external currency. 

 "In Hong Kong, we know from experience that interest rates are a function of the risk premium," said Chung. 

 Those premiums made a substantial contribution to the Asian crisis. Huge and volatile U.S. dollar inflows seeking high interest and no currency risk ramped inflation throughout Asia, swelling credit and building unsustainable asset price bubbles. 

 Those asset bubbles collapsed like dominoes after Thailand devalued the baht last July 2, sparking rapid capital flight. 

 If Indonesia fixes its currency again, those inflows could return and repeat a process clearly identified as dangerous. 

 "The risk that people will borrow U.S. dollars again, assuming its guaranteed, is not inconsiderable," said Mays. 

 Foreign investors were also sceptical of Indonesia's political will to allow the currency board to work independently -- and independence would be key to its successful operation. 

 "We're not even sure we have that political will here in Hong Kong," said Chung. "In theory, things can work out beautifully but in practice, politics does matter unfortunately. Politics is everything in Asia." 

 Hong Kong has faced criticism for acting to ease the interest rate burden during speculative attacks on the Hong Kong dollar, pegged at a rate of HK$7.80 to the U.S. dollar. 

 Although most commentators supported the Hong Kong intervention, others argued the currency board should be allowed to work in total isolation from interference, with rates moving only according to market demand for the domestic currency. 

 The fear among foreign investors is that Indonesia will refuse to abide by the currency board when rates shoot high enough to damage corporate activity. 

 Instead of allowing higher rates to force economic adjustment -- bankruptcies or bank failures -- Indonesia could instead resort to printing money to maintain the status quo, the fund managers said.

title: HK Dollar Higher Late; Investors Relax As Asia Mkts Calm
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--Quiet markets in the rest of Asia are having a calming effect on the Hong Kong dollar, which has moved higher late Tuesday. 

 The U.S. dollar is trading at HK$7.7375 at 1000 GMT (5:00 a.m. EST), down from HK$7.393 late Monday. 

 Last week, investors tried to push the U.S. dollar below HK$7.7350 without success. On Monday and again on Tuesday morning, they tried to move the currency in the opposite direction. 

 But after the U.S. dollar failed to break above HK$7.7410 Tuesday morning on aggressive buying by European banks, investors took profits, dropping the U.S. dollar down to its current level. 

 The head of money markets at a U.S. bank said investors don't believe the U.S. dollar can break above HK$7.7500 without risking Hong KongMonetary Authority intervention. As a result, they're not pushing the currency much above HK$7.7400. 

 'When it stays at HK$7.7350-7.7400, it's a very comfortable level,' the money markets chief said. 

 The money markets chief said investors in the Hong Kong market aren't motivated to move much, with the rest of the region's markets fairly subdued. Investors have either locked in long U.S. dollar positions for safety's sake, or Hong Kong dollar positions for rate arbitrage. 

 Forward foreign exchange premiums continue to fall, with the one-month premium dropping to 70 points from 90 points late Monday, the three-month to 520 points from 640 points and the six-month premium to 1,450 points from 1,700 points.

title: EMERGING MARKETS - HK dollar must sink or swim.
text:
LONDON, Jan 13 (Reuters) - The Hong Kong authorities must either stick with their existing U.S. dollar peg or float the currency freely because there is no half way house, foreign analysts said on Tuesday. 

 The existence of such an alternative is probably illusory despite some speculation to the contrary this week, they said. 

 Traders in London said there was talk on Monday that the Hong Kong administration was privately mulling alternatives to its existing fixed exchange rate system, one that would not involve allowing markets complete freedom to set the rate. 

 But a one-step devaluation and refixing or the adoption of a managed depreciation, like the so-called crawling peg, would be unworkable, they said. A watering down of the strict currency board system, on the other hand, by means of capping market interest rates would only risk undermining confidence further. 

 If the existing peg was forced to go, the only practical option is to let the currency find its own level, even if this meant an overshoot. Most economists, however, are betting this route will be avoided - at least until there is some substantial correction to currencies of Hong Kong's beleaguered neighbours. 

 "In some respects the Hong Kong peg is working brilliantly and is doing exactly what it is supposed to do. The problem is it's very painful," said Peter Von Maydell, senior currency economist at UBS in London. Devaluation and deflation are direct substitutes." 

 Hong Kong's Hang Seng index of leading stocks fell 8.70 percent on Monday as interest rates rose amid fresh speculation about the durability of the local currency's fixed exchange rate peg just above 7.7 per U.S. dollar. 

 The peg has been in place since 1984 but the Hang Seng has lost more than half its value since August. 

 The relentless currency turbulence across Asia in the second half of 1997 damaged sentiment in Hong Kong too as a analysts reckon the currency has become anywhere between 10 percent and 40 percent overvalued because of currency collapses elsewhere in the region. 

 Abandoning the existing peg for some other form of managed system would be hard to operate, however. 

 "If they were to devalue and refix the rate lower there would be an automatic assumption that the peg would be broken again. Either interest rates would soar to reflect that lack of confidence or a float would be forced eventually," said Von Maydell at UBS. 

Currency pegs hinge on local and international confidence in their rigidity. Tamper with that in the slightest, analysts argue, and capital will stampede to the exit and cause an overshoot that is impossible to manage in the short-term. 

 "If you convince people that the peg is unassailable and then you alter the rate or the system, it is very hard to do anything except float," said Paul MacNamara, emerging markets economist at Julius Baer Investments. 

 The net result over time, however, of either adjusting the peg or floating is also higher local interest rates because the risk premium required to hold the currency would rise. 

 As a result, the authorities are prepared to stick with the devil they know for now in the hope markets will calm further and that the HK dollar will regain some lost competitiveness as the other regional currencies rebound in time. 

 But analysts said the growing worry amongst officials in Hong Kong about the impact on the stock market of high interest rates will continue to gnaw away at international and domestic confidence that the currency board is absolutely rigid. 

 The currency board system set up 14 years ago is aimed at guaranteeing the base money supply at a fixed rate by matching notes and coins one-for-one with foreign exchange reserves. As a result, market interest rates automatically rise when there is speculation against the currency. 

 Analysts said the system has been diluted in Hong Kong because the central bank has been intervening in the interest rate markets to prevent excessive rate rises hurting the stock market too much and ultimately damaging the banking system. 

 "There's been a lot of confusion in the market about what exactly the HKMA (Hong Kong Monetary Authority) is doing," said Carlos Daurignac, emerging markets strategist at Credit Agricole Indosuez. 

 "If it sticks by its currency board, then it should allow interest rates to adjust automatically. But by not doing this, it is watering down the whole system," said Daurignac. 

 "This undermines confidence in the willingness to maintain the whole system and to ultimately suffer the pain of a currency board," he said. "As a result, the urge to hedge will continue."

title: HK Dollar Weaker Late; Pulled Down By U.S., China Accounts
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--The Hong Kong dollar was weaker in late trading Thursday from levels a day ago, thrown off intraday highs reached in London and New York on U.S. dollar buying by U.S. and Chinese accounts. 

 Dealers said mainland banks were buying to get cheap U.S. dollars, while U.S. accounts may be trying to sell the Hong Kong dollars short. 

 Around 0906 GMT (4:06 a.m. EST), the U.S. dollar is quoted at HK$7.7460, up from HK$7.7360 late Wednesday. 

 'There were some orders which is why the TT (U.S. dollar against Hong Kong dollar) went lower last night,' a treasury chief at a foreign bank said. 'But I believe there's some speculators that are trying to go long the U.S. dollar so that's why the TT is going back up.' 

 In overnight trading, the Hong Kong dollar strengthened to HK$7.7300 to the U.S. dollar at one point on a combination of large U.S. dollar sell orders and possible intervention by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority. 

 One U.S. dollar sell order believed to be around US$2.0-3.0 billion is said to have forced the Hong Kong dollar to its global intraday high right when the London market opened Wednesday. 

 However, local television reports in Hong Kong said the HKMA intervened to strengthen the local currency, which has been hovering near the psychologically-important HK$7.7500 to the U.S. dollar level for several weeks. 

 An HKMA source, however, said the quasi-central bank has kept a 'passive' stance in the markets, acting only as a counterparty to those who want to cover short positions.

title: HK Dollar Weaker Early -2: HKMA Says It Was Passive Wed
text:
News reports in Hong Kong have claimed that the HKMA was intervening in the money markets and currency market in Hong Kong, or in the currency market in London. 

 But an HKMA source said the quasi-central bank was 'passive' Wednesday, merely supplying the Hong Kong dollars necessary for short position holders to exit markets. 

 There were rumors in the afternoon that there might be another bout of speculation against the Hong Kong dollar, the HKMA source said. 

 The source explained that interbank rates climbed because bankers were reluctant to lend for fear that a sudden spike would leave them unable to cover their positions. 

 Interbank rates are rising again Thursday. For more interbank-related news, see Dow Jones page [1085]. 

 In the forward market, where heavy hedging activity and speculation were believed to have been going on Wednesday, premiums have begun to steady. 

 That indicates that hedging of local currency exposure and speculative short-selling of the Hong Kong dollar have diminished. The result is a slightly less bearish outlook for the Hong Kong dollar than in previous days. 

 The three-month premium is quoted at 1,450 points, compared with 1,500 points late Wednesday. The six-month premium is at 3,300, up a touch from 3,100 points. But participants said it will fall later Thursday. 

 For the spot market, dealers said they expect a U.S. dollar trading range of HK$7.7400-80 for the rest of Thursday.

title: Equities Insight: HK Shrs Seen Mixed; Mild Rebound Likely
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--Hong Kong shares are seen opening mixed Thursday, with more downside than upside. 

 But the blue-chip Hang Seng Index is likely to move within a narrow range, and the market might be poised for a mild rebound later Thursday after a 5.9% plunge Wednesday, said traders. 

 'Yesterday (Wednesday), we were close to panic for a while. I don't think that today (Thursday) we will see the same kind of price movement, or volume,' said Nial Gooding, head of sales at Schroder Securities (HK) Ltd. 

 However, the deepening Asian financial crisis will continue to put investors on edge, and to put a cap on any rebound, Gooding noted. Several Southeast Asian currencies slumped to new lows for the third consecutive day Wednesday. 

 Traders said adding to the nervousness are media reports that the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, the de facto central bank, was seen intervening in London, or New York foreign exchange markets to prop up the Hong Kong dollar. 

 But Gooding said the currency worries have already been reflected in the local share market. So 'if there's no further bad news, the market should rebound a little bit today (Thursday)' as bargain hunting set in. 'All technical reviews show that the market is oversold.' 

 China-backed red chips and major developers' stocks appear to be most attractive to bargain hunters, as both sectors got hammered in the massive sell-off Wednesday. The red-chip Index tumbled 11% while the property sub-index dipped 8.4%. The blue-chip Hang Seng Index, meanwhile, ended down 596.90 points, or 5.9%, at 9538.61. 

 Wednesday's move puts the benchmark index down 1,184.15 points, or 11%, in the first week of 1998, compared to its close on New Year's Eve last Wednesday. 

 Meanwhile, overnight on Wall Street, the Dow Jones Industrial Average shed 3.98 points, ending at 7902.27 Wednesday.

title: HK Dollar Steadying In London, NY After Sudden Spike
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--The Hong Kong dollar has steadied at stronger levels in the London and New York centers Wednesday after spiking to intraday highs near the end of active trading in Hong Kong. 

 The U.S. dollar, also referred to as the 'TT,' is quoted at HK$7.7355 at around 1600 GMT, down sharply from HK$7.7500 late Tuesday and the HK$7.7495-98 level at which it traded for most of Wednesday in Hong Kong. 

 Late night television news reports in Hong Kong claimed the Hong KongMonetary Authority had intervened in the London and New York markets to support the Hong Kong dollar. 

 But a 'TT' dealer at a London-based bank said he has seen no sign of Hong Kong's quasi-central bank in either trading center. 

 He said the Hong Kong dollar actually spiked just after 0900 GMT, with the U.S. dollar briefly touching a low of HK$7.7300 on what market participants believe was one large U.S. dollar sell order that was well-timed to move the market. At 0900 GMT, most Hong Kong-based currency traders are closing up shop, and active trading in London hasn't quite begun. 

 'Basically, because of the timing, most liquidity had dried up, most Hong Kong banks were done for the day, and the European markets aren't so liquid,' he said. 

 He said he heard the U.S. dollar sell order was for between US$2.0-3.0 billion and came from a U.S. investment bank. 

 'The selling was very heavy,' he said.

title: HK Dollar Flat Late; U.S. Dlr Sell Orders At HK$7.7500
text:
HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--Despite steep falls in most Asian currencies, the Hong Kong dollar stayed extremely flat late Thursday as few traders dare weaken the local currency since it would most likely prompt strong government intervention. 

 Dealers said that while Hong Kong stock and bond markets are dropping in reaction to the deepening Asian currency crisis, traders are reluctant to take the Hong Kong dollar substantially past the HK$7.7500 per U.S. dollar level. 

 That's because the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, which is said to have been intervening aggressively in the past weeks, has sell orders right above that level, a reminder that any punt against the local currency will be met with stiff resistance. 

 Around GMT, the U.S. dollar is quoted at HK$7.7498, virtually flat from HK$7.7500 late Tuesday. 

 'It's no surprise the TT (U.S. dollar against the Hong Kong dollar) is so stable,' one money markets manager said. 'There's some selling interest at HK$7.7500. It's believed the government is up there to cap the (U.S. dollar's) rise. But we haven't seen the HKMA name in the market today.' 

 Market participants, however, are showing their jitters over the Hong Kong dollar in the forward exchange market where premiums have been rising steadily since the beginning of this week. 

 However, one local trader said the rise in premiums is a definite sign some players are amassing Hong Kong dollars for another possible attack on the domestic currency. 

 In the forward foreign exchange market, the six-month premium is quoted at 3,100 points from 2,350 points previously. The three-month premium is quoted at 1,500 points, compared with 1,050 points late during the previous session.

title: HK Early Hibor Sharply Higher on  Currency  Fears

title: FOCUS-Asian  currencies  take heart as yen surges.
text:
SINGAPORE, Dec 17 (Reuters) - Asian currencies calmed down a bit on Wednesday as the dollar dropped dramatically against the yen following the Bank of Japan's unexpected -- and repeated -- interventions and news of a massive Japanese income tax cut. 

 The dollar lost what had looked like a firm grip above the 131 yen level and fell as low as 125.85 yen in Tokyo trade. 

 But no one was prepared to predict the end of its reign over Asian currencies just yet. 

 "Overall, sentiment in the whole of Asia is still very fragile so what we're seeing today may just be a technical rebound. I think the dollar demand is very real," said Jacqueline Ong, regional economist at I.D.E.A. 

Currencies in Southeast Asia, where the region's economic crisis had its beginning, had a much better day. 

 The Philippine peso reversed course, the Singapore dollar recovered from a heavy fall, the Malaysian ringgit moved higher and the Indonesian rupiah stopped falling. 

 The peso bounced to 39.904/937 to the U.S. dollar at 0530 GMT after hitting an all-time low of 41.60 earlier. 

 Manila traders said the central bank was seen selling dollars heavily at various levels in an effort to counter dollar demand amid shrinking supply. 

 News the Bankers Association of the Philippines (BAP) and the central bank had agreed to set up a dollar pool to cover the requirements of oil companies and other corporations helped boost the peso, they said. 

Central bank governor Gabriel Singson said the bank had also agreed to enter into non-deliverable forward contracts with dollar borrowers to ease demand in the spot market. 

 The Singapore dollar also staged a recovery as talk of intervention in overnight trade and possibly early on Wednesday by the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), the de facto central bank, spooked the market. 

 It was quoted at 1.6885/915 to the U.S. dollar at 0530 GMT after firming through the 1.6800 level against a morning low of 1.7010. 

 "The MAS was in in London last night. When dollar/Sing got to a high of 1.7175, they were in selling," a senior regional currencies trader said. 

 "I heard they were in again through some local banks this morning. But then again, other local banks were bidding on the other side," he said. 

 The Singapore dollar caved in to mounting pressure and dived through the key 1.70 level in thin London trade on Tuesday, reaching lows not seen in over six years. 

 The sharp drop meant the once static currency had lost nearly seven percent in three trading days as poor year-end liquidity exaggerated movements. 

 Dealers and analysts said it remained in a downtrend but the market was likely to avoid the 1.70 level for the time being. 

 "They (the MAS) don't mind a weaker Sing. In fact, they'd welcome it for now, but not too fast," the dealer said. 

 The Malaysian ringgit also pulled back from its lows on the yen's rebound and on talk of foreign inflows to the stock market. It was at 3.8300/400 to the dollar against 3.8825/925 late on Tuesday. 

 Dealers said the thin market was keeping the ringgit volatile, with small volumes causing wild gyrations. 

 The Indonesian rupiah hovered between 5,450 and 5,600 to the dollar all morning as spreads narrowed to 50/100 points amid dwindling interest. 

 Dealers said the dollar maintained a firm undertone against the rupiah, which gained little mileage from news that President Suharto would attend a public function on Thursday. 

 Worries about his health have sent the rupiah spiralling to new lows in the past week. 

 The Thai baht was little changed at 47.80/48.00 to the dollar onshore against 47.60/48.10 late on Tuesday. The offshore rate stood at 46.65/85 against 46.90/47.20. 

 Dealers said they expected the baht to have a steadier day as regional currencies should gain from the yen's rise. 

 In north Asia, the South Korean won slipped for the first time this week due to dollar buying for importer settlements due early next week. 

 The won was at 1,505/10 to the dollar against Tuesday's 1,425 close, but dealers said its decline would be limited by fears of central bank intervention. 

 The Taiwan dollar continued to be driven by external factors, firming to T$32.644/669 against Tuesday's T$32.820 close as traders watched the yen rebound. 

 The Hong Kong dollar was protected from weakening through the 7.75 level to the U.S. dollar by thin year-end conditions and the yen's rise. 

 Dealers said the Hong Kong Monetary Authority did not appear to have intervened in the foreign exchange market, but it was seen offering three-month money in early trade. 

 A European bank dealer in Singapore said the ringgit's ability to hold above the 3.93 per dollar level for the second time on Tuesday suggested i 

 The Philippine peso and the Singapore dollar had the most volatile morning, both rebounding sharply against the U.S. dollar 

 Asian currencies posted fresh losses on Tuesday as persistent dollar demand and dwindling trading volumes sparked fresh carnage in foreign exchange markets. 

 Only the South Korean won defied logic, surging nearly 16 percent to highs of 1,350 against the dollar after the central bank decided late on Monday to scrap its 10 percent trading band. It ended at 1,425.0 against Monday's 1,563.9 close. 

 Dealers said the won was benefitting from expectations of heavy dollar inflows under the IMF's $57 billion bailout scheme for South Korea, which had moved players to unwind long dollar positions built during the won's near 50 percent drop last week. 

 The government's decision to float the won, as requested by the International Monetary Fund (IMF), sell off one or two troubled banks and push forward with a $10 billion sovereign bond issue boosted Korean financial markets on Tuesday. 

 But dealers said sentiment could quickly turn negative if more of the pledged IMF loans were not disbursed soon. 

 The won was also expected to face selling pressure from importers seeking dollars towards the weekend. 

 Its improved fortunes gave the Taiwan dollar an opening boost, but it soon shed the gains in the face of strong U.S. dollar demand from importers. 

 Taipei traders said there was also concern about the previously sturdy Singapore dollar's sharp falls, which triggered renewed fears of a competitive depreciation in the Taiwan dollar. 

 The Taiwan dollar ended at T$32.820 to the U.S. dollar, its lowest close since November 1987, against Monday's T$32.746 close. It hit a low of T$32.950. 

 Dealers said the central bank appeared to have intervened in the last minute of trade in a bid to keep its dollar above the psychological T$33 level. 

 The Hong Kong dollar remained on the cusp of the key 7.75 level to the U.S. dollar, but forwards eased in the wake of the won's rebound. 

 Dealers said the Hong Kong Monetary Authority was heard buying the local dollar via a major commercial bank to limit the U.S. dollar's rise. 

 Southeast Asian currencies were off their lows but remained weak and weary as companies scrambled to buy dollars to meet loan payments amid shrinking liquidity and widening spreads. 

 "There's just a lack of liquidity in the market. There are very few interbank players around so if you're buying, the whole world knows you're buying," said Jimmy Koh, regional economist at I.D.E.A. in Singapore. 

 "Given the widening spreads, the pace of depreciation is much faster. People are just extremely bearish on the region," he added. 

 Dealers said transaction volumes had fallen sharply as players sought to limit their exposure to growing market volatility towards the year end. 

 "In the middle of the year, people would trade something like 20 to 50 (million) dollars. But lately because of the volatility and the fact that the big figure changes so fast ... positions have been reduced to one to two (million) dollars," said a European bank dealer in Singapore. 

 The Indonesian rupiah recovered in late trade as attempts to test the 6,000 level failed, causing a pullback in the currency which was reinforced by central bank intervention. 

 It was at 5,500/600 to the dollar at 1020 GMT after Bank Indonesia sold dollars at 5,700, dealers said. The rupiah hit an early record low of 5,980 to the dollar. 

 Dealers said it remained fragile on lingering worries about President Suharto's health despite clear signs he was gradually resuming work after a period of rest and corporate difficulties in meeting debt payments. 

 They said liquidity had practically dried up and spreads of 200 or 300 points were exacerbating the rupiah's moves. 

 The Thai baht's abrupt recovery from a record low of 49.35 against the dollar sparked speculation of central bank support. 

 Bangkok dealers said exporters sold dollars around the 48 baht level, but the Thai unit remained weak at 47.50/48.00 to the dollar against 47.30/90 late on Monday. 

 Offshore baht was at 46.90/47.20 against 46.90/47.40. 

 Finance Minister Tarrin Nimmanahaeminda appealed to Thais to refrain from speculating against the baht and said the government would use the limited resources at hand to defend it. 

 The Philippine peso ended at a record low of 40.214 to the dollar against a previous 38.853 close despite intervention by the central bank. Further falls were only prevented by the activation of volatility bands. 

 Poor market liquidity -- total turnover was a mere $9.5 million -- did little for the peso's condition and dealers expected more declines. 

Central bank governor Gabriel Singson said the peso would only recover if people stopped speculating against it. 

 Dealers attributed the peso's steep drop to panic buying of dollars by firms with dollar exposures and importers hedging future dollar requirements. 

 A slowdown in remittances from overseas contract workers was also contributing to the shortage of dollars. 

 The Singapore dollar fell within a hair's breadth of the key 1.70 level to the U.S. dollar, but fears of central bank intervention pulled it back from the edge, dealers said. 

 It was at its weakest in more than six years at 1.6935/55 to the U.S. dollar at 1020 GMT after hitting a low of 1.6995. Late on Monday it was at 1.6835/65. 

 There was no consensus among dealers about the likelihood of the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) selling U.S. dollars above the 1.70 level, or over whether it was behind a spurt of dollar sales that pushed the Singapore dollar up to an early high of 1.6660. 

 "I think they were in at least once or twice this morning, but it didn't really help because dollar/Sing is still biddish," a U.S. bank dealer said. 

 I.D.E.A.'s Koh was skeptical about the MAS intervening given the sharp falls in other regional currencies. 

 "The authorities have affirmed again and again that they look at the Singapore dollar, not just against the U.S. dollar, but on a trade-weighted basis," he said. 

 The MAS declined to confirm rumours about an intervention. 

 The Malaysian ringgit recovered as players took profit on the dollar's gains after the rupiah rose on Bank Indonesia's intervention. 

 It firmed to 3.8825/925 to the dollar against 3.9025/125 late on Monday.

title: HK Late Hibor: Rates Edge Down On Liquidity, Stable HK$
text:

title: No won-linked speculation on HK dlr - HKMA's Yam.
text:
HONG KONG, Nov 19 (Reuters) - Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) chief Joseph Yam said on Wednesday the territory's de facto central bank had detected no Hong Kong dollar speculation linked to the slide in the South Korean won. 

 "I haven't heard or seen anything that suggests people are borrowing quite a lot of Hong Kong dollars so they can take advantage of a particular event to short the Hong Kong dollar," Yam told reporters at a briefing. 

 Although the overnight rate has returned to about five percent from 300 percent during attacks on the Hong Kong dollar in October, long-term rates remain high, reflecting an increased Asian risk premium following contagious currency speculation, Yam said. 

 "I expect these rates to come down further but if there is yet another event in the region, for example in Korea, then sentiment may turn again and banks may become more cautious," he said. 

 The recent currency attack started in earnest on October 21 with massive selling of Hong Kong dollars for U.S. dollars, Yam said. Selling of Hong Kong dollars increased on October 22. 

 But on October 23, now known as Black Thursday due to the largest one-day point fall in the history of the blue-chip Hang Seng Index, Hong Kong banks were required to give the HKMA nearly HK$5 billion to settle their U.S. dollar transactions. 

 This left less than HK$1 billion in the banking system, Yam said. 

 "On Thursday (October 23), the net amount of balance, Hong Kong dollar balance in all accounts in all banks in Hong Kong was only about less than HK$1 billion, about HK$500 million or so," he said. 

 According to Hong Kong's currency board system requiring full U.S.-dollar backing for all Hong Kong currency in circulation, Hong Kong banks were left without local currency to settle Hong Kong-U.S. dollar trades. 

 This persuaded Hong Kong banks to bid up the overnight rate to 300 percent in a mad scramble for Hong Kong dollars, quickly forcing banks back to the HKMA to sell U.S. dollars to raise Hong Kong dollars to settle their earlier transactions. 

 Yam said the overnight rate might have gone as high as 1,000 percent had the HKMA not opted to lend banks Hong Kong dollars in advance of U.S. dollar transactions. 

 "We made exceptions and we actually did these foreign exchange deals for value the same day," Yam said. 

 "I also...started lending the money to them in order to relieve them for the weekend, in other words, creating Hong Kong dollars and lending to them over the weekend. In advance of settlement, I was actually providing money to the market." 

 This "discretion" earned the HKMA some criticism for interfering in the "auto-pilot" currency board mechanism and accusations that it squeezed rates so hard it added momentum to the Hong Kong stock market fall. 

 "We did not exercise that much discretion," Yam said. 

 "We are the lender of last resort," he added. "And if I had not done anything, the interest rates could have gone up to maybe 1,000 percent." 

 Hong Kong's foreign exchange reserves at the end of October increased rather than declined as a result of HKMA intervention during the attack, Yam said. 

 The end of October figures have yet to be released. 

 Yam, who stressed repeatedly Hong Kong's commitment to maintaining the currency link to the U.S. dollar, also said the HKMA did not intervene in the currency forward market.

title: FOCUS-Asian  currencies  uninspired as dollar drops.
text:
SINGAPORE, Nov 13 (Reuters) - Most Asian currencies softened on Thursday while the Indonesian rupiah found itself torn between its central bank and companies seeking dollars. 

 Dealers said IMF Managing Director Michel Camdessus's calming words about Southeast Asia's efforts to pull out of months of economic turmoil were largely ignored by the market. 

 Camdessus, on a tour of Southeast Asia, said he believed Asia would quickly rebound from its current crisis and should be able to return to high rates of economic growth. 

 He said Thailand had passed its first IMF review while Hong Kong and Malaysian banks were unlikely to face a crisis. 

 He also said Malaysia was in solid economic condition, though its current account gap was still on "the higher side". 

 In Indonesia, the rupiah was pushed to a high of 3,355 to the dollar in early trade on talk Bank Indonesia had sold dollars above the 3,400 level in Jakarta and Singapore markets. 

 But there was no official confirmation of the intervention and no clear sign the central banks of Japan and Singapore were involved in the operation, as was the case twice last week. 

 The rupiah drifted lower on dollar demand from offshore parties, especially Japanese companies, in afternoon trade. It was quoted at 3,400/10 to the dollar at 1010 GMT amid vague talk Bank Indonesia had checked rates above the 3,400 level again. 

 "We heard BI had been checking rates for the third time but I'm not sure if they actually sold dollars," a U.S. bank dealer in Singapore said. 

 "I don't think BI coming in alone would scare the market. It's unlikely they'll have that much effect unless they come in with the Bank of Japan (BOJ) and Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS)," she added. 

 The Japanese finance ministry and the MAS declined to comment on whether the BOJ had taken part in the intervention. 

 Other Asian currencies looked soft but dealers said the market lacked energy as many players were winding down for the end of the year and the dollar's abrupt drop against the yen on talk of BOJ intervention also dominated interest. 

 In Thailand, the baht was steady but weak at 38.70/80 to the dollar against 38.55/65 late on Wednesday. The offshore rate was at 38.30/31 against 37.999/00. 

 Dealers said the market was awaiting the announcement of Thai Prime Minister Chuan Leekpai's new cabinet. Chuan was due to present his cabinet list for approval to King Bhumibol Adulyadej later on Thursday. 

 Dealers said the baht did not react to comments by the IMF's Camdessus that the Fund had no plans to make changes to Thailand's economic programme. 

 In Bangkok, Supachai Panitchpakdi, expected to be named deputy premier in charge of economic affairs in the new cabinet, appeared to echo the IMF chief's statements. 

 He said Thailand did not intend to renegotiate the terms of the IMF-led $17.2 billion economic bailout package. 

 The Singapore dollar eased to 1.5795/10 to the U.S. dollar against 1.5746/66 on Wednesday on buying of the Malaysian ringgit/Singapore dollar cross. 

 "There's been some ringgit/Sing buying going through. There's talk that the cross might go to 50 cents but I think it has to break 48.20 first," a European bank dealer said. 

 The ringgit was at 47.70/89 Singapore cents at 1010 GMT. 

 Across the border, the ringgit showed little sign of stirring out of the range it has established against the U.S. dollar in recent sessions, hovering around 3.3000/100. 

 The Philippine peso ended lower at 33.93 per dollar against a previous close of 33.43 on dollar short-covering and offshore dollar demand. 

 Dealers said the central bank intervened to sell about $4 million at 33.98 pesos in late trade, but further falls were expected to be capped by inflows from overseas contract workers. 

 In north Asia, the Korean won ended up at 986.70 to the dollar as the central bank kept to its staunch defence, selling dollars at 988.00 won in opening trade while repeating its daily words of support. 

 "Our stance to maintain the won steadily stronger has not changed," said Lee Eung-baek, chief of the central bank's foreign exchange division. 

 The Bank of Korea has moved its defence line up by one won to the dollar for each of the last two days, steering the embattled currency away from the 1,000 level eyed by the market. 

 But its actions have taken their toll on the money market where the overnight call loan rate hit a yearly high of 14.90 percent on Thursday. 

 Seoul traders said the market was awaiting a government package of measures to stabilise financial markets. 

 The Taiwan dollar slid to T$31.105 against its previous T$30.992 close on jitters about the weak yen and won. 

 After the market close, the central bank said there was no change in its monetary policy for the time being and it reserved the right to intervene in forex market when needed. 

 The Hong Kong dollar ended lower at 7.7320/40 to the U.S. dollar from Wednesday's 7.7300/10 close as interest rates eased. 

 Dealers said liquidity improved after the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) clarified its rules on borrowing from its discount window. 

 On October 23, the HKMA had said it would levy penal rates on "repeated borrowers" at the window, making banks wary of tapping the facility and leading to a liquidity crunch. 

 The HKMA said on Thursday repeated borrowers are licensed banks which have borrowed through the facility on eight occasions in any period of 25 days or on four consecutive days in which the window is open.

title: China offers  Hong Kong  support, shuns  intervention .
text:
SHANGHAI, Oct 29 (Reuters) - China's communist leaders have offered soothing pledges of confidence amid Hong Kong's stock turmoil but have shunned intervention, leaving freewheeling markets to sort out problems on their own. 

 Their laissez faire stance in this first crisis since Beijing recovered the former British colony on July 1 has earned them high marks -- in this case at least -- for keeping their promise of a high degree of autonomy, analysts said on Wednesday. 

 Their style has also contrasted dramatically with the name-calling and finger-pointing of Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad, who has found a host of foreign forces to blame for a crisis that has dealt a blow to financial markets around the world. 

 "They have made all the right noises," said Richard Margolis, first vice president, research, at Merrill Lynch Asia Pacific, speaking of China's leaders. 

 "They have offered general support and have said they will leave Hong Kong to sort out its own problems," he said from Hong Kong. 

 Hong Kong's stock market had staggered under successive waves of selling, triggered by regional financial worries that have since spread to Wall Street. 

 Hong Kong's blue chip Hang Seng index sank a stunning 13.7 percent on Tuesday after a 5.8 percent drop on Monday, though it came roaring back with an 18 percent gain late on Wednesday. 

 While many critics in Hong Kong have viewed with scepticism China's "one country, two system" formula for Hong Kong -- in this case Beijing has been holding to its end of the bargain. 

 "On this test, it's been passed," said Margolis. 

 China's central bank has made it known it had weapons in its arsenal -- $134.07 billion in foreign currency reserves -- and was ready to offer support if needed. 

 President Jiang Zemin, speaking in the United States, said he had confidence in Hong Kong, echoing statements of the former colony's own leaders. 

 "China has handled the situation very well; it has left Hong Kong to handle its own problems," said Francis Leung, group managing director, Peregrine Investment Holdings Ltd. 

 "But senior Chinese officials have said openly if Hong Kong wants China's help, they are ready to help at any time." 

 Beijing has not been shy of intervening in its own unruly markets but it has felt content to keep a watchful eye on developments this time around. 

 China's tightly controlled news media has reported on the financial crisis but has avoided placing the blame on foreign speculators. 

 Qiu Xiaohua, chief economist at the State Statistical Bureau, told reporters the best weapon China had was to ensure its own economy remained on a sound footing, saying that would support Hong Kong. 

 Other Chinese economists agreed this was the right approach. 

 "Hong Kong's problems are temporary," said Yang Qixian of the State Commission for Restructuring the Economy, speaking from Beijing. 

 "I think Hong Kong can resolve its problems itself. And under the 'one country, two systems' formula we can't use mainland methods to deal with Hong Kong problems."

title: Hong Kong to survive speculative attacks - Greenwood.
text:
SINGAPORE, Oct 28 (Reuters) - Investors should not be too alarmist about the impact that recent speculative attacks on the Hong Kong dollar will have on the territory's economy, LGT Asset Management chief economist John Greenwood said on Tuesday. 

 Greenwood, the architect of the Hong Kong currency peg to the U.S. dollar, told a conference the Hong Kong economy was flexible enough to weather the fluctuations and the peg would survive the speculative attacks. 

 "I doubt Hong Kong will suffer the same downturn like Thailand," he said. 

 "The Hong Kong dollar is pegged by the means of a currency board. Currency boards are inherently stronger than central bank pegs," Greenwood said later in an interview with Reuters Financial Television (RFTV). 

 "Fundamentally, the Hong Kong authorities have reserves six or seven times greater than the issued currency notes," he said. 

 "More importantly, the monetary authority does not have to use its currency reserves to protect the currency. Under the current system, what happens is the whole economy adjusts to the exchange rate rather than the other way around," he said. 

 Asked if a sustained attack on the currency would hurt the economy, Greenwood said defending the Hong Kong currency would mean pushing interest rates up, which would attract money from abroad. 

 "The rates would have to stay up for several months in order to do any real damage to the economy," Greenwood said. 

 "I don't believe that a few days or weeks of high rates would do any significant damage to the economy. The high rates are only in the inter-bank market and have not percolated to rates for mortgages," he added. 

 Greenwood dismissed suggestions the Hong Kong dollar had to be devalued for the economy to stay competitive against other Asian countries which saw their currency values slashed drastically against the U.S. dollar in recent months. 

 Governments should put in place micro and macro policies and restore investors' confidence instead of adopting an interventionist approach, he said. 

 Greenwood said he expected the Hong Kong market would continue to see further adjustments in equities and property prices as interest rates changed. 

 "However, typically these interest rates adjustments last for weeks, not months. I would expect the same kind of thing on this occasion. The only caveat to that scenario is if we have continuing problems in the ASEAN region which have knock-on effects on Asia, then that will affect Hong Kong," he said. 

 ASEAN, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, groups Brunei, Burma, Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam. 

 Greenwood said he believed Wall Street's 7.18 percent plunge on Monday to 7,161.15 was a "short-term blow but not an end to a bull economy". 

 "It is a temporary event, a stock market event rather than an economic event," Greenwood said. 

 U.S. economic fundamentals would remain sound amid low inflationary pressure, he said.

title: Central Bank  Eased Grip On Hong Kong Rates During Tuesday's Turmoil
text:
HONG KONG -(Dow Jones)- The Hong Kong Monetary Authority eased its tight grip on credit conditions in the money markets Tuesday, in an apparent effort to ease pressure on the territory's battered banks. 

 There was little evidence of speculative attack on the Hong Kong dollar during the session, further reducing the need for high interest rates, said traders. 

 Even before stock trading began in the morning, the quasi-central bank was seen lending money overnight at rates as low as 5.0%. Almost a week ago, the HKMA's strategy to defend the Hong Kong dollar from speculative attack resulted in money market rates shooting to 300%. 

 "The HKMA was more aggressively lending money because of the impact on the stock market of shaken confidence from high rates," said a trader with a U.S. bank. 

 Market participants said the HKMA was signaling Tuesday that it wanted the overnight Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate at 7.00%. Officially, after a weekend rate hike, the HKMA targets the overnight HIBOR at between 4.00% to 7.00%. 

 The authority itself declined to comment on its market activity, but participants said it also offered enough one-week money to drop the one-week HIBOR to 13% from late Monday's level of 20%. 

 "We have observed that the HKMA has been in the market all day offering liquidity to the banking system. It was providing a signal to the market that it wouldn't like to see interbank rates high for a long time," said the head of treasury at a domestic bank. 

 While the rates have since eased, they remain above levels seen before the markets turmoil began last week, and money market players said they aren't convinced the lower levels are here to stay. 

 The Hang Seng Index, the leading measure of share price movements in Hong Kong, fell 14% on Tuesday to 9059.89. 

 There was less impact from the HKMA's activity at the longer end of the money market, where rates remained in the middle to high-teens. The three-month rate remained at 16% and the one year HIBOR stood at 15%, well above equivalent U.S. dollar interbank rates, though down of the levels seen at the top of the crisis last week. 

 Because rates remained high for longer terms, the Hong Kong dollar was little affected by the HKMA's money market easing, traders said. 

 The U.S. dollar was higher amid Tuesday's stock selling, even amid apparent direct intervention from the HKMA. It was quoted at HK$7.7325 in late trading, from HK$7.7300 around the same time Monday. 

 The U.S. bank trader said that the HKMA was buying Hong Kong dollars, but he didn't know how much it was intervening. Other participants said they saw no signs that the authority was directly intervening on Tuesday. 

 In fact, the Hong Kong-based bank's treasurer said that the steadying Hong Kong dollar on Tuesday confirmed to him that the currency hadn't really come under significant selling pressure last week. He said the HKMA overreacted, endangering asset values in the territory, such as properties and stocks. 

 "Today confirmed my view that the attack on the Hong Kong dollar has been minimal. The HKMA wanted to prove the government has the power and ability to maintain the pegged rate system. They succeeded in crashing the stock market," he said.

title: FOCUS - HK takes more steps to fend off speculators.
text:
HONG KONG, Oct 25 (Reuters) - The Hong Kong Monetary Authority made it more expensive for banks to borrow money on Saturday to keep currency speculators at bay, analysts said. 

 "It's a cautionary measure to fend off speculators," said Edward Chan, head of research at Amsteel Securities. 

 The Hong Kong Monetary Authority, the territory's de facto central bank, said it was adjusting the bid rate under the Liquid Adjustment Facility (LAF) to four percent from 4.25 percent. 

 Offer rates rose to seven percent from 6.25 percent. 

 "For banks trying to borrow money, the cost would be slightly higher," said Albert Chan, spokesman for the HKMA. 

 "The reason for doing it is higher volatility in overnight interest rates," Chan said. 

 Widening the LAF corridor would also allow the HKMA more flexibility on interest rate decisions. 

 "The market was much more volatile this week in terms of interest rates, so widening the bid and offer spread of the LAF rates will allow a certain flexibility for the HKMA to manoeuvre the interest rates in an indirect way," said Stanley Wong, regional treasurer at Standard Chartered Bank in Hong Kong. 

 The HKMA effectively declared war on speculators this week, intervening actively in the currency and interest rate markets to make the cost of attacking the Hong Kong dollar very high for hedge funds, many of them reportedly from the United States. 

 The Hong Kong dollar is the last Asian currency pegged to the U.S. dollar and the latest regional currency to come under attack. 

 Overnight rates rocketed to 300 percent on Thursday at the peak of the crisis then fell to six percent the next day. 

 "If (speculators) short the Hong Kong dollar, they have to borrow money from the system, so if you raise interest rates, you increase the cost on speculators," Amsteel's Chan said. 

 Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index plunged more than 10 percent on Thursday as interest rates surged but clawed back nearly seven percent on Friday on as rates eased. 

 The market turmoil is the worst crisis to hit the territory in decades and the first since it reverted to Chinese rule in July. 

 However, while the HKMA seems to have won the latest battle against speculator, it has not yet won the war, analysts have said. 

 Traders said the Hong Kong dollar rose sharply to 7.5 against the U.S. dollar on Thursday as speculators cut their losses. The currency was pegged to the U.S. dollar at 7.8 in 1983 but is allowed to move in a narrow range around that. 

 The currency eased to 7.7335/55 on Friday. 

 Analysts have said scaring away the banks which finance speculators was the HKMA's first step in halting attacks on the currency peg. 

 "For repeated borrowing, we don't think banks should come to our discount window. If banks manage their finances properly, they shouldn't need to come to us repeatedly," the HKMA's Chan said. 

 Widening the LAF spread would also help maintain Hong Kong dollar interest rates at a higher level, Wong said. 

 "To widen the spread so banks will have to borrow from the HKMA at 75 basis points higher than before will imply that Hong Kong dollar interest rates will be maintained at a higher level for a prolonged period," Wong said. 

 He said Hong Kong dollar interest rates would stay at double digits next week as policy-makers and investors keenly watch for any signs that speculators have abandoned the market. 

 "It's very much a wait-and-see attitude," Wong said.

title: China  central bank  says would help Hong Kong.
text:
BEIJING, Oct 24 (Reuters) - China would respond if Hong Kong's monetary authorities asked for help, a Chinese central bank official said on Friday, commenting on the speculative assault on the Hong Kong dollar. 

 "If anything happened to Hong Kong, and if Hong Kong monetary authorities requested us to do something, then the relevant departments would find concrete solutions," said an official in the spokesman's office of the People's Bank of China. 

 The official, who declined to be identified, was speaking in a telephone interview. 

 "When Hong Kong returned to China, the central bank stressed that the mainland and Hong Kong would have two separate monetary authorities and Hong Kong affairs would be mainly handled by Hong Kong," he said. 

 "Under any circumstances, China would not use Hong Kong's foreign exchange reserves," he said. 

 Hong Kong was returned to China by colonial power Britain at the stroke of midnight on June 30 under a "one country, two systems" formula, which guaranteed the territory's capitalist way of life would remain unchanged for 50 years. 

 Hong Kong stocks, pounded into the ground on Thursday, rose sharply on Friday and closed the morning session with the blue chip Hang Seng Index 470.75 points, or 4.52 percent, higher at 10,897.05, brokers said. 

 Overnight rates in Hong Kong came down to about 10 percent in early afternoon from a peak of 300 percent on Thursday, prompted by worries about the stability of the Hong Kong-U.S. dollar peg. 

 A Hong Kong newspaper on Friday ran an interview with People's Bank of China Governor Dai Xianglong in which he pledged support for the local dollar. 

 The interview was conducted by Peter Seidlitz, the Beijing-based correspondent with the German newspaper Handelsblatt. 

 Seidlitz said the interview took place on Wednesday, one day before the collapse of the Hong Kong stock market. 

 "I have full confidence in the stability of the Hong Kong dollar," Dai was quoted as saying. 

 "What is more important is that the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) has the competence to maintain its stability," Dai said. 

 "If it is necessary -- or at the request of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region Government or the HKMA -- the Chinese government will provide support to the Hong Kong dollar," he said. 

 "Besides, the International Monetary Fund will also give its support for Hong Kong's financial stability," he added. 

 The Hong Kong Monetary Authority is Hong Kong's de facto central bank. 

 The Chinese central bank spokesman said Dai's comments were "not directly connected to what was happening in Hong Kong". 

 Separately, an economist at a central bank research institute said China would certainly intervene to support the Hong Kong dollar if China believed its national interests were under threat. 

 "If they believe the situation over there is influencing the national reputation, and if it was necessary, we would definitely intervene," said the economist at the Finance and Banking Research Institute. 

 "We have the strength to do that," said the economist, who declined to be identified. 

 The Hong Kong dollar has been pegged to the U.S. dollar since 1983 at a rate of HK$7.80 to US$1. It is allowed to float in a narrow band, but normally trades on the strong side of the peg. 

 Chief Executive Tung Chee-hwa vowed to defend the peg after he returned to Hong Kong on Friday from Europe. 

 China announced on Thursday its foreign exchange reserves hit $134.07 billion at the end of September, up $29.04 billion from the end of last year. Hong Kong says it has reserves of $88 billion.

title: WSJE: Financial Meltdown In HK Puts China To The Test
text:
From Friday's Wall Street Journal Europe



HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--How long can Hong Kong prop up its battered
dollar? And will Beijing intervene?


 Those were the multibillion-dollar questions as a brutal attack on the territory's currency prompted monetary authorities to ratchet up interest rates as high as 300% in a spirited defense that drove Hong Kong shares down 10.4%, the biggest drop in their history, and sent shock waves through financial markets around the globe. 

 The nerve-wracking free fall on the blue-chip Hang Seng Index jolted investors in Europe and the U.S., rudely reminding bull-market buyers that stock prices can fall as well as rise. By the time the dust settled Thursday night, stock sellers had lopped more than 3% off the value of shares traded in London, Frankfurt and Paris, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 2.33%. 

 But the biggest shock probably came in Beijing, where the debacle will sorely test the communist government's hands-off policy toward its new territory. 

 The meltdown is just the sort of crisis that Hong Kong long feared would draw Beijing's meddling, particularly since the catalyst in this case is essentially political: the decision to defend the Hong Kong dollar's link to the U.S. dollar rather than devalue the currency along with those in the rest of Southeast Asia. 

 China could, foreign-exchange traders say, stop the speculation by stating that it will defend the Hong Kong dollar with the mainland's own reserves. Such a step would likely face stiff opposition, economists say, from Chinese leaders bent against spending mainland money to defend a currency that is arguably overvalued. But the consequences of not intervening may prove too grave for China to ignore. 

 The quickening deflation of Hong Kong's bubble economy threatens to undermine the territory's competitiveness against Asian countries that have already devalued. It could also choke off new investments by companies; pummel the local real-estate market, where Beijing owns loads of property; and wreak havoc on China's recent decision to accelerate economic reforms on the mainland by floating shares in state companies. 

 Thus Beijing faces a brutal choice: "Asset prices or the peg," said Andy Xie, an economist at Morgan Stanley Dean Witter in Hong Kong. "You can only choose one, because - if you defend the exchange rate - you have to maintain high interest rates." 

 So far, Hong Kong's worst financial crisis in a decade has failed to dislodge its currency, which for the past 14 years has traded in a fixed range of around HK$7.80 to the U.S. dollar. That's because the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, the former colony's de facto central bank, mounted a fierce defense of the currency on Thursday by pushing overnight interest rates up to as high as 300%, up from around 6% the previous day. 

 That actually drove the Hong Kong dollar above its normal peg, prompting some monetary authorities to gloat. "Now our exchange rate is at the most strong position we've seen for a long, long time," said Hong Kong Financial Secretary Sir Donald Tsang. He and other senior officials declared that there was no reason to adjust the Hong Kong dollar's peg. 

 In fact, the monetary authorities have used highly unusual means to prop up the currency in recent weeks, raising serious questions about the territory's monetary stability. The tactic involves using government reserves as well as official foreign-currency reserves to defend the Hong Kong dollar in the open market. 

 By Thursday, some hedge-fund managers had decided the tactic was a bluff and called it - expecting to win regardless of whether the U.S. dollar peg stays or falls. Some foreign-exchange speculators, roused by recent victories against central banks around the region, redoubled their attacks on the Hong Kong dollar, claiming that it was almost in their hands.

title: Hong Kong dollar peg not like the others.
text:
HONG KONG, Oct 23 (Reuters) - The Hong Kong dollar's link to the U.S. unit bears little resemblance to the currency pegs that have snapped like dry twigs throughout Asia, analysts said on Thursday. 

 Unlike many of its neighbours in Asia, the Hong Kong government by law must stand ready to redeem Hong Kong dollars for U.S. dollars at a rate of HK$7.80 per US$1. 

 The currency is permitted to trade in a narrow band around that level. 

 "There is a big difference when we talk about Hong Kong compared with Thailand, Malaysia and Indonesia," said Chi Lo, regional economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in Singapore. 

 "Because there is a currency board system, the HKMA (Hong Kong Monetary Authority) is not supposed to change the exchange rate policy just because of domestic economic concerns," he said. 

 Thailand, Malaysia and Indonesia had fixed exchange rate systems which they were eventually forced to abandon. 

 Central banks found that trying to maintain fixed exchange rates conflicted with monetary policy -- they would have to raise rates to support their currencies even as their battered economies cried out for easier policy. 

 But the HKMA is bound under law to take no account of the economy when it defends the dollar. 

 As Hong Kong's three note issuing banks buy or sell Hong Kong dollars from the HKMA's Exchange Fund, they are bound by law to undertake a reverse transaction by selling or buying Hong Kong dollars for the Fund. 

 This drains, or injects, liquidity in the monetary system, so pressures for a strong Hong Kong dollar will lower interest rates and vice-versa. 

 The local currency, linked to the U.S. dollar since 1983 after a speculative attack, is basically the last pegged currency in the region and an obvious target, analysts have said. 

 Interest rates surged this week as speculators sold Hong Kong dollars and liquidity tightened. Dealers said the HKMA also was actively mopping up liquidity in the money markets. 

 Overnight rates rocketted to 300 percent by noon and were at 200 percent at day-end. 

 The surge in rates wreaked havoc on Hong Kong's stock market, with the blue-chip Hang Seng Index diving 1,211.47, or 10.41 percent, to end the day at 10,426.30. 

 Hong Kong financial leaders said they would do nothing to stem the stock market slide and insisted that maintaining the peg was the government's main goal. 

 "The first priority is to defend the exchange rate. This is our top priority. We believe it is right to do so," Financial Secretary Donald Tsang told reporters on Thursday. 

 There is no specific mention of the dollar peg in Hong Kong's constitution, the Basic Law, which was hammered out by British and Chinese authorities in the years before the territory reverted to Chinese rule on July 1, 1997. 

 But the document states that the Hong Kong dollar would remain the territory's legal tender and would be allowed to circulate freely without any exchange controls. 

 Analysts have said that it is unthinkable that China would consider de-pegging the currency because that would shake confidence in Hong Kong just a few months after the mainland assumed control. 

 "There is still too much at stake here both economically and politically so that Hong Kong and China officials are still quite willing to keep the peg even at a high cost in the short term," said DMG's Chi Lo. 

 Like many countries in Asia, Hong Kong and China have signed bilateral repurchase agreements, pledging to help each other stabilize markets in times of currency crisis. 

 Hong Kong and China have combined foreign currency reserves of more than US$222 billion, a hefty arsenal against any attack. 

 But while the Hong Kong Monetary Authority has intervened to prop up the local dollar in recent months, China has not. 

 "Quite naturally, I think leaders in China are concerned about what is happening here, but so far, (China) has left us...to do our own work," Financial Secretary Tsang said. 

 The Hong Kong government said it dipped into its US$88.1 billion in foreign reserves most recently on Wednesday to defend the peg.

title: Hong Kong peg here to stay, but not painlessly.
text:
HONG KONG, Oct 22 (Reuters) - Hong Kong's currency peg has come under renewed scrutiny as the local dollar drifts and interest rates jump, but government officials and economists insist the peg is here to stay. 

 "There is no political or economic need for us to disband the Hong Kong dollar peg," the territory's Financial Secretary Donald Tsang told reporters in Hong Kong on Wednesday. 

 Speaking in London, Chief Executive Tung Chee-hwa said the Hong Kong dollar, backed by huge foreign reserves and sound fundamentals, maintained strength amid the Asian market turmoil. 

 The Hong Kong dollar, the last major pegged currency in Asia, is linked to the U.S. dollar at a rate of HK$7.80 per US$1, but traditionally trades on the strong side of the peg. 

 In recent days the spot rate has drifted to trade around HK$7.7500 per U.S. dollar from about HK$7.7375 a week ago. 

 The dollar's dalliance at that level caused some market jitters since HK$7.750 is widely regarded as a trigger for intervention by the monetary authority, but most of the actual selling was seen in the forward market. 

 The HKMA declined comment on intervention. 

 Some dealers said that the volatility in the Hong Kong dollar forward market was the worst since the 1994-1995 Mexico crisis, which wreaked havoc on emerging markets. 

 Interest rates soared on Wednesday as nervous investors sold Hong Kong dollars for U.S. dollars, damaging Hong Kong's blue chip stock index, which fell to a 13-month low of 11,637.77. 

 Hong Kong dollars that are sold ultimately must be absorbed by the HKMA, which is pledged to maintain the local dollar's peg to the U.S. dollar, causing tighter liquidity and higher rates. 

 Since Asia's troubles began in July, Hong Kong periodically has been the target of speculators attempting to break the peg. 

 Traders said the latest round of market jitters was set off by Taiwan's decision to float its dollar. The idea was that if the Taiwan dollar could go, so too could the Hong Kong dollar. 

 Rubbish, economists said. 

 "Can you see the headlines? Four months into Chinese rule and the Chinese screw up the peg. It's just not going to happen," said Andrew Freris, managing director at BA Asia. 

 China has vowed to retain the dollar link and the peg is enshrined in Hong Kong law. 

 "If China lets the peg go, there will be all sorts of imaginings. People will think that China might violate the Basic Law (Hong Kong's constitution)," said Chi Lo, regional economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in Singapore. 

 Unlike other currencies in Asia that had been pegged to the dollar or a currency basket, Hong Kong maintains a currency board system, meaning that every Hong Kong dollar is backed by its equivalent in U.S. dollars. 

 DMG's Chi Lo said the HKMA could run into trouble because it has adopted the role of lender of last resort, meaning reserves could be depleted if there was a catastrophic loss of confidence and people demanded U.S. dollars all at once. 

 "But that potential problem has been eased by very good cooperation between the central bank and the banks in Hong Kong, which provide the HKMA with information on what is getting done in the market and in what size," he said. 

 Economists and policymakers have said that concerns about Hong Kong's loss of competitiveness in a region where most currencies have been devalued is misplaced because goods exports make up a small part of the territory's economy. 

 But maintaining the peg will not be without pain. 

 "In the process of defending the (Hong Kong) dollar, interest rates may have to go up," said Tung. 

 Hong Kong's economy is highly interest rate sensitive because so much of the economy depends on the property sector. 

 "The peg will stay, but the stock market will go lower, wage rates will go down and unemployment will go up," said Steven Xu, regional treasury economist at Standard Chartered Bank. 

 "But what else can Hong Kong do? It is a small open economy. If the peg goes, there will be so much chaos the costs will be very high," he said.

SINGAPORE, Aug 15 (Reuter) - The steep plunge on Wall Street and fallout from the latest wave of currency weakness in the region were likely to keep Asian stocks markets unsettled in the week ahead, analysts said. 

 The Dow Jones industrial average fell 247.37 points, or 3.1 percent, to 7,694.66 on Friday. The sell-off, sparked by the weakening dollar and worries about corporate earnings, was the second biggest point drop ever and left the index at its lowest close since June. 

 In Jakarta, the stock market was hard hit on Friday and shed nearly four percent when the rupiah fell to a record low after the central bank abolished the currency's intervention band. 

 Brokers also warned that a market like Hong Kong, which previously was immune from the currency turmoil, was also starting to the feel the heat amid concern that the local dollar would be the next target for speculators.

 "The Dow's tumble is likely to hurt sentiment in the market because it will raise concerns that investors with global assets may decrease their holdings in Japanese equities," said Masaaki Higashida, strategist at Nomura Securities. 

 Before the Wall Street sell-off, Tokyo traders had expected the Nikkei index of 225 shares to drift around the 19,000 level.

 The Hang Seng Index fell 550.66 points, or 3.31 percent, last week, to close at 16,096.88 on Friday over fears of a speculative attack on the dollar and an upward spike in short-term interest rates.

 Friday's slide on Wall Street and the U.S. Federal Reserve policy-setting meeting on Tuesday will add to the market's woes, analysts said, although they expect U.S. interest rates to remain unchanged next week. 

 They said the Hang Seng Index should find support around 15,200 points.

 "Investors will step to the sidelines to see whether Wall Street will fall further," said International Investment Trust vice-president David Yu. "If Wall Street falls further, it will trigger overall downward corrections in global stock markets -- Taiwan also cannot exempt from this."
