title: Experts debate fate of HK dollar on volatile day.
text:
HONG KONG, Aug 15 (Reuter) - While Hong Kong money market dealers warily awaited monetary authority intervention and the local dollar slipped lower, analysts on Friday debated the future of Asia's last major U.S. dollar fixed exchange rate. 

 "With what's happening on the Indonesian rupiah, there's a little bit of tension here," Andrew Fung, head of Asian Capital Markets for Commonwealth Bank of Australia in Hong Kong, told Reuters Financial Television's daily programme Asia Today. 

 On Thursday, Indonesian officials effectively lifted the fixed exchange regime that had kept the currency's trade limited to a 12 percent band. 

 Spillover pressure from the managed flotation of the rupiah was being felt throughout Asia on Friday and was building up in Hong Kong where the local exchange rate has been fixed at HK$7.8 per US$1.00 since 1983. 

 Throughout the recent months of currency turmoil in Asia, the Hong Kong dollar has stayed on the strong side of its unofficial one percent trading band, rarely straying from HK$7.75 to the U.S. dollar. 

 But forward Hong Kong dollar rates have soared in response to regional pressures. 

 By Friday afternoon, six-month forward contracts were trading at a 1000 point premium to spot, and one-year money was at a 1500 point premium, making the carrying cost of a Hong Kong dollar short position very expensive. 

 In many traders' eyes, the Hong Kong dollar is starting to look very isolated in a region battered by waves of speculative pressure. 

 "I think there's definetely some reconsideration to be had," said Eric Nickerson, head of currency research at Bank of America. 

 "The fundamentals of Hong Kong are very much Asia-oriented, not U.S. oriented," said Nickerson. "Certainly the U.S. dollar is an important currency for this economy, but to have all of its financial policy dictated by the Federal Reserve really doesn't make any sense," he said. 

 Chi Lo, regional economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in Singapore, said Hong Kong authorities may well want to rethink the link to the U.S. dollar, but will not be forced to do so for some time, at least until the end of the century. 

 But Nickerson disagreed, saying the uncertainty associated with the July 1 handover of Hong Kong to China was in the past, making the political justification of the peg less viable. 

 While agreeing that the political uncertainty of the handover was no longer a factor for the Hong Kong dollar, Lo pointed to continued jitters over the "one country, two systems" model that permits a westernized, capitalist Hong Kong to exist inside a communist ruled China. 

 "Foreigners, as well as Hong Kong people, they are all skeptical," about one country, two systems, said Lo. "They need a kind of confidence booster, and the Hong Kong dollar peg will serve this purpose in the medium term." 

 Nickerson admitted the resolve of Hong Kong authorities to maintain the peg is strong, and that the combined financial resources of the HKMA and the Peoples Bank of China - if called upon - would total more than US$200 billion. 

 But he warned that the market may not care. 

 "That's not necessarily going to be sufficient to keep the market at bay given the uncertain circumstances in the rest of the region," said Nickerson. 

 CBA's Fung said that, while the market is nervous, he does not expect the Hong Kong dollar to be shoved from its U.S. dollar peg amid the current pressure. 

 "I think the forward will stay higher, at a signifcant premium against the U.S. interest rate, as the major disincentive for speculators to try their luck here," he said.

title: HK spent US$1.0 bln defending HK dollar in July.
text:
HONG KONG, Aug 12 (Reuter) - The Hong Kong government spent US$1.0 billion from its reserves fending off speculative attacks against the Hong Kong dollar in July, a government spokeswoman said on Tuesday. 

 "Everything was resolved in a very swift manner," she said. 

 Hong Kong government radio earlier quoted Financial Secretary Donald Tsang as saying that the government had repelled the attack against the Hong Kong dollar in about two hours on an unspecified day in July, spending US$1.0 billion. 

 The Hong Kong dollar has been pegged at HK$7.8 to the U.S. dollar since the currency plunged in 1983 due to worries over the future of the former British colony, which returned to China in June this year. 

 Several Asian currencies have been targeted by speculators over the last several weeks in the wake of Thailand's currency and financial crisis. 

 The spokeswoman said the government also knew the identity of the speculator, but said Tsang had declined to identify the attacker. 

 Another government official, who declined to be named, told Reuters that whatever the authorities might have spent on defending the currency was not lost because the government could reverse its position in the market later once currency volatility had eased. 

 Hong Kong foreign exchange dealers said the local currency held up well on Tuesday despite heavy selling of other Asian currencies, notably the Singapore dollar. 

 "The Hong Kong dollar was little changed despite the drop in the Singapore dollar and other Asian currencies, though there was some movement in the forward rates," said one dealer. 

 "The market is very concerned about the HKMA (Hong Kong Monetary Authority) coming in because they are very serious (about defending the currency)," he said. 

 But there was no sign of intervention in Tuesday's session, the dealer said. 

 The Hong Kong dollar was trading at HK$7.7433/43 to the dollar.

title: HKMA Confirms/HK$  Intervention  -2: Normally Doesn't Comment
text:
HONG KONG (AP-Dow Jones)--The Hong Kong Monetary Authority on Tuesday confirmed that it intervened on a single day in July to defend the Hong Kong dollar against the activity of a single speculator. 

 But a spokesman for the quasi central bank - which normally won't talk about its market activity - declined to talk about how the intervention was engineered or about amounts spent. 

Hong Kong media earlier in the day quoted the Financial Secretary Donald Tsang, who oversees the authority, as saying US$1.0 billion was spent to defend the currency, which is pegged to the U.S. dollar. 

 'That day in July, within two hours, the Monetary Authority intervened and the speculator lost money,' said Albert Chan, a spokesman for the HKMA. He said the activity took place on a Friday afternoon.

title: HK Used/Defending HK Dollar -2: Second Half Of July
text:
HK's Financial Secretary Donald Tsang reportedly made the comments after reporters asked him about the day-earlier announcement that Hong Kong would participate in the International Monetary Fund-sponsored bailout of Thailand. 

 Hong Kong is making US$1.0 billion available to the Bank of Thailand, through the aegis of the IMF. Tsang on Monday said that forwarding money to the Thai central bank would help stabilize the baht. A more stable baht would reduce the likelihood of spillover currency selling elsewhere in the region, and weakening of the Hong Kong dollar. 

 The official didn't say exactly when the speculative activity took place. But in the second half of July, Hong Kong interbank offered rates were pushed extra high for almost a week, as forward exchange rates for the Hong Kong dollar suggested the market expected currency would weaken later. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority intervened in the market on more than one day that week, traders said. 

 The HKMA, the quasi central bank, is charged with defending the peg that values US$1.0 at HK$7.8000. It also holds the foreign exchange reserves, which at mid-year were worth HK$67.9 billion.

title: HK Dollar Lower Midday As Traders Liquidate Long Positions
text:
HONG KONG (AP-Dow Jones)--Traders began the week Monday liquidating some long Hong Kong dollar positions, driving the local currency lower against its U.S. counterpart in remarkably quiet mid-morning dealings. 

 After scrambling for Hong Kong dollars in recent days amid intervention by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, traders reversed their positions and unloaded the local currency into the market early Monday. 

 However, trading is thin owing to fears any huge positions, which could bump the exchange rate around, could draw the wrath of the quasi-central bank again. 

 'Positions are being liquidated from Friday which is easing some pressure on the longer-dated forward market rates,' a chief trader at a Hong Kong bank said. 'But everything's pretty stable because nobody wants to challenge the HKMA.' 

 Forward rates eased below 1,000.00 points Monday, indicating that banks are no longer seeking long-term funding to hedge their Hong Kong dollar exposure. 

 The one-year forward contract slid to 930.00 points, down from 1,100.00 late Friday. 

 Around 0325 GMT (11:25 p.m. EDT), the U.S. dollar is quoted at HK$7.7410, up from HK$7.7405 late Friday. 

 The U.S. unit is expected to trade in a range of HK$7.7405 to HK$7.7415 Monday. 

 Short-term interbank rates stayed firm, with all but the overnight Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate above 7.00%. 

 Dealers said the HKMA is keeping market conditions tight to deter speculation by making the cost of funding painfully expensive. 

 The overnight Hibor is at 6.50% Monday, up from 6.375% late Friday. The one-week rate is flat at 7.00%.

title: HK$ Bonds Mostly Unchanged But Yields Remain Firm
text:
HONG KONG (AP-Dow Jones)--Hong Kong government bonds were mostly unchanged late Monday, but yields remained firm amid a continuing tight interest rate environment, traders said. 

 Dealers said activity calmed down from last week, when volatile currency markets and intervention by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority caused widespread selling in short-term bonds.

title: HK Dollar Up On Short-Covering Carried From NY, London
text:
HONG KONG (AP-Dow Jones)--A bout of short-covering carried over from the London and New York sessions is driving the Hong Kong dollar slightly higher against its U.S. counterpart midday Friday. 

 Speculation that the Hong Kong Monetary Authority intervened in New York or London, driving the U.S. dollar below HK$7.7400, prompted traders to cover short positions in the local currency. 

 'The U.S. dollar hit a low of HK$7.7365 in London...and whether the HKMA did the selling is not confirmed,' a trader at a European bank said. 'People are taking up short-term money in the market...and trying to cover up all their shorts. It shows the downside to the Hong Kong dollar will be limited.' 

 But 'the turmoil isn't over,' he added. 

 Around 0315 GMT (11:15 p.m. EDT Thursday), the U.S. dollar is quoted at HK$7.7417, down from HK$7.7445 late Thursday. 

 The U.S. unit has traded in a range of HK$7.7430 and HK$7.7400 so far Friday. 

 High short-term interbank rates - hovering around the 7.00% level - also encouraged selling in the U.S. dollar. 

 'I think the HKMA squeezed rates high enough that it pushed people to sell the U.S. dollar,' another dealer at a Hong Kong bank said. 'That's what's driving the U.S. dollar down compared to yesterday,' he said. 

 In recent days, currency markets have been buzzing with talk that speculators are poised to attack the Hong Kong dollar amid the turmoil affecting Southeast Asian currencies. Thursday, traders said the HKMA intervened in the currency and debt markets to stabilize the pegged exchange rate.

title: Speculators position for HK dollar attack - traders.
text:
HONG KONG, July 24 (Reuter) - Hong Kong money market traders said fund managers around the world were preparing to attack the Hong Kong dollar, buying currency forwards aggressively. 

 "It's the usual case where people want to speculate against the currency and they have to fund themselves first," said one head currency trader at a local bank. "Fund managers around the world will be trying to attack the Hong Kong dollar and they are trying to buy forwards." 

 Traders said the Hong Kong Monetary Authority was intervening heavily as currency forwards reached their highest levels since the 1995 speculative attack against the Hong Kong dollar, which followed the Mexican peso crisis. 

 Three-month currency fowards reached 350 points while the six-month soared to 550 from Wednesday's levels of 130 and 170 respectively. 

 The Hong Kong dollar spot rate remained steady at HK$7.7428/38. The unit is pegged at HK$7.80 to the U.S. dollar. 

 The Hong Kong Monetary Authority declined to comment on market conditions, or confirm its intervention. 

 "We will closely monitor the situation," said HKMA spokesman Thoman Chan. "I've just come back from the dealing rooms, I know what is happening in the market, I know what traders have said to reporters. The HKMA will monitor the market and we don't comment on money market rumours." 

 Dealers said funds were buying U.S. dollar foward, anticipating a fall in the Hong Kong dollar. 

 "It's speculation and the spillover from speculation," said Callum Henderson at MMS International. "Previously banks wouldn't necessarily hedge their short U.S. dollar exposure." 

 Customers bailing out of Hong Kong dollars are leaving Hong Kong banks short of U.S. dollars short-term. Banks are now going to the market to make sure they are not exposed to the Hong Kong dollar, Henderson said, where previously they would not bother. 

 Although the HKMA declined to comment, traders said the HKMA was mopping up liquidity in the short end, keeping conditions tight by buying up all the excess Hong Kong currency. 

 One dealer reported the HKMA selling one-month Hong Kong dollar Exchange Fund bills at 7.71 percent -- far above the one-month market yield of 6.56 percent. 

 "He (HKMA chief Joseph Yam) hit the market twice. We expect short-dated money will squeeze up dramatically on Friday," the dealer said. 

 Two initial public offerings were due to be released on Friday, which would tighten liquidity further in Hong Kong's small and tightly-traded money market. 

 The overnight shot above the key level of seven percent this morning before settling back to 6.75 percent after intervention. 

 Dealers said they were very nervous that rates would soar sky-high on Friday, forcing them to bail out of positions. 

 "We will take losses. The mood, in one word, is very frightened," the dealer said. 

 "(The spot rate) didn't do what (Yam) wanted it to after he intervened on Friday. It still went back to HK$7.75 and this made him crazy and angry. Tomorrow is a good day, he can do anything. He can squeeze rates up to 55 percent if he wants." 

 But some players said the activity was driven more by "prudent hedging" than speculation. Substantial scepticism about the likelihood of a successful attack against the Hong Kong dollar remained much in evidence as the morning session closed. 

 The HKMA holds at least US$63 billion in foreign exchange reserves, and has a commitment of support from China, which holds in excess of US$112 billion in foreign exchange.

title: Regional  Currency  Concerns Again Spill Into HK Markets
text:
HONG KONG (AP-Dow Jones)--Forward rates moved sharply higher Thursday for the second time this week in what some participants said might mean speculators are poised to attack the Hong Kong dollar. 

 When the rupiah plunged Monday, banks paid a hefty premium to hedge their Hong Kong dollar exposure. Likewise, pressure on the baht and ringgit Thursday sent banks back into the Hong Kong dollar forward markets. 

 'There's obviously a contagion effect from regional markets,' said a currency analyst at a European bank. 

 On Thursday, the U.S. dollar premium rose above Monday's 900.0 points, soaring all the way to 1200.0 points and above Wednesday's 500.0-900.0 premium in Asian trading. The premium has slipped slightly, but remains at 1100.0 points at 1042 GMT. 

 The premium level implies that participants expect a sharply weaker Hong Kong dollar at HK$7.8645 per U.S. dollar a year from now. The U.S. dollar is quoted at HK$7.7441 at 1042 GMT, down from HK$7.7475 earlier in the day. 

 Participants said concern that the Hong Kong dollar spot rate would weaken and that a window would open for speculators prompted the Hong Kong Monetary Authority to intervene in both the debt and currency markets Thursday. 

 The head of money markets at a North American bank said he believes the HKMA sold just under US$100.0 million of the U.S. currency at HK$7.7470 to signal it didn't want forward market volatility affecting the spot rate. 

 And a bond trader at a market-making bank said late Thursday that the forward market activity also prompted the HKMA to sell HK$100-200 million of one-month bills at around 0230 GMT to drain liquidity out of the system, drive up money market rates and discourage potential speculation. 

 A Monetary Authority spokesman declined to comment on the quasi central bank's activities Thursday.
